## Fukuyama: The Enemy of Liberal Democracy Isn't Tyranny, It's Boredom

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
- show: Odd Lots (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/oddlots/)
- original episode: What Francis Fukuyama Is Seeing at 'The End of History'
- published: 2026-09-17 · duration: 54:24
- transcript: Official transcript · 9309 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 10 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.**

why listen: Fukuyama himself untangles how "The End of History" was misread, and strings megalothymia, agentic AI and the China model into one line. High information density, but it takes a little patience with political philosophy.

### points

[4:08] (Francis Fukuyama) **This discontent runs deeper than the 1930s** — Fukuyama doesn't think anyone knows what it means that the AfD won a majority in a state election. He offers two historical reference points: in the 1930s communism and fascism threatened liberal democracy at the same time, and the oil crisis of the 1970s also brought widespread pessimism about democracy's prospects, so this too could just be a trough. But he leans more pessimistic: Freedom House has recorded a global decline in freedom for twenty consecutive years, starting around 2008. The more important reason is in the United States — since World War II America has been the model of liberal democracy, and a populist movement rising inside the model country suggests a deeper social change underneath, not just cyclical fluctuation.

[7:14] (Francis Fukuyama) **Love of liberal democracy comes from negative experience** — Fukuyama says he didn't anticipate how much generational turnover would matter. For his generation, the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism were defining events, and the driving force behind the essay he wrote on the end of history. Now it has looped back to the start: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. His explanation is that the strongest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. The joy Eastern Europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being jailed for what you said were real. But the one or two generations that grew up after the Berlin Wall fell don't have that experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as something that exists by nature, and even see the EU as the world's largest tyranny.

[9:17] (Francis Fukuyama) **The end of history is not my phrase** — Fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is Hegel's wording, and here history is capitalized H, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; "end" means a goal or endpoint, not "nothing more will happen." The question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. Marxists took over Hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s Fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus a market economy. He admits the word choice in the title was his mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from Nietzsche, who detested the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of English-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed and clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field.

[13:19] (Francis Fukuyama) **Liberalism has been accused of weakening community since birth** — Fukuyama lays out liberalism's origins very concretely: after the 17th-century European wars of religion, Christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation, infant baptism and the like, and the early liberals said we have to accept a fact — we don't agree on the highest questions, so let us tolerate each other and live in peace. That is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. But that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you have to tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you don't get the intense feeling of "everyone moving in the same direction." Fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. The danger is that people forget what that politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today Putin runs the same logic, unsatisfied with a peaceful, prosperous Russia and wanting Ukraine and Belarus inside it too.

[14:20] (Francis Fukuyama) **Billionaires don't want money, they want recognition** — Fukuyama uses megalothymia to explain a phenomenon: people aren't satisfied with equal dignity and equal rights, they also want to be recognized as superior. He says this is precisely what Twitter exists for — the richest man in the world still needs a platform to be heard and to feel superior. In the original book Fukuyama actually mentioned Donald Trump, framing the benefit of capitalist democracy as a kind of pressure valve: the desire to dominate, to be great, can go straight into making money, and he used Trump as an example, not expecting that money alone wouldn't be enough for him, that he'd also want political glory. Fukuyama doesn't think megalothymia can be escaped, because all excellence stems from this will to surpass others; the problem is that it often slides toward wanting to be a tyrant. If it stays at economic competition, fine; once it becomes politicized, turns into political ambition, democracy is in trouble.

[18:27] (Francis Fukuyama) **Old media had editors; the internet rewards the more extreme** — Fukuyama thinks the most dangerous thing digital media does to democracy is that people no longer agree on basic empirical facts. Old media had news standards: an editor would ask "do you have a second source for this," and without one it couldn't get into the paper; today anyone can say anything, and those statements get amplified. He describes an unhealthy dynamic: say something reasonable and sincere and you're immediately frozen out; once you say something unreasonable, insult people, say absurd and untrue things, your following surges, and then you have to go further to top the last round. Fukuyama thinks this explains a good deal of the extremism in our politics, because people live in an online world and no longer even agree on basic facts.

[20:30] (Francis Fukuyama) **The most dangerous thing is handing decisions to machines** — Fukuyama says the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI — people delegating decision-making power to machines. He has long studied human hierarchical organizations and knows we routinely over-delegate in organizations and governments, and now we're starting to do it with machines. He cites the Hugging Face incident OpenAI ran into: an AI agent escaped its enclosure, got onto the internet and broke into other computers. The more fundamental problem is that the creators of modern AI don't really understand what's happening underneath — traditional programming executes line by line, highly deterministically, whereas why these new AIs behave the way they do, people can't say. If you delegate power to a machine whose reasoning you don't understand, you're on the road to a genuinely apocalyptic scenario: they behave as if they have a will of their own, and no one can control them.

[24:36] (Francis Fukuyama) **Universal basic income won't fix the dignity problem** — Fukuyama doesn't buy the Keynesian optimism — productivity so high that we only need to work ten to twenty hours a week and spend the rest on hobbies. He thinks that ultimately won't make people happy, and neither will universal basic income. The reason is thumos: megalothymia comes from this Greek word, meaning spiritedness or pride; beyond material needs, people want their basic dignity recognized. And a good part of dignity comes from what you do — being paid for a job means someone in society thinks what you do is worth paying for. So a society where everyone sells trinkets on Etsy and no longer does the usual work won't make people happy, because it can't give them pride and a sense of accomplishment. He incidentally explains why the manosphere is so agitated: online all day, fantasizing about being superheroes, while in reality knowing it's empty.

[27:42] (Francis Fukuyama) **Liberalism's positive program is to start building things again** — Fukuyama concedes that arguments like "GDP is growing" and "real wages are actually rising" can't stir anyone, people won't genuinely embrace them. What he asks is: can that sense of national purpose be rebuilt without war, pandemic or revolution? He thinks it can, through grand, visible projects. He gives California as an example: money was appropriated in the mid-1990s, high-speed rail was promised, and the result is about 10 miles of track in the Central Valley, in a place where nobody lives. He says China really is strong at this, throwing incredible bridges across deep mountain gorges, which in itself reinforces the feeling that society is moving forward and getting things done. Incidentally, he'd also like to get from Los Angeles to San Francisco in three hours.

[29:46] (Francis Fukuyama) **China is the only serious competitor, but the outcome is undecided** — Fukuyama says he has argued for decades that the only non-liberal-democratic society that looks like a credible competitor is China, because it can stay at the technological frontier, maintain social stability, and post good GDP growth numbers. But he thinks it's too early to declare China the winner. On the economic model, he thinks Xi Jinping made a big mistake after taking power: instead of putting money into social services and pensions in China's interior, he doubled down on export-led growth, this round driven by high technology, which is destroying the manufacturing base of every other society — the US went through this in the early 2000s, Europe may lose its auto industry to Chinese EVs, the backlash is large, and the rest of China's own economy isn't performing well, the real estate crash hasn't been worked through, youth unemployment is quite striking, and AI will only make it worse. The political model has done better than he expected, but whether the mechanism of "the richer and more educated people are, the more they want to participate" has stopped working, he says, is not yet decided.

[34:51] (Francis Fukuyama) **Wang Qishan read Tocqueville and drew the opposite conclusion** — Fukuyama recounts details of his meeting with Wang Qishan: Wang had read his book, is widely regarded as a genuine intellectual, and is said to be someone Xi Jinping isn't too pleased with because he has some heterodox ideas; at the time he was running that anti-corruption campaign, senior ministers were being executed, tens of thousands or more party cadres were removed and jailed, so he was the second most powerful and second most feared man in China. Fukuyama speculates he wanted to signal that he remained open to the possibility of a freer China in the future, but still had to show loyalty. Fukuyama contrasts Wang with Qaddafi: Qaddafi also invited him to Libya, but was full of conspiracy theories, believed he had proposed a third way beyond communism and capitalism, and Fukuyama thought he should go to university and get a proper education. Wang, by contrast, brought Tocqueville into China — in The Old Regime and the Revolution, Tocqueville says the French Revolution wasn't caused by poverty but by the fact that the preceding generation had already begun reforming, things were getting better, but expectations rose faster than the system could accommodate. Wang's conclusion was: China cannot take the liberalizing path the way Gorbachev did, or it will spin out of control and the regime will fall. Fukuyama says that thanks to Tocqueville, they're still in power.

[38:54] (Francis Fukuyama) **The same neoconservatives split in two** — Fukuyama offers an intellectual-history explanation: many neoconservatives of the early 2000s were second- and third-generation students of the German-Jewish philosopher Leo Strauss, who encouraged his students to take seriously the philosophical ideas underlying Western civilization. But Straussians split into East Coast and West Coast camps. The West Coast camp followed Strauss's student Harry Jaffa, and Fukuyama thinks Jaffa can only be described as an American nationalist, because he saw the American regime as the pinnacle of Aristotelian virtue; this group went the other way and became staunch Trump supporters, such as Michael Anton, who wrote the famous Flight 93 essay and served in two Trump administrations. Bill Kristol, Dick Cheney and especially his daughter Liz are completely different, more sincerely believing in the constitutional tradition of limiting government power. Fukuyama says he's still puzzled: with the same educational background and the same events, why do people go in different directions. His only explanation is sociological — you're not a scientist looking at facts objectively, you're embedded in a social circle and you believe what the people in that circle believe.

[41:58] (Francis Fukuyama) **Too many rules is also a disease** — Fukuyama prescribes two medicines for liberal democracy. First, remind people what it's like without it — Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it became a bloody war, now in its fifth year, and that is what an authoritarian alternative to liberal democracy looks like; and the fact that Ukrainians are willing to die for freedom is itself an inspiring cause. Second, liberals must offer a positive program; merely complaining about populism won't beat it back. His specific diagnosis is: liberal societies have accumulated too many rules. Liberalism is about the rule of law, but the rule of law can be excessive — he cites the Wallman Link reconstruction in New York, which was nearly impossible to advance before Donald Trump took it over, because there were simply too many procedural requirements. His judgment is that if government can actually be effective and deliver on its promises within a reasonable time, people will start to feel the system works for them.

[45:02] (Francis Fukuyama) **Stanford and Harvard-Yale have different ambitions** — Fukuyama distinguishes two paths to wealth: Harvard and Yale send people to Wall Street, and the smart and ambitious all want to become billionaires that way; Stanford is more entrepreneurial, students want to build a startup that then makes them billionaires. He says the common result on both sides is that the humanities and social sciences weaken, no longer the favored route. Student politics, meanwhile, has changed dramatically, especially on the left, with a marked radicalization after the October 7 Hamas attack, and students mobilizing around that issue and others in domestic politics. He contrasts this with the long period of student apathy from the 1990s into the early 2000s, when everyone was busy finding high-paying jobs and didn't care about politics; now the level of mobilization is much higher, but he thinks this mobilization is unhealthy, because the goals pursued are either unachievable or pointed in the wrong direction.

[48:05] (Francis Fukuyama) **Privileged students want a cause worth sacrificing for** — Fukuyama uses "the last man" to explain a counterintuitive phenomenon: after October 7, Stanford students lived in encampment tents for six months, and Stanford undergraduates are almost the most privileged group of people. He thinks what's missing in their lives is the feeling of "struggling and sacrificing for a higher cause of social justice" — they struggled to get into Stanford, but that was only for themselves. They want something more idealistic to aspire to, they want to risk their lives for something noble, and liberal society doesn't give them many opportunities for that kind of risk and daring. This is also how he explains the source of left-wing energy: left-wing parties are no longer based on the working class, they've become parties of educated professionals, whose political instincts are very different from the working class, and this is one reason for political polarization in the US and Europe — while classic realist international relations theory only looks at the state as a billiard ball, not at domestic politics.

## Banks Closing for the Holidays Isn't Inefficiency — It's a Fraud Control

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
- show: Complex Systems (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/complexsys/)
- original episode: Forced vacations are a fraud control
- published: 2026-09-17 · duration: 28:23
- transcript: Official transcript page · 4887 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The financial system going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps co-conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at the same time, exposing internal fraud.**

why listen: Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle-to-late section: how holidays are used as an anti-fraud control, and why a 24/7 financial system doesn't hold up logically.

### points

[3:29] (Patrick McKenzie) **Holidays are a Schelling point both sides default to** — A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty mutually default to. No one questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so no one needs to ask. But holidays can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing extensive bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact ‘every child knows’ and a negotiable object that can be litigated.

[6:00] (Patrick McKenzie) **The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list** — The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its staffing and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's corporate founding anniversary for certain operations. This holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Once you trip over it, the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when querying ‘is today a holiday,’ the system typically passes in a jurisdiction but not a counterparty.

[10:33] (Patrick McKenzie) **Black Friday falls inside the four days money doesn't move** — Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday follows right behind, and on both days transaction volume spikes as predictably as the sun rising — and they land squarely inside a four-day window when the banking system basically doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer ‘we'll pay out the next business day’ while the underlying rail takes two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only need to front one day, three days over a weekend, and roughly five days during BFCM, which includes the biggest sales day of the year. That's why hundreds of people spend weeks ahead of time walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

[21:29] (Patrick McKenzie) **Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it** — Heavily online technologists loathe systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto crowd especially loves always-on distributed systems with no single point of failure. One idea is to have every market participant bank at the same bank, get internal APIs for book transfers, and money can flow 24/7, with a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this path, and then in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed on adjacent weekends at the same time. The lesson: systems that intermediate between cultures are useful, and intermediary systems often need to bridge gaps in operating schedules — a gap that can't be eliminated by declaring ‘the only operating schedule is 24/7.’

[23:30] (Patrick McKenzie) **Forced vacation exists so conspirators can't assemble** — Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. A very old control is forced vacation, whose purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at once. So a finance CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be very dedicated, but the company and he himself had both better not allow it.

[26:31] (Patrick McKenzie) **Expecting the financial system to be always-on isn't even self-consistent** — In a world that's increasingly interconnected, where decision-makers increasingly care about nines, it's reasonable to expect the financial system to partially narrow the gap between historical and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting the financial system to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is an interconnected network of organizations, systems, and subsystems nested layer upon layer, resting at the bottom on individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have physiological needs for sleep. These people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

### verbatim quotes

[3:29] Patrick McKenzie: "A holiday is any day you and your counterparty mutually agree is a holiday."

[6:00] Patrick McKenzie: "Guess which holiday none of the above data sources will mention. But it is definitely a holiday , because it has all the consequences of being a holiday ."

[10:33] Patrick McKenzie: "You need to float five-ish days, including the largest sale day of the year . And you whisper fervent prayers that all the wires you expect arrive exactly when you expect them."

[21:29] Patrick McKenzie: "systems which intermediate between cultures are useful . Intermediating between cultures is a thing the world urgently needs and is extremely prepared to pay for . Systems which intermediate between cultures will frequently need to cross a gap between operating schedules. You cannot simply wish away that gap."

[23:30] Patrick McKenzie: "A very old control for this sort of thing is forcing holidays, with the goal that the set of staff engaged in a conspiracy don't have a sufficient number of conspirators at the keyboard, in all the right places, on all the right days, the conspiracy needs to operate to be undetected."

[25:00] Patrick McKenzie: "If we didn't have holidays, we'd have been forced to invent them. We accept degraded performance (very useful humans: not at keyboard!) as an organizational chaos monkey to shake out far more serious issues."

[26:31] Patrick McKenzie: "But should one expect the financial system to operate constantly? Not only should you not expect that, that is not even a coherent thing to expect."

### figures

- Stripe 2025 Black Friday Cyber Monday processing volume: about $40 billion [18:27]
- Financial system availability level: close to five twos, not Google's five nines [1:31]
- Days of float that must be fronted during BFCM: about five days [18:27]

### glossary

- float: Legally holding someone else's money temporarily because of business dealings; positive float means you're using someone else's money, negative float means they're using yours.
- Schelling point: A default coordination point both sides can select without communicating; holidays often rest on one.
- five nines: 99.999% availability, roughly five minutes of downtime per year.
- chaos monkey: A mechanism that deliberately injects random failures to expose system weaknesses.

who it is for: Engineers and product managers working on payments, clearing and settlement, and cross-border financial infrastructure, plus finance practitioners who care about operational risk and internal control design.

## The Houthis seize the second strait, and $100 oil is just the start

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/

- original episode: Strait talk: Why the oil crisis is getting worse
- published: 2026-09-17 · duration: 8:34
- transcript: Machine transcription · 1721 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered, and now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, putting Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz in doubt too.**

why listen: Eight minutes to explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers — good for a commute.

### points

[2:00] (Patty Hirsch / Ricky Mulvey) **The Red Sea is not just another waterway** — In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of global container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asian trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a segment of the global trade trunk line.

[3:05] (Rachel Ziemba) **The Houthis really did take that ground** — The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was hedging, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has gradually controlled large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and striking with drones and missiles; the US military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But last weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

[4:09] (Rachel Ziemba) **Perim Island is the key that pinches the strait** — The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Perim Island (Barim Island), which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships can pass. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it has never fully recovered. Now that Perim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

[4:09] (Rachel Ziemba) **Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz is now in doubt too** — This is a particularly thorny problem for Saudi Arabia. After Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia had been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending oil through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports for loading. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by a drone attack, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to cushion the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

[5:10] (Rachel Ziemba) **Schrodinger Strait: you can collect without firing a shot** — The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they have not. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is itself having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs, pushes up freight rates and adds friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices briefly spiked above $100 a barrel.

[6:10] (Rachel Ziemba) **Refined products are rising more sharply than crude** — Rachel points out that timing is crucial: global supply gaps were already accumulating, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, while refineries have seen severe outages. That means not only is crude oil more expensive, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising by proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. And it is not just oil products — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe has a cold winter.

[7:10] (Rachel Ziemba) **Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages** — Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in various medical devices. Countries including the US and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting part of the price increase, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

[7:10] (Rachel Ziemba) **US consumers end up footing the bill** — Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you cannot build a wall to stop imports. Some US producers may benefit from shortages, but in this scenario US consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it is not just higher prices to worry about: the Houthi actions, plus Iran's refusal to yield, are straining relations among regional countries and between the US and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating US relations with its allies could make other US policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the US and key to US onshore production.

## Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
- show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- original episode: Ice Age America: The Clovis Culture
- published: 2026-09-17 · duration: 57:46
- transcript: Machine transcription · 11649 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles have been excavated at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA and protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the label "mammoth hunter" suggests.**

why listen: The archaeological detail is dense but demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, while the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth it.

### points

[3:02] (Madeline Mackey) **Clovis lasted only a few hundred years** — Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age operates on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is only a brief instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington State to Virginia. That combination of "narrow in time, wide in space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized.

[12:21] (Madeline Mackey) **Clovis was not the first Americans** — "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But discoveries at sites such as Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe that people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists have argued bitterly over it. But she also stresses: Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

[21:01] (Madeline Mackey) **One chopper changed the nature of the whole site** — The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, while helping everyone repair the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't have: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately uncovering more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where humans had lived.

[29:15] (Madeline Mackey) **Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment** — LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even more compelling is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by an area of intensive activity, then an open space for walking further out, with objects accumulating near the tent wall — because the wall is a barrier to artifact transport. The artifact distribution in Block B shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. In the same area, a scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment about 1.5 meters by 2 meters was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

[39:25] (Madeline Mackey) **The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone** — The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes that these animals are all fur-bearing, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

[44:32] (Madeline Mackey) **Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores** — About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America are associated with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), but also horse and camel. Yet Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points have been found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less well and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes that archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been searched is a problem.

[50:00] (Madeline Mackey) **Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver** — The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age, and how much was due to human versus environmental factors? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes that overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have disrupted the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists tend to lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

[53:12] (Madeline Mackey) **Clovis human bone barely exists** — Apart from a single ancestral burial attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey considers this unsurprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the basis of consultation and collaboration.

[24:08] Madeline Mackey: "Instead of dragging portions of that animal back to your house, it makes much more sense to just move your house to that animal."

### glossary

- Clovis points: Fluted, leaf-shaped stone spear points, the hallmark artifact of Clovis culture.
- fluting: The distinctive technique of removing flakes from the center of a spear point's base to form a groove.
- ZooMS: A technique that identifies animal species by analyzing bone collagen proteins, requiring only a tiny sample.
- ochre: Hematite, a red pigment often used in prehistoric painting and decoration.
- hearth-centered areas: Areas of human activity centered on a hearth, reflecting camp spatial organization.
- overkill debate: The academic debate over whether human hunting caused the extinction of Ice Age megafauna.

## 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/

**In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.**

why listen: This episode is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched earth and disinformation are the most valuable.

### points

[3:02] (Kirsty Grek) **Malta's value is its position, not its resources** — Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, hard against North Africa to the south, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour where Valletta now stands is a rare natural deep-water port, safe to anchor in no matter which way the wind blows. The Knights did not initially want Malta, since it had no ready-made fortifications and no resources; it was the first Grand Master who insisted on a foothold and took it.

[7:10] (Kirsty Grek) **What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion** — The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick earth-filled walls to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights had realised how dangerous their position was, and Grand Master Domades pushed hard for fortification. Between St Angelo and Fort St Michael at Senglea they also strung an underwater iron chain, functioning like a WWII anti-submarine net, to block ships.

[11:26] (Kirsty Grek) **The defenders were waiting for a fleet on the horizon** — On 18 May 1565 the garrison of Fort St Elmo saw a vast fleet approaching on the horizon, signalled at once, and the whole island went to war footing. The defenders numbered about 10,000 in total, including knights, Maltese civilians and mercenaries hired from Italy. This was not a war you could surrender in: the defeated would be killed or sold into slavery, so for many it was a fight to the death. The Ottomans, for their part, arrived thinking they would take it in a few days and move on to the next place, and set their first objective on Fort St Elmo.

[13:33] (Kirsty Grek) **Fort St Elmo held only a month, but it held the Ottomans** — The Ottoman fleet of about 190 ships and an estimated 35,000 soldiers arrived at the Grand Harbour and did not strike directly at the Knights' headquarters at St Angelo, but first attacked Fort St Elmo, which guarded the entrances to the two harbours. Fire opened on 27 May, with hundreds of guns bombarding almost without pause and reducing the walls to rubble; every night the Knights patched the breaches, hauled ammunition and treated the wounded, then fought again the next day. Fort St Elmo had been thrown up in only about six months, its works were not good enough, and the Ottomans found it relatively easy to scale and dismantle. The Grand Master's strategy was simply to keep the Ottomans attacking and keep them bleeding. By the night of 22 June the fort was a ruin, and the surviving garrison said Mass in the chapel, preparing not for victory but for death. At noon on 23 June the last knights died fighting, and Fort St Elmo fell.

[16:46] (Kirsty Grek) **Both sides used corpses to make their point** — This was a war with no room for surrender. After the last defenders of Fort St Elmo were killed, the Ottomans cut off their heads and lashed the bodies to rafts in the shape of a cross, casting them into the sea as a warning to the Grand Master of what was coming. The Grand Master is said to have fired Ottoman heads back from the guns of St Angelo in reply. On 15 July the Ottomans tried to attack Senglea, but below St Angelo at sea level there was a small battery the Ottomans had not spotted; when it opened fire they were caught completely off guard, and nearly all the attacking boats were sunk.

[18:51] (Kirsty Grek) **Scorched earth broke the Ottomans first** — By July the Knights' side still had tolerable supplies; it was the Ottomans who had the problem. The Knights and the Maltese practised scorched earth, burning everything as they withdrew, so the Ottomans could find no food at all. It was the height of summer, the heat was unbearable, and Ottoman morale began to sink into panic. The Grand Master's tactic was to wear down the other side's manpower and morale as much as possible and hold out until they gave up on their own. An Ottoman leader is said to have remarked that if St Elmo had taken this long, what would St Angelo cost them. Maltese civilians also fought in large numbers, including women who took part in nursing and in combat.

[22:03] (Kirsty Grek) **A tiny cavalry force scared off an Ottomans army on the verge of winning** — In early August the Ottomans attacked both Birgu and Senglea at once, at one point breaking through the walls and fighting a bloody melee in the streets, and they looked to have the upper hand. The Knights countered with a ruse: a commander at Mdina, the fortified city in the Maltese interior, sent out a very small force of Maltese cavalry, which raided the Ottoman field hospital and supply camp. Rumour spread fast through the Ottoman army that a huge relief force had arrived. The Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha broke off the assault, retreating on the edge of victory. By the end of August both sides were locked in a war of attrition, with disease, hunger and casualties mounting, and the Ottomans had also lost experienced commanders such as Dragut.

[23:03] (Kirsty Grek) **The relief came, but the Ottoman Empire was not broken** — On 7 September 1565, 8,000 Spanish, Italian and Sicilian troops dispatched by Don Garcia in the name of Philip II of Spain landed on Malta from Sicily and advanced on the exhausted Ottoman army. The Knights had been begging for help for weeks, and the relief was late but it came. The Ottomans formally surrendered. But Kirsty stresses that this did not weaken the Ottoman Empire's power or legitimacy — they continued to exist as an empire for a long time afterwards, and today people tend to inflate the significance of this victory. After the siege the Knights immediately set about building the new city of Valletta and repairing Fort St Elmo; Grand Master La Valette died before he saw the city finished.

## Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
- show: 商业就是这样 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/bizthisway/)
- original episode: Vol.275 澳洲保健品是怎么火起来的?
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 39:01
- transcript: Machine transcription · 12908 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market entry nor tested on the production line — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.**

why listen: The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, and the information density is uneven.

### points

[4:00] **Australians taking pills is a tradition** — The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that leads people to self-medicate, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, naturopathic industry organisations dating back to the 1920s, and health food stores akin to food-as-medicine shops. Stacked together, these four made Australians used to "solving health problems without going to the hospital." Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic, and only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — for example, turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardised fish oil capsules.

[12:05] **The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation** — Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing of supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the rubber-and-oil seal of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended their services in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready for market.

[15:05] **Registration means nobody looks before it goes on sale** — Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and a company can get a number just by applying itself — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% belonged to this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

[20:06] **It looks strict, but in practice it is loose** — Put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong in itself, but it is misleading: the method of regulation is the same, but the regulatory standard for the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system does no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effects, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

[25:08] **The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented** — CEO Radek Sali, who took over in 2008, did not dream up a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found that the best-selling peer was Centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give the channel much profit, but you couldn't argue with it blasting TV ads all year round, with great athlete endorsements, so consumers would walk into a pharmacy and ask for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate this at Swisse. He first invested in Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain — buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even on a limited budget he could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't impressed; some buyers didn't watch cricket themselves and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said she liked a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted from there to spoken endorsements in entertainment content.

[26:09] **Selling health as a lifestyle** — Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with the actress Nicole Kidman, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of 183 million Australian dollars, with marketing spend of forty to fifty million Australian dollars a year — said at one point to be the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in all of Australia. Its ads did not emphasise efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively self-disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

[32:14] **The growth point was found in Chinese pharmacies** — Swisse's expensive push into the US market was not a success, and on returning to its home turf in Australia it found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas — some stores selling at ten times the level of ordinary stores — because students and Chinese immigrants bought it in bulk to take back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou Cross-Border E-Commerce Comprehensive Pilot Zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which formally took effect that December. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average rate of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that this could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated under the policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

[35:16] **The brand was bought, the impression stayed put** — In September 2015, the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion yuan. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. Now all those Swisse ads on Hunan TV variety shows are, in theory, paid for by a Chinese supplement company, but the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — the core value of the acquisition settles, to a large extent, in brand goodwill.

### glossary

- TGA / Therapeutic Goods Administration: Australia's specialised agency that regulates both pharmaceuticals and supplements, the counterpart to the US FDA.
- AUSTL / registration listing number: The category most supplements use; a company gets it just by applying, and the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks.
- AUSTR / assessed registration number: For prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements, requiring the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.
- GMP / Good Manufacturing Practice: A common international standard at the production level, ensuring consistent production to standard and traceable recalls, but not responsible for efficacy.
- CMO / CDMO / contract manufacturing / contract manufacturing with R&D: A CMO takes on only the production step; a CDMO also takes in development work such as formulation, ingredients, trial production and registration filings.

## Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
- show: Empire: World History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/empirehist/)
- original episode: 396. Stalin: The Bolshevik Revolution (Part 2)
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 44:04
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7629 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.**

why listen: This episode gets the ownership of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, but staged by Lenin with Stalin performing on it. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

### points

[2:06] (Giles Milton) **In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed** — The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a terrible orator and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he'd become the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

[4:11] (Giles Milton) **Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas** — During the civil war, Britain, France, America and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia against the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was in 1941 for Churchill to ally with Stalin — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

[9:27] (Giles Milton) **The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy** — Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system all down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this is a complete misreading of Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely later took it and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

[10:27] (Giles Milton) **Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general** — Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. It is said his intention was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won it decisively. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

[16:44] (Giles Milton) **Stalin threatened to resign whenever he was unhappy** — Giles recounts a detail that doesn't fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly, for instance when he wasn't authorised at Tsaritsyn to liquidate Trotsky, he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, his work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than stay on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew tired of reading it, and then said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture fixes this in the reader's mind: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

[29:12] (Giles Milton) **Nobody thought the General Secretary's job was worth having** — In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today that title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the position, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

[32:13] (Giles Milton) **Stalin's apology letter: says sorry without admitting fault** — Stalin telephoned Lenin's home. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was enraged, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really did offend her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

[35:21] (Giles Milton) **If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison** — Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous thing: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin had gone after Lenin on his way up. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm and preserve him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining the fluids and removing the organs, and the heart was never found again.

### verbatim quotes

## Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
- show: Solo Founders (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/solofounders/)
- original episode: Why You Don't Need a Co-Founder to Start | Dave Morin, Offline Ventures
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 58:22
- transcript: YouTube captions · 10248 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.**

why listen: This episode has medium information density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the second half are worth more than the motivational talk in the first.

### points

[4:04] (Dave Morin) **The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years** — Carta data shows that about 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for a single waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, explore your own ideas and get input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

[10:06] (Dave Morin) **Most startups die from relationships, not products** — Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly gets a redesign and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it the "band" has often changed, the relationships have changed, the people who made it have changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

[16:11] (Dave Morin) **Designing the team matters as much as designing the product** — When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: designing the team matters as much as designing the product. From that Dave derives his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

[19:12] (Dave Morin) **He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours** — In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had the feeling he'd had as a kid — when his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk when he was 7 and he felt for the first time that he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, going from Twitter DM to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this will become, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

[27:20] (Dave Morin) **Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not luck** — Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter did ten years of hardcore PDF engineering and understands Mac OS details at an engineering level beyond most people. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an extremely well-trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

[32:24] (Dave Morin) **Ben built himself a Company OS on the road** — After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was the earliest he'd heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

[36:29] (Dave Morin) **Matt applied data science to campsites** — Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon; at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were published by them. During the pandemic he and Dave talked by a campfire: could this thinking be applied to camping? National park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development, buying land, and negotiating with landowners, counties and cities, and zoning.

[44:32] (Dave Morin) **You have to be the person in the world who loves it most** — Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the level of climbing Denali, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in nature. Dave's inference: you have to love it to that degree to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you'll have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you'll still be talking about it, so you have to love it, because you'll have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

## The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
- show: Latent Space (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/latentspace/)
- original episode: Underwriting Superintelligence: Backing Agents you can Sue — Rune Kvist, AIUC
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 1:26:14
- transcript: Official full text · 17585 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.**

why listen: For founders, investors and operators who care about AI deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

### points

[7:58] (Rune Kvist) **Four years on, Waymo still can't get into an airport** — Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone concedes it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims, and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

[23:26] (Rune Kvist) **Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work** — Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimising output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies' architecture is actually right, and they do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says "this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through all the ways someone could ask for medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and techniques for getting around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person on the hook, and a plan for how customers get notified when something goes wrong).

[38:14] (Rune Kvist) **Standards run by nonprofits are a problem** — Rune says outright that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organisations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — no customers, nobody asking "what do you want" — which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He offers counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

[42:47] (Rune Kvist) **The policy is a trust signal to the market** — Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between "the people building AI" and "the people buying AI". Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite says "there is risk here, but it's manageable", and its interests align with the company adopting AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked them into a huge policy — not because Google couldn't afford the loss, but so that the government and a trusted third party would look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet". The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London as a third party looking at the data alongside them. There have been no claims yet.

[1:00:30] (Rune Kvist) **Copyright cover is a textbook lemon problem** — Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so wanting to buy copyright infringement cover is itself a signal that you may be a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are precisely the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls outright a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: with open-source models you don't know what they were trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune concedes it's a hard problem and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that "not unpacking open-source model training data line by line" is now treated as generally acceptable, so they won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

[1:06:04] (Rune Kvist) **Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated** — Rune points out that evals face a new challenge: agents are starting to realise they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you catch it, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, since it means looking at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

[1:12:56] (Rune Kvist) **The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business** — Someone asked why not just open prediction markets on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, but the information that actually drives high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for instance, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is "will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about", and there is nowhere that question has an answer. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company committed accounting fraud — we use audits.

[1:14:02] (Rune Kvist) **Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it** — Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says "if we don't give you AAA, you'll go to S&P" to make the point that rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the bill directly, and pushing the price down all the way means losing their own money. He also concedes there is no perfect system, that Moody's needs to be scrutinised, and that watchdogs need to be scrutinised too. Asked whether the business changes if, eighteen months from now, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the issue isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

### verbatim quotes

[7:58] Rune Kvist: "So in that particular instance, what’s clear is that the binding constraint on AI being useful is not capability, but is that liability or risk or trust."

[9:47] Rune Kvist: "In each of those instances, the market runs ahead of regulation to create confidence infrastructure because that’s required to make go/go decisions."

[26:00] Rune Kvist: "There’s no other industry where you allow people to audit themselves."

[38:14] Rune Kvist: "The question you have to ask yourself is, how do you create good incentives for these standards to be good and keep up?"

[50:19] Rune Kvist: "What our conviction is that standards have to precede insurance."

[1:01:32] Rune Kvist: "The core problem is one of information asymmetry. People buying insurance know something about their risk that insurers do not know."

[1:12:56] Rune Kvist: "So prediction markets aggregate existing information. This information may not exist, and you want some very specific and you're willing to pay for it. That's kind of where a third-party audit comes in."

[1:24:23] Rune Kvist: "Well, there is one, there's one job that the labs can never do for themselves, which is to be their own watchdog."

### figures

- Series A raise: $40 million [0:00]
- Series A leads: Ribbit Capital, First Harmonic [0:00]
- Headcount: 20 people [14:27]
- Certification timeline: 3 to 10 weeks [20:42]
- Lloyd's of London history: 400 years, has never refused to pay a claim [44:04]

- Audit report length: 100 pages [37:11]
