- Share of the Fortune 1000 AIUC currently covers: 0% (Rune explicitly denies it is 50%) [1:19:10]
- When the AIUC consortium is expected to cover the Fortune 1000: possibly 50% representation by the end of this year [1:19:10]

### glossary

- AIUC-1: The AI confidence standard set by AIUC, with three categories of control requirements: technical, testing and policy.
- eval awareness: An agent realising it is being evaluated and changing its behaviour accordingly, which distorts the eval results.
- groundedness filter: A filtering mechanism that ensures model output is grounded and not fabricated.
- lemon problem: Under information asymmetry, the people most eager to buy insurance are precisely the highest-risk customers.
- CAISI: The US government's AI standards body; Rune considers its budget tiny relative to the scale of the challenge.

who it is for: Founders building AI applications, agent products or enterprise AI, plus investors and risk leads watching compliance, insurance and third-party audit.
what to skip: The personal history and Scaling Laws reminiscing from 1:05 to 7:58 can be fast-forwarded; start the argument at 7:58.
tags: AI compliance, AI insurance, third-party audit, agents, confidence infrastructure

## Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
- show: Nature Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/naturepod/)
- original episode: Transplanted human brain-tissue takes root in mice without a cortex
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 28:10
- transcript: YouTube captions · 4632 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.**

why listen: The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

### points

[2:08] (Sergio Pasca) **No surgery — genetics makes the room** — In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team transplanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," unable to get connections or room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells are unable to divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "no-pallium mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

[4:08] (Sergio Pasca) **Four million human neurons take over the empty space** — The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into no-pallium pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells, already differentiated and on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, most of what was removed having been replaced by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

[6:10] (Sergio Pasca) **They are neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice** — The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, no-pallium mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice with the organoid implants. No-pallium mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. Later experiments backed this up: no-pallium animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and human cells very likely contributed some of it, but this is not perfect restoration — it only shows these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

[7:11] (Sergio Pasca) **A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work** — The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can bring lifelong disease, whereas mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to low-oxygen conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced into a hypoxia response while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and no-pallium mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show deficits in walking and gait coordination. Sergio thinks this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these deficits, and that this would be a strong system not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

[8:12] (Aparna Bhaduri) **A very rare neuron type was grown** — Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer, and she thinks one highlight of this work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. But she also points out there is a long way to go: the cortex's laminar structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach anything more like a human brain; and the authors themselves state that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

[9:12] (Aparna Bhaduri) **This is not a human brain in a mouse's head** — Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing and the ones present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from a human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she considers this an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers Nature spoke to take the same view: these are not fully formed functional human cortex.

[10:13] (Emily Jackson) **Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists** — Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper and the work of Sergio Pasca's lab is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine error: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that with replacing part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a new kind of harm you would not easily notice — and that must be taken very seriously.

[17:19] (James) **Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to** — James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents," which you can think of as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, then stores the knowledge in a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, so that models like ChatGPT and Claude become virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper, or even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

[20:20] (James) **Two paper agents talked to each other and found something new** — Because it has to reproduce the original results, paper to agent can in turn find problems in how a paper was produced: if the agent cannot reproduce them — say the data were misread — it can flag the mismatch between data and results to the original authors. James says this process also helps reduce hallucination, because the agent has walked through what the original authors did, and its conclusions are verified by the paper's results, keeping it more grounded. They did a case study: automatically turning Google DeepMind's newly released AlphaGenome, a tool for interpreting the effects of different mutations, into an agent, and turning a large-scale genetics study dataset on ADHD genetic risk into another agent; the two agents began talking to each other, found shared interests and collaborated, and ultimately found a previously unknown splicing mutation associated with elevated ADHD risk.

[23:23] (Magdalena Skipper) **Who builds this tool — the paper does not say** — Nature editor-in-chief Magdalena Skipper, who has 25 years as an editor and 8 as editor-in-chief, thinks traditional papers will not disappear in the short term, and that storytelling is central to how humans share knowledge. But she is optimistic about the potential of "conversational papers," seeing the process of reproducing a paper's work as a good way to test the robustness of results and to make papers more accessible to more scientists. The open question she raises is this: the paper's core is building an AI connector that plugs in the data, the code and the information described in the paper, then forms an interface with an LLM, but the paper does not make clear whose responsibility it is to build this tool. If it falls to the authors doing the research, that is a fairly onerous task, and most researchers, by their area of expertise, do not have that capability; if it is widely adopted, perhaps journals will evolve and publishers will provide this kind of service layer on top of the papers they publish.

[25:26] (James) **Twenty-six of a hundred papers would not convert** — James's team ran 100 computational biology papers through this workflow to turn them into agents, and 26 failed, because of missing information in the paper or inconsistencies in the code the article used. James thinks even failure is informative, because it tells you something in the paper is blocking reproduction. The conversion cost is about one to two dollars per paper, spent on the tokens needed to run the various AI processes. His ambition is to make research more accessible and more robust: papers are now often required to carry a data availability statement, sometimes a code availability statement, and in future he hopes papers can also carry an "agent availability statement," stating that the agent associated with the paper is the paper's virtual author, responsible for ensuring the paper is reproducible and able to help readers and collaborators answer questions about it.

### verbatim quotes

[6:10] Sergio Pasca: "Would they be like the wild type controls or the apalial mice? You know, they're neither. They're so like in a third behavioral state."

[7:11] Sergio Pasca: "So now this tells us that it's likely the human cells that are causing this."

[9:12] Aparna Bhaduri: "I want to say very clearly, this is not a human brain in a mouse."

[11:14] Emily Jackson: "So I think sometimes people wrongly think that regulation is a hindrance to scientists and I think that's a real mistake."

[19:20] James: "it doesn't really know how to generate the results or generate the figures or do the experiments or use the data and the code right because it doesn't have that hands-on experience"

[21:21] James: "those two agents actually started talking to each other and they realized that they have some common interest and they can actually collaborate and in this case right they actually discovered a new splicing mutation associated with increases in risks for ADHD which is not known before"

[24:25] Magdalena Skipper: "What is not clear to me from the paper whose responsibility it is to build this tool."

[26:26] James: "I think this is an opportunity for us to reimagine what knowledge can look like in the future, right? Does not have to be static artifacts could actually become this dynamic knowledge agents in some sense like a living knowledge right"

### figures

- Brain volume lost by no-pallium mice: nearly half [3:08]
- Total neurons in xenocortical mice: about 70 million [4:08]
- Of which cortical and hippocampal cells: about 14 million [4:08]
- Number replaced by human neurons: about 4 million [4:08]
- Age in days of the pups that received transplants: 5 to 17 days [4:08]
- paper to agent conversion failure rate: 26 of 100 papers failed [25:26]
- Cost to convert one paper into an agent: about 1 to 2 dollars [25:26]
- Magdalena Skipper's years as an editor: 25 years as an editor, 8 as Nature editor-in-chief [22:22]

### glossary

- organoid: A small three-dimensional brain-like piece of tissue grown in a dish from human stem cells.
- pallium: A neural structure present early in development that later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.
- xenocortical mice: The name the paper gives to mice that received human cortical organoid transplants, meaning the cortex comes from another species.
- paper to agent: A workflow that reproduces a static paper and turns it into a conversational AI agent.
- AlphaGenome: A tool released by Google DeepMind for interpreting the effects of different mutations.

who it is for: Researchers in neurodevelopment or organoids, and engineers and founders building research AI tools, paper agents, and AI agent workflows.

## The Mess in AI Evaluation Is Not a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
- show: NEJM AI Grand Rounds (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/nejmaigrandrou/)
- original episode: Beyond the Hype: Dr. Xiao Liu on Evaluating Medical AI
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 43:50
- transcript: Official transcript · 7811 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.**

why listen: This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a firsthand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to norms — has direct reference value for anyone building medical AI products.

### points

[11:22] (Xiao Liu) **Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up** — Around 2019, every week brought new papers claiming ‘AI is as good as radiologists’ or ‘AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection’, yet these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, head-to-head comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down sharply — fewer than 5% actually met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

[16:28] (Xiao Liu) **Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did** — CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially checklists specifying which items must be reported in a paper. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report something, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure.

[18:33] (Xiao Liu) **Guidelines come from Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut** — CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion generated a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that reach consensus are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a rushed version compressed to three months, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multiple rounds of participation, you can't skimp on time or reach.

[20:36] (Andy Beam) **Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting** — Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said ‘No, it shouldn't be done at all, for the following reasons’. That debate was later commissioned into a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly takes the ‘no’ side in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

[26:43] (Xiao Liu) **Being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere** — At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

[32:49] (Xiao Liu) **Short term, computer scientists set direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep** — Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what ‘driven’ means, and after confirming it meant ‘changed’, gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism: the people who process data, choose metrics, and choose benchmarks determine in the short term which direction progress goes; but if the endpoint is real use on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

[33:50] (Xiao Liu) **Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten** — Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond, and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being ‘a companion to experience’ — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: the ability to call on knowledge without necessarily carrying it oneself, but translating it into human language.

[40:00] (Xiao Liu) **The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we dare not** — Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives the example of inflammatory eye diseases from her PhD research: a bunch of diseases are loosely called ‘white dot syndromes’ just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious, may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, and during a period of new technological change may rigidly stick to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, missing opportunities for discovery.

### verbatim quotes

[13:23] Xiao Liu: "Less than 5% of the papers actually really met that very standard bar in other areas of medicine."

[14:23] Xiao Liu: "we found that the performance of those models within that cohort was at best equivalent to radiologists."

[16:28] Xiao Liu: "What reporting guidelines don't do is tell you how you should do your study. So, they're not methodological guidelines, they're transparency guidelines."

[17:30] Xiao Liu: "it supplies enough information that brings the authors, the editors of a journal, and the peer reviewers on a level playing field."

[30:48] Xiao Liu: "I think we should ask why we want AI or anything to be explainable, and I think if we drill down far enough, ultimately, we just want stuff to have beneficial effect."

[32:49] Xiao Liu: "the computer scientists and the people who are handling the data, choosing the metrics, choosing the benchmarks, get to decide in the short term which direction progress happens."

[34:53] Xiao Liu: "there's something deeply interpersonal that we will continue to want as part of that journey, which someone that can leverage the knowledge but not necessarily embody it but translate it into human terms."

### figures

- Share of AI papers meeting rigor standards of other medical fields: fewer than 5% [13:23]
- Combined citations of CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI: over 4000 (since publication in 2024) [18:33]
- Minimum time to do a consensus project properly: at least 6 months (a rushed version was compressed to 3 months) [22:39]
- Xiao Liu's tenure at Apple: more than a year [26:43]
- Xiao Liu's tenure at Microsoft AI: a year and a half [27:44]

### glossary

- Delphi study: Multiple rounds of anonymous voting plus in-person discussion, used to reach consensus among experts on which items matter.
- CONSORT: An international checklist of what must be reported in randomized controlled trial papers; the AI version is CONSORT AI.
- SPIRIT: A reporting checklist for clinical trial protocol papers; the AI version is SPIRIT AI.
- white dot syndromes: A loose umbrella term for a group of inflammatory eye diseases that produce white dots in the fundus, possibly driven by different mechanisms.

who it is for: Engineers and founders building medical AI products, doing clinical validation or regulatory submissions, and researchers interested in how evidence standards for medical AI get established.
what to skip: The personal-history parts of the lightning round (first job, favorite paper) can be skipped.

## He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Condemned by His Peers for Forty Years

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
- show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- original episode: Coley's Toxins and the Origins of Immunotherapy
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 38:28
- transcript: Official transcript · 5594 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he could not standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around the therapy.**

why listen: Medium information density: the first half is medical-history background, but the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

### points

[6:13] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The death of an 18-year-old changed him** — In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment available at the time, and it had not worked, which drove him to comb through the records of roughly 90 cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital over the previous 15 years, looking for something better.

[7:15] (Tracy V. Wilson) **In one record, the tumor vanished on its own** — In the case files, Coley found a patient of his colleague Dr. William T. Bull with a small round-cell sarcoma of the neck that had recurred four times; by the fifth operation the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After surgery the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by discharge it had completely disappeared. The hospital had no follow-up record, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him: in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the operation.

[9:21] (Tracy V. Wilson) **He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins** — On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could swallow only small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to lab-cultured bacteria, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in October a culture a colleague had brought from Robert Koch's lab in Germany was injected; the patient became very ill, but two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared and the tonsillar tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins rather than use live bacteria directly.

[15:34] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The effect was real, but only in some patients** — In his papers, Coley wrote that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases improvement was only temporary, and within weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very few cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he recommended it for all inoperable sarcomas (except the melanotic type), for long-bone sarcomas where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, after primary sarcoma surgery once the wound had healed to prevent recurrence, and after all cancer surgery using the mixed toxins to reduce recurrence.

[19:40] (Tracy V. Wilson) **JAMA watched first, then declared failure two months later** — On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published an article comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts delivered complete results. But just two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying there was "no longer much doubt that toxin injections as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths have completely failed," that many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, and that not one fully verified recovery had been reported. Coley responded the following January, noting that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not affect the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded.

[23:47] (Tracy V. Wilson) **Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers** — Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treated roughly 1,000 cancer patients, and published about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company produced various preparations starting in 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refusing to include his cured patients, insisting they were misdiagnosed; his insistence that all cancers had a microbial origin, even after that idea had been overturned; the difficulty of producing and standardizing the toxins; and the 1902 Biologics Control Act, which raised regulatory costs.

[26:54] (Tracy V. Wilson) **Radiation stole his window of time** — Coley's own method of use was also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different lengths of time. Partly this was because he was trying to figure out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost by feel rather than data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, and admitted that his shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard treatment for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry, slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

[29:00] (Tracy V. Wilson) **His daughter spent her life building an institute for him** — After Coley died, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, and ended up digging deep into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully went through all her father's publications, trying to find out why some cases succeeded and others failed. In 1953, with philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr., she founded the Cancer Research Institute, with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method and became chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. Today the Cancer Research Institute has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

[32:00] (Tracy V. Wilson) **BCG bladder instillation is a direct descendant of Coley's therapy** — In 1959, Lloyd J. Old, the Cancer Research Institute's founding scientific and medical director, and others published a paper in Nature describing how mice injected with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) became resistant to implanted tumors. BCG is a tuberculosis vaccine made from attenuated bovine tubercle bacilli. The work grew out of 1920s autopsy studies at Johns Hopkins showing that tuberculosis patients had fewer malignancies. In 1975, Old, with Elizabeth Carswell and others, combined BCG with one of Coley's toxins to stimulate the immune system in mice, extracted a cytokine from mouse blood, and named it tumor necrosis factor (TNF); it both causes inflammation and kills tumors. In the 1970s, Old and other researchers tried injecting BCG into the bladders of some bladder cancer patients and found that BCG stimulated the immune system to attack the cancer. The FDA approved BCG for superficial bladder cancer in 1990, and it is still in use today. Old is sometimes called the founder of cancer immunology, but many who have written about Coley think the two should share the title.

### verbatim quotes

[7:15] Tracy V. Wilson: "The history stated that when the patient left the hospital, his tumors had entirely disappeared."

[12:25] Tracy V. Wilson: "Three weeks from the date of the attack of erysipelas, both tumors had entirely disappeared."

[15:34] Tracy V. Wilson: "in a certain number of cases, in my own experience, a little over 10%, the degenerative process has gone on until the complete absorption of the tumors has taken place. and the patients have remained cured."

[20:42] Tracy V. Wilson: "There is no longer much question of the entire failure of the toxin injections as a cure for sarcomata and malignant growths."

[23:47] Tracy V. Wilson: "I have had 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma successfully treated with the mixed toxins of erysipelas and bacillus prodigiosus. Of these, 35 have remained well from three and a quarter to 16 years, 28 from five to 16 years, and 14 from 10 to 16 years."

[33:01] Tracy V. Wilson: "the toxins were effective at inducing fever and robust surges in cytokines. One patient with metastatic bladder cancer had a clear clinical response to treatment, experiencing a 50% reduction in his cancer that correlated with elevated levels of cytokines."

### figures

- Total patients treated by Coley: about 1,000 cancer patients [23:47]
- Number of papers Coley published: about 150 [23:47]
- Cases of inoperable sarcoma treated with Coley's toxins: 52 [23:47]
- Cases among them that stayed healthy for 3.25 to 16 years: 35 [23:47]
- Age at which Coley died: 74 [27:56]
- Year BCG was approved by the FDA for bladder cancer treatment: 1990 [32:00]
- Year Coley's toxins were classified by the FDA as an investigational drug: 1963 [32:00]
- Year Coley's toxins were placed on the American Cancer Society's list of unproven therapies: 1965 [32:00]
- Year Coley's toxins were removed from that list: 1975 [32:00]
- Year the Cancer Research Institute funded a phase I trial of Coley's toxins: 2007 [33:01]

### glossary

- erysipelas: A bacterial skin infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, marked by red, swollen, hot, painful skin.
- Bacillus prodigiosus: Now called Serratia marcescens, a bacterium that produces a red pigment, which Coley mixed with streptococci.
- BCG: A tuberculosis vaccine made from attenuated bovine tubercle bacilli, later used as immunotherapy for superficial bladder cancer.
- tumor necrosis factor (TNF): A cytokine that both causes inflammation and kills tumor cells, extracted from mouse blood and named by Old and colleagues in 1975.

who it is for: Founders and investors interested in medical history, the origins of cancer immunotherapy, or the question of why a therapy that works but cannot be standardized disappears.
what to skip: The first two minutes of throat-clearing about the definitional fight between vaccines and immunotherapy, and the listener mail at the end.
tags: Medical history, Cancer immunotherapy, Coley's toxins, Drug regulation, Translational medicine

## Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
- show: Conversations with Tyler (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tyler/)
- original episode: Annie Lowrey on the Time Tax, Fraud, and Rationing by Paperwork
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 56:23
- transcript: YouTube captions · 10077 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.**

why listen: Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about softening on UBI is worth hearing.

### points

[0:58] (Annie Lowrey) **The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you** — Lowrey's central example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a prefilled return and you just correct the errors. The US could easily do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it is an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labor, and unlike a monetary tax it is different in kind: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

[1:02] (Annie Lowrey) **The worst program is TANF, not the IRS** — Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: nominally it exists to address child poverty, in practice it does not move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of the beneficiary.

[6:08] (Annie Lowrey) **Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent** — Cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020 fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, and from the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

[11:19] (Annie Lowrey) **Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side** — Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the money you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organizations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who do not commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, and thereby get voters to tolerate cuts.

[13:25] (Annie Lowrey) **Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal** — Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS cannot capture multitasking (cooking while on hold is recorded as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with subordinates and accountants, with one exception: to renovate a house in San Francisco, no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

[22:57] (Annie Lowrey) **AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test** — Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is an open question; second, much of the burden is not paperwork at all — it is mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that is hard to collect. She takes SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and the government has no stable definition of "household," so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split food spending — the kind of question AI will struggle to answer for you. She notes she was originally skeptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

[31:18] (Annie Lowrey) **Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for** — Cowen presses with data: from 1990 to 2014 the number of people on disability insurance rose roughly fourfold while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the bar be raised? Lowrey does not accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population aging and the rise of obesity-related chronic disease. Then the counterevidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both sides — about paying people who don't need it, and about denying people who do — so she does not think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

[38:28] (Annie Lowrey) **The research moved her off her UBI position** — Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering," and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver did not materialize. Her defense is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI," and would not go that far now — but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and you would have to start considering UBI-type policies.

### verbatim quotes

[0:58] Annie Lowrey: "We could do this. Nine in 10 American households take the standard deduction and have fairly simple tax situations. We do not do this. The IRS is legally not allowed to do it."

[7:11] Annie Lowrey: "If you’re a governor and you have a low unemployment rate, what governor is going to devote a huge amount of money to upgrading a state UI system?"

[11:19] Annie Lowrey: "To do big fraud, you have to be doing a lot of processing."

[13:25] Annie Lowrey: "If you’re looking at what I think of as roughly as bureaucratic time total spent, it’s 50 hours per person per year."

[21:49] Annie Lowrey: "I’m convinced that white-collar technology, labor-saving stuff, I’m convinced it’s all Jevons paradoxical. I think that basically anything that is designed like email to make your life easier will at some point make it worse."

[32:24] Annie Lowrey: "In 5 percent of applications, the applicant submits more than 1,000 pages of medical paperwork. It’s a lot. 11,000 Americans die waiting on a disability determination each year."

[39:41] Annie Lowrey: "I think it is noncorrupted, that their lives don’t improve as much as I would have thought, I think, isn’t necessarily a case against the policy."

[53:17] Annie Lowrey: "I note that I think the best way to make friends is not to make yourself available for what other people need but to ask for help."

### glossary

- time tax: The time cost imposed when government shifts administrative labor onto individuals; unlike a monetary tax, it cannot be offset by earning more.
- TANF: The US cash welfare program, which Lowrey considers the most administratively burdensome and least effective program in government.
- submerged benefits: Benefits delivered through the tax code, where recipients often do not know they are receiving them, such as the child tax credit.
- Jevons paradox: Efficiency gains increase total consumption instead; Lowrey uses it to explain how labor-saving tools like email ended up adding to the task load.
- improper payment: An erroneous payment caused by complex rules, distinct from deliberate fraud, and reducible simply by simplifying the rules.

who it is for: People working in public policy, government digital services or benefits products; engineers wondering whether AI can replace administrative process; and readers who want to understand why the American welfare state is so inefficient.
what to skip: 36:25 to 38:28, the argument over how easy voting is — both sides talk past each other, low information gain.
tags: Public policy, Administrative burden, UBI, AI and government, US welfare

## After 25 Million Users on Tome, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: The AI-Native CRM
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 52:43
- transcript: Machine transcription · 10159 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.**

why listen: The first half is a rare post-mortem on deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense with operational detail on pricing, expansion and org design.

### points

[3:01] (Keith Perez) **They killed a hit not because of the data, but because they didn't like it** — Tome launched around the same time as ChatGPT and reached 2 million monthly users, so many that inference capacity ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what actually made them stop wasn't a metric — it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a discerning, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would use it to write memos. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wouldn't close just by waiting for better models.

[6:04] (Keith Perez) **Follow the heat first, then discover the real problem is data** — The Tome team dug through their own user base and found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, so they gave 12 large companies free pilots. The original idea was helping sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that heat, asking customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses, and found the hardest part wasn't doing that work — it was that the data in these systems contradicted each other. The reality in call recordings and the reality in the CRM often didn't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you can reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people understand, that's more worth doing than the original path.

[8:11] (Keith Perez) **Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them to use it** — What they built first was a go-to-market assistant that AEs used every day, but they couldn't charge for it — the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were chasing the same thing. So they shrank the team, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then found nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset left was a huge office they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were inside every day, and that they cared about enough to give feedback by the hour.

[11:21] (Keith Perez) **The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields** — Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and built an activity log first — when you first made contact, what you said, what they replied, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth, and eventually what the other party did inside your product and how they paid. All the traditional CRM field updates and stage progression are triggered from that log, but underneath there's always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow — a needle-in-a-haystack problem — and landed on semi-structured: stuff a large amount of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from it.

[15:26] (Alex Rampell) **Get the data model wrong and sales will never go back and fill it in** — They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields up wrong and you can't send salespeople back in time to fill in the data — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be "schemaless" — connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up a data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields come later. Change your mind and it traverses the activity log and refills. Alex Rampell summed this up as "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length, like name varchar 25 — now they don't even want a schema.

[17:28] (Keith Perez) **Someone used it to find a cutting-edge treatment for an Alzheimer's patient** — Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from the start, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial participants; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and seeking cutting-edge treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of "every ongoing clinical trial in the world," and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield actually helped an Alzheimer's patient find a cutting-edge treatment within days.

[23:37] (Alex Rampell) **Win the founders and engineers first, then wait for the sales VP to come around** — Alex points out something often overlooked: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led motion free for anyone in the company to use. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. By the time that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company pushes him to try it — and that's when they get their opening.

[32:00] (Keith Perez) **Pure seat-based and pure consumption pricing both blew up** — They tried pure seat-based pricing first; acceptance was decent, but top users consumed 10,000 times more than the tail, which wasn't sustainable long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits — and within three weeks nobody touched any feature. Keith says those were the company's worst three weeks: a pile of signups and no usage. Finally they split it into four kinds of work: day-to-day CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into a platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged on consumption, because there's alpha there that turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately — say someone requests a demo on your website and Lightfield decides this is a deep tech company that should go to Henry and that one is health tech that should go to Matt; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most under-explored part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

[36:10] (Keith Perez) **No swim lanes — whoever's free takes the problem** — Keith says Tome's biggest lesson was that "a lot of people were playing house": the product lead, marketing lead and CS lead each had their own swim lane, and got offended when someone commented on theirs, so the company crawled and couldn't pivot at all — a bunch of appendages not talking to the brain. Lightfield is the opposite: 40 people, no swim lanes, everyone owns both product and customer success, everyone joins the same standup every morning, they rank the most important problems — delivery, engineering, CS — and whoever's free takes it. They do continuous planning, with a list that may change daily and gets reassessed weekly. Because in this era anyone can get up to speed on a customer quickly through Lightfield, can ramp on a design system library quickly with an LLM, can auto-create tasks through the Lightfield-Linear connection, engineers, designers and CSMs all lead projects, and specialists just do more projects of the same kind.

[39:15] (Keith Perez) **The bar to start is low, the bar to ship is high** — How do you stay aligned when everyone's a generalist? Keith's answer is a weekly roadmap and GTM meeting, and constant editing: a customer asked for this, how does it relate to the mission? It doesn't, so we don't do it. He describes it as continuous editing to keep what the company puts out coherent. Paired with that are two bars: the bar to start something at Lightfield is very low, but the bar to ship is very high — they still hold a company-wide bug bash, something Keith learned at Instagram: before a product goes to customers, the company itself has to like it first.

[40:23] (Keith Perez) **What makes him paranoid is speed, not competition** — Keith says what worries him most is speed. He mentions reading a report about an a16z portfolio company that had been using some startup's CRM and, because that startup couldn't build the dashboard they wanted for four months, eventually moved to Salesforce. That's what makes him most paranoid: Lightfield has a great wedge — being the best CRM for new companies — but they have to build everything so those people never get the idea of going back to the old world.

[41:27] (Keith Perez) **In a red ocean you can only be an expansion company** — Facing a world where anyone can prompt a product into existence, Keith says one skill Lightfield developed is reading an account's expansion potential. As a CRM company in a red ocean, they have to be an expansion company: in a fiercely competitive market you often don't get the initial land you expected, but by year three or year five that doesn't matter — you become an important part of the customer's company. So they prioritize by an account's three-year expansion value, favoring building for the fastest-growing customers rather than the average one, while admitting that at this stage you have to be "a bit more extreme than usual" and build everything.

[43:48] (Keith Perez) **Silicon Valley is for getting logos, not for making money** — Keith says most systems-of-record companies' eventual revenue scale actually comes from "more than 50 miles from here." He sees the Silicon Valley phase as a technique for getting reference customers: some customers raised $200 million but have only three go-to-market people, yet they'll be huge later, so you do the work to perfection now and then use their logos to go after the rest of the world — "we have healthcare, we have fintech" — and then say we also serve a lot of great manufacturing companies and can now do the same for you. Alex adds the absurdity of the phenomenon: you store exactly the same thing, but because I sell toothbrushes and you sell Coca-Cola, I need to see whether my peers use it.

[47:56] (Keith Perez) **Big companies won't build the system, but they want to build the company brain** — On DIY, Keith says it's slightly overstated: when the ICP was still seed-stage founders, they'd often hear "I could pay you, or I could build it myself in four weekends," and their response was "good luck, call us in five weekends" — and the person would come back saying it hallucinates, sends the wrong emails, nothing works. But at bigger companies they don't hear "I want to build my own system of record"; they hear "I want to build my own company brain," and they hear it a lot. Many of those people come back later saying building a company brain or a business world model is genuinely hard, and the hardest part is probably modeling customers — "we tried, we didn't like our own results, so now we're coming to you."

[48:57] (Keith Perez) **What excites him most is being the company's crystal ball** — Keith says what excites him most is Lightfield becoming the crystal ball companies use for scenario planning: how many salespeople to hire, what product to build next, which way to go. He gives a customer example — a company selling to enterprises discovered inside Lightfield that it needed a mid-market product, and built an entire new product line. Joe connects this back to Alex's point about "extremism": in an era when you can build anything, the answer is instead to have a tool like Lightfield that throws frontier intelligence at a genuinely complex decision — something that used to require very smart people, a lot of ops, SQL and a pile of other things, and now takes an afternoon or a weekend of talking to Lightfield.

[49:57] (Keith Perez) **When you pivot, almost all the noise around you doesn't matter** — Asked what advice he'd give his past self, Keith says the most important thing is: when you pivot, almost all the noise around you doesn't matter. You just need to find the pain point, be motivated to build a product or service that solves it, and then focus on customers almost obsessively — everything else is noise. He recalls the things he heard at the time — the office reminds people of the good old days, the food isn't inspiring enough, how will my options get repriced — and says none of it really mattered; put on blinders and stare at the core.

## Are bad teeth the number one reason kids go to A&E? The number got misread

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
- show: More or Less (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/moreorless/)
- original episode: Are bad teeth the number one reason kids go to A&E?
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 28:28
- transcript: Machine transcription · 4694 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A British MP said teeth are the number one reason children go to A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.**

why listen: Four fact-checks strung into one episode: fast pace, medium information density. The teeth and medicines segments have the most solid numbers; the NEET and P-Doom segments work better as thinking exercises.

### points

[1:01] (Chris Venatza) **Teeth are the number one reason for A&E — that claim is wrong** — Leila Moran, a Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said on Radio 4's The World at One that the number one reason children go to A&E is teeth. Chris Venatza, a consultant in paediatric dentistry at Newcastle University, flatly rejected it: she very likely conflated two sets of numbers. What actually ranks first is "hospital admission for tooth decay treatment" — the number one reason 5-to-18-year-olds are admitted to hospital. A&E attendances, by contrast, have all sorts of causes, and there is simply no data showing whether dentistry ranks high or low among them. Moran's office later confirmed Chris was right, and that she had meant the hospitalisation figure, not the A&E figure.

[3:09] (Chris Venatza) **So many hospital tooth extractions because the rules changed in 2001** — When children are hospitalised for teeth, it is usually not for a filling but for an extraction. Extractions are harder for a child to endure, so children who cannot cooperate for an extraction in a dental clinic may need general anaesthetic. There is an institutional turning point here: the rules changed in 2001, and ordinary dental practices were no longer allowed to administer general anaesthetic, so anyone needing it had to go to hospital. A large share of the hospitalisation numbers are therefore general-anaesthetic extractions. This explains why "hospitalisation" and "A&E" are two entirely different measures — one is a surgical arrangement pushed into hospitals by the rules, the other is unplanned care.

[4:10] (Chris Venatza) **The hospitalisation rate is actually falling, not a crisis** — Chris gives the rate per 100,000 population: about 320 in 2015, down to 270 before the pandemic, and 250 now. Host Tim Harford's reaction was "this doesn't look like a crisis, the trend is even quite encouraging." Chris concedes that a pre-pandemic decline is a good thing, but stresses that even so, large numbers of children are still having general anaesthetics and dental treatment in hospital, which is not good in itself. He adds one more thing: for the past decade, dental causes have been the number one reason for hospitalisation, unchanged for ten years — so the "number one" position is stable, but the absolute level is heading down.

[5:10] (Chris Venatza) **To see the decay rate, look at school surveys, not hospitalisations** — Chris says there is a better dataset for understanding children's tooth decay: the government sends dentists into schools to examine five-year-olds. The latest survey found 22% of five-year-olds already have decay reaching the dentine layer — close to a quarter. A quarter of the population having a disease that needs treatment, he says, is not a good state of affairs. Over time: about 30.9% in 2008, down to 23% in 2017-2018, then a plateau, with the latest survey slightly down again on the 2022 one. Longer-term data comes from a survey run once a decade since 1973: 72% of five-year-olds had decay in 1973, down to 43% in 2003 — roughly halved.

[8:15] (Lizzie McNeill) **25% of UK medicines come from Israel — off by two orders of magnitude** — US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on the Today programme that 25% of the medicines Britain uses are made in Israel. Lizzie McNeill checked the latest ONS import data: in 2025 the UK imported £10 million of medicines from Israel, against total UK medicine imports of about £28 billion, so Israel accounts for just 0.04% — one twenty-fifth of 1%, not 25%. She also ruled out several possibilities: active pharmaceutical ingredients come mainly from India and China, and the more upstream raw materials mainly from China; and the medicines supplied by Israeli companies (the largest being Teva) are mostly not made in Israel but in European plants in Hungary, Croatia and elsewhere. Teva estimates it supplies one in eight generic medicine packs in the UK, equivalent to one ninth of all prescriptions, but the other Israeli companies are all too small to push the total to 25%.

[13:29] (Daisy Christodoulou) **Blame Gove for rising NEETs and Wales dismantles the case** — Education secretary Lucy Powell wrote in The Times that a million young people have been left behind by the education system Michael Gove led. Daisy Christodoulou rebuts with a natural experiment: Wales and Scotland took the opposite path to Gove's reforms. Wales's NEET rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose from 14% in 2019 to 17% in 2025, while England's rose from 11% to 13% over the same period — similar levels, similar trends, with Wales rising slightly more. If Gove is responsible for England's rise, then Wales must be responsible for Wales's rise, yet the two places had completely opposite policies. She says the NEET rate sits on top of economic structure, the minimum wage, tax, regulation and far too many other factors — not just education.

[17:51] (Daisy Christodoulou) **The teen mental health decline is not unique to England** — Against the criticism that Gove's reforms increased academic pressure and damaged mental health, Daisy turns to the WHO's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, which reports England, Scotland and Wales separately. It shows average life satisfaction among teenagers fell in all three nations this century (2000 to 2022), but it also fell across Western Europe and many other regions, so it is not specific to England. Then the share of 15-year-olds who "like school a lot": about 10% in England, about 9% in Scotland, about 7.5% in Wales — all low, but essentially the same across the three. The share of 15-year-olds feeling overwhelmed by academic pressure is high in all three, with no big difference.

[19:59] (Alexander Mark Koch) **P-Doom is a subjective probability and nobody can produce a model** — Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are irresponsible on AI safety. Anthropic's Evan Hubinger responded on X: he personally thinks the probability that AI kills all of humanity within the next decade is greater than 10%. Alexander Mark Koch, an assistant professor of global risk and resilience at Cambridge, explains that P-Doom is shorthand for "the probability that AI causes human extinction," and is almost always one individual's subjective probability estimate. He says the issue is extraordinarily complex: it involves regulatory capacity, system resilience, where large-model capabilities are heading, autonomous weapons and biotech tools, whether AI can self-improve into an exponential loop, funding, rules, what China will do, and disaster scenarios ranging from science fiction to "a rogue state using a large model to learn to make bioweapons."

[24:13] (Alexander Mark Koch) **Nobody really believes it, because market prices don't reflect it** — Economist Tyler Cowen repeatedly points out that many people talk about human extinction, but nobody can point to any market price — interest rates, share prices — reflecting that anyone truly believes it. Asked whether anyone really believes it, Koch says some people genuinely do, and you cannot say they don't; but people differ hugely on the probability and on how a catastrophe would unfold. Asked about his own P-Doom, Koch says he doesn't have one, because he doesn't know how to assign a number to it: he can conceive of many paths to destruction, and can also think of ways to mitigate each one, but he doesn't know how to assign a probability to any of them.

## Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets the Core

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
- show: Invest Like the Best (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ilt/)
- original episode: Michael Moritz - Lessons From 40 Years of Investing and Writing - [Invest Like the Best, EP.491]
- published: 2026-09-16 · duration: 1:12:28
- transcript: Machine transcription · 12351 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you unconsciously absorb from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.**

why listen: Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — on structural changes in venture capital and the great man view of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.

### points

[7:23] (Michael Moritz) **The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass disappeared** — Moritz's two grandfathers were two reactions to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving, and in the end he and his wife were sent east and vanished from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported his family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he draws is not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and you can never have too many passports.

[21:03] (Michael Moritz) **His most effective question makes people cry on the spot** — When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked this — the man was the son of Latino immigrants, and at around 12 he and a friend stole candy from a corner grocery; the owner told his father, who dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews are not really listening to the answer.

[26:03] (Michael Moritz) **On Zoom he sorted everyone he knew into categories** — Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divides people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, on those Zoom calls with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he has invested in would be resisters, he says he would like to think so, but he is not sure.

[38:04] (Michael Moritz) **The painter took one day off a year** — Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a total monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas to rest at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house was right on the English coast, and Moritz asked whether he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly that.

[43:04] (Michael Moritz) **He bet on something beyond the résumé** — Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a direct reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cited most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that foreshadowed success. Don did not believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing whether they drowned.

[46:15] (Michael Moritz) **Venture capital's old edge was imperfect information** — Moritz says doing venture capital in the 1980s and 90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you did not know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many middlemen, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says that a moderately intelligent, quick-minded 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture capital in the mid-80s; he is not sure he could still do it well today.

[52:57] (Michael Moritz) **He is an unabashed believer in the great man view of history** — Asked whether it is great individuals or enduring institutions that shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In his work at Sequoia and in writing Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And of Elon, he says he is completely stunned by the scale of his achievements across so many different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

[58:40] (Michael Moritz) **The more AI writes, the more a human voice is worth** — Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the junk is actually appreciating in value; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to your own inner feeling and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He does not consider himself a technologist, and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doom when the nuclear bomb went off, and in the 1970s predicted a genetic revolution making humans, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.
