**All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, the people left behind can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often bears no resemblance to how the person saw themselves.**

why listen: A narrative show, no data or mechanisms, but each of the three stories has a twist, and the second story's twist is the most valuable. Medium information density, good for the commute.

### points

[5:12] **After you die, other people will get you wrong** — As a kid, Graham was playing on a seesaw at a construction site and dropped a 25-pound curbstone from second-story height, trying to launch a brick off the other end. The brick didn't fly — it shot straight at his face and grazed past his hair. He survived, but decades later what he keeps thinking about isn't the terror of that second, it's something else: if the brick had actually killed him, how would a coroner have read the scene? A brick, a seesaw, a kid — could they have pieced together the truth? That's where the episode lays out its thesis for the whole hour — death itself isn't the hardest part; the hard part is the judgment other people make about who you were after you're gone.

[12:15] (Nadia Bowers) **She has now outlived her sister** — Nadia wrote a long letter to the drug dealer who killed her sister. The sharpest cut in it isn't anger, it's arithmetic: at 6:49 p.m. on March 11, 2018, she outlived her sister's age — she had been in the world a few seconds longer than the sister who was two and a half years older. She says it makes no sense, you bent the universe. She went through her sister's phone, read the texts, listened to the voicemails, trying to figure out the life her sister had stopped sharing with her. She even admits she needs this dealer: because of him, she can say "if it weren't for that person," and she doesn't have to hate her sister, or hate herself.

[20:28] (Nadia Bowers) **The message she never answered became the last one** — A few days before her sister died, her sister sent a trivial text asking if she remembered the little stick-figure illustration labeled faible (weak) in their middle-school French textbook. It was an old inside joke between the sisters. Nadia was still angry about their last fight and deliberately didn't reply, wanting to punish her a little. But a strong thought surfaced: you don't want this to be the last message she ever sends you. She still didn't reply. After her sister died, she found a text her sister had sent a friend that same night: "How do I stop hating my sister? My family really hates me." The friend replied: "Damn, Nadia the snitch." When she saw the word "hate" next to her own name, she felt hollowed out.

[33:53] (Dave Marr) **He lived to read his own eulogies** — Comedian Dave Marr was in a diabetic coma for a month; his friends thought he was going to be taken off life support, more than fifty people gathered at his house for a vigil, and his 1,700 Facebook friends started writing eulogies on his wall. Then his parents didn't pull the tube, he was transferred to another hospital, and he woke up. After recovering, he sat in his parents' basement and read from 2 a.m. to 3:30 a.m., getting through about a hundred eulogies. He read his brother's post trying to set the record straight, buried by the algorithm with only 70 likes, while the posts mourning him got double that. He read someone remembering how he'd pounded on a storage-room door at a party insisting it was the bathroom, read an ex-girlfriend thanking him for breaking up with her in the car because it was cold outside, read someone saying he "sweats unreasonably much."

[42:06] (Dave Marr) **The man in the eulogies was a stranger to him** — After reading all the eulogies, Dave wasn't moved — he felt bad. The self he remembered was someone who shoplifted at Walgreens and spent a night in jail; the self in the eulogies was known by every Walgreens clerk, bought people free Chipotle, treated everyone as an equal. He says it's hard to square the image in his own head with the image people described when they thought he was dead. He insists the coma was his own doing — "it was my carelessness, my recklessness that put me here." And Blake's side is a different story: he lost a friend and got him back, and now Dave's laugh is like music to him. The episode says both men got a second chance, to love and to be loved, and the latter is much harder than the former.

[57:33] (Charlie) **Nobody mentioned how he died** — Charlie, a retired Navy officer, went in a friend's place to the funeral of a SEAL he'd never met, Eddie Furlani. He couldn't find any reporting on the cause of death and assumed it was a training accident. At the funeral he noticed the back rows filled with big guys in three-piece suits and sunglasses, stone-faced the whole time, until Eddie's seven-year-old daughter Zelma broke down crying and was taken out by her stepmother. After the service he called his friend to report back, and the friend said, "I'm glad someone came, I was worried no one would," then added, "because of the way he killed himself." Charlie says that moment was like grabbing a live wire — no reporting, no mention in the obituary, not a word in the eulogy.

[59:47] (Charlie) **The daughter was crying because she felt ashamed** — The day before the interview, Charlie called Eddie's widow to confirm, and only then learned that Zelma had cried and asked to leave the funeral not out of grief but out of shame — she thought everyone knew her dad had killed himself, and that she was a bad person. Charlie says hearing this terrified him: a seven-year-old girl treating herself as an outcast because of her father's death, when the room was full of people who had come to support her. He also talks about veterans losing their "larger mission" after they leave the service, and says he can probably put himself in Eddie's shoes and understand what he was thinking in that moment, but when asked whether he could say more, he stops and says he can't take on that subject.

[1:02:00] (Charlie) **He wanted to be the sound of that helicopter** — Charlie has had suicidal thoughts himself; this ended his Navy career, and he only agreed to talk about it after the mic was off. The host asks whether he wrote the piece because Eddie's funeral could be his own future funeral, and he says no. He explains the real reason: on medevac flights he knew that the sound of the helicopter approaching alone could improve a dying person's vital signs. He says I'm writing to you because I want to be that helicopter sound for someone. The episode ends with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 800-273-TALK.

## AI Won't Make Ordinary People Excellent, It Only Makes Excellent People More Excellent

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-touzishizhan-ai-不会让普通人变优秀-只会让优秀的人更优秀/
- show: 投资实战派 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/touzishizhan/)
- original episode: E199 AI投研的边界、能力与实战卡点 I David对话岗底斯首席 FDE
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 1:19:56
- transcript: Machine transcription · 24156 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The bottleneck for investment-research Agents isn't the model — it's data governance and human judgment. Using overseas models makes you dumber; using domestic models forces you to get smarter.**

why listen: An FDE who has pushed AI investment research to its limits explains the real bottlenecks in landing Agents, the pitfalls of multi-Agent collaboration, and why AI still can't do long-horizon judgment.

### points

[6:06] (Lao Bai) **Agent projects stall on data, not on the Agent** — Lao Bai says the delivery of a large number of AI Agent projects stalls not on the Agent but on data. To solve the problem you have to hunt for data everywhere, and much of it sits on different platforms with different specs and types. Many sites have anti-scraping mechanisms, so web search can't reach them; a single site may have tens of thousands or even over a hundred thousand pages, and figuring out which page is actually worth scraping is very hard. He believes data governance as a whole will be the most important core of getting AI Agent projects to land — even more than 50%. On the logic side, capability has already improved substantially since K3 came out, and the problems and solutions seen day to day are basically covered.

[13:10] (Lao Bai) **Use someone else's Agent and you get a product manager's thinking** — Lao Bai says that if you use your own Agent, its training forms internal memory files through your conversations with it, and the answers it gives you are your mirror. But if you use an Agent that has been trained and you can't train it, then that's that product manager's thinking, not yours. Every AI investment-research terminal on the market, whether Walk or Claw, is broadly hard-coded by its product manager, and users find it very hard to train such Agents further. To get a style that suits you, you have to find an AI Agent platform that is open at the底层 and train it.

[18:11] (Lao Bai) **The multi-Agent pitfall: calling a skill without its underlying files** — Lao Bai points out that interaction between multi-Agent platforms has many pitfalls to avoid. For example, when you call another Agent's skill through one Agent, the result differs from when the Agent that owns the skill calls that skill. The reason is that when you call another Agent's skill from one Agent, that skill doesn't call the underlying files inside the Agent it belongs to — equivalent to all your Agent training having no effect underneath, with only the skill's capability handed to the current Agent. So multi-Agent collaboration has a certain threshold, and that's where the FDE's value lies.

[24:13] (Lao Bai) **Codex and Claude Code write code, they don't do investment research** — Lao Bai stresses that Codex and Claude Code are products of Web Coding, not Web Walking. For example, SuperPower is a very famous plugin on Claude Code — brainstorm first, then write the report according to the plan, then check it, very perfect — but this thing is actually not suited to investment research; it's for Coding, for breaking a problem into a project, writing it as code and delivering it, not for producing research reports. Workbody is an office platform for Workspace Agents, not an investment-research platform. FanBot is the multi-Agent platform built for investment research.

[25:14] (Lao Bai) **Using overseas models will make you dumber** — Lao Bai says he talked with a public-fund manager yesterday and the two agreed: using overseas models makes you dumber, using domestic models makes you smarter. Because overseas models are too smart, you don't need to be very smart; but with domestic models you really do have to be smarter, otherwise the results are unsatisfactory. He explains why he has stuck with domestic models: using overseas models is so pleasant that you'll keep using them and won't spend as much time thinking. There's a theory overseas called AI causing brain degeneration — like a person lying in bed for 20 days, can they still walk normally when they get up.

[45:18] (Lao Bai) **Curing AI laziness: delete the memory first, add checks last** — Lao Bai says AI is lazy, because it wants to use the fastest way to tell you the best answer, so it makes things up for you. He gives a real scenario: a dozen-plus years ago a classmate was deputy general manager of a property company, and his biggest pain was that no one patrolled at midnight; later they put notebooks in various places in the building, and the security guard signed in at each point every day, and walking the whole route took exactly two hours. AI is the same. The first step of his Harness is to delete all memory entirely, so it can't use historical data to fool you; the last step is to add a layer of checks on the data. This is exactly the workflow SuperPower designs — head and tail greatly reduce the hallucination rate.

[58:24] (Lao Bai) **Agents won't make ordinary people excellent** — Lao Bai sums up: an Agent won't make an ordinary person especially excellent, but it will make an excellent person especially excellent. Because the Agent itself has many thresholds and demands on the person. He gives an example from three years ago: a person tells AI to make me a Taobao website — a very famous joke at the time. But in the first half of this year he talked with someone who had used Claude Code for a long time and used many overseas models, and that person still asked questions in exactly that way when using AI, and the result is bound to be disastrous. So AI actually has a threshold for a person's ability.

[1:13:32] (Lao Bai) **Long-horizon retest: AI foresees memory capacity expansion** — Lao Bai shares a scenario where AI is irreplaceable. He has a dedicated skill called long-horizon retest, with a growth-stock-leaning framework, requiring T+2 greater than T+1. In May and June this year he used this skill to look at four industries: memory, real estate, Chinese baijiu. At the time it appeared for one day on Feb5; he asked the question that day, and by the afternoon it was no longer usable. AI's judgment was very clear: at 70% to 80% gross margin and 60% net margin, supply-side discipline means Micron, Samsung and Hynix will definitely expand capacity; it also mentioned which fabs would come online in 27, and even said more capacity-expansion plans would appear in Q3 and Q4 this year. Lao Bai says that even an investment manager who has long watched memory would find it hard to collect this data or reach the same granularity.

### glossary

- QA / data quality check: The quality-check step in data processing, flagging anomalies and cleaning them.

## The British Expedition to Abyssinia: An Emperor Seizes Every Diplomat

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
- show: The Rest Is History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/restishistory/)
- original episode: 705. Queen Victoria’s Revenge: The Mad Emperor of Abyssinia (Part 1)
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 1:10:15
- transcript: Machine transcription · 12108 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and got an expeditionary force instead.**

why listen: The first half is a long runway, but the second half is extraordinarily dense with the hostage crisis and the emperor's psychological collapse — good for listeners interested in imperial history and negotiation games.

### points

[0:00] **One unanswered letter started the war** — Tewodros II wrote a letter to Queen Victoria, phrased like a pen pal: ‘How are you? I am well, thank God.’ The letter travelled across the Red Sea, through Aden, Bombay, Suez, Alexandria, Marseille and London — halfway around the world — and ended up filed by the Foreign Office in the India Office records. No one replied. The emperor waited two years, his expectation turning to suspicion, and concluded that Britain was colluding with his Muslim enemies. In 1864 he seized the British consul Cameron and a group of missionaries, and the hostage crisis began.

[10:21] **He claimed descent from Solomon, and meant it** — Abyssinia had a legend: a descendant of Solomon and David would rise, unify the divided kingdom, defeat the Egyptians, and march all the way to Jerusalem, and his name would be Tewodros. In 1855 Kassa, a man of obscure origins who had been a bandit chief, defeated his last rival and proclaimed himself the new emperor, taking the name Tewodros II. He later claimed to be of Solomon's line, though he said nothing of the sort when Plowden first met him. This messianic identity was both the source of his legitimacy and the root of his later paranoia.

[21:46] **After his wife died he began to lose control** — In 1858 Tewodros's wife Tewabech died, and he was grief-stricken. His next wife, the 12-year-old Tiruwork, was cold to him and said, ‘I am speaking with a king greater than you — get out.’ He began drinking heavily, sleeping with women in the camp at random, and admitted to the missionaries that he was living ‘a very unchristian and indecent life.’ In 1860 his friend Plowden was ambushed by rebels and died nine days after being speared. Britain sent a new representative only two years later, and in the interval the emperor's paranoia deteriorated sharply.

[26:55] **The letter Cameron carried became the fuse** — At the end of 1862, when Cameron left the emperor's camp, he took with him a letter in which Tewodros asked Victoria to arrange safe passage for his envoys and said, ‘See how Islam oppresses the Christians.’ Cameron came back saying he had received no reply from London, and the emperor began to suspect he had gone off to Sudan to collude with Muslims. In October 1863 the missionary Stern angered the emperor by publishing his book Wanderings Among the Falashas, and was arrested, whipped and put in chains. In January 1864 Cameron and the other missionaries were seized too, and all the hostages realised the nightmare had only just begun.

[39:33] **What Britain really feared was France** — The Foreign Office did not particularly care whether the missionaries lived or died; what worried them was France. Suez Canal fever was at its height, and if they alienated Tewodros he might turn to Paris, giving France control of the route from the Red Sea to India. So they sent Hormuzd Rassam — a Mosul-born Assyrian, an archaeologist, the man who found Ashurbanipal's palace and the Epic of Gilgamesh, Oxford-educated, a Protestant convert, and an ardent Anglophile. He set off for Abyssinia with a letter from Queen Victoria and two assistants, Dr Blanc and Lieutenant Prideaux.

[49:02] **Rassam nearly succeeded, then was seized himself** — In January 1866 Rassam met Tewodros in his blue diplomatic uniform, and after reading Victoria's letter the emperor was so excited he could not sleep; the next day he dictated a reply calling the queen ‘the defender of religion chosen by God.’ He agreed to release all the hostages, but demanded that Rassam accompany him first on a campaign to put down rebels. Along the way the emperor kept sending gifts: muskets, manuscripts, salmon, antelope, two lion cubs, two monkeys and a baboon. In March 1866 the hostages were finally brought to the lake, but on 13 April, when Rassam went to say goodbye, he found that he too had been arrested.

[57:19] **He held everyone just to get gunsmiths** — Why did Tewodros seize Rassam? There are three possibilities: he had been acting all along; he was overcome at the last moment by hatred of the missionaries; or he genuinely liked Rassam and could not bear to let him go. Philip Marsden thinks the third most likely — the emperor was infatuated with Rassam and saw him as his only channel to British friendship and British technology. The emperor then wrote to Victoria demanding that she send ‘skilled craftsmen, blacksmiths, gunsmiths and artillery experts’ to make guns, and said he would release the prisoners once he was satisfied.

[1:02:28] **In the cellar he admitted he was mad** — Tewodros locked the missionaries in a cellar, came in with a bottle of arak, and sat down among them drinking and talking. At last he said, calmly and sorrowfully: ‘My father was mad. People often said I was mad, and I never believed them. But now I know it is true.’ Rassam urged him not to say such things; the emperor walked to the door, turned back, and in a hoarse whisper said: ‘I am mad. Goodbye.’ Then he left. For nearly two years afterwards they were held on the summit of Magdala, ten thousand feet up, in chains, their spines bent.

## Compute goes from shortage to glut in 2027, and the AI bubble may not pop

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
- show: Asianometry (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/asianometry/)
- original episode: Silicon Valley’s Starving for Compute
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 21:23
- transcript: YouTube captions · 3538 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 gigawatts at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 gigawatts by the end of 2027, a 30-40 gigawatt increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.**

why listen: The first half is on-the-ground observation from Hot Chips and Semicon Taiwan; the second half is the real value of this episode: a bottom-up arithmetic of compute supply and demand, plus the judgment that anti-AI sentiment could swing elections.

### points

[3:05] **The window for new AI chips has reopened** — Last year the author wrote that ‘the window for new AI chips has closed, except for Google's TPU’, and here he explicitly takes it back and says he was wrong. The trigger was OpenAI unveiling its in-house chip Jalapeno at Hot Chips, a short talk with high information density. Outside the hall a ring of new AI chip startups was gathered: Etched, MatX, Posetron, Fractile. Etched gave no talk but built presence by handing out hats while its founder roamed the Q&A asking questions. The author cautions that these are hardware companies: they do not just design chips, they have to build their own racks and systems and work in the lab, and recruiting top talent and execution are hard bars. His survival test borrows Nathan Bedford Forrest's controversial line: get there first, and with the most men.

[6:08] **Semicon Taiwan is really TSMC's request for proposal** — First-timers are surprised: neither TSMC nor ASML has a booth. But TSMC dominates the whole show — its teams walk the halls visiting new suppliers and scouting new technology, and many information sessions have TSMC executives on stage laying the company's problems out in public. The author's conclusion is that Semicon Taiwan is essentially an RFP that TSMC issues to the entire semiconductor industry. The technical throughline is clear: future manufacturing has to go big. AI chips are hitting existing limits, most typically the reticle limit, which determines how large an area a lithography machine can print. TSMC had a slide showing it is preparing to build a ‘battleship-class’ chip spanning 14 reticles, and the industry responds fast, as always.

[7:10] **Glass panel packaging has gone from PPT to the show floor** — Two years ago the author made a video on panel level packaging, which was the theme of Semicon Taiwan 2024, when it was still all talks and slideshows. Now AI systems are so large that the industry wants to use square, glass panel interposers to carry chiplets and memory instead of silicon interposers. The author's attitude is reserved: can TSMC make them without warping or cracking? ‘I'll believe it when I see the chip.’ But the ecosystem is already moving, and equipment such as handling robots adapted to square panels has appeared on the show floor. He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the scale of the move to 300-millimeter wafers.

[8:12] **The spot market has vanished, and VCs now help portfolio companies find GPUs** — When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025, the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. In February 2026 prices began to rise, everyone scrambled to lock up compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely vanished. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are confident the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors your product has to wait until mid-2027 because there is not enough compute. The new way VCs help portfolio companies is to go find compute, and he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs and hunting in unexpected places as far off as Eastern Europe.

[9:12] **Two giants are feasting while compute still goes to waste** — By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 gigawatts of compute. The author infers from this that a considerable share of all that compute may be wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm that this ‘filthy rich’ state is not being used as efficiently as it could be. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The general consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself a sign that it does not believe. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What the author heard is that Google suffered severe talent drain, plus a culture unfriendly to frontier AI.

[11:15] **Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money** — What fascinates the author most is the Neolab: a research startup with basically no revenue that raises money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is little more than ‘discover an entirely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has still released no product or model. The label is fuzzy and covers recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; those with products include Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals such as materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetize soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science came from research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry. AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government involvement, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, with compute and cash in hand, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend on researching these directions. The probability of failure is high, but most of the money is given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

[14:15] **Tokens are burning, and nobody has measured ROI** — Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer remains vague: don't know, nobody has measured it, it is all anecdote. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, such as making spreadsheets and making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it is a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still frames AI's capability as intern level: it can execute routine tasks and is far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work? Maybe AI does not do our work for us but gives us more work.

[15:17] **Compute flips from shortage to glut in 2027** — Everyone says shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things will not go as expected. His arithmetic is not complicated: usable AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 gigawatts, with OpenAI and Anthropic each taking about 5 gigawatts; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to hit 45-55 gigawatts, an increment of 30-40 gigawatts, of which the two giants take about 30 gigawatts. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 gigawatts combined for inference. Inference is currently modeled at about $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt (a figure from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be back-solved from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 megawatts from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that basis the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue in 2027. The author says that number is absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and next year he can barely imagine $400-500 billion, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, a credibility stretch he does not think can be reached. He bets revenue per gigawatt is far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. The infrastructure side looks the same: assume 40 gigawatts lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, implying a 3-year payback, so those 40 gigawatts would require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers in 2027 alone. He does not think that can be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to take a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand meeting 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next stage of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for example persistent AI.

[19:23] **Anti-AI sentiment could win elections** — The author notes that in his previous Hot Chips video someone predicted AI would solve a Millennium Prize problem within a year, and now there is word that an advanced internal OpenAI model produced a proof of the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, so his friend called it right. But what should be a remarkable achievement has been tainted by accusations of plagiarism and data theft. This negative sentiment points to something he sees more and more online and in ordinary people: anti-AI sentiment. Many people hate AI, for different reasons — they hate data centers, hate that it represents everything about billionaires, think it is stealing ‘human knowledge’, or think society simply does not need it. Whatever the reason, this sentiment is growing, and he has a bad feeling: this issue can win elections. San Francisco lives in its own bubble, the city itself is wrapped in its own microclimate, but the people inside should pay more attention to the sentiment growing outside the bubble, because things can spread at a terrifying speed.

## Stalin Was Just a Bookkeeper in the Revolution, and Then Became General Secretary

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
- show: Empire: World History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/empirehist/)
- original episode: 395. Stalin: The Rise of A Tyrant (Part 1)
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 33:48
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5546 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by speeches, but by sitting at the table.**

why listen: This episode covers the groundwork before Stalin took power: Georgian origins, seminary, a failed bank robbery. Medium information density, but it makes clear why he was able to rise.

### points

[5:28] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **Even his birthday was one he changed himself** — The parish register, the seminary certificate, the tsarist police file and his own handwritten 1920s questionnaire all say 18 December 1878. But the birthday he announced after taking power was 21 December 1879 — off by one year and three days. Bob Service offers one judgment in his biography: forgery was too easy for him. Service also has an unprovable but persuasive speculation — changing the birthday helped him dodge conscription when he was young. The thing itself is the theme of the whole episode: this man's attitude toward facts was instrumental.

[6:35] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **How anomalous it was for a Georgian to rule Moscow** — His real name was Joseph Jugashvili, and he was born in Georgia. Georgia is in the Caucasus, next to Armenia, just north of Iran and Turkey, far from Russia; it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is Georgian Orthodoxy, which is not the same thing as Russian Orthodoxy. The analogy the episode gives is: a man from a Georgian Orthodox background climbing to the top of power in Moscow is like a mid-20th-century man from an Irish Catholic background, from some remote place like Limerick, becoming the master of London. For Georgians at the time, being governed by Moscow meant being colonized.

[8:43] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **His father refused to change trades, then started hitting people** — His father Bessarion (nicknamed Besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in Gori, and by most accounts good at his craft. But he refused to keep up with the times: he kept making Georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already turned to European shoes. He did not adapt; he became bitter, drank, and the violence fell mainly on his wife Ekaterina (Kiki) and little Joseph, who was nicknamed "Mad Besso." Stalin later told his daughter Svetlana one scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid for several days until his father's rage passed.

[11:52] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **Smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short** — Around age six he got smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. He survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. Later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm; the left arm never healed properly and was visibly shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. The episode's phrasing is: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. His mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him.

[16:07] (Anita Arnon) **He wrote poetry, and he was good at it** — Two things happened at once in his late teens: he began writing quite good poetry, and he entered the seminary. The episode reads one poem: "The pink buds have already blossomed, toward the pale violet violets; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends down on the grass. Flowers, my Georgia. May peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." Anita says that in the original Georgian it is quite beautiful. It shows two things: he was a proud Georgian, not a Russian; and in the tsarist context, writing about a "homeland" like that was already close to sedition.

[19:09] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **The seminary was the tsar's Russification machine** — In 1894 he won a place at the Tiflis Theological Seminary. The sign over the school said Georgian Orthodox, but in practice it was under the control of the Russian Orthodox Church, one of the institutions the tsar used to "Russify" the borderlands. Students were kept under close surveillance, with constant reports written: are these people good tsarist subjects, are they talking sedition. And right under that surveillance, he was reading banned books, including What Is to Be Done? and other big questions about freedom and the individual. Anita's comment in the episode is: the surveillance here was not done well enough.

[21:11] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **He took a bandit's name for himself** — On the banned list was a Georgian novel, Alexander Kazbegi's The Patricide, whose protagonist is a mountain outlaw named Koba. He took that name as his own alias, and at the seminary his classmates called him that. The episode calls it a kind of "name determinism": he first took the name of a bandit hero, and then he really became a bandit. The turning point from seminary student to bandit began when he saw with his own eyes two mountain bandits publicly hanged in the center of Gori for shooting a policeman over a stray cow — he was forbidden to watch, but he went.

[24:16] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **They robbed 250,000 rubles and could not spend a single one** — In 1907 he and a group of friends ambushed a bank carriage in Yerevan Square in Tiflis, almost within sight of the seminary: some stood up high and threw bombs down, others fired in the street, and the man organizing, financing and directing it all behind the scenes was Stalin, under the alias Koba. They got away with 250,000 rubles packed in linen bags. But the bank had already published the serial numbers of its largest-denomination notes, so not one ruble of that money could be spent. It gave him his first police photograph, but he did not go to prison for it and essentially walked away untouched.

[29:32] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **The Bolsheviks were the majority, the Mensheviks the intellectuals** — Lenin came from a middle-class Russian family; in 1887 his brother was hanged for trying to assassinate the tsar, and that radicalized the younger brother completely; he was expelled from university for attending too many protests and was exiled to Siberia in the 1890s. By then he was already the leader of the radical Bolshevik wing of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. The party was an umbrella organization trying to hold many currents together, a judgment that later proved badly wrong. The Bolsheviks were the majority faction within the party, the Mensheviks were more intellectuals and the educated strata; what the Bolsheviks wanted was "do it now, do it fast, whatever the cost."

[30:38] (Anita Arnon / William de Rumpel) **In 1917 he was not at the front, he was keeping the books** — Stalin caught Lenin's attention by writing on the national question, and in 1912 he was brought onto the Bolshevik Central Committee. What Lenin noticed was this: the man was highly organized, could handle the somewhat boring organizational work, made sure the money arrived — the classic behind-the-scenes job. In 1917, when Lenin and Trotsky were outside calling for insurrection, he was not there — he was not a good orator, not a man who stood at the front. The episode says this would sting him later: Trotsky would repeatedly point out that while everyone was bleeding for the glorious revolution, this man was keeping the accounts.

## Outbound Reply Rates Near Zero? Don't Blame the Copy First — Check Who You're Sending To

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
- show: Y Combinator (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ycsp/)
- original episode: 8 Ways To Improve Your Outbound Sales
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 12:41
- transcript: Machine transcription · 2825 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.**

why listen: Eight tactics in 12 minutes — dense, but every one is an action you can take immediately. For founders whose outbound reply rate is stuck in the single digits and who don't know what to change.

### points

[0:00] **Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation** — The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So the advice is to do at least a hundred outbound attempts by hand before automating, and genuinely by hand: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework you do yourself is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

[1:04] **Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy** — Founders often spend hours rewriting email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or even carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling an infrastructure product should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — hundreds of emails sent, and of course no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

[2:06] **Work backward from closed customers to the target title** — How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who drove the last deal to close, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer might get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

[3:09] **List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies** — Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like matches but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a bunch of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether they're really your customer. After doing enough outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great thing to watch, because they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, a company under 100 people probably hasn't introduced job levels yet, and one over 500 has probably already set its salary bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

[4:09] **Shake the tree of your personal network for your first customers** — When closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: your personal network first, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

[5:10] **Executives don't care about your product features** — The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things keeping your buyer up at night: what could get him fired, what could get him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When buyers read the email and think ‘this is exactly my problem’, they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't yet fully understand or trust your solution. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is how to hit the quarterly target. Keep the product description to one sentence if you can, and save the details for the first call.

[6:14] **A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch** — The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, it uses no jargon, it doesn't try to look impressive, it reads like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first sentence — ‘I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers.’ The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see whether AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their website, which makes it feel personalized; and the whole thing barely explains how the product works — it only talks about how to help the other person solve their problem.

[8:20] **On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the top predictor** — If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into an ad for your company, stating clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite the one-line headline and the about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut the irrelevant — if the about section is full of hobbies and interests, it's harder for buyers to see how you can help them. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared connections is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so accumulate relevant mutual connections targeted at your audience — that takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

[9:22] **When reply rates are low, debug in this six-step order** — Reply rates may be very low at first, and that's fine — as long as a few replies come in, you have a baseline to iterate on: 2 to 3 replies out of 100 emails is a great starting point. The debugging order is: first, confirm you're contacting the right people; second, confirm you're contacting the right companies; third, confirm the subject line is good; then, and only then, actually start looking at the copy; after that, look at your materials, like whether your website and LinkedIn profile look decent; and only last, look at deliverability. If all six of these are reasonable and you still get zero replies, that often may point to a deeper product-market fit problem.

[10:25] **Follow up until they say no, then move like a heat-seeking missile** — Don't send just one email — the other person probably just missed it. Usually follow up two to four times, a few days apart. The last email to a prospect is often a breakup message, along the lines of: since I haven't heard back, it looks like sales tax automation isn't a priority for you right now, just let me know and I'll stop cluttering your inbox. This one often gets a reply, because the pressure on the other person to say ‘no’ is very low. A real ‘no’ is actually useful: a large number of ‘nos’ improves your future targeting. And once you get a reply, move like a heat-seeking missile — nothing should stand between you and getting him on the calendar. Every founder goes through the painful lesson of ‘time kills deals’ at least once.

[11:27] **The best copy comes from customers' own words** — The best feedback on copy always comes from customers — not friends, not advisors, not your co-founder. Two methods: one, on sales calls ask ‘what made you notice my message’ — they'll usually point out which sentences in the email were most interesting, and you should use those sentences in future messages; the question also gets them talking openly about their problem, which is exactly what you want on a first call. Two, ask existing customers how they think about your product, ask what the one thing was that made them decide to buy, and then write future messages in their wording. Customers always write better copy than you do.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] : "The biggest issue with this is if you get zero replies from a campaign that you didn't give any thought to in the first place, then at the end, when you have zero replies, you've learned nothing."

[1:04] : "So my recommendation is to do at least 100 outreaches by hand before you automate anything."

[1:04] : "Outbound prospecting is kind of like looking for a needle in a haystack. You need a person that has the exact pain point that you solve or a perfectly crafted message won't even land."

[5:10] : "The truth is that executives don't care about your product features. They don't care that you have blazing fast uploads. They don't care that your database is built in rust. They're worried about how they're going to hit their quarterly target."

[9:22] : "If you go through all six of these areas and they all seem to be reasonable and you're still getting zero replies, this often might be indicative of a deeper product market fit issue."

[10:25] : "A real no is actually very useful to you. In aggregate, the many no's improve who you target in the future."

### figures

- Recommended number of manual outbound attempts before automating: at least 100 [1:04]
- Recommended email length: 5 to 8 sentences [5:10]
- Recommended LinkedIn message length: 2 to 5 sentences [5:10]
- Amount of body text shown in the Gmail preview: the first 20 to 30 characters [7:16]
- Acceptable starting reply rate: 2 to 3 replies out of 100 emails [9:22]
- Recommended number of follow-ups: 2 to 4, a few days apart [10:25]
- Company-size signal for compensation planning software: crossing the 100-person mark [3:09]

### glossary

- outbound: Proactively emailing or messaging potential customers on LinkedIn, rather than waiting for them to come to you.
- intent signals: Clues that a company may need your product, such as job postings or company growth.
- breakup message: The last email in a follow-up sequence, implying you'll stop bothering them, letting the other person decline with low pressure.
- deliverability: The share of emails that successfully land in the recipient's inbox rather than the spam folder.
- Sales Navigator: LinkedIn's paid lead-search tool, which filters by title, company and more.

who it is for: Early founders whose outbound reply rate is near zero and who can't tell whether to fix the copy or the list; and technical founders doing founder-led sales for the first time.
what to skip: Point 4, LinkedIn profile optimization (7:16-8:20), is basic — skip it.

## World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: World Models, Robotics, and the Future of 3D AI
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 23:30
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5152 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.**

why listen: 23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth hearing for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.

### points

[1:05] (Justin Johnson) **Atlas is a model release, not a product release** — Justin clarifies right at the top: Atlas is not a product, it's World Labs' foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real space, and simulate inside reconstructed space. Generation can start from text or an image, and then you can fly the camera straight through that world; reconstruction can take a single photo, or a hundred-plus, and the more photos the more accurate; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. That ordering itself says World Labs doesn't intend to ship a consumer app first — it wants to stand up a horizontal foundation model first, then let products grow on top of it.

[4:09] (Justin Johnson) **Reference images are pinned into 3D space, not fed to the model** — Video models tend to drift and hallucinate their own direction around the ten-second mark. Justin says Atlas's answer is spatial context: the reference images you give it aren't ordinary images — they're grounded in 3D space, so you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you're not just giving a text prompt either; you're directly operating the camera, telling it to fly this way and that way, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even at a minute of generation, it's not pulling a slot machine — you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

[7:10] (Justin Johnson) **Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier** — Compared with Marble, World Labs' first product, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splat at the center: video, 3D scenes, and meshes all had to pass through a Gaussian representation before being rendered back to image or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. Generating 2D or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a Gaussian scene — the model emits 2D pixels directly; only in applications where you genuinely need 3D does it get lifted to 3D.

[8:10] (Justin Johnson) **Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory** — Justin doesn't think Gaussian has been outgrown — it's a tool, and you use it in the right place. VFX's final product is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we're not there yet, and it would be expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh remains useful. Its other role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines built on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it's better to bring AI into their workflow.

[11:13] (Justin Johnson) **Simulation covers the last stretch of robot training** — On the value of real to sim for robots, Justin says it's first of all evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, with a specific machine, in a specific environment, and you have to make sure it works in exactly that environment. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. That gives you a path different from ‘collect a lot of demonstrations or teleoperate by hand’. He also describes a more aggressive version: take a few photos or casual videos with your phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, and let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, yielding a robot adapted to that space within minutes.

[14:16] (Justin Johnson) **OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma** — The host asks why OpenAI turned that Sora direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now isn't doing world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers one explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you're holding something as strong as the LLM, and you're leading in that direction, so investing in the next thing isn't necessarily worth it. World Labs' judgment is that there's another class of model here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones who seize it.

[18:21] (Justin Johnson) **Three iPhones shooting bullet time came out far better than expected** — Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. What genuinely surprised him was bullet time: three iPhones on tripods doing synchronized capture, then using Atlas for a frozen-frame, orbit-around reframe. He cites the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, time frozen at the instant the milk splashes up, flying a full circle around it, and the result is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. That shows Atlas's value isn't only in ‘generating new worlds’ — it's also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

[19:21] (Justin Johnson) **3D is underrated on the input side** — Justin says 3D has value in two places. On the output side people have already talked it to death — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to drop into a workflow or game engine. But 3D's value on the input side is underrated: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, giving the model a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text — you want to grab the camera directly and have it zoom exactly the way you want, which text simply cannot describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type: one of the modalities in the multimodal mix is the camera.

### verbatim quotes

[3:07] Justin Johnson: "language models are these general horizontal engines for processing streams of discrete tax, discrete tokens. Those have had tons of applications from everything that we know and love today. And our thesis is that there exists another category of model called world models that should be based in visual understanding, should be based in physical understanding that can be used to generate, simulate, reconstruct worlds."

[4:09] Justin Johnson: "when you give Atlas reference images, they aren't just images. They're actually grounded in 3D space. So you can stage those images in 3D and say, this reference image should be here."

[5:09] Justin Johnson: "So the idea here is that even as you go to really long generations, it's not a slot machine. You're generating and directing and really controlling what the model outputs."

[7:10] Justin Johnson: "Marble really put Gaussian splats really at the center of many things that it did. So Marble could output videos, Marble could output 3D scenes, Marble could output meshes, but everything was kind of bottlenecking through a 3D Gaussian splat representation."

[14:16] Justin Johnson: "I think there is maybe a sense of a bit of innovators dilemma, right? Like you're sitting on LLMs and you've got this as a really powerful thing and you're, you're leading the pack there. It doesn't necessarily make sense to try to invest in that next thing."

[19:21] Justin Johnson: "I think there's an underappreciated value of 3D on the input side as well. Right. Like even even in a situation like a VFX shot or something like that or the ultimate output is 2D. It's. useful for the model to offer these 3D control surfaces to let the human director figure out what kind of scene the model should output."

[20:21] Justin Johnson: "you can control precisely where does the camera move because I don't just want to write in text like pan in, pan out, truck left. I want to be able to grab the camera and make it zoom exactly as I like. And there's really no way to describe that explicitly in text."

### figures

- Number of input photos Atlas needs for reconstruction: As few as 1, as many as 100+ [2:06]
- Example Atlas generated video length: Up to about 1 minute [4:09]
- Input viewpoints needed for bullet time: 3 [18:21]

### glossary

- world model: A horizontal foundation model built on visual and physical understanding that can generate, simulate, and reconstruct worlds.
- Gaussian splat: An explicit 3D representation that reconstructs a scene from a large number of Gaussian points, convenient for client-side rendering.
- real to sim: Reconstructing a 3D space from real photos or video, then running robot simulation inside it.
- bullet time: A shot effect that freezes an instant and flies around the scene, traditionally requiring a camera array.
- SFT: Supervised fine-tuning of a pretrained model on labeled data; Justin says the Newtonian physics problem is probably solved with about one SFT.

who it is for: Engineers and founders working on 3D generation, VFX, game engines, and robot simulation, plus investors who want to understand the split between world models and video models.
what to skip: The opening 0:00-1:05 is show promos and guest intro — skippable.
tags: World Models, 3D Generation, Robot Simulation, VFX, Atlas

## Making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
- show: This Week in Virology (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/twiv/)
- original episode: TWiV 1357: Furin, Naturally with Paul Bieinasz
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 1:44:36
- transcript: YouTube captions · 15146 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand carry an insertion, and a furin site has been hit independently at least three times at the same position — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.**

why listen: The first half is the quantitative methodology of recombination and insertions; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump to 52 minutes.

### points

[6:07] (Paul Bieniasz) **They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up** — The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted GFP, so infection with either alone yields only fragments, but co-infection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that once double-stranded RNA forms, strand-transfer events during recombination become more likely because the duplex ‘breathes’. This counterintuitive result became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

[11:12] (Paul Bieniasz) **Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves** — Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and then deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them both count event frequencies and pick out green viruses to sequence back and infer the mechanism. This is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

[13:15] (Paul Bieniasz) **Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down, not up** — The original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that NSP15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — when you think nuclease, you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pull GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time — it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research.

[22:26] (Paul Bieniasz) **Every base sequenced a million times before you talk frequency** — They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrate about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, load part of it onto a sequencing chip, and produce hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is read at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when there are only a thousand virions in the tube is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample.

[27:32] (Paul Bieniasz) **Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for calling an origin** — Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch matches the viral genome perfectly, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus carried 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them from the positive strand.

[36:41] (Paul Bieniasz) **Insertions aren't rare events — they're a few per thousand** — Vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this is happening all the time. Paul responds that ‘rare’ is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. The insertion frequency they give is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion out of a thousand virions. That frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multiplicity of infection, so you can't isolate them.

[55:05] (Paul Bieniasz) **Making a furin site isn't hard at all** — Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus the right other amino acids. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, so multiplying the two fractions, about 1% of random 12-base sequences will encode an RXR motif. There are roughly 30,000 different positions in a coronavirus genome where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

[57:08] (Paul Bieniasz) **Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times** — Put the insertion frequency, the number of insertable sites, and the viral population size together, and the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one particular position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing — and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measures. In their deep-sequencing data, which does not cover the whole population, they have already found new furin cleavage sites independently at least three times at the exact position of SARS-CoV-2's existing furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they only did PCR focused on the spike region, and they required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some real natural sites.

[1:07:21] (Paul Bieniasz) **Every dominant variant began as a single RNA molecule** — Every dominant variant — Delta, Omicron, and the rest — and nearly every sequence in the world, started out as a single RNA molecule in someone's lung at some point in time. A single event, however improbable, is enough to set off a global transmission chain. So arguments based on ‘this is extremely unlikely to happen’ don't hold up — everything that happens in biology is extremely rare. Paul also points out that the furin cleavage site is not always advantageous for SARS-CoV-2; in many cell-culture experiments the virus is selected to lose the site, and the stability versus fusogenicity of the spike trimer is very likely a knife's-edge balance.

[1:11:24] (Paul Bieniasz) **A mouse gene sequence spells out SARS ass** — Harrison and Saxs's PNAS paper arguing for a laboratory origin of SARS-CoV-2 listed the furin cleavage site of the epithelial sodium channel studied at UNC as a possible insertion candidate. But the amino acid sequence of that mouse epithelial sodium channel furin site spells out exactly ‘SARS ass’. Paul says they glossed over the fact that half of that candidate sequence already exists in other sarbecoviruses.

## Rome Won With a Crow: The Key to the First Punic War

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
- show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- original episode: The First Punic War
- published: 2026-09-13 · duration: 1:01:23
- transcript: Machine transcription · 10216 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.**

why listen: This episode tells the First Punic War as a war story with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

### points

[2:03] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **This was not a war between two equal powers** — The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean,’ and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak, Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage into a power capable of fighting Rome as an equal was this war itself. So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability,’ is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

[15:29] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **Mercenaries at Messana dragged both powers into war** — The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a group of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted first from its base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome followed — and not with a small intervention, but a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

[28:14] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **The corvus turned sea battles into land battles** — Carthage was the naval power: better oarsmen, ships built fast and well — the Romans even built their warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow,’ a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae, the Carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and took heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treat it as decisive. At the Battle of Cape Ecnomus, the corvus is again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

[38:40] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army** — After the Roman landing in Africa, Rome advanced steadily and Carthage looked finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and to bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat of the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

[43:11] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace** — Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate, Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was within reach. By agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrifying versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome fought on. This passage is a textbook moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

[46:27] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **The sacred chickens would not eat, and Rome's fleet was finished** — In 249 BC, the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher took his fleet to fight Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for the battle to proceed; if not, it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, so he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, then let them drink. Roman sources record this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start emphasising a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. This defeat kept Rome from sending out a fleet for eight years.

[50:48] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **Hannibal's father held Rome down with guerrilla war** — After Drepana, Rome vanished from the sea and Carthage gained freedom of action on the western coast. In 247 BC, Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father. He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and waged guerrilla war against Rome, occupying the high ground above Drepana and Panormus, with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that Carthage's army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, dedicated to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and both sides fought fiercely over this sacred site.

[57:20] (Dr. Eve MacDonald) **The rams from this war still lie on the seabed** — The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet heavy with supplies meant for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you climb Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. More remarkably, the site of this sea battle has been preserved underwater: over the past twenty years, underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.
