## Bunsen Burners Don't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
- show: This Week in Microbiology (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/thisweekinmicr/)
- original episode: 363: Why Vegetables Are Good for Your Heart
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 58:04
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7308 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.**

why listen: The first half has a clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to those willing to chew through mechanism.

### points

[6:05] (Michael Schmidt) **Bunsen burners don't reduce plate contamination** — The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contaminated airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors don't say the burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta, then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

[10:13] (Michael Schmidt) **83 CFU per minute is the crossover point** — Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/minute, settle plates next to the burner tended to show less deposition; below that level, deposition tended to increase. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find it useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

[13:43] (Michael Schmidt) **Airflow isn't one-dimensional — don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood** — The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must draw replacement air from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner in a laminar flow hood, and the flame itself disrupts laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than fluid dynamics directly, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

[17:49] (Michael Schmidt) **Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual** — The authors draw a historical comparison with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there's no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode: changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives people a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there's no evidence it actually does anything. The authors don't argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

[28:14] (Vincent Racaniello) **Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway** — This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, is turned by microbes into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefit of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mainly mediated by microbially generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently believe in. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

[31:32] (Vincent Racaniello) **No DNIC found in germ-free mice** — They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissues. Signals were visible in the liver and kidneys of healthy mice, but when the same detection was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC could be found in the tissue — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can make DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

[39:55] (Vincent Racaniello) **DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO** — They used isolated mouse aortic rings, pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO, one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same goes for bacterially generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a mutant lacking nitrate reductase did not.

[47:16] (Vincent Racaniello) **DNIC suppresses leucine uptake, holding down mTORC1** — On the metabolic line, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

### figures

- Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab: 40%-60% [11:23]

### glossary

- settle plate: An agar plate with the lid removed, letting airborne particles settle naturally onto the surface.
- DNIC: Dinitrosyl iron compound, an iron carrying two nitrosyls and two thiol ligands.
- EPR: Electron paramagnetic resonance, a method for detecting molecules with unpaired electrons; DNIC has a characteristic signal.
- sGC: Soluble guanylate cyclase, the main nitric oxide receptor in the cardiovascular system, converting GTP to cGMP.
- mTORC1: Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1, the master switch integrating nutrient and energy signals in the cell to promote anabolism.

## Private credit's risk hides in insurance company ratings

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
- show: Excess Returns (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/excessreturns/)
- original episode: We Asked Fidelity's Ex-President What Made Peter Lynch Great — and Where Private Credit Risk Hides
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 1:00:48
- transcript: YouTube captions · 8582 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.**

why listen: The first half is industry lore; the real value is in the middle and back sections — the specific mechanics and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, and Social Security reform.

### points

[5:08] (Bob Posen) **A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks** — When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build internal consensus first — if you run a stock fund, you must keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's stated positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks "now is not a good time to buy stocks." That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

[8:12] (Bob Posen) **After doubling in size, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams** — Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international and so on — giving each group a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds in New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

[19:21] (Bob Posen) **Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first** — Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when hit by a medical emergency or when they reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity should only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the order of magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

[21:25] (Bob Posen) **The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole** — Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer immediately mark that investment up to par on its books even though it bought at, say, a 5% discount. He believes this rule must be changed. Valuation is already hard enough; this "instant markup" should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through to holders via NAV.

[24:28] (Bob Posen) **Private ratings systematically overstate private credit** — The private credit held by insurance companies, depending on how you count, can reach as much as $2 trillion, and a large share of it is "affiliated investments" — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then placed debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

[29:35] (Bob Posen) **Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call** — Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what was a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to your own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds such as Apollo and KKR have all found insurance companies to be handy investment vehicles.

[41:52] (Bob Posen) **Someone with $1 million investable should not hold 40% bonds** — Posen points out that most target-date funds arrive at retirement at 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks, which is reasonable for people who must live off their retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million Americans have investable assets (excluding their primary residence) of over $1 million; they do not live off investment income and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over 30 years, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — the equivalent of $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds acted as a hedge in only 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall deeply, but look at two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and surpassed.

[50:09] (Bob Posen) **Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings** — Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and a company's own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; moreover, the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: full 10-Qs and 10-Ks at mid-year and year-end, and a slimmed-down report in the first and third quarters — three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet, not a heavy burden. He rebuts the claim that "less reporting encourages long-termism": when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the firms that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

### glossary

- private credit: Debt that is not publicly traded and is lent directly by private firms, with poor liquidity and hard-to-value positions.
- affiliated investments: Debt held by an insurance company that is related to its parent or an affiliated party.
- rating shopping: An issuer picking, among several rating agencies, the one that gives the highest rating.
- auto-IRA: A retirement savings plan set up by a state government, with employers only handling payroll connection, that employees can opt out of.
- reversion to the mean: The tendency of extreme performance to swing back toward the long-run average.

## Humans Have Fought Bad Smells for Millennia; Perfume Began as Smoke Burned for the Gods

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
- show: ExtraCredits (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/extracredits/)
- original episode: The History of Perfume: Mankind's Millennia Long Battle Against Stank
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 16:29
- transcript: YouTube captions · 2855 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Perfume did not begin as luxury or pleasure, but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they walled themselves in with scent.**

why listen: Medium information density, but it strings together perfume's religious origins, the plague and the decline of bathing, and the transformation of Grasse in France into one line — suited to anyone interested in the history of the senses and the history of consumption.

### points

[0:02] **Ambergris comes from a battle inside a whale** — The episode opens with a very concrete image to explain where ambergris comes from: a sperm whale swallows a giant squid, the squid's hard beak lodges in the whale's intestine, gets coated in a mysterious bile secretion and expelled, then drifts in ocean currents for decades before washing ashore. Apothecaries buy it by gold weight, grind it into a fixative, and use it to control how fast a scent evaporates, so the fragrance shifts slowly over a whole day. The image shows how absurdly long the raw-material chain of perfume can be — behind one scent is a deep-sea struggle and decades of drifting on the currents.

[2:04] **Smell is the most emotional sense** — The episode offers a judgment: by some measures, smell is the most emotional sense, because it connects directly to the brain's memory center. Research shows that recalling a smell evokes memory more strongly than visualizing one. Host Rob says his earliest memory is grabbing the rope seat of a lounge chair on Oahu's North Shore while learning to walk — what he remembers is not the image but the smell of that old rope fiber soaked in sea-salt air. The other host's earliest olfactory memory is the old 1980s-formula Trix cereal. Smell can offend, can give pleasure, can summon the past like a ghost, and is essentially untouchable, changeable, and fleeting.

[3:04] **The earliest perfume was smoke burned for the gods** — Ancient perfume's origins were mainly religious, and it was not today's distilled liquid — the earliest was basically smoke produced by burning. Egyptian priests burned specific woods, plants, and resins to make pleasing smoke that both purified the ritual space and served as a channel connecting to the gods. The word perfume comes from the Latin perfumum, meaning "through smoke." In China, Southeast Asia, and Native American communities alike, these fragrances were believed to be vehicles for communicating with deities, carrying prayers and pleas up to heaven or the spirit world. In Asia this developed into an incense-making tradition that largely replaced personal perfume until modern times, because the scent stayed in clothing and rooms.

[7:07] **Ibn Sina invented steam distillation** — In the 11th century the Arab scholar Ibn Sina discovered steam distillation: boiling a solid substance in water, collecting the steam, and separating the oil or essence from it. The first things extracted this way were rose water and rose oil, still a mainstay of cosmetic perfume today. Like many chemical, scientific, and mathematical concepts, the method passed in the Middle Ages from Arab to European scholars, and then to Italy, which became Europe's center of perfume manufacturing throughout the Renaissance. The people making perfume then were often alchemists and apothecaries, and the perfumes they made were both drunk as medicine and worn on the body.

[8:08] **Scent was treated as an airborne barrier against disease** — Before germ theory, European medical thought rested on miasma theory: foul or bad-smelling air was the main route by which disease spread. In an age without science this was not absurd, because rotting flesh, industrial burning, and contaminated water really did make people sick. So Europeans concluded that inhaling sweet or pleasant air could ward off disease. The upper classes began using nosegays (a small bunch of dried flowers or herbs, held up to the nose when passing bad smells), gentleman's canes topped with containers of aromatic substances, and perfumes worn, drunk, or used to fumigate clothing as protection. Most famous is the plague doctor's mask, its hooked bird beak stuffed with flowers, spices, and herbs.

[9:08] **The Black Death killed the public bathhouse** — The Black Death may be the single biggest factor in Europe's adoption of perfume. The plague that swept Europe for three centuries killed off the public bathhouses left over from the Roman Empire, because people believed water was a vehicle of infection. Moral norms then shifted, religious concern about public nudity grew, and bathhouses came to be seen as places for trysts or sex work. People switched to cleaning their hands and faces with damp cloths, and soaking baths became increasingly rare. They began wearing more underclothes to absorb sweat and odor so the garments could be changed and washed. In this environment, not just the upper class but the emerging middle class relied more on perfume, often making it at home from rosemary in the garden or alcohol plus purchased ingredients.

[10:09] **Perfumed gloves set off a political scandal** — In the 16th century people usually scented their clothes rather than their bodies, and perfumed gloves, handkerchiefs, and fans were especially popular. The French queen Catherine de Medici brought Italian perfumery traditions to the French court and hired the Italian perfumer Renato Bianco (Master Rene) to blend exclusive scents for her. Legend has it that Master Rene had a secret tunnel connecting his residence to Catherine's bedroom, and that he also served as her poisoner. When Catherine's rival Jeanne III of Navarre died after receiving a pair of perfumed gloves as a gift from Catherine, rumors spread that the gloves had been soaked in poison. Whether the poisoned gloves were real or not, several deaths were reportedly attributed to them, to the point that William Cecil advised the perfume-loving Elizabeth I to refuse any gift of scented clothing.

[12:09] **Grasse shifted from leather tanning to perfume** — Catherine de Medici's passion for perfume changed the industry forever. The French city of Grasse realized the flower fields around it made it an ideal place for fragrance manufacturing, and with Catherine's support shifted its economic base from leather tanning to perfume making; the city, and the country as a whole, remains the center of world perfume manufacturing to this day. France began to dominate the spice trade, and the French empire could bring in novel, far-flung ingredients from the Caribbean, Indonesia, India, and China. French perfumers also created the language we use to describe perfume, and the three stages of a scent's evolution: top notes or head notes smelled in the first few minutes, middle notes that can last for hours, and base notes smelled in the evening or the next day. This evolution comes from fixatives controlling evaporation speed, such as ambergris or alcohol, revealing layers of fragrance over time.

[13:10] **We use more fragrance products than at any point in history** — By the time of Louis XV, the French court was called the "perfumed court," and nobles competed to wear rare exotic scents like chocolate and jasmine. Visitors were sprayed with perfume before entering, and there was even a perfume fountain. The Revolution did not change the elite's love of fragrance either: Napoleon ordered enormous quantities of eau de cologne, and his wife Josephine consumed just as much. In the 19th century the spread of scented soap meant making perfume was no longer mainly about masking odor but became more a part of the cleaning process. Scientific progress also brought scented and unscented antiperspirants, and the ability to bathe in hot water every day. But the episode offers a counterintuitive conclusion: even though humans as a whole are cleaner than ever before, we actually use more fragrance products than at any point in history.

### verbatim quotes

[3:04] : "Actually, the word perfume comes from this practice since it comes from the Latin perfumum or from smoke."

[8:08] : "Therefore, they concluded you could ward off disease by inhaling sweet or good-smelling air."

[9:08] : "In fact, the Black Death was probably the single greatest factor in European adoption of perfume because while people did try to use aromatics as protective medicine, the wave of plague which swept Europe for three centuries also killed off the communal bathhouses which still existed as a legacy of the Roman Empire."

[12:09] : "So with Catherine's support, it switched its economic base from leather tanning to perfumery and the city specifically, as well as the wider country, remains the center of world perfume manufacture to this day."

[13:10] : "But yet, even though we humans as a whole are living cleaner than we ever have, we actually use more scented products than ever before in history."

### figures

- Age of Assyrian cuneiform tablets: 3200 years ago [5:06]

### glossary

- miasma theory: The pre-germ-theory European medical belief that foul, bad-smelling air spreads disease.
- ambergris: A waxy substance formed from secretions in the sperm whale's intestine, used as a perfume fixative.
- nosegay: A small bunch of dried flowers or herbs, held up to the nose when passing bad smells.
- fixative: A substance that controls how fast a scent evaporates, letting the fragrance unfold in layers over time.

## Astra Crosses the AGI Threshold, but No One Can Audit It

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
- show: The Cognitive Revolution (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cogrev/)
- original episode: AI:AM Highlights: Astra as AGI, OpenAI's Pause, Mythos @ Mozilla & Human Agency vs Technocapitalism
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 1:42:06
- transcript: Official transcript page · 17603 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.**

why listen: The two hosts chain together the evidence for Astra's capabilities, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why auditing can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge by shorting — high information density.

### points

[3:30] (Nathan Labenz) **Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file** — In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can also search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight but genuinely new."

[6:19] (Nathan Labenz) **OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday** — In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," reporting that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

[21:03] (Prakash Narayanan) **External audits are structurally stuck at two or three days** — Prakash breaks down why external auditing can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial regulation remains unsolved to this day.

[31:12] (Nathan Labenz) **What was announced as a pause was only half a pause** — Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was paused first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue category labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the deployed one, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

[39:05] (Prakash Narayanan) **There is no adult in the room to take the blame** — Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — no external savior, the whole world is held together with duct tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, nor the legitimacy needed for execution. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

[46:03] (Prakash Narayanan) **Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor** — Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you would with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first remove the antitrust excuse. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded an exemption from vaccine liability claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retroactive reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree, it doesn't matter, because the only thing that binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

[1:00:40] (Raffi Krikorian) **FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop** — Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims a human in the loop but when it actually hands control to the user it doesn't give enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is completely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team only allows humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single line of which was written by a human — people only write the spec, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

[1:29:15] (Prakash Narayanan) **The takeover is already complete, no one just admits it** — The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market itself is the paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took about a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

### verbatim quotes

[0:08] Prakash Narayanan: "People are gonna use this thing. Token spend is is gonna increase dramatically. I think a lot of people are gonna be using it all the time. It is it is AGI. It is that kind of cleared the hurdle of AGI. It will do things better than most people you can hire and train."

### glossary

- METR: An organization that has long tracked how long a task AI can complete; its hours curve has stopped being updated.
- paper clipper: In the thought experiment, a runaway optimization process that turns all resources into paper clips.
- safe harbor: A legal provision exempting specific conduct from liability, which pharma companies secured in Operation Warp Speed.
- Dyson sphere: A megastructure wrapping a star to capture all its energy; here it refers to an extreme energy-growth target.

## Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
- show: Y Combinator (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ycsp/)
- original episode: Open Models Change The Economics of AI
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 57:15
- transcript: YouTube captions · 12055 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will run through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.**

why listen: The Ollama CEO brings first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look nothing alike, and the real constraint on enterprise purchasing is security, not cost.

### points

[1:03] (Jeffrey Morgan) **The driver behind open models is control, not saving money** — Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is ‘better control over AI and customising it for yourself’. Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once it is solved does customising the model to your own use case come up. The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting lever, you will misread why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European ones, while also evaluating Chinese models.

[4:05] (Jeffrey Morgan) **Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw** — The per-user token usage curve on Ollama's cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax shipped in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, support, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for that explosion.

[8:08] (Jeffrey Morgan) **Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill** — Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work gets crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to make sure it is fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the single biggest day of growth. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer and application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

[14:11] (Jeffrey Morgan) **The new scarcity sits above the token** — Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgement: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers will end up preferring the best standalone product at every layer rather than something bundled together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

[17:14] (Jeffrey Morgan) **Stateful things will not sink down into the model layer** — Asked whether harnesses will be absorbed by models, Jeff's judgement is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge separate problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolchain the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

[18:15] (Jeffrey Morgan) **80% of tokens run open, but only 20% of budget** — Jeff's steady-state judgement: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will run through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget goes to open source. The open community is driving cost extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spend lands on open models. The hardest work stays with the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is done by combining open and closed. He uses a law firm as the analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

[22:19] (Jeffrey Morgan) **Local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all** — On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, hit many hard problems, and lean mainly on large cloud models; end-to-end low-difficulty workflows like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

[29:25] (Jeffrey Morgan) **The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens** — Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually get back to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is exactly the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

[40:30] (Jeffrey Morgan) **Two years without finding the problem is scarier than having no hype** — Jeff says that when he entered YC in 2021, the direction he wrote down was ‘Kitematic for Kubernetes’ or ‘Docker Desktop for Kubernetes’, building security products like SSO for Kubernetes. The company entered YC in 2021, and Ollama did not launch until July 2023 — more than two years in between. He says the scariest thing is not whether there is hype, but that ‘you cannot even see the north star’ — customers are usually a good north star, and not being able to see it is scarier. The team was over 10 people at the time, and he is especially grateful to them for sticking through several pivots.

[42:31] (Jeffrey Morgan) **First version in two weeks, and Llama 2 shipped at exactly the right moment** — The trigger for the pivot was an all-hands discussion in Toronto: what would you build if you started from zero today. They saw two problems — one, build a gateway to access any model (framed at the time as Segment for LLMs, the router idea that came later), and two, they were ex-VMware, ex-Docker people who were good at making things run, so make open models run. They gave themselves two weeks to build the first version, and Llama 2 happened to launch at the end of those two weeks, so they shipped straight away. Jeff calls it bias to action: from idea to launch in two weeks, with more users than all their previous products combined.

[45:34] (Jeffrey Morgan) **Free and runnable anywhere took a hobbyist tool straight into the Fortune 500** — Jeff says what surprised them most was the speed from hobbyists to the Fortune 500. Two reasons: open models are free to start with, and they can run anywhere — which is critical for Fortune 500 IT developer teams, because they do not need to request permission to use them. What is good for hobbyists translated directly into what is good for developers inside enterprises. He draws a database analogy: MongoDB also went from developers to the enterprise, but LLMs are stateless, which makes that transition even easier than it was for databases.

[53:38] (Jeffrey Morgan) **The rules of the infrastructure era do not hold in AI** — Jeff gives two pieces of old muscle memory that have to be broken. One, ‘building a layer on top of someone else is dangerous’ — true in the infrastructure era, not true in the AI era, where moving up the stack can actually be better because you are closer to the customer. Two, the systems world demands that everything run exactly as designed, tested and verified, whereas an LLM by definition does not work that way — that is a feature, not a bug. He also mentions team size: some problems do not need that many people now, such as support pipelines, the way cloud services are delivered, and the fact that ‘no engineer knows how all the code works’.

### glossary

- open weights: Model parameters that can be downloaded and self-hosted, as opposed to closed models offered only via API.
- router: A middle layer that dispatches requests across multiple models by task difficulty and cost.
- MLX: Apple's local inference stack for running large models on a Mac.
- DGX Spark: Nvidia's desktop AI workstation, a device that sits on a desk and can run models from 20 billion to 120 billion parameters.

## One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for Decades

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
- show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- original episode: SYMHC Classics: Flexner Report
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 39:30
- transcript: Official transcript · 6619 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The Flexner Report is usually written as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years no new Black medical school appeared.**

why listen: Medium information density. The first half is a chronological account of Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half, on how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

### points

[6:09] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer** — Abraham Flexner was not part of the medical world. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to look at US and Canadian medical schools with the same critical eye. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording each one's admission requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

[14:23] (Tracy V. Wilson) **Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge** — In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic techniques and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admission standards were equally chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

[18:31] (Tracy V. Wilson) **He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools** — Flexner set standards first and then scored each school against them: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for practical training; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than physicians who practised on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time teachers. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within a decade the number of American medical schools was down to half, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were substantially modernised. In Canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

[23:43] (Tracy V. Wilson) **He never did the arithmetic on Black medical schools' books** — The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven "can make no valuable contribution at this moment", and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and already ran on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools", and said that one of the most important duties of Black people and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four by 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

[25:48] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The next Black medical school had to wait until 1966** — Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school aimed primarily at Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966 and was a response to the Black community's need for access to care; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were excluded from educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's line about "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors were the ones left without them.

[26:51] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project** — One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for this project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There are also unresolved questions — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. His accounts differed at different times: sometimes he said the man went with him, later he changed his story to say they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

[28:53] (Tracy V. Wilson) **Did he know he was restricting Black medicine?** — He knew. The report contains an idealistic passage saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions "shall not directly or indirectly take account of race, religion or sex". One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among their neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have made him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he studied educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

[35:01] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The hygiene line may not have been his own** — The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for judging Flexner a racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's phrasing may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he reached independently. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across racial divisions — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

### glossary

- Flexner Report: The 1910 publication Medical Education in the United States and Canada, which reshaped North American medical education standards.
- AAMC: The Association of American Medical Colleges, founded in 1876 and made up of 22 member schools, which had itself agreed on uniform standards for the medical curriculum.
- The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge: A memorandum Flexner wrote in 1921 for the board of the Rockefeller Foundation, later published as an essay, arguing that the pursuit of pure curiosity yields unexpected uses.

## Change One Law of Physics and Every Wish Backfires

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
- show: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/skeptics/)
- original episode: The Skeptics Guide #1105 - Sep 12 2026
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 1:23:10
- transcript: YouTube captions · 16888 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: change just one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity equals free energy, hyperspace travel equals handing the technology to every alien civilization.**

why listen: The first half is live improv riffing; the second half — the Roman telescope, robot babies, the falling-atom experiment on the Chinese space station, and the Verne details — is denser and worth skipping ahead for.

### points

[2:07] (Steven Novella) **Changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe** — The rule is hard: pick only one, and it has to be practical and feasible within the laws of physics — no perpetual-motion-style having it both ways. Steven starts by handing most science-fiction premises a death sentence — warp drive, shields, phasers, artificial gravity, antigravity — either they violate physics or they fall under non-trivial: theoretically maybe possible, but never going to happen. The real fun of the whole discussion isn't in what you pick, it's in finding the consequences inside each wish that nobody counted.

[8:08] (Jay Novella) **Antigravity means free energy thrown in** — Jay wants antigravity, on the grounds that transportation, construction and materials handling would all change. Bob points out it's a twofer: if you could feasibly turn gravity off, you'd turn it on while the water wheel goes down and off while you haul it back up, and you'd have a perpetual motion machine. Steven, as the buzzkill, patches it by force: the energy it costs to turn gravity off has to equal the energy you get out of it — no free lunch. The argument also incidentally kills science-fiction movies — single-stage-to-orbit is simply impossible in a 1g gravity well, and every shot of a ship reaching orbit in a minute is lying, because it assumes antigravity exists.

[10:08] (Bob Novella) **Hyperspace travel hands the technology to every alien civilization** — Bob picks entering subspace/hyperspace: run ordinary engines over there, come out having crossed a far greater distance — essentially practical FTL. He argues there's no downside risk, because hyperspace is separate from real space and doesn't affect our universe. Steven and Jay immediately push back: changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe, not just for you, and hostile civilizations could use it to colonize Earth just as well. Bob's answer is to hide — human radio signals dilute into noise a few light-years out, so in principle nobody could work backward to the conclusion that Earth has life. Jay offers a compromise, jump gates: both ends have to be built, so expansion can only be slow, and not every alien comes knocking.

[23:16] (Bob Novella) **Zero-point energy is too thin, and forcing it triggers a big rip** — Steven's second choice is free energy, specifically zero-point energy. Bob gives the objection: zero-point energy is observationally extremely thin, and lighting a single bulb might take several cubic light-years of space; and if you really injected that much energy into space, cosmic expansion would run away into a big rip that destroys all life. Steven's response is that this is exactly why these aren't laws of physics — every wish, once it actually lands, brings catastrophic consequences, so the fun of the thought experiment is finding the loophole that dismantles the wish. Julia adds her astrophysics-major perspective: if gravity had a knob, 90% of the observations used to infer stellar phenomena from gravity would all be wrecked.

[36:19] **Even a bucket of water can compute like a neural network** — The core of physical reservoir computing: any nonlinear system — a bucket of swirling water, time-varying mayonnaise — as long as you measure the right spot, its nonlinear interactions can be mapped onto an artificial neural network and made to ‘think’ for you. Someone gave a talk saying, ‘We got mayonnaise to think very slowly.’ Once that analogy holds, scale becomes a variable: if you had a nonlinear system the size of a nebula, you feed it input and measure output at the right point, and it can do the computation for you. The speaker himself admits this is a ‘wild idea’, but stresses that once you shrink physical constants down to something tiny, a pile of strange corollaries pops out.

[44:29] **Roman is a thousand times faster than Hubble, but cast as a supporting player** — The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a wide-field infrared telescope with a 3.4-meter primary mirror, the same size as Hubble, but its design goal isn't ‘better than existing telescopes’ — it's complementary: James Webb excels at deep space, Hubble at staring at specific objects, Roman at taking in a huge swath of sky at once. It can survey a thousand times faster than Hubble, covering in its five-year mission the sky area Hubble would take a thousand years to cover. Once it finds something interesting, you turn Webb and Hubble onto it for a closer look. It will also build a three-dimensional map of the universe and carries a coronagraph to block starlight glare and directly image exoplanets — able to find smaller planets farther from their host stars, correcting the transit method's and radial velocity method's bias toward ‘hot Jupiters’.

[55:41] **A robot baby kicks its legs and kicks up explore versus exploit** — The University of Hamburg and Czech Technical University did a ‘robot in a crib’: a baby robot, iCub, placed in a crib with a mobile hanging overhead carrying QR codes, one leg tied to it by a string, and their own deep learning algorithm run to predict the mobile's motion. The result was that the algorithm spontaneously produced the explore versus exploit trade-off — both curious exploration and exploitation of the causality already learned. The researchers treat it as a platform: you can't change a baby's learning algorithm, but you can swap algorithms in a robot, so you can test different versions of contingent learning theory. By contrast, the mainstream of current robot control is deep reinforcement learning: put thousands of copies of the robot in simulation, train with a reward function, then transfer once to the real machine — that's ‘do this and something good happens’, not ‘this causes that’.

[1:04:44] **The Chinese space station redid the Leaning Tower experiment with rubidium atoms** — On the Chinese space station, researchers redid Galileo's falling-body experiment with two clouds of rubidium atoms of different isotopes, one heavier than the other. The free-fall time was about 10 to 12 seconds, far longer than ground experiments, and averaged over many repetitions, the result was that the two clouds fell at rates identical to five parts in ten million. What this verifies is that gravitational mass and inertial mass are exactly the same — in Newtonian mechanics mass shows up in two ways, and in free fall the two effects cancel precisely. What Einstein asked was precisely: why must they be the same? There's no reason they must be. From that comes his thought experiment: in free fall gravity seems to vanish and you're in an inertial reference frame; and in an accelerating elevator light bends, so if gravity and acceleration are equivalent, gravity should bend light too.

### glossary

- physical reservoir computing: Treating any nonlinear physical system as a neural network and reading off its computational capacity.
- island of stability: A predicted region in nuclear physics where superheavy elements might be stable.
- coronagraph: An instrument that blocks a star's glare to directly image the planets around it.
- contingent learning: The way infants learn by kicking a leg to establish a causal link with a moving object.
- big rip: The hypothesis that dark energy makes cosmic expansion run away and eventually tears apart all structure.

## German Cars Lost to Chinese EVs, and AfD's Rise Is Just a Symptom

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-goodfight-德国车败给中国电动车-afd-崛起只是症状/
- show: The Good Fight (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/goodfight/)
- original episode: Judith Dada on the Rise of the AfD
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: —
- transcript: Official full text · 10272 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**AfD is not a German problem but a Western one: people feel tomorrow won't be better, and the simultaneous loss of competitiveness in Germany's proudest industries — cars, chemicals, rail — is the real fuel for the far right.**

why listen: The first half covers AfD and German social mood; the second half is the substance: the AI value chain, the 80/20 intelligence split, and Europe's real gap being a lack of people who can make the call.

### points

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **AfD is not a German disease, it's a Western disease** — Judith Dada argues AfD's rise is not a German phenomenon: the US, France, the Netherlands and the UK all show the same tendency — people feel left behind, feel tomorrow won't be better than today or yesterday, and feel a melancholy for ‘the slower world of the past, where their value in their environment was clearer’. She stresses at the same time that AfD is ‘the ugliest expression’ of this problem — among all far-right parties in Europe it is one of the most extreme, in some respects with regrettable similarities to Nazism. But she refuses to treat it as a fringe right-wing problem: in Saxony-Anhalt more than four in ten people voted for it, which shows the problem is societal and needs drastic political change, plus a vision of the future that can bring people along.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **The neighbour who votes AfD is actually very friendly** — Dada lives on the island of Rügen in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and in daily life she has not encountered xenophobia; her neighbours are very friendly to her, her husband, her children and her darker-skinned Nigerian father. But she notices her own fear growing: last weekend her father visited and the two walked around Stralsund, the streets full of AfD campaign posters, the occasional German flag hung in front of an apartment block or a parking lot, and she felt a kind of nausea, wondering ‘whether my father, whether I, am seen as not belonging here, as unwelcome’. She says if she saw a French flag in France she would not feel the same unease; but seeing a German flag in the country where she was born, she asks: is this because they love Germany, or because they are far right.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **Germany's last shred of face has been taken too** — Dada says the German model ‘very clearly no longer works’: the economy has long been in stagflation, pillar industries like cars and chemicals have lost competitiveness because of high energy costs, and large numbers of jobs have been cut or moved away. She takes German cars as an example: Germany completely misjudged the relevance of electrification and underestimated Chinese automakers' ability to catch up — it used to be assumed Chinese brands could never have the same prestige as German brands, but now go to markets like South Africa, where German cars once sold at a premium, and you see BYD and a crowd of Chinese brands pouring in, and people no longer care whether it's a BMW or a Mercedes. She says the last remnant of German pride — ‘nobody in China can build a high-end car brand’ — has now been taken away too.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **America's non-tech sectors are just as sick as Germany's** — Dada offers a comparison: the US has 150 companies with software revenue above a billion dollars, Europe has only about 30. The Mag 7 together are worth almost half of total global market cap, and economic growth is extremely concentrated in the single sector of tech. But she points out this is not just a European or German problem, it's a technology problem: America's existing non-tech industries are suffering exactly the same malaise as German and European industry, US economic growth is broadly driven by capex going into data centres, by the tech and AI boom, while non-tech sectors grow at the same rate as mature German and European industry. She stresses, however, that this does not remove a fact: in industries dense with technology and R&D innovation, Europe simply does not have as strong an industry as the US.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **Europe is absent from every layer of the AI value chain** — Dada breaks the AI value stack into three layers: the chip and infrastructure layer (chips, and the data centres that host them and turn them into training and inference compute); the model layer (the models that actually produce intelligence); and the application layer (using that intelligence to build concrete applications that bring value to people's lives). She says Europe plays too small a role at every layer, and the further down the stack you go, the starker the gap. She argues that without a structural answer to ‘what is American tech, what is Chinese tech’, no amount of transformation effort in Europe will solve this root cause — every other problem compounds and grows out of this root cause.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **80% of the economy doesn't need the strongest model** — Dada offers a ‘vibes-based number’: of the total value AI creates, 80% does not depend on the strongest Pareto-frontier model; many more efficient, cheaper, possibly open-source models can do the economically valuable work as long as they fall within the intelligence distribution the task requires. Her company is heavily betting on this direction, namely ‘model routing’ — you don't care whether it's model A, B or C, you only care whether at a given moment it is the cheapest, lowest-latency optimal intelligence. The remaining 20% she admits she finds hard to price: that is where frontier intelligence matters, such as drug discovery, adversarial markets like cybersecurity (there is always a better hacker, so you always want the strongest intelligence to attack or defend), hedge funds, critical infrastructure protection. She uses Einstein as an analogy: give a hedge fund a thousand Einsteins and its success rate rises sharply; give Coca-Cola a thousand Einsteins and it won't make it more successful, because that is brand, a century-old formula, distribution and a physical business.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **To build frontier yourself, it has to be a Manhattan Project** — Dada argues that for the 80%, Europe can get by with the existing model landscape, using Chinese models, American models; but for the 20% it is ‘absolutely critical’ — you cannot honestly tell a European that in ten years you can defend their life and secure their access to the modern medicine of that time if you have not secured access to frontier intelligence. There are only two ways to get access: produce it yourself, or trade for access. If you produce it yourself, being third or fourth is not enough, being ‘DeepSeek minus twelve months’ is not enough, it must be a Manhattan-style effort, extremely ambitious, extremely well funded. She admits Europe is already late on the recursive self-improvement loop, but ‘it's not over until it's over’, and even at the last metre of a marathon she will try not to come last. At the same time she says that even if Europe mobilises capital and talent, success is not guaranteed, so it must plan for failure.

[0:00] (Judith Dada) **What Europe lacks isn't money, it's people who can make the call** — Dada thinks the capital problem is real, but it is not that ‘Europe has no money’ — Europe has pension funds, insurance companies with huge balance sheets, and the European economy is about two-thirds the size of the US. The real problem is a structural lack of the kind of few players the US has: AWS, Google, Microsoft, xAI and OpenAI can coordinate at extremely low cost, xAI can just call OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft. Europe has national borders, different regulations, fragmented capital, far higher coordination costs, and not even a unified financial market. Her solution is not to wait for 27 member states but a ‘coalition of the willing’: the largest few companies plus the largest few governments, together pushing pension and insurance money to allocate more to venture capital. She thinks Europe's biggest structural gap is the lack of an Elon Musk figure — someone with enough influence, power and orchestration ability to put all the pieces together, lock people in a room for three days and get the deal done, Manhattan-style.

### glossary

- model routing: Not being tied to a single model, dynamically choosing the most suitable model for a task based on price, latency and capability.
- Pareto-frontier model: The most capable model at the very frontier of the capability-versus-cost trade-off curve.
- Migrationshintergrund: Official German term meaning a person or their parents have foreign ancestry; Mounk calls it his least favourite German word.
- Aktienrente: A pension reform under discussion in Germany that would be supported by returns from capital-market investment.
- tech-brosphere: A pejorative European media term for the Silicon Valley tech scene and its discourse, used to discredit it wholesale.
