## Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but a Loop Only Climbs to the Local Optimum

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: Why Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops | Anish Acharya on Lenny’s Podcast
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 1:18:04
- transcript: Machine transcription · 16474 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 9 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will carry you up to the local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.**

why listen: Anish strings agent deployment, model pricing and the consumer AI bottleneck into one line, and the second half — on moats and product problems — is worth more than the first.

### points

[0:00] (Anish Acharya) **Nobody funds an idea that is too small anymore** — Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would not invest; today it is the reverse — ideas that are too small, too local, they do not want to touch. The reason is that model capability has torn down the threshold of ‘can it be done’, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, the scale of what you want to do can be amplified too.

[6:10] (Anish Acharya) **It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic** — Anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people in the labs who understand it best do not say RSI (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own process, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow, and when he went back to his hometown he found people's lives had barely changed; second, many problems are simply not intelligence bound — give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs and it still will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush everything.

[8:16] (Anish Acharya) **Using AI and reorganizing around AI are two different things** — Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to factories actually reorganizing took 40 years, and it meant burning down the old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. He also cites the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone, including mechanics, to use the new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in the production environment.

[11:18] (Anish Acharya) **Companies will become a series of nested loops** — Anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, skill files), and after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing a task). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and a mature loop already existed — a bug report comes in, a reproduction is generated, it is fixed, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones ship directly, and the customer may even get an automatic reply. Above that there is loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company.

[14:18] (Anish Acharya) **A loop only climbs to the local optimum and stops** — The growth team's version of the loop: every variant is generated automatically, measured automatically, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left behind, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish stresses that a loop will hit the local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. His example is telling Claude ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’ — it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

[21:32] (Anish Acharya) **Frontier model pricing is actually irrational** — Anish explains model choice with Pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve — one more IQ point may cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries like drug discovery, where the upside is unbounded, that one extra IQ point may be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; whereas for work with bounded upside like law and finance, you just want Pareto efficiency, using a cheap open-weight model that is good enough. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

[31:46] (Anish Acharya) **People want to spend time, not save it** — Anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but in fact they want to spend time — the world's biggest products are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: the AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly over whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; the Instagram user just thinks ‘this is a better Google search’. He thinks this is not a model or capability problem, it is a product design problem: for the past 40 years we built technology that extends the intellect, and we did not build things that extend the soul.

[34:49] (Anish Acharya) **Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010** — Anish likens the present to iPhone 2010 — Airbnb, WhatsApp and Uber had not appeared yet. Three things hold consumer back: models are too expensive, so free products are hard; the interface problem, chat only suits ‘the highest-agency people in the world’ like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for ordinary consumers is TikTok, and something between chat and TikTok needs to be found; and the technology has been too skewed toward productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models have brought costs down sharply, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interface, and Brian Chesky has also set up a lab focused on the next generation of interfaces.

[37:58] (Anish Acharya) **People are strongest when the stakes are high, worst when they are low** — One of Anish's theories: when the stakes are high we are great, when the stakes are low we are in our absolute worst state. The world five years ago felt like a low-stakes world, so the whole society collectively did a lot of side projects that neither produced anything nor made people happier. Now everyone feels they are climbing the ladder of ambition. He cites GDP growth being stuck in a 2% rut for a long time, and asks who said we have to stay there, why can't it be 10%, 15%, 20%. He also says AI unbundles skill from desire: you do not need to play piano to want to make music, you do not need to be a programmer to want to make software.

[40:00] (Anish Acharya) **Making important things cheap is AI's best PR** — Anish thinks the most important thing for changing AI's public image is making important things cheap. America has two extremely important things that keep getting more expensive: healthcare and education. In healthcare, 45% is administrative cost, and removing the administrative burden would reveal healthcare cost deflation; education faces its strongest competition in 200 years, which will unbundle learning from institutions and also unbundle identity from credentials — you do not need a Harvard degree. He also offers an observation: revealed preferences show individual experience is getting better, while stated preferences show people think society is getting worse. Ask whether a data center should be built near your home, most say no; ask whether you use ChatGPT today, most say yes.

[42:02] (Anish Acharya) **‘Too dangerous to release’ mixes marketing and compute** — On OpenAI slowing RL training, and on the claim that ‘the model is too dangerous so we won't release it’, Anish is skeptical. He thinks the aura Anthropic gains from ‘the model is too dangerous to release’ is enormous, but behind it there may be confounding factors like a GPU shortage, capability not actually being there, or simply wanting to keep this proprietary model in-house to extend the lead. He says the concept mixes marketing, inference compute and economic considerations — do you actually want to externalize your competitive advantage, or use it to make yourself stronger. He takes offensive cyberattacks seriously: before making systems easy to break into, all systems should be hardened first.

[53:29] (Anish Acharya) **Moats are discovered, not designed** — Anish quotes Decagon's Jesse: most moats are discovered, not designed. When he was a founder he had this same flaw, insisting on forcing out a business plan that could withstand scrutiny from MBAs and BCG. Cursor is the example: early on it was criticized for having no moat, but a high-NPS DAU product is itself good, and later they accumulated all the reasoning traces and trained their own Composer model. He also says not one classic moat is built on ‘how hard the software is to make’ — network effects, scale advantages, brand, proprietary data, what history calls a cornered resource, the moats of five years ago are still moats today.

[59:49] (Anish Acharya) **There is no growth problem, only a product problem** — Anish says nobody has a growth problem now, only a product problem. The reason is that you can build a product that is extremely ambitious in any direction, functional or emotional, and you can charge a lot for it. His challenge is: is it really a growth problem, or a failure of our collective imagination? If you imagine your product charging a thousand dollars a month, ten thousand dollars a month, if it is the Birkin bag of software, what would it have to do to deserve that price? He also says it is now easier rather than harder for startups: Gemini, despite Google's massive cross-selling, nobody would say it has won; startups can build in directions incumbents are uncomfortable with, like companions; prices can be very high, people are willing to pay 200 dollars a month, and enterprises are willing to sign million-dollar ACV contracts without being quite clear what they are getting.

[1:10:14] (Anish Acharya) **The switch that makes AI change you is ‘joy’** — Anish says he has observed that people's attitude toward AI flips, and the trigger is often not an efficiency gain but some moment of joy AI created for them. His example is a Mother's Day idea — first ask yourself ‘if this worked, what would make me happy’, or ‘what can I do for someone else’. He treats this as an actionable starting point: do not start from technical capability and look for a scenario, start from a concrete thing that brings joy.

[1:11:20] (Anish Acharya) **The three books he recommends are all about the same thing** — Anish's three most-recommended books: Thomas Sowell's Conquest and Cultures, on how conquest changed cultures in different places, which he considers the best historical lens on ‘culture is the biggest driver of outcomes’, and which also maps onto the ambition-culture difference he felt after moving from Canada to the US; Seven Powers, on moats and compounding advantages in business; and the textbook Mark recommended to him, Increasing Returns to Scale (author Brian Arthur), a slightly dense study explaining why things like software have extreme economic effects. He says these three helped him understand ‘why our industry works the way it does’.

[1:12:25] (Anish Acharya) **He used Grokbot to grab IMAX tickets and got stuck on a captcha** — Anish says he kept failing to get IMAX tickets for Odyssey, so he had a Grokbot keep watching the ticketing site to find him good seats. But the captcha on the AMC site blocked it — you have to click three matching shapes. Lenny asks whether it is the pick-the-fruit kind, and Anish says yes, that kind, ‘come on, you can't even do this?’ This is the most concrete agent deployment case in the whole episode: a real task, a real point of failure.

[1:13:30] (Anish Acharya) **Grokbot made him doubt that models are a two-horse race** — Asked for his favorite AI product, Anish picks Grokbot, because it ‘so unabashedly’ caches credentials and completes tasks for you — he says he expects startups to do this, but did not expect a big company to do such a thing. He thinks it has a thoughtful UI and a strong foundation model, and from this draws a judgment: maybe the model side is not a two-horse race.

[1:14:31] (Anish Acharya) **Do not build a product and a platform at the same time** — Anish's life creed comes from his startup experience: do not discover through painful firsthand experience what someone else could tell you in one sentence. The version for his kids is ‘don't touch the hot stove’, and the version for founders is ‘don't build a product and a platform at the same time’. His first company wanted to be both a mobile-game social platform and a game studio, and someone told him to his face: being a studio is already hard enough, and you are doing a platform at the same time, pick one. They did not listen, and it took them several years to figure out they were wrong.

[1:15:32] (Anish Acharya) **Tape is the real watershed in music history** — Anish has DJed for 31 years (since 95), and he thinks DJ plus music models is a new form of expression: you supply the idea, the model does the heavy lifting. He gives a history of music media — at first you could only hear live performance, then there were recordings on the phonograph, and the real turning point was tape, because that was the first time a person could ‘create’ on their own, sequencing their own album. He thinks the music industry's troubles in the 2000s were precisely because this disappeared and it fell back to a broadcast model; now people are starting to make music again, and the music industry will be bigger than ever.

## Copper grades have fallen from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand is going to the moon

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
- show: Odd Lots (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/oddlots/)
- original episode: Robert Friedland on the World's Monumental Shortage of Copper
- published: 2026-09-12 · duration: 1:09:54
- transcript: Official transcript · 11379 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Global copper grades keep sliding, new mines take 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.**

why listen: Robert Friedland distills the copper supply-demand deadlock from 40 years in mining: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only show up in the second half.

### points

[14:30] (Robert Friedland) **The next 18 years will require mining all the copper of the past 10,000** — Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get back roughly 700 million tons. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years require mining the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

[22:51] (Robert Friedland) **The world's largest copper mine's grade is in freefall** — Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it's down to 0.8%, and within two years it will fall to 0.4%. Falling grades mean crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

[27:54] (Robert Friedland) **An AI search uses 30x the power of a normal search** — Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he uses ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30x that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old on the planet with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this studio itself is copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

[34:01] (Robert Friedland) **Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months** — About 25% of the world's copper requires sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell the acid to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

[51:25] (Robert Friedland) **Buying one large motor means waiting eight years** — Friedland tells a supply chain story absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and just the ring gear took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers trying to buy natural gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

[58:35] (Robert Friedland) **US miners earn $100 an hour; Congo engineers earn $800 a month** — Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast if you don't invest, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest ever.

[1:02:39] (Robert Friedland) **Tariffs could keep US copper mining alive, but they'd stoke inflation** — Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.80, taking copper to $7.80, and he could afford to pay American miners, making US mining viable. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

[1:04:42] (Robert Friedland) **Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and nobody can calculate supply and demand** — Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says nobody can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on yen weakness so they never have to repay. He thinks we're at an inflection point, where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinizable.

### verbatim quotes

[14:30] Robert Friedland: "at the rate of current global economic growth with 8 billion people on this planet, to maintain 3% GDP growth, absent the electrification of the world economy, absent electric cars, and let's not even get started on data centers, we need to mine that same amount of copper that we mined in the last 10,000 years in the next 18 years."

[23:52] Robert Friedland: "about 4% to 5% of all the energy produced on planet Earth is utilized in the crushing and grinding of rock, which is a huge number when we're worried about the generation of global warming gas."

[27:54] Robert Friedland: "when you do an AI search, and I use ChatGPT4, and we're using Cloud, and you do an AI search, you're using 30 times more electrical energy."

[34:01] Robert Friedland: "We cannot, as an industry, find and responsibly mine the copper that we need for an energy transition with yesterday's technology."

[52:27] Robert Friedland: "it was a four and a half year wait to get the ring gear. In other words, you order the motor, four and a half years later, Siemens or ABB could build it. Today it'd be an eight or 10 year wait, if ever."

[59:36] Robert Friedland: "today, mining companies in the aggregate only have the value of less than 1% of the S & P 500, which is an all-time low for mining."

[1:04:42] Robert Friedland: "What's happening is that governments are buying copper metal as a proxy on money. And they're not reporting it. And nobody can calculate the supply-demand balance on any of these metals because why would you?"

### glossary

- NPV model: A method of valuing an asset by discounting its future cash flows; Friedland argues applying it to mines systematically suppresses mining company valuations.
- heap leach: An extraction process that piles up ore and sprays it with a chemical solution (such as sulfuric acid) to dissolve the copper out for recovery.
- tailings dam: An embankment holding waste residue after ore processing; a failure can cause severe environmental and safety disasters.
- solid oxide fuel cell: A high-efficiency power generation device; Bloom Energy uses it to provide uninterruptible power to data centers, and it requires scandium metal.

## US Measles Returns: CDC Refuses to Count Two Child Deaths

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹卷土重来-cdc-拒绝承认两例儿童死亡/

**Pennsylvania's two measles deaths were erased from the CDC's weekly report on the grounds of "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the case: state-reported notifiable disease data can now be rejected by the federal government on undisclosed standards.**

why listen: A routine clinical update segment; the first half is scattered news on Florida dengue, rabies, and NIH funding shifted to the Department of Defense, with average information density. ### points

[4:06] (Daniel Griffin) **Florida's local dengue no longer requires leaving the country** — Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: Florida added 32 locally acquired dengue cases last week, bringing the cumulative total past 70, with 14 infected mosquito pools detected across five counties. In the same segment he also mentions the health advisory the CDC issued that day — since July 2026, rabies-related consultations are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including large-scale exposure events, against a backdrop of US pet owners becoming hesitant about vaccinating animals against rabies. His framing: US infectious diseases are rising, and these are diseases we have known how to prevent for decades.

[6:09] (Daniel Griffin) **NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense** — Nature reported that NIH is seeking to shift hundreds of millions of dollars in research programs from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense's biodefense programs, and two NIH employees said the two sides have signed a preliminary agreement. Responding to Nature, the Department of Defense called the agreement a "project-by-project strategic collaboration" and said "any suggestion that the agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response did not mention money. Griffin's criticism lands here: collaboration is fine, biodefense is fine, and the Department of Defense has plenty of its own money; it does not need to move funds out of an NIH that is already underfunded.

[10:09] (Daniel Griffin) **HPV vaccine coverage is only 77.7%** — Among adolescents aged 13 to 17 in 2025, only 77.7% had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, and only 63.4% had completed the full series — the fourth consecutive year without growth. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccine coverage has held at about 90% since 2019. Griffin's argument is direct: this is a cancer-preventing vaccine, it can prevent cervical, anogenital and head and neck cancers, and vaccination at ages 13 to 17 can prevent 100% of them; the studies he cites show a 90% decline in certain head and neck cancers and more than 80% across all head and neck cancers. He attributes the flat coverage to the anti-vaccine camp framing it as a "sexually transmitted infection vaccine."

[17:16] (Vincent Racanello) **CDC deleted the two state-reported measles deaths** — On August 25, the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly report, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying the available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from the new CDC director, Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. The key fact Racanello adds: the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

[22:20] (Vincent Racanello) **The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield** — The technical core of the dispute is how death certificates are filled out. Part I lists the chain of events leading to death, with the top line being the immediate cause, the lines below it the conditions it caused, and the last line the underlying cause that set off the whole sequence; Part II records other significant contributing conditions. So the immediate cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis or splenic rupture, while measles appears in Part II. The county coroner's statement that "no measles was the immediate cause of death" plays precisely on this structure. Racanello quotes former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury: states have always reported deaths, the CDC has always counted them, and the CDC's role has historically been to receive, tabulate, and reconcile afterward — reconciling afterward is normal, refusing a state's report at the intake point is not.

[23:20] (Vincent Racanello) **The real damage is that the data become negotiable** — Racanello frames the consequence as heavier than the individual case: if the CDC can refuse a state's notifiable disease report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. He stresses that this damage is independent of who holds office and applies equally to the next director. By contrast, the two children in West Texas and the adult in New Mexico were all counted directly after state reporting, with no independent federal adjudication. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC measles response team and that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation.

[29:24] (Daniel Griffin) **Flu antivirals within 48 hours cut hospitalization risk 81%** — A multicenter, retrospective case-control study matched by age and season included laboratory-confirmed pediatric outpatients with influenza seen at participating hospitals between 2020 and 2023; cases were children subsequently hospitalized or killed by influenza, and controls were matched by initial visit date and age. Among 1,492 children, starting antiviral treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset was associated with an 81% lower overall risk of hospitalization compared with delayed or no use, and the finding was robust across analyses. Griffin uses this to restate his long-standing point: for viral illness, timing is everything — you cannot "wait and see."

[32:24] (Daniel Griffin) **Vaccination cuts cardiovascular event risk by 80%** — A statewide cohort study and target trial emulation based on linked administrative health data for 2,391,456 adults in Victoria, Australia, from 2019 to 2025 examined the association between vaccination around the time of infection and major adverse cardiovascular events. MACE covered stroke, heart failure, heart attack, atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism. Vaccination was associated with lower risk of all these events, with an estimated absolute risk reduction of 21% — which Griffin translates into an 80% risk reduction. His landing point: every COVID infection carries the risk of heart attack and stroke, and what the vaccine truly reduces significantly is disease, not just infection for a brief window.

## A US measles death is erased from CDC data, and state reporting becomes negotiable

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/

### points

[4:06] (Daniel Griffin) **Florida now has locally acquired dengue** — Griffin says he no longer needs to leave the country to see dengue cases: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired infections, the cumulative total has passed 70 locally acquired dengue cases, and 14 virus-carrying mosquito pools have been detected across 5 counties. Put together, these two things show not an isolated outbreak of some pathogen but that the US has abandoned lines of defense against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

[6:09] (Daniel Griffin) **NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense** — Nature reported that NIH is seeking to transfer several hundred million dollars' worth of research programs from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense's (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense programs, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Department of Defense responded confirming it had signed a research agreement allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response never mentions the money. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Department of Defense has plenty of money, and it does not need to reach into the pockets of an already underfunded NIH.

[9:09] (Daniel Griffin) **HPV vaccination has been flat for four years, at just 77.7%** — An MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021, now stalled for a fourth straight year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose, and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the meningococcal rural-urban gap appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can 100% prevent cervical, anogenital and head and neck cancers — why aren't we doing it.

[15:15] (Daniel Griffin) **Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts** — MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; each confirmed case identified on average only 10.6 contacts, against a target above 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases are occurring outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, a number that should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths so far.

[17:16] (Vincent Racaniello) **The CDC removed a state-reported measles death from the tally** — On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying the available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key fact: state and local health departments do the case investigation, apply the case definition and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically has only received and aggregated, checking afterward. This time the CDC was itself embedded in the Pennsylvania investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

[19:18] (Vincent Racaniello) **Nobody routinely screens the dead for measles** — A SIDRAP commentary dismantles the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" line: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance for clinicians is to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then mention testing. So a positive measles result in a death investigation usually means there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but small enough that a rational person should shift their judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also fell severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born not breathing and could not be resuscitated, with measles virus detected in lung tissue.

[22:20] (Vincent Racaniello) **The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield** — Much of the dispute stems from how death certificates are structured, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part one lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line the immediate cause and the lines below it the conditions that produced it, ending with the underlying cause that started the whole sequence; part two, per the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate-cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in part two — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

[24:20] (Vincent Racaniello) **The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases** — Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury told STAT that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that, per the Pennsylvania health commissioner, the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

[32:24] (Daniel Griffin) **COVID vaccination cut cardiovascular event risk by 80%** — The study, published in the European Health Journal, used linked administrative health data on 2,391,456 adults in Victoria, Australia (2019 to 2025), a population-based cohort plus target trial emulation, to look at the association between vaccination around the time of infection and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE, including stroke, heart failure, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism). Vaccination was associated with lower risk of all these events, with an estimated absolute risk reduction of 21% — Griffin specifically corrects the phrasing: a risk reduction of 0.21 means an 80% relative risk reduction. His bottom line: every time you get COVID, without vaccine protection you face the risk of heart attack and stroke, and what the vaccine genuinely and substantially reduces is disease, not just infection.

[35:27] (Daniel Griffin) **A Medicare nurse told a 60-year-old stroke patient not to get vaccinated** — Listener Jill is a retired pediatrician in Nebraska whose 60-year-old husband had a stroke two days after a hip replacement seven years ago. Disabled and on Medicare, he is offered an annual virtual home visit by his Medicare Advantage plan, and this year he took it because it came with a $50 health-products credit. The nurse practitioner doing the visit, after asking about fall and depression risks, brought up the COVID vaccine on her own, and on learning he gets a shot every year told him to stop, citing an association with "cardiomyopathy in older men" and vaguely mentioning two enzymes and the need for more research before it could be called safe. Griffin's reaction is that this is deeply troubling: it amounts to spreading misinformation and discouraging evidence-based prevention, and he suggests Jill contact the nurse's supervising physician. He adds that the early signal appeared in younger men and after a first dose, and has not been seen in this age group.

## The AI Doom Narrative Is a Psyop, and the Target Is Open Source

- show: All-In Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/allin/)

- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:35:57

- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI may end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.**

why listen: The first half is the sparring over Doomer PR and IPO disclosure; the second half's breakdown of OpenAI's math breakthrough and Nike's collapse is worth more.

### points

[0:00] (David Sachs) **The resignation letter wasn't spontaneous — it was organized PR** — Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic after only six weeks and posted that the people building AI genuinely believe it could kill everyone by the end of this decade. Sachs points out this was not spontaneous: the account had almost zero followers and zero posts before, yet got hundreds of millions of views in a day; within the first 15 minutes three Doomer organizations amplified it, all funded by the same big EA donor, who also co-led Anthropic's Series A. More tellingly, the Wall Street Journal story went out minutes before the tweetstorm — meaning the reporter had been briefed under embargo. Sachs says if Coxon really came on the show, the first question would be: who introduced you to the Wall Street Journal?

[6:12] (David Sachs / Chamath) **The company didn't distance itself — it amplified him** — A normal company facing a whistleblower immediately pushes back and distances itself. Anthropic did the opposite: Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment, publicly replied that Jacob is right, that they genuinely believe AI could kill all of humanity, and that he personally puts the probability above 10% over the next decade. Sachs argues this exposes the contradiction — what he said matches the company's internal Doomer agenda exactly, which is why he got internal support. Chamath adds the knife: the company can't distance itself, because the moment it does, that whole internal bloc blows up.

[10:18] (David Sachs / Chamath) **Asking for a trillion-dollar valuation while saying the product could end civilization** — Sachs lays out Anthropic's IPO dilemma clearly: you are asking public-market investors to underwrite your company at a trillion-dollar valuation while your safety lead says the core product is unsolved and could end civilization. That is at minimum the seedbed of product-liability litigation. Chamath uses the Philip Morris analogy: we know cigarettes kill you, we'll say so, but we won't disclose it, we'll still go public and let you buy the stock, and we'll figure it out later. Sachs calls it "a time for choosing" — either publicly deny that Coxon is a Doomer operation, or admit Bernie Sanders is right and development should be frozen, in which case how do you IPO at a trillion-dollar valuation?

[22:45] (David Sachs / Friedberg / Chamath) **The real target of regulation is open source** — Sachs is blunt: this is a Doomer psyop, and the end goal is open source. Because FDA-style regulation won't say "ban open source" — it will say "the same standards apply to open and closed models" — and Dario has already testified in the Senate that models are dangerous if they can't be centrally monitored and rolled back. Once open-model weights are released they can't be rolled back, so the standard landing is equivalent to banning the release, use and hosting of those weights. Freeberg adds: open source has no corporate structure to file regulatory paperwork, and open source is precisely what cut AI costs by 50x and benefited everyone. Chamath's version: once open source is banned, you get a monopoly in partnership with the federal government.

[39:17] (Chamath / Jason) **AI can't even nail autocomplete yet** — The core anti-Doomer argument isn't theoretical speculation but everyday experience: autocomplete still isn't good, and AI can't even handle a chore like "bring the toiletry bag upstairs." If it can't finish one mundane task, why believe it can kill all of humanity? They call this humanity's insurance against AI taking over the world — company decisions still require humans to wake up, drink coffee and sit in the same room, and there is a natural 16-hour window between decisions.

[50:45] (David Sachs) **What's truly damning is that retweet endorsement** — From a legal standpoint, the key isn't Jacob Coxon's resignation tweet but Evan Hubinger's endorsement retweet — he is still a senior alignment executive at the company, running one of the safety teams, and his co-sign plus the "greater than 10% probability" figure is what made it go viral. If it were only Coxon, the company could call him a disgruntled employee; but an executive endorsement turns "was disclosure adequate" into a real question.

[1:00:12] (Chamath) **OpenAI solved the math problem with brute force, not divine inspiration** — The Navier-Stokes solution used roughly 130 billion output tokens, with 10,000 agents communicating with each other, equivalent to between 50,000 and 500,000 years of human work (estimated at 40 words per minute of typing). AI had no flash of insight humans couldn't have; it just did a huge amount of brute-force work, and every step of the message chain is recorded and human-readable. The conclusion is that AI is a leverage tool, not a math god above humans.

[1:15:40] (Sacks / Chamath) **De-identification doesn't remove the method itself** — De-identification can strip personal information and company-specific information, but the general method for solving a math problem is itself IP. A user iterates on that method inside the tool, and that conversation can be de-identified and used for training, making the model better at math. This is the network effect of closed models: they can see what the whole world is doing, and this observation system feeds them more data than anyone else, constituting a long-term advantage over customers.

[1:26:53] (David Sachs / Chamath) **It's not that the ads got worse — the shoes fall apart in six weeks** — Sacks says all his shoes used to be Nike, then he stopped buying them, and the reason wasn't advertising or the ordering experience but the product itself getting worse — shoes fall apart in about six weeks, thin and not durable. He walked into REI, tried on a pair of Brooks and switched. Chamath says he stuck with Nike a long time, buying a pair every six months, then it became every six weeks, and he finally switched to On because of knee problems, for a straightforward reason: Roger Federer represents mastery and excellence. Brooks is owned by Berkshire Hathaway, has posted nine consecutive years of double-digit growth, and has $1.6 billion in revenue; its CEO says Buffett gives just one instruction a year: make the product better than it was at the end of last year.

### glossary

- Doomer: The camp that believes AI will most likely cause human extinction, often overlapping with effective altruism (EA) funding networks.
- RSI / recursive self-improvement: The loop in which AI helps improve the next generation of AI; a mild version is already happening, while the extreme version means AI fully autonomously designs and launches the next training run.
- ZDR / zero data retention: A clause in which a model provider promises not to retain user data, but it is only a commercial best effort and cannot be guaranteed.
- S-1: The prospectus a US company files with the SEC before an IPO, which must accurately present both opportunity and risk.
- DTC / direct-to-consumer: A strategy of selling straight to end users while bypassing retailers; Nike pushed it aggressively and alienated retail partners.

## Active management giant moves HQ to Nashville, saves $85 million a year

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
- show: Masters in Business (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/mastersinbiz/)
- original episode: Finding Stability in Investing: Masters in Business with Seth Bernstein
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 59:00
- transcript: Official transcript · 9138 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, without forcing a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and personnel, and the bet is on hiring people New York can't reach.**

why listen: A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401ks. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

### points

[9:18] (Seth Bernstein) **When passive squeezes active, cut costs before talking growth** — The Alliance Bernstein Bernstein took over was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions sliding from 20 to 25 cents a share all the way down to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — post-merger AUM had touched nearly $900 billion intra-quarter, and by 2012 only $380 billion remained; in 2006 roughly 70% was equity assets, and by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced parts of the teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and an emphasis on distribution.

[21:39] (Seth Bernstein) **Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year, and nobody is forced to move** — The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being ‘wanting to be a big fish in a small pond’, which Charlotte or Dallas couldn't deliver. The move saves roughly $85 million a year, part real estate and part personnel. The key design: no portfolio manager is forced to relocate, because the firm is a ‘price taker’ for that kind of talent. As a result, nearly 100 portfolio managers chose to move. The challenges are concrete too: Nashville is the capital of healthcare services, and locally it is hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training; but the firm received a flood of résumés from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

[25:44] (Seth Bernstein) **Sell-side research with no cross-subsidy can only be a joint venture** — Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Nearly every peer cross-subsidises its research department with equity capital markets or prime brokerage, and Alliance Bernstein had none of those businesses to subsidise with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition entirely to SocGen. He specifically mentions the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Brits — so it had to be done step by step, very carefully. The transition period runs five years from the JV's anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

[37:08] (Seth Bernstein) **Banks are structurally unsuited to holding long-dated fixed-rate assets** — Bernstein uses his leveraged finance experience at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players running short money, structurally unsuited to holding long-duration, especially fixed-rate, assets. JPMorgan at the time spent a great deal of time and money trying to securitise its loan book, and credit derivatives started from there. Insurance companies and funds are a better home for these assets, because funds don't offer a genuine liquidity option and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that there is no maturity transformation in credit, and apart from interest and principal there should never have been any liquidity at all.

[40:14] (Seth Bernstein) **Private credit's problem isn't defaults, it's insufficient disclosure** — Asked how the industry gets past the first-half troubles this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure obligation, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and one should ‘over-communicate in periods like this’. He also frames the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are simply the normal state of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; what went wrong was a handful of companies, plus fraud which has always existed; what genuinely went wrong was structure and pricing getting out of balance for a while. His conclusion is that after going through this, now is actually a better entry point.

[43:14] (Seth Bernstein) **Private credit in 401ks: fees are not the obstacle** — Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401ks may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlisle to develop a vehicle that can sit alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He concedes the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years — but in ten years it will most likely be part of large plans. On the fee objection, his response: these are institutional buyers who will drive a hard bargain; and private assets are only a small slice of a target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

[47:18] (Seth Bernstein) **Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at it** — Bernstein points to Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and that one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at it. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mainly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people haven't saved enough to retire, and will delay retirement and look for supplemental income. He also proposes a specific mechanism: rather than buying an annuity in one lump at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income protection over a longer lifespan.

[51:26] (Seth Bernstein) **AB is the last publicly traded partnership** — Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits institutional willingness to hold. He describes the stock as ‘a bond with an equity option’ — essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure and make the stock pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock didn't pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is that it's not a sure thing.

### verbatim quotes

[11:30] Seth Bernstein: "you can have the smartest people in the world with the most impressive process deliver appalling returns. It's serendipitous why it works when it does work. So be careful mucking around in it."

[13:30] Seth Bernstein: "Your whole revenue stream is structured on ad valorem pricing. So even when you destroy value and markets go up, you make more money, kind of a wonderful thing."

[15:32] Seth Bernstein: "Look, either it's a fiduciary standard or it's not. It is that black and white."

[38:11] Seth Bernstein: "But ultimately, there is no maturity transformation in credit. You got what you got. And frankly, I think there shouldn't be any liquidity other than the payment of interest and credit. repayment of the debt itself."

[48:19] Seth Bernstein: "The last thing you need most people at age 65 is to be predominantly in short-term fixed income and cash. You need to be invested. On the assumption you have another 20, 25 years to go."

[56:29] Seth Bernstein: "My advice to them is never act like you know the answer if you don't because you don't People aren't going to trust you because of your experience. So if you lose that trust early, it's really hard to regain."

[57:30] Seth Bernstein: "People who think they can time the market and actually can prove out that they really do it well, you can count on one hand. Diversification, no one diversifies to get rich. You diversify to stay rich."

### glossary

- ad valorem pricing: Management fees charged as a percentage of the market value of assets under management, so revenue rises when markets rise.
- K-1: A tax form partnerships issue to their partners; institutional investors often avoid it because of the paperwork.
- glide path: The designed path by which a target-date fund shifts its stock/bond mix as retirement approaches.
- SMA: A separately managed account for a single client, allowing tax management and avoidance of wash sales.
- superannuation: Australia's mandatory retirement savings system, regarded as a thought leader in retirement planning.

## AI 2040 isn't about stopping AI, it's about pushing superintelligence to 2040

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-tbpn-ai-2040-不是停掉-ai-是把超级智能推迟到-2040/
- show: TBPN (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tbpn/)
- original episode: Fruitfly Hard Takeoff, Washington on AI Risk, 𝕏 Timeline Reactions | Thijs Simonian, Alex Heath & Guy Oseary, Mitesh Agrawal
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:45:49
- transcript: Official transcript · 20293 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 10 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute cap: pause new frontier training, allow inference only, and make stealing weights impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.**

why listen: High information density, but the topics jump around: AI regulation, robotics, how VCs read people, and the chip supply chain each get a segment, so it's good for picking and choosing.

### points

[0:00] (Speaker 1) **AI 2040 doesn't stop AI, it delays it to 2040** — Many people assume anti-AI sentiment is pushing to ‘stop AI’, but what the AI 2040 proposal actually says is: keep inference on existing models, keep doing capability research, just push superintelligence from 2028 to 2040. The concrete mechanism is a compute cap — pause new frontier training, apply ‘inference-only verification’ to data centers above 10,000 H100-equivalents (roughly $100M of equipment), and physically rip out the high-bandwidth east-west networking inside the data center so distributed training can't run but inference proceeds as normal. New R&D centers would have to be built from scratch inside a Faraday cage, with external connectivity capped at 1 MB/s — stealing the weights would take five years.

[0:00] (Speaker 2) **Anti-AI mobilization is nowhere near anti-battery-chicken** — Speaker 2 points out a contrast: the anti-flock (anti-battery-chicken) movement converts into real physical action by ordinary people, whereas on the anti-AI side you don't see a 100,000-like video teaching people ‘how to cut power to your local data center’. Speaker 1 adds that the volume on the anti-AI side comes more from concrete interests like ‘I'm an artist and I don't like AI-generated images’ than from x-risk arguments. Data centers are in remote locations, fenced and heavily fortified — far harder to get at than a chicken coop on the street.

[0:00] (Speaker 1) **The compute cap is the valve easiest to turn** — The most effective control lever in the proposal is judged to be the compute cap: chip controls plus slower data center construction. The goal is to make models stronger mainly by adding hardware rather than by new algorithms — because algorithmic breakthroughs can be hidden inside secret projects. Speaker 1 notes that Ilya's new lab recently got a large cluster from NVIDIA; even people on an orthogonal research path have to stack compute, which shows that ‘scale is a prerequisite’ is basically consensus in this circle.

[0:00] (Speaker 1) **Doomers don't bet, because they wouldn't live to collect** — Tyler Cowen demands that pessimists name the corresponding market price to validate their beliefs, but Deep Dish pushes back: why should short-term existential risk be reflected in market prices? ‘If everyone's dead, the contract that pays out is worthless to me.’ Speaker 5 twists the knife: in the nuclear-war era people built bunkers; nobody builds an AI bunker, because everyone thinks it's too totalizing for a bunker to help — so ‘you didn't build a bunker’ doesn't prove you don't believe. Paul Christiano is dug up as being 2x levered long and short 30-year US Treasuries, but that bet also makes money in the ‘good ending’, unlike a doomsday wager.

[0:00] (Speaker 1) **The fruit-fly agent moves the moral question forward** — Google mapped out all the neurons of a fruit fly, and once the code was open-sourced people started messing with it in every way: someone put the fruit-fly agent inside a Rabbit R1, and shaking the device makes its escape circuit light up; someone else had it play Doom. Speaker 1 thinks the real question is the next stop on this road — if you can simulate a person, hold a conversation, behave like a person, does it have moral status? His own judgment is not to overthink it and not to be in the business of torturing anything. He also mentions having Astra play Balatro with computer use last night, and it felt like giving it a reward rather than torturing it.

[0:00] (Speaker 3) **Once a reporter is in the room, he stops being escorted out** — Alex Heath describes the core mechanism of his changed status: when a reporter is in the room, you're brought in and then immediately escorted out; now he gets to stay in the room and slowly marinate on it. So his newsletter perspective changes — it's not about landing a scoop, but about letting a large volume of off-the-record conversation settle into a judgment, like the personal agents piece he's writing. He says explicitly that confidentiality still matters and he won't leak memos companies are worried about again; ten years in, that's enough.

[0:00] (Speaker 3) **A newcomer can hardly replicate his path now** — Asked whether now is a good time to become the next Alex Heath, his answer is the opposite: the traditional media environment is structurally challenged, many places aren't hiring, traffic is falling, and they haven't shifted to direct models like subscriptions and streaming. The only viable path he offers is ‘maniacally focus on one thing and become the best in the world at that’ — he himself started by focusing on covering Snap, broke a pile of Snap news, and after being noticed migrated that capability to other companies. And the niche has to be the intersection of niche and matters, not just obscure.

[0:00] (Speaker 2) **Fear of being left behind hands new players an opening** — One of the hosts besides Mitesh proposes a counterintuitive mechanism: because people fear AI, they're more willing to try new products — they don't want to be left behind, don't want to become a permanent underclass. The result is that people who've used various AI products for years are still willing to try new things, which keeps creating an advantage for second and third entrants. At the same time, once an AI brand gets big it starts accumulating baggage, and people become more willing to share and discuss something new rather than the one they use every day. That leaves a lot of room for startups.

[0:00] (Speaker 1) **The endgame for personal agents is network effects** — The discussion compares personal agents with the inference market for frontier models: every company will build a personal agent, and many already have. The key disagreement is whether this is a network-effects business — one side thinks yes, and that it can eventually take a cut of agentic commerce, e.g. you buy a car through it and it earns $500; Zuck has also said take rate is his business. The other side offers a counterexample: an agent isn't a person, so you may not care whether it's in the network; but if a given agent has never leaked, never crashed, never been hacked, you will indeed stay.

[0:00] (Speaker 1) **The window to rebuild social networks is opening** — One concrete judgment: now may be the best time to rebuild a social network, because you can have your agent open your Snap or LinkedIn, pull out every single person in there — they have no say in it — and add them back on the new network. The old arbitrage window of ‘export your contacts’ closed; now it's reopening. The immediate criticism: the old critique of social media was ‘we built social media for socializing, and it made people less social’; in the personal-agent era the new critique becomes ‘nobody talks to people anymore, only agents talk to each other’, and even chatting with grandma about a road trip becomes ‘talk to my agent’.

[0:00] (Speaker 4) **Chip companies are now asked whether they can build it** — Mitesh says that walking into a meeting room at a hyperscaler or frontier lab, the question isn't performance but two things: first, can you build enough of it — is the supply chain and component base robust enough; second, can you deploy it — does it need liquid cooling, and if so they may not have a data center for it, because it's already allocated to GPUs or TPUs. The threshold number he gives is gigawatt plus; at that scale, even counting ASICs as cheaper, it's tens of billions of dollars. His own cadence is tape out this year, volume ramp in the second half of 2027, and a plan to reach several hundred megawatts in 2028.

[0:00] (Speaker 4) **Using commodity memory to bypass the HBM and CoWoS bottleneck** — Positron's technical route is to bypass the queue for HBM and CoWoS — NVIDIA, TPU and AMD are all ahead of you. The approach is to use commodity memory, at the cost of being slow, so the technical innovation lies in how to solve the slowness. But commodity memory isn't freely available either; you can't just walk up to Samsung or Micron and ask for LPDDR5x, you still have to plan. He mentions the first-generation product was built on FPGA, with fewer than 20 people, delivering to the first customer in 15 months; Oracle now has 50 Atlas racks; the company just passed 100 people, more than 50 of whom joined in the last three months.

[2:20] (Thijs Simonian) **The robot takes one to two hours to draw a picture** — Thijs hooked Codex directly up to a Hugging Face open-source robotic arm to draw the TBPN logo; one drawing takes one to two hours, and he says himself it's ‘probably quite expensive’ and ‘definitely pretty slow’. His approach isn't to have the model look at an image and make one move, but to first have the model write a plan in the form of code, execute it, then take a picture every few seconds to monitor in the background and fine-tune the plan. He judges that a high-frequency image–small action–image loop would perform best, but the current ‘plan first, then monitor’ is a speed compromise.

[6:40] (Thijs Simonian) **Robotic arms went from thousands of dollars to two hundred** — Thijs says traditional robot hardware costs thousands to tens of thousands of dollars, whereas the Hugging Face SO-100 behind him is open-source, fully 3D-printable, and only requires buying actuators separately — currently about $200 (he adds that this price is on the high side, caused by supply chain issues). He compares it to the 3D printing boom: before industrial-grade machines became widespread, people would first buy these cheap plastic arms to clamp on a desk, plug in an off-the-shelf agent and use it.

[16:20] (Guy Oseary) **Guy Oseary put nearly a billion dollars into OpenAI and Anthropic** — Guy Oseary says that when he invested in Anthropic and OpenAI, they may have been the only fund betting that deep, and many people were confused at the time, but they were convinced these were long-term foundational platforms. He reveals they added more in the two companies' later rounds, for a cumulative total approaching $1 billion. But he also says that telling what's real from what isn't is far harder today than it was then — ‘It's not as easy as it was for us to really decipher’.

[22:10] (Guy Oseary) **Listen to a pitch the way you listen to a song: find the chorus** — Guy Oseary equates spotting founders with collecting demo tapes in clubs back in the day: at 17 he had 100 demos in hand, and the ones initially ranked top three had fallen out of the top 20 by the time he reached the 100th. He says he listens to every pitch like a song or an album, and the test is ‘is there a chorus’ — ‘I'm always listening for the chorus’; if he can't hear a chorus, he thinks the song doesn't work. Alanis Morissette played 30 to 40 seconds of Perfect in his office and he decided to sign her; Muse flew in from London, and after the first song he stopped them and said they could start.

[28:45] (Alex Heath) **Alex Heath spots fakes by having met the very best** — Alex Heath says he can see through marketing at a glance because he's spent a long time around the world's top founders — he just did Zuckerberg, and before that Sam Altman. Once you've seen people at the apex, with high integrity, dominating on the field, you can quickly tell who's pretending. He says he often has the instinct that ‘this looks like it'll pop’, and it's been right often enough. Guy adds that this instinct came from having to move fast back then: if you didn't decide to sign an artist immediately, Jimmy Iovine would outbid you and take them.

### verbatim quotes

## The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performance Copy

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
- show: The British History Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/britishhist/)
- original episode: Chansons de Geste and 12th Century Performance Sample
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 19:35
- transcript: Machine transcription · 3477 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by tracking dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.**

why listen: This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

### points

[1:03] **The most complete version is an English manuscript** — The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France itself — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was originally bound together with a completely unrelated book by someone later, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

[3:05] **Every stanza is a camera position** — The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut into four plus six in performance: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

[7:27] **At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times** — This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it uses consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of poetic slow motion. For example, Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "Roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

[9:29] **The performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript** — Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will not tell more." This line appears before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

[10:31] **Its pocket-book size gives away that it was for work** — The manuscript is only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket book you could carry on your person, not a wealthy man's finely bound volume. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator in a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. Such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler.

[12:31] **The dialect pins this performer to England** — The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests this performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French was also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

[14:34] **Accent drift alone can date a manuscript** — Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound.

[17:40] **A French epic, an English artefact** — Although this is a French poem about an old French king, this manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no equally complete other manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this manuscript, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departed from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience was constructed, and what the music sounded like.

### verbatim quotes

[7:27] : "when something gets really emotional or the action gets really intense, they will basically do the slow-mo matrix version of poetry, which is you see the same shot from three different angles."

[9:29] : "So the bard is like, I've gone as far as I want to go. My voice is wrecked. I'm getting a drink. Y'all on your own."

[10:31] : "It's like six and a half inch by four and a half inch. So it's like a pocket copy."

[14:34] : "they're pretty sure they can date the thing just based on this accent and how far it's drifted, which places this as between 1140 and 1170."

### figures

- Number of the manuscript's final line: line 4002 [9:29]
- Size of the Digby 23 manuscript: about 6.5 inches × 4.5 inches [10:31]
- Possible age of the oral tradition: by the 12th century it may already have been 150 years old [5:18]
- Dating of the manuscript: 1140–1170 [14:34]

### glossary

- Chanson de Geste: A 12th-century French epic genre; literally "song of deeds."
- laisse: The stanza unit of The Song of Roland, of varying length, one laisse to a scene or a mood.
- decasyllabic meter: Ten syllables per line, cut into four plus six in performance, with a pause in the middle.
- oliphant: The horn Roland refuses to blow in the poem, meant to call Charlemagne for help.
- jongleur: A medieval professional travelling performer; the word juggler comes from it.
- Anglo-Norman: The French dialect used in Britain after the Norman Conquest, already markedly different from continental French.
