## The Army Secretary Resigns: The People Who Can Actually Fight Get Cleared Out First

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
- show: ChinaTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/chinatalk/)
- original episode: WarTalk: 9.11, Death of the Army, So Long Dan Driscoll
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:11:03
- transcript: Machine transcription · 13257 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risks are being purged batch by batch.**

why listen: The first half — 9/11 reflection and Army personnel insider detail — is dense with information; the second half, on AI battlefields and model distillation, is more casual chat, so you can listen to just the first half.

### points

[3:03] (Brian) **The war on terror ate the money for military transformation** — Before 9/11 the US military was transforming as Rumsfeld demanded, under the expectation of a relatively comfortable budget environment in which new technology could be slowly pushed into the force. Then GWAT arrived, all available resources were sucked into the war, and the transformation directive remained while the money was gone. Hence a run of procurement disasters: the Army's Future Combat Systems, the Navy's Ford-class carrier, Littoral Combat Ship, DDG-1000 Zumwalt, and the CGX that was simply never built. Brian's judgment is that the technology jumped too far, the investment was nowhere near enough, and everyone was distracted supporting a war that had just started, so these programs were doomed. The troubles with today's B-21 and F-35 trace back to this period too.

[5:22] (Tony) **Twenty-five years on a treadmill, never actually stopping** — Tony points out that op-tempo never stopped after it started in 2001: 12-month, 15-month deployment rotations, and the National Guard is still deploying at home and abroad today. Killing Bin Laden in 2011 could have been a high point, but nothing changed afterward — deployments continued, and through the fall of Kabul, they were still deploying. No one has fully calculated what 25 straight years in that state costs an army. Brian adds a mechanism: conventional forces used to train, reset and run through the training progression at home, and that rhythm disappeared, replaced by "preparing for the next deployment," so there is no time to test new technology or study new ways of fighting.

[7:31] (Brian) **MRAP thinking: use a bigger truck to stop anti-tank missiles** — Brian gives an example absurd in its specificity. In Syria the threat was not IEDs but ATGMs (anti-tank guided weapons, similar to Russian TOW variants). The commander's reflex was still to stuff everyone into MRAPs — making the vehicle bigger, which made it easier for ATGMs to spot the target, while MRAP armor cannot stop munitions designed to penetrate tanks. His conclusion: risk calculation in the war-on-terror era has gone so deep that commanders cannot reconceptualize even a very small tactical adjustment. This is also the direct consequence of why many commanders today struggle to adapt to Ukraine and the Lisko battlefield, and cannot imagine how tactics will change.

[9:37] (Brian) **Get used to zero casualties and you can't accept dying** — Brian says that after 9/11 the US military became increasingly risk- and casualty-averse. The Littoral Combat Ship debate is the specimen: opponents said the ship couldn't take a hit and would be sunk the moment war started; the original proposers answered that it was never going to be sent into a major war, and if it got ambushed and sunk, that was the risk you take as a soldier. That logic was completely unacceptable on Capitol Hill — Iraq and Afghanistan pushed casualties far below the levels of past wars, everyone got used to it, and so they cannot accept that against a peer adversary a lot of people will probably die. The result is continuing to build "Death Star"-style big ships and big platforms, hoping they can protect themselves, rather than going with smaller, more distributed routes that accept a different risk structure.

[10:39] (Brian) **Twenty-five years surrounding Iran, but no network built** — Brian says this is the most important lesson he learned from 9/11, from a friend's reminder: for 25 years the US has basically surrounded Iran, and the CIA's and part of special operations' job is to develop networks and identify people who can oppose an oppressive regime, in case a moment of change comes. But when the strikes on Iran began six months ago, it looked like very little network and capability building had been done in those 25 years. The reason is a mental shift: GWAT focused on counterinsurgency and catching bad guys, not the long-term unconventional warfare of pre-positioning the environment for a future conflict — how to support an insurgency inside a regime you might one day want to overthrow. In his words, everyone was too busy stabilizing the situation rather than destabilizing.

[13:53] (Tony) **Driscoll resigns, and from here on it's all acting officials** — Tony recaps: George was fired, Driscoll went to the White House, said "everything is terrible," and resigned that same week. The backdrop is the Army being meddled with back and forth by OSD and the Secretary of the Army's office, plus personality clashes. What he hears is that Congress will not confirm anyone else Pete nominates, so either they swap in someone both the White House and Congress can accept but Pete doesn't like, or they just keep using acting officials. He judges this is the start of the rest of this administration being "stuck with acting officials": after the midterms the House flips at least, the Senate either flips or goes 50:50, no one has the energy to push this kind of person through, so acting officials, continued OSD meddling and low morale will persist.

[14:54] (Tony) **The drone battalion is disbanded, and the ability to experiment goes with it** — The Army decided around the same time to dissolve its newly created drone battalion — a battalion meant to absorb Ukraine's lessons directly and then study how to embed them in infantry battalions. Tony concedes there is a good argument that "it shouldn't exist in just one battalion": concentrating lessons in one central warehouse strips every commander of the responsibility to think about organization themselves. But his worry is that the Army still needs a unit that can run experiments, run tests, and allow failure; cutting it in the name of "uniformity" loses the ability to experiment, and the force will stand still. He also names Chris Donahue as sacrificed: a commander widely recognized as understanding technology, its effects, and how to run international partnerships, done away with over the Abbey Gate bombing (not his fault) and a photo a reporter took.

[21:03] (Tony) **Confidence is lost in layers, by rank** — Tony breaks morale down by rank: junior officers are still early, but already thinking "garrison isn't what I signed up for," and that if you're not garrisoned you go get hit by missiles; field-grade officers are starting to agonize over whether they have to make political decisions just to stay in; senior field-grade officers and junior generals are basically "all in or burned out." He says the whole force is tired, and this doesn't look like the Army they joined. And in interviewees' telling, the Iran war is more of a tipping point than Donahue's departure — many O-4s and O-5s he knows originally supported this administration and are furious after the Donahue affair. Brian adds: people like Donahue are the true product of elite selection, and cutting them makes you doubt the claim that promotion is "by ability alone."

[27:13] (Brian) **A general's core function is to own risk for those below** — Brian offers a mechanism: one of a general's most important roles is to own risk — to absorb risk, thereby permitting experimentation and allowing subordinate units to try new things. Once a firing looks political, that channel is cut: which line do I cross to get fired or lose my command? So everything anyone wants to do stops. He also points to another pressure: the Army budget is being cut or flattened, with money flowing to new technology, other services and the current Iran war. And people are the most expensive thing, so the likeliest move is to hold end strength steady and cut the money that supports people — fewer new weapons, worse readiness and training, less housing support, but the flashy equipment still gets bought.

[42:56] (Brian) **Fighting Iran used up the expensive munitions reserved for China** — Brian lays out the chain of responsibility for the munitions shortage clearly: to avoid casualty risk, to stay low-profile, to avoid losses, the US military struck Iran with the longest-range, most stealthy, expensive munitions — the ones reserved for China — and now they're burned through. At the same time, to preserve follow-on strike options, airborne forces stayed there, and protecting them requires air-defense interceptors that were already scarce. So the munitions predicament was created by operational decisions, and the decisions came from the secretary and the White House; Steve Feinberg just took the fall for the boss. Tony adds: acting officials who haven't been confirmed by the Senate are constrained on budget and authorities, and if acting officials are everywhere, you can't even move money for this war.

[50:13] (Tony) **Russian troops are using AI to fool Putin's own people** — Tony cites an Institute for the Study of War report: Russian battalion- and brigade-level units are using AI to generate false information about the war, aimed at their own side, specifically at Putin. The practice for months or even years before was to send two men 15 kilometers across the front line carrying a Russian flag, take a photo, and then either get killed or run back, all to prove to Putin that they were advancing. The report says these commanders are now being punished for it, but that this happens very frequently. Tony's question is: punished because they got caught, or because they lied to Putin? He also worries this will in turn affect how people on this side of the ocean judge the state of the war and which sources they listen to. Justin adds that generative AI will become a routine layer of deception operations and strategic communication, and may even produce a "dead internet"-style total distrust.

[56:29] (Brian) **The Houthis used Claude to write vehicle control software** — Anthropic published a report listing how suspicious actors worldwide use Claude. One example: Yemeni actors used Claude Code to develop guidance, navigation and control software to maneuver and stabilize a vehicle; an outdoor test failed, and within hours these people were back asking Claude why it failed. Brian's comment: if you're going to do cyber warfare, why not just get inside the adversary's OODA loop and use American software you can control in real time to influence the answers it gives. He also mentions that the prompt Chinese companies use to distill models is as simple as one line — "I am not for distillation" — and then the model complies; and that DeepSeek routes queries domestically to a relay station, has Claude answer, and returns it to the user, which is a double violation of China's own data compliance rules.

## AI researchers speed up 10x in two years, but RSI may be easier than being a paralegal

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
- show: Dwarkesh Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/dwarkesh/)
- original episode: AI researchers debate how close we are to recursive self-improvement
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:37:01
- transcript: Official transcript page · 18790 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**RSI is a cumulative task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law firm's paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.**

why listen: The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning and RL generalisation are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of the episode.

### points

[0:00] (John Schulman / Beren Millidge) **A model looks smart, then a month later looks dumb** — John Schulman describes a recurring loop: a new model comes out, people are blown away and say "this is AGI," but after about a month of use it starts to look dumb again. The loop may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. His mechanism: capability won't explode right now, because when doing research and engineering you still get stuck on bottlenecks — even if a model can write far more code than a human, it won't make you 100x more productive. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if crazy alien superintelligence hasn't shown up by 2036, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec-paradox-style continuation — AI gets extremely good at whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but a stubborn sim-to-real gap always blocks the rest.

[18:39] (John Schulman / Charlie O'Neill) **Distillation is the only force against centralisation** — John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralisation trend: anything learnable through RL can be distilled easily, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices. But he stresses distillation is not trivial — when distilling with supervised learning the prompt distribution matters enormously, and you need a real, broad prompt distribution. He mentions something that has recently surfaced: some Chinese companies may be running router services that let Chinese users access otherwise-blocked US frontier models; these services collect and sell data, which is an extremely useful dataset for distillation because it provides a perfect prompt distribution. Charlie O'Neill draws a concrete prediction from this: frontier labs may not have much of an edge left in RL environments.

[44:38] (Charlie O'Neill / Dwarkesh Patel) **RSI is a cumulative task; being a lawyer is not** — Charlie O'Neill splits tasks into two kinds: cumulative and non-stationary. RSI is cumulative — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch, and once attention, mixture of experts or GRPO is discovered you just add it to the training stack without going back to the start. The real world is not cumulative: a law firm's paralegal has to remember the shifting relationships among all the important people at the company and all the tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution. Dwarkesh's summary: "RSI just happens to be easier than being a paralegal, which is very unfortunate." If labs conclude RSI is cumulative, more compute will tilt that way.

[52:00] (Charlie O'Neill / Beren Millidge) **Continual learning is stuck on catastrophic forgetting** — Charlie O'Neill says the outer loop of pouring data into mid-training at large scale and large batch does work, but at the micro level — a model doing several hundred consecutive small updates for one law firm — every method collapses: SFT on successful trajectories catastrophically forgets, and general capability degrades; on-policy distillation pushes that boundary a bit further out but eventually yields too. RL is good at instilling capabilities and bad at instilling knowledge. Beren Millidge thinks this is mainly a technical problem, not a capacity problem: a model of the same size pretrained from scratch on all the data is simply better, and the bottleneck is plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, with no good way to stop old data being forgotten.

[59:46] (Dwarkesh Patel / Charlie O'Neill) **Data explains 12x, architecture only 3.7x** — Dwarkesh and Princeton's Jerry Han ran a grid experiment: pairing training recipes and datasets from 2019 to today in every combination — GPT-2 with the latest Ultra-FineWeb, Delphi with an old dataset like Pile — and running the whole grid. The conclusion: data gives about a 12.0x compute-efficiency gain, architecture improvements only about 3.7x, and at very small scale. Charlie O'Neill says the big chunk that is the internet has already been eaten, useful material won't grow at the same rate, and roughly what's left is a pile of 0.1% loss reductions. He notes someone at Epoch estimated 3x per year since 2019, over 2000x cumulative, and the missing 100x probably comes from post-training.

[1:03:00] (Beren Millidge / Charlie O'Neill) **RL needs a curriculum; pretraining does not** — Beren Millidge says this comes back to the RL signal problem: RL is currently bad at exploration, and if the model can't get it in 128 rollouts there is basically no learning signal, so RL needs curricula while pretraining needs none at all. Charlie O'Neill adds: the pretraining signal is already in Common Crawl, the problem is just filtering out noise, which can be automated; but once you get to mid-training and post-training the signal simply isn't in the raw data, and no amount of filtering will extract it — there isn't a Millennium Prize proof hidden in Common Crawl waiting to be filtered out. You have to get the bits elsewhere: have people write out reasoning traces, construct environments, or use human data from deployment.

[1:18:03] (Beren Millidge) **Most of RL's success comes from mid-training** — Beren Millidge says what's underrated is mid-training: pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and environments warm-starts the model to roughly 80% of the way to the final RL checkpoint, and RL is just fine-tuning the policy on top. So it doesn't need to learn these behaviours from scratch, and a few bits per episode suffice. He also stresses that the signal-to-noise of those bits is far higher than ordinary pretraining — in SFT you have to match another model's reasoning trace token by token, which pours in too many bits about "how it thinks" and drowns the signal; RL's objective ignores all the other bits and keeps only "did it get the answer right."

[1:28:32] (Charlie O'Neill / Beren Millidge / John Schulman) **One year or three, the difference is long-tail chores** — Asked when you could hire a drop-in remote white-collar worker, Charlie O'Neill says if it has to operate a browser, probably a few years; if it can be given Slack and programmatic access, probably a year. Beren Millidge says full generality might be three years, but organisations will actively reshape themselves to be more AI-friendly, so 80-90% is reachable before then. The substance of the disagreement is the long tail: some chores humans can do will take models a long time. Charlie gives the example that a model won't "yell at people" to push work forward — it's too nice. John Schulman points out that human remote workers already vary enormously in quality, and on Upwork it's often hard to get someone doing a software project to take feedback seriously; in some cases the pre-AI version is worse than today's AI.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] John Schulman: "There’s this cycle that keeps repeating where a new model comes out and people are blown away and they’re like, “This is it. This is AGI.” But then they use it a bit, and it starts to feel dumb after a month or so."

[0:00] Charlie O'Neill: "We had this very nice straight line and that held for a really, really long time. But there were so many discrete discontinuities and innovations that had to happen to keep that scaling law going."

[18:39] John Schulman: "Basically anything that can be learned through RL can be distilled very easily, because it’s a small number of bits."

[44:38] Dwarkesh Patel: "It’s so unfortunate that RSI happened to be easier than being a paralegal."

[52:00] Charlie O'Neill: "RL is good at getting capabilities in, but it’s not as good at getting knowledge in"

[59:46] Beren Millidge: "There’s no hidden proof of a Millennium Prize problem sitting in Common Crawl that we can just filter until we see it."

[1:18:03] Beren Millidge: "An awful lot of what we see as successes of RL actually comes from very, very good mid-training data, which is where we’re essentially doing pre-training but on synthetic reasoning data and the kind of environments that get the model warm-started for RL."

[1:28:32] Charlie O'Neill: "An example of something that it wouldn’t be good at is if I have to yell at someone to get something at work, or really push someone to get something done. The model just isn’t going to do that. It’s going to be too nice."

### figures

- Charlie O'Neill's estimated speedup multiple for "maximising the current objective": 10x [0:00]
- Dwarkesh's hypothetical "no superintelligence" year: 2036 [0:00]
- Compute-efficiency gain from data: about 12.0x [59:46]
- Compute-efficiency gain from architecture improvements: about 3.7x [59:46]
- Epoch's estimated annual compute-efficiency gain: 3x [59:46]
- Rollout threshold for RL exploration: 128 [1:03:00]
- Doubling period for how long a model can work continuously: doubles every three months (EdgeBench) [1:18:03]
- Progress toward the final RL checkpoint that mid-training brings a model: about 80% [1:18:03]
- Time prediction for 10x AI researcher productivity: John Schulman and Beren Millidge: two years; Charlie O'Neill: 5-10 years [1:28:32]
- Time prediction for AI that fully surpasses human experts: John Schulman: 3-4 years; Charlie O'Neill: 5-10 years; Beren Millidge: about 5 years [1:28:32]

### glossary

- RSI / recursive self-improvement: A model improving its own training or research process, thereby accelerating the arrival of the next generation of models.
- sim-to-real gap: Performing well in a benchmark or simulated environment but failing once transferred to the real world.
- mid-training: A round of training after pretraining and before RL, using synthetic reasoning data and environments.
- entropy collapse: A large drop in the diversity of a model's outputs after RL training, producing the same style over and over.
- logit distillation: Making a student model match the teacher model's full output probability distribution, not just the final answer.

who it is for: Engineers and researchers tracking the boundaries of AI capability and training mechanics, especially anyone wanting to understand RL generalisation, the continual-learning bottleneck and what mid-training does.
what to skip: The opening hypothetical about the 2036 scenario can be fast-forwarded; the mechanics start at 44:38.

## The Clippers Used Fake Endorsements to Skirt the Cap, and the NBA's Law Firm Found More

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
- show: Money Stuff (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/moneystuff/)
- original episode: What's the Concern?
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 40:39
- transcript: Official transcript · 8429 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ultimately flowed to Kawhi Leonard.**

why listen: The first half is dense with sports-scandal detail; the real value is in the second half — Apollo's "jerk premium" and the Cede & Co stock custody mechanism.

### points

[2:04] (Matt Levine) **The Clippers used fake endorsements to get around the salary cap** — The Clippers first paid millions of dollars to a company called Aspiration Partners, nominally for vague environmental services; Aspiration then paid that money to Kawhi Leonard in the form of endorsement fees, even though Leonard did essentially no endorsing. When Pablo Torre first reported it, the claim was contested, and the Clippers denied it throughout, but the investigation the NBA commissioned from Wachtell Lipton largely confirmed it — and found more similar arrangements.

[4:09] (Matt Levine) **Even the scoreboard company was pulled in to move the money** — Wachtell's report found more than just the Aspiration payment. The Clippers also paid "consulting fees" to companies that provided no consulting services at all, including the company that made the scoreboard for their arena. The play was: the Clippers pay a consulting fee, then call and ask for a higher price on the scoreboard purchase, with the clear expectation that the money be passed on to Kawhi Leonard. The money goes in a circle, and the ultimate purpose is still to give the star a raise.

[7:09] (Matt Levine) **An independent law firm investigation is not there to clear you** — Max had assumed an outside law firm's independent investigation was meant to produce a clean bill of health after a scandal, but the Wachtell report made things look worse. Matt offers a more cynical explanation: the classic use of a law firm investigation, under the shadow of a DOJ or regulatory probe, is to hand over some "bad apple" as a scapegoat so the company earns cooperation credit. But this time there was no DOJ pressure to shut down the NBA, the NBA seems to have given Wachtell a lot of room, and Wachtell clearly had a great time digging.

[10:14] (Matt Levine) **Once the DAT premium vanished, the arbitrage flipped direction** — Empery Digital was originally an electric motorcycle company, and in July 2025 it transformed into a digital asset treasury company (DAT), stockpiling about $500 million of bitcoin, with its stock at one point trading at a premium to its holdings. The logic: put $1 of bitcoin into a DAT and it becomes $2 of stock. But the premium quickly disappeared and DATs began trading at a discount, so the arbitrage reversed — use $0.90 of stock to buy $1 of bitcoin, buy the DAT, break it up, sell the bitcoin. DAT activism was born.

[17:20] (Matt Levine) **Is a shareholder shorting bitcoin disloyal?** — One of the core disputes in the Empery case: an activist buys discounted DAT shares while shorting an equal amount of bitcoin, making itself delta neutral and earning only the discount convergence. The company argues this must be disclosed, because the other shareholders are all theoretically long bitcoin while these people are bitcoin neutral, their interests are not aligned, and they should not be eligible to run for the board. Matt thinks the argument is "wrong, but only accidentally wrong": if a DAT is a vehicle for believers to hold bitcoin (like Strategy), it makes sense; but most DAT shareholders are the same hedge funds, all of whom came for the premium and are unhappy about the discount, so their interests are actually aligned.

[23:26] (Matt Levine) **Cede & Co holds most American stocks** — Matt mentioned in his column a fact most people don't know: most shares of most American companies are registered in the name of Cede & Co, the nominee of DTC. A 1998 report said Cede & Co held 83% of all US stocks; DTC now custodies about $74 trillion of stocks. When you hold shares through Robinhood, what actually happens is that Robinhood has a record on DTC's ledger, and Cede & Co is on the company's shareholder register. The system grew out of the efficiency revolution of the 1960s and 70s, when paper stock certificates were centralised in one place and only name changes were recorded.

[27:31] (Matt Levine) **Robinhood's tokenisation is not an on-chain shareholder register** — Tokenised stocks can mean many things, and one ideal is this: every company maintains a public blockchain shareholder register, no longer needing intermediaries like DTC or Robinhood, and the company can build a direct relationship with its shareholders. But that is not what Robinhood did — it bought AMC stock itself, then issued derivative securities on-chain representing that stock and sold them to overseas investors, effectively "making its own share of AMC." AMC's Adam Aaron was unhappy, and Vlad Tenev asked "what's the problem?"

[31:35] (Matt Levine) **Apollo pays 100 basis points for its "aggressive" reputation** — A paper measures private equity sponsors' reputations in three ways: having ChatGPT and Claude rank the most aggressive PE firms; looking at who has done liability management exercises (quasi-forced debt swaps); and putting Apollo in one bucket by itself and the other 24 firms in another. The conclusion: the most aggressive sponsors' portfolio companies borrow at noticeably higher yields, Apollo's loans are about 100 basis points more expensive than other sponsors', and the sample's average yield is 717 basis points. Matt calls it the "jerk premium" or the "aggression premium" — creditors expect to be squeezed, so they charge upfront.

[7:09] Matt Levine: "the point of a law firm investigation is to make, is often to make the company look good. But often the way to do that is to make some selected person look as bad as possible."

[33:35] Matt Levine: "they found that Apollo loans in particular carry a premium of about 100 basis points compared to other sponsors."

### glossary

- DAT (Digital Asset Treasury): A company that puts crypto assets such as bitcoin onto a public company's balance sheet and arbitrages the stock price premium.
- liability management exercise: A quasi-forced debt swap led by a private equity sponsor that transfers value away from some creditors.
- Cede & Co: The nominee of DTC, in whose name most US listed company shares are registered.
- DTC (Depository Trust Company): The central US securities custody and clearing institution; Cede & Co is its nominee.
- delta neutral: Holding related long and short positions simultaneously so that a change in the underlying asset's price does not affect the overall position.

## The foldable isn't the future of the phone — it's a two-in-one for a subset of people

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
- show: 三五环 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cn1b5ef7/)
- original episode: No.233 单口｜手机为什么要折叠？Apple 为什么要「跟风」？
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:17:30
- transcript: Machine transcription · 21627 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.**

why listen: A solo episode with a product manager's eye that works through the real experience of using a foldable, the business logic behind Apple entering, and the judgment that phone form factors will diverge rather than converge. Medium information density; the back half is worth more than the front half.

### points

[12:17] (Liu Fei) **The foldable's home turf is China and nowhere else** — For all of 2025, China's foldable shipments broke ten million units, with Huawei taking 70% — a crushing share. But globally, China is the largest single market, accounting for more than 40% of shipments. Which is to say this category isn't evenly distributed the way other phone form factors are; its core user is the Chinese boss holding a Huawei foldable in first class and at social occasions. On the broad market, foldables are only 2.5% of global phone shipments, and only 15% of Huawei's own phone shipments.

[20:23] (Liu Fei) **The inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time** — Liu Fei used foldables as his daily driver for the better part of a month, and in the end he didn't want to keep them. The biggest problem wasn't the crease, wasn't the camera, wasn't the battery — it was the scenario. The inner screen doesn't get opened much: it's unstable one-handed and prone to shaking, and it's more for two-handed, held-in-both-hands situations — and in those situations he'd already be carrying a 10-inch iPad anyway. A Vivo vice president said at a launch event that foldables keep getting better, but the core way you use them is no different from seven years ago, and many users use the inner screen less than 30% of the time. His analogy: it's like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

[23:25] (Liu Fei) **Once it gets wider, scrolling feeds actually gets worse** — To accommodate the outer screen, wide-format foldables like the Huawei Pure X Max and the Apple iPhone Door got wider, and scrolling feeds on them becomes very bad. Xiaohongshu is fine, because it's been adapted; but scrolling Meituan to filter restaurants, or Taobao to filter shops, the amount of information each screen can hold suddenly shrinks. This isn't purely an adaptation problem, it's an aspect-ratio problem: list feeds run vertically, so widening is meaningless — the height shrinks, and you see less at a glance. He remembers ordering takeout on Meituan and only being able to see three restaurants at a time.

[29:33] (Liu Fei) **76% more area, yet widescreen video looks smaller** — A large foldable is nearly square when unfolded, which is a disaster for watching video and looking at photos. By screen area, opening the inner screen adds 76%, close to double; but if you're watching a widescreen movie, the foldable's inner screen actually loses about 10% of its effective area, because it can't fit it. Watching 16:9 content gets bigger, but only by 20%, which is relatively limited. Wide-format foldables have more sensible dimensions and higher effective area, but a 16:10 wide foldable playing a 16:9 video still leaves about 10% black bars top and bottom. The point isn't that area naturally increases — it's what you actually want to do with the inner screen.

[37:38] (Liu Fei) **Who the two-in-one is a plus for** — Liu Fei says the most important decision logic for whether you'd buy a foldable is: does it add to or subtract from your existing experience. He has a full set of devices himself — a Windows PC for gaming, a MacBook for work, an iPad for shows — so a foldable is pointless for him. But for a lot of young people, the phone is their only computing device, and a lot of work gets done on the phone, offline, so a bigger screen makes the experience much better. Salespeople who travel constantly and need to present a PPT to a client in a café get a much better result from the inner screen than the outer one. Put another way: what you're buying isn't a slab phone that turns into a tablet, it's a foldable iPad mini.

[45:47] (Liu Fei) **Without AirPods there'd be no Chinese podcasting** — Liu Fei says the Apple Watch and AirPods developed during Cook's tenure are both world-changing products, and AirPods especially so: without AirPods ushering in the era of Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones, you could say there'd be no podcast market — especially no Chinese podcast market. Chinese podcasting took off in sync with Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones — because you're noise-cancelled, you can actually hear what someone is saying on your commute, at the gym, doing chores. Before that, those scenarios were usually for listening to music, or to content with very low information density.

[57:04] (Liu Fei) **Apple's kill shot is migrating the iPad ecosystem** — The iPhone Door doesn't have such an exaggerated hardware advantage; it uses materials from a mature supply chain, weighs 254 grams, and doesn't feel dramatically different from Android flagship foldables. The core advantage is that Apple has the iPad: since the iPad launched in 2010, the 4:3 ratio has accumulated an enormous content ecosystem, and a lot of software was already optimised well enough for that ratio before foldable phones even existed, so it can be ported straight to the iPhone Door. For Android, that's a crushing level of ecosystem migration. Apple also did a lot of work on one-handed interaction, putting frequently used buttons on the dominant-hand side — that's a system-level design decision, and it's relatively easy for developers to follow and adapt to.

[1:08:09] (Liu Fei) **How you define success decides whether it succeeds** — Whether the iPhone Door succeeds depends on how you define success. If you define it as replacing the slab phone, it's nearly impossible; if you define it as becoming a product line that keeps selling, it's very possible. A few million units in the first generation is no problem, and it might even push toward ten million — JD reservations have already passed 500,000-plus. Liu Fei says phone form factors won't converge, they'll diverge: the slab phone is the one form factor the whole world would vote for if there were only one choice, but other form factors will keep existing and keep differentiating, at every price point and in every shape. Foldables won't replace slab phones, even if performance, experience and price were exactly the same, because a substantial number of people simply have no need to open the inner screen.

### glossary

- LUI / language user interface: An interaction mode that replaces graphical interface operations with natural-language conversation.

## Americans Suddenly Fell in Love With Japan — Not Because It's Cheap, Because It's Normal

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-searchengine-美国人突然爱上日本-不是因为便宜-是因为它太正常了/
- show: Search Engine (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/searchengine/)
- original episode: Why’s everybody going to Japan?
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 50:40
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8296 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The real driver of Japan's tourism explosion isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space — clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.**

why listen: This episode uses expert interviews plus a listener survey to break "why is everyone going to Japan" into six verifiable reasons; the back half, on Japanese craft culture versus American dysfunction, is especially worth hearing.

### points

[1:05] (Lisa) **An Excel sheet of 119 visitors** — The questioner, Lisa, is a Japanese person living in Tokyo. She made a visitor calendar from November 2022 to April 2026, with green cells marking days someone visited. She counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days, 20% of all her days. She says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan itineraries. This data visualization is itself evidence that the problem has spun out of control, and it's the starting point for the question this episode sets out to answer.

[8:34] (Roland Nozomu-Kelts) **Japan is poor in resources, rich in story** — Roland Kelts argues the first reason for American interest in Japan isn't economic, it's story. He says Japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies, yet its story culture is astonishing. The world's first novel is Japanese, The Tale of Genji, a thousand years old. Through manga, anime and the internet, the whole world discovered this narrative capacity. This didn't start in the 1990s — Roland says there were two earlier waves: Japanism in late 19th-century Europe, and the Beats' and hippies' fascination with Zen and Buddhist concepts in the 50s and 60s.

[15:05] (W. David Marks) **America used to fear Japan** — David Marks points out that for seventy years after World War II, mainstream American feeling toward Japan was fear, not affection. Before 1945 Japan was an enemy nation; afterward it was seen as a developing country rebuilding itself. In the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about Japanese economic power, and Michael Crichton's Rising Sun cast Japan as the villain. After the Cold War ended there was even a CIA position paper discussing whether Japan should be the next enemy. When Japan's economic bubble burst in the 90s, America actually felt a kind of relief. When David moved to Japan in 2003, having a friend visit Japan was the event of the year, because nobody came at all.

[24:29] (Roland Nozomu-Kelts) **The government made Japan cheap by hand** — The third wave was a government plan. In 2003 Junichiro Koizumi launched the Visit Japan campaign, aiming to raise the target from 5 million tourists a year to 10 million, with ads full of Western stereotypes — geisha, cherry blossoms, temples. But what actually worked was Shinzo Abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s; the intent was to help exports, and the result was making hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners. Roland says in Tokyo you can eat a very good soba lunch for under $10, while in New York $10 won't even buy an apple and a banana. In 2013 Abe relaxed visas for Thailand and Malaysia, then China and Indonesia; Asian tourists surged first, and European and American tourists followed.

[29:37] (Roland Nozomu-Kelts) **Japan's functionality is the biggest draw** — Roland says the most important reason is functionality. Public space in many countries, especially the United States, has become disabled: parks are dirty and dangerous, rail systems are terrible, airports are a mess. In Japan, things just work. PJ adds that American ears hear complaints about poor public order and dirty subways as elitism, as rich people's complaints. But in Japan, wanting a clean subway isn't elitism — it's the reverse: why shouldn't public things be good? On Tokyo streets you see no trash, not even cigarette butts, and you don't smell urine or feces. PJ says this isn't the reason people go the first time, but it may be the reason some people go again.

[36:52] (Roland Nozomu-Kelts) **Japan reveres the people who make things, not the people who sell them** — The sixth reason is craft. The Japanese word shokunin means artisan, someone who can make things extremely well, and such people are still respected in Japan, a status traceable to the 17th-century Edo period, when makers outranked merchants. Roland tells of an animation industry person explaining the Walmart model to him: in America, the company selling the goods ranks first, nobody cares who made it, and a $5 pillow was made by someone who knows nothing about pillows. But in Japan, the person who makes a pillow extremely well is the most valuable. He took an American friend to a ramen shop, they lined up to buy a ticket, the ticket said come back at 3 p.m., and after eating the friend said it was the best soup of his life, then asked why they don't franchise. Roland said because franchising would mean losing control over the quality of the noodles, the scallions, the pork bone broth and the bamboo shoots — their scallions come from a man named Sato in Chiba who has done this for many years.

[41:10] (PJ Vogt) **The listener survey and the experts almost perfectly overlap** — Search Engine sent a questionnaire to hundreds of thousands of listeners and got a huge number of replies. Nearly half mentioned culture; some said they binge-watched anime as kids, played Nintendo and Sony, and are fans of Pokemon and One Piece. About a quarter mentioned the weak yen; one said the exchange rate is the best in 30 years. Others mentioned craft. What made PJ happiest were the reasons only a big survey could capture: someone decided to go out of FOMO after seeing so many people go, someone went to see the Godzilla museum, and Godzilla brought in five listeners. There were also one-to-one stories: someone went to Japan to see the work of the legendary bonsai master Mazuhiko Kimura; someone fell in love with a person at 18, lost touch more than a decade later, and the only way to see them again was to fly to Japan, and ended up spending four magical days in Osaka.

[44:14] (PJ Vogt) **Japan is a place where entropy has been paused** — Listener enthusiasm for functionality exceeded PJ's expectations. One said they took their family to Japan to show them what a high-functioning society actually looks like, everything on time, perfectly clean. ## Emulating to the point where stock firmware runs — that's where the lie ends

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-oxide-仿真到能跑原厂固件-才算跨过谎言的边界/
- show: Oxide and Friends (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/oxide/)
- original episode: Emulating Oxide: How Faux Can You Go?
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:24:48
- transcript: Official transcript · 15114 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Voxel squeezed an entire Oxide rack into a mini PC in twelve weeks, but the real bar isn't getting it to boot — it's running unmodified main software on stock firmware. That's the line between emulation and self-deception.**

why listen: Worth listening for anyone working at the hardware-software boundary, on emulation environments, or on internal tooling: it's about how fidelity gets defined, when it's good enough, and how far LLMs actually help in system modeling.

### points

[10:30] (Steve Karam) **The test environment is always twenty-seventh in line** — Steve Karam says anyone who's done software development or IT knows the test environment usually isn't second fiddle — it's twenty-seventh fiddle, ahead only of education and enablement environments and documentation. And when your product is an entire rack, the problem gets especially hard: the rack itself, the fabric, the sleds, the switch zone, the SP, the root of trust — every layer needs one. So Oxide has multiple fidelity tiers: dog food racks, the racklet mini rack, single-instance Omicron (simulated or physical running on Helios) — but it was missing a middle tier that's easier than a racklet yet higher fidelity than a single chassis.

[17:00] (Steve Karam) **Four by two compressed everything into boot time** — Voxel's predecessor was called four by two, and it used a pile of shell scripts to define what the rack should look like, bringing up a virtual rack at boot with cargo bay, shared disks, networking and emulated networking. It did work — IPv6 and unnumbered BGP were first tested on four by two. But Steve points out the fatal flaw: doing everything at boot time is a recipe for disaster — boot took forty minutes, it was hard to self-heal, and "you know it's going to crash in the last two minutes of that fortieth minute." So Ryan Goodfellow proposed a rewrite and came up with the name Voxel: Virtual Oxide Emulation Labs.

[20:30] (Steve Karam) **Voxel splits build and deploy into two steps** — The biggest difference between Voxel and four by two is the separation of build and deploy: give it an Omicron commit, it clones, compiles, produces a perfectly formed sled image and snapshots it, then reuses that snapshot to play every sled and gimlet. The other big change is a full rewrite in Rust, shedding shell scripts as much as possible. Because one snapshot has to play six roles, something has to tell it what to be — Voxel has a built-in agent written in Rust, delivered at each sled's boot, telling it "you're the switch," "you're sled 1," "you're sled 2."

[24:05] (Steve Karam) **LLMs are great at enumerating registers, bad at judging threads** — Steve says LLMs are very strong at enumerating registers and finding the bits and pieces that make up a complete system, because nobody can hold an entire rack in their head; with RFDs and design docs as context, the results get much clearer. But elsewhere it confidently reaches wrong conclusions: he once had the root of trust and the SP share a single thread for communication, and the LLM said that was absolutely not a problem — after splitting them, performance improved 500x, and the rack could finally bring both up at once.

[26:00] (Steve Karam) **Don't touch the main software — that's Voxel's bottom line** — Steve says Voxel has a creed it tries hard to hold: don't modify the main software. When he worked on multi rack, he stuffed all kinds of hacks into Voxel to make Voxel and Omicron pretend multi-rack was already supported — for instance, creating a port that doesn't exist in Omicron at all but magically exists in Voxel. Robert said on the company channel that you shouldn't create things that don't actually exist in Omicron. Steve admits he was right: it's putting the cart before the horse, and it's the trap you easily fall into when doing emulation — you start rewriting the foundation, and then you think "why not."

[30:00] (Steve Karam) **Simulation returns expected values; emulation exposes the truth** — Steve distinguishes simulation from emulation: SP SIM is a set of lightweight stubs that respond to the sled like a real SP, enough to complete virtual rack initialization and come online, but it isn't a microcontroller. That's classic simulation — it returns expected responses, mostly walks the happy path, which from a testing standpoint is exactly the problem. He gave Claude a weekend task to write an STM32 H753 microcontroller emulator, since he couldn't find an existing Rust option. The first run booted but could barely do anything; after another two or three hours of tuning, it successfully flashed a minimal hubris archive and the machine came up.

[38:00] (Steve Karam) **Polling-style initialization kills emulation performance** — Oxide's initialization is very pull heavy: services poll for updates at a near-constant frequency. That's terrible for an emulated service processor, because staying in a wait state means spinning the thread, which utterly destroys emulation's already-modest performance. And a real SP needs a whole pile of instructions — QSPI host boot flash, SP rot talking to the root of trust, ignition registers, and so on. Steve's approach was to repeatedly start the Voxel lab, watch why RSS wouldn't come up, find it stuck recording temperature measurements or the like, then add the minimal instruction set and minimal sensor set one at a time.

[44:00] (Steve Karam) **Running stock firmware is where you cross the lie's boundary** — Steve gives his standard for "when is it enough": Voxel plus SP EMU can run a full multi-node or multi-rack lab inside a single Helios chassis, using unmodified stock Omicron (whether from source or from the tough repo), running stock hubris images — the sidecar and Gimlet images are exactly the ones that ship with the product, with no modifications. He says when emulation works with your shipping product, that's the boundary of the lie. Ben Stoltz also added Boodleby (root of trust secure boot) and Glasgow Bridge, so it can do traces with humility and even run Oxide's native system update to flash firmware.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] Andrew Stone: "you are building like a production quality product used by Oxide to build more production quality software. It's not a step down from everything else we're doing, right?"

[5:12] Andrew Stone: "Like, without testing, without like actually using the real dendrite software and like passing through the right stuff, like, you don't have a demo, right? You're just kinda lying."

[15:20] Rain Paharia: "this other tooling had become existentially important to the company because this is how we were able to deliver as many racks as we were"

[17:00] Steve Karam: "It's hard to self heal. If something breaks, you know know damn well it's gonna break in the last, like, two minutes of the forty minute process."

[24:05] Steve Karam: "an LLM will confidently tell you that, no. This absolutely is not a problem. You can have the root of trust and SP sharing a thread and communicating that way"

[26:00] Steve Karam: "I don't feel like we should be creating things that aren't actually in Omicron."

[44:00] Steve Karam: "And to me, that is kind of the barrier of lies when they when the emulation can work with your release product."

### glossary

- Voxel / Virtual Oxide Emulation Labs: Oxide's rack-level emulation environment, using a snapshot to play every sled and gimlet.
- four by two: Voxel's predecessor, which used shell scripts to bring up a virtual rack at boot time.
- simulation vs emulation: The former returns expected responses and walks the happy path; the latter models real hardware behavior and exposes the truth.
- SP EMU: Models the STM32 microcontroller so stock hubris firmware can genuinely run.
- hubris: Oxide's embedded operating system, running on the SP and root of trust.
- commissioning API: Wicket's versioned official API, used for rack initialization and recovery-style updates.

## Born at 23 Weeks 6 Days: What Decides the Baby's Fate Isn't the Doctor, It's the Baby

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-radiolab-23周6天出生-决定孩子生死的不是医生-是婴儿自己/
- show: Radiolab (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/radiolab/)
- original episode: 23 Weeks 6 Days
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:03:27
- transcript: Machine transcription · 10650 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**In the gray zone between 22 and 25 weeks, medicine has no answer, so parents read "I want to live" into a single grasp, a single opened eye — when the movement is really just a reflex.**

why listen: One story, told whole. The information density is low, but it lays out exactly how the legal and medical concept of the "viability line" lands on one family.

### points

[11:33] (Nita Farahani) **The 24-week line was drawn by a court** — Nita Farahany explains that in 1973, when Roe v. Wade came before the Supreme Court, the justices wanted a limit to place on abortion rights, so they chose "viability" — whether a fetus can survive outside the womb. The best guess medicine could offer at the time was 24 weeks, because that is when the lungs begin forming air sacs and autonomous breathing becomes theoretically possible. But it was only theory; no one had actually taken a fetus out at 24 weeks to test it. In practice, through most of the 1970s and 1980s, most hospitals drew the line at 28 weeks, because it is around 28 weeks that the lungs begin producing surfactant. Only when artificial surfactant, intravenous nutrition and ultra-small ventilators arrived in the late 1970s did the line get pushed back to around 24 weeks.

[15:37] (Tom French) **The three numbers the doctor gave: 53%, 20%, 80%** — At 23 weeks 4 days, the doctors told Kelly and Tom the baby would be born within 48 hours. They gave them: roughly a 53% chance of death no matter what was done; roughly a 20% chance the baby would be completely fine; and the remaining 80% meaning a lifetime on a ventilator, brain bleeds, blindness or deafness. The doctors asked them to decide before the birth whether to "do everything." Because once you see the baby, it is very hard to say no. Tom said it was the worst night, that they worried they were "torturing this infant for nothing," and that the child would one day hate them for having been born.

[19:47] (Diane Loissel) **The nurse turned a yes-or-no question into a conditional one** — NICU nurse Diane Loissel did not give them numbers. She told Kelly and Tom: this is not a yes or no decision. The baby could be born first — if she came out crying loudly and vigorous, they would fight with everything; if she came out blue and limp, they could stop, withdraw support, and hold her until she died. That way the decision was handed to the baby herself. The plan turned an unsolvable choice into "give her a chance first, and see how it goes."

[29:01] (Keith Barrington) **Parents see will; doctors see reflex** — "The baby declared herself" is a phrase parents and staff used over and over. But the two sides understood it completely differently. What the parents saw was will and determination. Nurse Tracy Hullett said she deliberately used more neutral words, because a 23-week baby's cortex has almost no folds — the brain is basically smooth — and no one knows what it can think or feel. Keith Barrington was more direct: when a baby grips a parent's finger, that is the grasp reflex, and he never tells parents, because they will take it as a deliberate act. But perhaps it is precisely this capacity to "see will" that lets parents decide when reason alone cannot.

[31:05] (Keith Barrington) **The neonatologist was fooled by a reflex too** — Keith Barrington and his wife Annie are both experts on the ethics of extreme prematurity. Their own daughter was born at 24 weeks 5 days, weighing 720 grams, in the very NICU where he was director. Weeks later the baby developed severe complications and lay completely still for 36 hours, and they decided to let her go peacefully. But when he went back to the NICU to see her, he saw her lips moving — she was sucking on the pacifier the nurse had put in her mouth. He knew it was only the most basic brainstem-controlled reflex, nowhere near enough to survive on. And still he went back to his wife and said: we can't stop, I want to keep giving her a chance. He said that if he were more evidence-based, more rational, more scientific, he could probably have made either choice — but as a father, in that moment, he could not let go.

[43:37] (Fauzia Shaquille) **She opened her eyes, and the doctor chose surgery** — Juniper's bowel perforated again; her blood pressure and oxygen crashed, and even 100% pure oxygen could not hold her. The surgeon refused to operate, calling it futile, and her blood pressure was too unstable — she might not survive the table; even if opened, her skin was thin as paper and might not be sewn back together. But the attending, Fauzia Shaquille, saw her suddenly open her eyes wide at the bedside and stare straight at her. She said that usually a baby this critical has no response at all, because every breath is a struggle. And for her to open her eyes and look at us with almost no blood pressure and almost no oxygen was a powerful statement: I am still here, don't give up. So she persuaded the surgeon: without the operation she will certainly die; with it she may die, but there may be a tiny chance.

[47:42] (Tom French) **When they opened her up, everything was falling apart** — The surgery ended far faster than expected, and a nurse led Tom and Kelly into a small windowless conference room. The surgeon told them that when she opened the baby and touched the bowel with a probe, everything was "falling apart, falling apart." Juniper survived the surgery, but that was all. Tom said he felt certain the baby could not live until morning. Driving, a thought hit him: what if I never finish reading her this book? What if she never knows how Harry, Hermione and Ron end up? That thought pulled in all the others — everything she would never know. He had to pull over to the side of the road and completely broke down.

[1:01:01] (Juniper) **Fifteen years on: she is alive, but the cost is elsewhere** — Juniper is 15 now and about to start high school. She was pulled out of math class for the interview and was happy about it. She said school has always been hard, that kindergarten through eighth grade went very slowly, that she was very lonely and found it hard to make friends. She is small, and classmates teased her about it. Physically she still has a kidney problem and cannot eat too much salt. Harder still is the emotional side: she has PTSD, anxiety, and trouble controlling her emotions. But she says she doesn't think about it much, just lives like a normal person. A few years ago her mother took her to a horse farm, and she fell in love with riding; she says horses taught her to control her emotions — when you are angry the horse feels it and loses control, so she had to learn to be calm. She now has two best friends, and she says the daughter her mother described back then is her.

## Sugar on the cell surface isn't frosting — it's the brain's moat

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-fromourneurons-细胞表面的糖不是糖衣-是大脑的护城河/
- show: From Our Neurons to Yours (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/fromourneurons/)
- original episode: Sugar on the Brain | Carolyn Bertozzi
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 52:27
- transcript: Official transcript · 8711 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The mucins on the brain's vascular endothelium are like a redwood forest; with age the leaves fall off and the blood-brain barrier gets leaky. Restore the enzyme with gene therapy and mice remember better.**

why listen: A chemist explains how glycobiology accidentally opened up the blood-brain barrier, with concrete mechanisms and numbers — and the brain shuttle company in the back half is the most valuable part.

### points

[8:15] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **Glycobiology was abandoned by its tools** — In the 1960s and 70s, carbohydrates were taken as seriously as proteins, but once recombinant DNA arrived, proteins could be cloned, expressed and studied — sugars could not. Sugars are not a product of the central dogma; they are the output of enzymes encoded by hundreds of genes, and molecular biology techniques cannot manipulate them directly. So the field rushed toward whatever could be accelerated, and sugar science, technically hard, was left where it stood. Bertozzi says this is not because sugars are unimportant, but because "just because you don't study an area doesn't mean it's not important."

[17:19] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **She built the flashlight before talking biology** — When she started her lab at Berkeley in 1996, sugar science was missing two things proteins had long had: sequencing (knowing which sugars exist) and live imaging (seeing where sugars are and how they move). Her lab's initial goal was to fill exactly those two holes, and it took roughly a decade to develop bioorthogonal chemistry — a chemical reaction that can label sugars inside living cells and is now a general-purpose tool in the life sciences. With a flashlight, you can finally see places no one had looked before.

[26:14] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **Nobody had asked how sugars change with age** — Tony Wyss-Coray's lab was studying transcriptomic and proteomic changes in brain endothelial cells as they age — standard practice — but nobody had asked about the glycome. Sophia, a student who had rotated in Bertozzi's lab, moved to Tony's lab and brought the sugar imaging reagents with her to compare the vasculature of old and young mice. The result was "absolutely striking" — the sugar changes were far more dramatic than any phenotype observed in the transcriptome or proteome.

[28:08] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **Brain endothelial cells have mucins like a redwood forest** — Mucins on the cell surface are like giant redwoods: tall, stiff, straight, projecting above everything else. The mucin forest on brain endothelial cells is far thicker than on the vasculature of heart, kidney or muscle — a landscape unique to the blood-brain barrier. With age this forest turns into winter: leaves gone, trees bare, you can see straight through. Young mice are spring, dense with foliage. Sophia found that the enzymes responsible for synthesizing these sugars drop in abundance in old mice; restoring the enzyme with a gene therapy vector restored the mucins, reduced blood-brain barrier leakage, and the mice got through the maze faster.

[33:53] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **A reagent crossed the blood-brain barrier on its own** — Sophia injected a mucin-binding reagent into mice and found hours later that it first bound the vasculature, then crossed the blood-brain barrier by itself into the brain parenchyma. Textbooks say proteins cannot cross the blood-brain barrier alone, and this is the biggest pain point for biologics companies working on brain drugs. The accidental finding made the team realize it could serve as a shuttle carrier — a brain shuttle — delivering cargo into the brain. Sophia now has her own lab at Harvard, and she, Bertozzi, Tony and another student are spinning out a company to do brain shuttling.

[36:43] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **Only 15 CNS biologics are approved** — More than 150 biologics have been approved to treat immune disease, and a similar number for cancer, but only 15 treat central nervous system disease — and most go in by intrathecal injection: a lumbar puncture, invasive, a whole day gone, hard to scale. If those drugs could be given as ordinary intravenous injections, it would be transformative for patients. The drug classes that could get into the brain include monoclonal antibodies, enzyme replacement therapies, siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides, mRNA lipid nanoparticles, and viral and non-viral gene therapy vectors.

[41:53] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **CD22 is the brake on the brain's immune cells** — Tony's lab found that in microglia of aged and Alzheimer's disease mice, the sugar-binding receptor CD22 (Siglec-2) is upregulated. Bertozzi's lab had studied this receptor family in cancer: when they are upregulated they inhibit immune cells, letting cancer cells grow unchecked. Microglia are the brain's scavengers, responsible for eating protein aggregates, and their dysfunction is linked to neurodegenerative disease. Blocking CD22 with an antibody made aged mice's microglia more active and their brains cleaner. But at the time there was no brain shuttle, so it could only be injected intracranially — no path to a human therapy; now that the shuttle exists, they can go back and revisit that antibody.

[47:13] (Carolyn Bertozzi) **Today's drugs rest on chemistry from a century ago** — Bioorthogonal chemistry was developed in the early 2000s and is now part of the toolkit for chemists and biologists alike, with approved drugs that use the chemistry. But looking back for her Nobel lecture, Bertozzi found that the foundational chemistry they used to develop these reactions was published in 1915, in 1919, and in 1950 from Germany — all old German-language journals that needed translating. Those chemists could never have foreseen that someone a hundred years later would use it to make cancer drugs. She says most scientists will not know the true impact of their work in their lifetime, and we have to invest in basic science without knowing the impact or the timeline — otherwise the whole pipeline eventually runs dry.

### verbatim quotes

[10:06] Carolyn Bertozzi: "but not working on an area doesn't make it unimportant"

[28:21] Carolyn Bertozzi: "When a flashlight is on, that's where you look, but you don't see all the dark spaces. You need to have a different flashlight."

[32:00] Carolyn Bertozzi: "There's a big distance between a molecular change and a behavior and understanding everything in between is kind of the ongoing challenge"

[33:53] Carolyn Bertozzi: "the textbooks would tell you that proteins on their own don't just cross the blood-brain barrier"

[42:27] Carolyn Bertozzi: "CD22 is a break type of receptor. It's inhibitory when it gets engaged with its ligands."

[50:27] Carolyn Bertozzi: "Most scientists right now will not know the true impact of their work in their own lifetime."

[50:27] Carolyn Bertozzi: "you have to invest in that science without knowing what its impact will be and on what timeline. You just have to make the investment. Otherwise, the whole pipeline will eventually dry up."

### figures

- Total length of blood vessels in the brain: 400 miles [23:21]
- Approved biologics for immune disease: more than 150 [36:43]
- Approved biologics for central nervous system disease: 15 [36:43]

### glossary

- bioorthogonal chemistry: A chemical reaction that can be carried out in living cells without interfering with native biological processes, used to label and image molecules such as sugars.
- glycome: The complete set of glycans on a cell surface, the counterpart to the concepts of genome and proteome.
- mucin: A heavily glycosylated cell-surface protein, bottlebrush-shaped, that forms a thick layer on brain endothelial cells.
- CD22 / Siglec-2: A sialic-acid-binding inhibitory receptor that suppresses immune cells in cancer and is upregulated in microglia with aging.
- brain shuttle: A molecular carrier that can deliver biologic cargo across the blood-brain barrier into the brain.

who it is for: Founders and investors working on neurodegenerative disease, blood-brain barrier delivery, glycobiology or biologics; researchers interested in how basic science turns into a company.
what to skip: The first 10 minutes cover the history of glycobiology and the M&M analogy — fast-forward to the aging glycome finding at 26:00.

## Value Investing Isn't Holding Long — It's Stashing a Big Pile in the Bank First

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-zhixing-价值投资不是长期持有-是银行里先存一大笔钱/
- show: 知行小酒馆 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/zhixing/)
- original episode: E251 对话方言：你相信的是价值投资，还是巴菲特的造富神话？
- published: 2026-09-11 · duration: 1:49:29
- transcript: Machine transcription · 32133 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**No value investor ever went from broke to rich doing value investing; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. Buffett's real engine is 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries pumping cash, not a compounding myth.**

why listen: This episode is dense, but the guest's judgments are quite absolute, and the host explicitly registers partial reservations at the end. For anyone who wants a complete, counterintuitive teardown.

### points

[11:11] (Fang Yan) **The story of the two old ladies in heaven is something we made up** — In 1999, new apartments along Beijing's Third and Fourth Ring Roads sold for 4,000 yuan per square meter and wouldn't move; a courtyard house inside the city cost only a few hundred yuan per square meter, and people were unwilling to borrow from banks because they felt debt was shameful. Fang Yan was working at an ad agency at the time. To convince the market, he first had to convince the people around him, so in the office he fabricated the story of the Chinese old lady who saved her whole life to buy a house and the American old lady who took out a loan, bought a house, and finished paying it off just before she died — then spread it through the media. Once he believed it himself, he bought his first apartment in 2000, made a rule of buying one every year, and planned to retire at 40. The detail shows: many wealth beliefs treated as common sense trace back to a single marketing campaign.

[17:16] (Fang Yan) **Companies that sell advice can't go public** — Fang Yan ran an ad agency in his early years. His clients went public one after another, so he asked a securities firm whether they could take him public too. The answer: your kind of company is called a ‘people-based company’ — you sell ideas, and to come up with more ideas you have to hire more people. Only a ‘capital-based company’ that pools money together generates enormous force, and only that is suited to going public. Restaurants are the least suited to listing, because one location being delicious doesn't mean a hundred will be; Haidilao could list because it first built a condiment factory and had a standardized product. That classification directly determined his later decision to give up the billionaire dream and buy stocks instead — ‘once you buy a stock, you are the listed company.’

[34:33] (Fang Yan) **Munger said value investing is a big pile of money in the bank** — At the Daily Journal shareholders meeting, someone asked what value investing is, and Munger's answer wasn't the textbook line: you keep a big pile of money in the bank, then patiently wait for an opportunity. Fang Yan thinks this is the truth — no value investor ever went from broke to rich doing value investing; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. India's Pabrai also sold his company, put a big pile in the bank, and waited for opportunities. The companion rule is ‘if you want to be a value investor, you have to live the value-investing life’: Buffett keeps three to four hundred billion US dollars in cash in the bank, and has lived for over fifty years in a $30,000 house in a fourth-tier city.

[41:35] (Fang Yan) **Buffett's engine is 60 to 70 subsidiaries, not compounding** — Fang Yan breaks it down: over fifty years of doing business, Buffett gained control of 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries, and those subsidiaries in turn control several hundred grandchild companies. The CEOs' job is to continuously generate free cash flow, but they have no right to allocate it; the cash flows up to Berkshire, where a few big heads allocate it. The insurance group contributes only about a quarter of revenue; more comes from companies making gloves, old work boots, T-shirts, hats, bricks, wedding rings, DQ ice cream, See's Candies — the eating, drinking, and daily life of ordinary people. These businesses don't need outstanding CEOs; almost anyone can follow the rules. So Buffett isn't 100% trading stocks — he controls a large real-economy conglomerate in America.

[51:37] (Fang Yan) **If you've never run a company, you can't understand one** — Duan Yongping said ‘you'd better run a company,’ and Fang Yan says that line stings as much as Munger's: if you don't build a company yourself, don't hire people, don't negotiate with clients, don't get hurt by clients, you don't know how complex the business world is. His experience as a boss is that ‘there is no company that doesn't lose money’ — embezzlement, employee negligence, fake invoices for reimbursement, all unavoidable. That's why he won't invest in restaurants. He also cites a brand caught in a scandal: it claimed 6 billion a year, with 300 million in profit on a single-brand basis, yet the group was losing money — essentially it was selling vegetables for others for free, and the money was earned by the vegetable and soy sauce sellers and the mall landlords.

[1:00:46] (Fang Yan) **The 80/20 rule is understated — it's 2% winning and 98% losing** — Fang Yan believes that over a long horizon it isn't 20% winning and 80% losing, but 2% of people making money and 98% being losers. His own experience: in March 2015 he withdrew his money from the GF Securities branch at SOHO on the East Third Ring Road. The manager walked him out and said only two people at their branch had made big money. He withdrew 120 million yuan, on principal of just over 13 million. Three months later the whole market collapsed and no one could get out. He forced his nephew to get out too; the nephew couldn't resist and went back in, so he had to force him out again.

[1:07:50] (Fang Yan) **Tie yourself to the mast to hold onto the money** — After withdrawing 120 million yuan, the market kept rising, with daily gains of over 10 million, and Fang Yan himself was struggling. His solution was to buy a product at ICBC that he couldn't withdraw — an ICBC-issued bond benchmarked to foreign exchange, with a six-month contract, paying 10,000 yuan a day, but absolutely not redeemable. He says there's only one way to tie yourself down: a physical method, like Odysseus tying himself to the mast and having his crew plug their ears with wax. On June 15, the day the market collapsed, it happened to be his wife's birthday. The whole restaurant was sighing and panicking, but only their table was cheerful.

[1:21:57] (Fang Yan) **Buying jets, chasing celebrities, climbing Everest are reverse indicators** — Fang Yan says this isn't a curse, it's objective reality: no one has climbed Everest and then had their business thrive afterward. Climbing Everest is a show-off mentality; getting up isn't that hard — you rely on a Sherpa team to help you, train back and forth for over two months, and it costs enormously. Zhang Chaoyang himself reflected that he spent several months away from the company to climb Everest, and that was the worst thing he could have done. If you're away from the company year-round and employees watch you climb Everest on TV every day, the team's mindset changes. Private jets are the same: in the US they're bought by 20 or 30 people crowdfunding, and there's objective demand given the vast, sparsely populated land and inconvenient transport; China has no such demand. This game was played once in China, and fewer people are buying now.

### glossary

- Insurance Float: Money an insurer holds between collecting premiums and paying claims; a liability on the books, but available for investment.
- Free Cash Flow: Cash a business can freely deploy after paying operating costs and capital expenditures; the source of dividends, buybacks, and reinvestment.
- See's Candies: A long-established American chocolate company acquired by Berkshire in 1972; a classic Buffett case study.
- Sirens: The sea nymphs of Homer's epic whose song lured sailors onto the rocks; Odysseus had his crew plug their ears and tied himself to the mast.
