## An Account for Every AI Agent: Credit Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
- show: No Priors (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/nopriors/)
- original episode: Coinbase’s Everything Exchange: Agentic Finance, Stablecoins, and Tokenization with CEO Brian Armstrong
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 45:09
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9772 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.**

why listen: The part about how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

### points

[6:47] (Brian Armstrong) **76% of machine payments are under 30 cents** — Armstrong says agents are already generating a lot of few-cent transactions: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialised agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest argument for stablecoins and crypto rails cutting into the machine economy.

[11:42] (Brian Armstrong) **Build a "brain" for every service** — Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future scenarios, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing; Armstrong calls this "recursive self-improvement".

[15:00] (Brian Armstrong) **The CEO runs 10 agents changing code at once** — Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day — he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends a finished PR for review; he says it's addictive. He has also put the CEO back to writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten things each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 of those things got done and were waiting for his review.

[17:02] (Brian Armstrong) **What gets killed is tasks, not people** — On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that's a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He doesn't think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people it has can do vastly more and everything speeds up. At the same time, two-person and five-person companies will indeed produce volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people can produce far more, and margins should rise over the long run. He doesn't close the door — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

[18:33] (Brian Armstrong) **88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading** — Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, considers it digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenised equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking to regulators about a US path; he stresses that these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

[21:57] (Brian Armstrong) **Prediction markets are more than sports betting** — Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached about $100 million in annualised revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he thinks that's a form of entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it's much bigger than that, and the societal implications aren't fully understood yet. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation". Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God" — he calls that an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock: you're just betting it will get better or worse.

[31:53] (Brian Armstrong) **Restore cells to their youthful function** — New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it doesn't change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab-style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then does functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally goes into human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and immune-system T cells. The first Phase 1 trial is for alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates that this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

[41:10] (Brian Armstrong) **What America lacks isn't land, it's a sandbox** — Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, it's overregulation. He mentions that Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they've had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centres, nuclear power plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first test what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to test in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

## Take a Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
- show: The Rational Reminder Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/rationalreminder/)
- original episode: The Finances of Marriage | Rational Reminder 426
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 1:19:02
- transcript: YouTube captions · 13525 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they fight more about money and report lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.**

why listen: Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending and who holds financial decision power in a household — is worth more, so skim.

### points

[7:05] (Benjamin Felix) **A tightwad is not frugal — spending physically hurts** — Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core is not how much you spend but "anticipatory pain" — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel that pain too strongly and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel it too weakly and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your "ideal self" and your actual behavior, so a very wealthy person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

[22:15] (Benjamin Felix) **Tightwads and spendthrifts are exactly who marry each other** — Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people are poor at introspection about what will attract them in a real partner, and when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it reminds you of that negative trait. Hence "fatal fiscal attractions" — the other person lacks your spending vice, so at first they seem especially attractive. But the excitement is temporary. Afterward, tightwad-spendthrift couples have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital well-being; the wider the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, even controlling for household debt and savings.

[28:17] (Benjamin Felix) **Everyone already has a default prenup** — In Ontario it is called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still carry legal implications on separation. Why do so few use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate yet estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so any agreement they sign does not seriously contemplate the scenario it is meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself read as a negative signal of "lack of commitment to the relationship," which makes the other party less willing to raise it.

[40:23] (Benjamin Felix) **The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk** — A 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. The couples with the lowest divorce rates spent under $1,000 on the wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and taking a honeymoon — neither related to price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 with 150 people, saving money via a free photographer, a friend making the cake and gifts.

[46:29] (Benjamin Felix) **The benefit of merging finances may come from thinking, not doing** — A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances report higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found joint accounts foster communal norms, shared goals and a good feeling of "managing money as a team." But more counterintuitive is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to an existing joint account rather than to their separate accounts produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as "ours" rather than "yours and mine" itself makes people talk about money more, and more effectively, regardless of how the accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

[53:32] (Benjamin Felix) **Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements** — Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of, and then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to drift toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and this predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; the finding holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts increase transparency, but if someone is deliberately hiding things, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from money to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to a split — which is already beyond the scope of financial planning.

[57:36] (Benjamin Felix) **In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified** — A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, in household-level asset allocation, on average incorporate 60% of the husband's risk tolerance and only 40% of the wife's — which the authors call a 20-percentage-point bargaining-power gap; half of it comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable, but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, which the authors say is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism indicated by randomized experiments: female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice ideas, while male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's input.

[1:00:41] (Benjamin Felix) **Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year** — Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading is costly: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women simply did less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he deals with, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, the conversation is more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, it is more about planning. He also observes that some male clients ask questions they "feel they should ask," more like performance, while female clients almost never do.

### verbatim quotes

[0:03] Benjamin Felix: "Like a tight wad is not someone who uh just doesn't get a lot of pleasure from spending. It's someone who deep down wishes they could get more pleasure from spending than they're actually getting."

[23:15] Benjamin Felix: "the result is what the authors describe as fatal fiscal attractions where someone who doesn't share your same shortcomings from a spending perspective is initially exciting and appealing to you for that reason."

[30:17] Benjamin Felix: "the act of requesting a primup prenup functions as a negative signal showing a lack of commitment to the prospective relationship which makes it less likely for a partner to ask for one in the first place."

- Men's trading frequency relative to women's: 45% higher [1:00:41]
- Drag on net returns from overtrading: Men 2.65 percentage points a year, women 1.72 percentage points [1:00:41]

### glossary

- tightwad: Someone who feels spending pain too strongly and spends less than they ideally would — not the same as frugal.
- spendthrift: Someone who feels spending pain too weakly and spends more than they ideally would.
- unconflicted consumer: The middle of the spending scale, where actual spending roughly matches ideal spending.
- financial infidelity: Engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of and deliberately hiding it.
- prenup: Called a marriage contract in Ontario; used to override the default terms of your jurisdiction's family law.

who it is for: Founders and investors who are married or about to be, especially anyone negotiating a prenup, merging accounts or planning a wedding; also readers who want to understand how gender norms distort financial decision power inside a household.

## MLB Built Baseball Castles in the Dominican Republic, and Also Grew the Lenders

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-papertrail-mlb-在多米尼加建了棒球城堡-也养出了放贷人/
- show: Paper Trail (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/papertrail/)
- original episode: The Predatory Industry Behind MLB’s Dominican Superstar Pipeline
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 44:28
- transcript: Machine transcription · 6139 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**MLB spends as much as $400 million a year in the Dominican Republic, but there is no draft and teams may sign players privately before they turn 16 — spawning a shadow industry of high-interest loans to players' families, with David Ortiz alleged to be part of it.**

why listen: Investigative reporting with high information density; the mechanisms and numbers are concrete. Worth hearing for anyone interested in the sports industry, platform governance, or emerging-market arbitrage.

### points

[3:07] **MLB built 30 baseball castles in the Dominican Republic** — MLB has built a talent pipeline in the Dominican Republic: all 30 teams have physical facilities near Santo Domingo, and a 20-minute drive from the airport brings you to gleaming complexes bearing Yankees and Mariners logos, which the show calls ‘baseball castles.’ The system generates as much as $400 million a year locally, and roughly 10% of current MLB players come from this Caribbean island. The castles are where the most promising prospects live and train; for an ambitious Dominican boy, getting in is the whole goal.

[9:25] **You can't sign until 16, but you can agree at 14** — MLB rules say teams cannot sign players under 16, but when Belfi was 14, his coach pulled him and his parents into a video call, and on the screen was a representative of the Arizona Diamondbacks saying they wanted to make Belfi part of their family. In the Dominican Republic this practice is called an ‘early agreement,’ and all 30 teams do it. One MLB scout told the reporter that if you don't do early agreements, you'll be eaten alive and won't sign a single player you want. The United States has a draft; the Dominican Republic does not, so teams can only compete by locking up prospects earlier and earlier.

[15:43] **80% of Dominican signing bonuses are tied to loans** — Early agreements create an awkward time gap: Belfi's family knows $1.8 million is coming, but they won't see a cent for two years. The reporter describes these families as being in a state of mental whiplash — ‘about to be rich, but not rich yet’ — and some people saw a business in that. One lawyer estimates that 80% of MLB signing bonuses paid to Dominican prospects come with loans attached. The reporter found lenders on WhatsApp openly advertising to families with early agreements. Caraballo's first loan to Belfi's family was $25,000 in cash in exchange for $180,000 down the road; the second was $70,000 at 7% monthly interest, roughly 84% annualized — an illegal rate in most U.S. states, but nothing in Dominican law prohibits it.

[22:08] **On signing day they went to the bank, and Belfi left empty-handed** — The signing bonus was paid in two installments, the first $900,000. When Belfi and his family got to the bank, Caraballo and the coaches were all there waiting for their cut: the coaches ultimately took $720,000, and Caraballo took the $180,000 he claimed he was owed. On his first trip to the bank, Belfi got nothing. Asked whether he realized it would go that way, he said he was somewhat disappointed but had more or less expected it — he trusted that his parents needed the loan, and trusted even more that the man who treated him like a mentor wouldn't take advantage of him.

[23:13] **The second payment was talked into ‘a fund with Ortiz’** — Four months later the second payment arrived. Caraballo picked them up in a parking lot and told Belfi's parents on the way: you're poor, you don't know how to manage money, I can put the rest into a fund together with David Ortiz that pays you a monthly dividend, so you won't have to manage it yourselves. In a private room, Belfi watched in silence as his parents signed, handing over nearly the entire second installment. Then the scene at the bank spun out of control: a family friend and former coach publicly called Caraballo a ladrone (thief) and chased him around the bank, while Caraballo shot back that the coach just wanted a cut for himself. In the chaos Belfi put $196,000 into his personal account, and Caraballo left with the rest of the money and his bodyguards — without even leaving the family a car, after having driven them there.

[27:25] **A company co-owned by Ortiz and Caraballo** — The reporter obtained more than a dozen of Caraballo's contracts, signed by players' parents, with children as young as 10, handing Caraballo control over the child's finances and baseball career decisions. Nearly everyone interviewed said Caraballo told them Ortiz was his business partner. The reporter found registration records for a Florida company called Big Poppy Sports Group listing both men; what the company did is unclear, and it was dissolved about a year later. Around the same time, Ortiz and Caraballo signed a contract with the parents of a 13-year-old Dominican prospect, promising training, housing and meals in exchange for 35% of a future signing bonus, and barring the child from leaving the baseball academy while securing his representation rights. The family later sued, saying the two failed to perform and the child never signed; the case was dismissed on procedural grounds.

[34:38] **One Ortiz voice memo killed the international draft** — MLB has long wanted an international draft, so that players from the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and elsewhere would be picked in order like American players, with signing bonuses determined by draft position rather than private deals struck years in advance with the families of teenagers. In 2022, during contract negotiations between MLB and the players' union, the international draft was an issue close to being settled. But a retired player sent a voice memo to a group of Dominican players and coaches, claiming in his usual hyperbolic style that more than 40% of the Dominican population depends on baseball for a living and that a draft would destroy the income of future generations. That man was David Ortiz. The day after the voice memo went out, the league and the union reached a contract, and the international draft idea was abandoned.

[36:41] **Ortiz called the reporter himself, then hung up** — Before the reporter had even contacted Ortiz, Ortiz heard about the reporting and called him unprompted, but would not allow recording. It started friendly; he admitted he had invested in Caraballo's business, to the tune of millions of dollars, but wouldn't say how much or which business. He said he doesn't deal directly with players, and that if anyone says otherwise, he has no idea what they're talking about. When the reporter asked whether he opposed the international draft because he holds previously unreported stakes in the Dominican baseball industry and a draft would destroy that business model, the friendly atmosphere ended and he hung up quickly. In a statement sent through his lawyer, Ortiz said his opposition to the draft was not out of personal interest but based on what he believes a draft would do to Dominican baseball; he confirmed a close friendship with Caraballo and a business relationship involving lending to coaches, but said he never knew about the investment fund and never agreed to take part in Caraballo's other businesses.

[41:53] **Dropping the charges: put in a car, and signed** — Belfi's parents hired a lawyer and filed a complaint with prosecutors, saying Caraballo's promised investment was in fact fraud and that he exploited Belfi's vulnerability as a minor. But according to Belfi, Caraballo had an arrangement for that too: one day after training he sent a driver to pick Belfi up, a man with a gun on his hip, and Belfi got in when told to. Caraballo told Belfi that as long as he had an open case, he wouldn't be allowed to go play baseball in the United States — which isn't true, but it scared Belfi, so he signed the document withdrawing the complaint. Belfi is now 19, still in the Arizona Diamondbacks system, playing in the Dominican Summer League; the game the reporter attended had no spectators, only scouts, staff and family, and he waited the whole game without seeing Belfi take the field.

## Insects Are Disappearing, but Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
- show: Science Vs (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sciencevs/)
- original episode: Where Have The Insects Gone?? With Dr. Jessica Ware
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 45:53
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7563 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture — it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.**

why listen: Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value; but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful eradication of the giant hornet are worth hearing.

### points

[8:55] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **The 70% decline was challenged, but the data keeps piling up** — A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one location had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles with light mosquitoes — maybe it's just the composition that changed. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots of the insect evolutionary tree to its tips, and keep seeing the same pattern — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but the insects in the other column that are declining are "still astonishingly high, and increasing."

[19:02] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **Pesticides aren't an agriculture problem, they're your backyard problem** — The host assumed the answer would be agricultural pesticides, but Jessica turned the spotlight on ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on both volume and type, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But "you and I" can go out tonight and buy any pesticide and spray it wherever we like, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordering a pesticide from the US that is banned in Australia, and her response is "wear gloves and a mask." She calls the overall picture what her colleague David Wagner calls "death by a thousand cuts" — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land-use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species — with no single cure.

[22:24] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **Colony collapse was only ever the story of managed honeybees** — The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago actually concerned only Apis mellifera, the European managed honeybee, not native North American species. They're trucked around the country in huge trailers, living under heavy stress, on top of Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's criticism: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct except the cow we like to eat. What's really needed is pollinator health as a whole, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — planting native plants for every pollinator in the environment.

[24:13] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn** — NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has more than 30 million acres of lawn, including golf courses, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, stop mowing the edges and let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house, and got "garden shamed" by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and looks ugly for the first few years.

[27:16] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold** — The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap; an all-liquid diet means its excrement is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have more than 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they'll also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

[30:28] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated** — The so-called murder hornet has been renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica finds the old name a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case for human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect in their tree and, instead of ignoring it, reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up funding, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is now on display at the Smithsonian, because it held a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

[33:46] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **Cockroach milk is secreted through modified spiracles** — Most cockroaches lay an egg case, an oothika, that looks like a little coffee bean; when it hatches, all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the "little box" open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and have no nipples, so they modified their spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and cloudy white in color. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually requires sacrificing the mother.

[37:36] (Dr. Jessica Ware) **Fear of bugs is learned from your mother** — Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran experiments: put babies together with tarantulas and the babies aren't afraid; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the baby shows disgust too. Same with snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so her son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

[20:00] Dr. Jessica Ware: "So it's my colleague, David Wagner, calls it death by a thousand cuts. You know, there's not one stressor that you could just be the panacea. You fix that and insight declines over. There's all of these little pieces that together are just too much."

[24:13] Dr. Jessica Ware: "It would be like getting, not worrying about any mammals going extinct and only worrying about a cow, right? About the cow that we like to eat, right?"

[32:31] Dr. Jessica Ware: "It took the person, the homeowner saying, hey, I don't recognize this. Yes. Notifying someone in the scientific community, getting the funding, because that was also an important part of the story is that the government supported this action."

### glossary

- colony collapse disorder: The phenomenon of managed honeybee colonies suddenly dying off en masse, mainly affecting European honeybees.
- Varroa mite: An invasive mite that parasitizes bees and harms colonies.
- neonicotinoid: A class of pesticides with negative effects on bees and other pollinating insects.
- pollinator garden: A garden planted with native plants to provide habitat for all kinds of pollinating insects.
- oothika: The egg case laid by cockroaches, shaped like a little coffee bean.
- spiracles: Openings on an insect's body surface used for breathing; some cockroaches modify them to secrete milk.

who it is for: Founders and investors watching ecology, agriculture, food safety and urban policy; engineers who want to understand how regulatory blind spots create systemic risk.
what to skip: The dragonfly penis anatomy and gold-coating segment (roughly 5:19–8:23) can be skipped — pure spectacle.

## A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
- show: 故事FM (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cn907a40/)
- original episode: E909.我们给残障人写「爽文」戏剧，把健全人写成弱势群体
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 41:16
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8540 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the ones born in sin, the ones who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.**

why listen: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; its value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment.

### points

[7:15] (Yaoyao) **Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm** — Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanyā (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, a woman she calls jiejie, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at New Year, what she felt was ‘like being walked like a little dog or cat’. Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

[11:19] (Yaoyao) **Disabled people's friends are all disabled people** — A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; they hung the chairs front and back with belongings and hauled load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would have been done in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance at integration to speak of’. That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

[14:19] (Yaoyao) **Writing the able-bodied as the discriminated ones born in sin** — Leyi Theatre's first play, Huí Zhuǎn Wèi Lái (“逆转未来”), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the surviving minority of able-bodied people, guilty of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become the ones born in sin, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning every right disabled people now have to fight for into a right the able-bodied have to fight for. She calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The plot's core: an original-sin father, to spare his son from suffering for his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original-sin people and modified people.

[22:25] (Wang Xiaomin) **How the one who can't see and the one who can't hear partner up** — Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in as a partner by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition, and his first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, ‘absolutely no way they could ever communicate’, a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

[25:28] (Yaoyao) **Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones** — Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without any trouble, so the director had no way to assess them and could only marvel at how fast the visually impaired actors got their lines down. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while grinning on the sidelines, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

[30:36] (Yaoyao) **She received the best production award from the ICU** — In 2024 Huí Zhuǎn Wèi Lái was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao's heart gave out and she went into the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more after finishing, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won Best Production, the festival's top prize, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, the first integrated disability production, and the only one in the ‘Nothing Is Impossible’ section.

[35:45] (Yaoyao) **After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born** — The second play, Wǒ Xuǎnzé Chūshēng (“我选择出生”), is set in a world where every country legislates that parents must use brainwaves to inform the fetus of its health status and family environment once it reaches eight months, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families: deaf parents who must tell their child truthfully that you will be deaf too; a husband who deceives his wife into having a child; a family that favours boys over girls; and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the illness differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice at all.

[36:45] **The same question, and Cai Cong gives the opposite answer** — The episode sets the deaf couple in Wǒ Xuǎnzé Chūshēng against the real-life Cai Cong (蔡聪): Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume, merely because the child might also be visually impaired, that such a life was not worth starting; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument over this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have.

### verbatim quotes

### glossary

- situs inversus (镜面人): A congenital condition in which the internal organs are completely reversed from the normal position; Yaoyao has it

## Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
- show: Huberman Lab (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/huberman/)
- original episode: Essentials: Genes & the Inheritance of Memories Across Generations | Dr. Oded Rechavi
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 35:38
- transcript: Official transcript page · 7525 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.**

why listen: 35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with the experimental designs and the key numbers; on mammals the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

### points

[4:37] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page** — Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of them still not understood. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and the remaining question is whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

[11:35] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits** — Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make.

[12:46] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **It was opposed and desired, and not entirely for data reasons** — This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is sitting right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He takes Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

[16:20] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD** — Why trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, raised in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

[21:20] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses** — The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, while if it's destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes get infected and clear the virus, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring have no ability to make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still stay black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring stay black, and the resistance carries on for several more generations. Sequencing can read those small RNAs directly, matching the viral genome, and only offspring whose parents were infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

[24:46] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **The brain and inheritance don't speak the same language** — The boldest question in this episode: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something may just mean removing a particular odorant receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how the information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route sidesteps the translation problem: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of natural small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

[28:17] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **Mammals lack an RNA amplifier** — Why can nematodes do it while mammals are suspect? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: when there are just a few cells, perhaps even acting on the placenta formed during pregnancy, and from there gradually steers development off course, with problems like metabolism following. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

[31:07] (Dr. Oded Rechavi) **RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics** — The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples planning to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism were clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there may be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if you make the mice exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; when doing IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has imagined telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, and that would change your RNA profile.

### verbatim quotes

[4:37] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "This is like the IKEA book that you have in every cell in your body, the instructions to make everything that you need in your house, the chairs, the kitchen, the pictures. But in every room, you want something else."

[11:35] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "The man who first thought about this barrier is called Weismann, August Weismann. … Separation of the soma from the germline, only the germline transmitting information to the next generation. And this is also called the second law of biology."

[12:46] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "So to preserve this, we erase all these modifications and start anew. And this is in mammals and in humans, this is largely true. Most of the modifications in the sperm and in the egg are removed, so about 90% of them."

[16:20] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "In the worm, we now have very obvious and clear-cut proof that there is inheritance of acquired traits. So much so that I don't think that anyone pretty much in the epigenetic field argues against it."

[21:20] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "We demonstrated this very clearly using a fluorescent virus. If the virus replicates successfully, the worm just turns green, and if the virus is destroyed, the worm stays black."

[28:17] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "What we did in C. elegans is we showed that the brain can communicate with the next generations using small RNAs, and that this can change behavior."

[31:07] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "For example, there are experiments in rodents where they show that overfeeding the rodents creates problems for the next generations, for the children. However, if you let the rodent exercise, then it corrects the aberrant inheritance."

[32:22] Dr. Oded Rechavi: "The beauty is that this, unlike DNA, it's plastic. So with DNA, this is your DNA, perhaps we can choose another embryo."

### figures

- Share of the genome encoding messenger RNA: less than 2% [4:37]
- Share of epigenetic modifications cleared in sperm and eggs: about 90% [12:46]
- Cell count of C. elegans: 959 [16:20]
- Neuron count of C. elegans: 302 [16:20]
- Offspring per C. elegans mother: about 250 [16:20]
- Generation time of C. elegans: 3 days [16:20]
- Generations of offspring behavior affected by changing small RNAs in the nematode brain: all the way to three generations later [28:17]

### glossary

- Weismann barrier: The separation of soma and germline: only germ cells can pass information to the next generation
- C. elegans: A transparent nematode with a fixed cell count and a 3-day generation, a classic model organism
- small RNAs: Short RNAs that don't encode protein and can recognize and silence sequence-matched genes
- RNA interference: The mechanism by which double-stranded RNA triggers small RNAs to degrade messenger RNA and shut genes off
- epigenetic reprogramming: The process in which most chemical modifications are erased and reset in sperm, eggs and the early embryo

## Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail. Retail Theft Is Now an Industry

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/

**Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences strip the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.**

why listen: High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation — with plenty of hard numbers.

### points

[8:19] (Scott Glenn) **A third of shrink is self-inflicted** — Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious — in Scott's phrasing, the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The figure that has circulated in the industry for years: of malicious shrink, roughly 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only a few points a year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that they have been underreported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting capture the full picture.

[22:52] (Scott Glenn) **Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone** — The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their minds — get the goods out and turn them into cash — so they will fight, and they have fought. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and people have even been killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he will trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board will back that decision.

[23:53] (Scott Glenn) **RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store** — Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, effectively a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you have to use an active-signal approach. He also says tag cost is now essentially zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits costs a fortune. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single drill you'd have to rework an entire production line, and it's very hard to scale.

[25:58] (Scott Glenn) **Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms** — The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs, then go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store labels and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a crew of just a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

[35:19] (Scott Glenn) **One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times** — Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately get that it's a gross margin problem — as long as locking up breaks even or even makes a little money, it's justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate who opens it in an average of 90 seconds; and locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the product is finally in stock.

[39:23] (Scott Glenn) **A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away** — In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion — a whole container gets rerouted at the port or a transload warehouse and hauled somewhere else, sometimes even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he's asleep someone pries open the trailer doors and hauls boxes out; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, and the driver pulls in, says he's there to pick up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new may not be the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly deteriorated over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get cracked open by a group; and the other side has good intelligence, they don't touch every car, they pick the one carrying guns or electronics.

[41:28] (Scott Glenn) **AI in security is an efficiency tool** — Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closure and handoff to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores so the existing cameras can run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

[44:30] (Scott Glenn) **Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill** — He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsors, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalization and defunding the police.

### glossary

## Baseball's stadium music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
- show: Throughline (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/throughline/)
- original episode: How baseball got its beat
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 32:03
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5364 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns the crowd from spectators into part of the game.**

why listen: Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the Nancy Faust story in the back half is worth the price. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

### points

[0:00] (Randa Abdel Fattah) **One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan** — Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco in 2022 changed that. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to announce to the opponent: the show's over, this one's ours. The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, the mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play trumpets, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says that if you were in the stands then, the feeling was electric.

[6:18] (John Thorne) **The official historian finds the ballpark too loud** — MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like entrance music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet makes the other sounds louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit, and when Josh Gibson did; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio, the endless fight for fans' attention, may have robbed a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

[10:31] (John Thorne) **Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song** — The seventh-inning stretch was originally literal: stand up, move your legs, get the blood flowing. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist in the original lyrics is Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire blows a call, and knows what to do when the score is tight — she gets the whole crowd to sing the song. From this a new genre was born, the "baseball song," flooding sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

[12:35] (John Thorne) **The baseball song boom was publishers, not fans** — John Thorne points out that the 1910s wave of baseball music was less about fans liking it than publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But despite Tin Pan Alley producing so many baseball songs, large-scale singalongs at actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

[17:47] (Nancy Faust) **That 1977 singalong broke the opposing pitcher** — On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox trailed the Kansas City Royals by two. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, someone in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, the sound grew, more than 45,000 fans joined in, and the announcers had to raise their voices to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then erupted — bases loaded, cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans "saw him off" even louder. Nancy Faust says she was thinking, "Did I hear that right?" because it wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like mockery.

[23:51] (Nancy Faust) **She gave players songs; fans fed her ideas** — In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played a set repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when the crowd filed in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, the crowd would leave the bathrooms and popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went wild. Fans sitting around her booth started offering her ideas: one player used to work at a watch counter, got stuck there when the store closed, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to whatever was happening," not just scoring the players.

[25:52] (Nancy Faust) **An opposing pitcher admitted the singing shook his confidence** — After that 1977 singalong, an opposing pitcher told reporters: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye, and that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound, and flinched when they heard na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know whether they came to see us or we came to see them, but I can tell you it fired us up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

[28:56] (Randa Abdel Fattah) **She can't read music — it's all by ear** — Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she can't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she'd play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former President Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth she occupied for decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes out of retirement for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

## Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
- show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- original episode: Iron Age Ireland
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 52:48
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9573 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.**

why listen: Medium information density, with a long setup in the first half. The real value is in the second half, on Celtic identity, sacral kingship and the Fianna warband, and it suits listeners interested in pre-Roman Europe.

### points

[2:18] (Dr John Waddell) **Why the Irish Iron Age is the murkiest period** — John Waddell says the Irish Iron Age is the darkest of all Ireland's prehistoric periods, partly because the people of the time practised cremation. In much of Europe people were buried with large quantities of fine grave goods, whereas cremation followed by burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. So although there are very fine metal objects and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this history unusually hard to read. He also points out that using the phrase "Celtic Iron Age" to describe the period amounts to sticking an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story.

[9:28] (Dr John Waddell) **Sea routes connected people rather than isolating them** — Waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. Ireland and Britain are both islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. Before the Romans built straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. This means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric Britain and Ireland were. The Irish Sea was itself a connecting force, and the English Channel linked England to the continent.

[10:31] (Dr John Waddell) **Sacred sites sat on high ground, not by rivers** — Tristan asks whether Iron Age settlements were all close to rivers and coasts. Waddell's answer is unexpected: famous sites like Tara, Rathcroghan and Navan Fort are not obviously located on major routes. Each sits on high ground in its own different way, and these locations may have carried a kind of sanctity since the Neolithic. Tara was already an important burial place before 3000 BC, and its story runs into the medieval period, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. The importance of these places comes from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes.

[15:38] (Dr John Waddell) **A sacral king who fails or is wounded is deposed** — Waddell draws a key concept out of medieval Irish texts: sacral kingship. The king of Tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain the cosmic order. If a sacral king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. Another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacral king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. Waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of Britain and Ireland, suggesting that in the Celtic era, the pre-Roman period, certain tribal rulers did indeed carry a sacred quality.

[21:43] (Dr John Waddell) **The Celts were not invaders but a language community** — The traditional story is that around 500 BC a Celtic-speaking people brought knowledge of iron to Ireland. Waddell says this is wrong. His best definition of the ancient Celts is "people who spoke Celtic", not an ethnic or racial definition. Ireland in the pre-Roman period was undoubtedly Celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of immigrants in the Iron Age or the Late Bronze Age. Instead, from around 1000 BC there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between Britain and Ireland, with the Thames, the Rhine, the Rhône, the Saône, the Ruhr and the Danube all serving as major corridors. Trade and exchange means the movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. The Celtic languages most likely took shape gradually amid this Late Bronze Age surge of connectivity.

[31:04] (Dr John Waddell) **The Banquet Hall is really a ceremonial processional way** — On the hill of Tara there is a monument called the "Banquet Hall", a pair of very long parallel earthworks. Waddell's colleague Conor Newman established that it was never a banquet hall — it is far too large to be any kind of hall. Standing between the banks, you find you cannot see the world outside, because the banks are still high even in their ruined state. Newman proposed that it was a processional way running from the northern end of the hill to the centre of the summit, used for royal inauguration rituals. There are gaps in the banks that let the procession look left and right at the burials and other monuments on either side, reminding the man about to become sacral king of the stories of his ancestors and predecessors. Waddell compares it to Rome's Appian Way, lined on both sides with tombs.

[33:07] (Dr John Waddell) **Beneath Tara lies a timber circle bigger than Stonehenge** — Geophysical survey on the hill of Tara revealed a huge circular timber structure, four to five times the scale of Stonehenge. It was built around 2000 BC and at the time would have stood on the hilltop as prominently as Stonehenge, yet today there is no trace of it on the ground — only aerial photographs show the faint outline of the circle. Waddell says this reminds us that large timber circles earlier than Stonehenge are a feature of the prehistoric landscape of Britain and Ireland. Tara's burials have another detail: many of them intersect one another, as if new graves were deliberately laid partly over old ones to connect with ancestral remains, both legitimising one's own existence and conveying some kind of story.

[39:22] (Dr John Waddell) **The forgotten king Dathi and a Swiss myth** — Waddell tells the story of an almost forgotten king, Dathi, associated with Rathcroghan in western Ireland. In medieval legend Dathi was the last pagan king of Ireland, said to have campaigned on the European continent, possibly reaching the foot of the Swiss Alps, and to have been struck dead by lightning at the foot of the Alps, with his body carried back to Ireland and buried at Rathcroghan. The story was especially popular in the 19th century, because some people took it as proof that Irish military power reached far overseas. But Waddell says it looks like pure invention: there was never any Irish invasion of Switzerland. Dathi most likely only raided Britain occasionally. He was later overshadowed by the more famous warrior Cú Chulainn and gradually forgotten.

[48:57] (Dr John Waddell) **The Fianna were a prehistoric gang of juvenile delinquents** — The Fianna in medieval Irish stories are the warriors under the hero Finn MacCool. But Waddell points out that these stories are largely a medieval invention. The original Fian was a warband, with traces in pre-Roman Gaul and elsewhere. The earliest Fian were a group of landless young men, permitted to roam in a lawless manner, engaging in plunder, robbery, occasional murder and possibly sexual violence. They roamed the countryside like juvenile delinquents until they reached adulthood and became members of the community. Early Christian writers mention them with evident disgust and irritation. Waddell says this makes us uncomfortable: prehistoric society tolerated juvenile delinquents for all those years, but the medieval Irish evidence indicates that this was indeed the case.

### verbatim quotes

[2:18] Dr John Waddell: "Part of the reason, I think, is that the population in later prehistory had the unfortunate habit of cremating themselves, if that's the right way to put it."

[7:26] Dr John Waddell: "In fact, if you think hard about it, certainly in prehistory, both in Britain and in Ireland, sometimes travel by land was far, far more difficult than travel by sea and by river."

[15:38] Dr John Waddell: "Their fundamental role was to maintain cosmic order. And if, for example, a sacred king wasn't able to produce good harvests, he would be deposed."

[21:43] Dr John Waddell: "the best definition of an ancient Celt is somebody who spoke a Celtic language"

[38:19] Dr John Waddell: "Ritual permeated daily life."

[50:00] Dr John Waddell: "And I think it's something we're rather uncomfortable with, that there were notions of juvenile delinquents tolerated in prehistory for a number of years before they got sense."
