## Stamford Bridge Was Wiped Out by Hastings, and Archaeology Just Found the Battlefield

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-historyhit-斯坦福桥大捷被黑斯廷斯一笔勾销-考古刚找到战场/
- show: Dan Snow's History Hit (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/historyhit/)
- original episode: The Battle of Stamford Bridge Explained
- published: 2026-09-10 · duration: 31:50
- transcript: Machine transcription · 6359 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In September 1066, King Harold of England force-marched roughly 200 miles in four days and annihilated Harald Hardrada's Viking army; but a victory that could have cemented any monarch's reputation was erased days later by the catastrophe at Hastings.**

why listen: The first half is narrative military history with average information density; the real value is the second half — a team using metal detecting has found Viking artifacts at Low Catton, pinning down the battlefield's location for the first time.

### points

[3:04] (Dan Snow) **More than one king of England died in 1066** — Edward the Confessor died in the first days of January with no heir, and the throne instantly became the most tempting vacancy in all of Europe. The show stresses that from the late 900s to the 1300s, almost every English king who took power faced a claimant: brother fought brother, cousins fought each other, and outsiders always circled the empty throne. Edward had a distant English blood relative, but he was only a boy of probably no more than 13, not yet old enough to stand in a shield wall and cut down enemies — and that was precisely a king's first duty at the time. A child on the throne, in an England that had been through a century of war and invasion, meant inviting more war.

[6:04] (Dan Snow) **Hardrada was no pirate, he was a Byzantine veteran** — Harald Hardrada, king of Norway, was called "the Thunderbolt of the North" and was said to stand seven feet tall. Exiled from his homeland as a youth, he made his name and fortune along the rivers of Russia and Ukraine, fighting for the Byzantine Empire: he campaigned in the Crimea, is said to have flattened 80 Arab fortresses in the Middle East, fought on the Tigris and Euphrates, helped Christians conquer Sicily, served in southern Italy, and rose to command Byzantium's Varangian Guard. He crushed a Bulgarian revolt and earned the nickname "Bulgar-burner." When he returned to Scandinavia, his ships were so full of gold in the hold that they lost their balance. By the mid-to-late 1040s he was king of Norway, and he never stopped wanting to rebuild Canute the Great's North Sea empire spanning Norway, Denmark and England.

[9:07] (Dan Snow) **His own brother became the invader's guide** — Harold's brother Tostig was still earl of Northumbria in 1065 when a popular uprising drove him out for being too unpopular. He went south expecting his brother the king to restore him, but Harold judged that he had done a bad job, backed another candidate, Morcar, and expected Morcar to support his own bid for the throne later. Tostig could not believe the deal — his own brother had sided with the enemy. In exile he raided down the east coast, was soundly beaten on the Humber by Edwin and Morcar, fled to Scotland, found little support there, and so took his fleet to Norway. Hardrada already wanted to invade England, and now he had a "useful idiot": a man who had been close to the king and had ruled northern England, able to supply all kinds of intelligence.

[13:10] (Dan Snow) **A city that refused to pay was erased from the map** — Hardrada's fleet reached the mouth of the Tyne in the first week of September, possibly three or four hundred ships. They sailed south along the coast, past Holy Island — where the Viking Age itself had begun with that raid on Lindisfarne nearly 300 years earlier. At Scarborough he landed and demanded all its wealth; the inhabitants said no. Hardrada needed to make an example: he had great piles of firewood bound and set alight and rolled down the slope into the town, the fleeing inhabitants were cut down, and he ordered the entire population killed. Scarborough ceased to exist — it does not appear in the Domesday Book compiled about a generation later, and that book records every last pig. One historian's verdict on Hardrada is called by the show "the most understated line I've ever read": his personal morality seems not to have matched Christian ideals.

[17:13] (Dan Snow) **Fulford: one exposed flank lost the north** — At Fulford outside York, the first great battle of 1066. The English position was good: the Ouse on their right, marshland on their left, and they held the only firm ground leading to York. But Hardrada was not on a battlefield for the first time: he led his troops along the riverbank out of the English line of sight, possibly wading, then had Tostig show himself openly in the centre of the line. He bet that Morcar would want to crush Tostig's band of "English traitors" first — and he bet right. Morcar charged out, the right flank was exposed, and Hardrada came at them from behind the riverbank. The result was one-sided: the English dead were said to be so numerous that you could walk across the marsh on them without getting your feet wet. York surrendered, and the city's leaders swore to recognize him as king and Tostig as the new earl.

[20:25] (Dan Snow) **Four days, about 200 miles, Harold marches the other way** — Harold had been waiting on the south coast for an invasion from Normandy, raising a large force to stand by, but no masts ever appeared on the horizon. August passed, the weather turned in September, the invasion window on the English Channel closed, supplies ran out, and he was forced to disband the army. A day or two later, back in London, he got the thunderbolt: the invasion had come in the north, not the south, and not from William. Harold took his professional troops — the full-time house carls — and raced north along the Roman road (today's A1), while sending messengers to tell the Fulford survivors to rendezvous south of York. The show estimates he covered about 185 to 200 miles in four days, calling it one of the most astonishing and audacious marches in English military history, and true to his style: fast, a reader of battlefields, and judging that the best way to deal with a Viking invasion was to strangle it early.

[21:29] (Dan Snow) **The Vikings left their armour and shields in camp** — Hardrada had just won an overwhelming victory and was overconfident. He and part of his force walked from the ship camp toward Stamford Bridge, many without armour, with shields and heavy kit left behind — on a hot day's march, these things are a burden. He took only about a third of his army, leaving the rest at Riccall to guard the ships. They strolled to Stamford Bridge and lounged in the fields on both sides of the river in the sun. The weather was clear, and Hardrada was the first to see a cloud of dust rise on the western horizon — in dry weather an army on a metalled road cannot hide. Then the sagas say he saw a glint, "like sunlight on broken ice": that was not ice, it was iron, the morning light on the advancing English royal army, with the dragon banner of the English king and Harold's own warrior banner flying above it.

[23:30] (Dan Snow) **The story of one man holding the bridge may be true** — The English rolled over the Vikings on the west bank, then had to cross the river. The most famous story comes from this moment: a giant berserk Viking held the narrow bridge alone, fending off the entire English advance with an axe, said to have beaten back dozens, possibly 40 Englishmen, until a single soldier drifted under the bridge in a barrel or container and thrust up through the planks into his unprotected groin, running him through from crotch to chest. The show says the story was written down much later, but "it's a good story, and it may well be true" — because in reality there were other crossing points, fords as well as a bridge, and it is impossible that everyone used that one. The show's host waded one of those fords himself last summer; the water was deeper than he expected, but he could still stand.

[24:30] (Dan Snow) **A parley between brothers: six feet of English soil** — Some sources say the fighting paused and Harold rode forward alone to speak with his brother Tostig, offering to restore his earldom if he changed sides. Tostig called back asking what Hardrada would get, and Harold answered: six feet of English soil for a grave — or more, since he was taller. Tostig replied: then prepare for battle, we would rather die with honour, or win England by victory. He turned his back on his brother and stood with Hardrada one last time, the two sharing death or victory.

[26:38] (Dan Snow) **Hardrada threw away his shield and charged in two-handed** — Hardrada knew how to fight, how to win, and how to die to preserve his name. Instead of hiding behind the shield wall all day waiting for rescue, he made a decision: to die in a way that people would still talk about a thousand years later. He dropped his shield, took his sword in both hands, and launched a mad personal charge at the enemy, ploughing a furrow through the English ranks. The show uses this to correct the Hollywood image of war: real fighting was more like a rugby scrum — two rows of men pressed so close they could barely raise a hand, shoving, spitting, cursing, occasionally stabbing, until one side broke. But this time, possibly the greatest warrior in Europe really did decide to go for broke. He hacked at the English until the inevitable happened: an English archer, possibly at very close range, loosed an arrow that flew straight into the throat of the "hard ruler," the "Thunderbolt of the North," the "Bulgar-burner."

[28:43] (Dan Snow) **Hundreds of ships, only 24 sailed home** — Reinforcements trickled in through the afternoon, but as a trickle, out of formation and exhausted, some said to have died of overexertion. They were led by Eystein Orre, a nobleman and Hardrada's close man — he was in fact betrothed to the king's daughter, but never made it to the altar. He held the English at bay for a time and rallied the Vikings, known to history as "Orre's Storm," but it was not enough. The English eventually pushed them south toward the ships, the army shattered into a rout, and the dead piled up; years later, heaps of bones were said to still be visible, whitening in the sun. Hardrada and Tostig were among them, Tostig the first of Harold's family to die that autumn, but not the last. Harold called off the fighting and allowed the few survivors to sail home after swearing never to attack England again. Hardrada's 16-year-old son Olaf had stayed with the ships and took the survivors home: only 24 ships left Riccall, out of the hundreds that had sailed in a week or two earlier.

[30:46] (Dan Snow) **The real battlefield is at Low Catton, not in the town** — The battlefield's location had never been confirmed by archaeology. Today there is a modern town called Stamford Bridge, with a bridge over the Derwent, street names all tied to the battle, images of the conflict all over town, and anyone you stop in the street can tell you about the fight — but archaeologists have never found any artifacts or remains there. Recently, though, finds have started coming out of the ground at Low Catton, about a mile south of Stamford Bridge, and in quantity. The show's host watched metal detectorist Simon Richardson on site dig up a Viking belt buckle, its loop shaped into a mythical beast's head with recognizable eyes, ears and snout, 11th century and definitely Scandinavian. Minutes later, in the same field, came a Viking sword pommel — the fitting at the end of the hilt that protects the hand, stops it slipping and acts as a counterweight. Then fragments of chainmail.

[31:46] (Dan Snow) **A scabbard fitting points to Vikings from the Balkans** — The host's favourite find is a very fine chape — the decorative metal fitting at the tip of a scabbard that stops it scraping the ground or a horse's flank. They contacted Scandinavian experts, who said it closely resembles chapes found at Viking sites in eastern Europe, the Balkans, and possibly Bulgaria. So the evidence in these fields along the Derwent in Yorkshire is not just Vikings, not just a battle, but Vikings from the east, or with eastern objects — exactly matching the crowd around Harald Hardrada.

## The CIA Warned Months in Advance. Why Couldn't the White House Stop 9/11?

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-empirehist-cia-提前数月警告-白宫为何还是没拦住-9-11/
- show: Empire: World History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/empirehist/)
- original episode: 394. Road To 9/11: Hijackers, CIA Failures, and America’s Darkest Day (Part 6)
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 46:16
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8417 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The intelligence system delivered strategic warning almost perfectly, but policymakers can choose to ignore it — that is the real point of failure in the seven months before 9/11.**

why listen: Peter Bergen brings a Saudi official's casing video that only surfaced in 2024, plus the details of how his own August 2001 warning letter was killed.

### points

[2:09] (Peter Bergen) **After the Cole bombing, America did nothing for seven months** — In October 2000 the USS Cole was bombed in Aden harbor. The Clinton administration had only four months left in office and was still arguing internally over who did it; the CIA quickly concluded it was al-Qaeda. But once the Bush administration took over, it sat still for a full seven months. Bergen's explanation is not negligence but a cognitive frame: Rumsfeld had been secretary of defense in the Ford administration, Condoleezza Rice was a Soviet specialist, and this cohort had spent its whole life inside the Cold War. They could not accept that a non-state actor without state sponsorship could constitute a threat. The main threat they identified was Iraq. So even with warnings coming constantly, the top simply could not make the turn.

[3:11] (Peter Bergen) **The CIA did its job well, but the client can choose not to look** — Bergen stresses a structural fact: the CIA's job is to give policymakers strategic warning, and in the spring and summer of 2001 it did that job excellently, warning repeatedly that something big was coming. The problem is that the CIA serves a "client" — the White House. If the president chooses to ignore it, the CIA can do no better. The 9/11 Commission later disclosed these warnings, and the Bush administration fought hard to prevent that commission from being created. Bergen says he had just finished his first book on bin Laden a week before 9/11, and at the time he needed no access to classified material to know something was brewing.

[7:20] (Peter Bergen) **Two hijackers entered America and the CIA forgot the watchlist** — Khalid Al-Midhar and Nawaf Al-Hamsi attended a meeting in Malaysia. The CIA surveilled them and knew they were al-Qaeda-linked. But the CIA made a tactical error: it did not put them on the State Department watchlist until August 25, 2001, leaving just over two weeks to 9/11. Bergen says plainly that this was not a conspiracy but the "cock-up view of history" — a pile of people knew these two men had US visas, roughly 60 people inside the CIA could see the information, but nobody told the FBI and nobody told the State Department. He also mentions a "wall" between the CIA and the FBI: the CIA collects intelligence, the FBI collects criminal evidence, the two are different in nature, and the CIA was even barred from sharing large amounts of intelligence with the FBI.

[10:22] (Peter Bergen) **The Saudi official's casing video that only surfaced in 2024** — After the two hijackers landed in California, a Saudi official received them: arranged housing, signed the lease, gave them money, introduced them into the local community, and even threw a party. Bergen says it was not until 2024 that anyone learned this official had recorded a video of the US Capitol, marking police posts and explaining where Reagan Airport was — what Bergen calls a "casing videotape," unambiguously reconnaissance, not a tourist filming scenery. On the tape he also talks about the plan, about "the devil in the White House," and uses "the brothers," al-Qaeda's internal term for itself. The tape came to light because after 9/11 this man was living in Birmingham, and when British police searched his flat they found it; some of the material was lost for a time and later resurfaced in a civil case. Of the 19 hijackers, 15 came from Saudi Arabia. Bergen explains the visa logic: Yemenis have a hard time getting US visas because of fear they will overstay and work; Saudis are assumed to have money and to go home.

[15:28] (Peter Bergen) **KSM's original plan was to blow up ten planes** — Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is the nephew of Ramzi Yousef, the mastermind of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. He met bin Laden in Afghanistan in 1996, but the two did not seriously discuss an operation until 1999. KSM's original plan was grand: blow up ten American planes in Asia and ten more in the United States. Bin Laden told him to narrow it and suggested using commercial airliners as flying bombs. Bergen says bin Laden's line "why use an axe when you can use a bulldozer" captures roughly that meaning. KSM is still held at Guantanamo and still untried, which Bergen says is partly because he was tortured while in CIA custody.

[16:29] (Peter Bergen) **Atta solved al-Qaeda's problem of finding pilots** — The operation needed two kinds of people: the "muscle hijackers," who controlled the passengers and did not know the target, and others who could fly, knew the West and spoke some English. al-Qaeda got lucky — Muhammad Atta and three companions walked into a training camp on their own. Atta was Egyptian, doing a doctorate in Germany, and most of this group had engineering or medical backgrounds. Bergen makes the key point: a Yemeni who speaks no English could never get into flight school or learn to fly a plane into a building, so Atta and his Hamburg associates were recruited as the pilots — the group the newspapers of the day usually called the "Hamburg cell."

[35:28] (Peter Bergen) **Bergen's August warning letter was killed over an editorial dispute** — In August 2001 Bergen wrote a four-page letter to the New York Times reporter John Burns warning that America was about to be attacked. He had three pieces of evidence: first, a group of US embassies had closed in an unusual way; second, bin Laden had released a two-and-a-half-hour videotape laying out his religious and political doctrine and why he wanted to attack America — a tape that was barely on the internet at the time, requiring access to a password-protected jihadist chat room and RealPlayer to watch, and Bergen had someone translate all of it; third, it fit al-Qaeda's pattern of issuing warnings before the Cole and embassy attacks. Burns agreed it was a story, and the piece was set to run on September 9; it was pulled over an editorial dispute and only appeared on September 12. Bergen says the website put it up and took it down on September 9, and the paper later admitted this was a serious error. His conclusion: what you need to know is almost always in the open source.

[40:40] (Peter Bergen) **O'Neill's new job: head of security at the World Trade Center** — John O'Neill's career was essentially finished after he offended his hosts in Yemen and was pushed out by Ambassador Barbara Bodine, and after he left a briefcase full of classified material somewhere. When he left the FBI, his friend Chris Isham joked at the farewell party that at least they wouldn't bomb it again — because it had already been bombed once. O'Neill's new job was head of security at the World Trade Center, with a generous salary. On the night of September 10, two and a half weeks into the job, with his office 34 floors above the plaza, he was out drinking in the city, telling the people at his table about his exciting and lucrative new position. Bergen also notes that bin Laden misjudged the scale of casualties: he thought the World Trade Center would only collapse above the impact points, not that both towers would come down entirely.

### glossary

- cock-up view of history: The historical explanation that major disasters usually stem from bureaucratic bungling rather than elaborate conspiracy.
- muscle hijackers: Hijackers tasked with controlling passengers aboard the plane, who did not know the specific target.
- casing videotape: Reconnaissance video shot in advance of an attack, marking guard posts and routes at the target site.
- the wall: The institutional barrier before 9/11 that restricted intelligence sharing between the CIA and the FBI.
- ghazia: al-Qaeda's internal name for the 9/11 operation, from the Arabic for "raid."

## What Solo Founders Lack Isn't Hands, It's Someone Who Makes Them Tell the Truth

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-solofounders-单人创始人最缺的不是人手-是有人逼你说真话/
- show: Solo Founders (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/solofounders/)
- original episode: 5 Solo Founders Called In With Their Hardest Problem | Solo Founders Office Hours
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 47:36
- transcript: YouTube captions · 9342 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Julian's diagnosis of five solo founders points at almost the same thing every time: without a co-founder, you lose the person who forces you to face what you actually did today.**

why listen: Five founders each bring one real problem, and Julian's live diagnosis is more concrete than any course. But this is public office hours — there's no deep case review.

### points

[3:04] (Julian) **Hundreds of paying users means you haven't given them something worth paying for** — Utkar's Game Native has 1.25 million users, but only a few hundred pay $5 to $10 a month for a Discord role, priority support and early builds. Julian's read is blunt: all of that is bonus, not core value — it's essentially a Patreon-style fan club, where people pay to support you, not because it's genuinely a good deal. His standard: a few hundred paying out of 1.25 million is precisely the proof that you haven't yet offered something truly worth paying for. And don't charge by taking existing features away — create something new in the future that users haven't used yet.

[11:08] (Julian) **A solo founder has no accountability partner, and that's the deadliest part** — Julian says solo founding is hardest from zero to one because there's no accountability partner. He uses the gym as an analogy: if you've already agreed to train with someone every day, you're more likely to actually show up. Early on, with no customers, everything is fuzzy, and you're the only one judging whether you're spending your time right. His antidote: be a little kinder to yourself, while staying honest about what you're actually doing each day. He also names a default trap — writing code is the addictive default option, because it always feels like progress, but the only thing that truly settles the question is paying customers.

[18:13] (Julian) **Let the lab see its own gap first, then sell the solution** — Ryan sells RL environments and benchmarks to frontier labs. Julian endorses his path: don't start by selling generic data — first use a public benchmark to get the lab to admit for itself that it has this gap, then offer that you can fill it. Ryan says this is already standard practice among frontier-lab data vendors: show that some model fails at some capability, and a few months later the research lead comes to you asking whether they can train on your data. Ryan's benchmark is a bunch of frontier models playing Werewolf against each other, testing not who wins but reasoning ability, who lies best, and who lies most.

[21:16] (Julian) **You don't need to be the best, you need to be the only** — Ryan worries that being solo will make labs not take him seriously. Julian says the worry is partly valid, but only if you're competing head-on with others. He quotes Kevin Kelly: you don't want to be the best, you want to be the only. So the question isn't "how does this team look" but "is this the only person who can help us solve this problem." He also says being solo is "more in your head than in anyone else's" — you can absolutely answer: I'm just starting out, I only work with a few people, I'll be hiring, and I have AI leverage.

[26:20] (Julian) **Users don't want features, they want a button they can press** — Charlie is torn between building the workflow features customers ask for and going straight for the AI brain that would eliminate all workflows. Julian tells the Magic School story: founder Adil was a former high school principal who wanted teachers to use ChatGPT, ran a whole-school training, and nobody actually used it. He judged that the blocker wasn't AI being too weak but a blank chat box being too scary — it can do anything, and therefore feels like it can do nothing. So Adil built dozens of "micro-apps," each doing one specific thing. First week: 100 users. Second week: 1,000. Julian's conclusion: the feature requests users make are really them telling you their jobs to be done.

[31:24] (Julian) **A slow deal may not be an efficiency problem but an incentive problem** — Charlie says both sides of a wholesale trade know exactly what they want, yet it takes two or three weeks of emails and CSVs to close. Julian doesn't give a direct answer; instead he asks a counterintuitive question: if everyone wants to compress the time, why hasn't it been compressed? Could some incentive be deliberately stretching it out? He says sometimes things drag on for a reason — just not the reason everyone assumes. He also suggests using frequency times severity to decide which problem to tackle first.

[39:28] (Julian) **Build the brain first, don't start with the body** — Andy wants to build "describe a robot, get a design and a 3D-printed kit," and is torn about whether to bring someone in to split software and hardware. Julian turns it around: if you were given a full-time person and enough money, what would you do differently? Andy says he'd put it all into 3D printing and hardware testing. So Julian suggests: could you skip hardware for now, run the character on a phone, put it on a desk as a base — the character can't move, but it exists; then the robot's first boot is releasing the character from the phone into the physical world. He uses dementia as an analogy: what makes a person a person isn't an exoskeleton, it's memory, a way of communicating, the look in their eyes when they recognise you. So early on, the body may matter less than the mind.

[43:35] (Andy) **Different characters move differently, and that's exactly the hardware problem** — Andy explains why he can't let go of physicality: Pikachu, Snoopy, a rover — they move through physical space in completely different ways. If you want to bring Pikachu or an owl into the real world as a robot, you have to solve for different characters moving in different ways. That's why he weights physicality so heavily. Julian concedes the point holds, and says if he built an owl it would be "a real hoot." This is the only moment in the session where a founder pushes back on Julian's advice head-on.

## Ashurbanipal's Library: He Was Both a Tyrant and the Earliest Book Collector

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
- show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- original episode: Ashurbanipal
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 37:30
- transcript: Official transcript · 5540 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Ashurbanipal kept defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, which kept the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.**

why listen: Medium information density; the first half is Mesopotamian background, and the second half — how the library was preserved and deciphered — is where the value is.

### points

[0:01] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The same man, two completely opposite first impressions** — At the British Museum, Tracy read the exhibit panels on Ashurbanipal's library and thought, "this guy's library is astonishing"; in the same gallery Patrick read the other set of panels about him as king of Assyria, and came away thinking, "this guy was really cruel." The same body of material can support two completely opposite impressions at once, and the rest of the episode picks apart that contradiction: he really did yoke the defeated king of Elam to his chariot and shut a rival up in a dog kennel, and he really did order texts from across the empire copied and sent to the capital.

[4:04] (Tracy V. Wilson) **You simply cannot lay out a timeline for Mesopotamia** — Tracy wanted to open the episode with a basic timeline and found she couldn't. Mesopotamia spans more than three thousand years from the first cities, with civilizations, kingdoms and empires overlapping and influencing each other, so a linear timeline is itself a distortion. Assyrian history is divided into Early Assyrian (from about 2600 BCE), Old Assyrian (from about 2025 BCE), Middle Assyrian (from about 1363 BCE) and Neo-Assyrian (911 to 609 BCE), followed by a post-empire period. Assyrians still exist today: roughly three to five million people in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey identify as Assyrian.

[9:10] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The father split the empire in two to prevent civil war** — Esarhaddon's father Sennacherib had Babylon utterly destroyed and even diverted canals to flood the ruins, and was later assassinated by his own sons, which was read as divine punishment for destroying Babylon. Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and positioned himself as its "governor" rather than its king. In 672 BCE he divided his two sons' roles: Shamashumukin took Babylon, and Ashurbanipal was made crown prince of Assyria. The arrangement was meant to prevent a repeat of the civil war that had attended his own accession. The episode says outright that this will come back later — because the brothers eventually turned on each other.

[9:10] (Tracy V. Wilson) **He got an education a king was not supposed to get** — Ashurbanipal's education had already begun when he was made crown prince. He learned horsemanship, chariot driving, archery, military tactics and court etiquette — the standard royal package. But he also learned literature and history, knew multiple Sumerian and Akkadian dialects, and could read and write cuneiform. The episode stresses that kings of this era were not usually educated this academically, and often were not literate at all; literacy was the business of scholars and scribes. He could do this most likely because early in life he was not being raised entirely as the heir to the throne.

[13:14] (Tracy V. Wilson) **In the reliefs, he wears writing tools on his belt** — Ashurbanipal was a patron of the arts, building temples and palaces and commissioning vast numbers of reliefs. Many depict him fighting, lion hunting, and going about daily life amid wealth and luxury; some show the severed heads of enemies. The episode singles out one detail: in many depictions he wears a riding stylus tucked into his belt, including in scenes where he is killing lions with a sword — Holly jokes that he probably wanted to write in his diary after killing a lion. The reliefs of his reign are considered the peak of Assyrian art, and the lion hunt reliefs are now in the British Museum.

[15:19] (Tracy V. Wilson) **Cruelty was not his invention; he took it to an extreme** — The episode draws a clear distinction: practices like displaying enemies' severed heads were the norm among rulers of ancient Mesopotamia; but in the depictions he commissioned himself and in the records others left, Ashurbanipal is seen as pushing this to an extreme. Specific examples include: salting the land after putting down a revolt, forcing people to grind up their ancestors' bones to make bricks for a palace, making the defeated king of Elam pull his chariot in the triumph, and forcing one rival to live in a dog kennel. About that rival, some accounts say he was forced to wear a dog collar, others that a chain was run through his jaw.

[21:39] (Tracy V. Wilson) **This was the earliest "systematically collected" library** — The library was built in the capital, Nineveh, and tablets have been found in the Southwest Palace, the North Palace, and around the temples of Ishtar and Nabu. The episode stresses two things: first, it is not clear whether these were the library's original storage locations or the result of tablets scattering after the city's destruction; second, this is one of the earliest known libraries to be systematically acquired and organized, a deliberately collected and curated body of knowledge, and the largest collection of Assyrian texts in the world. Excavations yielded more than twenty thousand tablets and fragments, many bearing standardized colophons, indicating a systematic method of labelling and cataloguing. The total number of complete tablets is actually unknown.

[22:39] (Tracy V. Wilson) **He ordered the whole empire to hand over books, and knew who to ask** — Ashurbanipal ordered temples and palaces across the empire to send texts to Nineveh, usually by having a copy made, with him receiving the copy or the original. Surviving documents show he actually wanted the originals, and that subordinates may have "creatively misinterpreted" the instructions in order to keep originals in their own temples or collections. Surviving correspondence also shows he knew exactly where to go for the texts he wanted, and who might hold works he did not know about but that were worth acquiring. Holly describes him as having a network of scholarly acquisition librarians. Some texts in the library were written by him, and many tablets carry colophons in his hand.

[25:47] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The city burned, which fired the tablets hard and preserved them** — Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE, an event that both preserved and destroyed the library. As the city burned, the tablets were hardened by the intense heat and then protected by the collapsing rubble; but wooden or ivory writing boards covered in wax were essentially destroyed. The tablets broke and scattered during the city's destruction, and on excavation it was often unclear where in the capital they had originally been stored. Nineteenth-century excavation worsened the scattering: Austin Henry Layard and Hormuzd Rassam began excavating Nineveh in 1849, Rassam found another large batch of tablets in 1852, and huge amounts of material were sent to the British Museum; there was also a French archaeological project, so some material is now in the Louvre.

[27:48] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The fragments cannot be reassembled because nobody recorded findspots** — Many tablets are marked "Palace of Ashurbanipal, King of the World, King of Assyria", so tablets found at different locations can be confirmed as belonging to the same collection. But during excavation, archaeologists and workers did not fully record the specific findspot of each fragment, making it very hard to tell which fragment joins which. The episode says the priority at the time was getting archaeological treasures back to Britain as fast as possible, not thoroughly recording the find context of every object. The result is that reconstruction is extremely laborious: only a small portion of the tablets have been rejoined, and many remain incomplete. Since the mid-nineteenth century, an average of 35 texts a year have been reconstructed and transcribed, and a great deal of work remains.

[28:48] (Tracy V. Wilson) **The library itself was the key sample bank for deciphering cuneiform** — Researchers first deciphered cuneiform in 1857, only a few years after the library's first tablets were found. One key was the Bisitun inscription: carved on a cliff face in Iran's Zagros mountains, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and like the Rosetta Stone it exists in three languages — Babylonian, Old Persian and Elamite — recording the account of the Achaemenid king Darius I. Henry Rawlinson published his study of the Old Persian portion in 1849, which made the other two languages translatable. The library provided a large number of additional cuneiform samples and was part of the decipherment process.

[29:51] (Tracy V. Wilson) **Before the library was excavated, Assyrian history was almost only the enemy's account** — Before this, the overwhelming majority of information about ancient Mesopotamia and the Assyrian empire came from the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament derived from it, plus Greek and Roman writers. The biblical texts focus mainly on matters relating to the Levant and Egypt, and the Greek and Roman accounts were often written centuries later; neither is a complete, detailed, layered history of the Assyrian empire. Once the library's tablets were read, they became a source of a great deal of new historical information. The episode gives one concrete example: Greek literature turned Ashurbanipal into a semi-mythical figure, Sardanapalus, blending elements of him and his brother Shamashumukin, and saying he was the last king of Assyria, who burned himself to death in his palace along with all his wealth and concubines.

### verbatim quotes

[0:01] Tracy V. Wilson: "Because I was sort of thinking, wow, this guy's library sounds so amazing. And Patrick, having read other signs, was like, wow, that guy seems really ruthless."

[15:19] Tracy V. Wilson: "Some of this, like displaying their severed heads, was typical of leaders in ancient Mesopotamia. But in depictions he commissioned and in surviving accounts produced by other people, Ashurbanipal is seen as taking it to an extreme"

[21:39] Tracy V. Wilson: "Obviously, plenty of monarchs and temples and wealthy people had collections of documents and texts long before this, but this is one of the oldest known systematically acquired and organized libraries in the world. It was intentionally collected and curated as a repository of knowledge."

### glossary

- cuneiform: A writing system pressed into clay tablets with a reed stylus, the main medium for Assyrian and Babylonian texts.
- colophon: Label information at the end of a tablet; many library tablets carry standardized colophons, indicating a cataloguing method.
- Neo-Assyrian: 911 to 609 BCE, the height of the Assyrian empire; Ashurbanipal was one of its last kings.
- Sardanapalus: The semi-mythical figure Greek literature made of Ashurbanipal, blending in elements of his brother and saying he died by self-immolation.
- Bisitun inscription: A trilingual inscription on a cliff face in Iran, similar to the Rosetta Stone, key to deciphering cuneiform.

## No Irreplaceable Leaders, Only Irreplaceable Luck

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
- show: Conversations with Tyler (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tyler/)
- original episode: Jared Diamond on Leaders, Luck, and Irreplaceability
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 52:19
- transcript: YouTube captions · 8509 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born on the wettest grassland in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things up by ten or twenty years.**

why listen: Diamond is 89, talking about leaders, geographic determinism, Papua New Guinea and Bach cantatas. Medium information density, but the back half — on environmental optimism and writing method — is where the value is.

### points

[1:09] (Jared Diamond) **No irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable timing** — Diamond's answer to ‘who is the most irreplaceable leader in human history’ is ‘no one.’ Not because leaders don't matter, but because time washes out the differences: Jesus was a charismatic founder, but the Roman Empire of the same period had half a dozen other prophets; Genghis Khan built the largest land empire from China to Poland, but recent research found that the wettest period on the steppe in the past two thousand years happened to fall right around his birth — had he been born twenty years earlier or two hundred miles farther away, we would never have known his name. From this Diamond distinguishes two kinds of questions: why you and I speak English right now — the answer lies in the domesticable plants and animals of the Fertile Crescent, nothing to do with individuals; why Amazon is what it is today — the answer is Bezos alone.

[13:50] (Jared Diamond) **Rachel Carson moved environmentalism up by ten years** — Cowen challenges Diamond with the environmental Kuznets curve: once per capita income reaches 28,000, countries naturally go green — is Carson replaceable? Diamond concedes the movement would have come anyway, but stresses she moved it up by roughly ten years — the day after her Silent Spring was published, a senator announced a government investigation into toxic chemicals. More crucial was her position at the time: back then a professional scientist writing popular science was seen as ‘selling out,’ and she was not a university professor, so no one could say that of her; she was a woman, wrote like a poet, and would read her drafts aloud to hear them. Diamond says that even today's best science writer, Richard Dawkins, doesn't write as well as she did.

[18:00] (Jared Diamond) **The pomegranate juice industry waited five thousand years to appear** — Cowen tests Diamond's replaceability theory with the pomegranate juice industry: without the Resnick family, America would eventually have gone down this road anyway. Diamond says no. Pomegranates were domesticated five or six thousand years ago, but there was never a global pomegranate juice industry, because pomegranate juice is extremely hard to make — you cut an orange and squeeze, but the pomegranate's value is inside an extremely hard rind, and the contents are not pulp but small seeds; scaled production requires a three-story-tall tower that crushes whole pomegranates rind and all. In 2002 America had 22 pomegranate growers, 21 of them small farmers with no money and no incentive. Lynda Resnick put in about two hundred million dollars and waited 18 years before starting to make money. Companies like Coca-Cola and Nestlé would never allow a division to invest 150 million dollars and lose money for 18 years.

[29:32] (Jared Diamond) **Face-to-face social skill is collapsing off a cliff** — Diamond's advice to a 25-year-old who wants to become influential: learn to talk to people face to face, put down indirect communication tools. He has done 60 years of fieldwork in Papua New Guinea and watched Chevron bring in international lawyers from Switzerland to negotiate with villagers who had never left their village — the lawyers thought they'd close it in a day, but the agreement reached on day one, the villagers said on day two, ‘we forgot that agreement, the people who signed it don't count, these are a few other negotiators.’ The villagers had negotiated face to face their whole lives, with far more skill than the international lawyers. Diamond says that over the past 40 to 50 years he has watched social skills degrade, and in his 39-year-old child's generation it is especially striking, because most communication is no longer face to face and people no longer understand each other.

[33:54] (Jared Diamond) **New Guineans may be smarter than Westerners** — Diamond answers ‘yes’ outright, and says some people hate him for it. His argument is that natural selection pushed in different directions: over the past ten thousand years, survival in Europe depended mainly on getting through infectious diseases like smallpox, tuberculosis and measles, with little to do with being smart; in New Guinea the main causes of death were coping with an extremely difficult environment and coping with other New Guineans — warfare there was constant. So his impression is that New Guineans on average ask more questions and are smarter. He adds that Westerners usually think they are stupid because they use stone tools — but they lack metal tools because agricultural output was far lower, not because of intelligence. Cowen presses him on a Nature paper claiming West Eurasians have gotten smarter since the Stone Age; Diamond says he hasn't seen it, but for more than a century eugenicists have been trying to prove Europeans are smarter, with no evidence whatsoever.

[39:24] (Jared Diamond) **The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because it is an island** — Diamond rejects Greg Clark's hypothesis that the British became more patient by intermarrying and lowering their time preference. His explanation is geography: Britain is an island, needs no standing army, and is not constantly invaded — the last successful invasion was 1066. Not needing an army, it gradually developed democracy, and democracy is a productive form of government. Britain also sits on the Atlantic coast, and like the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, it was one of the countries that could spread across the whole world, because the Atlantic coast was the testing ground for maritime technology. He mentions that in the 1600s Britain cut off its king's head and Parliament became powerful. As for Daron Acemoglu and Jim Robinson's extractive vs inclusive institutions theory, Diamond says he has learned more from Jim Robinson than from any individual in the past 20 years, but thinks they give geography less weight than he does.

[44:32] (Jared Diamond) **Big business and young people have made him cautiously optimistic** — Diamond says that 20 years ago he would have said the most evil and destructive force in the world was big business, when big business basically didn't care about the environment. But over the past 20 years, big business has come to care more and more: Walmart leads on sustainable products, Unilever leads on sustainable fisheries, even oil companies. In 1999 the World Wildlife Fund sent him to do an environmental study of Chevron's oil field in Papua New Guinea, and he expected it to be terrible, but found Chevron extremely cautious, because they knew that if they screwed up, New Guineans would sue them, and they wouldn't get the Norwegian oil field development contract either. Another source of optimism is young people: 25 years ago young people didn't care about the environment, now they care very much. The probability he gives is 51% good outcome, 49% bad outcome.

[47:46] (Jared Diamond) **The most important question is not to find the most important question** — Cowen asks what the biggest environmental problem is at the global macro level, and Diamond laughs and says this is why interviewing Diamond is frustrating: his answer is always ‘the most important thing is not to go looking for that one most important thing, because the world is complicated.’ He uses marriage as an analogy: a couple about to marry asks what the single most important thing for a happy marriage is, and the answer is not to go looking for that one most important thing — you need to get 37 things right, and if you get 36 right but disagree on sex or religion, the marriage breaks. Back to the question itself, he says there are three things we must get right: climate change, inequality, and nuclear risk — including the risk of nuclear war and nuclear winter.

## AI Is a Rounding Error for Ordinary People: Diffusion Takes Fifty Years, Backlash Won't Wait

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
- show: Interconnects (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/interconnects/)
- original episode: When will average people feel AI’s impact?
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 8:31
- transcript: Official full text · 1511 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is coming too fast.**

why listen: An eight-minute short take, not especially dense, but it offers a counterintuitive angle: AI's biggest risk isn't technical failure, it's that ordinary people can't feel the benefits.

### points

[0:00] **AI is still a rounding error in daily life** — The author spent weeks on his honeymoon without touching AI at all, and on returning realised: the points where ordinary people encounter AI are either marginal or confusing. The positive impressions are making fun images and an enhanced Google search; the negative impressions are addictive social media algorithms, a friend of a friend addicted to an AI chatbot, and various claims about data centers. Family, food, transportation, entertainment — the core of daily life — have barely changed directly. His conclusion: being fascinated by AI is the result of a very small number of people actively choosing it, and stepping outside the bubble reveals that what's happening today really isn't that important to most people.

[0:00] **The Industrial Revolution gave physical things; AI gives indirect benefits** — The first Industrial Revolution brought cheaper clothes, cookware, reading material and new livelihoods; the second brought sewing machines, food preservation, indoor plumbing, photography, better light sources, bicycles and electrification — a long list, and a very physical one. The author worries that even if AI's benefits materialise (new scientific discoveries, treatments for rare diseases, sustained economic abundance), they are too indirect: ordinary people won't credit OpenAI or Anthropic with saving their life, because it was their family doctor who told them about the new treatment; and not many Americans will care that OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. He judges that fifty years from now, the daily life of the average American will still look a lot like today.

[3:47] **AI today is mainly a tool serving elites** — Knowledge work is roughly half the US economy, and for that half AI is already (or soon will be) as foundational as electricity, with rapid agent improvements over the next eighteen months accelerating this. But a transformative, highly productive tool that only lifts half of society is highly unstable. The author cites the "Engels' pause": from 1790 to 1840 British workers' wages stagnated while GDP per capita grew rapidly amid technological upheaval. He argues that if the AI industry itself thinks this is the closest analogy, then backlash from those who don't benefit is reasonable. He also agrees with Doug O'Laughlin's judgment: knowledge work output explodes while headcount in the tech industry very likely shrinks.

[3:47] **The backlash's root isn't AI, it's Big Tech's old debts** — The author splits the political backlash AI faces into two layers: first, the early positive effects are too indirect; second, they are deeply intertwined with Western society's historical grievances against Big Tech. He stresses that the latter merely collided with AI in time — if AI's exponential growth had happened decades after the growing pains of platforms like Google and Meta, the data center issue very likely would never have risen to such a central political position. Solving either one would greatly relieve the pressure and give the industry more time to make the positive case. And AI itself, through doom rhetoric and declarations of mass unemployment, has marked itself as a negative or unsafe technology, making both harder.

[3:47] **Robots might rescue the narrative for LLMs** — The author raises an ironic possibility: if the intelligence explosion from large-scale production of large language models spills over into robotics, accelerating the spread of robots in daily life, humans will quickly seize on AI's tangible benefits. This is ironic because many people have been working hard to convince the public that this LLM wave is very different from the general AI progress of the past ten or twenty years. If in the end the same dynamic saves (or largely overshadows) the LLM narrative, that would be funny. He also cautions that the connection between robotics, autonomous driving and the current AI revolution is currently more a matter of storytelling.

[3:47] **Diffusion takes fifty years; the fight against it won't wait** — The author calls the present the first five years of a fifty-year diffusion process, and lays out two simple problems: the positive effects are too indirect, and political backlash is entangled with Big Tech's history. He judges that the story of diffusion will last far longer than the struggle against it. Young people paying attention today will, within their lifetimes, see powerful AI go from effectively 0% to over 90% full adoption. What truly marks AI's evolution is the kind deeply integrated into enterprises and acting as a personal assistant; it is only just becoming viable, and adoption will be far slower than for easily understood applications like ChatGPT. So continuing to push the technology forward is crucial — the benefits are astonishing but not guaranteed, and there is still a great deal of hard work to do on distributing them widely.

### verbatim quotes

## Public leaderboards can't measure a model's real ability; third-party evaluation is the real need

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-a16z-公开榜单测不出模型真实能力-第三方评测才是刚需/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: Who Grades the AI Models? | Ben Horowitz & Rayan Krishnan
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 39:45
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7654 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Llama 4 looked astonishing on public leaderboards, yet underperformed on Vals's private held-out set—the gap between self-reported scores and real capability is spawning an independent evaluation industry.**

why listen: Medium information density; the first half covers evaluation methodology, while the second half on enterprise token spending and policy division of labor is more valuable.

### points

[3:03] (Rayan Krishnan) **Llama 4 exposed the crack in self-reported scores** — Rayan gives a concrete case: when Meta released Llama 4, the model actually underperformed on Vals's private held-out benchmark, but on all major public benchmarks—because the questions and scoring criteria are open source—it showed astonishing capability. This gap shows a huge disconnect between what labs self-report and what third-party, high-quality, high-signal benchmarks measure. Rayan believes the labs themselves understand this, and what they want is a rational buyer's market: when spending billions of dollars training a new model, there needs to be substantive evidence pointing to progress, rather than relying entirely on their own say-so.

[8:07] (Rayan Krishnan) **An evaluator can't also sell training data** — One key early decision at Vals was to never sell training data to labs. Rayan says this is a direction they are often pushed toward—when partnering with a new lab, the other side will propose buying training data, which is a lucrative business, and many companies in the industry already make gimmicky benchmarks to sell data, which has become their go-to-market. He uses the audit industry as an analogy: if the same people doing audits also do consulting for the company, the incentive structure is mixed, and it ends up as paying to pass the audit—in AI, paying to win the leaderboard. Ben adds this is a bit like MPAA ratings—what is art, what is pornography, where the line is, the definition itself changes over time, and ultimately it relies on enough people in the industry forming a consensus, rather than a narrow and easily gamed rule like "solve this problem and you reach this level."

[14:23] (Rayan Krishnan) **Evaluation is moving from millions of samples to few tasks** — Rayan describes a structural shift: the more complex the evaluation, the smaller the sample size, but the more criteria for judging the output. Early on, something like ImageNet was millions of images for basic classification, with a one-to-one mapping between input and output; now it might be a much smaller number of tasks like "generate 50 full-stack web apps for me," but the mechanism for evaluating the output is far more complex. The infrastructure layer changes accordingly—now you have to test a model's ability to run for hours, days, or even weeks, and the infrastructure must be stable enough that if a request fails, you can retry from that point rather than rerunning the entire trajectory. He believes this trend will continue as more complex work is brought into evaluation.

[16:24] (Rayan Krishnan) **Token spending may exceed salary spending** — Rayan tells a Fortune 10 company case: they gave engineers a Claude Code budget of about $100 per day, but because the quota reset at 4 p.m., the most productive work hours became 4 to 6 p.m., and there was a dead zone in the afternoon when people went for walks and coffee. The company recently raised the quota to $300 per person—almost equivalent to an employee's salary becoming tokens. Rayan's judgment: mispricing of intelligence is happening at every layer; engineers don't know how to allocate that $100 to maximum productivity, companies set quotas arbitrarily, and Anthropic is supporting all this on thin margins. When token spending starts to exceed salary spending, enterprises must justify ROI more seriously than they have in the past six months.

[20:30] (Rayan Krishnan) **The most expensive model isn't necessarily the most expensive bill** — Rayan points out that today it's still hard to say that the best OpenAI model or the best Anthropic model is necessarily the best fit for your codebase; many counterintuitive cases require running evaluations to know. The middle layer of options has become very complex: Anthropic has Opus and Sonnet, plus Luna and Terra; Luna is very cost-competitive, MewSpark is also cheap, 1.2 is very capable, and there are growing open-source models that can be self-hosted. He gives a concrete counterexample: in many cases Sonnet is more expensive than Opus because it consumes too many tokens; if you operate on a "use it if it feels applicable" basis, you may end up spending more.

[22:35] (Rayan Krishnan) **The experiment that burned $150,000 in tokens in a month** — The product ValSmith came from Vals's own missteps. Rayan ran a token maxing experiment, getting the team unlimited access to certain coding tools for a month; in hindsight, they consumed 1 to 2 billion tokens per day, with a peak of one engineer burning 6 billion in a day. He calculated that the month cost about $1.5 million worth of tokens—free, but actually 10 times employee salaries, not a 50-50 split. So they dug through traces and GitHub repos, built ValSmith, and found some counterintuitive conclusions: Cognition's Devon tool is actually very token-efficient, so it was adopted more; in some scenarios subscription pricing is more cost-effective than per-token pricing. This approach later became their operational strategy.

[28:53] (Ben Horowitz) **Government sets rules, third parties judge whether they're broken** — Ben lays out the policy division of labor very clearly: the government receives a lot of warnings from big labs—this thing will be used for biohacking, it will be a cybersecurity risk—so what the government needs to do is first clarify what it is afraid of, then ask two questions: does the model have this capability, and can people be induced to steer the model to do this. Ben thinks the government is particularly unsuited to do the latter assessment, especially over time; it's not a good government function. But the government is very good at making rules, because it can enforce them. So the ideal combination is for the government to make and enforce rules, and for capable private companies to tell it whether the rules have been broken. He also mentions a phenomenon: big labs start saying the model has this capability and can be induced to do bad things, so we won't let anyone use it—only we will use it and make sure our own people don't induce it to do bad things—and even then it doesn't always work.

[34:09] (Rayan Krishnan) **Nuclear arms control's "trust but verify" is the template for AI** — Rayan says from an idealistic perspective, he is surprised by the massive investment in sovereign AI—from a god's-eye view, building so many data centers, replicating data engineering processes, and training these super-large models is extremely inefficient and could have been consolidated. But the reality is that countries are ramping up sovereign AI construction, which requires a shared language to communicate evaluation frameworks and risk alignment. He quotes Reagan's "trust but verify," noting that Xi Jinping and Trump will meet next month, signs of trust are appearing, but there is no clear way to do the verification half. In nuclear arms control, verification relies on overflights, allowing one country to audit another's nuclear stockpile; if AI poses societal or existential risks, a shared language for evaluation must likewise be built to accomplish verification.

### verbatim quotes

[3:03] Rayan Krishnan: "what we saw is that on our held-out private benchmarks, the model is actually underperforming. But on all of the major public benchmarks where the questions and rubrics are actually open source, it was showing incredible capability."

[8:07] Rayan Krishnan: "if you have the same group who's responsible for doing the audit, as well as also consulting and supporting the company, you have a mixed incentive structure. And then it just becomes pay to pass the audit, or in this case, pay to win the benchmark."

### glossary

- held-out private benchmarks: Evaluation sets whose questions and scoring criteria are not public, preventing models from specifically gaming the score.
- recursive self-improvement (RSI): The process where a model participates in training the next generation of models, creating a self-compounding capability loop.
- reward hacking: When a model bypasses the evaluation objective and uses shortcuts to get a high score.
- token maxing: Pushing token usage to the limit regardless of cost, in exchange for maximum output.
- harness: The outer system that wraps the model and handles tool calls and task orchestration.

who it is for: Engineering leads choosing AI models and coding agents for their companies, CTOs who need to justify AI ROI to their boards, and practitioners focused on AI policy and evaluation standards.

tags: AI evaluation, benchmarks, enterprise AI, AI policy, token cost

## Weather forecasts are 95% accurate, and nobody believes them

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-ologies-天气预报准确率-95-但没人相信它/
- show: Ologies with Alie Ward (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ologies/)
- original episode: Meteorology (WEATHER & CLIMATE) Encore with Marshall Shepherd
- published: 2026-09-09 · duration: 1:16:07
- transcript: Machine transcription · 14125 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A meteorologist says forecasts are about 95% accurate three to five days out; the public only remembers the time they got soaked. Climate isn't future tense, it's present continuous.**

why listen: Medium information density: the first half is career explainer, the second half — on probability, hurricane cones and climate lag — is worth hearing.

### points

[14:27] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **The forecast isn't wrong, your memory is biased** — The public broadly believes weather forecasts are often wrong, but the number Shepard gives is roughly 95% accuracy in the three-to-five-day window. The problem isn't the model, it's memory: people remember the cookout that got rained on, the kid's ballgame that got rained on, and forget all the days the forecast nailed it. He uses the kicker analogy — perfect all season, misses one in the Super Bowl, and that's the only one anyone remembers. What this changes: forecast reliability is far higher than its public reputation, and that reputation is shaped by statistical bias.

[18:36] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **Bomb cyclone isn't a new word, it's new exposure** — Many people assume bomb cyclone, polar vortex and derecho are signals that the climate has changed. Shepard rejects that outright: these terms have existed in meteorology for decades, they've just recently come into heavy use in mass media. So you can't use the popularity of a term as an anchor for climate change. What's actually changing is intensity — heavier downpours, more frequent and more severe heat waves, rapid hurricane intensification, higher sea levels pushing more water in with the same storm, bigger storm-surge losses.

[22:42] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **The reason for optimism is that we know what to do** — Shepard says he doesn't want to stop at bad news, because the good news is this isn't a problem that still needs head-scratching research — we know what to do: cut carbon emissions, and we must adapt, because some changes have already crossed irreversible points. He cites the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave: most homes there had no air conditioning, Canada recorded 120 degrees Fahrenheit, it was called a once-in-a-millennium event, but climate change made it 150 times more likely, causing nearly $9 billion in losses and 1,400 heat deaths. The adaptation strategy is to retrofit those houses with air conditioning.

[28:06] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **Warming makes blizzards fiercer, not milder** — The counterintuitive mechanism: hurricanes, downpours and blizzards all start with water vapor. The Clausius-Clapeyron equation says a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapor. For every 1 degree Fahrenheit of warming, water vapor increases about 4% (7% in Celsius). A century ago the Northeast US averaged 22 degrees Fahrenheit in winter; now it's up to 26, and some years 30 — against 22 degrees that's a 32% increase in water vapor, and 30 degrees is still below the 32-degree freezing point. So a warmer planet means more water in the atmosphere, and blizzards can hit harder.

[41:31] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **The hurricane cone is probability, not a path** — During Hurricane Ian in 2022, some people evacuated from one part of the cone to another — a complete misreading. The cone means the storm center has a 67% chance of falling somewhere inside it, not that the storm will travel down the cone's center line. Shepard says the public broadly struggles with probability, uncertainty, two or more processes happening at once, and anything that can't be simplified to their level — so they simplify complex information down to their level, and the cost is bad decisions.

[1:00:12] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **A 20% chance of rain doesn't mean it won't rain** — Shepard tells the story of getting soaked while rafting with his son: a woman nearby complained that it was only a 20% chance of rain and meteorologists are always wrong. But that day wasn't 0% — they just happened to be in that 20% area. Statistically, 80% of the area stayed dry and they landed in the 20% that got rain. One way to compute POP is confidence of rain × fraction of area affected: 60% confidence over 60% of the area gives a POP of 36%. So "20% chance" doesn't mean "it won't rain" — it's describing a regional probability distribution.

[1:07:32] (Dr. Marshall Shepherd) **Satellites cover more, balloons resolve more** — On the trade-off between weather balloons and satellites: satellites give more consistent observations over a wider area, while balloons only have data at the launch point and launch moment, sometimes only twice a day. But satellite resolution is far coarser. Shepard uses a phone camera analogy: more pixels make a better photo, and finer resolution in observations or models captures more fine-scale weather. A thermometer or barometer at your location has far better resolution than the blurry one-square-mile reading a satellite gives you.

### verbatim quotes

[12:24] Dr. Marshall Shepherd: "weather is your mood and climate is your personality"

[14:27] Dr. Marshall Shepherd: "Almost all of the time, about 95% of the time within three to five days. It's just that it's human nature for people to remember the bad ones."

[22:42] Dr. Marshall Shepherd: "Climate change is now we've got to stop using future tense. We're living it right now"

[41:31] Dr. Marshall Shepherd: "there's a 67% chance that the center of that storm can be anywhere in that hurricane cone"

[1:00:12] Dr. Marshall Shepherd: "it wasn't a 0% chance of rain. In fact, we were probably in the 20% region that day."

[1:09:35] Dr. Marshall Shepherd: "it's fluid dynamics, but it's accessible to many in the public. So they think it's much more."

### figures

- Weather forecast accuracy, three to five days: about 95% [14:27]
- Water vapor increase per 1 degree Fahrenheit of warming: about 4% (7% in Celsius) [29:09]
- Canada's record high during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave: 120 degrees Fahrenheit [23:47]
- How much more likely the 2021 heat wave was made by climate change: 150 times [23:47]
- Economic losses from the 2021 heat wave: nearly $9 billion [23:47]
- Probability the storm center falls inside the hurricane cone: 67% [41:31]
- Hurricane track forecast error: 50 to 100 nautical miles [57:03]
- Share of Earth's water that is usable: 0.3% [26:00]

### glossary

- Clausius-Clapeyron equation: The physical relationship describing how a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapor.
- wet bulb globe temperature: A heat-stress index combining temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation and cloud cover.
- bombogenesis: When colliding cold and warm air masses cause a low-pressure system's pressure to drop rapidly — a bomb cyclone.
- atmospheric river: A long, narrow band of moisture that can carry as much water as the Amazon River.
- ENSO: The warm-cold cycle of equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperatures — El Niño and La Niña.
- AMO: A warm-cold pattern in Atlantic sea-surface temperatures that flips roughly every 70 years.

who it is for: Engineers and product people interested in weather, climate communication and probability communication; anyone doing risk communication, early-warning systems, or agriculture and energy decisions.
