## When Investors Say They Don't Back Solo Founders, It's Usually Just a Polite No

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-solofounders-投资人说不投单人创始人-多半只是个体面的拒绝/
- show: Solo Founders (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/solofounders/)
- original episode: Why Investors Say "We Don't Back Solo Founders" (And What They Mean)
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 21:41
- transcript: YouTube captions · 3961 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**65% of startups die from people problems, and in an early-stage company the only "people" are the co-founders — so "we don't back solo founders" is often just the easiest exit for an investor who doesn't want to tell the truth.**

why listen: Medium information density, but two judgments — the denominator delusion and the idea that a pass is a face-saving excuse — can directly change how you handle your own fundraise.

### points

[1:05] **A co-founder isn't table stakes, it's a high bar** — They've spent seven years helping people find co-founders, and they still believe an excellent co-founder is enormously valuable — but the bar should be absurdly high. Don't force a convenience co-founder just because "people think you should have one." Their position isn't "don't find a co-founder," it's "don't let the search for a co-founder stop you from starting."

[2:05] **Companies die from people problems, and early on the only person is the founder** — About 65% of companies fail because of people problems, not product or customers. And when a company is just getting started, the only "person" in it is the co-founder — so the co-founder is itself the leading source of company death. That leads directly to a counterintuitive conclusion: a solo founder actually sidesteps the biggest cause of early-stage death.

[3:05] **The number one killer of solo founders is loneliness** — Solo founders have no co-founder, so the most common early-stage blowup cause doesn't apply to them; their real failure point is loneliness. With no teammate, no one with equal stake and equal incentive to carry it with them, things hit extremely hard when they go wrong. Their solution isn't to force you into a pair — it's to build solo together: gather solo founders each building their own company, giving each other context, connections and insight, without forcing anyone into a team.

[10:11] **Not backing solo founders is the easiest rejection line** — Investors really do have a bias against solo founders, but more often it's just the least offensive reason to say no. Saying "I'd love to back you, but I don't back solo founders" is far easier than saying "I don't believe in you, your company, or your market." So don't take a pass too seriously, and don't expect them to change their minds — they usually won't. But equally, don't over-read the reason for the pass: unless they gave you very direct, very brutal feedback, it's mostly just relationship maintenance.

[11:12] **With no co-founder, investors can only read your hiring** — Investors will care especially about who you hire next, because without a co-founder they've lost the ready-made yardstick for judging your talent bar. Every person you hire adds a cultural signal to the company: you're founder and CEO, but after three hires, 75% of the people aren't founders. So investors want to know what your talent standard is. The exception is a company like Pulseia's Ben, pursuing true solo and hiring as few people as possible.

[13:12] **Solo founders don't have to optimize only for valuation** — If the company is split three ways, dilution hurts much more, so you might accept a higher valuation from a lower-quality firm just to dilute less. Solo founders don't have that pressure and can prioritize a firm with a better reputation, one more likely to help you than hurt you. The conclusion: valuation is just one of many variables when choosing a lead investor, and it shouldn't be the only one.

[15:15] **The denominator delusion: failed companies had co-founders too** — The data argument against solo founders is that "most of the most successful companies were co-founded" — which is true as far as it goes. But it's missing the denominator: how many failed companies were also co-founded? Once you count the denominator, you find that far more co-founded companies fail. The denominator is so large for two reasons: everyone thinks you must have a co-founder, and co-founders are precisely why most companies die. Solo founders have a smaller numerator and a smaller denominator; you still have a chance to be a winner, you just have to keep going.

[17:16] **People who worry they have solo founder syndrome usually don't** — Solo founder syndrome is roughly understood as "can't work well with others." Their retort: then what syndrome do the 65% of companies that break up over co-founders have? There really are people who want a co-founder but can't find one because they're a jerk, but the people who worry "am I a jerk?" are exactly the ones who don't need to worry — the ones who should worry would never let the thought enter their heads.

[2:05] : "about 65% of the reasons that uh companies fail are because of people issues. It's not about product or about customers. It's about people. And when you're starting a company, the only people are the co-founders."

[15:15] : "How many of the companies that have failed also have co-founders? And if you include the denominator in this, you'll see that not only of course are many great companies started with co-founders, but many many many more are started that ultimately fail."

### figures

- Applications for the first cohort of the solo founder program: 1,000 applications for 6 spots [7:08]
- Applications for the fourth cohort of the solo founder program: 4,500 applications for 10 spots [7:08]

### glossary

- co-founder of convenience: A co-founder you settle for because you feel you "should" have one, rather than someone genuinely right.
- denominator delusion: Looking only at the share of successful companies with co-founders while ignoring that failed companies also had co-founders.
- true solo: Going as long as possible without hiring any human teammate, building the company entirely alone.
- talent bar: The threshold a founder actually enforces when hiring, which investors use to judge team quality.

who it is for: Founders who are considering going solo or have already been rejected by investors with "we don't back solo founders," and early-stage investors who want to understand what actually kills early-stage companies.

## AI writing's moat isn't the model, it's the proprietary data you feed it

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
- show: AI & I (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/aiandi/)
- original episode: How a Professional Writer Writes With AI
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 47:58
- transcript: Official transcript · 7899 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Every writer Katie spent two years turning ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.**

why listen: Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer uses AI as a mode of production: the substance is concentrated in the last 30 minutes, and the personal story up front provides the motivational background.

### points

[2:09] (Katie Parrott) **The biggest value of an AI coach isn't saving money** — After being laid off she was at a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20-a-month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing her thoughts out and letting AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalise her thinking, counter catastrophising, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of that experience wasn't the money saved, but that it made her believe AI really can drive concrete change in a life. At the time she was hesitating over whether to take Every's freelance offer, and it was ChatGPT that gave her the push to just try it.

[8:26] (Katie Parrott) **Throughput comes from upfront context, not clever prompts** — She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she knew how to write a smarter one-line prompt, but because she did a great deal of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience profiles and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content repurposing, and AI is good at rewriting one long piece into versions for different platforms. The rule she distilled: set the scene up front, and only then can you move fast later.

[11:28] (Katie Parrott) **Give the model a fence first, then talk tone and word choice** — Before Claude Projects existed, she could only keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into context each time. This structure didn't fall from the sky; it comes from the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what the pain points are, how the product maps to them, who the competitors are and where the differentiation lies. She says this amounts to giving the model a playground with a fence: first make sure it won't wander off, then talk about word choice, tone and reading difficulty. Later, as soon as Projects launched, she built a separate project for every client and every column.

[15:40] (Katie Parrott) **AI writing's last mile can only be covered by a human** — She believes there is a "last mile" problem in AI writing: the model has a knowledge cutoff, and it isn't in the real physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw the model a single line like "write a blog post about style guides", all you'll get is generic content it already knows, which is commoditised information; what really makes writing distinctive is fresh ingredients the model has never seen, such as internal company research, third-party reports and personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human is responsible for providing good ingredients.

[22:50] (Katie Parrott) **AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output** — She talks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster, but reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care doctor for three years, and in the end just had Codex find doctors who accepted her insurance and were taking new patients and complete the booking; email is first filtered by automation, and only messages that genuinely need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't treating AI as a production tool, but as assistive technology that makes her day-to-day running "as a person" easier.

[27:03] (Katie Parrott) **Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritise for you** — Two years ago she was just asking ChatGPT whether it could be her career coach; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her role profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a folder of reader praise and her OKRs. She doesn't maintain a board herself; she uses voice conversations to have the system prioritise by highest impact, and the system also maintains her Kanban for her. The key to building this system was letting AI interview her repeatedly and then sedimenting the interview content into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

[32:27] (Katie Parrott) **Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted** — The core of the Compound Writing plugin is compounding thinking: every piece of feedback given to AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and reworked it into a writing workflow: code and writing both have brainstorming, planning, drafting and review stages, except writing focuses more on structure, voice and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that works sentence by sentence, and a final pass that checks before publication. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window, but feeds the day's fresh material into this system.

[39:19] (Katie Parrott) **Vonnegut as editor gives you a perspective, not a verdict** — She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's principle of suspense about the bomb under the table, and the expressive styles of Sorkin and Sedaris into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether "the story starts as close to the end as possible" and whether "every sentence earns its place"; Hitchcock's perspective asks whether the reader will want to keep reading because of this. She stresses that this isn't letting the masters' ghosts grade your draft, but giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject; non-professional writers may actually benefit more, because they're less likely to be picking at themselves while they write.

[44:49] (Katie Parrott) **AI's compounding may only compound for the few who got in early** — She says her core thesis about AI today is this: access to education and to using it will matter more than ever. She lives in Columbus, Ohio, and has never lived in New York or San Francisco, which makes her care more about how opportunity is distributed. She admits she got where she is because she had financial slack, a time budget and a network with access to excellent peers; she hopes the AI community will actively create conditions for more places and more kinds of people to get on board. Because she sees clearly that AI has enormous compounding effects, and the cost is that the returns may only compound for the few who happened to get in early.

### verbatim quotes

[5:13] Natalia Quintero: "Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt."

[15:40] Katie Parrott: "And our job as the humans is to close that last mile and provide the real world experiences that AI can't get because they come after the knowledge cut off and it's also out there happening somewhere in the real world and AI is not in the real world, the physical world yet."

[22:50] Katie Parrott: "We think about AI as a productive technology, right? We value it for its ability to produce output and get things out of our, like just put stuff out. And what I found in my personal experience is that AI is just as powerful as a supportive technology."

[32:27] Katie Parrott: "compounding is the idea that every piece of feedback that you give to AI should feed back into the system to improve the next output."

[44:49] Katie Parrott: "My thesis on AI today is that education and access are going to matter more than they ever have before."

[46:32] Katie Parrott: "But the risk there is that value is going to compound to the small subset of people that happen to be early. And I just think that a much more compelling vision for an AI future is one where everyone is able to come along for the ride."

### figures

- Human career coach hourly rate vs ChatGPT monthly fee: about $150/hour vs $20/month [3:11]
- Time spent putting off booking a primary care doctor: about 3 years [23:53]
- Number of security vulnerabilities Codex found in her Tastemaker project: 5 [43:24]

### glossary

- context engineering: Pre-organising information such as brand, audience, product and differentiation into a fixed background so every AI conversation heads in the right direction.
- last mile problem: Model training has a knowledge cutoff, so humans need to supply the latest data and real-world experience for writing not to fall into generic platitudes.
- compound engineering: Sedimenting one-off feedback given to AI into the system so the same good decisions automatically take effect again and again in future.
- computer errands: Having an AI agent handle administrative chores you keep putting off, such as booking doctors, filing insurance claims and sorting your inbox.

who it is for: Independent writers and content entrepreneurs struggling with the quality of AI-generated writing, and anyone who wants an AI agent to take over life and administrative tasks.
what to skip: The layoff story and the ad break in the first few minutes can be fast-forwarded; start on the methodology at the 8:26 delivery case.

## Stronger Models Make Dirty Data Deadlier: Cleaning Is Worth More, Not Less

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
- show: Signals and Threads (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/signalsandthre/)
- original episode: Wrestling the world into rows with Eric Mannes
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 1:25:00
- transcript: YouTube captions · 13499 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model, the more dangerous it gets; pinning down "what was known at the time" is worth more than tuning the model.**

why listen: This episode is a dense account of how data engineering actually creates value; the second half, on corrected data, timestamps and cost models, contains judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

### points

[2:06] (Eric) **Once a pattern is found, competition erases it** — This is what Eric defines as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, the patterns you find are often quickly absorbed by other people and the market, and then stop working; knowledge that can accumulate over the long term like a law of physics is rare. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio of trading data is inherently ugly — the whole mechanism of the market is to keep squeezing out extractable signal, and what's left gets closer and closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you have to keep finding new facts, not guard old patterns.

[19:21] (Eric) **Prices can go negative, so don't hard-code assumptions into the system** — On April 20, 2020, the settlement price of near-expiry crude oil futures on the CME closed negative — just for that one day, and the final settlement price later returned to positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage space at the delivery point, Cushing, was nearly full and nobody wanted to take physical delivery. Order and risk systems that had long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some people couldn't place orders, some didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion is that a large part of trading is understanding the dumb details of reality: tank capacity, contract multipliers, quote units — only when the system gets these details right can you draw a ceiling on risk.

[32:33] (Eric) **Domain experts don't know how good good tools can be** — For data and systems to be genuinely usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have a high tolerance for painful workflows, worn down by Excel and manual processes to the point where they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the domain's real mechanics to engineers, and to explain "how good it could get" to traders. Jane Street now has such an embedded developer on every desk, and that role grew out of exactly this.

[59:04] (Eric) **The number of parking spaces is not the sales figure** — The classic example of alternative data is counting cars in Walmart parking lots — the fuller the cars, the better the business. Eric says this example is actually terrible: what you want to infer is consumer spending, but parking spaces only tell you foot traffic, very indirectly; about 20% of Walmart shopping happens online, and a city like New York has no parking lots to count. The more direct signal is on the transaction side: card-issuing banks, the Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit unions' processing systems know how much people actually spent, and can sell anonymised aggregate statistics to buyers.

[1:04:08] (Eric) **Corrected data turns a backtest into a time machine** — When deciding "should we subscribe to this dataset," the vendor may already have corrected past errors; backtesting on the pretty corrected data doesn't test the data you would actually have received back then, but the right answer you only learned later. Eric says this is equivalent to simulating that you have a time machine. Jane Street's solution is to keep every piece of raw data and the local timestamp at which it was received, so that no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct "what exactly we knew at that moment." This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data's arrival time.

[1:08:10] (Eric) **LLMs know the future, so keep them off historical data** — AI hits alternative data on two levels: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make it easy to extract features from text. But watch out for a causal trap — using the latest LLM to featurize old documents drags in what happened later: it knows how Enron ended, and it may have seen later revisions of this financial report in its training data. This amounts to creating a new leak of future information, and when handling historical data you especially need to pin down "which point-in-time model was used."

[1:11:26] (Eric) **The stronger the model, the more data cleaning is worth** — A common expectation is that as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric's view is the opposite: once models can do more on their own, you can do less manual feature work, but the data you feed in has to be more correct. If the data isn't point-in-time and quietly leaks future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models also have different tolerances for outliers and patches of dirty data. All told, cleaning data is worth more, not less.

[1:16:34] (Eric) **Usage-based billing pushes teams to keep pinching pennies** — Jane Street runs its data warehouse in its own data centre, and it isn't purely about control. Eric's observation: move the same queries to a cloud vendor billed by reads or compute time, and the price is high enough that you'd feel "this money could buy a pile of hardware." More important is the distorting effect of the cost model — usage-based billing makes teams constantly optimise the bill and reshape workloads to accommodate the billing; once self-hosted, cost becomes a one-off hardware investment, and the team spends its time on research and queries themselves rather than on saving money.

### verbatim quotes

[32:33] Eric: "the domain experts like who are not themselves software engineers like don't understand how good things can be if we build the right software for it."

[59:04] Eric: "Like the thing you're getting at is like how many people showed up which is different from how much they're spending."

[1:04:08] Eric: "you're not actually studying like what trades you would have done if you'd been subscribing to the data set. You're uh simulating what you would have done if you had a time machine, right?"

[1:08:10] Eric: "if you use like a really up-to-date LLM to like that knows stuff about old data and trying to, you know, use it to featurize some old data, like you're going to get very confusing things happen because the LLM is smart. It knows things about the future."

[1:12:27] Eric: "It seems like an enormous amount of like human judgment is incredibly important."

### figures

- Number of data engineers at Jane Street: The first one only arrived in 2023; today about 20-plus [43:42]
- Walmart's online shopping share: About 20% [59:04]
- Negative crude oil futures settlement event: Closed negative for one day on April 20, 2020; the final settlement price turned positive [19:21]
- Data engineer intern development timeline: Interview in 2026, summer in 2027, join in 2028, fully productive in 2029 [1:22:40]

### glossary

- alt data: External data used for investment judgments but not traditional data such as exchange quotes, e.g. satellite imagery and consumer aggregates.
- anti-inductive environment: An environment where patterns get competed away once discovered, making knowledge hard to accumulate over the long term.
- point-in-time data: Data that records only "what was already known at the time" and contains no future information.
- desk dev: An engineer embedded in a trading desk who combines domain understanding with systems development.

who it is for: CTOs who want to build a data team, quants evaluating data vendors, and engineers who believe large models will clean data automatically.

## The most valuable step in writing with AI isn't the prompt — it's compounding your revision feedback

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-every-用-ai-写作最值钱的一步不是提示词-而是把改稿反馈沉淀成复利/
- show: Every (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/every/)
- original episode: How a Professional Writer Writes With AI
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 48:26
- transcript: YouTube captions · 7899 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 2 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Katie took AI from professional coach all the way to writing plugin: first load the model with context, then store every revision note back into the system and let it compound. For her, AI's value isn't just speed — it's a support system that steadies her emotions and gets her past execution roadblocks.**

why listen: Not another prompt demo, but a rare record of how a writer grows her own AI workflow: how to build context files, how to choose reviewers, even how a non-technical person avoids the pitfalls — concrete enough to copy.

### points

[2:09] (Katie Parrott) **Hiring AI as a coach is about being questioned, not being thought for** — After being laid off while working as an editor and ghostwriter at a crypto company, Katie tried agency-side, client-side and freelancing, and still felt she had hit the end of what her own ideas could do. A real career coach was too expensive — she estimated about $150/hour — so she switched to ChatGPT at $20/month. She wasn't looking for someone to think for her, but to use it as an object to externalize her thinking onto: lay out her situation, have it question and push back, especially pull her out of herself when she tends to catastrophize. She later called this approach a ‘thinking tool’. She even used it to decide whether to accept Every's column invitation — at the time ChatGPT suggested she try it first, and she ended up going all the way to where she is now.

[8:26] (Katie Parrott) **One person delivering five channels runs on context, not typing speed** — In early 2025, while freelancing, Katie badly overcommitted: within a two-week deadline she had to deliver 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, 16 Instagram posts. Getting it done wasn't about writing fast, but about what she only later realized was called context engineering: first write out the company's brand information, product details, audience and differentiation point by point, then let the model generate. Building that context up front was laborious, but once the foundation was laid, production speed afterward became very fast. She admits that six months later she repeated the overcommitment — the method didn't cure her overcommitting habit.

[13:36] (Katie Parrott) **Without underlying information, style constraints just spin in place** — On what to put into a project first, Katie is clear: not rules like ‘use these words, avoid those’ or ‘keep reading difficulty low’, but first give the model a foundational file on who the reader is, where it hurts, how the product maps to that pain, who the competitors are and what the differentiation is. She says this was her instinct from writing style guides in content marketing, just now fed to AI. Only after the foundational material is in place does it come to constraints at the level of tone, wording and syntax. Her positioning on ‘style’: wording debates will drag on forever, but without underlying information, style constraints just spin in place.

[16:40] (Katie Parrott) **The model is the kitchen; fresh ingredients can only be brought in by a human** — The ‘data’ she means isn't generic background, but first-hand material that happened after the model's knowledge cutoff, or that only exists in the real physical world: research the company did itself, third-party reports, specific personal experiences. If you just let the model write a ‘style guide’ from what it already knows, the output is commoditized information. So what she needs a human to own is the ‘last mile’: bringing new material the model doesn't have into the system. Her metaphor is that the model is the kitchen and the process is chopping and cooking, but the fresh ingredients must be carried into the kitchen by a human — the quality and freshness of the input ultimately determine whether a piece is worth reading.

[22:50] (Katie Parrott) **AI as supportive technology is as strong as AI as production tool** — Katie talks about a layer rarely said publicly: she has bipolar disorder, experiences high-energy periods, and also faces very, very long lows. For her, AI's value isn't just ‘high output’, but reducing friction in daily life and making it easier to be a person who functions normally. She put off booking a family doctor for three years, and finally had Codex automatically find nearby doctors who accept her insurance and take new patients, and book it; her inbox is also handed to automation to first filter out the mail that genuinely needs her reply, rather than her digging through a pile of subscription notifications every day looking for a ‘bomb’. In her own words: AI as supportive technology is as powerful as productive technology.

[27:59] (Katie Parrott) **A career coach isn't one prompt, it's a project** — That simple ‘be my career coach’ prompt from back then has now become a standalone project in Codex: it contains her own profile and role positioning, Every's brand positioning intelligence, article performance data exported from the CMS, a validation folder specifically collecting reader praise, and Q2/Q3 OKRs. Much of the material wasn't organized by hand: she learned Alex Duffy's method of having AI interview her, drawing the thoughts out of her head and turning them into documents. She now increasingly talks to it directly by voice, ‘thinking out loud’, having it prioritize, do project management, maintain the kanban. She has even forgotten what's on the kanban, and only asks about the deadline for a given deliverable when she needs to.

[32:09] (Katie Parrott) **Writing should be like engineering: correct the same problem only once** — Compound Writing started by forking Kieran's Compound Engineering: in engineering, the system should remember every piece of feedback, correct the same problem only once, and do it right automatically next time; writing should be the same. She mapped the engineering version's brainstorming, planning, working, reviewing onto writing's brainstorming, outline, draft and review, and designed three kinds of review: substantive edit looks at overall structure and argument, line edit polishes sentence by sentence, and finally a publication-ready final check. She no longer opens a web chat window, but runs this system on the Claude or ChatGPT desktop app, with the style guide, sample articles and other context inside, and the human only needs to bring in fresh information. At the time of recording the plugin was already downloadable from Every's GitHub.

[40:19] (Katie Parrott) **This plugin is a gym, not a ghostwriting machine** — She calls the plugin a gym, with the goal of making the user stronger rather than letting AI ghostwrite. She breaks favorite authors into invokable reviewer skills: Vonnegut says ‘start as close to the end as possible, every sentence must earn its place, give the reader a character to root for’; Hitchcock says ‘bomb under the table’ — if you first let the audience see the countdown, one second of shock becomes five minutes of suspense. She builds these frameworks directly into the editing step, so after writing you can invoke Vonnegut, Hitchcock, Sorkin, Sedaris to look at your draft. She thinks non-professional writers may benefit even more, because there's no stock attachment of ‘how I used to write it better’ in the way.

### verbatim quotes

[5:13] Natalia Quintero: "Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt."

[10:28] Katie Parrott: "But when you have that environment set up, you can just kind of run and like run fast."

[17:45] Katie Parrott: "So the data is the unique insight, the data point that the model doesn't have access to yet, the personal experience, all of those things that are working are ultimately going to make the writing unique."

[46:32] Katie Parrott: "what I want to challenge the AI community with is thinking about how we can expand those kinds of opportunities to more people and more kinds of people in more different places."

### figures

- How long she put off booking a family doctor: 3 years [23:53]

### glossary

- Compound Engineering: Having AI remember every piece of feedback, give the same correction only once, then apply it automatically so output keeps improving.
- Compound Writing: Katie's port of Compound Engineering into the writing process — a plugin that accumulates style, structure and review feedback.
- context engineering: Before letting the model write, load brand, audience, competitor and other background information into the system to set boundaries for the AI.
- supportive technology: AI that isn't responsible for producing content but reduces friction in life and execution, making it easier to get done what needs doing.
- MCP: A general interface standard connecting models to external data and applications; Katie uses it to link small apps with the tools she uses.

who it is for: Reporters and editors doing content, WeChat public accounts or long-form pieces, plus indie developers building AI as a personal productivity system; especially suited to anyone stuck with homogenized AI output who wants to build their own workflow.

## Nvidia Has No Monopoly, Only First-Mover Advantage — Take 90% of the Money and Someone Will Come Dig Up Your Foundation

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-cn561550-英伟达没有垄断只有先发优势-赚走九成钱就等着被挖地基/
- show: 科技乱炖 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cn561550/)
- original episode: 从抢 GPU 到喂 AI，互联网正在悄悄更换主人
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 1:09:49
- transcript: Official transcript · 20788 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Nvidia's moat is the CUDA software layer plus a hardware lead, but it has not formed a monopoly. The higher the gross margin, the stronger the incentive for model makers to build their own chips — swinging that shovel is partly about answering to the capital markets.**

why listen: The first half has high-density detail on the GPU black market; the second half has real judgments on how AI rewrites product logic; the model-evaluation section in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

### points

[1:01] **Taking 90% of the money means everyone wants to dig you up** — Nvidia's moat is software plus hardware: the hardware is the GPU, the software is the CUDA middle layer that acts as a bridge between human programming and the GPU. But it has not formed a monopoly, only a leading first-mover advantage. The problem is that when you run especially fast and take 90% of the world's money, the price is that everyone wants to settle that money with you, with a crowd behind you chasing with guns. And the higher the gross margin, the greater everyone's incentive to chase. Model makers themselves have an interest in raising gross margins, whether through cost cuts or efficiency gains; squeeze to a certain point and the knife naturally swings at Nvidia's ecosystem — even if it is only a test swing.

[3:49] **Swinging this shovel is about answering to capital** — Why do model makers insist on developing their own chips even knowing how hard it is? This is not just a technology-selection question, it is even a question of how to answer to the capital markets. I want to swing this shovel to tell the capital markets that I am trying to do this, that I have not raised my hands in surrender and been monopolized by a single ecosystem. Amazon and Google have already proven that building your own chips is feasible, and the bigger the scale, the more money you save. So OpenAI also announced it would make its own chips, with the evaluation score called Mexican chili pepper. But this takes too much money — OpenAI said it would spend 45 billion US dollars to rent compute; can 45 billion build its own? Probably not enough.

[6:01] **An eight-card server is 14 million RMB in China spot** — Take the relatively advanced B300 server as an example: 4T of memory, eight cards per unit, spot price in China over 14 million RMB. The same machine in the US costs only just over 500,000 US dollars, about six to seven million RMB, three times the price. There are multiple reasons for the high cost: US government export controls — the so-called defense is about preventing you from shipping it out. You can order on Amazon in the US and have it delivered to a home in Silicon Valley, but it cannot leave the country — it needs KYC, it cannot be China, and it needs IDC proof. When the machine is routed through layer after layer of forgery to Southeast Asia, say Thailand, it basically doubles; then from Thailand it breaks through layer after layer of defense into the mainland, going through both sides, and it triples.

[10:10] **512 units delivered means plugging in and lighting up 512 times** — Spot trading is like housing, generally sold in powers of two: two units, four, eight, 128, 256. Someone ran into 512 units quoted at over 7 billion. The transaction process: first you screenshot your bank account to prove you really have the money, and the other side has to shoot a video proving the goods really exist, saying the company name and holding that day's newspaper. On delivery it is one unit at a time: plug in and light up to show it is good, wire the money, haul one away, then the next, repeated 512 times, taking almost a day — because lighting up one server with cards pulled takes half a day. The 80 billion HKD Alibaba raised is only enough to buy 5,000 units.

[11:28] **Futures are all fake, and 70% of spot is brokers** — In the flood of futures inquiries, an 8 million quote is cheaper than the 14 million spot price, but nobody dares do it; now it is full-payment letters of credit. A letter of credit is a bank guarantee, understandable as an old paper version of Alipay, used for bulk commodity trade, and it also needs a third-party warehouse: goods go into the third-party warehouse, the warehouse receipt goes to the bank, the bank pays on seeing the receipt, and the buyer takes the receipt to the warehouse to collect the goods. But the current play is: the buyer issues a full letter of credit, the seller takes the letter of credit and the buyer's documents to the bank as collateral, gets the money and goes to buy the goods. So futures are 100% all fake — as long as the goods arrive, there is no compensation risk, and you can sell spot directly, who wouldn't do it? Spot is also estimated to be 70% fake, with 70% of sellers being brokers.

[19:21] **What must a 14 million machine run to pay for itself** — Do the math: 14 million buys eight cards; for training, one or two units is definitely not enough, you need at least several hundred; for inference, how much does buying tokens cost? When does it pay back? It used to be said ten months to pay back, now that has already fallen. Someone saw the news of DeepSeek's IPO and said model makers have pretty high margins, seemingly reaching 60-70% — but that does not count the investment, nor the servers; with hardware assets amortized, plus data center, power and maintenance costs, maybe you calculate a 60-70 gross margin. The key is whether there is a steady stream of writable content to keep the cards fully loaded. Many businesses do not make money because there is too much idle time, just like a restaurant: if it can be full 24 hours a day, the margin is also very high.

[24:44] **A domestic GPU runs a top model; Nvidia falls then rises** — Zhipu released GLM 5.3 Flash; the score is not first, but it basically caught up with Opus 4.8, and it claims to have entered the top tier. The most important thing is not the score, but the line in the article: our compute runs on domestic GPUs, and after optimization, the computational efficiency of domestic GPUs has caught up with that of overseas GPU products. That sentence went viral. The timing of the news was also bad, landing during the evening development window. Nvidia fell only a little yesterday and rose over 6% today. The market is now either extremely optimistic or extremely pessimistic; one piece of news seriously affects the direction, and a couple of days later it comes back.

[31:42] **Models split in two: top price for creativity, cheapest for repetition** — Now blind tests cannot tell the models apart, so people start choosing on price. But the enterprise side actually splits into two scenarios: creativity-driven scenarios, such as writing code or doing long-horizon analysis to produce reports, where no matter how cheap it is you will not use it — you will definitely use the top tier, because the sunk cost is too high and redoing it after a bad job is not worth it, wasting both time and money. The other is work like content analysis, where the output directly determines enterprise revenue, so you must choose the model with more reasonable ROI. It is like hiring people: for cleaning, even at a monthly salary of 10,000 the best still feels unnecessary, so among the cheapest you find one that is passable; for an engineer, you are willing to pay a higher salary to buy creativity. Two ends — stand in the middle and you are backed by neither.

[39:14] **The official website is read by AI; more words is an advantage** — A report says 70% of internet traffic is already AI. If the official website is read by AI, it must be written more complexly and give complete information to gain an advantage from the GEO angle. SEO used to be about stuffing keywords, but AI does not look at those; if it cannot summarize, it skips over you, so you must write it clearly with a relatively complex and complete narrative logic — do not fear too many words, fear not covering it. Technically, the old dynamic pages no longer work; AI scraping on the device side can only get an empty page, so you must use SSR backend rendering and put all the content into HTML returned in one go. There is another approach: the large model sends header information about acceptable content types; if it is TXT plus markdown, return pure markdown with nothing in it that could cause hallucination.

## An explorer died for a phantom city, and the source was a political forgery

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-stuffmissed-fawcett-的-z-城执念可能始于一份政治伪稿/
- show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- original episode: Percy Fawcett, Manuscript 512, and a Lost City in the Amazon, Pt. 2
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 37:11
- transcript: Official transcript · 6073 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The Z city Fawcett spent his life hunting traces back to a fragmentary 18th-century manuscript of unknown provenance, suspected of being a political fabrication from post-independence Brazil; his final coordinates sit about 200 miles from the public version, and no hard evidence of his disappearance has ever surfaced.**

why listen: The core mystery is concentrated in the back half: the manuscript doubts, the coordinate contradiction and the archaeological vindication all land after the 20-minute mark; the front half reads long quotations and can be sped up.

### points

[1:03] (Holly Frey) **Fawcett read far more out of it than the manuscript supports** — Manuscript 512 describes an expedition finding a vast ancient city: black stone pillars, Roman-style spires, swarms of bats, stone carvings, cave tombs and river gold — but the text never gives any actual location. The manuscript runs only ten pages with large stretches of missing words and broken sentences, and the hosts have to pause at the gaps when reading key passages aloud; they cannot even read straight through whether it is ‘a coastal city or a royal court.’ The narrator hears roosters crowing in the city, while the scouts report no one lives there, so the whole party walks in armed at night. What Fawcett read out of it clearly goes far beyond what the text itself can support.

[7:10] (Holly Frey) **The manuscript may be a new nation manufacturing an ancient civilization for itself** — The manuscript is said to have been found in 1839 in the archives of the National Library of Brazil, but no one knows how it got into the archives; soon after its discovery it hit the newspapers, and multiple Brazilian groups sent expeditions to find the city, all of them coming back empty. The manuscript's authenticity is still disputed, and even if it really is an 18th-century document, it could have been fiction at the time. National Geographic reporter Jordi Canal Solar offered an explanation in 2024: Brazil only broke from Portugal in 1822, and the new republic needed a document proving that an ancient civilization had existed within its territory, something like the great Maya sites of Central America. Note: this is a ‘possible’ explanation, not a settled conclusion.

[8:12] (Holly Frey) **The lost-city obsession had no single aha moment** — Manuscript 512 is often described as the single origin of Fawcett's obsession, but the hosts stress one thing in particular: there was no ‘aha moment’ that made him certain a lost city existed. Each time he went deeper into the Brazilian jungle he went farther, and he saw with his own eyes that the dense vegetation could hide anything, which convinced him a city could be hidden in there. In 1911 Hiram Bingham's discovery of Machu Picchu (more accurately, his bringing it to the outside world's attention) caused a global sensation and further fed Europeans' fever for jungle cities. At the same time Fawcett claimed he knew from other documents and from Indigenous people that Z existed, yet never once cited a specific source — which became the handle later used to accuse him of being a fraud or an exaggerator.

[11:17] (Holly Frey) **Money that cannot be traced became the handle for fraud accusations** — Fawcett did not have an easy time applying to the Royal Geographical Society for funding. His peers thought he had been bewitched by the golden-city legends circulating in Brazil, and no one wanted to dig deep for a project wrapped in that kind of ‘atmosphere.’ He wrote: I have no doubt whatever that the city exists; I have myself seen the remains of one of them. Right at that juncture, according to some accounts, a mysterious financial group called The Glove stepped forward with money; the names of its members are entirely unknown, as if the money appeared out of thin air. This kind of unverifiable thing, plus his habit of never naming the documents he cited, led many contemporaries to brand him a deceiver or an exaggerator.

[16:27] (Holly Frey) **The last letter holds no clue, only insects** — On April 20, 1925, the party set out from Cuiabá, and on May 29 Fawcett wrote his last letter to his wife Nina at ‘Dead Horse Camp’ (where in 1920 he had been forced to shoot his sick horse). There is no dramatic clue in the letter, only concrete torment: flies from dawn to dark and even through the night, smaller than a needle yet biting like mosquitoes, plus swarms of bees; Jack was in good shape, and Raleigh still had a bandaged leg but refused to turn back. He admitted he could not be sure of lasting longer than the young men, but he gave precise coordinates and said ‘you need not fear any failure.’ After this letter, the three were never heard from again.

[20:34] (Holly Frey) **The only physical evidence the search party brought back was a decade-old discard** — In 1928 the Royal Geographical Society sent the pilot and travel filmmaker George Miller Dyott to find out what had become of Fawcett — directly against Fawcett's own wishes: before setting out he had said that if he failed, no one should come looking for him, it was too dangerous. Dyott's party was large, with a photographer and a radio operator; after contact with the Kalapalo and Nahukua peoples he claimed to be in danger, sent stories back to the newspapers, and brought back a uniform case stamped with the maker's mark. But Percy's younger son Brian countered: that case was an old item his father had discarded in 1920. Dyott's later book even says the medium he consulted saw Fawcett killed by a tribe, and the hosts judge the whole book to be a kind of old-fashioned ‘big-man jungle adventure’ narrative.

[23:38] (Holly Frey) **He most likely died of hunger and thirst, not at the hands of a tribe** — In 1931 a crew filming an Amazon documentary stumbled close to the truth. The ethnographer with the party, Vincenzo Petrulo, recorded on the east bank of the Kuluene River what the Kalapalo said: three white men were led to the village by Nahukua guides, the Indigenous people gave them food and urged them not to go on, and the next day ferried them across the river anyway; the two young men had ulcers from blackfly bites and clearly did not want to go forward. Over the following five days the Indigenous people saw the smoke of the overnight campfires every day, and on the sixth day the smoke stopped. Petrulo concluded that Fawcett had not been killed but had died of hunger or disease in the dense forest on the east bank of the river. He added one more thing: Dyott had not asked about this account back then because he had no interpreter, and the Indigenous people did not like him.

[29:44] (Holly Frey) **The coordinates are 200 miles apart, yet archaeology sides with him** — In 1951 Villas-Boas claimed to have found Fawcett's remains through the Kalapalo, and testing proved they were not his. In 1953 Brian published his father's “Exploration Fawcett”, and people immediately noticed the coordinates did not match: the Dead Horse Camp coordinates Fawcett made public were 13°14′ S, 54°35′ W, while the ones he sent Nina were 11°43′ S — about 200 miles apart, and to this day it is unknown whether it was a slip of the pen or a deliberate error to throw off anyone following him. Modern archaeology has partly confirmed his intuition: in 2008 Michael Heckenberger published results of work with the Kuikuro, showing that a complex settlement network once existed in Mato Grosso; today descendants of the tribe also insist their ancestors did not kill Fawcett, and the related accusations were further clarified in David Grann's “The Lost City of Z”.

## Superconducting chip claim: don't change the process node, change the temperature zone — 28nm logic can hit 5nm performance

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-techtechpotato-超导芯片宣称-不换制程换温区-28nm-逻辑能到-5nm-性能/
- show: TechTechPotato (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/techtechpotato/)
- original episode: What if Computers Ran Cold, Like Liquid Helium Cold?
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 11:47
- transcript: Machine transcription · 1747 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Move logic into the liquid helium temperature zone and replace transistors with superconducting switches. That's Snowcap's bet: tape out RISC-V first, then claim 28nm-class logic can deliver 5nm-class performance.**

why listen: If you're watching the power wall in compute, this episode lays out a third route — don't squeeze transistors, move the whole logic stack into the liquid helium temperature zone; a former Intel CEO has already placed a bet. The risks and the numbers are both on the table, and it's worth a listen.

### points

[0:00] **The ceiling on extreme overclocking is heat removal, not the chip** — This episode opens up from the overclocking industry: everyday chips rely on air cooling, higher-power parts use water cooling, and beyond that you need sub-zero media like dry ice and liquid nitrogen. Extreme overclockers add voltage to chase the highest frequencies, the chip gets hotter and hotter, and the only way to deal with it is ever more extreme cooling. The host says he was an extreme overclocker himself and once held the world number two spot — though it only lasted a day and a half. The key reference point he gives: this kind of overclocking exists just to run a benchmark for a few minutes at 8.5GHz, whereas real superconducting computing isn't chasing an instantaneous record but logic at close to zero power.

[2:01] **With liquid helium overclocking, the expensive part isn't the helium, it's the transfer line** — Going from liquid nitrogen to liquid helium, physics starts to interfere. Liquid helium costs about 20 times as much as liquid nitrogen (liquid nitrogen is about one dollar a litre), but that isn't the main expense: getting liquid helium from a large storage tank into a 3-4 kilogram copper overclocking pot through the transfer line costs 5000 dollars for a single use. Both Intel and Asus have done liquid helium overclocking, and records have broken past 9GHz. The host warns that when temperatures drop this far, material behaviour changes drastically — some platforms have a ‘cold bug’ where the system simply won't boot below a certain temperature; only platforms without a cold bug are suitable for liquid helium play.

[4:03] **The lure of superconductivity isn't faster, it's zero resistance** — Overclocking is about squeezing frequencies out of existing materials; superconductivity is a different story: electrons flowing through a superconducting material meet no resistance, which amounts to free transport. The vast majority of superconductors today require extremely low temperatures, and room-temperature superconductivity is still stuck in a state of research back-and-forth. The key inference here: if an entire chip's switching logic could operate in the superconducting state, energy per operation would be ‘several orders of magnitude’ better than today's laptops. The host deliberately states it fully and then pulls back — superconductivity is still the holy grail, not yet in hand. This sets up Snowcap's entrance later.

[5:07] **What the former Intel CEO bet on is a temperature zone, not a process node** — Snowcap Compute has just closed a seed round, with former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger on its board. Their bet is that they can build superconducting chips that run at roughly 4-15K, the liquid helium temperature zone. Structurally it's no longer billions of transistors but a new kind of switch that works at superconducting temperatures — the Josephson junction. At this stage Snowcap's goal is to first build a RISC-V-class CPU at low temperature, getting power consumption close to free; the price is that the whole machine must stay in the liquid helium temperature zone, and the cooling itself consumes energy.

[7:08] **The new variable in superconducting logic is fitting into a standard EDA flow** — There is no shortage of long-term researchers: a US defence contractor built chips integrating tens of millions of Josephson junctions, IMEC reached hundreds of millions, and built accompanying logic and EDA tools. Snowcap's differentiator is compatibility: they say this kind of superconducting logic can go into a standard EDA flow and can be taped out on ordinary CMOS processes, with niobium titanium nitride as the material. The core conclusion the host takes away: the energy-efficiency advantage superconductivity brings is equivalent to achieving near-5nm chip performance with 28nm logic — note this is not a smaller process node but the equivalent gain from lower power consumption.

[8:12] **Cryo CMOS is only an intermediate state; the real hurdle is scale** — Snowcap plans to deliver its first chip in 2026, followed by a deployable RISC-V design. For the intermediate state you can look at cryo CMOS: it runs in the roughly 72-77K liquid nitrogen temperature zone, and although there's no superconductivity, the low temperature itself pushes power consumption down. The real hurdle to cross is going from cryo CMOS into superconductivity; the host's doubt about this is ‘can you scale it up at high performance’ — being able to run and being able to commercialise at scale are two different things.

[9:12] **Cold booting is nothing new; keeping the whole machine in liquid helium is the hard part** — This section provides a reality check on low-temperature tape-outs: when AMD was most short of money, the first Zen 1 A0 sample it taped out could only boot at dry-ice sub-zero temperatures because of a design flaw, and was later fixed to run at room temperature. So low temperatures in the test and boot stages are nothing unusual; but keeping an entire processor in the liquid helium temperature zone is an infrastructure problem, including helium supply — liquid helium is also the lifeblood of the superconducting magnets in MRI machines, and there was a helium shortage a few years ago.

[10:14] **Snowcap isn't selling IP, it's selling a closed all-in-one machine** — Snowcap positions itself not as selling IP but as delivering a complete system. The host's judgement is that precisely because of the infrastructure barrier of the liquid helium temperature zone, the product form will be a near-closed all-in-one machine, with the software stack rebuilt from scratch. A seed-stage company still has A/B/C rounds ahead of it; however, they have already brought in advisors and former employees with Apple, Nvidia and Google backgrounds. This topic is worth being sceptical about, and worth following.

The main cost is actually the tube you need to get it from this massive compressed gas sewer into your massive 3-4 kilogram copper pot. That tube, single use, is five grand."

[3:03] : "When you go down to those cold temperatures, the way the materials work is incredibly different. In some chips and in some platforms, you might experience what's called a cold bug. It gets too cold for the system to boot or to work."

If that happens, one day we may have free energy. Right now, we don't. Right now, superconducting is the holy grail."

[5:07] : "But what if you could make a chip that was superconducting? Suddenly, you now have a processor that can do compute for next to no energy. And we're talking orders of magnitude better energy consumption per operation than this laptop, for example."

## Writing family history taught Moritz: you can never have too many passports

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-tyler-写家族史让莫里茨明白-护照永远不嫌多/
- show: Conversations with Tyler (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tyler/)
- original episode: Michael Moritz on Origin Stories, Exile, and Obsessive Curiosity
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 41:54
- transcript: YouTube captions · 6745 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**He didn't apply for German citizenship because he feared being expelled from America — he learned from writing his parents' story of escape that the history of the 1930s was only truly burned into a nation's memory in Germany, and a passport is the only insurance you can carry with you.**

why listen: Medium information density; the first stretch on art and Jewish literature is more casual chat. What's actually valuable is Moritz on how he stumbled from journalism into Sequoia, and his read on Britain's decline.

### points

[8:36] (Michael Moritz) **Only ugly paintings are worth hanging on the wall** — Moritz and his wife collect "ugly paintings" — Otto Dix, Frank Auerbach and the like. His reasoning: a decorative painting is exhausted at a glance, whereas a difficult painting has many layers you can keep exploring as you age; it carries history and tells stories. He traces this habit of "looking carefully" back to his reporting career — looking at landscapes, buildings, people, all the same thing. But he explicitly denies that this directly improves his investing; he only says the three are connected when he sizes up a person and considers building a business relationship.

[13:00] (Michael Moritz) **Children don't ask because they don't think their parents have stories** — Asked why children don't ask their parents more about family history while they're alive, Moritz is blunt: they're too self-centred, not curious, they don't understand that everyone has a story and that the deeper you dig the more interesting it gets; they don't know how to ask questions, and they don't know how to listen. He says if he could question his parents now, it wouldn't be one question but hundreds — because one answer leads to the next. But he adds a layer: these were people who lived through extreme trauma, memory gets suppressed, and even with the will, it's hard to dig the answers out.

[19:16] (Michael Moritz) **He starts his questions at his grandparents' age ten** — Moritz says he would start with what his grandparents' lives were like around age ten, because he believes the first ten to fifteen years of a life are shaped profoundly, and everything afterwards echoes off that base. The concrete picture he gives: imagine a ten-year-old boy in 1890 or 1891, living in a small village by a river in central Germany — who woke you up in the morning? Did anyone share your room, your bed? Do you remember what you ate for breakfast? What clothes did you wear to school? His grandfather Max fought in World War I and survived Verdun, and that stretch alone could yield countless questions.

[23:37] (Michael Moritz) **He got into Sequoia by writing a letter; four firms turned him down** — Moritz says his move from journalism to venture capital was entirely unplanned, pure luck. When he was in San Francisco in 1981 and 1982 he knew nothing about Silicon Valley; there were almost no tech companies in San Francisco then, unless you counted Charles Schwab. It was covering Apple, Atari, Microsoft and Oracle that made him realise for the first time that people started companies, and that founders could be just 18 or 20. He couldn't start one himself, so he joined a small publishing company. Later he wrote letters to the heads of five venture firms — in that era you could only write letters, not send email — four rejected him, and Don Valentine brought him into Sequoia. He says Valentine's peers thought he was insane for hiring someone with a history degree, a reporting career and no technical background at all.

[30:53] (Michael Moritz) **You can never have too many passports** — Moritz has obtained German citizenship. He rules out several guesses himself: he isn't afraid of being expelled from the United States, he already has British citizenship; he doesn't think he'd be threatened or intimidated in San Francisco; and he doesn't plan to move to Munich. The real reason he applied came from an observation while writing the book — whether in Western Europe or the United States, the only country that truly drummed the history of the 20s, the 30s and the Holocaust into its entire population was Germany; not France, not England and Wales, not the United States. He sums it up in one line: you can never have enough passports.

[38:43] (Michael Moritz) **Britain's problem is imperial afterglow plus too much government** — Moritz explains Britain's predicament as "the residue of imperial arrogance": the pound was once the world's reserve currency, Britain had the world's largest navy and was the global hegemon, then that position was taken by a more entrepreneurial country, and Britain never recovered from the loss — everything since has been a weak, low-grade stress response. He concedes Britain went through a cycle where government was the answer, and through Thatcher and later Blair, Brown and Cameron, when government was not seen as the answer, but his conclusion is that Britain is broadly trapped by a government that does too much.

[43:34] (Michael Moritz) **In China he saw where capitalism burned hottest** — Moritz attributes Sequoia's nearly two decades of success in China to collective decisions, but gives his own path of observation: going to the mainland in person, having many preconceptions washed away, then quickly realising that if you wanted to see where capitalism burned hottest in the early 21st century, it wasn't in America but in China — despite everyone talking about the Communist Party and state control. The mechanism he offers: there was almost no social safety net, so people had only education or their wits to live by. He also concedes that the last few years have tightened a great deal, and the atmosphere and conditions are no longer the same.

## The first cancer vaccine to work: every dose is a new drug for one person

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-a16z-癌症疫苗首次成功-每剂都是一个人的新药/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: Inside Moderna’s Personalized Cancer Vaccine
- published: 2026-09-02 · duration: 40:10
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7478 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**After more than a thousand failed clinical trials, an mRNA personalized cancer vaccine has cleared Phase 3 for the first time. About 90% of the antigens differ from person to person, so personalization isn't an edge case — it's the precondition for this drug to exist at all.**

why listen: The first half covers mechanism, the second half covers manufacturing and regulation: 42 days needle to needle, cramming machines into cleanrooms, and approving by process rather than by product. Worth hearing for anyone trying to understand how personalized medicine scales.

### points

[4:05] (Stefan Bancel) **The first success after more than a thousand failed trials** — Stefan says this is the first therapy to beat Keytruda monotherapy in melanoma, and the first time a cancer vaccine has actually worked. The field has spent over 20 years and run more than a thousand clinical trials, all of them failures. This Phase 3 hit its primary endpoint, recurrence-free survival — meaning a significant drop in the risk that a patient relapses or dies. More surprising, it also hit a secondary endpoint, distant metastasis-free survival; distant metastasis takes longer to mature and wasn't expected. He repeatedly stresses that this is only the first interim analysis, not the end of the study.

[6:05] (Stefan Bancel) **Keytruda's ceiling is 40% of people treated for nothing** — Checkpoint inhibitors like Keytruda work by "letting the dog off the leash" so the immune system attacks the cancer, but only 60% of patients are disease-free at five years. The other 40% go through the treatment, endure immune-related side effects, and get none of the benefit. The side effects aren't chemo-style; they're autoimmune disease — type 1 diabetes, lupus, Crohn's disease. Stefan's words: think about those 40% who don't respond — most of the time they get an autoimmune disease and they don't get the benefit of the drug. Moderna's mechanism is orthogonal: it doesn't unleash the dog, it tells T cells at the molecular level exactly what to look for.

[13:21] (Stefan Bancel) **The point of mRNA is letting the immune system see it from the inside** — Stefan breaks the difference into two parts. First, delivery: injected into muscle, the mRNA reaches lymph nodes and APCs (antigen presenting cells), gets translated inside the immune cell and presented "from the inside." Cancer vaccines built from proteins or peptides in the past were manufactured in a reactor and then injected; once in the blood they circulate, and the immune system sees them in a completely different way. Second, personalization: cancer is a disease of DNA, sequencing costs have fallen dramatically over 20 years, so you can biopsy the tumor, read out every DNA letter, compare it letter by letter, nucleotide by nucleotide, against healthy cells, and use an algorithm to pick the most relevant mutations.

[14:22] (Stefan Bancel) **90% of antigens differ between people, so it can only be one drug per person** — Moderna picks the 34 most relevant mutations out of hundreds to thousands and strings them into one large mRNA, made for that one patient in about 30 days. The data presented at ASCO: roughly 90% of the antigens are different between patients. Stefan says that when they started they had no idea whether it would be 2%, 5% or 90%, because the whole field had gone down the shared-antigen route. That number directly determines the business shape — if 90% don't overlap, personalization isn't an optional feature, it's the only way this drug can work.

[16:25] (Stefan Bancel) **The algorithm was written ten years ago, and this is only version 1.0** — Stefan says the algorithm used in Phase 3 is the same one used in Phase 2 and Phase 1 — an algorithm from ten years ago. It already gets 80% of patients to five years disease-free, but 20% still don't respond. Now, with all the blood samples and sequencing data from Phase 3 patients, they plan to go back and mine the data to figure out why some respond and some don't, then talk to the FDA about whether they can move from 1.0 to 2.0 — provided they don't lose efficacy. His analogy: everyone jokes that today's AI is the worst AI we'll see in our lifetime; Intismeran is the same, this version is the worst version in the history of medicine.

[20:28] (Stefan Bancel) **42 days needle to needle, and no need to take out your cells** — From taking the biopsy to the vaccine being ready at the hospital is now about 42 days, needle to needle. The biggest difference from CAR-T: you don't have to take out the patient's immune cells, engineer them in a factory reactor and ship them back to the hospital. Moderna only needs information — the sequences of the healthy cells and the cancer cells, i.e. a file. After that it's fully synthetic, fully enzymatic, done in water, then wrapped in lipids. Because you don't have to grow cells, the reactor can be made extremely small. Stefan says they've been working on "shrinking everything" since before entering the clinic; the first version of the machine was like a big refrigerator, large and hard to handle, because at that point the only requirement was quality, not efficiency.

[23:36] (Stefan Bancel) **What he's really obsessed with is square inches, not science** — Only after the Phase 2 data confirmed the science did Moderna move its smart engineers over to work on efficiency. Stefan names two vectors: one is cycle time — the faster the turnaround, the more times an asset turns over in a year; the other is square inches — cleanroom area is a fixed envelope, and if you can fit 2x or even 10x the machines into the same area, throughput goes up, fixed costs get spread thinner, and ultimately the product price comes down. He says every time he goes to the factory he's picking at things, looking at how much space can be saved, even moving some of the compute out of the cleanroom. The Marlboro plant can produce tens of thousands of doses, and the incidence of melanoma means tens of thousands of doses would cover the entire market.

[27:51] (Stefan Bancel) **The FDA approves the process, not a single dose** — Every dose is different, so approving dose by dose is impossible. Stefan says the precedent is CAR-T: approved as a process BLA rather than a product BLA. Moderna has five products approved as products; this one has been a process IND since it entered the clinic. The FDA's question is very concrete: if you start with the same sample — tumor and blood — does the same product come out of the black box at the end. That requires proving it to yourself first, then proving the robustness of the whole process to the FDA with data. He stresses this isn't a case of not talking to the FDA for ten years and then suddenly showing up; they've been in meetings, answering questions, and incidentally educating the regulators along the way.

[30:56] (Stefan Bancel) **Three directions to expand, including where Keytruda does nothing** — Moderna has already shown it can generate de novo new T cells that didn't exist in the body before treatment. Three directions: first, everywhere Keytruda works, because the mechanism is orthogonal — lung cancer in Phase 3, kidney and bladder cancer in Phase 2; second, early disease, where checkpoints aren't used yet, such as a Phase 3 in early lung cancer starting in spring 2026, using Intismeran as monotherapy, because early-stage patients don't deserve a lifetime of autoimmune side effects for a checkpoint; third, places where checkpoints do nothing at all, pancreatic and gastric cancer, where past trials were all negative, but the mechanism is different so it's worth a try. He also mentions combining with Revolution Medicine's recently approved pancreatic cancer drug.

### glossary

- distant metastasis-free survival: The time before the tumor spreads beyond the original site; the secondary endpoint unexpectedly met here.
- APC (antigen presenting cell): An immune cell that the mRNA enters, gets translated inside, and presents antigen from.
- process BLA: Approval based on the manufacturing process rather than a single product; CAR-T was approved this way.
- Intismeran: The code name for Moderna and Merck's personalized mRNA cancer therapy.
- de novo T-cell: A new T cell that didn't exist in the body before treatment, taught by the vaccine to recognize the tumor.
