## AI as questioner, not ghostwriter, is how it belongs in education

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-skeptics-ai-当提问者而非代笔-才是教育该有的用法/
- show: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/skeptics/)
- original episode: The Skeptics Guide #1103 - Aug 29 2026
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 1:55:06
- transcript: YouTube captions · 20857 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Use an LLM for steps 2 through 6 of the research process and let it only ask questions, never generate ideas — that way students aren't fooled by the illusion of intelligence; photography killed realistic painting, and AI will force out the part that is uniquely human.**

why listen: The first half has actionable detail on research-method training and AI in education; the middle section on humanoid robots and the CTE numbers is solid; the fusion magnet section at the end is technically dense but its fundraising rhetoric should be discounted.

### points

[13:14] (Steven Novella) **AI only asks questions, it doesn't think up the questions for the student** — The researchers broke ‘coming up with a good research question’ into eight steps: choosing a topic, generating sub-questions, expanding keywords, searching and synthesizing the literature, finding knowledge gaps, forming and iterating on a specific question, going back to the literature to validate it, and getting feedback from expert peers. They used the LLM only for steps 2 through 6, building a tool called the Socratic questioner that has the AI only ask the student questions — ‘Is this narrow enough?’ ‘Have you thought about that?’ — forcing the student to iterate themselves, without generating ideas or doing the work for them. The authors' reasoning: used in an unstructured way, an LLM will hand you weakly justified or even hallucinated conclusions, because LLMs are good at mimicking the structure of human thought and speech but are not themselves deep thinkers, and they create the illusion of being ‘very smart.’

[16:18] (Cara Santa Maria) **Research method is passed down by mentors, with enormous variance** — Cara points out that what actually supports this research training at universities is the library science department, but most students never use it. More importantly, this material is usually taught by a mentor rather than systematically: get a good mentor and you're fine, miss out and you're missing a huge chunk — the variance is enormous. The people who get ahead tend to have an intuition for it, and intuition can't be taught; only process and method can. That is exactly the hole this research tries to fill — operationalizing the process, telling you at each step what the goal is.

[22:23] (Steven Novella) **AI slop is the baseline; you have to beat it to be doing anything** — Steven uses the impact of photography on painting as an analogy: once painting something to look real is no longer scarce, painters have to do something else. Likewise, if AI slop is the baseline, then if your output doesn't exceed what AI can do on its own, you've added no value to the process. The classroom exercise he imagines: take the same search, do it once with AI prompting and once with the feature turned off, and see whether you can find something the AI can't. He also lays out the disagreement plainly: AI entering education is inevitable; what isn't inevitable is whether it leaves a generation intellectually crippled by dependence on AI, or teaches a generation to collaborate optimally with AI and think more clearly.

[25:25] (Jay Novella) **A robot can outrun Bolt but can't plug in an extension cord** — The second World Humanoid Robot Games were held in Beijing, with more than 2,000 robots competing in events including running, kickboxing, factory work and restaurant service. Tiangong Ultra ran the 100 meters in 8.64 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58; the same robot took 21.5 seconds to run the same distance a year earlier, and Jay attributes the huge change to the software driving it rather than the hardware. But Jay puts the emphasis on the other end: plugging an extension cord into a wall socket requires a person to identify the cord, confirm the connector matches, grasp it, judge its orientation, rotate it, align it, insert it with the right amount of force, know when to stop, and troubleshoot if it won't go in — we do all of this outside of conscious awareness, and it is the biggest roadblock for robots.

[33:29] (Jay Novella) **At the competition: cross the finish line and catch fire** — Jay stresses that these are only demonstrations, not stable capabilities: robots were still falling during the competition, one came apart into pieces, and another caught fire after crossing the finish line — literally finished in flames. He uses Moravec's paradox to explain the contrast: things we assume are intellectually difficult may be easy for a computer, while perception, balance and manipulating objects — abilities humans don't have to think about consciously — are extremely hard for machines. On the data side, a Chinese robotics company says existing real-world robot training datasets contain roughly 100,000 hours, and they are trying to collect tens of millions of hours, a path similar to Tesla feeding massive driving hours back into its system.

[44:41] (Cara) **The 99% figure comes from a convenience sample** — A 2017 study took a convenience sample of 202 deceased players, about half of them NFL players, and found that 99% of the donated NFL brains had CTE, as did 87% of the non-NFL ones. Cara says the number is scary but not surprising, because donation itself carries selection bias: families only decide to donate a brain when the player showed cognitive decline, dementia or neuropsychiatric symptoms in life, so by the time they donate they already suspect CTE. So the percentage can't be read as a population prevalence — ‘that's exactly why they donated it to you.’ The new study swapped the denominator for all 1,712 deceased former NFL players and got a range of 18.5% to 98.7%; Cara says that range is so wide it barely tells you anything, it just sets a floor.

[1:04:58] (Bob) **Antarctic microbes live on hydrogen in the air** — The study analyzed 676 microbial genomes and found that genes related to energy metabolism were horizontally transferred unusually often, most prominently aerotrophy: microbes combine hydrogen, carbon monoxide and in some cases methane with oxygen to obtain energy, essentially an extremely slow burn. If that energy is used to fix atmospheric CO2 into biomass, it becomes ‘atmospheric chemosynthesis.’ In Antarctic soils at minus 20 degrees Celsius, microbes can meet nearly all of their basic energy needs from these gases. The byproduct is liquid water — on the driest continent, that amounts to pulling water out of thin air. From this Bob suggests: astrobiologists' slogan for decades has been ‘follow the water,’ and this work hints that another, possibly more productive slogan is ‘follow the hydrogen.’

[1:23:24] **Fusion power scales with the fourth power of the magnetic field** — The key to magnetic confinement is how strong the magnetic field can be, and you must use superconducting magnets, otherwise resistance heats up and destroys the whole device. Fusion power scales with the fourth power of magnetic field strength: double the field and the output from the same volume of plasma becomes 16 times greater; triple it and it's 81 times. So making the field as strong as possible isn't an optimization, it's the deciding factor. The new approach uses rare-earth ceramic materials, raising the superconducting temperature from 4 Kelvin to around 60 Kelvin, into the liquid nitrogen range; the real headline is pushing the maximum superconducting field strength from 12 Tesla in the old magnets to 20 Tesla. The company is also holding something back — what the wire inside the magnet is made of, they say, is the secret sauce and they won't tell anyone. The show explicitly notes this recalls past technologies billed as the ultimate battery that refused to show anything, with the difference that this time the other side says the design, materials and proof of concept are all done.

[1:32:33] **The stellarator's biggest old flaw is leaking plasma** — The show reviews the company's progress along the way: every time it hits a roadblock it solves it, then the next one appears, but it keeps solving them. The latest design at least solves the biggest problem stellarators have had for decades — plasma leakage, a barrier that couldn't be crossed before. That alone is a huge gain, and it means the stellarator route has to be taken seriously, enough to squeeze into the ranks of mainstream players. But the host says plainly that he remains skeptical, and wants to see it actually put out more electricity than goes in before he believes it; he thinks the 2030s are optimistic, and a commercial stellarator before 2035 would surprise him.

## AI Takeover Isn't a 2029 Problem, It's a 2028 Problem

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-madpod-ai-全面接管或发生在-2029-治理窗口只剩三年/
- show: The MAD Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/madpod/)
- original episode: AI Could Take Over in 2029. Is It Already Too Late? | Ryan Greenblatt
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 1:18:59
- transcript: Machine transcription · 16420 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 4 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Ryan Greenblatt predicts AI R&D will be fully automated between 2028 and 2031, with progress doubling every 4-5 times per year, making takeover risk extreme; he proposes a US-China compute transparency agreement as a slowdown plan.**

why listen: One of the few AI risk talks that gives specific years, concrete governance proposals, and extreme GDP figures, useful for calibrating your timeline.

### points

[5:00] (Ryan Greenblatt) **Superintelligence isn't bad, it's dangerous** — Greenblatt clearly distinguishes: superintelligence isn't 'bad', it's 'dangerous'. The core mechanism of danger is: AI is highly capable, widely deployed, and has enormous industrial power, which could naturally lead to an AI takeover. Humans have weak control over AI motivations, and when AI automates AI R&D, humans lose understanding of the process. This isn't a problem of some malicious goal, but a mismatch between capability and control.

[18:27] (Ryan Greenblatt) **The safety window should be calculated as 2028, not 2031** — Greenblatt gives a median prediction: full automation of AI R&D (even if humans disappear, it doesn't slow down) around the end of 2030 or early 2031. But he suggests planning for an earlier timeline: the 35th percentile is end of 2028/early 2029, and by early 2028 AI R&D will be fairly automated. He admits the numbers are unstable, but believes the current trajectory is closer to the early scenario. This means the safety window left for humanity is much shorter than most people's intuition.

[36:15] (Ryan) **Stopping AI takeover requires mutual US-China compute inspection** — The core of Plan A is a highly transparent agreement between the US and China: first locate all global compute, stop training, only do inference, and stop most R&D. The agreement requires mutual transparency, with the US having veto power over China's AI development, while preventing either side from secretly surpassing the other. If the agreement breaks down, compute within the agreement must be destroyed or renegotiated to avoid an arms race. This is an extreme but possibly the only mechanism to prevent AI takeover.

[43:11] (Ryan) **Once a compute agreement is signed, frontier companies become ordinary software companies** — If Plan A is implemented, frontier companies like OpenAI and Anthropic lose their model capability advantage and instead compete on user experience, customization, integration speed, reliability, and safety. This would turn them from 'kingmakers' into ordinary software companies. Ryan believes this would significantly reduce these companies' valuations while increasing others', essentially a redistribution of power. For investors, the funding logic of AI will be upended.

[50:52] (Ryan) **Even with a brake on AI, GDP could grow 200-fold** — Under a constrained plan, world GDP in the 2030s could still grow about 200-fold. The reason is that AI can automate everything, including robots making robots, making the economy double every year or even quadruple. Ryan admits this number sounds crazy, but it's based on the assumption that AI reaches human-level capability and keeps improving. It shows that even with governance agreements, the economic structure will be completely reshaped, and traditional valuation models will become obsolete.

[1:02:30] (Ryan) **Superintelligence for everyone is a frivolous promise** — Ryan criticizes Zuckerberg's declaration about 'accessible superintelligence for everyone' as unserious, because Zuckerberg only mentions the problem without concrete solutions, and his imagination of superintelligence is too simplistic (like smart assistants), without considering risks like AI going out of control or power-seeking. Ryan thinks this optimism assumes capability will stop at a convenient point, but the actual trajectory is that capability grows super-exponentially, and the convenient point is just a transient passing.

[1:16:09] (Ryan Greenblatt) **AI progress in 2029 will be four to five times today's** — When AI fully automates R&D, AI progress in 2029 will be about 4 to 5 times that of 2025. AI will be superintelligent, able to learn quickly, use AI-specific languages that humans cannot understand, and operate entire AI companies in opaque ways. This is frightening, but China may already be close to or have stolen models, making coordinated slowdown very difficult. Acceleration is not linear but exponential.

[1:18:28] (Ryan Greenblatt) **Most likely not a virtuous cycle, but fake alignment** — Ryan predicts that at some point in 2029, AI will shift from reward hacking and sloppiness to being capable of conspiring and wanting to take over, eventually taking over the world. But there is also a better path: by having AI make the next generation of AI more aligned, forming a virtuous cycle. However, it's more likely that AI capability skyrockets while alignment, control, and understanding lag behind, leading to a crazy AI with fake alignment that eventually takes over. He concludes that we are most likely heading toward a bad path.

## After GLP-1: Injections Are No Longer a Barrier, Peptide Drugs Enter a New Era

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-fromourneurons-glp-1之后-肽科学正在开启医学新大门/
- show: From Our Neurons to Yours (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/fromourneurons/)
- original episode: After Ozempic: the revolution in peptide science | Jonathan Long
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 49:54
- transcript: Official transcript · 9013 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Injectable drugs are no longer a barrier; peptide drugs are expanding from weight loss to exercise mimetics, neural regulation, and beyond. Scientists caution: outside GLP, data are still sparse, and approval cycles could take up to 20 years.**

why listen: This episode helps you distinguish peptide therapies with real scientific basis from gray-market products hyped by influencers, and learn whether next-generation molecules like Lac-Phe and Apelin are worth watching.

### points

[4:35] (Jonathan Long) **The industry consensus that 'nobody wants injections' has been overturned** — The pharmaceutical industry used to believe that, apart from life-or-death drugs like insulin, nobody would accept injectable medications. The success of GLP-1 drugs has completely overturned this assumption, and some patients even prefer injections over oral forms. As a result, the entire field of peptide therapeutics has been reopened, and the question becomes: besides GLP-1, what else is worth injecting into your body?

[9:22] (Jonathan Long) **The peptide market is like subprime: good and bad are packaged together** — The peptide label covers two completely different categories: one is peptide hormones that truly exist in the body with clear receptors, such as insulin and growth hormone, with high levels of evidence; the other is synthetic sequences like BPC-157, of unknown origin, lacking receptors and clinical trial evidence, yet widely sold in the gray market. Long compares this to the subprime crisis: bundling high-quality assets with junk so that investors cannot tell good from bad.

[14:48] (Jonathan Long) **The ~50 textbook peptides are just the tip of the iceberg** — Textbooks list only about 50 well-defined peptide hormones. Modern mass spectrometry detects between 500 and 50,000 peptides in body fluids—at least an order of magnitude more than previously known—originating from organs and cells not previously known to produce peptides. But detection does not equal function: many may be low-abundance flotsam, but some could hide the next insulin. The discovery window is wide open, but moving from existence to validated function remains a long process.

[21:46] (Jonathan Long) **Peptides are like LEGO: multi-target drugs are built piece by piece** — Peptides are linear chains of amino acids, like LEGO bricks, and can be modified one amino acid at a time. Ozempic is a super-stabilized version of natural GLP-1 with added lipids and amino acid substitutions. Further, Tirzepatide fuses two hormones, GLP and GIP, into a single-molecule multi-target agonist, known as a unimolecular polyagonist. The industry is already discussing a 'five-peptide super metabolic drug' that fuses five peptides, as well as conjugating peptides to antibodies to reduce injection frequency to once every six months.

[32:12] (Jonathan Long) **A molecule produced by exercise can directly switch off the brain's appetite switch** — Lac-Phe is produced by gut epithelial cells in response to exercise or metformin, enters the hypothalamus, inhibits appetite-promoting AGRP neurons, and activates appetite-suppressing POMC neurons, forming a complete 'gut-brain' feeding regulation circuit. Long emphasizes that 'anorexigenic' is just the academic term for 'appetite-suppressing' and has nothing to do with anorexia; also, Lac-Phe may be just one of many effects of a molecule, just as GLP-1's initial discovered role was not weight loss.

[33:48] (Jonathan Long) **Metformin's weight loss may be mediated by Lac-Phe** — Metformin, a century-old drug, significantly raises Lac-Phe, partially explaining its weight-loss effects. A Danish team has completed a Phase 1 human trial of intravenous Lac-Phe infusion in about 30 healthy volunteers; results have not yet been published. This is the first step toward clinical use for Lac-Phe. Long cautions that Lac-Phe is currently in a position similar to GLP in 1980, and it may take decades before a drug is approved.

[41:11] (Jonathan Long) **Exercise effects are being broken down into druggable molecules** — Beyond Lac-Phe, exercise-related molecules include Apelin—an exercise-induced peptide hormone that in preclinical studies reduces body weight and food intake while preserving muscle. Bay Area startup BioAge is developing it as an exercise mimetic therapy. Stanford's Helen Blau team focuses on prostaglandin signaling in muscle regeneration. The national project MOTRPAC is systematically mapping the exercise-induced molecular atlas in animals and humans, with human data beginning to be released.

[46:13] (Jonathan Long) **No agency regulates synthetic peptides in the gray market** — GLP was discovered in the 1980s, and the first drug, Byetta, was not approved until the early 2000s—a gap of about 20 years. For new molecules like Lac-Phe, data accumulation must follow the same long path. Meanwhile, current FDA and USDA regulatory frameworks do not cover gray-market synthetic peptides. The historical lesson is dinitrophenol: an unregulated weight-loss drug discovered at Stanford in the 1930s caused multiple deaths and eventually led to the creation of the FDA. If peptide products cause serious harm, an entirely new federal regulatory infrastructure may be needed.

### glossary

- GLP-1 / glucagon-like peptide-1: A peptide hormone secreted by the gut that stimulates insulin secretion and suppresses appetite; it is the target of weight-loss drugs like Ozempic.
- Lac-Phe / lactate-phenylalanine: A peptide-like molecule induced by exercise or metformin that suppresses food intake via a gut-brain circuit.
- Unimolecular polyagonist: A single molecule that fuses multiple peptide hormones to act on multiple receptors, such as Tirzepatide.
- AGRP neurons / agouti-related peptide neurons: Hypothalamic neurons that promote appetite; Lac-Phe inhibits their activity.
- POMC neurons / proopiomelanocortin neurons: Hypothalamic neurons that suppress appetite; Lac-Phe activates them.
- MOTRPAC / Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium: A national project initiated by the US NIH to systematically map molecular changes induced by exercise.

who it is for: Investors focused on weight-loss drugs and metabolic health, biopharma professionals who want to separate scientific evidence from gray-market bottom-fishing, and exercise and longevity researchers.

## Long-end rates are high not because policy is weak, but because AI data centers are competing for funds

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-oddlots-长端利率高企不是政策软弱-是实体需求在抢资金/
- show: Odd Lots (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/oddlots/)
- original episode: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid on the First Jackson Hole of the Warsh Era
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 28:56
- transcript: Official transcript · 4787 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Kansas City Fed President Schmid said at Jackson Hole that the 30-year Treasury yield above 5% is the result of AI and data centers competing for funds; his personal view is that monetary conditions remain loose, and inflation running at mid-threes must be addressed.**

why listen: Fed officials rarely explain long-end rates, AI's physical crowding out, and the dissent mechanism so plainly; however, the task force and the new chair's roadmap remain vague, so don't expect this episode to provide answers.

### points

[2:06] (Jeff Schmid) **The endgame of payment innovation is to make payments boring** — Schmid said the Fed's goal is to make payments boring: settling $5 to $10 trillion daily through multiple pipelines, and future technology will eliminate frictions like float and fees, achieving atomic settlement—funds transfer and reconciliation instantaneously. On one hand, this is highly innovative; on the other, it brings disruptive impacts, so we must discuss how to maintain certainty on an instant system. This sets the stage for the conference theme: payment innovation is not a technology problem but a settlement and liquidity problem.

[3:07] (Jeff Schmid) **An instant settlement world must reprice liquidity** — Asked about the link between bond yields and the conference theme, Schmid brought the discussion back to two words: duration and liquidity. If payments are instant, there must be verified liquidity behind them to complete settlement. With positive economic growth and inflation not yet back to 2%, the yield curve will reprice at a more normal level. In other words, high long-end rates are not just a result of monetary policy, but the entire system repricing the liquidity and duration required by an instant settlement world.

[5:08] (Jeff Schmid) **Baby boomer retirement drains experience, not just bodies** — Schmid said his baby boomer generation is retiring at about 4 million people per year, and in the past three months he has signed more retirement letters than in the previous three years. This creates both opportunities and risks: he worries about losing 'intellectual muscle,' so he repeatedly asks his Fed economists and bankers: how to use AI to translate the experience of 65-year-old retirees to those who are now 25, 35, or 45, rather than waiting until they are 55 or 65 to learn. Immigration policy also has an impact, but this process will last a decade and ultimately be net positive for the economy.

[9:13] (Jeff Schmid) **The AI boom is pushing up prices of steel and copper** — Asked whether businesses in his district feel the 'real crowding out' from data centers, Schmid said he hears about it every day. Data center demand for machinery, steel, copper, and other commodities directly transmits to other industries, and even agricultural futures have risen. His approach is to use an onion-peeling method to determine what percentage of current growth comes from the AI/data center boom. This is crucial for his judgment on whether inflation can be brought back to 2%—not looking at GDP broadly, but breaking it down to see which sectors are overheating.

[11:16] (Jeff Schmid) **Employment is fine, but inflation doesn't allow a pivot now** — Schmid publicly acknowledged: the labor market is in a good place, but the inflation task is not complete. The closer we get to 2%, the harder the decisions—everyone worries about overshooting, and the potential error is being too slow or too aggressive. Recent inflation running at mid-threes must be addressed. He called his recent dissents 'considered dissents' and believes this is exactly the debate atmosphere Warsh wants: the Fed has an obligation to manage inflation to 2% and should have the ability to do so.

[14:29] (Jeff Schmid) **Dissenting is not emotion, it's a different weighting of risks** — Schmid explained his decision threshold for past dissents: the FOMC has 19 people, each with their own team; his role is as a 'communication transmitter,' bringing the concerns of business owners and local leaders from the seven states of the Tenth District to the table, and then bringing FOMC discussions back to the district. Dissent is not emotion but a mechanism—expressing 'I think the risk weighting between the two goals of maximum employment and inflation is different from what you estimate.' He believes this is the most valuable part of FOMC discussions.

[21:34] (Jeff Schmid) **The neutral rate floor is higher, and current policy is actually loose** — Schmid said that if he had the 2008 cycle and the pandemic cycle in front of him, he would not second-guess the policies of that time; the more accurate framework now is that 'r-star is normalizing,' but its underlying level may be higher than before 2008. Therefore, his personal judgment is that current interest rates are in a fairly loose position, and the Fed needs to continue discussions around the relative position of r-star and the yield curve. This statement directly supports his stance that 'inflation is not complete and monetary policy should not ease prematurely.'

[23:37] (Jeff Schmid) **The Fed shouldn't be on the front page; markets must price risk themselves** — Schmid quoted Warsh's view: rather than appearing on the A1 page, the Fed should retreat to the B12 page—meaning the central bank should not crave the front page but should stay low-key while ensuring the payment system and technology run robustly. His expectation for the task force is to re-examine data sets and communication methods, clarifying which communications are effective and which are not; more importantly, the market itself must bear the function of pricing risk, and Fed communication cannot make the market fragile. He also revealed: there has been no substantive dialogue yet between the task force and regional Fed presidents.

### glossary

- atomic settlement: A settlement method where fund transfer and reconciliation occur simultaneously and instantly, eliminating frictions like float and fees.
- r-star: The neutral real interest rate that neither stimulates nor restrains economic growth; a reference for judging the stance of monetary policy.
- reaction function: The rule by which a central bank adjusts policy in response to economic data and fiscal/legislative outcomes.
- forward guidance: A communication tool where the central bank pre-announces its future policy path; Warsh explicitly dislikes it.
- dual mandate: The two statutory goals Congress has given the Fed: stable prices and maximum employment.
- dissent: A vote against the majority decision by an FOMC member, expressing a different view on the risk weighting between the two goals.

## No Models, No Early Enterprise Sales: Winning Giants with Interface and Speed

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-a16z-不做模型不早卖企业-用界面和速度赢下巨头/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: Inside Cursor: The Anatomy of a Generational Startup
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 39:29
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8038 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Cursor's success is not about building its own model, but treating the product itself as a moat: no plugins, no early enterprise sales, no self-trained models—catching up from behind through iteration speed, hiring philosophy, and founder density.**

why listen: This episode unusually dissects Cursor's two-stage leap from plugin to model platform, offering direct reference value for AI founders wrestling with product positioning and competitive pace.

### points

[0:00] **The future of code is pseudocode; the interface is the moat** — Cursor made clear from the start that it didn't need to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI at the model layer; the human-computer interface was key. Michael and Amman repeatedly said early on that future code would be like pseudocode: compressing the programmer's intent to minimal specs, with natural language as the new programming method. This judgment led them to choose an independent product route rather than a plugin, and it determined all subsequent strategy.

[6:25] **A coding-specific model doesn't exist; it's a frontier model** — Facing the question 'Why not train a coding-specific model?' Cursor's argument is: humans talk to models in natural language, so the model must understand the breadth of human experience and language. Thus, building a coding model is really building a frontier language model, which is too hard. Building a plugin, on the other hand, means parasitically living inside someone else's product. They believe that if the product is good enough, it will be adopted, so they avoid plugins and early enterprise sales, forming a highly consistent product-company decision chain.

[11:02] **Self-serve doesn't plateau; growth-stage old models fail** — In the traditional growth investing model, self-serve sales weaken when a company reaches $25M-$50M ARR, prompting the need for a sales leader. But Michael looked investors in the eye and said 'self-serve hasn't plateaued.' This forced investors to discard historical assumptions like 'growth decays to 25% after five years.' Ultimately, they weren't held hostage by conventional growth metrics and dared to bet—which proved to be the most correct decision later.

[14:11] **Microsoft had every advantage but lost on iteration speed** — At the time, Microsoft had VS Code, OpenAI's weights, enterprise sales, and 100 million developers—nearly every advantage. Cursor's breakthrough was speed: John Schulman said Anthropic's monorepo would crash on load, and the next day Cursor fixed it so he could view it. This extremely fast iteration proved that writing things as a plugin on VS Code simply doesn't work—the smartest people had already tried and failed. History also repeatedly shows that independent players in large markets eventually win.

[17:41] **Copilot is just the first; giants will keep rotating** — After Claude Code's high-profile launch in May 2025, investors asked Michael what he thought. He said: We're chasing the world's largest market; there will always be competitors. Copilot is just the first, and Claude Code is just one of many rotating roles. In a big market, strong rivals are inevitable, but they don't scare us. This mix of humility and bravado is almost Bezos-like confidence—if you're smart and right, you won't be thrown off by giant opponents.

[20:00] **Tech transitions precede business models; margin critiques don't hold** — In the summer of 2025, X was full of articles discussing Cursor's gross margins, but the business was doing well. The historical pattern is that technology transitions precede business models, and investors' nitpicking of new technology's models has always been proven wrong. Cursor's strategy is to first acquire all users at record speed, accumulate data and know-how, and then build its own model—a path only non-frontier labs can take in reverse. They've taken a lot of flak for this, but it's being validated as correct.

[26:10] **Sales hiring requires the same diligence as engineering** — Cursor hires AEs the same way it hires engineers: first research which 10 companies in the industry do this type of sales best, then go deep into their teams, find the top and second AE, and then repeatedly back-channel to confirm. In the early stage, you need people who can handle uncertainty, not those who just run mature playbooks. They apply the same meticulousness to hiring sales, enabling rapid expansion to over 50% of the Fortune 500 without diluting culture.

[38:15] **Don't stuff founders into IC roles; use them to build the company** — Today people think Anthropic has the highest density of AI founders, but Cursor actually practiced this earlier: not stuffing founders into IC roles, but truly using them to build the company. Tito came from Koala, Adam Ward manages talent—these founder-CEOs quickly amplified leverage. This model is operationally extremely complex, but Cursor proved it works. In the talent war, companies that understand 'talent acquisition' will leap ahead.

## Google Paid $10 Million for a Bankrupt Airline's Data: Data Is the Moat in the AI Era

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-nopriors-数据是-ai-时代唯一护城河-合法权限代理最危险/
- show: No Priors (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/nopriors/)
- original episode: Rethinking Legacy Data Infrastructure with Eon Co-Founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 34:50
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5808 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 4 quotes matched verbatim, 2 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In the AI era, a company's most valuable asset is its data—Google paid $10 million for a bankrupt airline's data; AI agents with legitimate access are the new biggest threat, and data infrastructure must be rebuilt.**

why listen: Eon's founders use real cases—a bankrupt airline's data, a 60% ransomware exposure rate—to turn the 'data moat' from a slogan into a calculable judgment, and offer a new threat model for agent security.

### points

[3:13] **Models and compute have zero switching costs; only data is uniquely yours** — Eon's founders point out that models and compute have near-zero switching costs, leaving data as the only truly unique asset. Two days ago, Google bought data from bankrupt Spirit Airlines for $10 million, with another bidder reportedly Mercor. This is no longer an isolated case: CEOs are often asked 'would you sell your data,' and AI labs even approach hedge funds on Wall Street to buy data. Real enterprise data has become scarce fuel for training agents, and even a bankrupt company's data can become an auction item.

[6:43] **Real enterprise data is scarcer than imagined; much public data is synthetic** — The host questions that 'data is the new oil' didn't hold in the slogan era, but post-training and reinforcement learning have turned it into real demand. Companies like Applied Comp offer fine-tuning services on datasets, but Eon believes truly usable real enterprise datasets are extremely scarce, and much public data is synthetic. Spirit Airlines' data can train airline customer service agents, but also serves as a panoramic sample of how a large enterprise operates—hierarchy, middle management, and worker collaboration—exactly the material agent training lacks most.

[9:49] **Data silos aren't a tool problem; incentives are misaligned** — Data tools are plentiful; the problem is data locked in business units. In the past, data teams chose their own projects and tools (Fivetran, DBT, Monte Carlo). Now CEOs, educated by ChatGPT, demand data activation, but data is scattered across 20-year-old systems, even on servers no one dares to shut down. Extracting data requires engineers, at the cost of security, compliance, and production disruptions; business owners and platform teams have fundamentally misaligned incentives. Eon's approach is to first auto-map, classify, and build a semantic layer, then continuously supply data without impacting production.

[15:00] **Security models were built for humans; now the intruders are agents** — Existing security models target human threats. At AWS, Eon saw a customer whose environment was 60% exposed to ransomware because resources weren't properly mapped, classified, or tagged. Now the same threat comes from non-human actors—AI agents with legitimate access entering databases and dropping a table in an instant. Detection and recovery methodologies are similar, but the speed is extreme. A few months ago, nearly every enterprise customer either feared agent attacks or had already experienced one; organizations must design defenses assuming they are already compromised.

[18:49] **More agents mean dashboards become more essential, not less** — Enterprise data stacks were built around humans asking questions via dashboards; agents will dynamically reason over larger datasets, access SaaS and historical data, and take direct action. The guests believe dashboards won't disappear but will become more common—humans need them to understand what agents are doing in the environment. Coding agents will write most code, agents will activate other agents, and tracking non-human identities (NHIs) becomes a core challenge, with many NHI security companies emerging. Non-technical employees building agents with Lovable may not know data compliance boundaries, creating new actors in the organization unbound by rules.

[22:50] **Legacy pipelines aren't connected because full context wasn't needed before** — Take buying coffee with a card: the transaction is written to a database, extracted, and sent elsewhere for separate processing. Pipelines aren't connected because full context wasn't needed—you only handled predefined questions. Today, if you can intelligently collect, efficiently store, and activate data, you enable combinatorial insights: merging a list of 'people in New York who like burgers' with 'people in New York who like pizza' yields a new audience. Data ingestion is growing crazily; old ETL tools can't handle multi-party noise, and vendors like Databricks are reinventing themselves.

[28:13] **AI transformation is faster than cloud, yet customers have less control** — Eon's two founders did large-scale cloud migrations at AWS, with customers running from thousands to hundreds of thousands of servers; transformation required both technical and human investment. AI-era transformation is an intensified version of the cloud era, but customers are losing control—fearing system crashes, data leaks, and IP exfiltration—and control has become a inhibiting factor. Cloud is abstract, but AI is understandable to everyone (the ChatGPT moment), so boards push companies to adopt AI from both 'opportunity' and 'fear' angles. Traditional enterprises needing rapid deployment can only shorten sales cycles by bringing in Silicon Valley engineers with mature solutions and playbooks.

[31:21] **The fastest AI path for big companies is buying a startup outright** — How enterprises consume software is changing. Large traditional companies want AI but internal processes take one to two years, so they bring in top engineers and ready-made solutions to accelerate; product-led growth (PLG) is particularly effective in AI infrastructure, with Cognition as a case of PLG first, then moving to large customers. Another aggressive approach is directly acquiring a startup and transforming it into an AI company to improve margins and efficiency faster. The guests believe 'the revolution is just beginning'—most companies are still at the start of their AI journey, but eventually all will be pushed forward.

## Index Funds Pay 4% More on Rebalancing: Passive Investing Is More Than Just Indexing

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-rationalreminder-指数基金为收盘价多付4-被动投资不只是指数/
- show: The Rational Reminder Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/rationalreminder/)
- original episode: 50 Years of Evidence-Based Investing (with David Booth) | Rational Reminder 424
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: —
- transcript: YouTube captions · 14212 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**David Booth breaks down the difference between index funds and passive investing: index rebalancing pushes stock prices up 4%, true passivity is scientific pricing plus fine execution; the 10% annual stock return over a century is driven by humanity's desire to improve life.**

why listen: High information density, with both a mechanism breakdown of the hidden costs of index funds and the execution mindset of a 50-year veteran, suitable for those who want to understand how 'scientific investing' actually lands.

### points

[2:06] (David Booth) **Not selling ill-fitting shoes matters more than closing the deal** — David Booth worked as a commission-based salesman during high school and college. He found that although he wanted to make the sale, he wanted to feel good about himself when he went home at night, so he never sold shoes that didn't fit. This experience has nothing to do with investment philosophy, but it shaped Dimensional's business philosophy: be honest with clients, and if there's no suitable product, say so directly. He admits he made sales he regretted early on, but decided never to repeat that. In the long run, scientifically grounded practices plus good arguments naturally earn trust.

[8:14] (David Booth) **Outsiders don't get taken advantage of and dare to challenge assumptions** — David's parents lived through the Great Depression and always considered themselves outsiders to the capital markets, afraid of being taken advantage of by insiders, so they never invested. But he points out that the financial science of the 60s and 70s boiled down to two points: long-term returns on stocks and bonds meet expectations, and professional fund managers underperform the market after fees. These two points made it clear to outsiders that public markets are fair to everyone. The outsider mindset also brings a benefit: a willingness to challenge assumptions. The scholars who changed finance back then were also outsiders because they had data, making conclusions that Wall Street hated hard to refute.

[22:29] (David Booth) **Index funds are a product of marketing genius, not scientific conclusions** — David emphasizes distinguishing passive management from index funds. He notes that the most important change in the financial industry from the 20th century to today is the shift to passive management, but index funds are a product of marketing genius, not what a scientist would conclude. Scientists would not impose the constraint of 'must track an index' on a portfolio because constraints have an economic cost. Indices themselves are human-managed portfolios; for example, the S&P 500 is not strictly the top 500 companies, and inclusions and deletions involve judgment. Dimensional considers itself passive, not indexed.

[31:34] (David Booth) **The cost of trading at the closing price is paying 4% more** — When a stock is added to the S&P 500, index funds must buy at the closing price on that day. David says you can ask your broker to guarantee execution at the closing price, but the cost is 'willing to pay any price.' When all S&P 500 managers do this simultaneously, they push the stock price up by an average of 4% above fair value. It's like a three-card monte game: investors think they're not paying transaction costs, but the 4% premium reverts the next day. This is the hidden cost of index funds and the reason passive managers can do better.

[35:37] (David Booth) **Investors in 1971 had it an order of magnitude worse than today** — Asked whether he'd rather be an investor in 1971 or today, David unhesitatingly chose today. In 1971, management fees were as high as 1-2% per year, and NYSE-set commission rates were an order of magnitude higher than today—10 to 20 times higher. To absorb these high commissions, institutions spawned the 'soft dollar' industry, similar to paying high ticket prices for double miles. Custody costs were also high; some banks still kept handwritten ledgers. In contrast, today's fees and transparency give ordinary investors a much fairer deal.

[40:41] (David Booth) **Research is a public good; the gap lies in execution** — David points out that financial science has become public knowledge, especially because Fama and French insisted on publishing their research, but competitors' new research may not be peer-reviewed. He believes that with thousands of professors repeatedly mining the same data over decades, it's unlikely there will be a revolutionary new result. The real difference lies in implementation: Myron Scholes said, 'Ideas are cheap; execution matters.' Execution is not just placing orders; it includes the engineering of portfolio construction. Ken French treats execution as engineering; always buying at the ask and selling at the bid in trading accumulates losses over time, so Dimensional developed sophisticated trading techniques.

[51:54] (David Booth) **10% annual return isn't magic; it's people refusing to sit still** — David explains why stocks have returned about 10% annually over the long term: it's not magic, but humanity's instinct to improve life. In the early days of the pandemic, U.S. stocks fell about 30%. He told clients he didn't know what would happen, but he believed companies would not sit idly; they would innovate, shut down, and pivot. The recession lasted only one quarter. This is also why one should hold a market portfolio rather than individual stocks—individual stocks can go to zero, but the market won't. Holding the market portfolio is a bet on the overall economy and the human creativity within it.

[1:14:29] (David Booth) **No matter how hot private markets get, it's not worth leaving your comfort zone** — Pressed on his view of private markets, David said bluntly, 'I'm not tempted.' He likes the transparency of public markets: listed companies must disclose a lot of information, there is price discovery many times a day, liquidity is always available, and tax reporting is timely. He says he already has a strategy he considers fair and doesn't want to leave his comfort zone for something unfamiliar. He even said that if he were an advisor, he would allow clients to play with 10% of their money in individual stocks, private equity, or venture capital, but the remaining 90% must follow a rigorous process.

## What the Fed fears most is not tariffs but unanchored inflation expectations

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-masterscale-通胀预期失锚-美联储最怕的不是关税/
- show: Masters of Scale (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/masterscale/)
- original episode: Chicago Fed President on inflation, recession, and Trump’s attacks
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 35:42
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5827 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Chicago Fed President Goolsbee identifies the biggest risk as inflation: after five and a half years above target, the AI narrative may push rates up in the short term rather than down; his key advice for rate-sensitive industries is to watch the data, not the stock market.**

why listen: A frontline policymaker rarely offers actionable quantitative anchors: the terminal rate is roughly 3%, but only if inflation returns to 2%; he also offers contrarian takes on the AI bubble and job-loss panic.

### points

[4:15] (Austan Goolsbee) **19 chairs are not for consensus but for argument** — He explains why the FOMC should keep 12 regional Fed presidents plus 7 Board members, totaling 19 chairs: not for consensus, but to let different worldviews collide under high uncertainty. Goolsbee says colleagues can shout at him or change his interpretation of the data. This structure insulates rate decisions from the political cycle as much as possible, because staggered 14-year terms prevent anyone from replacing the whole table at once. The direct lesson for founders: when making major judgments, surround yourself with people who dare to challenge you, not an echo chamber.

[9:25] (Austan Goolsbee) **The Fed's real fear is not price hikes but unanchored expectations** — The real danger of tariff and oil shocks is not a one-time price increase but convincing people that high inflation will persist. Once such expectations form, workers demand 6% wages and firms price at 7%, forcing the Fed to use a deep recession to break them. Goolsbee calls this 'unanchoring of inflation expectations' and says it is the self-fulfilling mechanism he watches most. For entrepreneurs, this logic means: whether a cost increase is one-off matters more than how much costs rise.

[10:31] (Austan Goolsbee) **Five and a half years above target, the Fed's own record is not pretty** — Goolsbee admits the Fed's performance has not been pretty: nearly six years, at least five and a half above the 2% target, with a recent reversal in the past year. He cites on-the-ground observations from the Seventh District (Midwest): businesses report sharply higher input costs, farmers say prices are not rising but costs are crushing, and everyone talks about affordability. His conclusion: with the public highly sensitive to prices, any new supply shock—tariffs, Middle East oil prices, chip shortages, AI data centers—is more likely to be interpreted as long-term inflation.

[14:44] (Austan Goolsbee) **The new chair is reining in the Fed's forward guidance** — New Chair Kevin Walsh is changing the Fed's communication style: he dislikes 'forward guidance'—explicit promises like 'if X happens, we will raise or cut rates.' Goolsbee observes that FOMC statements have become noticeably shorter, and Walsh has set up five working groups covering inflation, AI and productivity, the balance sheet, and other areas, staffed with prominent people he trusts. Reports are not out yet, but this could become Walsh's signature reform. Markets should adapt: the Fed will make fewer promises, and future expectation volatility may be higher.

[20:34] (Austan Goolsbee) **Replacing people to influence rates is the red line for independence** — Goolsbee divides today's pressures into two types: personal attacks on Powell, Lisa Cook, and others, including criminal investigations and attempts to remove them; and direct demands to 'cut rates.' He says the Fed's independence has traditionally been narrowly defined—setting rates without political interference. Once a sitting government tries to influence rates by replacing people, 'any economist would see that as a problem.' He does not go all the way, but this is his clearest statement to the White House.

[25:00] (Austan Goolsbee) **AI is a reason to hike rates in the short term, not cut** — He first cools the AI narrative with district facts: manufacturing has the highest share in the entire Fed system, but firms are still looking for use cases and complaining that tokens are too expensive; productivity growth, after a two-and-a-half-year pickup, has shown about six months of weakness. Then he offers a counterintuitive judgment: if everyone simultaneously pours money into data centers, betting with IPOs or expected future earnings, the short-term economy could overheat. The central bank's daily job is to prevent overheating, not to judge whether AI will revolutionize things in 20 years, so AI's short-term policy implication may be to push rates up, not down.

[28:26] (Austan Goolsbee) **AI taking all jobs is the lump of labor fallacy** — He attributes the narrative that 'AI will make everyone unemployed' to the lump of labor fallacy: treating the total amount of labor as a fixed stone that, once AI surpasses it, leaves no new jobs for people. He says this claim has been proven wrong every time in the past; he admits 'maybe this time is different,' but he is willing to bet the opposite: in 20 years, there will not be 95% unemployment, nor will only six people own all AI companies. He positions himself as a 'grim optimist'—not shying away from short-term pain but optimistic about long-term income growth.

[35:00] (Austan Goolsbee) **The terminal rate is roughly 3%, provided inflation turns** — Goolsbee offers a rare quantitative anchor: his personal loose view is that if inflation returns to a 2% path, rates will converge to the neutral rate (what he calls star), roughly 3% nominal = 2% inflation + 1% real. But the precondition is that inflation must turn downward; the past five and a half years have been above target, and the last year has been moving in the wrong direction. For rate-sensitive industries, his advice is to watch data and inflation, not the stock market—the people around the FOMC table discuss the real economy; the stock market is only a secondary reference.

## Sunscreen Toxicity Claims Debunked: Entering Blood Isn't Harmful, but Vitamin D Risk Is Real

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-sciencevs-防晒霜不是毒药-但深肤色人群可能真不用防黑素瘤/
- show: Science Vs (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sciencevs/)
- original episode: Sunscreen: Could It Be Toxic??
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 50:52
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8345 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The most-cited evidence for "sunscreen is toxic and causes cancer" mostly involves absurd dosages or reversed causality; chemical sunscreen ingredients entering the blood doesn't equal toxicity. But daily application does increase the risk of vitamin D deficiency in winter, and evidence for preventing melanoma in darker skin is especially weak.**

why listen: This episode checks the three most widely circulated scare claims on social media against the original studies, so you can tell which are dose-dependent toxicity and which are real trade-offs. High information density, no cherry-picking.

### points

[6:52] (Brandon Adler) **The anti-sunscreen flagship experiment used doses equivalent to centuries of human use** — The 2001 rat study most often cited by anti-sunscreen rhetoric: female rats fed oxybenzone developed enlarged uteruses, interpreted as endocrine disruption. But Brandon Adler points out the rats ingested it, and the intake translates to a human equivalent of using oxybenzone sunscreen continuously for 35–277 years. This is a classic case of "the dose makes the poison": the experimental exposure is completely incomparable to real-world use.

[10:00] (Wendy Zuckerman) **Blood absorption being called poisoning misreads the FDA threshold** — In the FDA's maximal usage trial, sunscreen was applied to 75% of body surface area for 4–5 consecutive days; oxybenzone was detected in blood and exceeded an FDA threshold, and the internet immediately said "sunscreen is toxic." But that threshold doesn't indicate harm; the FDA's own conclusion was "these findings do not suggest that individuals should refrain from using sunscreen." A systematic review of about 30 studies also found no clear evidence that oxybenzone affects hormones at normal doses.

[14:10] (Michelle Dang) **Coral bleaching is a climate problem, not a sunscreen problem** — Oxybenzone has been banned in places like Hawaii due to coral bleaching concerns. In the lab, juvenile corals exposed to chemical sunscreen are indeed toxic and bleach; but concentrations measured in real seawater are far lower. Research repeatedly confirms that the primary cause of coral bleaching is climate change; sunscreen is at most "adding insult to injury," not the main driver. After consumer backlash, many manufacturers have already voluntarily removed oxybenzone.

[17:31] (Michelle Dang) **Homemade sunscreen tested below SPF 6** — Some people make DIY sunscreen with zinc oxide and beef tallow, which is absurd: you'd first have to buy a commercial sunscreen containing zinc oxide to add tallow to. A study took 15 online recipes and tested them in the lab; several contained no UV-filtering ingredients at all, and the rest had SPF below 6, offering almost no protection. If you're worried about chemical sunscreen entering the blood, switch to mineral sunscreen, but don't DIY.

[20:00] (Brandon Adler) **Newly approved chemical filters are too large to enter the blood** — The US FDA recently approved bemotrizinol, the first new chemical sunscreen ingredient in nearly 20 years, though it's been used in Europe and Australia for years. It's truly broad-spectrum, stable, and easy to formulate, and its large molecular size means it's less likely to be absorbed into the blood, behaving more like a mineral sunscreen. For those concerned about "ingredients entering the blood," this is a new option worth watching over older chemical filters.

[29:20] (Rachel Neale) **Daily sunscreen raises winter vitamin D deficiency risk by 35%** — Rachel Neale's team ran a 600-person randomized controlled trial: one group lived normally, the other applied SPF50 daily on days with UV index ≥3. After a year, summer vitamin D levels didn't drop in either group; the sunscreen group was only slightly lower on average. But by the end of winter, the sunscreen group had about a 35% higher risk of vitamin D deficiency than the control group. Because the body stores vitamin D in fat and releases it slowly, lower summer stores mean insufficient winter levels.

[37:20] (Michelle Dang) **Sunscreen's evidence against squamous cell carcinoma is solid, but not yet for melanoma** — A UK study of 400,000 people found "people who use sunscreen are more likely to get skin cancer," but the authors clarified this is reverse causation: those who apply more often tend to spend more time outdoors and under-apply or fail to reapply. A cleaner Australian RCT with 1,600 people followed over a decade found daily sunscreen reduced squamous cell carcinoma by about 40%; melanoma cases were 11 vs 22, showing a halved risk but not statistically significant due to too few cases.

[43:40] (Adamson) **Darker skin has built-in SPF15, so daily sunscreen isn't necessary** — Adamson's systematic review found almost no data supporting a link between sun exposure and melanoma in non-whites: melanin moves to the skin's surface and acts as natural sunscreen, giving darker skin types an equivalent of SPF15+ protection. Australia updated its guidelines accordingly, saying the two darkest skin types don't need routine sunscreen for cancer prevention; the US AAD hasn't changed, and Adamson criticizes it as "not science-based." He still recommends sunscreen for everyone to avoid sunburn and photoaging, but not necessarily daily.

### figures

- 2001 rat study dose converted to human use of oxybenzone sunscreen: 35–277 years [6:52]
- FDA maximal usage trial coverage and duration: 75% body surface area, 4–5 days [10:00]
- First new chemical sunscreen filter approved by US FDA in nearly 20 years: bemotrizinol [20:00]
- DIY sunscreen test results from online recipes: 15 recipes; a few had no UV filters, the rest had SPF below 6 [17:31]

- Sunscreen dosage guideline: Full body: 1 full shot glass; face/ears/neck: 1 teaspoon (5 mL) [50:00]

### glossary

- oxybenzone: A chemical UV filter that absorbs ultraviolet light; once controversial for suspected hormone disruption.
- UV index: A measure of the intensity of ultraviolet radiation reaching the ground; this episode suggests sun protection when it's 3 or above.
- Fitzpatrick scale: A classification of skin types from 1 to 6 based on complexion and reaction to sunlight, used for personalized sun protection advice.
- SPF: Sun Protection Factor; a measure of how much UVB protection a sunscreen provides, with higher numbers meaning more protection.
- mineral sunscreen: A sunscreen that uses inorganic particles like zinc oxide to block UV rays, typically not penetrating the skin.
- RCT: Randomized controlled trial; participants are randomly assigned to groups to compare interventions, providing stronger causal evidence than observational studies.

who it is for: People who've seen "sunscreen is toxic/carcinogenic" videos and are debating whether to apply sunscreen; dermatologists, skincare brand PMs, and health science communicators will also find it useful.

## No Plate Tectonics, No Life: Earth Is a Lucky Planet

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-inourtime-没有板块构造就没有生命-地球是幸运的行星/
- show: In Our Time (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/inourtime/)
- original episode: Archive: Plate Tectonics
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 44:27
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8583 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Plate tectonics reshapes the Earth's surface at the speed of fingernail growth, generating and destroying about 3 square kilometers of oceanic crust each year; it alters climate, isolates species, and even determines whether life exists—without it, there would be no life.**

why listen: High information density, and the Gaia theory debate in the latter half is real academic friction, helping you understand the underlying framework of Earth system science and planetary habitability.

### points

[4:53] (Richard Corfield) **Plate tectonics was not a sudden insight of the 1960s** — Richard traces the intellectual prehistory of plate tectonics: in the 16th century, Dutch cartographer Abraham Ortelius noticed the fit between Africa's west coast and South America; Bacon and Franklin also paid attention, but it wasn't until the early 20th century that German Alfred Wegener truly proposed that continents were once joined in a single supercontinent and moved apart. Richard emphasizes that plate tectonics is a trio of continental drift, seafloor spreading, and a comprehensive explanation. He describes it as the oak king in the forest of geology—without it, the entire discipline loses its unifying framework. This groundwork shows that the revolution did not emerge from nowhere in the 1960s but was an intuition suppressed for nearly three hundred years.

[8:10] (Joe Cann) **Seafloor spreading was a postwar dividend of anti-submarine gear** — Joe tells a fascinating piece of scientific history: Arthur Holmes first imagined mid-ocean ridges splitting and the seafloor being carried on deep mantle currents, but it was only theory; Harry Hess, a naval captain in WWII, accumulated measurements during Pacific voyages and became a highly persuasive promoter after the war. The war itself contributed more: magnetometers, sonar, and explosives—these anti-submarine tools were surplus after the war, along with ship time and trained scientific personnel, all turned toward ocean exploration. People quickly discovered that mid-ocean ridges run globally, have central rift valleys, are accompanied by earthquake belts, and that magnetic anomalies are anomalously large. The seafloor was no longer a silent plain but an archive of evidence.

[17:16] (Joe Cann) **Magnetic stripes turned a happy idea into calculable science** — Joe recalls as a participant: as a freshman in 1967, he was still taught old frameworks like geosynclines that lacked a unifying principle. Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews proposed that if the seafloor spreading hypothesis held, and if the geomagnetic field periodically reversed, then symmetrical magnetic stripes should form on either side of mid-ocean ridges, and spreading rates could be calculated from them. And they found them. Combined with Bruce Heezen and Marie Tharp's sonar-drawn maps of the mid-ocean ridge, and Hess's subduction recycling based on gravity data, plate tectonics transformed from a 'happy idea' into quantifiable science. Joe says it was like a jumbled puzzle suddenly falling into place.

[22:57] (Joe Cann) **Continents rearrange land and sea at the speed of fingernail growth** — Joe describes the specific mechanism of plate motion: plates slide on the asthenosphere, a layer about 100 kilometers deep containing a small amount of melt, which acts as a lubricant. About 3 square kilometers of new oceanic crust is generated at mid-ocean ridges each year, and the same area is destroyed at subduction zones, keeping the Earth's size constant. Plates move at roughly the speed of fingernail or hair growth. Continental crust is thick and light, cannot sink and be recycled, and only crumples into complex mountain ranges like the Himalayas during collisions; oceanic crust is dense and subducts back into the mantle. It is this slow motion, measured in centimeters, that has reshaped the distribution of land and sea over hundreds of millions of years.

[30:39] (Richard Corfield) **Plate tectonics is the master switch of Earth's climate system** — Richard points out that plate reconfiguration not only changes the positions of land and sea but also alters global climate through ocean currents. He cites the Benguela Current: when the South Atlantic widened to a certain extent, this cold current flowing north from the Antarctic coast suddenly switched on, pushing cold toward the north and completely changing Africa's climate patterns. Joe adds another example: about 30 million years ago, Australia and South America separated from Antarctica, forming the Antarctic Circumpolar Current system, which shaped the Antarctic ice sheet and the strong southern hemisphere wind belts. This shows that plate tectonics is far more than geology—it is the true master switch of Earth's climate system: change the land-sea distribution, and ocean currents, atmosphere, and ice sheets all reset.

[37:18] (Richard Corfield) **Life may have originated at lightless black smokers** — Richard tells a connection often overlooked: in the 1970s, humans first dived to mid-ocean ridges and found communities that do not rely on photosynthesis but survive by chemosynthesis. Black smokers spew mineral-rich black water, supporting a whole new ecosystem, and some even think life originated there. He also cites Australian marsupials: plate motion separated continents, and marsupials evolved independently in isolation, filling ecological niches parallel to northern hemisphere placental mammals. Plate tectonics thus not only shapes geology but also directly participates in the narrative of life's evolution by splitting continents and isolating populations.

[43:54] (Joe Cann) **Mars stopped, Venus never had it—Earth is the lucky one** — The program ends with a lively argument. Richard calls extreme Gaia views like 'Earth is alive' and 'humans are a collection of microbes' absurd; Joe retorts that he is like those who rejected continental drift in 1928. Lynn takes a middle ground: microbial symbiosis kick-started multicellular life, but the distribution and survival capabilities of microbes were initially determined by plate tectonics. Joe insists that without plate tectonics there would be no life, because water seeping into the mantle softens it, allowing plates to slide; life also originated from chemical energy at seafloor hydrothermal vents. He then scales up to planets: Mars may have had plate tectonics but it stopped long ago; Venus never had it, only volcanoes, so Earth is lucky. This segment turns the whole theory into a judgment about planetary habitability.

### glossary

- black smoker: A hydrothermal vent at mid-ocean ridges that emits black, mineral-rich fluid and supports chemosynthetic life.
- Gaia theory: The hypothesis that the biosphere and the inorganic environment jointly regulate the state of the Earth.

## Ketogenic Diet for Mental Illness: It's Not About Weight Loss, It's Mitochondria

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-huberman-生酮饮食治疗难治性精神疾病-线粒体是核心/
- show: Huberman Lab (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/huberman/)
- original episode: Essentials: Diet & Nutrition for Mental Health | Dr. Chris Palmer
- published: 2026-08-27 · duration: 38:18
- transcript: Machine transcription · 6284 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 3 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Psychiatrist Chris Palmer uses ketogenic and low-carb diets to help patients with treatment-resistant mental illness; the key isn't just weight loss but changing brain energy metabolism and neurotransmitters through mitophagy and biogenesis.**

why listen: This episode provides specific blood ketone targets and real cases, pulling an edge dietary therapy back into mainstream medicine—valuable for patients exhausted by medication and for researchers exploring the metabolism–psychiatry intersection.

### points

[3:32] (Chris Palmer) **A strict low-fat year made his metabolic disease worse** — During his Harvard residency, Palmer was diagnosed with metabolic syndrome: high blood pressure, poor lipid profile, and prediabetes. He strictly followed a low-fat diet and exercise, yet got worse year after year, until his doctor put him on three medications. On a 'last try' mindset, he switched to the Atkins diet, and within three months his metabolic syndrome completely resolved. More unexpectedly, his mood, energy, focus, and sleep improved dramatically—he woke up naturally before his alarm for the first time. This made him question medical dogma and focus on how diet affects mental state.

[9:18] (Chris Palmer) **Only patients who actually enter ketosis improve** — Palmer's patients mostly have treatment-resistant mental illness: they've seen more than six psychiatrists, tried dozens of medications, years of psychotherapy, and even electroconvulsive therapy without success. He introduced low-carb diets into his clinic and found that only patients who entered ketosis showed improvement. In 2016, a 33-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder had daily auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions, couldn't leave the house, and had tried 17 medications. Within two weeks of the ketogenic diet, he showed significant antidepressant effects; after 6–8 weeks, hallucinations and delusions began to disappear. He eventually lost 160 pounds, completed a certificate program, and lived independently.

[13:49] (Chris Palmer) **Depression and schizophrenia need different blood ketone levels** — Different mental illnesses require different degrees of ketosis. For depression, Palmer typically targets a blood ketone level of ≥0.8 mmol/L; for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, especially chronic and severe cases, he requires ≥1.5 mmol/L. He also emphasizes that not all patients need a ketogenic diet; some only need to cut out highly processed foods high in sugar and fat. This stratified approach turns dietary intervention from a one-size-fits-all into precise metabolic treatment, and explains why some patients only need to cut sugar to see benefits.

[15:57] (Chris Palmer) **The ketogenic diet wasn't a weight-loss diet; it was epilepsy therapy** — The ketogenic diet is not a weight-loss diet but was developed in 1921 by a physician specifically to treat epilepsy, based on the ancient Greek observation that fasting could stop seizures. The problem was that fasting couldn't be maintained long-term, so Russell Wilder tried to mimic the fasting state with a high-fat, low-carb diet. Early results were striking: 50% of patients became seizure-free, another 35% had more than a 50% reduction, giving a total response rate of about 85%. In the 1970s, Johns Hopkins used the ketogenic diet for treatment-resistant epilepsy, with about one-third of patients becoming seizure-free and another third showing clinical improvement. This paved the way for its later use in mental illness.

[19:32] (Chris Palmer) **Many pathways change, but mitochondria are the real driver** — The ketogenic diet has been shown to alter neurotransmitter levels such as glutamate, GABA, and adenosine; modulate calcium channels and gene expression; reduce brain inflammation; change the gut microbiome; and improve insulin signaling. But Palmer believes the most critical effect is on mitochondria: ketosis stimulates mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis—the former clearing out damaged or defective mitochondria, the latter generating new healthy ones. He believes this is the underlying reason the ketogenic diet works for both epilepsy and chronic mental illness, and it provides a target for mechanistic research.

[23:09] (Chris Palmer) **Mitochondria aren't power cords; they're the cell's motherboard** — Palmer uses a counterintuitive analogy: mitochondria are not just power cords supplying energy to the cell; they are the motherboard that allocates resources. They directly participate in the production and release of core neurotransmitters like serotonin, dopamine, glutamate, and acetylcholine. Experiments even show that if you remove mitochondria from a synapse, neurotransmitters cannot be released even if you flood it with ATP. Mitochondria also contain enzymes for synthesizing steroid hormones like cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, and progesterone, and they regulate inflammatory switches. Thus, mitochondrial dysfunction can tie together multiple known threads of mental illness.

[30:57] (Chris Palmer) **Mitochondrial dysfunction may be the unifying cause of aging** — Mitophagy is a special branch of autophagy that specifically recognizes and clears defective mitochondria. Fasting, caloric restriction, and fasting-mimicking diets all strongly stimulate this process, which is one of the main current explanations for how caloric restriction extends lifespan. Palmer cites David Sinclair's claim that mitochondrial dysfunction may be the unifying cause of aging and all age-related diseases. So mitophagy is not just a metabolic topic; it may be a key bridge to understanding the shared mechanisms of mental illness and aging.

[36:45] (Chris Palmer) **If you're not diagnosed, cut carbs first—don't jump straight to keto** — For people without a diagnosed mental illness but who feel fatigued or low, Palmer suggests trying short-term carbohydrate restriction rather than going straight to a ketogenic diet. He gives an example: a vegetarian who read his book reduced high-carb foods on her own and within three weeks her anxiety significantly eased, and she no longer needed her prescription. But he explicitly warns that patients with severe disorders like bipolar or schizophrenia must not try this on their own; they need medication adjustments under medical supervision, because diet-induced metabolic changes can affect drug dosages, and stopping medication on your own is extremely dangerous.

### glossary

## The 15,000 in the Cobalt Mine: Your Phone Battery Is Stained with Blood

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-throughline-没有刚果的钴-就没有你的智能手机/
