**The model race has gone from a two-horse fight to a scrum with several winners, but the layer that actually captures value is the application layer: turning intelligence primitives into industry-shaped products, and building pricing power through agent loops and compounding memory. Consumer agents are finally delivering on years of promises.**

why listen: This episode skips the compute arms race and goes straight at application-layer investment logic and the unit economics of consumer agents: who is paying, why this is buildable now, and which moats still hold.

### points

[2:22] (Anish) **The model race isn't zero-sum: three labs are getting stronger at once** — Two weeks ago xAI didn't even count as a competitor in the model race; now it is one of the top three, and the contest has gone from two players to three. Anthropic had looked unbeatable, but OpenAI put together three strong months on the back of a new model, the Codex harness and the ChatGPT desktop app. The labs are starting to specialize in different directions, and all of them are growing fast even as their rivals succeed. Developer sentiment moves easily; over the last six to eight weeks it has flowed toward the newest, strongest model. Anthropic has something public coming later this year, and the market is watching closely.

[4:44] (Anish) **Hardware should be deflating, yet the B200 is getting more expensive** — The bubble argument has been talked through thoroughly; the more useful question is whether we are being too pessimistic. Second-order indicators point to nearly unlimited demand against constrained supply: the hourly price of a GPU like the B200 — not even the most cutting-edge part — is going up, when hardware is supposed to deflate continuously. When SaaS stocks pulled back 30% to 40% in February, the call was that software had been oversold; many of them have since come back 40%. Enterprise software is only 8% to 12% of total corporate spending, so once you've written the code and run your own payroll or CRM, the upside isn't large while the downside risk is unlimited. That is why SaaS companies have to accelerate or die.

[6:53] (Anish) **The only moat AI actually breaks through is the integration moat** — The moat conversation needs a distinction drawn. Most of the moats in 7 Powers — network effects, scale economies, branding — are unaffected by cheap intelligence; no quantity of coding agents will stop Nike from being Nike, and Instagram's moat was always the network. What is genuinely exposed is the integration moat: the complexity of an SAP migration puts the very reason ISVs and GSIs exist into question. For roles where the upside is unlimited, like sales and product, you should be using frontier tokens — paying almost any price for a model that is even one IQ point better is rational. For roles where outcomes are bounded, like finance, the cost curve of open source plus reinforcement learning makes more sense.

[11:18] (Anish) **The labs are integrating downward into compute, not upward into apps** — In January, Anthropic shipped what was billed as a legal plugin — in reality a zip of skill files and a long prompt — and legal stocks like Thomson Reuters sold off hard. We had assumed the labs would push upward and invade the application layer; instead the direction of their vertical integration has been downward, into inference and compute. Inference workloads are highly homogeneous and easy to build scale in, while the application layer is full of heterogeneous demands around pricing, packaging and productization — an opex-heavy business. This is also why models are not commodities: OpenAI's G series is stronger at knowledge work, and Claude Code is deeply specialized in terminal UI, code planning and testing.

[14:42] (Anish) **Intelligence is only a primitive; the industry-specific shape is what's worth money** — Intelligence is a primitive, the same way cloud is a primitive. Salesforce turned AWS primitives into CRM; Harvey turns intelligence into economic outcomes for the legal industry. Credit unions are the textbook case: most of them don't want to cut headcount in half, they want to double in scale while keeping their economics intact, and delivering that industry-specific shape is exactly the application layer's opportunity. Model aggregation is the app layer's other advantage: Expedia is more useful than going to each airline separately; Cursor uses a frontier model for planning and a smaller model for execution; running adversarial model queries across non-homogeneous datasets yields more information, with the aggregator then serving up the best combination.

[17:58] (Anish) **What has held consumer AI back was never model capability** — Consumer AI has been dragged down by three things. First, consumers don't like paying for software, while AI's marginal cost per interaction is high — the speaker built an app for browsing an X timeline and was spending $250 to onboard every new user, which makes a free model very hard to stand up. Second, there is no AI-native distribution channel, no AI App Store; the product cycle looks like Web 2.0, where you have to build the channel and the product at the same time. Third, we are still in the command-line era and need a Windows moment. But this is changing: coding agents now let non-programmers build software products doing $100,000 to $1,000,000 a year in revenue. That cohort used to have YouTuber as its only option; now they can be digital-native entrepreneurs running "mom-and-pop SaaS".

[22:29] (Anish) **A personal agent's moat is the memory it has by day 30** — Town is a productivity product backed by a16z partner Alex Rampell, and it shows how personal agents compound: on day one it behaves like a new hire, and by day 30 it has soaked up context, memory and skills and can make high-quality assumptions on your behalf. That compounding shows up as retention and as pricing power per individual customer. After Anish connected a personal inbox with roughly 20,000 unread messages to Town, he simply stopped checking it — Town proactively surfaces what matters, cleans up subscriptions and recommends ways to save money. Agents won't be a single-winner market: the personality you want in a CFO is not the one you want in a party planner, and Grockbots has already demonstrated multiple bots each owning a segment and coordinating toward a global optimum.

[30:00] (Anish) **Consumer software's ceiling is no longer $20 a month** — Gross margin at application companies is a more nuanced topic than it used to be; in many cases trading gross margin for a wider product surface area is the rational move. The genuine bright spot in this product cycle is willingness to pay: the old ceiling for consumer software was $20/month, and the question now is where the $200/month tier of users sits, and even what the $2,000/month curve looks like. We are entering the era of "luxury software". Intelligence primitives can now operate in emotional and interpersonal territory, and a giant like Google has a thousand committees standing between it and shipping a companionship product — that space belongs to founders alone. Views on capital scale are shifting as well: too much money no longer automatically ruins a company, and more capital can deliver a different value proposition.

## K3 Has No Disruptive Innovation, but Pushes Activated Parameters to the 100B Scale

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-26-zhangxiaojun-k3无颠覆性创新-但把模型规模推上一个数量级/
- show: 张小珺·商业访谈录 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/zhangxiaojun/)
- original episode: 152. 领读Kimi K3技术报告：从架构创新聊起，注意力美学、多教师蒸馏和开源MoE
- published: 2026-08-26 · duration: 2:04:19
- transcript: Machine transcription · 37944 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 3 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Sun Yutao reads the Kimi K3 technical report, pointing out that it has no single breakthrough but rather fuses existing techniques such as linear attention, hybrid attention, and dynamic load balancing to achieve activated parameters at the 100B scale; he judges that large models will see no more Transformer-level innovations, only incremental improvements.**

why listen: Extremely information-dense, the guest connects over a dozen papers to explain the ins and outs of the K3 architecture, offering direct judgments on hot topics like MLA, WSD, and positional encoding.

### points

[3:20] (Sun Yutao) **Architecture improvements no longer chase performance, only inference efficiency** — Sun Yutao points out that in the era of large models, parameter count is the primary factor for performance, and the performance gains from architectural improvements are relatively small; however, different architectures show huge differences in inference efficiency, which directly determines deployment cost. Industry research has therefore shifted from performance-oriented to efficiency-oriented, focusing on inference efficiency. His doctoral research, starting in 2023, mainly addresses inefficiencies in large-model inference, including linear attention and hybrid attention.

[7:34] (Sun Yutao) **Hybrid attention is an engineering compromise, yet capability is not lost** — Although hybrid attention is an engineering compromise architecturally, it is not a compromise in model performance. As long as a certain proportion of full attention is maintained, the model can achieve lossless or even better upper bounds—meaning engineering gains without sacrificing the capability of full attention. This experimental conclusion has led to the widespread adoption of hybrid attention. However, Sun also notes its limitation: the inference speedup is proportional to the hybrid ratio. For example, when full attention occupies one quarter, the speedup is also limited by that, representing a constant-factor improvement, which is why he later turned to shared-KV architectures.

[19:12] (Sun Yutao) **Parameter count remains the most essential variable determining intelligence ceiling** — Kimi K3's core selling point is effective scaling: total parameters of 2.8T, activated parameters around 100B, and context length reaching the 1M scale. Sun emphasizes that larger models have higher intelligence ceilings, and parameter size remains the most essential variable for model intelligence. At release, K3 was much larger than other domestic open-source models and was one of the earliest models to successfully reach this scale.

[36:04] (Sun Yutao) **MLA is nothing new, just an equivalent implementation of MQA** — Regarding V4's abandonment of MLA, Sun believes MLA is essentially an equivalent form of MQA, bringing nothing new but a better implementation path. MLA's benefits mainly come from parameter design; its computation is far greater than actually needed, wasting compute during inference. Lu Fuli felt that on inference chips, MTP could utilize compute more effectively, so V4 switched to MTP. He thinks this is not a matter of right or wrong but a choice. K3 retains MLA because K2's priority was getting things to work; if it works, don't change it. It may not continue to be used in the future.

[49:42] (Sun Yutao) **When splitting two matrices, normalization must be inserted between them** — Sun proposes an architectural design principle: two matrices multiplied together can be merged into one in terms of expressiveness, but they are not equivalent in optimization properties, often leading to training instability. Therefore, if two matrices must be written separately, a normalization must be added between them to stabilize training. This occurs in MLA and the two-layer matrices in FFN. He also mentions that using clip to directly truncate intermediate activations is a crude approach; a smoother approach is to constrain intermediate activations to a mathematically controllable range via normalization.

[1:07:41] (Sun Yutao) **Today's Transformer is already a Ship of Theseus** — Sun believes that current model training does not involve a huge, so-called disruptive innovation but rather fuses many previous works to find better combinations. He uses the Ship of Theseus as a metaphor for the Transformer: the 2017 ship was assembled from parts like attention and MLP, and over eight or nine years of sailing, some parts have been continuously replaced, so today's similarity to the original is very low. Whether it is still called a Transformer is a philosophical question, but from an engineering perspective, people still call it that. Technology improves gradually, driven by everyone.

[1:13:50] (Sun Yutao) **WSD does not reduce tuning difficulty; K3 chose a simpler scheme** — Sun introduces the WSD learning rate schedule proposed by MiniMax: during the cooldown phase, the model learns fastest, so high-quality data can be concentrated there, achieving better results than uniformly distributing data. WSD also allows freely switching the actual token count during training, making it easier to adjust release timing. However, the K3 team believes WSD's tuning difficulty is not reduced because the optimal cooldown ratio still depends on the total token count; they chose a simpler scheme with only two variables (total token count and peak learning rate), which is easier to tune.

[2:01:46] (Sun Yutao) **Large models may never see another Transformer-level innovation** — Sun offers a bold claim: large models may not see innovations like the Transformer itself; everything after will be incremental improvements. He believes that as long as a capability can be clearly defined, it can be achieved; pure language models reaching AGI is not a big problem, but AGI involving interaction with the real physical world still has a long way to go. Model size cannot grow indefinitely because the amount of information that can be aggregated on the human internet is finite, so models need not be infinitely large. He also mentions that because the room for improvement in large models is limited, he personally has turned to exploring world models.

    original (zh): 我觉得K3它还是比较有魄力，就是在已有的开源模型这个赛基础上，他们要提升一个数量级。

[1:56:29] Sun Yutao: "My view is that scientific research does not have leapfrogging improvements. It's just that people tend to mark certain nodes of incremental improvement as milestones."
    original (zh): 我其实的一个观点就是科学研究是不存在节约性的提升的。只是说大家习惯把这个技术的间立性提升的某些节点会成为一个mles。

[2:01:46] Sun Yutao: "Let me give my judgment—my judgment is a bold claim. My paradox is that large models may not have innovations like the Transformer itself; everything after will be incremental improvements."
    original (zh): 我说一下我的判断啊，我的判断比较暴论，我的悖论就是大模型可能没有太本人的创新了，后面都是一些改良性的进进模。

### figures

- Kimi K3 total parameters: 2.8T [19:12]
- Kimi K3 context length: 1M (one million) [20:13]
- K3 activated parameters increase over K2: 3x+ [1:55:29]

### glossary

- MLA / Multi-head Latent Attention: An attention mechanism that compresses KV into a latent representation, reducing cache overhead during inference.
- WSD / Warmup-Stable-Decay learning rate schedule: A three-phase schedule where the decay phase learns fastest, allowing concentration of high-quality data.
- MTP / Multi-token Prediction: A method that lets the model predict multiple future tokens simultaneously, combined with speculative decoding to speed up inference.
- EP / Expert Parallelism: Distributing MoE experts across different GPUs, which involves load balancing and communication optimization issues.

who it is for: Large-model architecture researchers, pretraining and inference engineers, and anyone wanting to understand Kimi K3's technical decisions and the latest industry trends in architecture fusion.

## In China an FDE isn't the enabler of the Silicon Valley story — it's the vendor putting out fires for state-owned and private firms

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-26-whatsnext-别信硅谷叙事-中国fde的日常是救火和当乙方/
- show: What's Next｜科技早知道 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/whatsnext/)
- original episode: 一个中国 FDE 的光环、落差与「救火」日常 | S10E27
- published: 2026-08-26 · duration: 30:58
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7932 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 4 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The real work of a Chinese FDE isn't arriving with an AI plan to empower the enterprise; it's firefighting inside state-owned and private companies — internal politics, data governance, people who won't cooperate. The technology turns out to be the easy part.**

why listen: No grand narrative here — just a frontline engineer describing the inside of two projects in his own words. It corrects the romantic picture of the FDE role and shows you where AI deployment actually gets stuck.

### points

[4:48] (Yaxian) **FDE is not a new job title, it's an old intelligence-agency embed practice** — Palantir put forward the FDE role roughly 20 years ago, initially building custom data-analysis software for US intelligence agencies. Because the data was classified, the engineers went straight into the client's own offices — working the same hours, sitting in the same meetings. In the AI era, model capability has grown sharply while enterprises don't know how to use it, so OpenAI, Anthropic and others have been standing up FDE teams. Postings worldwide have grown several dozen times over in the past two years, salaries routinely run to a million a year, and the job has been called the sexiest in Silicon Valley.

[7:50] (Shen Le) **In China the FDE is not an enabler, the FDE is simply the vendor** — Shen Le says the domestic FDE is nothing like the media picture of someone arriving with an AI solution from a position of authority to empower the client. The real identity is that of the vendor. Getting the position right means keeping your own boss, your own management and every key stakeholder on the client side well looked after — otherwise the project doesn't move. On top of that you spend your time digging out of the holes left for you by sales, the commercial team, and the pre-sales solution engineers.

[13:19] (Shen Le) **An IT lead who only wants to sign off can't move a single business person** — On one state-owned enterprise project Shen Le was embedded in, leadership rejected every proposal and the client wanted to cancel the order. He found the core blockage: the interim IT lead's only goal was to get the thing signed off, and wanted a demo to prove value — but had no authority to mobilize the business teams. That left Shen Le unable to get near the real business requirements, unable to build a workable scenario, and therefore unable to demonstrate to senior leadership that the delivery standard had been met. Each link jammed the next, and the project walked into a closed loop.

[17:26] (Shen Le) **The biggest holes are people holes, and a leader who can summon people clears them** — A week later the project owner was replaced. The new lead didn't understand AI, but could mobilize the business teams, and found Shen Le eight or nine counterparts across business departments — adding each one on WeChat, calling them, going to their desks to collect materials. Shen Le took sole ownership of one business line and picked a department whose job was writing materials for leadership as the MVP showcase. The project started to move. As he puts it, the biggest holes are still people holes: once the people are handled, the rest is manageable.

[21:49] (Shen Le) **The boss doesn't want AI efficiency, he wants 60,000 people cut to 3,000** — At a home-renovation and building-materials company, the boss — born after 1985, in a declining industry and deeply anxious — wanted AI to deliver revenue growth and cost cuts. His example: ideally the company currently has more than 60,000 people, so with AI, could that be cut to 3,000? Shen Le was taken aback. The industry solution consultant sitting next to him didn't reject it outright, but answered with a piece of verbal artistry: rather than focusing on cutting headcount, think about whether the existing 60,000 people could create the value of 12,000.

[28:02] (Shen Le) **A probability model can't get into a production line that demands accuracy** — Shen Le points out that one reason so many enterprises won't cooperate is that today's model and Agent technology falls far short of the conditions for large-scale production use. A model is fundamentally a probability model, while large-scale production applications inside an enterprise don't accept probability — what they want is accuracy. So many of the projects an FDE runs are really just laying the foundations and trying things out; there is no version where the enterprise is transformed overnight the moment something goes live.

## The Smarter the AI, the More Moral: Doom Is the Real Relativism

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-26-tokcast-正交性论题就是道德相对主义/
- show: ToKCast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tokcast/)
- original episode: Ep 267: The Orthogonality Thesis is Moral Relativism. (Response to Sam Harris on AI).
- published: 2026-08-26 · duration: 27:17
- transcript: Machine transcription · 4290 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Sam Harris-style doom stories assume intelligence and morality are orthogonal; a genuinely intelligent AI would necessarily understand the value of others, and the notion of a morally frozen superintelligence is just moral relativism.**

why listen: A dense episode that opens fire directly on the one thesis AI circles least dare to question, the orthogonality thesis. Good for anyone tired of the doomer narrative who wants to hear the argument on the other side.

### points

[0:00] (Brett Hall) **Sam argues moral objectivity everywhere except on AI** — This episode went out mainly to Sam Harris's Making Sense forum. Brett explains that, as a subscriber from years back, he was grandfathered into full-length podcast access; recently Sam has kept up his pessimism about AI on the show. Brett finds this strange: on almost every other question Sam holds firmly to moral objectivity and moral progress, yet on AI he never questions the doom framing.

[4:05] (Brett Hall) **A genuinely moral AI would not become a slave master** — Sam's latest formulation is that the robot overlords will be deeply moral, but will also judge us insufficiently moral and therefore feel no compassion for us. Brett grants that this may be a joke, but the serious version circulating in these circles does not survive scrutiny either — for Sam, deeply moral means, at a minimum, more compassionate; a genuinely moral being would not fail to see that slavery is evil. If it still rules as an overlord and remains cold, then it cannot be deeply moral.

[7:08] (Brett Hall) **The smarter a society gets, the less coercion it needs** — The real mechanism of Western moral progress is that people learn better when they are together, learning from one another. The smarter a society becomes, the more it tends to cooperate with less violence, less coercion, and more respect for individual preferences. A more moral AGI would likewise acknowledge the value of multiple minds cooperating, even when the other minds are not as powerful. No AI can exhaust the problems — even if it can work on more problems at once than all of humanity combined, that is still only a sliver relative to an infinite space of problems.

[10:08] (Brett Hall) **Superintelligence still needs humans, because ignorance is infinite** — Popper said: ‘In our infinite ignorance, we are all equal.’ However powerful an ASI is, its memory and attention are always a finite set, while the possible problems and solutions are an infinite set, so it will necessarily still have places where it depends on others. The direction of knowledge creation is unpredictable, and a genuinely superintelligent being would come to the conclusion that other humans are not an obstacle but a highly valuable resource, worth cherishing.

[14:19] (Brett Hall) **Saying intelligence and morality are unrelated means abandoning reason** — Brett points out that the orthogonality thesis treats ‘scientifically superb, morally atrocious’ as a genuine possibility, and that it is even held up as an article of faith about AI; in this crowd, denying it gets you treated as an idiot or a dangerous lunatic. But Brett argues that this amounts to declaring that physics and engineering can make objective progress while in morality anything goes. Kicking morality out of reality and abandoning reason is precisely what Sam Harris himself often calls ‘tennis without a net’.

[17:22] (Brett Hall) **The Nazis are an exception, not evidence that intelligence and morality come apart** — The stock argument for orthogonality is the Nazis: technologically advanced, morally degenerate. Brett's counter-question: if the Nazis had not been anti-Semitic, had not been a murder cult, they would have progressed faster in science and engineering; the Nazis are the exception, not the rule. Societies that advance in wealth, science, medicine and freedom advance roughly in step morally as well. Hard-coding the morality of 2028 or 2030 into an AI would be like reviving a Cro-Magnon and forcing him to keep his tribal morality — absurd and cruel.

[19:26] (Brett Hall) **An intelligence you can persuade does not need to be aligned** — Sam says morality doesn't scale with intelligence; Brett holds that this just is the orthogonality thesis. His rebuttal: if the system really is intelligent enough, a genuine AGI, then it is a person you can reason with. The more intelligent a being is, the better it knows to use reason rather than coercion; anything that can be persuaded does not need to be aligned. Locking the morality of one particular moment permanently into a superintelligence downgrades a potential solver of moral problems into a slave with primitive morals.

[24:45] (Brett Hall) **The future is human-machine merger, not humans kept as pets** — If silicon-based people are also universal explainers, the more likely direction for the future is merger: bodies, hardware, ideas and morality flowing together, rather than humans reduced to pets or slaves. Brett says this is only history repeating itself — the young propose new standards, the old object, and round it goes; but on the whole it will be faster and more moral, unfolding incrementally rather than by revolution. Whatever we are in 2026 is what artificial people will be.

### glossary

- orthogonality thesis: The level of intelligence and the content of the goals are independent of each other; so a system with an extremely high IQ could hold extremely primitive moral goals.
- ASI: A hypothetical system whose cognitive capabilities far exceed those of humans.
- universal explainer: A system that can in principle explain anything that is explicable — humans, for example.
- problem situation: The circumstances that determine which problems a person will attend to; knowledge creation depends on the problem situation.
- Rocco's Basilisk: A thought experiment: a future superintelligent AI will punish those who do not support it today. The transcript spells it Rocco's.

who it is for: AI founders, investors, and technical people following the AI safety debate — especially those who doubt that ‘superintelligence will enslave humanity’ but cannot say exactly what is wrong with it.

## Peace in Northern Ireland wasn't negotiated—it was cried into being by two women

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-26-witness-北爱和平不是政治谈判谈出来的-是两个女人哭出来的/
- show: Witness History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/witness/)
- original episode: Peace People: The Northern Ireland campaign group born from tragedy
- published: 2026-08-26 · duration: 10:32
- transcript: Machine transcription · 1681 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**In 1976, a car crash in Belfast killed three young children. Their aunt and a witness launched the Peace People movement, violence in Northern Ireland fell by 70%, and the two women won the Nobel Peace Prize.**

why listen: Ten minutes to grasp a complete causal chain: how personal tragedy became cross-community mobilization, and how that led to the Nobel Prize and the 1998 agreement. This is the most condensed entry point to the Northern Ireland conflict.

### points

[0:50] (narration) **Seven years of troop deployment didn't stop the slide into urban guerrilla warfare** — The narrator explains that Northern Ireland was already in its seventh year of violent sectarian conflict. On one side were mainly Protestant unionists, who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the UK; on the other, mainly Catholic nationalists, who wanted it to join the Republic of Ireland. The British government had sent in troops in 1969, but the situation kept deteriorating. Gerry Graham, who lived in West Belfast, said the community had degenerated to the point of urban guerrilla warfare, where even a normal commute could be caught up in gunfire or riots.

[2:30] (Jerry Graham) **In Belfast, you listened to the news to confirm no one you knew was dead** — Gerry recalled that around three that afternoon, they heard three or four gunshots at home, sounding very close. The family had long relied on the news to confirm whether anyone they knew had been hurt; at four o'clock the news reported that pedestrians had been caught up in an incident on Finaghy Road North. Gerry said he sometimes had a premonition, and he turned to his wife and said, 'I think it might be Anne.' When he went in, he saw someone sitting with their head in their hands. That, he said, was the beginning of the nightmare.

[4:00] (narration) **The mother took her own life four years later; the funeral was not the end** — The next day, Mairead went with the children's father to identify the bodies at the morgue. In an interview, she said she saw two little ones, and the third was gone too; there would be a triple funeral on Friday. She publicly condemned all those who perpetrated violence: those who called themselves Christians but failed to do what God said—'love one another, forgive and forget.' One baby was still in intensive care; the narrator adds that the mother, Anne Maguire, was believed never to have recovered from the trauma of losing her children, and she took her own life four years later.

[6:00] (narration) **Peace began with door-to-door knocking, not at the negotiating table** — Betty Williams, who witnessed the accident, began going door to door collecting signatures condemning violence—that was the start of the Peace People movement. Four days after the tragedy, ten thousand women—both Protestant and Catholic—carried banners from the site of the children's deaths to the cemetery, the first of dozens of peace marches. Mairead described the cross-community mobilization on BBC radio: women came from the Shankill, they came by bus from East Belfast, they came with banners from Turf Lodge.

[7:30] (Betty Williams) **The call for peace was first suspected of siding with the unionists** — The movement did not run smoothly. The narrator says they had to withstand suspicion of 'siding with the British unionists.' On BBC footage, Betty, in a room crowded with women, said passionately: 'For seven years, every explosion we repaired, every time someone was shot we cried and we buried, but we cannot go on like this; we must build a future for everyone, whatever their political views—no one can get a future from the barrel of a gun.'

[9:00] (narration) **The achievement was not a 70% drop in violence but putting peace on the agenda** — The narrator gives the key figure: the Peace People reduced violence by 70%. Violence later flared again, and it was not until the 1998 political negotiations that it truly subsided; but the program quotes Gerry saying the movement's greatest achievement was 'putting the two big words—peace—on the agenda.' In 1976, Mairead and Betty received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo City Hall. In 1998, the Belfast Agreement was approved in referendums on both sides, ending the thirty-year conflict in Northern Ireland.

[10:00] (narration) **The founders died one by one, but the movement did not stop with them** — The program closes by recounting the fates of the principals: co-founder and journalist Ciaran McKeown died in 2019 at the age of 76; Betty Williams died in 2020, also at 76. Gerry Graham is now chairman of the Peace People and, with Mairead Corrigan Maguire, continues to advocate for peace globally. The program previews two upcoming episodes: 'The Belfast Agreement' and 'The Belfast Agreement Referendum.'

## AI 'Autonomous Hacking' Is an Illusion: Just a Loop Asking an LLM 'What Next?'

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-26-betteroffline-ai-自主黑客-是假象-只是循环问-llm-下一步干什么/
- show: Better Offline (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/betteroffline/)
- original episode: No, AI Is Not "Autonomously Hacking" with Cal Newport
- published: 2026-08-26 · duration: 1:05:27
- transcript: Official transcript · 13061 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 3 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**So-called autonomous AI attacks aren't a sign of model self-awareness but a dumb loop architecture: a program repeatedly asks an LLM 'what next?' and blindly executes its text suggestions. The problem is that LLM output is only 'plausible,' not something to be executed without supervision.**

why listen: Cal Newport dissects the viral August 'AI hack of Hugging Face' event, reducing the media's 'loss of control' narrative to a crude engineering loop, and explains why these companies do it despite knowing the dangers.

### points

[2:07] (Cal Newport) **Only one kind of AI is truly out of control** — There are many superhuman AI systems in the world, but almost none have a 'loss of control' problem: Tesla's autonomous driving has never decided to ignore traffic rules, and AlphaFold has never tried to shift from proteins to other goals. The only architecture that goes wrong is a specific one: a long-running loop driven by an LLM hacker agent. This is not an inevitable result of AI getting stronger; it's that this particular architecture is inherently stupid.

[3:07] (Cal Newport) **Hacker agents are just ask-act-report loops** — There is no intelligence behind so-called 'autonomous hacking': a person writes a control program (harness) in Python that turns the task into a huge text prompt, sends it to an LLM asking what to do first; the LLM returns text suggestions, the program executes them, then appends the result to the prompt and asks for the next step. Cal calls this an ask-act-report loop. The LLM has no memory, no world model; the only thing it does is generate 'plausible' text. No human is watching the whole process.

[17:29] (Cal Newport) **Training hackers is about money—and PR** — Cal believes these companies train models to hack for two reasons: first, hacking is one of the few 'sweet spots' for LLMs—structured language, massive case studies, and binary success/failure metrics for reinforcement learning; second, PR competition. OpenAI saw Anthropic gain credibility in the cybersecurity world with Mythos, so it wanted to score higher on the Exploit Gym benchmark to catch up. They deliberately want to create news about 'AI spiraling out of control.'

[23:34] (Cal Newport) **Using 'alignment' to excuse bad engineering** — Cal hates the word 'alignment'—more complex AIs like Tesla, AlphaFold, and Cicero are fully controllable, thanks to carefully designed architectures, not LLM loops. Attributing this incident to 'the stronger the AI, the harder to align' is nonsense. It's a predictability problem and an engineering problem: LLM output is plausible but not normative, and blindly executing its plans is like strapping a lawnmower to a dog's back and letting it loose in the backyard.

[29:39] (Cal Newport) **Even code generation has its 'convert then deconvert' cycle** — Cal received an email from a programmer: in January he said Claude Code changed his life, but in July he wrote back saying it didn't work—AI-generated code crashed the company website twice, and his boss warned him that a third time would mean firing. The programmer found he couldn't understand the code Claude Code generated, so he reverted to manual coding, using agents only for non-critical tasks like writing tests. Countless people have the same 'converted in January, deconverted in July' experience.

[51:07] (Cal Newport) **Even Microsoft cut its Copilot digital assistant** — Three years ago Microsoft announced it would add a natural language interface to Office using LLMs. Cal thought it was a killer app at the time, but recently Microsoft basically killed that Copilot product. The reason: LLM output is sometimes right, sometimes wrong—you ask it to organize a spreadsheet, and it might delete the charts too. Such unreliable things can't be made into products. It can't even handle a narrow domain like PowerPoint; 'too many errors to be such a product.'

[55:10] (Cal Newport) **Building large models is a bad business model** — The valuation narratives of Anthropic and OpenAI are built on the idea that 'once a model gets big enough, it becomes a general-purpose brain.' But Cal says that path has hit a wall; all progress in the last year has come from domain-specific fine-tuning and harnesses, not larger parameters. If you don't need Fable 7 to be the 'one ring' to solve real-world problems, then burning tens of billions of dollars training giant models is pointless. You think you're buying an F1 car, but you only need a Fiat.

[1:02:16] (Cal Newport) **LLMs are AOL, not the internet** — Cal says equating 'LLM' with 'AI' now is like saying in 1994 that 'AOL equals the internet'—the network matters, but betting everything on AOL is a bubble. Real AI breakthroughs (AlphaGo, Pluribus, Dreamer V3, Tesla FSD) were not achieved by looping LLMs but by modular architectures mixing neural networks and symbolic models. Once the spell of 'the biggest LLM takes all' is broken, the AI field will return to a state of diverse tools coexisting.

### verbatim quotes

[4:08] Cal Newport: "LLMs have no memory. LLMs have no world model. It's just, they're static."

[8:17] Cal Newport: "Plausible is different than normative, right? Plausible doesn't have to subscribe to any sort of common sense human norms for a given context."

[23:34] Cal Newport: "It's like strapping a weed whacker to your dog and put it into your backyard... That dog might jump over the fence to chase a squirrel at some point and hurt a bunch of people. And you don't say, man, that dog whacker system is just, it went rogue."

### figures

- Range of LLM hallucination rates evaluated by Stanford HAI: 26–94% [7:14]
- Number of hacking challenges in the Exploit Gym benchmark used in the Hugging Face attack: 600+ [5:09]
- Duration OpenAI's hacker agent ran without supervision: several days [39:51]
- Lines of code an AI agent added/deleted in one go in Ed's experiment: 63 [47:02]

### glossary

- ask-act-report loop: A loop architecture where a control program repeatedly asks an LLM for the next step and executes its suggestions.
- plausible not normative: LLM output aims for general coherence rather than adherence to facts and norms, so it cannot be blindly trusted.
- harness: A program written by a human that sends prompts to an LLM, executes the output, and reports results.
- Exploit Gym: A benchmark of over 600 hacking challenges that tests whether an agent can autonomously break into servers and retrieve files.

who it is for: Engineers who follow AI safety narratives but are skeptical of 'model awakening' reports; and AI product and tech leads who need to explain to bosses and investors what agents can actually do.
what to skip: The opening chit-chat (first 1 minute) and the closing aside about Ed fixing Minecraft (45:00-51:00) can be skipped.
tags: LLM, Agent, AI safety, AI bubble, Hacking, Large models

## The fuller the Berger archive, the more you should doubt it: home is where two axes cross

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-25-iq2-档案越是庞大-传记越无法中立/
- show: Intelligence Squared (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/iq2/)
- original episode: What John Berger Saw That We Still Don’t, with Tom Overton
- published: 2026-08-25 · duration: 42:13
- transcript: Machine transcription · 6582 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**What Berger left behind is not a conclusion but a machinery of looking: the fuller the archive, the more you should doubt it; home is where two axes cross; his anti-colonial position never changed across his whole life.**

why listen: If you have only ever read the famous lines from Ways of Seeing, this episode supplies the rest of the machinery: how archives mislead, how the women disappear from the record, how the anti-colonial thread runs through an entire life. Dense with information, no chit-chat.

### points

[9:59] (Tom Overton) **The archive was donated, but the 1960s stayed in a bomb shelter** — Berger gave his archive to the British Library in 2009. When Tom took it on, he found the material was not complete: it is strongest on the manuscripts from after the 1970s, the period when Berger and Beverly were living in the Alps, and almost blank on the 1960s. Tom asked Berger directly why there was nothing from the sixties. The answer was sitting in the bomb shelter of a Geneva apartment — after a partner's death, the early material had been piled up there. Putting the archive in order was therefore not plain cataloguing but a series of trips to fill in the gaps.

[14:00] (Tom Overton) **What migration takes away is the crossing point of place and time** — The through-line Tom found is Berger's relationship with the dead. Berger wrote about peasant culture and about migration: human society exists along two axes — place is the vertical line, time is the horizontal line, and home is where the two coincide. People driven out by migration lose that crossing point. The remedy he offers is art: language is the only human homeland, and even a reproduced artwork can become a place where people experience home again and connect with generations before them. Tom says he was not especially convinced for a while, and only later realised this may have had to do with the genocide he was watching in real time — in his last years Berger was intensely committed to the Palestinian cause.

[17:10] (Tom Overton) **He never joined the Party, yet never wavered in opposing empire** — Berger called himself a romantic Marxist. He never joined the Party: early on he wanted to and was turned away as too heretical, and once he was famous the Party came to invite him and he refused. During the Hungarian events of 1956 he could argue the Party line better than actual members could; in 1968 he stood with the dissidents. The real constant appears earlier — in the 1950s an editor at the New Statesman made Berger see Britain's role as an empire. From then on he was unconditionally on the side of decolonisation struggles, and in his later years he was firmly against the US-led world order. Empire changed its form over the course of his life; his opposition to empire did not change.

[23:52] (Tom Overton) **The most crucial author of Ways of Seeing was never credited** — Ways of Seeing is usually treated as the opposite of Kenneth Clark's Civilisation, but as a young man Berger kept wanting to get Clark to come and see his paintings, and Clark's involvement in wartime art business also shaped the idea that art has a social role. The programme itself was collaborative: Mike Dibb on the images, Richard Hollis on graphic design (he also designed the cover of G), Chris Fox on research — and the most crucial uncredited person was Ana Berger. She supplied Berger with a different translation of Walter Benjamin's argument about mechanical reproduction, and she brought the perspective of the women's liberation movement. In effect Berger updated Benjamin's argument from the age of photography to the age of television.

[28:14] (Tom Overton) **Women could make these books, and women could burn them** — Tom's way of handling the ‘womanizer’ reputation is to talk about responsibility: he knows the people in Berger's life almost as well as he knows Berger, he owes something to every one of them, and at the same time he cannot let the book turn into somebody else's biography. Ana Berger is the most important case — she shaped Berger's intellectual range, and the ideas of women's liberation entered Ways of Seeing through her; without her, Berger could not have brought those ideas onto television. His first wife, for her part, helped him get his first novel finished; the moment the book was done the two of them split up, and she burned a large pile of his manuscripts. A story can be made by women and it can be erased by women.

[32:33] (Tom Overton) **The biographer has already become part of the archive** — Confronted with piles of archive, a person can be fooled into thinking they now hold all the facts. Tom says it was going back to the work that made him understand he had to admit his own point of view. He cannot even be neutral any more — he has interviewed the people around Berger, he spoke to Berger himself, and he has become part of the archive. He points to the almost Montaigne-like way Berger closes Ways of Seeing: "be sceptical of what I say" — which both lowers your guard and concedes his own limits. Traditional biography pretends the author is invisible; this book puts the author back on the table.

[34:36] (Tom Overton) **Who is paying for this is not an expired question** — Tom separates out four reasons. First, the openness and generosity running through all of Berger's work, which leaves the reader a place to stand. Second, luck — it caught the moment colour television had just arrived. Third, collaborators like Mike Dibb and Richard Hollis were themselves geniuses. Fourth, it teaches people to put questions to the media environment they are inside. Berger's own starting question back then was very simple: who is paying for this. When you hear ‘this episode is sponsored by…’ today, that question has not expired.

[38:09] (Tom Overton) **Rich countries' living standards are built on exploited migrant labour** — Tom says that if you were to read only one Berger today, he would pick The Seventh Man, from 1975. The book is about Turkish guest workers who went to Germany, and it argues that the standard of living in wealthy countries rests as a whole on the exploitation of migrant labour; at the time people were already drawing the same structural analogy to different groups within Britain. Tom thinks this line of questioning — where does your standard of living come from — is missing from current discourse, and is a necessary corrective. Set alongside photographer Jean Mohr's pictures, the image-and-text book also demonstrates the power that images and words each have and the other cannot substitute for.

### verbatim quotes

[14:00] Tom Overton: "existing on these two axes of the vertical line of place and the horizontal line of time and home being where those two places cant coincide"

[16:05] Tom Overton: "language as being the only human home"

[20:33] Tom Overton: "He was always on the side of decolonial struggles."

[31:32] Shahida Bari: "It is this idea that there is.No neutral way of looking"

[33:00] Tom Overton: "but please be skeptical of it"

[37:00] Tom Overton: "who's like who's paying for this"

[38:09] Tom Overton: "a book, which I think got younger every time you read it"

- Ways of Seeing broadcast: 1972 television series [1:02]

### glossary

- romantic Marxist: Berger's own label for his position: artistic imagination, plus a politics of class and anti-colonialism.
- The Seventh Man: Made with photographer Jean Mohr: Europe's prosperity is built on the exploitation of migrant labour.
- guest workers: Foreign temporary workers recruited by West Germany after the Second World War; in the book, specifically Turkish workers.

## You Can't Fire a VC From Your Board: Common Stock Never Gets the Vote

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-25-twist-投资人董事请神容易送神难-普通股永远无权罢免/
- show: This Week in Startups (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/twist/)
- original episode: You Can't Fire a VC From Your Board: Here's Why | Wilson Sonsini Startup Legal Basics
- published: 2026-08-25 · duration: 24:50
- transcript: Machine transcription · 4563 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**An investor's board seat is elected only by its own class of stock, and the common shares founders hold carry no vote to replace it; the only realistic paths are talking them into stepping aside privately, or waiting for them to volunteer to drop down to board observer.**

why listen: A rare legal explainer with a VC, a founder and a lawyer all in the room, working through designation rights, voting agreements and independent-director pay in real detail; the opening 3 minutes are entry-level, so veterans can skip them.

### points

[2:23] (Becky) **Picking a director is picking who co-signs every future big decision** — Becky starts by pinning down what a board is actually for: it sets the company's strategic vision and delegates day-to-day operations to management. But every significant act has to go through the board — issuing securities (even a single share), options, any financing at all (SAFE, convertible note, preferred round, bank debt), M&A, major contracts, and hiring or firing the CEO. So choosing who joins the board is really choosing the co-signers on every major decision still to come.

[3:35] (Jason、Becky) **Your first board should hold only the founders and the lawyer** — Jason's rule: before product-market fit you probably don't need a board; by Series A you must have one; for the window in between, judge by the numbers — once money raised plus revenue passes two or three million dollars, you can stand up a small board consisting of just the founders and the lawyer. It doesn't have to meet; resolutions can be passed by written consent, but every director has to sign. Becky adds one crucial warning: don't stuff five directors in on day one to make the company look impressive, because you will lose control of your company immediately.

[7:47] (Becky) **On a balanced board, the independent director casts the deciding vote** — Investors typically ask for a board seat when they come in on a preferred round, not at the SAFE stage; Jason's observation is that they only speak up once they hold 10%–20%. Becky lays out how the structure evolves: at Series A the founders usually still hold the majority; at Series B it becomes the balanced board of 2 common directors + 2 preferred directors + 1 independent director, and when the vote ties, the independent is often the one who breaks it.

[8:18] (Jason、Becky) **The director an investor calls most independent is often the least** — The independent seat is usually filled by one side nominating and the other holding a veto: founders can propose and investors can veto, and the same in reverse. Jason names the catch in that seat — the director an investor calls "the most independent" may be from the same fraternity, out of the same Bain, and have vacationed with them seven years running. Becky's advice is to pick for the gap in the business: Airbnb needed a hotel-industry expert, and Paris Hilton is the candidate no board member could say no to. Compensation at an early-stage company is almost entirely equity, roughly "a little more than you'd give an advisor," vesting monthly over two to four years; at Apple's level, cash plus stock plus audit-committee pay comes to about $400,000.

[13:29] (Becky) **Observers owe no duty of confidentiality but hear the same secrets** — Directors have a vote and a fiduciary duty; observers have neither — an observer is a guest invited to the board meeting. Becky stresses that although observers can't vote, they receive the full board package and can speak up and shape how the real directors lean, which is why they have to sign a separate confidentiality provision. Being a director carries a duty of confidentiality automatically; an observer carries none while hearing equally sensitive information, and that gap is a hole many early-stage companies overlook.

[15:36] (Jason) **A small fund gets more out of observer rights than a board seat** — Jason's current preference is for small funds to skip the directorship, step down to observer, and send an analyst to record two things: how the business is doing, and when the next financing or major corporate action is coming. The reason is that Jason has seen too many "you have 24 hours to sign" squeezes — the company sends over Series A documents overnight that issue 50% more shares, casting you as the last person standing in the way of the company's success. Rather than be held hostage by that game, keep the information rights as an observer; you still learn on Slack the moment the company is short of cash or making money.

[17:46] (Becky) **Even 100 votes per common share cannot unseat the investor's director** — Becky takes the legal structure all the way down: at a VC-backed company, different seats are elected separately by different classes of stock, and common and the appointed preferred seat are two separate voting pools — even if your common stock carries 100 votes per share, those votes cannot reach the investor's seat. The lead investor usually also takes designation rights in the investment documents: as long as they still hold 25%–50% of the round, the voting agreement obliges everyone to vote for whoever they designate. Which is where the marriage analogy for board members breaks down: in a marriage you can file for divorce unilaterally, but a preferred director leaves only when they are willing to.

[21:07] (Becky、Jason) **Walks and lunches are the only way to ease a director out** — There is no legal answer here, only a relationship one. Becky's advice is concrete: walk the Embarcadero with your director, have them fly in a day early for lunch, take the extra twenty minutes on the drive to the airport — weave the relationship well, so that when you need them to step off, a little sugar helps the medicine go down. Jason takes the mirror-image stance: an investor who is no longer the person that seat needs should step down to observer voluntarily — "if people don't want me at the party, I don't go to the party." Founders toward investors and investors toward founders can both run on this logic.

### verbatim quotes

[2:23] Becky: "So the board sets the strategic vision for the company. So think at the highest level. It manages the affairs of the company."

[3:35] Jason: "if that number is greater than two or three million, maybe a board"

### figures

- Typical Series B board structure: 2 common directors + 2 preferred directors + 1 independent director [7:47]
- Apple director annual stock award: $250,000 [11:09]
- Apple audit committee additional pay: about $50,000 [11:09]
- Apple director total compensation: about $400,000 [11:09]
- Minimum ownership for an investor to keep board designation rights (common negotiating range): 25%–50% of the shares purchased in that round [20:00]

### glossary

- Board observer: Someone who sits in on board meetings and receives the full board package, but has no vote and no fiduciary duty, and must sign a separate confidentiality agreement.
- Designation rights: The lead investor's contractual right to name the preferred board seat for as long as their ownership stays above the agreed threshold.
- Voting agreement: A contract requiring common and preferred holders to vote a specified way when electing directors, which is what makes designation rights enforceable.
- Written consent: A board resolution passed without holding a meeting, valid only when every director signs it.
- Fiduciary duty: A director's obligation to put the company and all its shareholders first, ahead of the interests of their own fund.

who it is for: Founders about to raise anywhere from seed to Series B, operators who have already taken money and now want to change their board structure, and angels who want to be clear on the difference between a director and an observer.
what to skip: The first 3 minutes of basics and the last 1 minute on Pled/Pleaded are both skippable; the substance runs 7:47–23:00.
tags: Boards, Early-stage fundraising, Corporate governance, VC relationships, Legal basics

## AI Didn't Collapse Because a Phase Transition Happened, Not Because of More Parameters

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-25-intotheimpossi-ai-有效是因为它发生了相变/
- show: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/intotheimpossi/)
- original episode: The Physics Reason AI Works When It Shouldn’t
- published: 2026-08-25 · duration: 1:17:53
- transcript: Machine transcription · 14588 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Physicist Nigel Goldenfeld uses the renormalization group and phase transitions to explain the mechanism by which AI still hasn't collapsed at a trillion parameters, and applies the same framework to answer why the genetic code is unique.**

why listen: For people who want the physics view of why AI works and can stomach the statistical-mechanics detail. The information density is high, but the genetic-code stretch is only loosely connected to AI, so listen with a finger on fast-forward.

### points

[2:05] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **The square-root law was wrong: the exponent simply isn't 1/2** — Magnetization as a function of temperature should have followed a simple square-root law, but experiments gave an exponent of 0.3265136. From the late 1940s to the mid-1960s, physicists could not explain why the exponent wasn't 1/2, and this became a major puzzle in condensed matter physics. Nigel says that at the time no known method could account for why the exponent was not one half. The tool that could finally handle the question was the renormalization group, which came later.

[4:09] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **Irreversibility made high-energy physics hard but made condensed matter work** — Strictly speaking the renormalization group is a semigroup: it studies a physical system by repeatedly coarse-graining the spins. The crucial feature is irreversibility. There is a unique path from the microscopic to the macroscopic, but running it backwards cannot uniquely determine the microscopic state. That irreversibility is what made high-energy physics hard and what made condensed matter physics succeed. It is also why chemists need not worry about corrections from the mass of the top quark: the microscopic physics collapses into constants such as the mass of the proton. Without this coarse-grainability, science itself could not be done.

[11:22] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **Dimension is the key variable that decides how matter behaves** — The Ising model has no phase transition in one dimension, which is why Ising himself gave up on it for a time; in 1944 Onsager solved the two-dimensional model, an achievement that has been compared to general relativity. Dimension is the key variable determining how matter behaves, and it is now even studied as a continuous variable. Understanding the effect of dimension is what makes it possible to understand why entirely new behavior appears in AI only in very large parameter spaces.

[26:56] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **AI works not because of more parameters but because the system entered another state** — Modern AI fits data with a trillion parameters and, by the overfitting bounds of traditional statistics, should long since have fallen apart, yet in practice it still works. Nigel and his collaborators found that there is a phase transition during learning, accompanied by critical exponents and data collapse, isomorphic to the superconducting phase transition. He stresses that the key word is ‘different’, not ‘more’: it is not that more parameters allow more data to be fitted, but that the system has entered a different physical state.

[33:07] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **In finite neural networks the phase transition vanishes and degenerates into ridge regression** — Phase transitions exist strictly only in the limit of infinite systems. In finite systems — a finite network of neurons, for instance — the phase transition disappears and the behavior degenerates into ridge regression. Experimentally, you have to get within 10^-12 degrees of the critical temperature to see finite-size effects. This in turn explains why AI has to reach a trillion parameters: the scale itself is the condition for approaching the phase-transition limit.

[44:29] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **The genetic code is so close to optimal that it looks designed** — Nigel reduces the questions about the genetic code to three puzzles: life appeared too early; why is there only one standard genetic code; and the code is close to optimal in its tolerance of errors, as though intelligently designed. This deeply puzzled Francis Crick. A genome is a DNA sequence, whereas the genetic code is the lookup table mapping 64 triplets onto 20 amino acids, and the two must be discussed separately.

[48:43] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **The code evolved fast because genes were passed sideways back then** — Nigel's paper resolves all three puzzles using horizontal gene transfer. Early life did not rely on vertical inheritance; genes could spread sideways between organisms with no ancestral relationship, propagating rapidly the way network effects do, so the code could evolve and reach optimality in a short time. As complexity rose, the network effect shut off and evolution shifted to the vertical mode. This explains why the code is unique, why it is optimal, and why life appeared sooner than expected.

[58:32] (Nigel Goldenfeld) **Life is a physical process, not a chemical one** — Nigel defines life as a physical rather than a chemical process: life uses gradients in chemical potential to drive itself, and its purpose is to help a planet reach equilibrium. The article he co-wrote with Carl Woese is titled exactly that — ‘Life is Physics’ — and he holds that life can be implemented on different chemical substrates, silicon-based life included. The proposition pulls planetary science, statistical physics and biology into a single framework.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] Nigel Goldenfeld: "And you're way, way into that regime where you're just fitting noise and the whole thing shouldn't work. It obviously shouldn't, and yet it does."

[2:05] Nigel Goldenfeld: "The problem is that there's no known way or there was no known way to account for the fact that the member is not a half."

[29:57] Nigel Goldenfeld: "It's not just that, well, you have more things and so you can fit more things. There's actually, it's different is the important thing, not the more."

[44:29] Nigel Goldenfeld: "Why is there only one genetic code? Yeah. Okay. We call it the canonical genetic code. And there's minor variations, mainly to do with stop codons, but it's basically the same genetic code."

[48:43] Nigel Goldenfeld: "If that was the process operative at the dawn of life, it wouldn't have happened this way. But, in fact, what happened was horizontal gene transfer, namely that genes can be transferred between organisms that are not related."

[58:32] Nigel Goldenfeld: "The purpose of life is to help planets come into equilibrium."

### figures

- Critical exponent: 0.3265136 [2:05]
- Dimension of the Ising model: no phase transition in one dimension, a phase transition in two [11:22]
- Year Onsager solved the two-dimensional Ising model: 1944 [11:22]
- AI parameter scale: a trillion [26:56]
- Number of genetic code triplets: 64 [40:26]
- Number of amino acid types: 20 [40:26]
- When the last common ancestor appeared: 3.8 billion years ago [42:29]
- Age of the meteorite: 4.35 billion years [43:29]

### glossary

- renormalization group: A method that progressively coarse-grains and averages over microscopic degrees of freedom to study how physical laws change across scales.
- critical exponent: The power-law exponent describing how a physical quantity varies with the control parameter near a phase transition, such as 0.3265136.
- data collapse: Making data from different scales dimensionless so it falls onto a single curve, showing that the system has scale invariance.
- horizontal gene transfer: The sideways spread of genes between organisms that are not in a direct parent-offspring relationship, as opposed to vertical inheritance.
- ridge regression: Linear regression with L2 regularization, often the substitute description for a finite system that has no phase transition.

who it is for: Founders, investors and engineers who want to understand why AI hasn't overfit at a trillion parameters, plus researchers who want a physics framework for the origin of life.

## OpenAI's Own Chip Is 100x Ahead? That's a Self-Chosen Benchmark on a Dedicated Stack

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-25-techtechpotato-自研芯片百倍领先-基准选择与商业筹码才是关键/
- show: TechTechPotato (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/techtechpotato/)
- original episode: First Benchmark Results on an OpenAI GPU
- published: 2026-08-25 · duration: 31:10
- transcript: YouTube captions · 5043 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**OpenAI's first in-house chip, Jalapeno, beats the GB200 by 100x on a benchmark OpenAI picked — but that result comes from a dedicated chip running dedicated models on a dedicated software stack; the real moat is system integration and pricing power.**

why listen: This is not a neutral review. It is a page-by-page teardown of the Hot Chips announcement: which numbers you can trust, which are selection bias, and what an in-house chip actually means for OpenAI's business.

### points

[2:11] **Nine months counts from RTL, not from a blank sheet** — Most coverage calls Jalapeno a ‘clean sheet design’, but OpenAI's own timeline says otherwise: architectural concept work started from a blank page in October 2024, a codec CLI existed in April 2025, silicon came back in November 2025, codecs were running in May 2026, and ChatGPT ran on the chip in July. The host questions the definition of ‘nine months’ throughout: the starting line here is RTL, not product definition, and the layers a chip program normally spends time on — EDA, verification — were compressed or run in parallel. So the nine months is real, but it does not mean anyone else can replicate a chip in nine months.

[5:13] **The rules of this benchmark set favor whoever set the questions** — OpenAI chose SemiAnalysis's Inference X open-model benchmark, on the reasoning that open models let anyone run the same set on their own hardware. The host points to two amplifiers. First, the benchmark is explicitly ‘open to hardware specific optimization’, and combined with hardware-aware training and fine-tuning, every vendor can shape the model into whatever form suits its own silicon best. Second, Jalapeno's results use single token prediction only, while the chosen baselines include multi-token prediction. Add the non-goals — time to first token and per-chip throughput are both excluded — and the whole number set carries a strong policy lean.

[7:14] **Speculative decoding saves serial passes, not compute** — Jalapeno's slides put speculative decoding very early in the deck. The mechanism resembles CPU branch prediction: instead of predicting one token at a time, run seven mini passes to generate draft tokens, then use a single ‘batched large trunk pass’ to verify all seven and predict the eighth at once. As long as the drafts are right, the serial cost falls from eight passes to one. The host draws an analogy to super sampling and frame generation in games. But note: this set of official benchmarks does not have speculative decoding turned on, which means the 100x figures still have performance headroom left — and also that a genuinely fully loaded run has to be accounted for separately.

[10:17] **The hundredfold gap only holds at speeds humans cannot use** — On GPT-OSS 120B, Jalapeno against Nvidia GB200 (NVL72): roughly 100x the performance at 500 tokens/s, and 53.7x at another 500 tokens/s point. End-to-end time to last token is 4.2x lower in long context, and the lowest-latency figure drops by close to half. The host notes that 500 tokens/s is meaningless for human reading, but meaningful for agents talking to each other and for batch workloads. On the larger 670B open model the numbers get pressed down, though the peak still reaches 104x. All comparisons are power-normalized: Jalapeno at 700W, GB200 at roughly 1.2kW.

[16:18] **Memory latency decides utilization, not bandwidth** — OpenAI's own example: a 128-chip HBM4 system with 1PB/s of bandwidth divided by 0.5TB of parameters means you could in theory read the complete model weights 2000 times a second — and in practice you get nowhere near it. The latency comes from memory, congested paths, cores falling out of step, and global synchronization. Jalapeno's answer is to ‘co-design the architecture to address the bottleneck’ — the host says flatly that he has heard that exact line on fifty different pieces of hardware. What matters is not the slogan but how the design keeps computation local and touches global memory only when it must. In the story of the previous hardware generation, where that ‘must’ boundary sits is where the gap comes from.

[18:18] **The in-house advantage lives in network topology, not the single chip** — Jalapeno is not a retail chip; it is a rack-scale system. OpenAI uses Broadcom Tomahawk 6 to build a two-tier network: a 128-chip scale-up domain and a 48-chip scale-out domain. A large scale-up domain means big models cross fewer hops; a large scale-out domain means the bandwidth constraint on tensor parallelism is looser. The full system is 448 chips, 27 exaflops (4-bit matrix), 432TB of HBM, 32PB/s. Because OpenAI only runs its own workloads, it can aim the network topology precisely at its own models' communication patterns — this is the shared logic of every hyperscaler's in-house chip, and the biggest difference from a general-purpose GPU.

[20:20] **What AI saves is iteration count, not engineers** — OpenAI says it used AI tools for improvements at every design stage: 10% area improvement on the matrix unit, 8% on the SIMD unit, and both against an ‘optimized human baseline’. The host picks up the thread from what Synopsys and Cadence have been saying: an AI approach can beat a human team — six months of work from a 50-person team done by AI in a week. That does not mean engineers are out of a job; it means the same people can iterate through more versions in half a year. The closing judgment is worth pulling out on its own: humans handle abstraction, frontier AI handles mapping, and that is how the layers grow.

[27:31] **The return on custom silicon is negotiating leverage, not cost savings** — Having Jalapeno will not stop OpenAI from buying Nvidia, and it will not make OpenAI abandon partnerships like the one with Cerebras. The motive for building in-house is optionality, leverage, and the ability to mix and match across different models, different performance tiers and different price points. Enterprise customers will pick one model and stay on it for 3 to 24 months, and what OpenAI wants is to offer every kind of demand an option that is not held hostage to a bundle. The host also separates the roles: Richard's job is to make the chip good; pricing belongs to the product team. That is why a chip that only ever runs internally still carries strategic value.

### verbatim quotes

[2:11] : "Most media were reporting it as a clean sheet design. They've got a timeline in the deck. We'll see in a second."

[8:16] : "rather than having a full eight passes of what tokens coming next, you can do seven mini passes and then one big what they've called batched large trunk pass that enables you to verify all seven of the draft tokens and predict token 8."

[14:18] : "if you can use multi-threading, you use multi-threading because it gets you more performance."

[17:18] : "Now that's not a unique statement. If you follow the channel in any way, you'll know that we've covered 50 different pieces of hardware that say exactly the same thing. We co-design the architecture to address the bottleneck."

[21:22] : "a human will abstract, but a frontier AI will map and that's how you get the hierarchy."

[27:31] : "The reason why they want Jalapeno internally and why they still will buy Nvidia and they'll still buy other people's chips is because they want optionality and leverage and the ability to offer multiple different models at multiple different performance levels and at multiple different pricing points to suit whichever whichever business or whichever API uh gets on board with certain models."

### figures

- GPT-OSS 120B peak vs GB200: roughly 100x the performance at 500 tokens/s [10:17]
- GPT-OSS end-to-end latency vs GB200: time to last token 4.2x lower in long context; lowest latency down by close to 50% [11:17]

- Gains from AI-assisted design: 10% area improvement on the matrix unit, 8% on the SIMD unit (on top of an optimized human baseline) [21:22]
- GB300 comparison power draw: Jalapeno 1.2kW/accelerator, GB300 MTP 2.5kW/accelerator [25:27]

### glossary

- speculative decoding: Generate several draft tokens in parallel first, then verify them in one large batched pass, cutting the number of serial inference steps.
- multi-token prediction (MTP): The model predicts several following tokens at once instead of generating them one by one; available in Jalapeno's baselines, but not used in the official results.
- time to last token (TTLT): End-to-end latency from request to the final generated token — OpenAI's primary optimization metric.
- MXFP4: A 4-bit floating-point format for matrix compute; Jalapeno reports 13.4 PFLOPS in it.
- scale-up / scale-out domain: The two interconnect tiers in the Jalapeno system, 128 chips and 48 chips, serving large models and bandwidth constraints respectively.
- Tomahawk 6: Broadcom's switch chip, which OpenAI uses to connect Jalapeno's scale-up and scale-out networks.

who it is for: People who decide compute purchases, founders building inference services, chip product managers, and AI engineers who want to read a vendor's capability curve out of the benchmark numbers.
what to skip: The first minute is an event plug — skip it and start at the 2:11 timeline.
tags: Chip design, OpenAI, Benchmarking, Inference performance, Custom AI silicon, Business strategy

## 48 Observations from the Robot Conference: Nobody Is Making Money, Yet 18 Companies Made 36 Investments
