## Food Safety Standards Born of Space Food: Testing the Finished Product Is Never Enough

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-stuffmissed-haccp-为防止宇航员食物中毒而生的全球食安标准/
- show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- original episode: SYMHC Classics: Astronaut Origins of Food Safety
- published: 2026-08-22 · duration: 36:42
- transcript: Official transcript · 5684 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**HACCP, the core of the global food safety system, was born out of NASA's space food program: testing the finished product is never enough, and the whole process from ingredient to person has to be controlled; a 1971 botulism case and the 1993 Jack in the Box outbreak turned it into a mandatory global standard.**

why listen: HACCP, the underlying system of food safety worldwide, came out of NASA trying to keep astronauts from getting food poisoning — not from the food industry or governments acting on their own; its path from defense-world FMEA to a mandatory standard is far more roundabout than you would assume.

### points

[1:02] **Produce traceability in America is still only law on paper** — The Food Safety Modernization Act passed in 2011 and required meaningful food traceability rules for produce, but the rules were not actually written until 2022. The FDA had set enforcement to begin on January 20, 2026; industry resistance and budget problems pushed it back to July 2028. At the time of recording, the second Trump administration was making deep cuts to several federal food safety agencies and programs. Listeners need to register what this means: produce traceability in the US is still a law that has not landed, not a protection consumers already enjoy.

[14:27] **Food safety is not inspected in, it is controlled in** — Early NASA food was tested as raw ingredients and then again as finished product; any batch that failed was destroyed whole, which left almost nothing fit to fly to space — evidence in itself that the process was the problem. Pillsbury's Howard Bauman realized that if a product's safety has to be inferred from large amounts of destructive testing, concentrating that testing on ingredients and finished goods misses a great deal of what happens in between. The only way out was to control the entire process: ingredients, the processing environment, the people. That insight moved food safety from ‘inspection’ to ‘process control’.

[16:29] **One link fails and the whole system has failed** — NASA worked with the Army's Natick laboratories, with Pillsbury as prime contractor. The team borrowed the military's ‘failure mode and effects analysis’ (FMEA) — going one by one through every way a process can fail and what follows from each — and treated food production as a system where ‘one link failing equals the whole system failing’. Three principles came out of it: analyze every possible hazard; identify the critical control points (CCPs), meaning every point in the process where a pathogen could get into the food; and build a system to monitor all of those points. That ‘branching tree’ style of enumeration is enormous — even a telephone on the factory floor can become a source of cross-contamination.

[20:32] **A precise recall runs on records, not on testing** — In March 1971 Pillsbury recalled a farina hot cereal product on its own initiative — a glass safety shield in the plant had shattered and contaminated part of the output. But because its record-keeping was so detailed, the company knew exactly what to recall: 27.5-ounce packages with one specific code, shipped only to western Massachusetts and Connecticut. At the time that sounded like something out of the future; most companies had no such record-keeping capability. A few days later, Pillsbury publicly presented for the first time the system that would come to be called HACCP (at the 1971 US food safety conference). This is an early case of ‘record-keeping capability becoming competitive advantage’ — the ‘process documentation’ Bauman had pushed for showing immediate value in the commercial world for the first time.

[23:33] **What forced mandatory regulation was not space, it was a can of soup** — Later in 1971, Samuel and Grace Cochrane contracted botulism after eating canned soup; Samuel died and Grace was hospitalized for months. The case exposed something more frightening: the plant involved had not been inspected by the FDA in more than four years, and the company had known beforehand that the production line had a problem and had not dealt with it. The government seized 1.5 million cans of the company's product. To keep the canning industry as a whole from being boycotted, the National Canners Association proposed industry-wide reform itself, much of it based on HACCP principles. The FDA promptly asked Pillsbury to run a course for FDA inspectors, and in 1973 wrote HACCP principles into the low-acid canned food regulations. That is the pivotal turn that carried HACCP from space into mandatory regulation.

[28:39] **A burger outbreak bought mandatory rules that still could not close a plant** — In 1993, hamburger patties at Jack in the Box restaurants set off an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak: more than 700 confirmed cases across four states, and four children dead. The strain had only been identified in 1972, and was not considered a foodborne pathogen until 1982; it took this outbreak for the public to really know it. Jack in the Box then became the first fast food company to implement HACCP; the International HACCP Alliance was founded in 1994; in 1996 the USDA issued the ‘Pathogen Reduction / HACCP Final Rule’, requiring every meat and poultry slaughter and processing establishment to design and implement HACCP. But critics point out that the USDA rule does not fully conform to HACCP: it calls for retesting rather than immediate correction, and the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals later ruled that the USDA has no authority to shut a plant down over failed tests, which weakened enforcement. Even so, in the 20 years after the US adopted HACCP, foodborne illness is estimated to have fallen by about 20%.

[31:42] **US food safety is not one system, it is seven agencies stitched together** — HACCP is not a cure-all: Codex Alimentarius is only advisory guidance, not law. The American food safety system is a century-old patchwork — at least 7 federal agencies split up the different pieces, with the FDA covering food other than meat plus shell eggs, the USDA covering meat, poultry and egg products processing, and fish and seafood grading falling to NOAA; 27 states have their own inspection programs, equivalent to or stricter than the federal one; and meal delivery companies land in the gray zone between ‘locally regulated restaurant’ and ‘federally regulated food manufacturer’. The WHO estimates that about 600 million people a year — close to 10% of the world's population — get sick from food, and 420,000 die, 125,000 of them children under five. That is why HACCP, as a ‘by-product of the space program’, still matters: it remains the most widely used system for preventing foodborne illness.

### verbatim quotes

[3:08] : "It was developed for NASA to make sure that astronauts did not get food poisoning in space."

[14:27] : "we concluded, after extensive evaluation that the only way we could succeed would be to establish control over the entire process, the raw materials, the processing environment, and the people involved."

[19:30] : "Baumann was so impressed by the end result of all of this that he pushed for Pillsbury to implement something similar for its consumer products, not just for the space program."

[22:32] : "Sounds like a really normal way for a food recall to happen now, but at the time like this was a level of record keeping that a lot of places just did not have."

[24:34] : "The company had also apparently known about the problems on its production line, but hadn't taken steps to address them."

[27:39] : "Some inspectors joke that hassup stood for have a cup of coffee and prey."

[35:46] : "I just really like the fact that one of the big methods to try to get that in a better place came from the Space program."

### figures

- Original date for FDA enforcement of the FSMA produce traceability rule: January 20, 2026 (later pushed to July 2028) [1:02]
- The specific lot in Pillsbury's farina recall: 27.5-ounce packages, a single code, shipped only to western Massachusetts and Connecticut [21:32]

- How long the cannery involved had gone without an FDA inspection: More than 4 years [24:34]
- Scale of the Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak: More than 700 confirmed cases across 4 states, 4 children dead [28:39]
- Decline in foodborne illness after the US adopted HACCP (estimated): About 20% [30:42]
- Number of federal agencies involved in US food safety regulation: At least 7 [32:42]
- Number of states running their own food inspection programs: 27 [33:43]

### glossary

- HACCP / Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points: A food safety management system: identify the critical points across the whole production process where hazards can be introduced, and put monitoring and corrective measures on them.
- CCP / Critical Control Point: The specific step in HACCP used to prevent, eliminate or reduce a food safety hazard.
- Codex Alimentarius: Food standards and guidelines set by the FAO and WHO; advisory in nature, with no binding force.
- FMEA / Failure Mode and Effects Analysis: A systems analysis method out of defense work that goes item by item through every way a process can fail and the consequences of each.

who it is for: Founders in the food industry, supply chain and compliance leads, agricultural policy researchers. Also worth hearing for anyone who wants to understand how NASA technology turns into global regulation.
what to skip: The first 12 minutes of American and European food history background can be skipped; start where NASA needs space food free of pathogens.

## A question is defined by the act of seeking information, not the question mark

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-phibites-真正的问题不是问号-而是寻求信息的行动/
- show: Philosophy Bites (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/phibites/)
- original episode: Lani Watson on the Power of Questions
- published: 2026-08-22 · duration: 16:28
- transcript: Machine transcription · 2896 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A real question is defined by its function, not its form; asking is a power you can practise — and most of the answers AI hands out today have not answered any question that was seriously posed.**

why listen: The conversation runs only 16 minutes, and the stretch on philosophical definitions is slow, but the counter-question — ‘ChatGPT is the answer; what was the question?’ — is worth the time.

### points

[0:00] (Lani Watson) **Neither the question mark nor intonation marks what a question is** — Nigel begins by assuming a question is whatever ends in a question mark. Lani counters that spoken questions carry no question marks at all, and we ask them all day long; intonation is no more reliable, since intonation systems differ completely across languages and cultures. In the online survey she has been running for 15 years she includes a "how are you" case, and participants split almost 50/50 — the disagreement turning on whether the speaker actually wants to know the answer. So the mark of a question does not lie in its form; form is only the surface.

[2:31] (Lani Watson) **A question is an act, not a sentence** — Lani's formal definition is that a question is an information seeking act: whether something counts is settled by function, not by form. Many participants counted looking both ways before crossing the road, consulting a dictionary, even raising an eyebrow as questions, because all of these are non-verbal acts of seeking information. A rhetorical question is therefore not a real question, since on her view it is not aimed at acquiring information; what is genuinely blurry is where we draw the line on what counts as rhetorical.

[5:15] (Lani Watson) **An insincere question is still a question** — Nigel presses: must the asker sincerely want the answer? Lani says no. Her analogy is a hammer — a hammer hung on a wall as a piece of art is still a hammer, because driving nails is its function; an insincere question, so long as the information-seeking function attaches to the act, remains a question. That sits in contrast with the 50/50 split on the "how are you" test earlier: sincerity is not part of the definition, only one dimension of whether a question is being used properly.

[7:30] (Lani Watson) **Philosophy can sit comfortably inside questions that have no answers** — Nigel asks why other disciplines simply applaud after a talk while philosophy insists on questioning and hunting for holes. Lani says philosophy has a tradition thousands of years old of pursuing questions that have no answers, so it is comfortable sitting inside a question; 15 minutes of Q&A is nothing. She also accepts the other view of philosophy: test an idea to destruction, check its robustness with the harshest criticism available. But she cautions that this is easily read as rude, and that what matters is the manner and the intent of the asking — if you are genuinely seeking the truth, you should not simply antagonise the other person.

[10:30] (Lani Watson) **Before asking whether ChatGPT is good, ask what it is answering** — She worries that in the technology world answers are everywhere and everyone is racing to answer rather than to ask first. Her favourite question at the moment is: what question is ChatGPT the answer to? If it is a solution, an answer, then what was the question it originally answered? The framing pulls the assessment of AI away from ‘how good is the answer’ and towards ‘is the question itself worth answering’. Once the question has not been thought through, no quantity of answers amounts to more than solving an object nobody has defined.

[13:00] (Lani Watson) **The collapse in children's questioning is taught, not the price of growing up** — Once children enter school the volume of their questions drops quickly, and by secondary school it has all but fallen off a cliff; the silence that follows a teacher's ‘any questions?’ is the everyday face of that collapse. But Lani says the neurochemistry that drives questioning at ages 3 to 5 is still running in the adult brain — exploring and asking still deliver a dopamine reward. So we should not accept ‘you grow up and stop asking’; we should embrace that natural impulse and resist the way an answer-oriented culture suppresses questioning.

[16:13] (Lani Watson) **The best question can be the simplest one** — Nigel closes by asking her what the best question anyone has ever asked her is, and she laughs and answers: the one you have just asked. It is both the show's closing joke and a live demonstration of the whole episode's argument — the best question need not be complex or profound; it can arrive in the simplest possible form, so long as it really is seeking something.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] Lani Watson: "I don't think a question is defined by having a question mark at the end. I think we've got lots of questions that don't have question marks at the end."

[2:31] Lani Watson: "a true question stands or falls on, not its form, not its intonation, but its function when you think about the function of a true question for me that's information seeking, so I define a question as an information seeking act."

[5:15] Lani Watson: "It's kind of like using a tool. And we know that if you're using a hammer to do something other than say, hammering in a nail, there's this kind of sense in which you're not using it for its original intended purpose. Maybe you're displaying it as a piece of art, say, but it's still a hammer because it has that function of hammering in nails"

[5:15] Lani Watson: "I think of questions as a form of power, and it's a form of power that we've underappreciated in modern life and that we can all learn to harness for positive change."

[10:30] Lani Watson: "one of my favorite questions at the moment is what is chat ET an answer to, if it is a solution, if it is an answer, what was the question"

[13:00] Lani Watson: "when children enter school, their questioning typically starts to decline pretty quickly and it more or less drops off a cliff by the time they're getting into secondary education"

[13:30] Lani Watson: "it still wants us to explore the world. it still wants us to ask questions. it rewards us when we do with dopamine."

### figures

- How long the online ‘what is a question’ survey has run: more than 15 years [1:30]
- Participant disagreement over whether "how are you" counts as a question: roughly a 50/50 split [1:50]
- How long ago Socrates lived: two and a half thousand years [4:00]
- Length of the Q&A session at a philosophy conference: 15 minutes [7:30]
- Time children spend developing their questioning before school: 4 or 5 years [12:30]
- The neurochemical period still active in the pre-school brain: ages 3, 4 and 5 [13:00]

### glossary

- information seeking act: An act whose function is to obtain information, not necessarily in verbal form.
- rhetorical question: A question in form, but not aimed at obtaining information.
- private questions and social questions: The split between questions you ask inside your own head and questions asked in interaction with other people.
- answer oriented model: Chasing answers from the system without ever going back to check whether the question was worth answering.

who it is for: People who build products, write criticism, or design interviews; founders and investors who are forever asked for answers; educators trying to understand why children stop asking.
what to skip: The opening display of defining terms is slow; if you are short on time, start from ‘asking is a power’ and listen on.

## AI Can't Replace the Plumber, but It Will Take Out Everyone Sitting at a Computer

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-goodfight-ai-取代不了水管工-但会端掉所有坐电脑前的人/
- show: The Good Fight (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/goodfight/)
- original episode: The Eras of Francis Fukuyama: Building Things
- published: 2026-08-22 · duration: —
- transcript: Official full text · 6918 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 2 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Fukuyama says AI's bottleneck isn't intelligence, it's the physical world: nobody in Dhaka lacks the knowledge to build a water system, the water mafia won't let them. What actually gets taken out is the middle layer of people sitting at computers.**

why listen: Medium information density. The first half is a hobbyist's woodworking chat; the second half — on AI and material constraints, and on democracy — is the part worth your time.

### points

[4:30] (Francis Fukuyama) **Making furniture is the antidote to big tech dependence** — Fukuyama elevates his hobby into a question of ‘individual autonomy’: we live in a world dominated by Meta, X, Apple, Amazon and Google, and being so-called tech-savvy just means knowing how to use their software — it doesn't penetrate any deeper. What he hates about Apple is that it deliberately stops you from opening your own machine: even opening the computer requires Apple's proprietary fastener, it isn't modular; a PC you can take apart. When the OS on his big home PC recently broke, he took the whole thing apart, reinstalled the system, put it back together, and it worked again. He worries the AI era will raise a whole generation that can't do anything without AI, the way most young people today can't read a map — if GNSS went down, they wouldn't know how to cross the city to visit a friend.

[9:00] (Francis Fukuyama) **His survivalist template is Ukraine** — Fukuyama says the world state in a lot of survivalist scenarios — Cormac McCarthy's The Road, Octavia Butler's Parable of the Sower — amounts to a return to the cave age, and nobody can prepare for that. The more realistic case is Ukraine's situation after Russia invaded in 2022: suddenly facing a far stronger enemy, able to rely only on their own brains, and it turned out they were very good at robots, drones, and standing up command-and-control systems — and they built it all themselves. He says that's roughly his own technical level: he can wire sensor inputs to an Arduino and a Raspberry Pi, drive servos, and has built a pile of robots (not the lethal Ukrainian kind). Drop him into a situation where he has to work with that tier of technology himself, and he can do it.

[13:00] (Francis Fukuyama) **The path to learning any craft is YouTube** — Fukuyama never took a woodworking class or a robotics class; it was all self-taught. His furniture making began in the 1980s, before YouTube existed — it was PBS's This Old House, and the carpenter on that show had his own furniture-making program; watching him build simple tables and desks is how he got started. He says YouTube is simply incredible: there is no hobby so obscure that it doesn't have a whole set of instructional videos. The visual part is what matters, because with any hobby that involves handling physical things — fixing cars, fixing computers, making furniture — if you don't actually watch someone do it, you won't understand how it works.

[15:30] (Francis Fukuyama) **The price of using Claude Code is skill atrophy** — Fukuyama used Claude to migrate several large databases: years ago he wrote a database program himself in Python, without SQL, which he now sees was a dumb move; migrating it to a more robust open-source product was only possible with ChatGPT and later Claude. He says he has written thousands of lines of code, and he used to always get stuck at the point of ‘I want to do something but I can't figure it out even digging through the manual’; now with Claude Code he just says add a button that does such-and-such, and it does it, he runs it to see if it works, and if it doesn't he says ‘can you fix it’, and that's that. But he sees the danger: he has already forgotten a lot of the programming he once knew, because he no longer needs those abilities. He also admits software skills come back — the way he once drew furniture plans in AutoCAD, built a Georgian house in software with 3ds Max, tuned the lighting to watch morning light come through the windows and fall on the furniture, and could even make a video of walking through the house; he can't do that now, because you have to be immersed in that highly complex software.

[21:00] (Francis Fukuyama) **What outsourcing threw away was tacit knowledge you can't say out loud** — Fukuyama thinks the loss of American manufacturing capability didn't have to happen, and the blame lies with economists: the outsourcing frenzy was driven purely by efficiency — if someone else can make a mouse more efficiently, why not buy it? They didn't understand the tight link between high-level skills like designing a computer or writing complex software and the low-level skills that turn it into a physical product, involving complex supply chains, social relationships with suppliers, and a great deal of basic engineering capability grounded in tacit knowledge — once it's gone, it's gone, and it's extremely hard to rebuild. He gives the example of tightening a bolt: loosen the bolt on a gasket cover and too much force strips the thread, too little and it won't come off — it's all feel, and a good mechanic knows how. Japan and Germany preserved these mechanical skills longer than the US — Japan has Living National Treasures, about a hundred people socially honoured for a particular skill, some cultural like the tea ceremony, others machinists who can make extremely complex parts to high precision.

[27:00] (Francis Fukuyama) **Government is the only organisation that can do a moonshot** — Fukuyama traces ‘can't build anything’ back to the political turn that began in the 1970s and 80s: in the Progressive era and the New Deal, Americans had strong confidence in their own government; an ambitious young progressive in the 1930s would want to go to the Roosevelt administration and run a federal agency, electrify the upper South through the TVA, or be an engineer building the Hoover Dam; by the 1960s there was a backlash, and Reagan fixed it in his inaugural address as ‘I'm from the government, and I'm here to help’ being the scariest words. He concedes the backlash had a point — Robert Moses was cast as a villain for tearing up communities, and many agencies really were captured by corporate interests — but the result was a general abandonment of government, and government is the only social organisation capable of undertaking a project like the moonshot. Today people who want to do social justice graduate from Yale or Stanford Law School and don't go into agencies; they go to public-interest law firms to sue the government and stop it from doing things.

[33:00] (Francis Fukuyama) **AI's weakest link is that it can't connect to the physical world** — Fukuyama says the weakest part of the AI revolution is the interface between LLMs and the real physical world. He cites Musk's interview with The Economist's Zanny Minton Beddoes: asked what money will be like in ten years, Musk said people won't need money because everyone will have everything they want — Fukuyama calls the idea absurd, because it's completely detached from the material preconditions of economic growth; close the Strait of Hormuz and the entire global economy staggers, because it depends on oil and gas as a physical resource. He thinks a lot of the AI speculative frenzy comes from very smart people who are only smart in a mathematical sense, and who overestimate intelligence's own capacity to solve every problem. He heard an OpenAI engineer talk about AI ending global poverty, every village in every developing country having clean water — and he has taught cases on water supply in South Asia: in a city like Dhaka, what good water supply looks like isn't rocket science; it doesn't get built because a water mafia controls the existing supply and makes big money from it, and the Bangladeshi government is too weak to enforce the law against them. How does a smart machine solve that? It's a purely political constraint, and no amount of intelligence gets around it.

[39:00] (Francis Fukuyama) **AI will take out the middle layer, and that's bad for democracy** — Fukuyama thinks AI will be far more transformative than the internet, because it's a general-purpose technology usable in almost every aspect of a modern economy; and most of the wealth in a modern economy like America's isn't generated by physical interaction, it's generated by people sitting at computers providing cognitive services, and these machines will replace them. He says many of the people pushing the technology downplay the impact, because it will take away a lot of people's livelihoods. He judges AI's immediate effect to be economies of scale: giants like Meta and Google exist because they're software-based, and software scales more easily than manufacturing; AI is slightly different in that it has a physical substrate — you have to build large data centres — but the returns flow to the people at the top of the corporate hierarchy building these systems, while taking out the livelihoods of the middle layer (the bottom still needs plumbers and electricians). That inequality and concentration of wealth is bad for democracy, possibly to the point where the state itself can no longer check these private companies. Cartels and monopolies like the Standard Oil Trust at the end of the nineteenth century triggered a political backlash and antitrust, but he isn't sure future governments will still have the power to control these big companies.

## A 20-Person Team Burned $2 Billion: AI Rewrites the Ceiling on Capital Efficiency

### points

[5:57] (Martin Casado) **Adding people never sped things up; adding money now does** — Martin's example: a well-known multimodal model that everyone uses was built by a team of about 20 people and cost more than $2 billion. Ten years ago, $1 billion would only have bought you a huge headcount and a botched result; today the team knows how to convert capital directly into capability and growth. This is a level of capital efficiency without precedent in the history of engineering, and it redefines the upper bound on how much money venture capital can put to work. The old mythical man-month held that adding people cannot speed things up — but in the AI era capital buys compute and data directly, which is what lets a small team absorb an enormous sum.

[10:33] (Martin Casado) **Early-stage investing reads position in the stack, not the financials** — Early-stage investing cannot be done off the balance sheet, gross margin and churn alone. This is the lens that makes the Cursor and OpenRouter deals legible, and it is the dividing line between early-stage investing and late-stage financial thinking.

[11:41] (Martin Casado) **The case for and against the labs winning everything is equally strong** — Martin separates out two paths: the labs win everything, or they don't. For winning it all: over the past three years they have held 95% of the market, they raise more than everything downstream combined, staying just slightly ahead is enough to keep pricing power, autocatalytic effects widen the gap, and they control supply. [16:09] (Martin Casado) **By dollars the labs win; by tokens the long tail wins** — Martin offers a specific guess: supply constraints ease around 2028; the big labs still take 80% of the market on a dollar-weighted basis, because that is how it has always gone with large incumbents in history; but on a token-weighted basis, 60% belongs to the long tail and open source. He cautions that this is not a settled call — it is, in his words, a complete guess.

[17:19] (Martin Casado) **OpenRouter's value is aggregating the long tail, not smart routing** — On the surface OpenRouter is an API router; in practice it is a two-sided marketplace: developers get a single entry point, visibility and analytics, and model providers get distribution and demand. Its value lies in aggregating long-tail supply, not in intelligent routing. Martin says intelligent routing is an AI complete problem; the gains actually being realized in deployment today are cost-performance optimizations — holding quality constant while cutting token consumption.

[25:00] (Martin Casado) **A $200 subscription gets resold to someone else for $20** — Martin reveals that highly sophisticated operators in China subscribe to a $200-a-month model plan, burn through the tokens within three days, cancel the subscription, collect a prorated refund for the remaining 27 days, and then resell the full service to other people for around $20. [28:11] (Martin Casado) **$60 billion for Cursor does not actually count as a premium** — SpaceX acquired Cursor for $60 billion, the largest standalone private acquisition in history. He stresses that this is two companies added together, not any single resource.

[34:22] (Martin Casado) **No single layer takes it all; every layer is growing value** — Martin argues that right now no one layer is eating all the value — applications, models, inference and media are all creating it. His advice to founders is to stop thinking in zero-sum terms and to worry less about moats, and instead to think about what is strategic in this new world. That judgment is the direct explanation for why a16z is willing to pay a premium for strategically positioned companies that are losing money.

## Giving Tamiflu too late in critical flu doubles the risk of death

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-twiv-重症流感太晚用达菲-可能反而提高死亡风险/
- show: This Week in Virology (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/twiv/)
- original episode: TWiV 1350: Clinical update with Dr. Daniel Griffin
- published: 2026-08-22 · duration: 1:01:12
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9749 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 11 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Critically ill flu patients who start Tamiflu only about five days into symptoms face roughly double the 90-day risk of death compared with no antiviral; an mRNA flu vaccine is approved, but only 50-64-year-olds got traditional approval.**

why listen: The most valuable thing in this episode is that it separates "effective early" from "harmful when given too late," and it draws the boundaries of the evidence for the mRNA flu vaccine by age group. If you have no time for the weekly outbreak reports, take the conclusions straight.

### points

[3:07] (Daniel Griffin) **The money is still appropriated; the people who could spend it are gone** — Daniel points to an Alzheimer's program Congress still funded with $41 million this year and a tobacco-control office funded with $246 million: the appropriations went through, but the experts who were supposed to execute them have been laid off by the Trump administration or placed on leave and barred from working. On the ledger the programs are alive; in function they are dead. The conclusion is not a vague complaint about budget cuts but a precise distinction: "the money exists" and "the capacity to do the work exists" are two different things, and money approved by the legislature cannot buy back the positions that were cut.

[9:16] (Daniel Griffin) **This DRC Ebola outbreak is the deadliest one ever recorded** — Africa CDC's language is heavier than the usual news coverage: the current DRC Ebola outbreak is already the deadliest in the country's history and the fastest-growing on record, with a case fatality rate approaching 50% and roughly one life taken every 30 minutes; there are 5105 confirmed cases and 2420 deaths. They do not treat the figures as a death tally but call for a humanitarian ceasefire, guaranteed access for health workers, and the lifting of unscientific travel bans, while urging African local production of diagnostics, treatments and vaccines.

[14:28] (Daniel Griffin) **Vaccines don't block infection, but they cut transmission about 400-fold** — A systematic review found 70 people who had been vaccinated against measles and still transmitted the virus, producing 237 second-generation cases, with 812 cases traced in the end; so "the vaccine prevents infection" does not hold absolutely. Daniel's conversion matters more: one unvaccinated person infects 20 others on average, while among vaccinated people it takes roughly 20 of them to produce a single secondary case, a difference in transmission risk of about 400-fold. He stresses again and again that vaccines prevent severe disease and do not prevent all infection and transmission, and that what deserves attention is immunity gaps at the school and school-district level, not the average coverage rate.

[21:39] (Daniel Griffin) **The mRNA flu vaccine is proven superior only in 50-64-year-olds** — FDA approved Moderna's mRNA-1010 flu vaccine: traditional approval for ages 50-64, accelerated approval for 65 and over. The key evidence is in the 50-64 group, where the vaccine reduced disease by 27% relative to a standard dose; for 65 and over it only demonstrated "no worse than the high-dose vaccine" and has not yet shown superiority, hence the conservative approval. Vincent says plainly that he falls in the 50-64 band and would choose the mRNA version; Daniel expects it to be available for shots in late September or early October.

[24:41] (Daniel Griffin) **Tamiflu's problem is not that it fails, but that it arrives too late** — A randomized controlled trial in 442 critically ill flu patients found 90-day mortality of 13.7% with no antiviral, versus 19.8% and 19.4% in the 5-day and 10-day Tamiflu arms, an adjusted OR of about 2.1 and a 98% posterior probability of harm. Daniel points to the reasons: enrollees had been symptomatic for about 5 days on average and most were already on high-flow oxygen or intubated, and the evidence for early antiviral use within 48 hours has not been overturned; the real signal may be that giving the drug too late is useless or even harmful, and that the observation endpoint should be extended to 90 days.

[33:03] (Daniel Griffin) **Winters when RSV overwhelms children's hospitals may not return** — A French nationwide matched cohort enrolled 74672 infants in 2023 and 175526 in 2024; among nirsevimab recipients, the first-year rate of RSV lower-respiratory-tract hospitalization was 0.8% versus 2.4% in the unimmunized group (in 2024, 0.5% vs 1.9%), for effectiveness of 66% and 72% respectively; there was no protection in the second year. A separate UK study of maternal RSV vaccination during pregnancy put adjusted effectiveness against hospitalization in infants under 6 months at about 61%. Daniel's hope is a concrete one: the scene of children's hospitals swamped by RSV each winter may be rewritten.

[40:21] (Daniel Griffin) **Data on 150,000 pregnant women shows no link to miscarriage** — This item responds to a Republican official treating Fauci's old text messages as evidence that vaccines cause miscarriage. Daniel starts with the background: whether or not a woman is vaccinated, 10%-20% of known pregnancies end in miscarriage. A 2022 pooled analysis of 23 studies covering roughly 118,000 women vaccinated during pregnancy, and a 2023 set of 21 studies covering 150,000 people, both found no association with miscarriage, and the 2022 analysis in fact found a reduced risk of stillbirth. The comparison figures are starker: in the first half of 2020, nearly one third of pregnant women infected with COVID required hospitalization, against only 6% of non-pregnant women the same age, with a 70% higher risk of death.

[43:27] (Daniel Griffin) **Viral infection outlasts the acute phase; discharge is not a cure** — A JID commentary takes apart three myths: viral infection is not merely an acute respiratory problem, and brings fatigue, brain fog and declining physical function; long-term damage is not confined to the very young, the very old and the immunocompromised, as a marathon runner infected with SARS-CoV-2 could not run three miles three weeks later; and third, "after the acute phase we provided the care that was needed" does not hold, since many specialty long COVID clinics in the United States have closed because they do not make money. Daniel uses this to argue repeatedly for pushing the endpoint of interventions out to 90 days and beyond, rather than counting a patient's discharge as success.

### glossary

- cyclosporiasis: A foodborne parasitic disease acquired from contaminated produce; the oocysts are extremely hard to wash off, and the typical presentation is persistent watery diarrhea.
- New World screwworm: Fly larvae that infest open wounds in warm-blooded animals and eat flesh; in recent years it has spread from South America toward North America and also infects pets.
- nirsevimab: A long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody injected into infants; one shot covers an entire season, with no waiting for active immunity to mature.
- test-negative case-control: Compares the vaccination histories of test-positive and test-negative patients within the same hospitalized population to estimate real-world vaccine effectiveness.
- adaptive analysis: A trial sets rules in advance to pause and look at results midstream, in order to decide whether to stop enrollment or change the later arms.
- non-medical exemption: Lets parents keep a child unvaccinated and still enrolled in school on religious or belief grounds, with no tie to any medical contraindication.

## A community's sound change always outruns the individual, and innovation mostly happens in adolescence

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-becauselanguag-社群的语音变化永远快过个人-创新大多发生在青春期/
- show: Because Language - a podcast about linguistics, the science of language. (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/becauselanguag/)
- original episode: 144: Sociophonetics Deep Dive (with Jennifer Nycz, Lauren Hall-Lew, and Kelly Wright)
- published: 2026-08-22 · duration: 1:08:13
- transcript: Official transcript page · 13074 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Your accent barely changes over a lifetime, yet an entire city's speech keeps moving: new changes are mostly added once in adolescence, then each person freezes with them, and the next generation adds a little more.**

why listen: The first 27 minutes are mostly the researchers narrating their own pronunciation, and the density is low; skip past that and the two mechanisms worth the time — adolescent entrenchment and media affecting only perception — are what pay it back.

### points

[17:46] (Lauren Hall-Lew) **Perfectly identical accents would actually be harder to understand** — Daniel asks: if the goal is to be understood, the easiest route is for everyone to talk the same way, so why isn't that how it works? Lauren says it's anatomically impossible — every person's vocal tract is different, so variation is built into speech. And once variation exists, it gets recruited for other jobs: little boys and little girls have the same vocal tract anatomy, yet they deliberately amplify gender differences, because that matters to their social world. She offers a counterintuitive corollary: if someone whose body differs a lot produced exactly the same sound, that would actually hinder understanding, because we're used to normalizing what we hear against the body we see. The other face of the same mechanism is what they call the "Social McGurk Effect": show a listener only a photo and tell them this is the speaker, and they will "hear" an accent that isn't there.

[35:48] (Jennifer Nycz) **The more intuitive the story, the more you should doubt it** — Daniel floats a hypothesis: Australian Indigenous languages generally lack fricatives, which might be tied to a high rate of hearing loss in the population — in 2018-2019, more than two-fifths of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged seven and over were assessed as having some degree of hearing loss. Jennifer doesn't accept the explanation: she says she wasn't aware of that feature in Indigenous populations, questions the premise, and presses that such an account could explain losing certain subtle contrasts but not why an entire fricative series would disappear. She offers a methodology: the more intuitive and plausible a story is, the more she wants to doubt it, especially when the generalization is about a group underrepresented in academia. Daniel himself concedes up front that it sounds like a Just-So Story.

[36:50] (Lauren Hall-Lew) **The individual freezes, the community keeps moving** — The book poses a paradox: sound change in a community is faster than in any individual in it. Lauren says this is almost logically necessary — if an individual changed more than the community, he would no longer belong to it, and the community already contains individuals' changes. The actual mechanism is called the adolescent peak: innovations are usually introduced into the grammar by adolescents, who then keep using them for the rest of their lives but never more than that. Take /u/-fronting: one generation pushes it to a certain point and stops, the next pushes a little further from there, and the community thus travels a road no individual could walk in a lifetime. Hedvig follows up by asking "why people always think the music they loved at 13 to 17 was the best," and Lauren says that's exactly the period when you're shaping "who I am" — speech is just one of many markers that set along with you.

[41:42] (Jennifer Nycz) **Media changes listening, not pronunciation** — The baseline judgment in sociolinguistics is: put a kid in front of Peppa Pig or Bluey and he won't permanently change his accent — what people want to learn is the person next door. Jennifer says media is more likely to have an indirect effect: if a show presents an accent, or people from a certain community, positively and as cool, the social payoff of adopting that feature in real life goes up, and change may be accelerated. She notes that past research mostly looked at asymmetric broadcast systems like radio and television, whereas podcasts and social media are more invested and interactive — listeners feel the host is like a friend in their ear, and that might affect vowels and consonants at a finer grain. Lauren adds: media's influence is probably more in perception than production — what it changes is your ability to understand various accents.

[44:10] (Lauren Hall-Lew) **You're unaware of 95% of what you say** — Daniel asks how much of our own accent we're conscious of — fifty-fifty? Lauren's answer is "95% not aware," and for linguists about 85%. She stresses this doesn't mean we only take in 5% of the information: we're taking in 100% all the time, but only 5% of it enters awareness. Her example: the moment you open your mouth you have to pick a language, which immediately tells others something about you, and you weren't thinking about it at all. Jennifer gives the reason from the other end: in one second we produce roughly ten to twelve phonemes, on top of stress, neighboring segments and morphological categories, so it's impossible to "choose" how to pronounce each one. So accusations like "someone is deliberately using an accent to be annoying or insincere" don't survive the arithmetic.

[50:59] (Lauren Hall-Lew) **A rare male-led sound change** — Lauren says what she's focused on now is East Asia and West Africa. East Asia has a large body of research on various feminine voice qualities: the "cute" voice popular in Korea, Japan, Taiwan and parts of China, and what happens when male bodies start using it. She gives Seoul Korean as an example — vowels after nasals used to be nasalized and are now denasalizing, an ongoing sound change. What's special is that it's rarely male-led: nasalization and hyper-articulated speech are already bound up with a hyper-feminine "cute" style, so men are leading the shift in the opposite direction. She then responds to a listener's claim that American women are more nasal, arguing that, like creaky voice, it's embedded in a higher fundamental frequency and so is more noticeable, and probably doesn't hold up when you actually measure it.

[56:23] (Jennifer Nycz) **Teach people the game, and also point out the game** — Hedvig asks: since the ideal that all accents should be treated equally won't be realized any time soon, should schools teach the prestigious variant so people suffer less discrimination? Jennifer uses an analogy: it's like "capitalism is terrible, but I also have a 401k" — an individual has to survive inside the system, and that doesn't mean giving up your judgment of the system. She separates two things: knowing that high rising terminals and creaky voice are linguistically no worse than anything else is one thing; telling a woman who feels she has to change her voice "don't change, you're fine" is another, because in her own situation she probably isn't fine. Lauren aims at the stigma around style shifting: every few months a politician gets slammed in the media for switching registers and being insincere, yet all of us switch all the time.

[1:03:03] (Lauren Hall-Lew) **Deaf schools create dialects in sign language** — Sign languages have no sound, but they have phonology and social variation just the same. Lauren says the most distinctive thing about sign-language sociophonetics is this: most deaf people are born to hearing families, so there's no intergenerational transmission the way there is in spoken language, which makes deaf schools play a far bigger role than spoken-language schools in "what counts as input," and people will say certain signs belong to this school or that school. Hedvig mentions a Catholic deaf school that separated students by gender and ended up with gender dialects — Lauren corrects the location to Ireland; in the US, racial segregation produced Black ASL, distinct from white American Sign Language. At the articulatory level, sign languages have two hands, non-manual features like the face and body, and a range of arm movement far larger than the mouth, so signing height, the size of the signing space and the speed of movement can all become individual variation.

### verbatim quotes

[17:46] Lauren Hall-Lew: "So, the second that you have variation, which is introduced just by differences in the meat of the human body, then that variation becomes available to be used for all sorts of interesting things. So, variation is just inherent to speech."

[38:12] Lauren Hall-Lew: "So, an individual is not going to go through all those stages. They're going to go through the first stage and then just hang out there for the rest of their life."

[41:42] Jennifer Nycz: "there can be this sort of indirect effect where if you are watching a show that portrays speakers of a particular accent or from a particular community in a positive way, like makes them seem cool or something then that can sort of accelerate the acquisition of a change IRL because that kind of enhances the social benefit of taking on that feature."

[45:12] Lauren Hall-Lew: "Oh, I'm saying we're picking up on 100% of it all the time. It's just we're not aware or consciously aware that we're doing it, five percent is conscious."

[50:59] Lauren Hall-Lew: "It relates to this cuteness thing because unlike most sound changes, it's male led. … So, you see men leading in the change away from vowel nasalization."

[56:23] Jennifer Nycz: "It's one thing to know that there is nothing like linguistically lazy or wrong about high rising intonation or creaky voice or something. It's another to tell a particular woman who feels like she has to alter her voice … because she's probably not fine in her context."

[1:01:57] Daniel Midgley: "Ben's not here, but when we talk to him about this, we usually come up with some version of: Teach people the game, but call out the game."

[1:06:12] Lauren Hall-Lew: "We need more sociophonetics of sign language, particularly those from Deaf backgrounds. So, this is my call to arms."

### figures

- Share of linguistic social-signal processing we do unconsciously: 95% (about 85% for linguists) [44:10]
- Phonemes produced per second: about 10 to 12 [53:46]
- Hearing loss rate among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians: in 2018-2019, more than two-fifths of those aged seven and over had some degree of hearing loss [33:26]

### glossary

- sociophonetics: The study of how phonetic variation is bound up with speakers' social identities, contexts and listeners' expectations.
- actuation problem: Why a given phonetic variant gets assigned social meaning at a particular moment, thereby setting off a sound change.
- adolescent peak: Sound-change innovations mostly enter an individual's grammar in adolescence, after which they are only used, not deepened.
- chronolect: A coinage Hedvig wants to popularize, meaning the shared way of speaking of the people of a given era.
- style shifting: The same person adjusting how they talk between classroom, family and friends; everyone does it, yet it's often taken as insincerity.
- denasalization: Vowels after nasals losing their nasalization — an ongoing, male-led sound change in Seoul Korean.

who it is for: Readers interested in sociolinguistics and phonetic variation; engineers working on speech synthesis, accent recognition or dubbing, who can take concrete judgments from the production-versus-perception distinction.
what to skip: 0:00-27:00 of personal pronunciation self-description can be fast-forwarded; the mechanistic discussion is essentially all after 27:33.

## Western Restaurant Brands Go Chinese-Owned; The Real Moat Is In Fragrance Compounds

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-fengtouquan-洋餐饮纷纷让位中资-硬壁垒藏在香气里/

- original episode: 145 ✪ 改属中资的餐饮洋品牌

- verification: 3 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**McDonald's, Starbucks, Burger King and their peers have handed their China businesses to Chinese capital one after another. In restaurants, localisation is the line between life and death — but the fragrance compounds upstream of perfume are still monopolised by four European and American giants. It is the barrier inside the supply chain, not the brand on the door, that decides where domestic substitution actually stops.**

why listen: It uses the ownership changes from McDonald's to Häagen-Dazs to explain what restaurant localisation really requires, then uses the four fragrance giants to make the opposite point: the rise of domestic brands does not mean anyone in China holds power over the supply chain.

### points

[2:01] **Buying the brand and hiring a local team beats running it from across the Pacific** — McDonald's sold its China business to CITIC Capital and Carlyle in 2017. CITIC took 52%, McDonald's globally kept only twenty-something percent, and from that point the operating company — Golden Arches (金拱门) — was Chinese-controlled. The past two years reversed the plot: McDonald's globally bought its stake back up from 20% to 48%, and Carlyle exited after holding for several years, realising a return of roughly six to seven times. The hosts' read is that this deal was the demonstration case for every foreign restaurant handover that followed: put up the money to buy the brand, then hire a local operating team, and you have far more fighting power than you do issuing orders from the other side of the Pacific. That is now industry consensus.

[7:08] **Starbucks giving up control is the watershed moment of this wave** — The deal flow reached its peak in 2026. In February, Yuanfeng Fund (元丰基金) injected US$350 million into Burger King China for an 83% stake, at an overall valuation of about 2.8 to 2.9 billion yuan. In April, Starbucks headquarters settled a partnership with Boyu Capital, with headquarters retaining 40% and Boyu taking 60%. The two hosts joke that the investment firms appear to be copying each other's homework — finish grabbing Starbucks, then go grab Burger King. What makes the Starbucks deal the marker is that Seattle gave up control of the China business for the first time, and that the new shareholder had already moved in and taken over operations before closing.

[11:30] **Pizza Hut's China business alone is worth almost all the rest of the world** — In June this year, Yum China paid US$1.2 billion to buy the brand ownership of Pizza Hut China from Yum's US headquarters, turning itself from a large franchisee into the owner of the brand. In the same period, Yum US dumped Pizza Hut everywhere outside China on a US private equity firm for only US$1.5 billion — one region's price coming close to the total for the entire rest of the world. The hosts take this as evidence that Yum picked the right road: it started running localised operations and listed the China business separately twenty years ago, and because it did the job well the brand was absorbed internally rather than handed to outsiders.

[17:47] **Restaurants are cheap to enter and brutally hard to scale past HK$100 billion** — The footnote to "low barrier to entry, high barrier to getting big" is market capitalisation: out of every listed restaurant company in China today, only one — Yum China — stands at the 100 billion Hong Kong dollar level. Mixue Bingcheng (蜜雪冰城) and Haidilao (海底捞) have both fallen back to the tens of billions, having exceeded it only at their peak. Restaurants are an enormous category worth three to five trillion yuan, yet the hundred-billion mark is a threshold that is extremely hard to cross, because every brand is taking hits from competitors on all sides at once. If a company is not decisive about localisation, even a famous one can easily lose the fight.

[20:53] **Starbucks refuses the delivery price war and localises the space instead** — The most immediately visible change after the acquisition is the playlist: the English background music that Seattle headquarters used to decide centrally has been replaced with a great deal of Mandarin pop, and the choice of songs has been pushed all the way down to each store's manager — a neighbourhood store plays something warm, a trend-heavy shopping district plays something more fashionable. This year it also opened a themed store at Yongqingfang (永庆坊) in Guangzhou built around a Cantonese intangible-heritage parlour, moving Yue opera costumes and a stage set inside the coffee shop. The hosts' read: Starbucks is not fighting the 9.9-yuan delivery price war; it is making "the experience of the space" — its actual foundation — more local.

[31:13] **Häagen-Dazs lost because a packaged-food company has no restaurant DNA** — Häagen-Dazs has had its own localisation high point in China. Twenty years ago, to move expensive ice cream, the China team opened experience stores in shopping malls and used the 50-yuan-a-scoop price inside the store as an anchor for the 30-yuan tub in the supermarket. Both the packaged business and the stores took off, and at its peak the chain came close to 1,000 stores. But General Mills is a packaged-food company with no restaurant DNA, and once that team left, the stores fell steadily behind on product, price and model, losing ground to Yeren Xiansheng (野人先生) as the latter gained it. In the end, General Mills sold the store business to Ningji (柠季) in June this year, in an announcement that did not even state the transaction price. Since the handover, Häagen-Dazs has started showing up with pushcarts and 19.9-yuan promotions.

[38:31] **Zero delivery is precisely why Yeren Xiansheng is winning** — The most counter-intuitive fact about Yeren Xiansheng: delivery is 0% of sales, and yet over the past year it has been the standout fast-expanding brand. Its logic for giving up delivery is that ice cream consumption happens in social settings — families, couples — and is emotional value rather than a functional need. Delivery damages the taste and cannot catch that occasion anyway. The hosts argue that its conviction about one insight — a family finishing dinner and sharing a single ice cream in the mall — is why it is stronger than its foreign-owned rivals. Next it is pushing ice cream cakes, aimed at birthday celebrations and emotional sharing, using only the odd corners and nooks around its stores for a few seats rather than copying Häagen-Dazs and spending heavily to fit out large stores.

[54:08] **Chokepoints do not sit only in hard tech; they sit in smell too** — Whether domestic perfume brands are really rising has to be judged across the whole supply chain: brands like Guanxia (观夏) and Wenxian (闻献) are only "assemblers of scent", while the actual R&D sits upstream — four chemical giants, two Swiss, one German and one American, which between them all but monopolise the world's supply of smell. The largest has annual revenue of 100 billion yuan. Three barriers have kept them standing for a century. A patent wall: the molecular formulas are not disclosed. A talent wall: there are only a few hundred top perfumers in the world, and training one takes more than ten years. A customer wall: Chanel and Dior are not going to switch raw-material suppliers to save money. Chokepoints do not exist only in hard tech — they exist in smell as well.

## Simulating real people is not a reasoning problem: frontier models get only 20–30% accuracy

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-21-latentspace-前沿模型太聪明-反而模拟不了真人/
- show: Latent Space (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/latentspace/)
- original episode: Simulation: the new Scaling Law — Joon Sung Park, Simile AI
- published: 2026-08-21 · duration: 1:09:38
- transcript: Official full text · 12378 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Joon Sung Park's argument: treating people as trainable objects does not call for a stronger reasoning model but for a model that makes the same mistakes people make — frontier models reach only 20–30% accuracy predicting the behavior of niche populations, and Simile has pushed that to 85% using two-hour deep interviews plus RCT data.**

why listen: Worth listening. It lays out a post-training route completely unlike coding or reasoning, plus a market structure that already has paying customers but no clearly stateable TAM.

### points

[5:59] (Joon Sung Park) **Agents fail at your errands because they do not know who you are** — When he ran a time machine exercise in 2022, simulation and ‘an extremely personalized personal assistant’ came out as the top two, side by side. Joon chose simulation not merely out of a taste for science fiction, but on a judgment about ordering: you ask a model to buy your dinner and it orders a Hawaiian pizza, and you do not eat pineapple. That failure cannot be repaired with stronger execution; only a deep understanding of ‘who I am’ fixes it. His bet is that an accurate representation of a person is causally prior to automated agents. His hot take is that no personal assistant to date has actually reached that level of ambition; ChatGPT and Claude do know a good deal about their users, and their output fits better, but the key ingredient is still not in place.

[9:50] (Joon Sung Park) **Public models have not learned the social physics of human beings** — He offers a test. If a model has to learn the underlying physics of the world it operates in — a new social physics — then you must train or post-train it. If that physics is already inside the model and you only need it to react to a situation, a prompt is enough. He does not think public models have learned a complete map of human social physics, and the reason lies in what the data is made of: web data is essentially people's ‘self-disclosed attitudinal data’, with behavioral data only scattered through it in fragments. The blank space between what people say they do online and what people actually do in the real world is what he calls humanity's dark knowledge, and it has to be collected afresh and brought into the modeling process. OpenClaw's Markdown memory shares the same intuition as the 2022 generative agents work: clever, but with a ceiling.

[11:21] (Joon Sung Park) **Data describing why is the scarcest and also the most valuable** — The first bucket is deep interviews: asking directly, ‘tell me your life story’ — childhood memories, trauma, first love. This long-tail material is what gives ‘the person as a model’ its texture, and it works in ways that are hard to predict. The second bucket is observational behavioral data: transaction data, scrapable web data. It supplies the base statistics of behavior and is also the easiest to obtain. The third bucket he considers the most important — data that describes causal mechanism, data that describes why — and it comes mainly from RCTs: same setup, move one variable, watch how behavior changes. That kind of data is both scarce and critical, because the world is ground truth, but it happens only once. Simile runs a large number of RCTs itself, and treats ‘the decision carries a real cost’ as the dividing line between attitude and behavior: in their experiments, what you buy actually gets shipped to your house.

[14:08] (Joon Sung Park) **Telling a client sales will collapse in two quarters says nothing at all** — ‘Your sales will collapse two quarters from now’ is of no use to a decision-maker; all they can say is ‘well, that's terrible’. What they need to know is what to do now to avoid that future — which is causal mechanism, and which is the boundary between simulation and prediction. The highest form of simulation takes as input not a question but a goal: as in Foundation, ‘compress the turmoil to a thousand years’, and then it outputs every step. And those steps are frequently counterintuitive — the first one turns out to be exiling the scientist who issued the warning to Terminus. Brought down to business: an automaker wants to know how to market EVs so as to push its stock price up, and the simulation might return ‘marketing it this way will change how consumers perceive your non-EV models, and actually pull total sales down’ — a conclusion you could never arrive at by watching EV sales alone.

[26:02] (Joon Sung Park) **The denominator of that 85% is a person replicating themselves** — The method in Generative Agent Simulations of 1000 People: recruit 1000 people, a representative sample of the US population, into a virtual lab; collect two hours of data per person (the interview script taken from the American Voices Project, plus as much behavioral data as possible); send them away for two weeks and use that data to build digital twins; then bring the real people back after two weeks for a full battery of behavioral-economics games, the Big Five, the General Social Survey, and RCTs that have been published in PNAS, and have each twin predict what its person would do. The result is replication accuracy reaching 85% of a person replicating themselves. The denominator is a person's own test-retest consistency, not absolute correctness — that is the only correct way to read this number.

[28:24] (Joon Sung Park) **The more rational frontier models get, the worse they simulate real people** — Frontier models are moving toward being ‘hyper-rational, objective machines’: data from Mercor and Scale, annotation by professional programmers and scientists, all aimed at reasoning ability. Simile's training objective runs the other way — it wants to build a model that makes the same mistakes he makes; whatever error he commits, the model has to commit it too. That is an entirely different set of data and training objectives, and it also explains the performance gap: on the niche populations and topics customers actually care about, frontier models' behavioral prediction accuracy falls to 20–30%, and on gen pop it is roughly 50–60%, not enough to make decisions on. Another post-training route is scraping pre-registered studies from the Open Science Framework — tens of thousands of high-quality RCTs that come with stated hypotheses and protection against p-hacking — and using them to significantly improve behavioral prediction. That model is part of open science and is not being commercialized.

[37:30] (Joon Sung Park) **Combinatorial prompts only retrieve knowledge the model already holds** — Faced with Tencent's billion persona paper (a Cartesian product of occupations and backgrounds used as prompts), he first grants the scale, then gives the core of his objection: that approach depends heavily on statistics that have already entered the model's parameters — you are only retrieving knowledge the model already has. If that route worked, simulation would already be solved, and what the market shows is not that. Real people carry a great deal of fine-grained, niche knowledge; any single piece of it looks unremarkable, but assembled it is extremely rich, and that part can only come from bespoke data collection. The same logic determines which social data they want most: Facebook, rather than LinkedIn or Twitter. On LinkedIn people are professionally guarded; on Twitter people are performing a persona; Facebook is closer to a person's base state.

[40:04] (Joon Sung Park) **Scale is not for significance, it is for sieving out subpopulations** — He says Simile is already seeing early signs of a scaling law in simulation: the more data about people and the more compute it takes in, the more predictable the gain in simulated-person performance. But be clear about what the scale is for. Today they collect data on tens of thousands of people a week, and panel partnerships reach tens of millions of people worldwide, while actual deployments use only tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand, because what customers want is not stronger statistical significance but the ability to sieve out the subpopulation they care about. And the same person can be reused across every subsequent study, because the model is domain-agnostic: what it learns is that person's social physics, and traits such as risk preference do not change over time in the first place. Looking forward, he judges that within some years there will be simulations that cost as much to build as training a foundation model; if a single simulation could solve climate change, he would go raise that money today.

### verbatim quotes

[9:50] Joon Sung Park: "I don’t think the models that are out in the open have yet learned the complete mapping of social physics of humanity. … it has yet to learn the really deep behavioral nature of people, not just what people say they do online, but what they do in real life."

[28:24] Joon Sung Park: "Simile doesn’t care about any of this. The models that we’re talking about here, what we’re trying to create are models that are as dumb as I am, right? So if I make some mistakes, the model has to make the same mistake."

[40:04] Joon Sung Park: "The thing that we’re seeing is the early glimpse of scaling law in simulations. The more data about humans and more compute you ingest, you start to get predictive and predictable gains of the model performance in simulating it, simulating people."

[48:35] Joon Sung Park: "I do think in the next some number of years, we will start creating simulations that will cost as much as training a foundation model. But perhaps it’s going to be so valuable to the society that it would be a no-brainer."

[55:01] Joon Sung Park: "So market research is a $100 billion industry. … But the thing about simulation is not a tool for market research. Simulation is a tool for human decision-making."

### figures

- Google Scholar citations of the generative agents (Smallville) paper: 7,200 [1:46]
- Accuracy of digital twins replicating a person's behavior and attitudes (denominator: the person replicating themselves): 85% [26:02]
- Data collection and follow-up design of the 1000-person study: 2 hours of data collection per person; full battery of tests at a follow-up 2 weeks later [26:02]
- Frontier models' behavioral prediction accuracy on niche populations and topics customers care about: 20–30% [28:24]
- Frontier models' behavioral prediction accuracy on gen pop: 50–60% [28:24]
- Number of people Simile newly collects data on each week / panel partnership reach: tens of thousands of people per week; panels reach tens of millions of people worldwide [45:31]
- Size of the market research industry: $100 billion [55:01]
- Simile team size and number of co-founders: about 60 people, 4 co-founders [1:05:16]

### glossary

- social physics: The underlying regularities that govern how a population behaves; a model lacking it must be trained, and a model that has it only needs a prompt.
- attitudinal vs. behavioral: The line is whether the decision carries a real cost — it counts as behavior only if what you bought actually ships to your house.
- concept testing: A marketing-side practice: taking different messages, products or ideas out to test how a population reacts.
- synthetic panel: A model-generated pool of virtual respondents that can be queried over and over, standing in for a panel of real people.
- agent-based modeling: A method dating to Schelling in the 1970s: give each agent one simple rule, then watch what emerges at the group level.
- Open Science Framework pre-registration: Publishing hypotheses before running the experiment so they cannot be changed after the fact; it has accumulated tens of thousands of high-quality RCTs.

who it is for: People building consumer products, doing growth, or running user research; investors in the AI application layer looking for a non-coding post-training route; engineers who care about the cost structure of multi-agent simulation.
what to skip: 58:27–1:03:03, small talk about painting and life philosophy; no added judgment.
tags: Simulation, Post-training, Behavioral data, Synthetic panels, Scaling law, Market research

## Being Itself Has No Content: Peirce Overturns Substance-Centrism in Nine Pages

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-21-pel-peirce的范畴论-存在无内容-实体是当下的它/
- show: The Partially Examined Life (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/pel/)
- original episode: PEL Presents Closereads: Peirce's New Categories (Part One)
- published: 2026-08-21 · duration: 1:01:06
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9857 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 2 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In a nine-page paper from 1868, Peirce takes ‘a concept must be able to unify the content of consciousness’ as his test, deriving being from substance and then the intermediate categories such as quality. Being itself has no content; it only connects a predicate to a subject.**

why listen: This episode reads Peirce's most compressed 9 pages line by line, checking it against Kant and Aristotle throughout. Once you have precision and ground, you can see how he turns the transcendental deduction into a method for deriving categories.

### points

[4:04] **A concept earns its place only if nothing works without it** — Peirce states it at the outset: the function of a concept is ‘to reduce the manifold of sense impressions to unity’, and a concept is valid if and only if the content of consciousness cannot be unified without introducing it. This is a reworking of Kant's transcendental deduction — not a complete table read off from transcendental logic, but a test run backwards: ‘it cannot be done without this’. Wes points out that Peirce, unlike Aristotle, never announces outright that he is doing metaphysics; he enters through a much shorter introduction, so reading him means supplying the systematic intention yourself.

[10:00] **Substance is not a natural kind, only an unsayable ‘it’** — The first universal conception is ‘present in general’ — that is, ‘it’. It stands closest to sensation but carries no content, no predicates whatsoever, only the mind's pure capacity to point. Peirce gives it a philosophical name, one sense of substance: substance cannot be made the predicate of anything, and cannot be in a subject. Unlike Aristotle, who takes substance to be a natural kind, substance here is the ‘given’ before any cutting up has occurred, the X in the stream of perception that can be indicated but never said.

[23:25] **Being carries no content; it only fastens the predicate to the subject** — The unity of a proposition comes from the connection of predicate to subject, and the being expressed by the copula ‘is’ is precisely the element that completes that connection. Peirce says the conception of being ‘plainly has no content’ — it contains only the connectibility of a predicate to a subject, what the two kinds of verb (is in fact / would be) have in common. Substance and being thus form the two ends: substance supplies no unity at all, being does all the work of unification. Further categories are still needed in between to fill the space.

[31:26] **Color can be prescinded from space, but never space from color** — Peirce redefines three kinds of mental separation: discrimination only draws a line at the level of meaning; dissociation pulls two images apart when the association between them is absent; precision sits between the two, attending to one element without supposing that the other actually exists. Then comes the crucial break in symmetry: color can be prescinded from space, but space cannot be prescinded from color, and red cannot be prescinded from color. This directionality is the leverage for the derivation of the categories that follows.

[44:19] **Categories come from the direction of abstraction, not from a list** — Peirce turns the asymmetry of precision into method: to find a universal conception lying between substance and being, ask whether a given conception reduces a manifold to unity, or connects an already unified object to another conception. The element that is prescinded can be thought before the conception, while the conception can be thought apart from the element. Working in that direction he derives three intermediate categories — quality, relation, representation — as the couplings between substance and being.

[49:10] **A property is not an accident of substance but a prior abstraction** — Quality is the first intermediate category on the way from being back toward substance. The example ‘stove is black’ shows what the move requires: to make this proposition you must first detach ‘black’ from the stove itself and grasp it as an independent quality. Black is a pure abstraction, and applying it to the stove is hypothetical and fallible. Peirce uses this to insist that a property is not an accident inhering in a substance, but an abstract term that has to be separated out in advance.

[58:12] **A quality need not exist, but being cannot do without quality** — Peirce names this pure abstraction the ground: when two things agree in some respect, that respect is the pure abstraction we use to compare them, such as black. The crucial asymmetry is this: the ground cannot be prescinded from being — being cannot do without a determinate quality; but being can be prescinded from the ground — a given quality need not exist. The ground therefore both connects substance and being and serves as the formal expression of quality.

### verbatim quotes

[4:04] : "This paper is based upon the theory already established that the function of conceptions is to reduce the manifold of sensuous impressions to unity.And that the validity of conception consists in the impossibility of reducing the content of consciousness to unity.Without the introduction of it."

[23:25] : "The conception of being, therefore, plainly has no content."

### figures

- Length of the paper: 9 pages [0:00]
- Year written: 1868 [2:02]
- Related episode number: Episode 396 [3:03]

### glossary

- manifold: The multiplicity of sense impressions; in Kant, the manifold content that is given to the mind.
- precision: Peirce's own term for the kind of abstraction that attends to one part of an object without supposing another part; it runs in one direction only.
- ground: Peirce's name for the pure abstract quality a predicate stands for, such as black, which serves as the respect in which objects agree.
- copula: The word ‘is’, which joins subject and predicate.
- substance: As Peirce uses it here, the ‘present it’ closest to perception: a pure object of indication with no content.

who it is for: Philosophy readers who want to see how Peirce rebuilds the categories out of an argument from unity, and anyone who likes analyzing conceptual systems by holding them against Kant and Aristotle.
what to skip: The ad and subscription reminder at 3:03-4:04 can be skipped.
tags: Philosophy, Categories, Peirce, Transcendental Deduction, Abstraction, Unity
