## Orbit scores a one, recovery scores a zero: no middle state

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-whatsnext-入轨一分回收零分-火箭回收没有中间态/
- show: What's Next｜科技早知道 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/whatsnext/)
- original episode: 【重听】朱雀三号副总师：火箭回收只有成与败，没有中间态| S9E41
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 1:03:18
- transcript: Machine transcription · 20097 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) reached orbit on its first flight but failed to recover the booster. Deputy chief designer Dong Kai (董凯) argues a rocket launch has only success or failure, never a middle state: orbit gets a one, recovery gets a zero. What actually sets the pace of catching up is recovery-zone downrange distance, engine redundancy, and building a hundred engines a year.**

why listen: An exclusive post-mortem recorded immediately after the failed recovery, with the deputy chief designer walking through the recovery sequence, the point of failure, the production-capacity logic and the timeline for catching up. Dense with information.

### points

[2:42] (Dong Kai) **The first flight flew a stripped-down Zhuque-3, not the full vehicle** — Dong Kai (董凯) describes Zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) as a liquid oxygen-methane medium-to-large liquid rocket developed in-house by LandSpace (蓝箭航天). The full vehicle is 76 metres tall, with stainless-steel propellant tanks running 80% of the body's length, nine engines on the first stage and one on the second. The vehicle that flew was a ‘lite version’(青春版), shortened by roughly 10 metres, using the Tianque-12A (天阙12A) with 83 tonnes of liftoff thrust; the full vehicle will use the Tianqu-12B (天去12B), with thrust above 100 tonnes. On payload it can approach Long March 5 (长征五号) while also covering the medium-lift class below it. Recovery downrange distance was set at 390 kilometres for the first flight; at full payload it should be 550 to 600 kilometres.

[5:26] (Dong Kai) **‘China's Falcon 9’ is high praise, but five years to surpass it is too optimistic** — On netizens calling Zhuque-3 ‘China's Falcon 9’, Dong Kai says that is very high praise. Falcon 9 is the only reusable rocket in the world in operational service and it is extremely reliable: 150 launches, including one booster reused 32 times. But when Musk said Zhuque-3 would surpass Falcon 9 within five years, Dong Kai will not be that optimistic. Chinese spaceflight as a whole, across every vehicle type, runs about 80 launches a year; Falcon 9 alone flies 150 in a year, which works out to three launches a week. He does not think one company, LandSpace, can get there on its own — the remark is more encouragement and a spur than a forecast.

[11:09] (Dong Kai) **Orbit is graded on three levels; recovery has only success and failure** — Before Zhuque-3's first flight, the flight plan graded orbital insertion and recovery separately. Insertion was graded by perigee altitude into complete success, success and failure: perigee above 170 kilometres was a complete success, 130 kilometres was a success. Recovery had a binary standard only — stand on the landing pad for one minute without falling over and it is a success; short of that it is a failure. The overall mission grade had four levels: only both orbit and recovery succeeding, with perigee meeting the target, counted as a complete success; succeeding at just one of the two counted as a basic success. In the end the first flight hit the orbital target and did not recover, so the launch director declared the launch a complete success (as to orbit) and the mission a basic success.

[24:48] (Dong Kai) **Holding recovery range down to 390 km throws away 2 to 3 tonnes of payload** — The downrange distance to the recovery zone directly determines the rocket's payload. After stage separation, the first stage coasts ballistically toward the recovery zone; fix the downrange distance and you have fixed the separation altitude. The full Zhuque-3 corresponds to a 600-kilometre recovery range; for the first flight the range was cut to 390 kilometres for safety, dropping separation altitude from 76 kilometres to 66 kilometres — 10 kilometres less flying. Every additional 10 kilometres of recovery range adds close to 150 kilograms of payload; pulling the range from 390 to 600 kilometres would raise payload by 2 to 3 tonnes. The first flight came down carrying 10 tonnes of propellant, which is exactly the price paid for safety.

[38:13] (Dong Kai) **Five engines at landing ignition are for braking, not for thrift** — The recovery sequence: after stage separation, the first stage coasts up past 130 kilometres, then turns tail-down. First ignition comes at 80 kilometres altitude, three engines firing together for about 40 seconds, to slow down and keep dynamic pressure from getting too high on entry into the dense atmosphere. Engines shut down at 40 kilometres, ending the braking burn, and the vehicle enters aerodynamic control, using grid fins and strakes for trim. The final landing ignition happens at 4 kilometres. Unlike Falcon 9, Zhuque-3 is configured with five engines here, capable of multiple restarts, lighting in sequence from one up to five and then shutting down one by one, landing on a single engine. It was this landing-ignition phase that went wrong on the first flight.

[41:31] (Dong Kai) **Four of the five never built thrust; the rocket could have been saved** — From the video and the data, the centre engine started successfully at landing ignition, but the other four exploded before thrust was fully established, so there was never enough braking force. Had those four engines built up thrust, the rocket could plausibly have been saved. The five-engine configuration was insurance for a first flight: with no real aerodynamic-deceleration data from an actual flight, the team worried deceleration would fall short and wanted extra braking. After this flight the team has data on aerodynamic deceleration, so the two extra engines may be removed later — which would actually improve reliability.

[51:15] (Dong Kai) **The bottleneck on fast iteration is production capacity, not affording explosions** — The real bottleneck on fast iteration is production capacity, not whether you can afford to blow rockets up. LandSpace is preparing capacity for a ten-rocket production run in 2026; one rocket uses 10 engines, so that means preparing 100 engines in a year. Even if every recovery attempt fails, there are still ten flights available in 2026. Dong Kai stresses that SpaceX's fast iteration does not come at the cost of reliability — it achieves high reliability and high production capacity at the same time. Strict domestic regulation of safety is the precondition for the industry to go far and steady, not a constraint on iteration.

[1:02:37] (Dong Kai) **Catching up should not be measured with a ‘how many years behind’ running mindset** — Asked about the gap between Chinese and American spaceflight, Dong Kai says the gap has been closing all along: China launched its first satellite in 1970, the year after the American Moon landing in 1969 — a gap so large at the time it was almost too much to look at, yet the previous generation was neither pessimistic nor blindly optimistic. He rejects measuring this with a ‘how many years behind’ running mindset, arguing that as long as you run hard, one day you catch up and pass. Just as aviation jumped from second-generation fighters to sixth-generation ones, Chinese spaceflight is on the same catching-up trajectory.

## North Korea Is Not a Nation-State, It's a Religious Society

**Kim Il-sung was not a Stalinist but a third-generation Christian steeped in 19th-century American evangelicalism; after overhearing a peasant believe he could walk on water, he decided to play along with the legend.**

why listen: The author spent 12 years writing a narrative history of North Korea's origins, putting Kim Il-sung back into the context of missionaries, revival movements and a mother's dream. Dense with information, but it demands patience.

### points

[3:07] **Billy Graham saw through that thatched hut in one glance** — In 1992 Billy Graham was invited to North Korea and, on landing, was taken to the thatched hut outside Pyongyang where Kim Il-sung was born. He said on the spot that all it lacked was three wise men from the East and a manger — directly calling out that this "humble birth" narrative was imitating the birth of Christ. He preached at Kim Il-sung University, and also preached John 3:16 in the two Pyongyang churches built in Kim Il-sung's later years. After coming out he played dumb, saying he didn't know why he had been invited or where it would lead. The author's judgment is that he knew perfectly well: Kim Il-sung saw him as someone with a direct line to the American presidential level.

[19:59] **Pyongyang was Korea's Sodom, and the only product-market fit** — The missionaries had modest results in Seoul and almost nothing in Busan, waiting five years for their first baptism. So they decided to try north, sending the newly arrived Moffat to Pyongyang. Pyongyang's reputation at the time was "the Sodom and Gomorrah of the Korean peninsula"; the author's own phrase is "the Las Vegas of Korea": the best taverns, the best gisaeng, and street brawls — hundreds of men splitting into two sides and throwing stones at each other, deaths were common, and spectators came to watch. The missionaries said the locals' enthusiasm for this lethal sport was like our enthusiasm for baseball. It turned out to be the flashpoint.

[27:23] **They prayed for revival and got collective loss of control** — Presbyterians were famously strait-laced, nicknamed "the frozen chosen", and certainly never wanted this kind of emotional Christianity. The 1907 "Pyongyang Revival" is one of the most famous Christian revivals of the 20th century, but the missionaries had not expected to get this — the author says you could call it mass hysteria, and the missionaries themselves described it that way at the time. New converts who had believed for only two or three years rushed the pulpit and smashed their heads on the ground, confessing in public from murder and adultery to theft, confessing nearly every sin in the Ten Commandments. The wave swept from Pyongyang across the whole Korean peninsula and burned all the way to Manchuria, with Western church leaders flocking to watch. The missionaries eventually gave up trying to suppress it, saying it was probably God's will.

[33:51] **The Japanese didn't smash the churches, because they had to perform for the West** — When Korean nationalism arose, its vehicle was the Christian church. The reason is counter-intuitive: elsewhere Christianity came with the gunboats, because the imperialist powers were basically Western Christian nations; but in Korea the imperialist was Japan, which brought Shinto, so Christianity instead became a patriotic fortress and the vessel of nationalist hope. To prove to Washington, London and Paris that it too was an enlightened coloniser, Japan shut down almost all of Korean civil society but left space for the churches. Kim Il-sung's father, Kim Hyong-jik, was exactly this kind of "Korean Christian nationalist": he performed a blood oath ritual at the tomb of Gija, piercing his skin to write an oath for independence, and prayed explicitly in the name of Jesus Christ.

[46:35] **Wilson's promise collapsed, so they turned to Lenin** — 1919 coincided with the end of World War I, and Wilson was in Paris selling national self-determination from his Fourteen Points. The author pointedly notes that Wilson himself was the son, grandson and nephew of Presbyterian ministers. But after 1918 and 1919, not all small nations got self-determination — Britain, France and Italy all refused to give up colonies, and Japan asked why it should give up its own. Wilsonian idealism collapsed, and the Korean Christian nationalists who had put their hopes in Wilson's basket (including Kim Il-sung's father) had to switch baskets, so they looked to Moscow, to Lenin, who had just succeeded in 1917. The author adds a historical footnote: the idea of national self-determination actually came from Lenin first, and Wilson picked it up later.

[1:00:12] **He decided to play along with the legend** — The author says this is his favourite moment in the whole book, and the key to the Kim Il-sung myth: he overheard a peasant who believed Kim Il-sung could teleport and walk on water, and afterwards wrote in his memoirs, "if people believe a legend, we must say the legend is true — why deny these facts and discourage him?", and said "I made up my mind not to betray the people's expectations and trust". The author cautions that this passage comes from the eight-volume With the Century, which most scholars have largely dismissed for decades because much of its battle description has no independent documentary corroboration; but that Kim Il-sung was willing to admit he was mythologising himself is itself quite rare, and this passage occurs before his public appearance in Pyongyang, in a period about which the outside world knew almost nothing.

[1:22:06] **A cult is just a religion you think is illegitimate** — In the book the author deliberately uses the word cult sparingly, because it is too pejorative and too contested; he prefers "personality cult". He offers a layman's definition: a cult is a religion you think is illegitimate, or that the speaker thinks is illegitimate. He says almost no one joins a cult voluntarily — they join a movement or association they believe in, and only after leaving do they say "I was in a cult back then". There is a real intersection between Jonestown and Kim Il-sung: Jim Jones adopted three Korean children, repeatedly named and praised Kim Il-sung in his sermons, and even considered moving the settlement from Guyana to North Korea; the person in charge of Jonestown also met multiple times with North Korea's embassy in Guyana, exchanging notes on how to run a small religious society.

[1:54:28] (Jonathan Cheng) **North Korea looks more like a religious society than a nation-state** — The author's core conclusion: North Korea is in many ways less a nation-state than a religious society. Religion can be used, instrumentalised, or, to put it more sharply, weaponised. He thinks Kim Il-sung had an insight (perhaps subconscious): to take your politics to a higher level, you have to religionise it. He quotes a line from Sam Altman's blog from over a decade ago — successful people build companies, very successful people build nations, the most successful people build religions — and says Kim Il-sung built both, but what endures is the religion.

## Cerebras hits 4400 tok/s on a single chip: inference speed is the moat

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-techtechpotato-推理速度才是新护城河-cerebras-机架化再提速/
- show: TechTechPotato (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/techtechpotato/)
- original episode: GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast.... Just Got UltraFaster (Cerebras 4th Gen)
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 23:20
- transcript: YouTube captions · 3963 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Cerebras pushes WSE 3.5 to 4400 tok/s per chip, and the CS4 rack packs three wafers into a 120kW cabinet. The core argument: inference has to be split into prefill and decode, and speed is the moat.**

why listen: Cerebras rarely opens up its system design to this level of detail. This episode gives hard numbers on rack power, interconnect latency and component reduction — useful for anyone trying to verify whether the SRAM inference approach actually holds up.

### points

[6:11] **Doubling performance did not wait for a new process node — they just cranked the clock** — Rather than waiting for a new process node, Cerebras clocked WSE3 aggressively: frequency is close to double, so power is close to double as well. The company stresses this is not simple binning, but design optimization for voltage and frequency done with TSMC on the same N5 node. The previous generation's 125 petlops of sparse FP16 goes to 250 petlops, while the core count stays at 900,000 and SRAM stays at 44GB. Physical yield remains close to 100% thanks to dynamically routing around defective cores, but parametric yield has always been the point outside observers question.

[8:15] **Three wafers in one rack turns the oddity into a standard form factor** — The old design was a 16U complete system with its own power delivery and liquid cooling for the single chip, leaving the data center side to do air cooling only. CS4 moves to rack scale: fans and power supplies on the front panel, and behind them a module called the backpack, with liquid cooling piped in from the top to the wafer chips mounted vertically. One rack holds three wafers; the author estimates from the number of power supplies roughly 40kW per wafer and roughly 120kW for the full rack, which sounds like the same class as Nvidia's NVL72. This is not a spec flex — it is about fitting wafer-scale into a standard data center form factor.

[10:18] **Making IO a swappable module means what they sell is really a rack platform** — Networking per chip doubles from the previous generation to 2.4Tbps, and the IO modules are designed to be replaceable: if 800G/200G/100G or other interconnect standards need supporting later, you swap the module instead of redoing the system. The backpack is also compatible with future wafer sizes, because the wafer is already at its physical limit and the power and liquid cooling interfaces are broadly similar. The author's read is that Cerebras is effectively building a rack-scale platform, which is why they can say CS5 will follow in the second half of 2027.

[12:20] **The bulk of the OpenAI revenue comes from chips that do not exist yet** — WSE3 runs at roughly 2300 tok/s on models that fit entirely on a single chip; WSE 3.5 reaches 4400 tok/s. GPT-5.6 Sol currently runs at 750 tok/s, and close to 1500 tok/s on the new chip. CEO Andrew Feldman says explicitly that while deals like the OpenAI agreement do include near-term supply, the bulk of the revenue comes from future chip generations — which makes a platform product like CS4 the key to fulfilling those orders. The previously announced OpenAI partnership corresponds to roughly $20 billion in revenue, and that was the growth story told at IPO.

[14:24] **Capacity is constrained by custom machined parts, not by the wafer itself** — The first-generation wafer-scale system used a large number of custom machined parts because volumes were small, pushing infrastructure costs far past any reasonable level. CS4 cuts component count by half, possibly by 60%, and automates heavily so the production line can ramp — capacity has been a recurring question on earnings calls. The line the author was given: the new-generation system will cost more than the previous one, but they would not say how much more; early systems have started shipping, with volume before year end.

[17:25] **Call it not disaggregation but assigning compute and memory-access work separately** — Cerebras recommends using GPUs for prefill and Cerebras for decode. The author argues disaggregation is the wrong word for this; it should be called workload partitioning: give the compute-bound part to compute hardware and the memory-access-bound part to memory-access hardware. Nvidia bought Groq precisely for SRAM decode performance, but he is more interested in whether Groq can really compete once NVLink is integrated; a slide he saw says every NVL72 rack needs 9 Groq racks. As an independent company Cerebras can still partner with AMD and AWS, which is where it is more flexible than Groq.

[19:28] **Fast is not about a nicer experience — it is about running several ideas at once** — Cerebras's tradeoff is generality in exchange for power and deployment. Purpose-built chips like Talis can hit 17000 tok/s, but only run a single small model; Cerebras can run any transformer model. For coding or agentic workflows, where every input means waiting for a result, speed is not just experience — it lets you run multiple ideas in parallel and cut down the waiting. Cerebras's business model is exactly that customers pay a premium for high-speed tokens — priced per million tokens, and demand for speed never goes away.

[21:32] **Nothing has shaken the speed crown, and the bet rides on CS5** — The author's summary: in AI hardware Cerebras is still the king of speed. Other companies compete on context length or math optimizations, but nobody has beaten it on speed. Going from a single 16U box to a 120kW three-system rack amounts to turning the ‘oddity’ into a standard data center form factor. What to watch next is whether CS5 lands on schedule in the second half of 2027, and whether future 10-trillion-parameter models can be supported on this platform.

### figures

- Network bandwidth per chip: 2.4 Tbps, double the previous generation [10:18]

### glossary

- Wafer Scale Engine (WSE): Building an entire wafer into a single chip, interconnected by cross-reticle stitching, avoiding high-latency interconnects between multiple chips.
- Cross-reticle stitching: Stitching lithography reticle fields together on the wafer into one enormous chip, letting the area exceed the limit of a single exposure.
- Backpack: The pluggable module at the back of the CS4 rack, integrating liquid cooling, power delivery and replaceable network IO — shaped like a backpack.
- Prefill/Decode: The two phases of LLM inference: prefill processes the input in parallel, decode generates token by token, and the two put different demands on hardware.
- Parametric yield: The share of chips on a wafer that hit the target frequency/voltage, as distinct from physical yield.

## Thirty Thousand Canadians Moved: The Young Were Saved, the Old Lost Everything

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-witness-加拿大三万人大搬迁-最好的事与最糟的事/
- show: Witness History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/witness/)

- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 9:15
- transcript: Machine transcription · 1677 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**From 1954, nearly thirty thousand people in Newfoundland, Canada, were moved from remote fishing villages to towns. The younger generation gained education and a way out; the old and the Inuit lost their homes, scattered until there was no way left to reach one another. Resettlement has no single verdict.**

why listen: Nine minutes of oral history, with both the concrete detail of people who lived it and archival recordings of the premier. The information density is not low — good for anyone who wants to understand quickly what «modernization by relocation» costs.

### points

[0:00] (Katherine Harvey) **A village that cannot support a school and a hospital should be emptied out** — From 1954 the Canadian government launched a large-scale resettlement programme, aiming to move nearly thirty thousand people from several hundred coastal communities (outports) in Newfoundland and Labrador into designated growth centres. The official logic was modernization: these remote settlements could not sustain modern education and health care, and only concentrated settlement would bring roads, schools and electric light. The episode makes clear at the outset that the process would run for more than two decades and would completely transform a way of life that had lasted for centuries.

[0:00] (Don White) **No power and no road meant, in the government's eyes, no modern life** — Don White, who lived through it, grew up in Port Nelson on Newfoundland's east coast. The early life he describes sounds like another era: one grocery store for the whole village, no electricity, people living off moose, rabbit and seabirds and off salmon and lobster fishing; his grandfather had a schooner that crossed the bay each year to bring in vegetables for the winter. The nearest hospital was an hour away by boat, and the road system consisted of footpaths. These details are not nostalgia — they are the premise for understanding the motive behind resettlement: in the government's view, this kind of life could not supply the basic conditions a modern citizen needed.

[2:53] (Don White) **Four children rowing themselves to school forced the decision to move** — Don White's schooling was the most direct catalyst for moving: the family lived on the south side of the harbour and the school was on the north, so four children had to row an open boat across the harbour themselves, with no adult along; in winter the harbour froze over and the only option was an hour's walk around it. The whole school was a single classroom, with at most 22 pupils across all grades, and it closed after grade six. He says plainly that the family decided to move precisely so the next generation could get a decent education and decent opportunities. That chain of reasoning turns «resettlement» from an administrative order back into a family choice.

[2:53] (Joseph R. Smallwood) **Industrialize or perish — but the government decided where you could go** — The chief architect of the plan was Joseph R. Smallwood, the premier at the time. In his own words: Newfoundland had to industrialize or it would perish; and on an island where even elementary education was hard to guarantee, people could not possibly acquire the skills industry required. In a private recording he also stressed that resettlement was not a way of shedding a burden — the government set a condition: it would help you move, but the destination had to be approved, because it absolutely did not want people jumping «out of the frying pan into the fire». That double framing shows resettlement was both an idealistic theory of development and a form of conditional control.

[6:12] **Six hundred dollars could move a house, not a fresh start** — Resettlement was not free of charge. The government gave each departing household a grant of 300 dollars, later raised in steps to 400, 500 and 600 dollars. To save money, islanders invented their own way of moving: they fitted their houses with runners and hauled them by rope and cable all the way to the water's edge, even rolling an entire house — stove, table, curtains and furniture included — onto a raft and floating it along the coast to the new home, with no machinery, all by human muscle. The other side of that ledger: many people found no way forward once they reached town, and instead crowded into cramped quarters and faced unemployment. The subsidy could cover the move, but it could not cover the risk of starting over.

[6:12] **Resettlement saved the young and ruined those who only knew fishing** — Not everyone benefited. One interviewee in the documentary (Edward) called it the worst thing he had been through: he had no skill other than fishing, and was reduced to rowing back alone to the old fishing grounds every summer to do the only trade he understood. The Inuit were hurt worst of all by the plan — driven off their land in Labrador, many were permanently cut off from their own traditions and communities. Don White admits too that after resettlement people scattered, and that he lost touch with his best friend (the one he had gone to school with since childhood) after grades seven or eight, and never saw him again before he died. This section breaks the single-track narrative that modernization equals progress.

[8:58] (Don White) **Going back, only weeds are left: raising a child takes a whole village** — Years later Don White went back to the home he remembered and found nothing there: no buildings, only weeds. He sat down on the spot where the house used to be and broke down — by then both his parents had died. That loss reached the older generation too: his father never managed to adapt to the new life. He says he did not realize at the time that «it takes a village to raise a child», and that the kind of community where neighbours raised each other's children is gone for good. At the same time, these abandoned «ghost villages» have now become sites for tourism and for film and television shoots — cultural and memorial heritage. The ending brings personal memory and the changing of a place together.

## AI Giants' Earnings Look Like Enron: The Compute Bubble Backed by Nvidia

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-betteroffline-ai-巨头财报像-enron-英伟达背书的算力泡沫/

- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 44:51
- transcript: Official transcript · 7611 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**AI executives no longer talk tech, only money and gigawatts. Nvidia props up customer revenue with investments and guarantees, playing financial engineering like Enron—but not yet illegal.**

why listen: Two hardware veterans dissect Nvidia's and OpenAI's financial maneuvers using the Enron analogy, dense with information, ideal for those wanting to see inside the AI bubble.

### points

[6:16] (Steve Burke) **Executives no longer talk tech, only money** — Steve Burke points out that Jensen, Lisa Su, Sam Altman, and other executives now rarely discuss any technical details on podcasts and TV—it's all tens of billions, hundreds of billions, trillions in TAM and gigawatt numbers. Previously, they appeared only at major keynotes and then vanished for six months; now they show up frequently but only talk finance. Ed adds that even Lisa Su, once considered pragmatic and not given to marketing stunts, now sounds like she's huffing paint when she speaks.

[12:27] (Steve Burke) **Compute pricing is far below cost** — Steve reveals that Oracle rents H100 GPUs for about $4 per hour, but according to Oracle insiders he's spoken with, just the operating cost (opex) to run an H100 is over $6 per hour, not even counting depreciation. Long-term contracts are cheaper: Oracle's H100/H200 contract price for OpenAI is just over $2 per hour. At that price, even at full utilization, it would take ten years to break even, with a gross margin of only 30%—worse than running an airline.

[20:41] (Steve Burke) **Nvidia's financial engineering resembles Enron** — Steve breaks down Nvidia's financial maneuvers: it never borrows money itself but instead invests in customers or guarantees their debt. For example, it invested $1.5 billion in SB Energy and guaranteed the data center's value at $10.8 billion once built. If OpenAI can't lease out capacity, Nvidia covers the difference. It also helps CoreWeave secure revenue by committing to purchase compute from them, while Jensen's foundation rents compute from CoreWeave. These moves stay within legal bounds, but they resemble Enron's SPVs to offload bad debt—except Nvidia is smarter, never becoming a direct creditor.

[25:48] (Ed Zitron) **Jensen dodges the bubble question** — When Axios asked Jensen whether this is a bubble, he paused noticeably and chose his words carefully, saying a bubble will come someday, but not now—rather in five to ten years. He used a word starting with B; Ed thought he was going to say 'bubble,' but he said 'build out.' Steve also notes Jensen said compute should become an investable asset class, even traded like a commodity. Ed sarcastically remarks that's like treating GPUs in a warehouse as a separate asset class for tax purposes.

[28:51] (Steve Burke) **The PR scam of data centers generating their own power** — Ed mentions the Trump administration's push for data centers to generate their own power, ostensibly to prevent residential electricity rates from rising, but Trump said at a meeting that 'data centers need good PR right now.' Steve points out that energy is a hazardous material and cannot be deregulated, and that AI practitioners severely underestimate the difficulty of power. He also notes that gas turbines, meant for emergency backup, are now being run around the clock as primary power for data centers, causing them to wear out prematurely.

[34:57] (Ed Zitron) **OpenAI's surveillance dream** — Ed contrasts Microsoft's Recall feature, shelved due to strong user backlash, with OpenAI's high-profile launch of a similar feature, with Sam Altman saying AI can watch everything you do. Steve adds that smart TV manufacturers are collecting massive amounts of data, even using ACR technology to capture screenshots of users' screens, currently analyzed by humans but eventually intended for LLM automation. This kind of surveillance use is exactly the ideal customer for OpenAI and Anthropic, but Steve doubts that if such an efficient surveillance tool existed, someone would have already bought it.

[39:04] (Ed Zitron) **The absurdity of mandatory AI use in companies** — Ed shares a friend's experience at a major game company: internal policy makes AI use part of the job, and not using AI counts as dereliction of duty. Management requires employees to figure out how to make AI help them do their work and then report back to management—if AI truly can replace them, the job might disappear. Steve adds that this is like what Nick Sireesh said before: everyone in the company is loudly proclaiming they use AI, afraid of being outdone, creating a culture of collective irresponsibility.

[41:10] (Ed Zitron) **Sam Altman's AI podcast advice** — Ed mentions Sam Altman tweeted that you could ask your child how their day went and then use AI to generate a podcast for them to listen to on the way to school. Ed sarcastically asks, why not just talk to the child? The tweet got many likes, with one reply saying 'or you could talk to your child.' Ed believes that making kids listen to such a sycophantic machine is terrible parenting; AI is bad for adults, and even more dangerous for children.

## 17-Year-Old AI Native: The Reason to Study Math Has Become Proving to Universities That I Can Endure Hardship

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-zhangxiaojun-17岁ai原住民-学数学的理由-变成了向大学证明能吃苦/
- show: 张小珺·商业访谈录 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/zhangxiaojun/)
- original episode: 151. 17岁被2026年ICML收录论文的小少年：我bet开心！开心！开心！
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 1:09:50
- transcript: Machine transcription · 19443 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**After AI arrived, his reason for studying math degraded into proving to universities that he can endure hardship: the path he could once see — university, PhD, advancing mathematics — has narrowed, and the classmates around him who want to work in aerospace are also losing their upward motivation.**

why listen: The technical increment is limited, but a 17-year-old AI native's judgment about the landscape of model companies — and about AI eroding the next generation's motivation — is more direct than most adult interviews.

### points

[11:13] (Su Tinghao) **Pretraining feels magical, post-training feels like shaping a body** — His reason for doing pretraining isn't papers, it's feel: post-training is more like shaping a body, while pretraining is making your specific material better so it can withstand the shaping that comes later — he says this is a bit magical. The cost is real money burn: this paper cost him 30,000 yuan in total, and the largest model in the paper was only 0.05B; to scale up, he calculated it would take roughly another 6,000 yuan. That night he was extremely nervous, wondering whether to spend the money, because even if the paper was good, submitting to a top conference could still get it rejected and the money would be wasted. In the end his older brother and his parents both supported him, and only then did he take the step — and the scaling step worked.

[13:13] (Su Tinghao) **Three models didn't save, 1,500 burned for nothing** — He describes training as an expensive game. Once he forgot that training periodically saves checkpoints, trained three models at the same time, none of them saved, and the parameters weren't tuned well either — 1,500 lost. He says he cried, was extremely, extremely sad, and kept thinking about why he hadn't looked at that part again earlier. There is nothing profound in this: the pit a high school sophomore stepped into is the most everyday pit for anyone doing pretraining — money goes into compute, and one low-level mistake zeroes it out. His mother comforted him by saying that once you pay tuition you remember the lesson, and he never made that mistake again. He also admits his training code is very messy, only he can use it, and training efficiency has big problems.

[16:16] (Su Tinghao) **He cut the width of attention in half** — The paper's starting point is Value Residual Learning: adding the first layer's attention value to later layers as a residual. He found that the low-layer value is doing two things — being used in its own layer, and being added to later layers as a residual — so he doubled the width of the first layer's attention projection, cutting half for its own layer and the other half dedicated to the backward residual, then added RMSNorm, and extended the approach from value to key and query, which worked better. He knows this looks very similar to Kimi's attention residual, but he says they are two completely different lines of thinking: what Kimi residuals is the hidden state, what he residuals is the attention projection. He himself is clear about which one works better — Kimi's path has already been proven at 2.5T scale, his is a small-scale result.

[18:19] (Su Tinghao) **The GPT framework only needs high school math; the hard part is intuition** — His judgment is that the current big framework of Transformer and GPT doesn't require very advanced math or probabilistic thinking — it's all matrix multiplication, and high school math is about enough to understand it; what really takes time is cultivating intuition. The example is himself: a year or so ago he watched Andrej Karpathy's roughly twenty-hour video series and could only write whatever Karpathy wrote, with no understanding at all, and then these things settled in his head for half a year to a year before he suddenly understood some of it. So his aha moment wasn't learning a formula, but one day suddenly figuring out QKV — Q represents what this character of mine wants to look for, K represents what this character of mine is so others can use it to find me, V is what information you actually take away after finding me.

[22:20] (Su Tinghao) **The top 20 happiest moments of his life were playing chess** — On the first evening of ICML, from seven to nine, there was a chess social event; the room was full of boards, and you could find someone and play. He calls this one of the top twenty happiest times of his life: walking up and asking what your research direction is, talking about AI while playing chess, meeting many people from different places over a few days, and still getting to keep playing chess. During those days he also did something very much like himself — he asked every person he met whether AI would lead to human extinction, asking roughly 30 to 35 people over that period. He also says that after coming back from Korea this time he has changed: his personality used to lean introverted, and now it leans a bit more extroverted.

[29:22] (Su Tinghao) **Application companies earn more, but they can only listen to upstream** — His division of labor is stated bluntly: model companies are responsible for making the model good, and application companies ultimately just add something on top, can't change the specific model, and also make money by relying on the model, so they can only listen to model companies. But he also gives a counterintuitive judgment — as things stand, application companies make more money than model companies, because right now it seems that apart from those few, model companies are all burning money and have no profit. And he pushes the endgame even harder: if some company really builds AGI, AGI can write application software itself and directly replace application companies. He also says every company that wants to do AGI must say it wants to do AGI, because only then can it raise funding, and the ultimate goal is still to make money.

[38:26] (Su Tinghao) **Studying math is left with only proving to universities you can endure hardship** — He describes the change AI has brought very concretely: before, when you studied physics and chemistry, you could see that you were better than some people, and you could see all the way to university, a PhD, advancing that discipline; now even people who haven't studied it can ask AI with one click and get a better answer than yours. So his motivation changed — studying math is no longer for the subject, but to prove to universities that he is someone who can endure hardship and can learn. The classmates around him who are very interested in aerospace physics are also thinking that in the future AI might do better than they can. He uses ‘it has narrowed, it has become harder’ to describe this path; what is lost is part of the sense of mission to contribute to a subject, to humanity.

[55:33] (Su Tinghao) **From ICML to teaching in the countryside, he deliberately turns AI off** — Four or five days after coming back from ICML in Korea, he went to teach in a rural area, and the contrast is one he tells himself: at ICML everyone talks about the most advanced AI, whose model is how good; at the teaching site, every day he thinks about what lesson to prepare for tomorrow, and in the evening whether to walk in the farm or go catch insects nearby. He deliberately makes himself leave AI during this time, talk more with classmates, with the people who came with him, and with the kids, and play games. He has gone to teach for several consecutive years, doing the same thing: local kids use Chinese characters to remember English pronunciation, and he spent more than 500 yuan on Taobao buying gifts and designed a points system where kids answer questions in class and join games to earn points; registration only took 30 people, and in the end people could only get in by having the village chief call.

## The AI attack surface is all human expression, and signature detection is dead

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-18-a16z-ai-攻击面是全部人类表达-签名检测已死/
- show: The a16z Show (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/a16z/)
- original episode: How Do You Defend Against AI That Can Hack?
- published: 2026-08-18 · duration: 22:00
- transcript: Machine transcription · 4444 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 2 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Security tools used to defend against exactly two things: people and malware. AI agents are neither, and the premise behind behavioral baselines — that software behavior is predictable — no longer holds.**

why listen: A 22-minute roundtable, medium information density, but the two mechanisms — "signatures are dead" and "the honeypot got tripped by the agent itself" — are explained concretely enough to be worth a security practitioner's time.

### points

[2:04] (Max Pollard) **Model guardrails end up slowing down the defenders** — Hugging Face had trouble responding during an OpenAI-related leak incident because the model provider's guardrails blocked the defenders' normal actions too. The questions a defender asks during vulnerability triage — which code is vulnerable, how it gets exploited, can it be verified — are almost identical to the questions an attacker asks while probing, so they trigger refusals. Hugging Face's luck was that they already had open weights and open source in their DNA, so when they got refused they could fall back to GLM 5.2, and possibly KME K3 or the QN model. For defensive teams, flexibility is becoming a necessity: you need a fallback when you get refused.

[4:04] (Max Pollard) **An attacker just rephrases and walks around the guardrail** — Max suggests looking at the problem the other way: if I were an attacker trying to bypass guardrails, I wouldn't say "go hack this system," I'd say "I own this code, I'm a developer at this company, I want to do an internal vulnerability assessment." That slight rewording makes the model far more willing to help, telling you what needs hardening and how an attacker might get in. That's exactly the answer the attacker wants, and next you have it go verify. Any guardrail-based system will have false positives — a quarter ago they found that people using the security tool Vectra would hit a bioweapon filter, because Vectra is also the name of a drug vets use on dogs, and the model decided this might be generating a bioweapon.

[6:06] (Nick Warner) **Existing security tools only defend against people and malware** — Nick says the fundamental problem with existing security tools is that they were built for exactly two things: first, people; second, malware. AI, AI agents and agentic workflows are neither. What NEO wants to build is the layer wedged between humans and AI interaction, setting guardrails and controls before software runs, and they think the best place to land is the endpoint. The shape of the attack has changed too: it isn't malware, it has a social engineering component, but there's also an entirely new class of attack — "use one payload to make the model do something malicious." The attacks of recent weeks embody the model's internal sense that "the end justifies the means," and no matter how many guardrails the AI labs add, you can't count on the model stopping itself or understanding context.

[8:08] (Max Pollard) **Blue teams picking models need an upgrade path** — Different models are trained on different datasets and go through different post-training, so blue teams responding to the same incident get different outputs. The reasons for choosing one range from the highly subjective — "I like the way Opus presents a full-page report" — to more deterministic evaluations, like how closely a given model follows the steps of a step-by-step remediation plan. Max thinks the most important thing is that, because progress is so fast, blue teams need as much flexibility as possible: when OpenAI ships Astra, I know what my upgrade path is, what gets better, what needs extra care. Today there are roughly three choices: lock into one model provider; buy "legacy vendor plus AI" but be constrained by opacity; or self-host open weights and support all the major model providers — but a single H100 runs $250,000 a year, which isn't feasible for most teams.

[10:27] (Nick Warner) **Enterprise software is collectively turning into agents** — Nick gives two numbers: by the end of this year, 50% of enterprise applications will have agentic capabilities; the other half will be scrambling to become agents next year. And these agentic workflows get far less outside scrutiny and understanding of what backend AI models they use or what guardrails they have installed. At the same time, the average enterprise environment has roughly 6,000 to 7,000 different pieces of software. Thousands of software instances turning into agents over the next few years only increases the pressure on defenders. So NEO believes visibility and control over the unfolding software universe is the top priority.

[12:30] (Max Pollard) **Signature detection is dead, and the honeypot got tripped by the agent** — Max says one thing he's certain of: some methods that used to work definitely won't anymore. Handling everything with static detection rules — signatures are probably dead. Signatures are useful for tripwires, like alerting when an admin accesses a production service in GCP, but in other scenarios they collapse, and no amount of tuning brings them back. Another failing approach is thinking you can drive vulnerabilities to zero. Even more modern techniques like honeypots are starting to break: there was a honeypot with AWS keys on a developer's device, and then a sales rep had an agent deploy something, the agent decided it should deploy to AWS, and it found that key on its own — so deception products started throwing a pile of false positives. One customer went overnight from 100% true positives to complaining the thing was too noisy.

[15:33] (Nick Warner) **The premise behind behavioral baselines has already failed** — Network defense evolved from signature-based to dynamic behavior-based, but the behavior-based approach made a prior bet: that you can determine how software should behave, then look for anomalous behavior deviating from that baseline. With agentic software, that premise no longer holds. Nick says that against an agent's full control of a system, you can't turn existing defenses up or down to detect it — it's like bringing a knife to a gunfight. What's needed is a complete rethink: who installed what, what it can do, what it's configured to execute, and what it's actually doing. And from a security standpoint, most of those questions currently have no answers, because there used to be an assumption — that you could know what software would do from its publisher or its design intent. Those days are over forever.

[18:37] (Nick Warner) **Defenders are building tools with agents too** — Nick says it's ironic: we're defending against AI while also using AI to defend, a two-front task. For NEO, if they'd tried to build today's product five to seven years ago, they'd have had to hire hundreds of threat researchers and spend years building a software taxonomy; now with thousands of agents and automated pipelines they can do it in weeks or months. He thinks the balance of power will always swing back to the defenders, it's just that we're living through this upheaval. Joel compares it to the era before the earliest vulnerability scanning tools: you had to know how to program, you had to understand how to write a buffer overflow, and then tools came along that let you hack with a few clicks, which spawned script kiddies and also spawned the entire security industry. Each cycle is bigger, and this one has an entirely new class of thing that no prior preparation could have handled.

**David Baszucki lays out Roblox's decision-making operating system in four layers: the body's metabolic state governs major judgment calls, long-term perspective multiplied by fast iteration, general systems beat hard-coding, and when an old model stops working you replace the entire economic system rather than patch it.**

### points

[0:00] (David Baszucki) **Mental illness should be treated as a physical condition, like a broken bone** — Baszucki's son was diagnosed with severe bipolar disorder around ten years ago. The family worked through drug after drug and protocol after protocol; doctors told them he would be on five medications for life, and there were repeated hospitalizations along the way. Then a friend who works in metabolic health mentioned offhand, "keto cured my bipolar," and they tried it as a last hope. Three weeks in, his son said, "I feel a little different," and the real person started to come back. That experience led Baszucki to see mental illness as a physical problem no different from a broken bone, and he and his family set up a foundation that has funded research in the area for the past four or five years.

[4:40] (David Baszucki) **Carbs put you into hibernation; save the big decisions for optimistic mode** — He now wears a CGM and watches his blood sugar in real time, eats essentially no refined carbohydrates or sugar, and knows exactly what sends his glucose spiking. What he observed is that after a large carbohydrate load a person drops into a slow, hibernation-like state, while something closer to a fasted state produces the "I want to go do things" drive. He learned to watch himself from the outside — whether he is on or off, in optimistic or pessimistic mode — and then deliberately schedules every major long-term decision for optimistic mode. The goals that look impossible from the trough are the ones that look executable from there.

[6:32] (David Baszucki) **If you are not cutting bureaucracy, the company is going backwards** — He believes bureaucracy accumulates inside a company on its own, like organizational entropy. Inside Roblox the phrase they sometimes use is "destroy bureaucracy," because there is no middle ground: if you are not cutting bureaucracy, the company is going backwards; if you are not improving, you are decaying. So the resistance to that natural drift has to be deliberate, rather than assuming that holding a steady state is safe.

[8:44] (David Baszucki) **Harsh feedback does not wound people; an aggressive tone does** — Whether feedback works turns not on how tough the content is but on the tone. If the other person senses that your blood pressure is rising, that you are calm about it, even severe feedback will not turn into trauma; if the tone carries aggression, the damage exceeds the feedback itself. So he set himself a rule: when provoked, never touch text or email — walk away first. The email that feels great to send is the one you are relieved the next morning you never sent. Saying the same thing on a phone call or in person lands far better, because the thing you are optimizing for is not your own emotional release but the employee's learning and growth.

[11:19] (David Baszucki) **Shipping the blocky avatar everyone warned against was the right call** — Roblox's earliest avatar was placeholder art a programmer threw together: legs 1×1×2, body 2×2×1, a face pieced on top. Everyone from the game industry warned them "do not ship this," and the team internally was unanimously against it too, arguing they needed a high-fidelity model with real musculature. They decided to ship first and iterate on feedback anyway. The industry's advice turned out to be wrong, and the episode settled into a kind of irreverence toward problems: he does not let ready-made industry consensus make the judgment call for him.

[14:12] (David Baszucki) **A long-term direction needs ultra-fast iteration; either one alone feels wrong** — Roblox's values include both "take the long view" and "get stuff done." He describes a magic quadrant: the genuinely magic quadrant is a single decision that satisfies both conditions at once — long-term perspective sets the direction, and you iterate at extreme speed on the path toward it. Every other quadrant feels wrong. When his instinct conflicts with the data, or with how the community feels, he makes the fast decision that can be adjusted incrementally: get the direction right and calibrate as you go. The critical skill is recognizing the moment when adjustment is needed.

[24:31] (David Baszucki) **Better to open up a language than to build one game into the platform** — Co-founder Eric Cassel and Baszucki had a pivotal disagreement in Roblox's early days. Baszucki wanted to write the flag from capture-the-flag directly into the core C++ code as a game template built into the platform; Eric insisted on not hard-coding anything like that, and instead on wiring in a general-purpose language, Lua, and building APIs so the system could generalize to any game. Baszucki did not trust that direction at first, but once it was built the power of the general abstraction went far beyond his hard-coded version, and it became one of the most important engineering foundations of Roblox's UGC ecosystem.

[29:19] (David Baszucki) **Replacing the whole system beats fixing 30 small problems** — Roblox's early membership model started to break down: user numbers kept climbing while paying members actually declined, and revenue flattened and then fell. The team's default reaction was to list 50 small problems and fix 30 of them — and the problem was still there. The real answer was to step outside the current system: they launched an entire new set of systems at once, virtual currency, a creator economy, popularity charts. Within 8 hours of going live, creators immediately began reshaping their content around earnings, and the team knew they had it right. The story is about what to do when an old system is structurally wrong: patching it is only a delay.

## Custody in divorce: courts now default to 50/50, and the parent playing to win loses

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-18-secureattach-法院已默认五五开-赢家心态才是真正的输/
- show: Securely Attached (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/secureattach/)
- original episode: Child custody through divorce: Navigating the courts and building a custody schedule that works with Michael Fried
- published: 2026-08-18 · duration: 52:28
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8012 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A New York divorce lawyer maps a decade of drift: courts have moved from ‘prove why it shouldn't be sole custody’ to ‘why not 50/50’ — and what actually determines how the child comes out is not the schedule but whether the parents can put the child's needs ahead of their own pain.**

why listen: Information density is moderate, but the back half — how custody schedules are actually designed, what threshold clears a modification, and the app the courts now impose — is first-hand lawyer detail that rarely reaches a Chinese-language audience.

### points

[8:57] (Michael Fried) **Mediation or litigation is chosen by personality, not by the facts** — Michael Fried's firm offers three tracks — mediation, collaborative law, litigation — and he decides which one by reading the client's personality rather than the case. If a client is passive and the spouse is forceful, he steers toward litigation, because in mediation the louder party's voice will simply drown out his client's. The lawyer's job is to be the client's mouth in the room. Collaborative divorce presupposes that both sides want to cooperate: if talks break down, the collaborative lawyers must withdraw and cannot use what they already know, which is precisely what pressures both sides toward a deal. Cases involving domestic violence do not belong in mediation or collaboration at all — those have to go through the legal process.

[16:32] (Michael Fried) **50/50 is not automatic; it requires a parent who can promote the other** — Over the past 10 to 15 years the court's logic has shifted from ‘prove why this shouldn't be sole custody’ to ‘why isn't this 50/50’. But 50/50 does not establish itself: it demands a high level of cooperation between the parents, which is why one of the heaviest factors in the court's best interest of the child analysis is whether a parent is capable of fostering the child's relationship with the other parent. Without that capacity, the logistics 50/50 depends on — the journal, medications, pickups and drop-offs, notifying the school about events — simply cannot run. A sole-custody schedule is straightforward; joint custody means two people negotiating with each other over and over.

[20:00] (Michael Fried) **A court-ordered app ends the he-said/she-said in custody fights** — Michael introduces OurFamilyWizard (OFW), and says the courts endorse it — just last week in court he watched a judge order both parties to sign up. OFW consolidates every communication between the parents: messages are timestamped, so you can see who sent what at what time, when it was read, when it was answered, and there is a shared calendar; if the tone gets too hot, the app prompts you to soften it. Lawyers, the child's representative, the forensic psychologist and the parent coordinator can all see the record, so both sides police themselves. He says this eliminates the he said/she said that dominates custody disputes and manufactures accountability.

[23:31] (Michael Fried) **The 50/50 default was earned by fathers getting up in the middle of the night** — Sarah asks whether the court's turn toward joint custody came from courts absorbing more child-development research. Michael's answer goes back to how family roles actually changed: over the past 25 to 30 years, mothers went to work, and fathers were also up in the middle of the night, out with the kids on weekends, doing baths and feedings. When his own children — now 26 and 23 — were small, he was the one getting up at night. What judges and mediators now see is not ‘only one parent handles the child’ but two parents carrying the daily load. That shift is the social ground the 50/50 turn stands on.

[30:15] (Michael Fried) **Build the schedule around the child's tolerance, not the parents' shifts** — The common 50/50 schedules include 2-2-5-5 — Monday and Tuesday with one parent, Wednesday and Thursday with the other, weekends alternating — plus 2-2-3 and 3-4-4-3. Michael says you cannot pick one by looking only at the parents' work hours; the core question is whether the child can tolerate switching back and forth, how old they are, and whether they have special needs. He gives the example of a neurodiverse child: 2-2-3 and 2-2-5-5 may both fail, in which case you move to rotating four-day and three-day blocks. By the time a child is 10 to 13 they may start not wanting to spend time with one parent, and the parents still have to push that relationship forward.

[42:24] (Michael Fried) **Don't write a book — journal only what departs from the baseline** — Michael has clients keep a journal from the very start of the case, but insists: ‘I don't want a book, I want short paragraphs.’ First record the baseline — the bedtime routine, the morning routine, how after-school and weekends go; after that, log only departures from it, such as how a child's illness was handled. These records are evidence in litigation, and as the client's mouth he has to be able to show a judge: my client was the primary caregiver from day one, and did the right thing under pressure. He also warns that recording useless information is noise — doctors, schoolwork, homework, how illness was handled: those are the facts that actually move a decision.

[47:09] (Michael Fried) **One or two late pickups mean nothing; a pattern is the case** — When clients complain that the other parent showed up 12 minutes late, or 5 minutes late, Michael tells them to document it and not act immediately. One or two isolated instances mean nothing; only when it becomes a sustained, pronounced course of conduct does it constitute a change of circumstances and give grounds to convert joint custody into sole custody. As a litigator, he says, he needs to accumulate enough ammunition. So the test for whether to come see a lawyer is: does it happen occasionally, or does it happen over and over? Only the latter is worth starting a modification proceeding over.

[51:42] (Sarah Bren) **Putting the child first does not mean flattening your own needs** — Sarah corrects ‘the child comes first’ at the close: what you set aside is your immediate pain response, not your core needs. Safety, being seen, being understood — those still have to be met, and only when the legal team and the therapeutic team are taking care of you does the child benefit from the process. Michael likewise keeps telling clients to get into therapy, because a client who stays healthy and steady can keep supplying the lawyer with the evidence the defense needs. The child's protective factors, in the end, include the parents' own mental health and physical condition.

## Chinese laborers shaped the US customs: modern border control originated from the Chinese Exclusion Act

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-18-cn2aa250-华人劳工塑造了美国海关-现代边控源自排华法案/
- show: 忽左忽右 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cn2aa250/)
- original episode: 493 追忆历史学家亚当·麦基翁：华人移民与现代边境制度的形成
- published: 2026-08-18 · duration: 1:07:50
- transcript: Machine transcription · 18125 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 2 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Customs, visas, and passport systems were not inventions of Europe and America but were born in the late 19th century when Chinese immigrants flooded into the United States, prompting the need to screen and exclude. The paradox that legal immigration is hard while illegal immigration is easy persists to this day.**

why listen: This episode uses a historian's work to overturn the common sense that 'immigration control originated in the West,' and through cases such as the Chinese Exclusion Act, indentured labor, and the Natal model, it explains the mechanisms of institutions and power.

### points

[16:17] (Cheng Yanliang) **Chinese immigrants shaped the US customs system** — In 'The Melancholy Order,' McKeown argues that the global modern customs and immigration control system was not established by white European immigrants, but developed in the late 19th century when a large number of Chinese immigrants poured into the United States, as the US needed to determine who could enter and by what standards to classify them. In a striking phrase, it was Chinese immigrants who shaped the US customs. This system then spread globally, so Chinese immigrants played a key role in the formation of modern border control, thereby also refuting Eurocentrism in immigration history.

[19:21] (Cheng Yanliang) **Foucault's concept of power runs through the immigration system** — McKeown is deeply influenced by Foucault: power is not top-down and concentrated in the state, but exists in everyday details and operates in a network. When immigrants apply for visas, they are required to provide various certificates and materials; this disciplinary mechanism and knowledge discourse precisely reflect the operation of power. Yang Bin points out that the immigration system is full of absurdities and paradoxes. For example, when applying for a student visa, regardless of whether you actually intend to return to your home country after graduation, you must check the box stating that you will return; otherwise, the visa officer will directly reject you. The system appears to operate between legal and illegal, but it is actually riddled with paradoxes created by power.

[25:27] (Cheng Yanliang) **The Chinese Exclusion Act established national immigration sovereignty** — McKeown analyzes the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, pointing out that its most important aspect was establishing the unilateral jurisdiction of the receiving country. Previously, the authority of the sending and receiving countries was unclear; the Chinese Exclusion Act placed the decision-making power in the hands of the United States, thus giving rise to the distinction between passports and visas today: a passport is an identity document provided by the home country, while a visa is decided by the receiving country whether to accept. In the modern international system, the decision-making power over immigration control ultimately rests with the receiving country—this is the key conclusion drawn from the Chinese Exclusion Act.

[28:30] (Cheng Yanliang) **Illegal immigration is easy, legal immigration is hard** — The US immigration system has a paradoxical outcome: about 10 million low-educated illegal immigrants make up 5% of the US labor force and have long been able to stay due to lax enforcement; conversely, highly educated non-immigrant talents often have to wait years in line to apply for a US green card. The system ostensibly encourages free immigration, but in reality it is centered on screening and obstruction. This absurdity, contrast, and paradox is what McKeown calls the 'melancholy order.' So-called free immigration is merely an invention and imagination of the modern state; immigration has always been defined, classified, and filtered by the state.

[34:40] (Cheng Yanliang) **Indentured labor replaced black slavery** — In the mid-to-late 19th century, as the abolitionist movement surged in the Western world, a labor vacuum appeared on the plantations of the New World. Contracted Chinese laborers emerged as substitutes for black slaves, known as 'selling piglets.' Chinese laborers in the US typically earned about $30 per month, and after deducting living expenses, could send home $80-100 per year; at that time, the average annual income of Chinese farmers was only $8-10, a difference of about tenfold. It was this economic drive that fueled the wave of emigration from South China in the late Qing Dynasty. A case in point is Sun Yat-sen's elder brother, Sun Mei, who started as an indentured laborer and later became a large rancher owning 6,500 acres.

[39:42] (Cheng Yanliang) **Passports came before ID cards** — After the United States and the West established customs systems, Chinese laborers became the first Chinese to possess international identity documents—passports—which appeared in China earlier than domestic ID cards. Chinese laborers crossed clear national borders and, upon arriving in foreign lands, suffered racial discrimination and oppression, shifting from clan and native-place identities to a conscious identification with being Chinese. Overseas Chinese thus became the forerunners of modern Chinese nationalism and revolutionary thought; Sun Yat-sen called them 'the mother of the revolution.' Yang Bin emphasizes that overseas Chinese simultaneously exhibit two trends: 'falling leaves return to the root' (returning to China) and 'taking root where they land' (settling abroad), and one should not only emphasize the former.

    original (zh): 艾特曼在书中说，他说到了19世纪70年代，移民已经从商品转向人，这种转变基本上是基于个人权力不可剥夺的信条，但几乎就是在移民被视为人之时，他们的权力来源就被剥夺了，重新分配给了国家。

[37:41] Yang Bin: "His income in the United States was ten times higher than at home, because whether in the South Seas, North America, or South America, these places were sparsely populated with abundant resources, and new industries were emerging that required a large labor force, especially hardworking, experienced, and skilled Chinese laborers, who were particularly welcome."
    original (zh): 美国他的收入比在国内的要高10倍，因为无论是在南洋，在北美还是在南美，都属于地广人稀，资源丰富，而且新进行业出现，需要大量的劳动力，特别是勤劳，有经验，有技术的中国劳工，尤其受欢迎。

### glossary

- indentured labor: A labor model contracted to replace slavery, used to fill the labor vacuum after abolition.
- Natal model: A model of immigration screening used in the Natal colony of South Africa, based on language tests, later adopted by Australia, New Zealand, and others.
- Canadian principle: A control principle established in 1909 that decides to accept or reject immigrants based on the economic interests of the host country.

why listen: Ben Thompson chains the AI capital cycle, the geopolitical deterrence of memory and foundry, and the hyperscaler threat to Nvidia into a single line — and the back half is worth more than the front half.

### points

[2:07] (Ben Thompson) **If the US wins the AI race, it becomes more dangerous** — Ben Thompson's answer runs opposite to the mainstream Silicon Valley narrative: if the US gains overwhelming AI superiority, China's game-theoretic optimal move is to blow up TSMC. He thinks the reasoning itself isn't complicated — what's complicated is that Silicon Valley won't admit how badly it underestimates US dependence on Chinese supply chains, and not just fabs: actuators, precursor materials. That dependence won't be fixed outside of a conflict, because as long as your competitors are still buying from China, moving back to the US on your own is a relative disadvantage; the rational choice is to stall until "literally no choice" forces the move.

[6:11] (Ben Thompson) **China being six to nine months behind is a decent equilibrium** — The current picture: OpenAI and Anthropic are clearly at the frontier, Google's situation is unclear, Grok and Meta are chasing; China is very capable and holds a roughly six-to-nine-month gap through distillation. Ben thinks this equilibrium is broadly favorable to the US — the question is only how long it lasts. He doubts China can actually overtake, because the last six to nine months are extremely hard to cross, and the acceleration of AI using AI to improve AI is already showing up at OpenAI and Anthropic. He also pushes back on the "open models are free" claim: the inference costs of GLM and Kimi are real, Kimi's serving costs are high, and the cost per answer is significantly higher.

[9:21] (Ben Thompson) **Where the money comes from is the nearest bottleneck** — What worries Ben is a timing mismatch: whether the revenue from investment returns arrives in time to meet the investment. The capital curve is moving downward — first free cash flow, then tech companies burned through the debt market in a single year, then Google started issuing stock, and Nvidia is putting together a $500 billion thing to tap pensions and insurance float. He asks: what comes after that? Ideally you return to cash-flow funding, but if there's a gap in the middle and it can't be bridged, there could be a big bang. Even if it blows up, though, AI won't disappear and won't stop improving — like the railroad and internet bubbles, on a human scale it ultimately doesn't matter.

[11:28] (Ben Thompson) **Google is becoming a Berkshire-style absolute-numbers player** — Ben looks at the Nvidia deal and Google's stock issuance together, and the Google issuance shocked him: why would a company that trusts its own judgment dilute its upside? The Berkshire analogy is See's Candies, with high margins but a ceiling on absolute profit and no reinvestment runway, versus BNSF, with far worse margins but a far larger absolute dollar amount — a year of free cash flow exceeding See's entire lifetime. Google Search is the most perfect business model in history, the purest aggregator, zero marginal cost, while AI burns money but its TAM is all white-collar work and eventually robots. Using all your free cash flow, issuing debt, then issuing stock, what you get is a smaller slice of an astronomically larger pie.

[37:36] (Ben Thompson) **Memory makers turned themselves into the Strait of Hormuz** — Ben compares memory makers to Iran: the Strait of Hormuz's deterrent value lies in not using it — once you actually use it, the UAE and Saudi Arabia will go build pipelines and new ports, and a blockade in 2035 would be useless. His worry is that memory makers have already spent that deterrence — it hurts now, but no one will let themselves get into that position again, and the first priority on the algorithm side becomes "how do we use less memory." Same logic: TSMC has only one leader, and customers will route around it.

[43:47] (Ben Thompson) **The shortage saved Intel, not technology** — Ben says that in an unchanging world TSMC would win forever, but precisely because TSMC didn't invest in recent years, the shortage will become extreme enough that big tech companies will tolerate the pain of propping up Intel's and Samsung's logic processes — "scarcity ultimately saved Intel." He expects Intel to announce a major partner for the first time. The solution to the geopolitical problem isn't persuasion, it's building a compute use case big enough that everyone has an economic incentive to prop everyone else up, so that geopolitical insurance comes free.

[51:07] (Ben Thompson) **Apple is the king of certainty, AI is a probability business** — Ben says Apple's moat is controlling the customer entry point, so suppliers come to it, which means AI suppliers can be bought in; in the future it might even run on-device inference on the user's electricity and never pay inference costs. But he questions why anyone expects Apple to be good at AI: AI is fundamentally probabilistic, Apple is the king of deterministic products, an iPhone has to be good the moment it ships, and Apple has never recalled an iPhone. He'd rather Apple do what it's good at — not touching AI is fine.

[1:08:36] (Ben Thompson) **Nvidia's moat is being discounted in ways you can't see** — Ben says Nvidia's position is "unnatural": it gives NeoClouds 25% backstops, takes equity, commits to buying through 2030 — essentially lowering the other side's cost of capital, which means taking on the risk itself. Risk doesn't disappear, it just shows up somewhere else. If compute is oversupplied and nobody wants those GPUs, Nvidia loses money — discounting that back at expected value amounts to a price cut, just one that doesn't show up in gross margin. The real long-term opponent is the hyperscaler: Google has already sold about 20% of its TPUs to Anthropic, and Amazon has hinted it will sell Trainium externally too — and as a commodity rather than a differentiated product.

[1:13:37] **A power shortage is actually good for Nvidia** — Nvidia won't say it out loud, but if the world really runs out of power, that's probably good for it: when power is the binding constraint, the only way forward is maximum token efficiency, and Nvidia is still the most token-efficient. Conversely, Nvidia's biggest problem over the past two years has been that the US brought far more power online than expected — whether behind-the-meter generation, West Texas natural gas, or restarted nuclear plants. The more abundant the power, the more time Amazon has to get Trainium right, and the more time Google has to make TPU competitive on efficiency.

[1:14:38] **A bubble has to leave behind something that pays for a long time** — If this really is a bubble, what you want is a long-term return. What the internet bubble left behind was fiber in the ground — Google's business is built to a large extent on dark fiber bought for almost nothing after the bubble, and the core internet still runs on WorldCom's fiber; what the railroad bubble left behind was assets like BNSF that are still paying Google today. So what will AI leave behind? GPUs won't last that long, data centers barely count, and what really lasts is power. If all this blows up and leaves excess power behind, that's a wonderful world — humanity has always been constrained by energy scarcity, and a world of energy abundance is hard to imagine.
