- published: 2026-08-16 · duration: 2:03:02
- transcript: Machine transcription · 18036 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**This episode shows the anti-vaccine movement is as old as vaccines themselves; phage SPO1 uses liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates to switch transcriptional phases; ancient smallpox DNA from South America confirms transmission by European colonization; and declining reading plus AI-generated content threaten our powers of discernment.**

why listen: It covers phage phase-separation mechanisms, the evolutionary history of variola virus, the historical thread of anti-vaccine argument, and the fight over vaccine policy. Dense with information, and worth the time.

### points

[7:26] (Vincent Racaniello) **A vaccine is not a bottle of soda; it is half a milliliter** — The United States has signed an executive order that attempts to reduce the number of childhood vaccines and to split up the MMR vaccine. The hosts call this ‘absurd’ and cite a commentary by Jake Scott at CIDRAP, which notes that Trump claimed children are injected with a volume of vaccine equivalent to a bottle of soda, when a vaccine is typically only half a milliliter — a difference of more than 200-fold from a 20-ounce soda. The piece also rebuts claims such as vaccines causing autism.

[10:45] (Rich Condit) **Experts were replaced by ideological loyalists, and a court ruled it illegal** — Rich fills in the background: after taking office, RFK fired the sitting Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), a body made up of experts whose recommendations are the basis on which states distribute vaccines. RFK installed non-expert ideological loyalists in their place, and the vaccine schedule they proposed was ruled illegal by a court. The new executive order is another attempt; it is expected to be challenged as well, but it will create confusion among parents and damage trust in the medical system.

[41:51] (Jolene Ramsey) **The phage has to act early, because once σA binds it cannot be evicted** — GP27 is the key protein that forms the condensate: its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) binds DNA, while its folded region interacts with the beta subunit of RNA polymerase. GP33 is an inhibitor of the host sigma factor σA; it binds between σA and the beta subunit and blocks the transcription complex from entering a productive transcription state. Competition experiments show that if σA binds first, GP33 cannot displace it — which is why the phage must suppress host σA early.

[57:54] **Smallpox was carried into the Americas by European colonization: the first molecular evidence** — A new paper reports the earliest ancient smallpox genomes from South America, recovered from two individuals from the Inca colonial period in northern Chile, dated to roughly 1492-1631. The phylogeny places them within a European medieval lineage, providing the first molecular evidence that smallpox entered the Americas through European colonization.

[1:19:55] **Smallpox gene loss is a continuing process that had already begun in medieval times** — In the CAM208 genome, 49 genes are deleted or inactivated. Of these, 37 are inactivated in both the ancient and modern genomes, 2 are unique to the CAM lineage, and 10 are inactivated in CAM and in modern smallpox but variable in the medieval genomes. This supports the view that gene inactivation is an ongoing process, and that some genes had already begun to be inactivated in the early medieval period.

[1:40:45] (Rich) **The marginal notes in Jenner's own book are today's anti-vaccine talking points** — Rich shares a scan he found of an original copy of Jenner's An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, and discovered that the book once belonged to the Southampton Anti-Vaccination League: its pages carry a large number of handwritten annotations by anti-vaccinationists. For example, where Jenner says cowpox virus can render a person permanently immune to smallpox, the annotation reads ‘nonsense’; where Jenner notes that blacksmiths are often resistant to smallpox inoculation, the annotator attributes it instead to their being physically fit from their labor. These notes are indistinguishable from contemporary anti-vaccine rhetoric.

[1:52:54] (Brianne) **Reading is not an instinct, and AI makes judgment scarcer still** — Brianne shares The Atlantic's article ‘The End of Reading’, which notes that in 2022 fewer than half of adults had read any book at all. The article argues that reading is not a human instinct — it has to borrow other regions of the brain — and that television and the internet have crowded out the time for it. ## The Roman Empire ran on enslaved people, not on its legions

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-16-ancients-罗马帝国是奴隶制的产物-无奴隶则无帝国/
- show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- original episode: How Slavery Built the Roman Empire
- published: 2026-08-16 · duration: 1:07:26
- transcript: Machine transcription · 11181 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Rome's administration, its army, its domestic work, its workshops and its mines ran almost entirely on enslaved people; after Carthage fell in 146 BC slavery became the engine of the economy, and once Augustus stopped expanding, that population reproduced itself by birth.**

why listen: Dense with information, and it explains the mechanism through specific people and specific laws rather than generalities. It corrects the impression that ‘slavery was just one facet of Rome’. Worth hearing all the way through.

### points

[2:27] (Emma Southern) **Take slavery out of Rome and the whole stool falls over** — Emma answers the title head-on: the Roman Empire simply could not have existed without slavery. From the bureaucracy to paying the army, almost everyone who handled the paperwork was enslaved or freed; hauling stone, building roads and keeping cities running all depended on enslaved labour. Her image for it: pulling slavery out of Rome as a whole is like pulling one leg off a three-legged stool — the whole thing cannot stand. She then stresses that the experience of enslaved people was deliberately fragmented. People at different ranks under the same roof competed with each other rather than combining, and that was an order the rulers maintained on purpose.

[8:25] (Emma Southern) **A freedman's freedom could be taken back at any time** — Rome wrote slavery into law very early. The Twelve Tables already contain clauses on the sale of people and on manumission. The freed were called freedmen: legally neither free persons nor slaves, but a stratum wedged between the two, barred from holding public office, unable to enter into certain contracts, with the restrictions reaching their children as well. Crueller still, being ‘insufficiently grateful’ could be grounds for re-enslavement. Emma stresses that this design was not an accident but an extension of Rome's bureaucratic character: a human being is a special kind of property, but property all the same.

[13:03] (Emma Southern) **Saying ‘slave’ finishes the Romans' work of turning people into things** — Emma argues that the word ‘slave’ is itself an instrument of dehumanisation, converting a person into an abstraction. She advocates ‘enslaved person’, which forces the speaker to pause for half a second and remember that the other party was a living human being. Her example is the gravestone of a three-year-old boy who died in an aristocratic household, paid for by his parents, who describe themselves as husband and wife — something legally impossible for them. From the stone you can work backwards to the mother's pregnancy, her work, her labour and delivery, even though none of it was ever written down. Archaeological material gives you fragments only; the rest has to be completed by imagination.

[19:59] (Emma Southern) **Only after Carthage was destroyed did Rome become a slave economy** — Emma dates the change in the character of Roman slavery to the fall of Carthage. Before it, Rome won and lost against the Samnites and the Etruscans in turn, citizens on the losing side could themselves be enslaved, and people flowed back and forth between wars. Once Carthage was destroyed, Rome swept the Mediterranean with no rival left and the number of war captives exploded; a few great estates were worked by whole blocks of enslaved labour, and Rome formally became a ‘slave economy’ — one that could not have held up for two hundred years without enslaved labour. Empire is extraction at bottom: alongside gold and silver, people were a resource being extracted.

[26:37] (Emma Southern) **Breeding kept the slave economy going for another 800 years** — After Augustus proclaimed the Pax Romana and closed the Temple of Janus, Rome stopped waging large-scale wars of expansion, and the supply of captive slaves fell sharply. But the slavery Rome practised was hereditary: a child born to an enslaved woman was born a slave. By then the enslaved population was already large enough to sustain itself by reproduction. Emma also points to an explicit incentive: an enslaved woman who bore three sons could obtain her freedom; daughters did not count. This self-reproduction extended the slave economy by roughly another 800 years.

[33:18] (Emma Southern) **The worst position of all was being enslaved with no master** — Not all enslaved people were foreigners. A Roman citizen could be sentenced to become a gladiator or sent to the mines or the quarries, which counted as a form of the death penalty. Emma calls them servus poenae, slaves of punishment: they had no particular owner, so there was nobody who could grant them favour and never any possibility of improving their situation. Beyond that, only two categories of enslaved people were protected in law: first, the stewards and outward-facing representatives of prominent families or the emperor's household; second, the publicly owned civic slaves of a city, for whom the city guaranteed housing, food and a small wage.

[1:00:16] (Emma Southern) **Buying your way to freedom was a road open only to men** — Emma points out that older scholarship overstated how common manumission was: the claim that ‘every slave was freed before thirty’ comes mainly from the experience of male bureaucrats and household slaves. In practice there were four routes: a gift from the owner, release by will, release after promotion through service, and saving up to buy yourself. Augustus restricted release by will: the individuals had to be named, and there was a ceiling on the proportion freed. But buying freedom was open almost exclusively to men. Emma says she cannot think of a single example of a woman purchasing her own freedom; an enslaved woman was usually freed by marrying her former owner, and in the same move was locked into a marriage that was very hard to leave.

[1:05:54] (Emma Southern) **A ‘good master’'s favour could be withdrawn at the last moment** — Emma closes with the case of Pedanius, a senator under Nero who was murdered by an enslaved member of his own household. By law every enslaved person in his house was to be put to death as collective punishment, and on that occasion 400 people were crucified. One motive Tacitus records is that Pedanius had first agreed to let his killer buy his freedom, then went back on it at the last moment. Emma uses this to show how fragile the Roman moral imagination of the ‘good master’ really was: favour at the very top could be revoked at any time, and the price of resistance for enslaved people was dozens or hundreds of lives.

### figures

- How long the slave economy lasted in Rome: about 800 years [27:42]

- Age by which older scholarship said slaves were freed: before 30 [1:00:16]

### glossary

- manumission: The procedure by which an enslaved person obtained freedom, used more often in Rome than elsewhere in the ancient Mediterranean; the freed still sat between slave and free.
- verna: A person born into slavery in the household, regarded as more reliable and often occupying one of the higher positions in the house.
- servus poenae: Someone condemned to slavery as a punishment, with no specific owner, so nobody could grant them favour and there was never a way back.
- dispensator: The enslaved steward in charge of finances and household management in a prominent Roman family; very high in status, and could even own slaves of his own.
- freedmen: A legal stratum sitting between free persons and slaves, barred from public office and from entering into certain contracts.
- Pax Romana: The long period of stability opened by Augustus, in which wars of expansion declined and the source of slaves shifted from war captives to birth within the household.

who it is for: Readers interested in Roman history, ancient economies, or in how systems run on labour that is kept invisible; especially useful for writers and museum curators.

## America Rescued the Yen for Its Own Trillion in Treasuries, Not for Japan

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-patrickboyle-美国救日元不是为日本-是为自家万亿美债/
- show: Patrick Boyle (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/patrickboyle/)
- original episode: The Hidden Risk in the US-Japan Yen Rescue
- published: 2026-08-15 · duration: 31:36
- transcript: Machine transcription · 4686 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The first US intervention in the yen in 28 years was officially a favor to an ally. The real calculation was to stop Japan from selling $1 trillion of US Treasuries to defend its currency — which would push up America's own cost of borrowing.**

why listen: One episode explains three things that make no sense on their face: why America intervened in the yen, why it sold euros to do it, and why Bessent is afraid of Japan selling Treasuries. You come away understanding what the disappearance of the Treasury convenience yield means.

### points

[0:00] (Patrick Boyle) **The Treasury Secretary's sticky note broke a 28-year taboo** — The episode opens on an absurd detail: a sticky note carried by US Treasury Secretary Bessent into a cabinet meeting, reading "buy yen, $5-10 billion," with the currency code JPY thoughtfully appended. Trump later explained it aboard Air Force One as doing a friend a favor, and even brought up Pearl Harbor. The genuinely strange thing is not the note but the nature of the act: the last time the US Treasury stepped in to support the yen was 1998, 28 years ago. By convention a Treasury Secretary does not do this, which makes it worth asking what actually happened.

[4:14] (Patrick Boyle) **Carry trade profits are not free money but a fee for holding the grenade** — There is no mystery to the mechanics of yen weakness. The Fed raised rates to roughly 3.75% to fight inflation, while the Bank of Japan held at zero for years and only recently moved to 1%. That enormous gap created the global carry trade: borrow yen in Tokyo at almost no cost, swap into dollars, and buy Treasuries paying around 4%. The textbooks say this should not produce a free lunch — the low-yielding currency ought to appreciate by exactly enough to cancel the rate differential. For years the market has done the opposite, and economics calls the gap the forward premium puzzle. The more popular explanation is that what you earn is not free money but a commission for holding the grenade on everyone's behalf. When it blows up, everybody runs for the exit on the same day, and the yen appreciates violently.

[9:25] (Patrick Boyle) **America bailed out the currency of a country on its own watchlist** — The US Treasury's official position has not changed in decades: it does not intervene in exchange rates, it lets the market set value, and intervention is only a short-term band-aid. To police everyone else, it publishes a report every six months naming trading partners that manipulate their currencies. The latest report, in July of this year, listed 10 countries, and Japan was on it. Yet in that very same month the US Treasury went into the market itself to help Japan bid the yen up. Strictly speaking, what the report criticizes is holding a currency down to push exports, and this time the intervention pushed the yen up. But spending American taxpayers' money to move a currency you are actively monitoring makes it plain that the rules are there to constrain other people.

[12:31] (Patrick Boyle) **Washington funded the yen rescue by quietly selling euros, not dollars** — The execution is stranger still. When the New York Fed placed the orders with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley on the Treasury's behalf, what it sold was not dollars but euros — and the European Central Bank was kept in the dark. The bulk of the euro assets in the US Exchange Stabilization Fund are French government bonds, so there is a strong chance America was in effect dumping a batch of French sovereign debt. A senior ECB official described this to the FT as "an unprecedented breach of central bank etiquette," and the IMF handbook explicitly advises central banks not to intervene in other countries' currencies. It amounts to driving off in your neighbor's car without asking, hitting a tree, and then explaining to him why his premium is going up.

[14:43] (Patrick Boyle) **The rescue was aimed at Japan's trillion in Treasuries, not at the yen** — Friendship with Tokyo is not the point; America's own borrowing costs are. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US government debt, with more than $1 trillion. If Japan spends another $50 billion or $80 billion defending the yen, the most convenient way to raise the money is to sell Treasuries — and heavy selling would push Treasury prices down and yields up. That is exactly what Bessent most fears, which is why he wants to help Japan steady the yen. His résumé makes it more ironic: in 1992 he was at the Soros fund and watched the Bank of England get picked off, and he later made his name shorting the yen. Now, sitting in the US Treasury Secretary's chair, the thing he is defending against is precisely the playbook he ran 30 years ago.

[18:56] (Patrick Boyle) **A Treasury Secretary should not place directional bets through debt issuance** — For most of the past two years Bessent has tilted issuance toward short-term bills and been unwilling to issue long bonds. The stated reason is that long-end rates are high right now, so there is no need to lock in for 30 years. Underneath it is a directional bet — a wager that inflation comes down, long rates fall, and the debt can then be swapped into long bonds. That bet is fine coming from a hedge fund, but not from a Treasury Secretary, whose job is not to guess rates but to fund the government regularly and predictably. Unfortunately rates have not fallen: the 10-year has risen to roughly 4.6%, and the 30-year has broken 5%. As long as rates do not come down, his funding strategy is stuck in a loop of rolling short-dated paper at ever higher cost.

[25:09] (Patrick Boyle) **$88 billion bought two weeks, and half the gain was given back** — The intervention did work at first: at the end of July the US and Japanese authorities spent roughly $88 billion over two days, and the yen went from around 164 to 155, a move of about 5%. Within two weeks it had slid back to 159, giving up half of that gain. The reason is plain — the FX market trades trillions of dollars a day, and $88 billion is small change. Obstfeld calls this set of contradictory policies cakeism: America wants a weak dollar but no inflation, low borrowing costs alongside enormous deficits, and Japan to keep buying Treasuries while the yen strengthens. America's own tariffs and its pressure on Japan to invest in the US are themselves pushing the yen down. It is bailing water out of the boat while drilling holes in the hull.

[27:21] (Patrick Boyle) **Treasuries are no longer scarce, and that is the real foundation here** — The real foundation of this drama is not the yen but the scarcity of US Treasuries. A paper by Harvard professor Wenxin Du finds that the convenience yield the world pays for the safety and liquidity of Treasuries has been narrowing for decades and has recently vanished, even turning negative. The cause is supply: too many Treasuries have been issued, and they are no longer scarce. Thursday's 30-year auction cleared at 5.22%, already the highest 30-year borrowing cost for the US since 2001. If the goal is a stronger yen, the cleanest route is for the Bank of Japan to raise rates. But Japanese government debt is already above 200% of GDP, debt service eats a quarter of government spending, and the new prime minister is opposed to hikes. Intervention does not change the trend; at most it buys a few days.

### verbatim quotes

[5:14] Patrick Boyle: "The carry trade works right up until the point where it doesn't, and when it stops working, it stops for everyone, on the same afternoon."

[8:21] Patrick Boyle: "It's a bit like gauging the British economy by the price of a burrito. You'll get a number, it just won't mean very much."

### glossary

- carry trade: Borrowing in a low-rate currency and swapping into higher-yielding assets to pocket the spread; the yen is the world's funding currency.
- forward premium puzzle: Theory says the low-rate currency should appreciate until the rate differential is cancelled out; reality has diverged from that for years.
- Cakeism: Wanting everything at once and refusing to pay any price; used here to describe the self-contradiction in US fiscal policy.
- Treasury Convenience Yield: The extra yield investors give up for the safety and liquidity of US Treasuries, now compressed into negative territory.

who it is for: Macro traders who follow Treasury yields and global liquidity, corporate treasurers with cross-border funding in Japan and the US, and investors watching fiscal sustainability.
what to skip: The Pearl Harbor joke and the lead-in before 2:09 can be skipped.

## Sufism Is Not a Low-Carb Islam — It Is a Backlash Against the Caliphate

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-litandhist-苏菲主义不是低配版伊斯兰-是哈里发国的反弹/
- show: Literature and History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/litandhist/)
- original episode: Episode 128: Early Sufism
- published: 2026-08-15 · duration: 1:56:24
- transcript: Official transcript page · 16053 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**European Orientalists described Sufism as a mysticism spanning Eurasia; modern Western promoters call it a message of "love, harmony and beauty" — but its roots are thoroughly Islamic, inseparable from the cultural history of the first caliphates.**

why listen: Medium information density, but the back half is very detailed on the mechanics of fana, the Path of Blame, and al-Hallaj's death — worth listening to.

### points

[3:00] **Sufism is not a low-carb Islam** — European Orientalists described Sufism as a mysticism spanning Eurasia, rooted in India and Persia rather than Islam; modern Western promoters call it a message of "love, harmony and beauty"; and readers of Rumi and Hafiz treat it as a kind of low-carb Islam — keeping monotheism and compassion while detaching from Islamic law and hadith study. The episode explicitly rejects all three simplifications: Sufism's roots are thoroughly Islamic, inseparable from the cultural history of the first caliphates.

[10:33] **Sufism was a backlash against caliphal secularisation** — The most common explanation is that Sufism arose in the early Islamic empire as a reaction to the worldliness, injustice and alienation of the Umayyad and early Abbasid dynasties. From the Indus valley to the Iberian peninsula, millions were ruled by a single and unstable state system; by 722, when Islam turned one hundred years old, the Umayyad caliphate was full of ethnic, economic and sectarian divisions. After the Abbasids replaced the Umayyads in 750, many Muslims felt the new regime served them no better. Eighth-century Muslims lived inside a paradox: they were heirs to the Persian, Greek and Syrian intellectual inheritance, yet ruled by hereditary monarchy; they recited the rhythmic Qur'an, yet lived under a despotism of greed and pleasure grossly out of step with the teachings of charity and equality. What the Qur'an demanded was an interdependent umma — a community of believers bound by gratitude to God and kindness to one another; the typical Umayyad or Abbasid city was a jumble of people ruled by often impious tyrants, characterised by anonymity and commerce rather than faith and community.

[25:36] **The earliest Sufis were bookish, not bohemian** — People who know Sufism today might assume the earliest Sufis drank and loved like the poets of their era. But the real forerunners were more scholarly than bohemian, hardcore theologians rather than religious dabblers. Hasan al-Basri was a major Qur'an commentator; al-Muhasibi (c. 781-857) lived in Baghdad and studied under al-Shafi'i, one of the four Sunni schools of law; Dawud al-Ta'i, Abd al-Wahid ibn Zayd and Shaqiq al-Balkhi were students of Abu Hanifa, founder of another school of law; the recluse al-Fudayl was a student of Ja'far al-Sadiq.

[50:10] **For Nuri, salvation does not happen after death** — The most counterintuitive point about the early Sufis: salvation is not Abrahamic, not post-mortem. Believe in God, be a good person, enter Jannah rather than Jahannam after death — that is the standard script. But Nuri wrote that the heart was created with light first; the light grows bright, becomes a ray, becomes a moon, becomes a sun; at the stage of the sun, a person "sees neither this world nor the next," because all worlds are God. The goal is not to move a clunky individuality from earth to heaven, but to dissolve one's own uniqueness into God's eternal being before death. This framework of "annihilation in life" is the prototype of the later doctrine of fana.

[57:42] **fana is not the end — it is the qualification to come back and teach** — Junayd handled fana (annihilation, the extinction of the self) differently from his contemporaries: annihilation is an important step, but not the end of the journey. The person who has passed through fana and fallen back to earth brings back a richer, truer understanding of God — he has gained clarity and can teach others. Junayd compared the Sufi who reaches fana to a banner of truth and a lighthouse, a chosen group of guides who can not only teach Sufism but use that clarity for exegesis, law, hadith study and other mainstream Islamic disciplines. So Sufi identity and muhaddith (hadith scholar) or faqeeh (jurist) are not mutually exclusive.

[1:04:37] **Nuri raced to be beheaded first and saved himself and his companions** — Seventy Sufis were brought before the caliph and all sentenced to decapitation. Nuri rushed forward and asked to be beheaded first, because he loved his companions and wanted to give them as much extra time alive as he could. The executioner put down the axe, unwilling to believe these prisoners were heretics, and the seventy were handed over to a judge for questioning. The judge asked about their prayers, asked how they kept themselves pure, and found nothing to reproach. At the critical moment Nuri said: "God has servants who hear by God, see by God, go by God, and come by God, eat by God, and are clothed by God." The judge is said to have declared: "If these people are heretics, then there is not a single monotheist on earth!" The narrator says plainly: it is a great story, but I do not know whether it is true.

[1:11:08] **al-Hallaj died of politics, not of being a Sufi** — The fourth figure, Mansur al-Hallaj, died in 922. In his early years he travelled the northeast of the Islamic world, going as far as India as an itinerant preacher, and settled in Baghdad around 900. He lacked his contemporaries' sense of where the line was drawn, plunged headlong into political controversy, and was ultimately ordered by the caliph's vizier to be tortured, flogged and beheaded before a large crowd on the bank of the Tigris. In later Sufi legend he said "I am the Truth" and did not retract it under torture; to a vizier looking for a reason to get rid of a political agitator, the phrase sounded like a claim to be an incarnation of God, because "The Truth" is one of the 99 names of Allah. But the narrator points out: he died not for Sufism, but as a political provocateur and a religious iconoclast. The execution did not trigger any larger crackdown on Baghdad's Sufis.

[1:26:41] **Path of Blame: the lower self cannot be transcended** — In Nishapur, in northeastern Iran, there appeared the al-Malamatiyya, the "Path of Blame." Early Sufis divided the self into two parts: the higher part can, through training, commune with God; the lower part is bound to worldly concerns, and the Sufi must reach up toward God while dragging this chain. But the people of the Path of Blame did not believe the lower self could be transcended — the lower self is base and at the same time insurmountable, so the best a believer can do is humbly recognise his own limits. They lived quiet, unpublic lives, holding that publicly showing off good deeds or declaring one's doctrine correct is merely an expression of egoism that strengthens the lower self. They wore no distinctive clothing, and seem to have come from the urban guilds of craftsmen, groups already inclined toward communal solidarity.

### verbatim quotes

[35:09] : "Piety is not in one’s clothing. It settles in the heart and is confirmed by one’s work and deed."

[36:00] Christopher Melchert: "persons called ‘Sufis’ by their contemporaries [early on] seem to have been [understood as] disreputable, marginal figures, often involved with political opposition and certainly not demonstrably mystics. Only in the second half of the ninth century does it appear that there were persons called Sufis who were also acceptable to the Sunni mainstream."

## Wi-Fi signals can identify you, and you don't even need to carry a phone

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-skeptics-wi-fi-信号能认出你-而且不用你带手机/
- show: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/skeptics/)
- original episode: The Skeptics Guide #1101 - Aug 15 2026
- published: 2026-08-15 · duration: 1:54:01
- transcript: YouTube captions · 20911 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Since Wi-Fi 5, the BFI that devices send back is unencrypted — anyone within RF range can set up a receiver and read it; identifying individuals by how their bodies perturb the signal hit up to 99.5% accuracy in experiments.**

why listen: The first half on vaccine politics and the second half on the origin of life and early black holes are information-dense; the middle sections on vegetable diversity and UAPs are more routine and can be fast-forwarded.

### points

[9:10] (Steven Novella) **An executive order on vaccines was always beyond his authority** — Trump signed an executive order called ‘gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations’. Steven's judgment: the president has no authority whatsoever over the CDC's recommended vaccine schedule, and this is a completely out-of-bounds intervention. Mechanically, childhood vaccine requirements in the US are decided by the states — states set which vaccines are required for school entry and which exemptions are allowed; professional organizations like the American Academy of Pediatrics issue their own recommendations. The job of that CDC committee is to review evidence and issue recommendations, not to have them rewritten by executive order. So on its own the order ‘has no teeth’, but it is paving the way for a later, systematic weakening of vaccines.

[16:15] (Steven Novella) **‘Only one vaccine and one ingredient were studied’ is a talking point** — RFK Jr. said the scientific community has not proven vaccines don't cause autism, that only ‘one vaccine and one ingredient’ have been studied. Steven points out this is a standard anti-vaccine talking point: what was studied is precisely the two things the anti-vaccine camp itself named — the MMR vaccine and thimerosal — plus aluminum adjuvants, and studies of total vaccine dose, and none showed a signal. The other side then demands a randomized controlled trial of ‘vaccinated vs. unvaccinated’, and such a trial will never be done, because you cannot randomly assign people to the group that doesn't get standard care — that is an ethical red line.

[22:19] (Steven Novella) **There is no autism epidemic; the diagnostic net just has smaller mesh** — The anti-vaccine narrative depends on three parallel curves: the vaccine schedule increasing, cumulative thimerosal dose increasing, autism increasing. Steven says the true autism rate has not risen: the number of diagnoses rose because the definition was broadened, surveillance is denser, and because of diagnostic substitution — these people existed thirty years ago, they just weren't diagnosed or were diagnosed as something else. Go back through medical records from different eras using the same surveillance and diagnostic methods and you get the same rate. He adds one caveat: you can't rule out that a very small increase, for demographic reasons, is hidden in there, but the bulk of it is a diagnostic artifact.

[30:23] (Jay Novella) **Wi-Fi's BFI feedback is unencrypted; anyone can listen** — A team at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in Germany built a system called BFID that identifies specific people by how their bodies perturb Wi-Fi signals, reaching up to 99.5% accuracy in experiments. The key mechanism: early Wi-Fi sensing relied on CSI, which required modifying hardware and firmware and had a high barrier to entry; the new method uses beamforming feedback information (BFI), introduced with Wi-Fi 5, in which devices send wireless channel information back to the access point — and BFI is transmitted unencrypted. An attacker only needs to set up a receiving device within RF range to read it; they don't need your Wi-Fi password, and you don't need to be carrying any Wi-Fi device.

[38:29] **Privacy fatigue is itself an attack surface** — The show acknowledges a counterintuitive psychological mechanism: when privacy threats come in wave after wave like a tsunami, the psychological defense isn't heightened vigilance but ‘everything is going to track me anyway’, so people end up doing none of the protection they should. The speaker calls this state being saturated with privacy concerns. His proposed remedy isn't individual self-discipline but raising the political salience of cybersecurity and online privacy, so that voters keep treating it as an issue. He also points to an asymmetry: there is ready-made legal infrastructure (search warrants and the like) for requiring the government not to violate privacy, but constraining private companies from violating privacy is far harder — and the government often ends up outsourcing its programs to exactly those private entities.

[1:00:46] **The same reaction, two completely different enzymes** — The research reconstructed about 420 core metabolic reactions — reactions that synthesize amino acids, DNA components and other necessities of life, using only simple molecules like CO2, H2 and ammonia as inputs. As expected, the ancient chemistry shared by bacteria and archaea is itself universally conserved; but what surprised the researchers is that roughly half of the enzymes catalyzing these same reactions are not conserved between the two, and the differences are not the result of homologous enzymes diverging — they are entirely different enzymes. So the authors propose that the other half of the key reactions were catalyzed by environmental metals at the time, with geochemistry working alongside biochemistry at the origin of life. Corresponding author Joseph Moran's phrasing is that the closer you look, the more you see that early biochemical evolution was a hybrid of enzyme catalysis and metal catalysis.

[1:06:53] **‘Life arose twice’ is clickbait** — Science Alert's headline read ‘radical study hints life on Earth arose twice’, but the paper's title is “intermediate stages in the origin of metabolism and phosphorating hydrothermal vent”. The authors are not saying the non-life-to-life transition happened independently twice — that would be a genuinely astonishing finding. What they are saying is: bacteria and archaea still evolved from a common ancestor, share the same basic genetic code, and merely evolved independently into fully free-living cellular life. Senior author William Martin's own words are ‘what we see is one origin of the genetic code, two origins of life’, where ‘life’ uses his own definition of ‘free-living, autonomous’. The show also notes that the same study addresses the energy problem: ATP itself requires enzymes, and in these hydrothermal environments phosphate can drive reactions without ATP and without enzymes.

[1:43:18] **Billions of times brighter than fusion — it can only be a black hole** — How do you rule out that it's just a giant star? Because the energy it produces is billions, even tens of billions, of times what hydrogen fusion can produce, so the energy source can only be a black hole, from an accretion disk. Then why doesn't the accretion disk outshine all that hydrogen? Because it is filtered by a dense hydrogen envelope the size of a solar system. There would be no significant fusion in the envelope — even at that density it is several orders of magnitude thinner than a stellar core, and lacks gravitational confinement. The observational data comes from JWST.

### glossary

- LUCA (last universal common ancestor): The common ancestor of bacteria and archaea before their divergence; this study argues half of its metabolism depended on the environment.
- Balmer break: A spectral feature left by hydrogen atoms absorbing light at specific wavelengths, used to determine whether the surroundings of an object are clean hydrogen.
- CSA (community supported agriculture): Consumers pay a fixed price up front and periodically receive a box of seasonal vegetables, sharing the farm's operating pressure.

## The Order Calls Vaccines Soda and Splits MMR Into More Shots: Every Sentence Is a Lie

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-twiv-行政令里的谎言-拆mmr与汽水比喻都是伪科学/
- show: This Week in Virology (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/twiv/)
- original episode: TWiV 1348: Clinical update with Dr. Daniel Griffin
- published: 2026-08-15 · duration: 55:00
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9063 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Every sentence in the ‘gold standard’ executive order gets called a lie: splitting MMR to add needles, vaccines as bottled soda, Merck refusing outright — and the new CDC director will have to pick a side.**

why listen: High information density but no major scientific breakthrough; worth it for the policy fight, the outbreak numbers, and two mechanisms that are easy to overlook — mAbs interfering with vaccine response, and the wastewater score having no units.

### points

[2:03] **The order is not a scientific assessment — every sentence in it is a lie** — The August 10 executive order asserts that ‘pure nations sustain high vaccination rates through public trust and education, while American states instead use mandatory school-entry requirements’. The conversation immediately dismantles that frame: this is not a scientific assessment, ‘every sentence in it is a lie’, and ‘gold standard’ is nothing more than a label. There is a real counterexample from the COVID period — some countries invested in education and had people scrambling to get vaccinated. But the 50 US states differ enormously, and trust and education alone cannot hold vaccination rates up.

[9:15] **Splitting MMR has no scientific rationale — it just means two more needles** — The order ‘acknowledges’ that measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis and polio, among others, should be recommended for all children — and then demands that MMR be broken into three single-disease shots, each given at a separate visit where possible. The key judgment: this adds needles and office visits, with no scientific reason at all, and no manufacturer is willing to make them. The reason Trump gave when signing was that combination vaccines contain a ‘dangerous amount of fluid’, describing a single shot as being like a bottle of soda; in fact most vaccines are only about 0.5 milliliters. Merck's answer was 10 years and hundreds of millions of dollars — and an explicit no.

[14:30] **Vaccination has always been a state power, so the order is an overreach** — Vaccination decisions in the US have historically belonged to the individual states; the federal role is to issue ACIP recommendations that the CDC director signs off on, which makes the executive order an overreach. This is the third executive order aimed at vaccines in under a year; the previous one was already blocked by a judge, and this one will most likely go the same way. The new CDC director previously said ‘they would never ask us to put children at risk’; now the order is sitting in front of her, and how she answers becomes the first test. HHS is also soliciting members for the National Vaccine Advisory Committee, and someone joked that being selected would mean the clinical updates have to stop.

[21:45] **The Cyclospora season has not closed out, and the risk sits in one production line** — CDC has received 13,895 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, with at least another 10,455 awaiting further investigation; Michigan alone accounts for 12,485 cases and 279 hospitalizations, and there have already been deaths. Missouri has 1,577 cases, New York City 594. August should be near the tail end of the imported season, some sources have been pinned down and the products pulled from shelves. The remaining risk is that 40% of US lettuce comes from Taylor Farms, and contamination on the Mexican production line is the main worry.

[23:51] **Screwworm kills not through the maggots but through secondary sepsis** — The US now has 45 screwworm cases, concentrated in New Mexico and West Texas. Mexico reported 204 cases between April 2022 and March 2026, of which 202 were analyzable: 72% male, mean age 61, 55% on the lower limbs, 77% with at least one comorbidity, six deaths, and only one attributed directly to the myiasis. The larval stage is an obligate parasite: eggs hatch in 12-24 hours, and the larvae feed on living tissue for 5-7 days before dropping to the ground. The mechanism of death is that in people with neuropathy the wound is eaten open, bacteria enter the bloodstream, and sepsis follows.

[28:58] **The county RFK once went to lobby has become the measles epicenter** — Measles has already reached 2,484 cases this year, with 10%-20% hospitalized, and there have been deaths. The New York Times dug up RFK telling the Amish community in Lancaster, Pennsylvania five years ago that the CDC and agencies like it ‘cannot stand that you are healthy’, and joking that the treatment for measles is chicken soup plus vitamin A. That same county is now one of the largest outbreak sites in the country, with the state reporting 230+ cases and physicians reckoning it is badly undercounted. The attitude here is unambiguous: hundreds of children hospitalized and unable to catch their breath is not something to discuss lightly.

[40:22] **Get a monoclonal first and the later vaccine's B cell response is suppressed** — A study in JID asked whether people who received a COVID monoclonal antibody during acute illness have an altered immune response to a subsequent mRNA vaccine. An analysis of 43 people showed that at day 140 neutralizing antibody titers were lower in the mAb recipients than in the placebo group, and RBD-specific memory B cells were reduced at both day 56 and day 140 — but spike-specific CD4/CD8 T cells were unaffected. The conclusion is that anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonals limit the RBD-directed B cell response to a later vaccine while leaving T cells intact. The unanswered question Griffin cares about is whether waiting three months or six months before vaccinating avoids the suppression.

[53:59] **The 2 on the wastewater chart has no units and is not a concentration** — A listener asked what the ‘2’ on the CDC wastewater chart actually is. The answer lays out the whole pipeline: sampling → concentration → nucleic acid extraction → qPCR or dPCR to get a concentration such as gene copies per liter → normalization for rainfall and sewage composition → conversion by service population into gene copies per person per day → and finally a 7- or 15-day rolling average with a regression fit. But Vincent stresses that the ‘2’ itself has no units; it is only a categorical score. Read on its own the number will be misinterpreted — it has to be looked at alongside hospitalization and emergency department trends.

## The universe doesn't end in heat death — it gets steered back on course infinitely many times

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-tokcast-宇宙的终点不是热死-而是被无限次驾驶回正轨/
- show: ToKCast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tokcast/)
- original episode: Ep 265: David Deutsch's "The Fabric of Reality" Chapter 14 "The Ends of the Universe" Part 2 The Omega Point
- published: 2026-08-15 · duration: 1:28:35
- transcript: YouTube captions · 14189 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Tipler's omega point theory was wrecked by his own extravagant religious claims, but Deutsch says there's a valuable core inside: the universe must be continuously piloted to complete infinite computation in finite time.**

why listen: This episode is medium density, but the back half — on dark energy and the Church principle falsifying each other, and on predicting future knowledge being self-contradictory — is worth hearing.

### points

[8:09] (Brett Hall) **Tipler's theory was destroyed by Tipler himself** — Deutsch has a precise criticism of Frank Tipler's omega point theory: the theory itself is ‘about the fabric of all reality’, belonging not to any one of the four strands but irreducibly to all four — which is very high praise. But in “The Physics of Immortality” Tipler made extravagant claims for his theory, and the result is that most scientists and philosophers threw the whole thing out, missing the valuable core idea inside it along with it. Deutsch says that discarded core is what he is about to explain.

[22:20] (Brett Hall) **Tipler holds the line on unitarity against observation** — Faced with observations of accelerating expansion, Tipler refuses to give ground. He invokes Hawking's result: an eternally expanding universe requires all black holes to evaporate via Hawking radiation, which destroys all the information inside them and thus violates the unitarity of quantum physics — probabilities must sum to one. Tipler's argument is: the accelerating expansion you see now is only a local fact about us at this moment; wait long enough and contraction will begin, because unitarity cannot be violated. Brett points out that Tipler is also engaged in a kind of motivated reasoning, trying to derive from the omega point theory that Christianity is true and that a Christian-style resurrection of everyone will occur.

[36:34] (Brett Hall) **The world is comprehensible because it is comprehensible** — Deutsch's argument is: if we want to explain why the world appears comprehensible, the explanation may simply be that the world is comprehensible. And a theory that the world is ‘half comprehensible’ has no explanatory power at all; it merely restates the problem and introduces an inexplicable constant of 1/2. Brett says this is his new favourite sentence from rereading the chapter, a thorough refutation of those who say the human mind can never understand ultimate physics — including Neil deGrasse Tyson, who worries that only an alien mind could understand the successor theory to quantum mechanics. The reason is in “The Beginning of Infinity”: we are universal explainers.

[36:34] (Brett Hall) **The omega point needs someone at the helm the whole way** — Deutsch points out a technical detail: the spacetime oscillations that make the omega point possible are of the classically chaotic, unstable kind, growing more violent the closer you get to the omega point. Any tiny deviation from the correct shape is rapidly amplified, enough to destroy the conditions for continued computation, so the big crunch would arrive after only finitely many steps of computation. So to satisfy the Turing principle and reach the omega point, the universe must be continuously ‘steered’ back onto the right trajectory. Tipler has already shown in principle how to do this by manipulating the gravitational field of the whole of space.

[47:43] **Cramming infinitely many thoughts into the last second** — Deutsch's argument: the stabilisation mechanisms and the technology for storing information must be improved infinitely many times, with density and stress rising without limit, which requires continually creating new knowledge — and Popperian epistemology says new knowledge requires rational criticism, and therefore requires intelligent entities. So in the final frenzy, an infinite amount of stabilisation and knowledge creation happens in finite time. Someone will ask: with only a second left, why not rest? Deutsch says this is the biggest misunderstanding — these people's minds are programs running on computers with no upper bound on speed, and thoughts are virtual realities rendered by those computers. The subjective duration of a virtual experience is not determined by the time that elapses but by the computation executed during that time. Infinite steps of computation contain the time for infinitely many thoughts.

[52:46] **The Kardashev scale is pseudoscience** — The host says flatly that he regards the Kardashev scale as pseudoscience. The reason: how do you calculate how much energy is there? You can look at the amount of luminous matter, make various assumptions, but we don't know what dark matter is, we don't know whether zero-point energy can be tapped, there are too many unknowns — especially when you're talking about the distant future and about ‘harnessing all the energy around a star’, you might find another energy source. He lumps it together with the Drake equation: not a law of physics but a string of choices about variables, some constrained, many completely open. He also grumbles: Musk is very keen on it, so tech people are keen on it too.

[1:02:56] **Dark energy and the Church principle falsify each other** — There are three independent lines of evidence for accelerating expansion: type 1a supernovae (white dwarfs accrete to 1.38 solar masses and explode, giving a standard luminosity, and they measure as dimmer, hence farther, than they should be), the acoustic peaks of the cosmic microwave background being larger than they should be, and the matter distribution of baryon acoustic oscillations. All three are most parsimoniously explained by accelerating expansion. But the host says this poses a two-way problem: the Church principle makes the dark energy observations suspect, and the dark energy observations make the Church principle suspect. The possible ways out are that one of them is false, or that both are true and the universe will recollapse in the future, or cycle as Penrose says, with something odd happening at the end that lets information leak into the next universe.

[1:25:09] (Host) **Predicting future knowledge is self-contradictory** — Deutsch cites Pa's argument: future human affairs depend on the growth of future knowledge, and we cannot predict which specific knowledge will be created in the future — because if we could predict it, by definition we would already have that knowledge now. This is not ‘prediction is hard’ but logically impossible. So any large-scale prophecy about future human or posthuman affairs cannot be reliable. The host says this sentence is the closing point of the whole picture of the future, and is the core content of “The Beginning of Infinity” appearing early in “The Fabric of Reality”.

**Antibiotic bowel prep before colon cancer surgery is meant to prevent infection; but in patients whose cancer recurs, the resistant bacteria in their gut are unfazed, and on the day of surgery their total bacterial load is 23 times higher than in non-recurring patients. The prep may be precisely what selects for future recurrence.**

why listen: This is not just another 'microbiome and cancer' correlation. It links 16S sequencing, resistance genes, in vitro cancer cell experiments, and 19 clinical samples into a chain of evidence; for surgeons operating on colorectal cancer, it directly affects the choice of perioperative antibiotics.

### points

[12:39] **Bowel prep cannot wash away the microbial signature of recurrence** — The cohort is indeed small: 19 patients, 6 of whom recurred about 10 months after surgery, roughly 30%, with sites mostly in the lung, liver, and anastomosis. Fecal samples taken on the day of surgery captured the key feature: after mechanical bowel prep, oral neomycin and metronidazole, plus intravenous cefoxitin, the originally clear microbial differences between the left and right colon and the rectum were all flattened, but the compositional difference between the 'will recur' and 'will not recur' groups remained. All these patients received standard bowel preparation, meaning that by the time the surgeon closed, the gut microbiota of the recurring patients had already diverged from that of the non-recurring ones.

[13:41] **Bowel prep is nearly ineffective against resistant microbiota** — Each patient served as their own control: after bowel prep, the total bacterial load in the non-recurrence group dropped about 10-fold; in the recurrence group, the bacterial load was almost unaffected. Thus, on the day of surgery, the total bacteria in the stool of recurring patients was 23 times higher than in non-recurring patients (calculated by 16S rRNA gene copy number). This is not because the prep was done incorrectly—oral neomycin plus metronidazole, laxatives, and an intravenous push of cefoxitin 30 minutes before skin incision were all strictly followed. The problem is that this perioperative regimen at best clears susceptible bacteria, but has almost no effect on the bacteria in the recurring patients' guts that can withstand all three drugs.

[15:42] **Bowel prep amounts to an in vivo selection screen** — Resistance gene sequencing provides the material basis for the 'selection' hypothesis: the total number of resistance genes in the gut of recurring patients, as well as the number of resistance genes against the three bowel-prep drugs—neomycin, metronidazole, and cefoxitin—were higher than in non-recurring patients. Petra Levin pointed out on the show that this is not a vague 'selective pressure' but the most standard selection in a microbiology lab—like screening for successful transformants on an ampicillin plate, except here the entire gut microbiota is being screened. But genes and phenotype do not fully overlap: the authors did not observe functional resistance to neomycin, and they acknowledged that the small cohort can only yield directional conclusions.

[18:51] **The pathogenic phenotype only appears after bowel prep** — Before surgery, collagenase gene abundance did not differ between the recurrence and non-recurrence groups; only by the day of surgery did the difference emerge. The recurrence group had higher relative abundance and absolute counts of collagenase genes, as well as higher collagen-degrading activity of the microbiota; among the 13 patients who did not recur, 12 had no collagenolytic colonies with clear zones. The authors put it directly: antibiotic bowel prep is a prerequisite for revealing this pathogenic phenotype. Before prep, enzyme-producing bacteria are inconspicuous mixed in the intact community; after prep clears susceptible bacteria, the remaining resistant and enzyme-producing taxa gain the upper hand in the residual community.

[25:00] **Enzyme-producing enterococci promote cancer cell metastasis** — Functional experiments distinguish correlation from causation. Adding the supernatant from the day-of-surgery microbiota of recurring patients to the upper chamber of a transwell significantly enhanced the migration of human and mouse colon cancer cells, as well as invasion through a collagen-coated layer; supernatant from the non-recurrence group had no effect. From the 72 colonies picked from recurring patients' samples, Enterococcus was the dominant genus; when cancer cells were treated separately with collagenase-producing and non-producing strains, only collagenase-positive strains induced migration and invasion, while negative strains had no effect. Whole-genome comparison between enzyme-producing and non-producing strains revealed 8,961 variant alleles, and the enzyme-producing strains also carried more virulence-related genes such as adhesins and type IV secretion systems.

[47:15] **Phage uses size to pull off bacterial pili** — The second story in this episode is unrelated to cancer, but the mechanism is counterintuitive. The single-stranded RNA phage uses type IV pili as its receptor, and its MAT protein is responsible for binding the pilus; experiments showed that the N-terminal 200 amino acid residues of the MAT protein are sufficient to induce pilus shedding, and the amount of shedding is proportional to the number of viral particles. To rule out enzymatic cleavage, the researchers attached a large fluorescent microsphere to this protein segment—it also caused pilus shedding. This shows that the effect is due to size, not catalytic activity: when the pilus is about to retract into the cell, it gets stuck by this 'big head,' and the connection is mechanically broken. Since type IV pili are involved in motility, adhesion, and biofilm formation, the truncated MAT protein could become an anti-virulence tool that does not kill bacteria.

## The Fed Was Not Born Precise: What It Was Supposed to Do Was Still Being Figured Out in the 1970s

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-14-cn2aa250-美联储不是天生精密-它该干什么到1970年代还在摸索/
- show: 忽左忽右 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cn2aa250/)
- original episode: 492 刘怡、于杰谈保罗·沃尔克与现代美联储制度的形成
- published: 2026-08-14 · duration: 1:17:43
- transcript: Machine transcription · 23546 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Before the 1970s, even Fed chairs could not say clearly what the Fed was for, and presidents simply ordered rate cuts to protect employment. Volcker pushed rates above 20% to fight inflation head-on, and in doing so set the modern template: the chair watches inflation and unemployment, nothing else.**

why listen: Yu Jie, who brought The Changing Fortunes to Chinese readers, questioned Volcker in person and spoke repeatedly with Toyoo Gyohten, the Japanese negotiator of the Plaza Accord; every judgment comes with a source, not a textbook history of the dollar.

### points

[8:08] (Liu Yi) **The Fed's mandate was only settled in the 1970s** — Liu Yi stresses repeatedly that today everyone is used to treating the Fed as a precision machine, as if it had known from birth what it was supposed to manage. But before Volcker, no one could say clearly what a Fed chair was supposed to do: Keynesian economics was still new at the time, Friedman's doctrine was popular only in a small corner of Chicago, and the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate left monetary policy little room to operate. More common was direct pressure from the president, ordering the central bank to cut rates to protect employment. Only after Volcker had rolled through decades in the Treasury and the Fed did the template take hold — the chair mainly watches inflation and unemployment, and does not manage GDP growth. The mature system on which dollar hegemony depends is in fact only a little over half a century old.

[21:14] (Liu Yi) **Had Keynes's plan passed, America would be fined every year** — At Bretton Woods, Keynes proposed that the major powers crowd-fund 35 billion dollars into a very powerful IMF, with accounts kept in a virtual currency unit, the bancor: deficit countries could apply for aid, and surplus countries that refused to invest abroad would be fined, using coercion to prevent mercantilism. White rejected the plan, because he saw clearly: after the war the United States held more than half the world's export trade and a third of its industrial capacity, so under Keynes's design America would inevitably be fined every year; and Britain and France simply could not put up the crowd-funded money, so the 35 billion would basically have to come from the United States. So the IMF was designed to be very weak, and the real anchor became the dollar fixed to gold at 35 dollars an ounce. Bretton Woods was not an idealist design; it was a product of American interests.

[27:21] (Yu Jie) **35 dollars an ounce was set in 1933** — Yu Jie points out that the real foundation for writing the dollar's gold parity at 35 dollars an ounce into Bretton Woods in 1944 lay in 1933: after Roosevelt took office he declared private gold holdings illegal, nationalised the people's gold, and the gold in the Fed's hands was transferred to the Treasury; the president then, under congressional authorisation, devalued the dollar by nearly 60% to 35 dollars, and authorised the Treasury to exchange gold freely with foreign central banks. He stresses that the crux of a strict gold standard is free entry and exit across the border — once you have exchanged dollars for gold, you can load it on a ship and take it away. This 1933 exchange commitment later became the cornerstone of Bretton Woods, and it also explains why after the war countries like France flew planes to America to exchange gold: what they were cashing in was in fact Roosevelt's promise, not merely a 1944 agreement.

[33:27] (Liu Yi) **Ten billion in gold cannot back forty billion in promises** — Bretton Woods's fatal flaw was the Triffin dilemma: countries needed dollars, and the more dollars flowed overseas, the more everyone doubted whether they could be converted back into gold at 35 dollars, because the dollar and gold had become competitors. By around 1971, the market value of the gold reserves in American hands was only a little over 10 billion dollars, while a full 40 billion dollars circulated overseas; the London gold price was one-seventh higher than New York's, and arbitrageurs sold dollars, bought gold, and shipped it to America to demand conversion. Even without the Vietnam War and inflation, a 4-to-1 gap made "convertible at any time" arithmetically impossible long before. Nixon's suspension of convertibility in 1971 was not a sudden default but an outcome long destined to arrive.

[48:38] (Yu Jie) **Volcker's rate hikes crushed Latin American debt first** — Petrodollars poured into American commercial banks, and Chase, Citibank and others lent them on to Latin American countries desperate for funds. Latin America borrowed in the era of low dollar interest rates, and when Volcker raised rates above 20% to crush inflation, Latin America was hit doubly at once: the dollar appreciated against every currency, and Latin American currencies collapsed relative to it; American rates soared, and the new debt that had to be borrowed to roll over old debt also became more expensive, forming a debt spiral outright. West German Chancellor Schmidt left behind the lament that since the birth of Jesus, he had never seen numbers with interest rates this high. American farmers drove tractors to Washington saying they would smash their heads to death under the Fed's windows — but Volcker did not stop, inflation came before everything.

[59:45] (Yu Jie) **The Plaza Accord was not the culprit behind Japan's bubble** — Yu Jie asked Toyoo Gyohten, who was present on the Japanese side at the Plaza Accord and later became vice minister of Japan's Ministry of Finance, many times: should the bursting of the bubble be blamed on the Plaza Accord. Gyohten's answer was that the dollar had long needed adjusting, and moving in 1985 was already late; Japan's real problem was a misaligned monetary policy — it failed to tighten when it should have tightened, and failed to loosen when it should have loosened. The Plaza Accord itself was neither an agreement nor a treaty, only a statement, with no binding force on any country. After the yen appreciated, Japan's fiscal discipline loosened, it went in for heavy infrastructure spending, and together with rate cuts it pushed real estate and stocks to the top; in 1991 the new central bank governor raised rates sharply, and the bubble burst at once. Pinning the lost thirty years on the Plaza Accord is to oversimplify a complex history.

[1:13:55] (Liu Yi) **Greenspan invented Fed-speak** — After Volcker left office, the role of Fed chair switched tracks. In his first year Greenspan ran into the 1987 stock crash, and through the media he built himself into a figure whose word was decisive, bold and tough, and from then on he had enormous say at the White House; his briefcase was chased by the media, and he also invented the so-called Fed-speak — using obscure wording to make a simple question sound as suspended and uncertain as could be. Liu Yi says that from Greenspan onward, the Fed chair became a public figure who appeared on camera often. Today Kevin Warsh takes another path: saying little or even nothing, using mystery to manufacture weight with the market and the public. Mystery and Fed-speak are the same in essence: the credibility Volcker earned by holding the line has become image management in the media age.

## The cure for picky-eating anxiety: no judgment, no rewards, dessert is just another food

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-14-raisinggh-挑食焦虑的解药-不评判-不奖励-甜点也是普通食物/
- show: Raising Good Humans (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/raisinggh/)
- original episode: Picky Eating & Food Guilt with Jennifer Anderson
- published: 2026-08-14 · duration: 46:02
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8503 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A child's relationship with food does not hinge on whether they ate any particular thing. It hinges on whether the parent sorts food into good and bad, whether dessert gets used as a reward, and whether the parent gives themselves permission to feed according to what the child actually needs. The earlier picky-eating signals are recognized, the easier they are to change.**

why listen: For parents whose feeds are saturated with "good food, bad food" and who are simultaneously locked in battles at the dinner table with their kids and their own parents. Information density is moderate; the picky-eating warning signs and the scripts for hard conversations are the biggest additions.

### points

[3:07] (Jennifer Anderson) **Loving your body and caring for your body are one thing, not two** — Jennifer uses her own coined phrase, "embodied independence," to make the point: a child needs to live inside their body and love it, and also be able to answer rationally what that body needs — bathing, a balanced diet. She insists these were never two separate things but a single one. Once the culture splits enjoying your body and caring for your body into two goals, the child ends up divided between "what I like to eat" and "what I should eat." Putting the two words side by side is precisely an attempt to pull that connection back together.

[6:57] (Jennifer Anderson) **Unless there is an allergy, every food can fit in a child's diet** — She argues social media's biggest distortion is sorting individual foods into good and bad. Those labels make parents anxious and guilty, and they transfer easily to the child. Her replacement is a flexibility frame: absent a diagnosed allergy or other medical reason, all foods can fit into my child's diet. The parent hosts the experiment — observing firsthand what works for their own family. The shift does not abandon health goals, but it takes fear and shame off the table, and parents become more confident as a result.

[13:49] (Jennifer Anderson) **Dessert should go directly onto the dinner plate** — Against the rule of "finish your meal, then you get dessert," Jennifer offers two alternatives. First, do not announce dessert before the meal, so the cookie is decoupled from dinner. Second, put a small portion of dessert right on the dinner plate and serve it as an ordinary food. She acknowledges the second is a culture shock for many families and may not suit them, but it has worked in her house. The key move is that the parent acts as the restaurant's chef: what goes on the table is your call, rather than something you direct verbally, nonstop, at the child.

[14:57] (Jennifer Anderson) **Balance is not taught by lecturing but by how often a food appears** — She rejects defining food through lectures and argues for teaching through frequency on the table: hyper-palatable foods are only "extra delicious," so they appear rarely; plain, high-fiber, high-protein foods appear often. Without hearing a single word, the child learns balance from the family table. She also warns against using food as a reward — "eat your spinach and you get a cookie" carries the subtext that the cookie ranks above the spinach, children grasp that instantly, so it is best not to make that trade at all.

[19:09] (Jennifer Anderson) **What decides the outcome is not which strategy you pick but how you say it** — The core is "not which strategy, but how you use it." The same sentence — "you can only have one piece of cake" — lands completely differently said with fear and moral judgment than said matter-of-factly. Jennifer suggests parents first work out whether they need a stricter or a looser environment, then give themselves permission to choose whichever fits their own relationship with food. A strategy that does not match the household's atmosphere cannot be sustained, however correct it is.

[23:52] (Jennifer Anderson) **The red flags for picky eating were visible at 10 months old** — Her son showed red flags at 10 months: he avoided purees and needed 20 exposures before he would eat a given food, at an age when children are usually very open. She did not wait for a doctor to say "let's keep watching" — she used the extreme-picky-eating screener (PSAE) as early as possible. Her son turned out to be an ordinary picky eater and never became an extreme one. Her rule of thumb for parents: a full year with no improvement, and still picky at 6, puts you in red-flag territory that needs to be taken seriously.

[31:09] (Jennifer Anderson) **Toddlers eating less is usually fine; rescuing the meal is the problem** — A toddler's falling appetite is not necessarily a problem: growth slows sharply after age 1, so eating less is a normal physiological change. But the moment parents panic and pull out chicken nuggets, snacks and other hyper-palatable foods to "rescue" the meal, the child loses interest in plain food instead. What really warrants attention is a sudden shift in eating around age 6 — starting to ask about sugar content, abruptly eating very little, or a 7-year-old coming home from school saying "I'm too fat." These are not parental failures; they are the signal to find a professional.

[39:12] (Jennifer Anderson) **"Don't tell your mom" is the line with grandparents that cannot be conceded** — When conflict with grandparents over snacks arises, Jennifer's approach is: first, expect to feel bad, and accept feeling bad; second, communicate through the channel the grandparents are used to, and offer concrete, cheap alternatives (buy a balloon, go to the zoo, rather than ice cream every time); third, when necessary, sit with the discomfort and set a hard boundary — she once told a relative that giving her child candy was fine, but "do not say don't tell your mom," and that was non-negotiable. She adds a further warning: comments about a child's body made to their face can affect them for life, and if the other person will not change, a short-term separation is safer than continuing to expose the child.

## Straight women's dating pessimism isn't melodrama — it's political rollback and economic dependence

**Sarah Jones argues that straight women's awkwardness and pessimism about dating men is both genuine feeling and performance, sitting on top of political rollback, economic dependence, and a reality that social media amplifies.**

why listen: The episode digs into the phenomenon of ‘heteropessimism’, separates the performance from the real feeling, and traces its political and economic roots — distinctive value for anyone trying to understand contemporary gender relations.

[1:52] (Sarah Jones) **Straight women hold fewer rights now than they did at birth** — Asked whether straight women are okay, Sarah Jones answers flatly: no. Romance is difficult to begin with; now it carries the added weight of economic inequality and political rollback. History does not progress in a straight line, she says, and people are working to make sense of that fact.

[34:15] (Sarah Jones) **Economic dependence makes moving out not a real option at all** — Sarah Jones spells out how economics blocks women from leaving unhealthy relationships. Her examples: moving in together sooner than planned because rent is unaffordable, marrying for health insurance, becoming disabled after marriage and needing a caregiver. Structural facts like these make ‘moving out’ a decision women can barely make — down to whether they can find a job, or take the pet with them. Economic inequality, she stresses, is central to why women can't get out.

[40:59] (Sarah Jones) **Men and women aren't opposed; the opposition narrative is the danger** — Sarah Jones warns that reducing the heterosexual predicament to men versus women is dangerous. Men and women are not really in conflict, she says; they are facing the same unfavorable cultural, social and economic reality together. That adversarial framing feeds the manosphere's zero-sum thinking — the belief that women's gains must come at men's expense. She worries that heteropessimism could inadvertently reinforce exactly that mistaken idea.

### verbatim quotes

### glossary

- heteropessimism: A pessimistic, embarrassed stance toward heterosexual relationships, usually voiced as self-deprecating humor.
- hopeful pessimism: A position that concedes a bleak reality but believes change is possible, and acts on that belief.
