**Henry I made his knights dismount and fight on foot, then used a hidden fourth division to ambush the flank and take his brother Robert prisoner, ending the struggle for Normandy.**

why listen: For listeners who like medieval political intrigue and military tactics; the early church dispute is a bit slow, but the tactical deployments and source criticism in the second half are the main event.

### points

[4:25] (Jamie) **The church dispute costs Henry two and a half months** — Henry had originally set May 3 to cross the Channel and invade Normandy, but was held up by an open conflict with Archbishop Anselm. Anselm, who had been on his sickbed one moment and recovered after eating a stolen partridge the next, kept raising his demands on Henry: return Canterbury's church property, pardon the fines on married clergy. Henry was forced to agree to everything, even making Anselm regent of England, before he could get him onto a ship. As a result the campaign started two and a half months late, and Count Geoffrey of Anjou was killed by a crossbow bolt on May 19, plunging Anjou into a succession crisis and costing Henry a key ally. This section shows how politics and military timing wreck each other.

[10:00] (Jamie) **Robert only had to hold his ground to win** — Henry had to attack; Robert only had to defend. But Normandy was already fractured from within: nobles warred with one another, western Normandy swung to Henry, and Robert could not even suppress the chaos in his own lands. Henry judged that a frontal assault would cost too much and decided to go the political route, turning Robert's allies one by one. This was precisely the grand strategy he later attempted: not to wear the other side down with sieges, but to end the war in the council chamber. This section provides the background for the later quick victory at Tinchebray: Robert's military strength was not weak, but political collapse left him unable to organise a unified line of defence.

[13:05] (Jamie) **The trap at Saint-Pierre is turned against its makers** — The abbot of Saint-Pierre came to Henry with his castle, offering to hand it over, and advised him to bring only a small retinue to receive it, saying the garrison was all willing to swear allegiance. Henry agreed verbally, then turned to his advisers and asked, "Isn't this too suspicious?" He immediately gathered 700 knights, rode 20 kilometres through the night, and arrived before dawn. The garrison had set a trap: Saint-Pierre held a large ducal garrison of 140 men, and Robert's relief force was about to arrive, intending to wait for Henry to walk into it. What arrived instead was an entire army. Henry, having been mocked, flew into a rage and ordered an immediate assault, even setting fire to the abbey; the garrison fled or burned to death. This section shows Henry was neither a hothead nor a puppet to be led by the nose.

[23:09] (Jamie) **Green wheat humiliation forces Henry to take personal command** — Henry sent Thomas of Saint John to build a siege castle outside Tinchebray, tasked with stopping William of Mortaine's troops from sallying out to raid. But after William entered the town with a large force and supplies, Thomas only dared hide inside his fortress. Seeing the other side would not come out to fight, William simply had his soldiers harvest the unripe green wheat outside the walls — good as fodder, but more importantly to humiliate Thomas utterly. When Henry heard, he flew into a rage, believing he had overestimated Thomas, and came in person with troops to tighten the siege. The result was that William really was trapped inside the town, able to send only secret letters begging for relief. This section shows the practical value of "humiliation" and "reputation" in medieval siege warfare.

[25:00] (Jamie) **A lesson in reading sources: Robert did not declare war** — Robert's warning letter has been paraphrased by some historians as "if you do not lift the siege, I declare war," as if Robert did not even realise the two sides were already fighting. But Orderic's original text says: Robert gathered his army and demanded that Henry lift the siege of his lands, otherwise he would challenge him to a decisive battle — which means something entirely different from "declaring war," suggesting Robert was well aware the two sides were already at war and simply desperately wanted to avoid facing his own brother in combat. Jamie specifically says he checked multiple translations and they all read the same, warning listeners not to trust second-hand paraphrase. This episode's awareness of source criticism is stronger than that of most history podcasts, and is one reason it is worth hearing.

[30:00] (Jamie) **Henry offers deliberately humiliating terms for partition** — Henry did not attack directly at first; he sent a letter full of moral blackmail: claiming he acted not from ambition but to protect the church and the poor; calling Robert a "duke in name only" who tolerated wicked men destroying Normandy. His terms were very specific: hand over all the fortresses of Normandy and all judicial authority, and give me half the duchy; you keep the revenues of the other half, and the English treasury will pay you an equal sum each year; you may enjoy yourself to the full, and I will do the work. To Robert, an old comrade-in-arms, this was a double humiliation — it also hinted at his refusal of the throne of Jerusalem and his God-cursed laziness. Robert's men, on hearing it, were furious and demanded to attack at once. Henry's rhetoric struck precisely at the most sensitive spot in Robert's camp.

[35:00] (Jamie) **Refusing the throne of Jerusalem becomes a fatal public-relations wound** — Robert had been offered the kingship after the First Crusade took Jerusalem, and he refused. Church authors such as Henry of Huntingdon interpreted this as laziness so great he would not even serve God, and said God therefore punished him in Normandy. Jamie points out this was extremely effective propaganda: Henry's camp repeatedly invoked "Robert's God-cursed laziness," so Henry's letter telling him to "go to feasts, hold games, enjoy yourself" was not a blessing but a poisoned barb. He also suspects this narrative likely came out of Henry's court. This case shows that in medieval warfare the war of opinion was as crucial as the war of arms.

[42:08] (Jamie) **The fourth division in ambush decides the battle** — At nine in the morning the horns sounded, and Robert's army, led by William of Mortaine, launched a fierce assault on the royal line; many were First Crusade veterans, and they at one point drove the royal lines back. But Henry had hidden a fourth division of more than 1,000 men far off on the flank of the battlefield, commanded by Count Helias, and they had not dismounted. They suddenly slammed into William's flank and killed 225 men in the blink of an eye. Robert of Bellême, who should have led the rear division in support, simply retreated, abandoning the main force and the duke. The ducal army collapsed and nobles were captured one after another. This was the first time Henry had truly taken the field and won, and he won through deployment and concealed positioning, not brute force.

## DNA repair is the secret to a long life: bowhead whale repair proteins are already in human trials

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-07-naturepod-长新冠或源于休眠病毒-dna修复或为长寿关键/
- show: Nature Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/naturepod/)
- original episode: Briefing Chat: Is DNA repair the secret to a long life? Whales and mole-rats offer tantalizing hints
- published: 2026-08-07 · duration: 13:52
- transcript: Machine transcription · 2381 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Research shows that in nearly half of hospitalised COVID-19 patients, dormant viruses in the body were reactivated, with higher inflammation and cell damage a year later; and what long-lived animals like the bowhead whale have in common is not tumour-suppressor genes but stronger DNA repair — drugs for it are already in human trials.**

why listen: Both stories challenge the intuition that disease comes from outside invaders: the real enemy may be something asleep inside the body, and repair capacity may matter more than natural gifts. Medium information density, worth a listen.

### points

[1:37] (Charmani) **Some viruses are never cleared, only held down** — Over a lifetime a person is infected by a great many viruses, but as long as the immune system is healthy, most infections are defeated. Some pathogens, however, are never fully cleared — they quietly lie dormant in the body, held in check by a healthy immune system. Once immunity is weakened, they resurface; many of the complications seen in people with HIV, for instance, are caused by reactivation of dormant viruses. Researchers therefore wondered: could a severe infection like COVID-19 also weaken the immune system and wake dormant viruses, becoming a source of long COVID? This hypothesis determines what has to be tested next.

[1:37] (Charmani) **Nearly half of hospitalised patients had old viruses revive, but causation is unsettled** — The team looked back at COVID-19 patients hospitalised in 2020 and 2021, testing blood samples, nasal swabs and lung fluid for reactivation of common viruses. Nearly half showed viral reactivation. After a year of follow-up, these people had higher inflammation levels, stronger immune-cell activity and more cell damage. But the study did not directly diagnose long COVID, and it is only correlational: COVID-19 may induce stress that triggers reactivation, and reactivation may then amplify the inflammation COVID-19 caused, forming a loop; or reactivation may simply be another symptom of immune exhaustion rather than a cause of long COVID. A phase 2 clinical trial is testing antivirals against herpesviruses, on the reasoning that if the reactivated viruses are themselves harmful, the therapeutic target should shift to those reactivated viruses.

[6:11] (Charmani) **DNA damage is not just carcinogenic — it is upstream of ageing** — DNA damage can mean a change in a base pair (A, C, G, T), or a change in the chemical structure of the base itself, such as the addition of an oxygen atom. It is not only the cancer-causing mutation people worry about. DNA damage is strongly correlated with ageing and is thought to underlie hallmarks of ageing such as inflammation, cellular senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction. Conversely, long-lived animals such as naked mole-rats and bowhead whales tend to have outstanding DNA repair capacity; bowhead whales live past 200 years and rarely get cancer. So researchers wondered: can we transplant their repair mechanisms to extend human healthspan?

[8:22] (Charmani) **The repair protein works when moved into human cells and fruit flies too** — Last year the podcast reported a clue from the bowhead whale: a protein called cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRBP), linked to extremely strong repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Double-strand breaks are the most destructive form of DNA damage. The bowhead whale's rare cancer seems to stem mainly not from the usual tumour-suppressor genes but from this repair capacity. More importantly, putting the protein into human cells and fruit flies works just as well, showing it does not depend on the whale's special environment. The question thus shifts from ‘why do they live long’ to ‘can we transplant this mechanism’ — and that is the most tantalising part.

[8:22] (Charmani) **Boosting only one repair system can sometimes make things worse** — It is far from that simple. Enhancing human DNA repair is an old problem, and the difficulty is that there are too many systems: about six major repair systems, which interact, overlap, and sometimes one system needs the product of another. When only one of them was boosted in the past, the effects seen were very limited, and sometimes it made things worse. So you cannot simply say ‘just switch the repair genes on’. We are still at the stage of figuring out how these species work, and of trying experiments in petri dishes.

[10:59] (Charmani) **The hope for longer life is in human trials, not supplements on the shelf** — The same team moved from bowhead whales to rodents: beavers can live 10 to 12 years, while mice may live only a few. They found that overexpression of an enzyme called Sirt6 is linked to longer species lifespan; human centenarians may also carry favourable variants of Sirt6. More practically, Fucoidan, a compound naturally present in brown algae, can activate Sirt6 and is already being treated as a potential therapeutic. A study is now giving Fucoidan to men aged 50 to 80 to observe the effects. But the researchers also caution: there is a lot of hype around NAD+-related supplements on the market, and not much evidence. The hope exists, but it needs to be verified in human trials, not cashed in by supplements.

### figures

### glossary

- dormant virus: A virus not fully cleared after initial infection, held in check by the immune system, which can reactivate when immunity weakens.
- double-strand break: A break in both strands of DNA at once, one of the most severe forms of DNA damage; failed repair can cause genomic instability.
- CIRBP (cold-inducible RNA-binding protein): A protein found in the bowhead whale, linked to enhanced repair of DNA double-strand breaks.
- Sirt6: An enzyme linked to DNA repair, metabolism and lifespan; overexpression is seen in long-lived rodents and some centenarians.
- Fucoidan: A natural compound in brown algae that can activate Sirt6 and is in human trials as a potential anti-ageing drug.
- NAD+: A coenzyme involved in metabolism and DNA repair; related supplements are hyped but clinical evidence is limited.

## The US-Iran War Burned Through the Ammo Meant for China, and Japan Is Preparing to Hold the Line Alone

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-07-chinatalk-美伊战争打光了打中国的弹药-日本开始准备独自扛/
- show: ChinaTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/chinatalk/)
- original episode: WarTalk: Out of Ammo for Real + Are CCAs Dumb?
- published: 2026-08-07 · duration: 1:17:54
- transcript: Machine transcription · 14701 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The US fired nearly all of its long-range munitions — stockpiled for a war with China — at Iran, is preparing to abandon its Middle East bases, and Japan is rewriting its defense strategy to hold out on its own for a while.**

why listen: Two defense analysts go item by item through munitions stockpiles, the strategic pivots in Japan and Australia, and the hard lessons of CCA drone wingmen. High information density, but you need a little military background.

### points

[2:09] (Brian) **The munitions used on Iran were the ones stored for China** — These long-range munitions — Tomahawk, JASM, El Razum — were stockpiled for a future great war with China. In the first months of fighting, 850 Tomahawks were fired, against a planned inventory of about 4,000 a few years ago; add earlier expenditures against the Houthis, and perhaps only two thousand or fewer remain. JASM and El Razum are essentially at zero, the Army's ATACMS is nearly gone, and its replacement, PrSM, is nearly gone too. At roughly 30 Tomahawks per surface warship, what's left can't even fill out the existing fleet, let alone reload it. The conclusion isn't "we can't keep fighting" — it's "we can't keep fighting without risking pilots," and we are no longer prepared for a conflict in any other theater.

[7:23] (Brian) **Iran switched to ballistic missiles and aimed straight at the US weak spot** — Iran, like Russia, shifted its main attack to ballistic missiles because they're cheap and the US has no cheap way to intercept them. The Navy's SM-2 is thirty-year-old technology: great against cruise missiles and drones, still plentiful in inventory, but it can't stop ballistic missiles. So you have to use SM-6 or PAC-3 — and those are essentially gone too, leaving Jordan and other places exposed to ballistic missile threats. Brian's judgment: every future adversary will have Iran's capabilities or better, because these technologies have proliferated. So long-range precision munitions are no longer optional; they're a necessity in every conflict. What's needed is lots of cheap long-range munitions, not a small number of exquisite ones plus a pile of ordinary bombs.

[17:42] (Brian) **The war ended up forcing the pivot to Asia** — Brian says the unintended consequence of this war is that it genuinely advanced the pivot to Asia: after it ends, US bases in the Middle East basically won't be rebuilt — according to Pentagon people he's in touch with, "we're not going back." Future operations in the Middle East will be mainly from the sea and air, expectations for the ability to intervene in regional affairs must be lowered, and missions like escorting shipping will fall more to allies. Iran's biggest strategic goal since 1979 has been to shrink the US presence in the Middle East, and after this round the US footprint is smaller, its ties to allies weaker, and Iran has de facto influence over strategic chokepoints like Hormuz. Brian's exact words: "This regime could not have asked for a better outcome."

[22:57] (Brian) **Japan is no longer just the US military's logistics base** — The preview of Japan's new defense strategy names China directly as a revisionist state, states plainly that a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency, and names Russia too while stressing China-Russia coordination. More critical is the execution level: heavy investment in unmanned systems, including one-way attack drones launched from shore and from ships, creating denial zones around the home islands — the so-called "porcupine strategy." This breaks the old understanding: the US military defends Japan, and the JSDF defends the bases the US military uses. The new strategy makes clear Japan must be able to defend itself, at least for a period, because the US may be tied down by China, may not be sufficiently motivated, or may simply have nothing left to spare. Japanese defense spending rises about 25% over the next few years, focused on unmanned and autonomous systems, new technology and space.

[30:30] (Brian) **Australia bet everything on nuclear submarines** — Japan is adding money; Australia isn't. Its investment plan says defense spending will increase, but apart from AUKUS submarines the real growth hasn't materialized — most of the increase goes to paying the US to stay in the program. Brian says Australia's "denial strategy" doesn't add up: the military is too small, it's unclear what it's denying, and in practice it relies on distance and on being a secondary theater to China's actions elsewhere. The submarine concept: if China hits northern Australia with ballistic missiles, Australia retaliates against the Spratlys with submarine-launched cruise missiles. But the cost is that the manpower side keeps shrinking, leaving only a small fighter fleet, a few tankers and AWACS, and a small army for border protection. If China sends maritime militia to surround Christmas Island, Australian ships have low readiness rates — one sortie would exhaust the entire fleet.

[49:10] (Brian) **Manned-unmanned teaming has proven to be a false premise** — Brian's wargames at the Naval War College with senior Navy leaders produced two conclusions. First, forward-deploying a "bespoke force" of large numbers of autonomous systems is extremely costly: it takes land, people and money — possibly billions of dollars a year — whereas the traditional model is to spend money building a ship or a squadron, sail it over when needed, and bring it back when not. Robots are slow, short-ranged and can't self-deploy, so the rotation model can't be copied. Second, manned-unmanned teaming basically doesn't work: a robot is valuable precisely because you can sacrifice it, but once it's alongside people, you have to protect the robot too; robots also slow down manned ships or need frequent refueling, leading to mutual sub-optimization. Only very narrow cases like decoys actually work.

[59:31] (Brian) **CCA was meant to save money and instead built another F-35** — The Collaborative Combat Aircraft was conceived as a "loyal wingman" and extra weapons bay. But the problem: it has to be as stealthy as the manned aircraft, or it gives away the manned aircraft's position; to find targets on its own it needs passive sensors on par with the F-47's; to launch from the same base it needs runways and long range. Add it all up and the cost rapidly approaches an F-35 — Brian's exact words: "Then you might as well build an F-35, except there's a robot inside." So the Air Force opened a separate program for the next batch of CCAs, letting them launch from different locations, not operate alongside manned aircraft, and only pass information over long distances. Brian says that no longer counts as manned-unmanned teaming — it's just a kill chain.

[1:06:50] (Jordan) **VCs fund the weapons; what's missing is people who know how to fight** — Jordan attributes CCA's detour to the absence of people genuinely close to the use case at the design stage: VCs will fund an idea that sounds interesting and maybe feasible, and then it just keeps going, without first doing wargaming and concept development with warfighters. He says some funds now require founders to have advisors, but the hard part is finding advisors who aren't just there for equity. Brian adds that this is why technologists need to be integrated with military planning early — he cites the IVAS headset as an example, saying it's obvious at a glance that no one who served designed it. Both agree that if CCA had been written into legislation from the start, with a promise to produce in 50 states, it would have become impossible to cancel.

### glossary

- CCA (Collaborative Combat Aircraft): The US military's envisioned unmanned wingman operating alongside manned fighters; this episode discusses its cost and stealth problems.
- AUKUS: The Australia-UK-US trilateral security partnership, with two pillars: the first is providing nuclear submarines to Australia, the second is cooperation on other defense technologies.
- standoff munitions: Precision munitions that can be launched far from the target, keeping the launching aircraft outside enemy air defenses.
- porcupine strategy: Using large numbers of dispersed unmanned and shore-based weapons to create denial zones that make an attack difficult.
- man-unmanned teaming: Having manned platforms and unmanned systems operate together in the same space; this episode argues it doesn't hold up in most scenarios.

who it is for: Founders, investors and policy researchers watching the US-China military balance, defense industrial capacity and allied strategy; anyone working on drones, autonomous systems or defense tech should especially hear the CCA segment.

## Don't Teach Your Kid Empathy — Show Them You're Listening

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-07-raisinggh-别只让孩子换位思考-要让他看见你在听/
- show: Raising Good Humans (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/raisinggh/)
- original episode: How to Disagree With Your Kids Without Fighting
- published: 2026-08-07 · duration: 55:22
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8663 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The key to teaching kids to disagree well isn't empathy or perspective-taking; it's proving with words that you're listening. The HEAR framework and the curiosity sandwich are usable right away.**

why listen: The guest is an empirical researcher who directly dismantles the usual "empathy" advice; the second half gives a replicable HEAR framework, suited to parents talking with adolescents at the dinner table.

### points

[4:56] (Julia Minson) **Well-intentioned moral righteousness is freezing family conversation** — She starts with something from her own home: her daughter stopped her from saying "I'm so OCD" because it offends people with OCD. Her daughter was actually defending a friend who wasn't there, out of a strong moral impulse. The trend comes from good intentions but has unintended negative consequences: many topics become off-limits, conversation freezes, real parent-child concerns go undiscussed, and judgment accumulates on both sides. The point isn't that kids are bad — it's that moral righteousness, without practice, makes family members afraid to speak.

[10:29] (Julia Minson) **Making people try harder to empathize barely works** — Her experiments randomly assigned people to "shift your mindset," "try harder to empathize," or "take the other person's perspective," and the results were almost no different from the control group. One reason is that in a disagreement we assume we're right and that we've already granted the other person plenty of latitude; after genuinely running through the other side's position, we often end up more certain they're stupid. Another reason is that "trying to listen" is invisible from the outside — the other person just sees you zoning out. So the key is making the processing visible to the other person.

[16:20] (Julia Minson) **Listening that isn't said out loud didn't happen** — The effective move is to prove with words that you're listening. When you want to understand the other person, verbally flag your curiosity and willingness to learn, e.g.: "It sounds like we disagree on this, and I really want to know your view; from where I sit, here's how I see it; but I know there are lots of different takes, so I want to understand where you're coming from." This doesn't mean agreeing with them, and it doesn't require giving up "I might be right." If the other person's position is very strong, you can also just say it: "I'm pretty sure I'm right, but I want to hear why you disagree."

[19:32] (Julia Minson) **In a conversation, the kid holds more power than the parent** — Formal power is boss over subordinate, parent over child; but power in a conversation is different. A teenager can walk out of the kitchen and slam the door at any moment, and the conversation is over. So wanting the other person to stay in the conversation is itself a form of power; even if you're 100 percent right, once they cut off communication you've lost the chance to persuade. This explains why adults need to acknowledge the disagreement and express curiosity first, rather than leaning on "I've lived a few more decades than you."

[25:15] (Julia Minson) **Adults won't discuss these topics themselves but demand kids do** — She pushes back: grab any adult at random and ask whether they'd discuss genocide, trans rights, or abortion with a colleague, and 99% would say absolutely not; so why do we expect teenagers to dive enthusiastically into these extremely hard topics in front of their peers? The fix is to tie constructive disagreement to career aspirations — for example, the Kennedy School tells students outright: to make policy for the country, you have to be able to have this conversation. Harvard College has already turned her research into a required pre-orientation module for incoming freshmen, and the lab is also building a version for high schoolers.

[31:36] (Julia Minson) **Arguing in front of your kids is good; fighting is not** — She argues explicitly: you can argue in front of your kids, but don't fight in front of them. The difference is that the former models disagreement with curiosity — one parent says the daughter shouldn't go to a friend's house until her room is cleaned up, the other says it's been a busy week and she can play first and tidy up after — and what the kid absorbs is that a disagreement can be voiced and handled this way. Modeling how to ask questions, how to offer choices, how to ask about preferences should start when kids are very small, so that by adolescence the default setting is "I can talk with Mom properly."

[40:49] (Julia Minson) **We badly overestimate how extreme the other side is** — She cites research on "false polarization" and "perception gaps": when Democrats and Republicans report their own views and then guess the other party's views, people badly overestimate how extreme the other side is and underestimate how complex and nuanced its positions are. In a real conversation, people aren't caricatures. Media and social networks make money off inflammatory content, so the most extreme material is what gets pushed in front of you. This is also why "it's hard to hate someone up close" — once you meet the actual person and hear the full account, the sense of polarization comes down.

[46:05] (Julia Minson) **Swapping a few words can change where a conversation goes** — H is hedging: using words like sometimes, maybe, perhaps to lower certainty, which is usually more accurate and keeps the other person from being provoked. E is emphasizing agreement: find a shared value or shared concern first and put both of you back on the same side. A is genuinely restating the other person's view, rather than a perfunctory "I heard you." R is positive reframing: swap no, can't, hate for "it would be great if..." or "thanks for telling me," because people mirror each other's tone; using a positive tone is actually how you steer the conversation.

## Screening embryos isn't doing everything you can — it's moral coercion

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-07-grayarea-胚胎筛选-父母该为孩子做到哪一步/
- show: The Gray Area with Sean Illing (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/grayarea/)
- original episode: What does a parent owe their child?
- published: 2026-08-07 · duration: 27:47
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5312 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 1 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Genetic screening can lower disease risk, but its statistical significance is often overstated and it may worsen social inequality. Parents should aim for "good enough" rather than "optimal," and stay wary of commercial companies' moral coercion.**

why listen: It dissects embryo screening from both ethical and scientific angles, challenges the notion of "optimal parenting," and offers a value-pluralist perspective — illuminating for anyone concerned with reproductive ethics and the impact of technology.

### points

[4:30] (Sigal Samuel) **"Doing everything you can" isn't care — it's moral coercion** — The phrase in the listener letter — "shouldn't I do everything I can?" — touched the moral-optimization trap Siegel herself once fell into. She points out that this mindset loads parents with guilt and shame, especially when they face social scrutiny before a child is even born, as if they were already "bad parents." This sets the emotional tone for the discussion that follows.

[9:24] (Sigal Samuel) **Polygenic screening measures correlation, not causation** — Distinguish PGT-A from polygenic testing: the former is simple and long-established, screening for Down syndrome and sex; the latter is complex, involving traits influenced by thousands of genes, such as depression and IQ. Polygenic testing rests on correlation rather than causation, gene-environment interactions are unknown, and many researchers believe its predictive power is overstated.

[12:13] (Sigal Samuel) **"12% lower risk" doesn't mean you won't get the disease** — "12% lower risk" sounds appealing, but disease is a continuous spectrum, not an on-off switch. Lowering risk may only delay onset or reduce severity rather than eliminate it. For example, lower diabetes risk might mean shifting from diabetes to prediabetes, or onset a few years later. Consumers easily misread it as a "health guarantee."

[15:00] (Sigal Samuel) **Screen out the anxiety gene and creativity may go with it** — Traits like anxiety and obsessive-compulsiveness can bring suffering, but they are also linked to creativity and focus. Both Siegel and Noam say that even with a magic wand, they wouldn't want to eliminate these traits in themselves. So screening out "mental illness" genes may simultaneously forfeit potential advantages, which makes the decision more complicated.

[17:05] (Sigal Samuel) **One gene does more than one job — screen one spot, move the whole set** — The case for screening faces a scientific challenge: pleiotropy means one gene affects multiple traits, and our understanding of it is limited. If depression-related genes were widely screened out, other traits could be affected unexpectedly. The population-level consequences are unknown, and this is an important reason to oppose screening.

[18:19] (Sigal Samuel) **Once the price drops, it's the parents who don't screen who get coerced** — Polygenic testing is currently expensive — Orchid, for example, charges $2,500 per embryo, so testing 10 embryos costs $25,000. This could lead the wealthy to screen for smarter, healthier offspring, widening class gaps. More worrying still: once the price falls and the practice spreads, parents who don't screen may put their children at a disadvantage, creating implicit coercion.

[20:00] (Sigal Samuel) **A selected child may come to feel they are a disappointment** — If parents choose sex, a child may grow up to discover they are transgender, and feel that the parents' costly sex selection is a burden — even that they are a "disappointment." This knowledge can bring new psychological weight and add complexity to the parent-child relationship.

[23:09] (Sigal Samuel) **The standard for a good parent is good enough, not optimal** — Borrowing Nobel laureate Herbert Simon's concept of "satisficing," Siegel suggests parents choose "good enough" rather than "optimal." For example, preventing fatal Tay-Sachs disease is reasonable, but pursuing "high IQ, blue eyes" is excessive. This offers a practical framework for ethical decisions.

### glossary

- PGT-A / preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy: Screens for abnormal chromosome number, such as Down syndrome, and can also identify sex.
- polygenic testing: Assesses complex traits influenced by multiple genes, such as depression and IQ, but with limited predictive power.
- pleiotropy: One gene affects multiple traits, so screening may produce unknown knock-on effects.
- satisficing: A decision strategy of choosing "good enough" rather than "optimal," proposed by Herbert Simon.

## Her Studio Contract Locked Her Weight: Gain and You're in Breach, Diet and You're Dead

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-07-cautionary-制片厂的合同里写着-女演员的身体不得改变/

- published: 2026-08-07 · duration: 41:39
- transcript: Official transcript · 4737 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In the 1920s, the actress Molly was benched by her studio for gaining weight and ended up on an operating table; in the 1990s, the bride Mary died from the diet drug fen-phen. When the body becomes a commercial asset, punishment and shortcuts lead to the same place.**

why listen: The dual narrative uses specific contract clauses, surgical details and litigation figures to expose the commercial coldness behind body standards; the conclusion is a touch restrained, with the real informational payoff concentrated in the middle.

### points

[1:21] **The contract locked down her body** — In 1920s Hollywood, the big studios controlled production, distribution and theaters, and treated actors as assets on the balance sheet. Molly's contract specified working hours, exclusivity, and one special clause: as long as she wanted to work, she had to keep the same bodily contours forever. When her body changed naturally, the studio invoked the "facial and bodily disfigurement" clause, treated adolescent weight gain as breach of contract and stopped her pay. The contract gave commercial power a legal basis to intervene in the body — that is the foundation of the whole episode's narrative.

[11:43] **The ultimatum: slim down or you're out** — Production manager Al Rockett summoned Molly and delivered the ultimatum: you can get as fat as you like, but the studio won't use you until you get down to the "correct size." At the time Molly weighed only about 20 pounds more than the average screen actress of her height. She wasn't indulging herself — she was a teenager still growing, and always hungry. But 1920s aesthetics demanded the pencil-thin flapper figure. The punishment cut off her income directly and forced her to comply.

[15:56] **A twelve-week deadline to lose weight** — The studio gave Molly twelve weeks to restrict calories and fit back into her old costumes. In the industry of the day, Lila Lee drank only orange juice and lost eight pounds in under two weeks, and Vilma Banky had to lose fifteen pounds before she was hired. The press publicly humiliated Molly's "solid flesh," even inventing a rumor that she wanted to lose weight by catching influenza. Fans wrote letters of protest, but the studio was unmoved. What this shows is systemic pressure: not one person's judgment of her, but an entire industry's standardization.

[19:03] **The diet black market: from tapeworms to thyroxine** — The 1920s "diet craze" spawned a flood of dangerous products: laxative chewing gum, slimming corsets, soaps claiming to dissolve fat. More extreme still were swallowed tapeworms, and Rido Fat, an over-the-counter drug containing concentrated thyroid extract — in 1926 a dieter who overdosed on it quickly developed heart disease and died at 33. Molly tried and still couldn't fit into her costumes, so she turned her gaze to surgery.

[25:18] **Surgery: ten pounds of fat cut away** — Molly found the star surgeon Robert Griffith to perform a lipectomy. The doctor made long incisions at her hips and legs, scraped away about ten pounds of fat, then pulled the skin tight and stitched it. Anesthesia was primitive, there was no penicillin, and open wounds were highly prone to infection; two years earlier a woman in Paris had developed gangrene after similar surgery and had her leg amputated. After the operation Molly looked slender, but was so weak she needed crutches. She satisfied the studio, but paid with her health and her comeback.

[29:23] **Millions of fen-phen prescriptions** — After lawyer Alex MacDonald took on Mary's case, he discovered millions of fen-phen prescriptions being written every year, meaning millions of people — the vast majority women — were sitting on a medical time bomb without knowing it. Mary had taken it for only 23 days, and the damage was already permanent. The Mayo Clinic later confirmed dozens of cases of a rare heart condition linked to fen-phen, and the FDA pulled the drug in September 1997. The companies chose to conceal the risk reports they received in order to protect profits.

[35:31] (Tim Harford) **Not vanity — the decisions were rational** — Tim Harford's conclusion is that Molly's and Mary's decisions were not vanity or naivety, but entirely understandable. Molly's employer was the source of her income and demanded she get thin; Mary's specialist recommended fen-phen to her. They trusted people who seemed to know what they were doing, and ran into a ruthless commercial logic. Technological shortcuts persist today: GLP-1s have real health benefits, and Brazilian butt lifts can kill. We treat body diversity as a bug rather than a feature, rewarding fast visible change regardless of the cost.

## AMD buys Talus: burning AI models into silicon, 17,000 tokens per second

**AMD has acquired Talus, a startup that builds chips customised for specific AI models and hits 17,000 tokens per second. It marks AI inference moving toward non-programmable, model-specific silicon.**

why listen: This episode surfaces a new trend in AI chips: model-specific silicon. For readers tracking AI infrastructure and chip investment, it is the key signal for understanding where inference cost and performance will inflect.

### points

[1:05] (Host) **Talus's founding idea: burn the model into the chip** — Talus was founded by Ljubisa Bajic, the founder of Tenstorrent, and its core concept is burning an AI model directly into the chip, producing non-programmable custom silicon. The idea drew scepticism at launch, because models iterate fast and custom chips can go obsolete quickly. But Talus argues that even if a chip only works for one specific model, its 100x speedup is enough to offset the cost of replacing it.

[5:09] (Host) **Hardcore One: 53 billion transistors, 17,000 tokens/s claimed** — Talus's first chip, Hardcore One, is built on TSMC's 6nm process, is close to reticle size, packs 53 billion transistors, and draws at least 300 watts. On Llama 3.1 8B it claims 17,000 tokens per second, far above Nvidia H200's 230, Groq's 600 and Cerebras's 2,000. That figure was verified in a demo, where it actually reached 14,200 tokens/s.

[8:13] (Host) **AMD keeps Talus as an independent team under Boppana** — AMD has signed an agreement to acquire Talus. The team will report to AMD AI head Vamsi Boppana and will keep operating as an independent team. Ljubisa previously worked at AMD and knows Jim Keller, so the acquisition can be seen as a homecoming. The deal value was not disclosed and is expected to close by the end of the year.

[10:16] (Host) **Talus slots into AMD's mix-of-chips AI strategy** — AMD CEO Lisa Su stresses that AI deployment is a mix of many kinds of chips. Talus's chip suits the small-model calls inside agentic AI, complementing AMD's Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs and the rest. AMD already partners with Cerebras, but Talus's model-specific nature offers another option.

[12:17] (Sally Ward Foxton) **Sally Ward Foxton: all-SRAM, best paired with a GPU** — Sally Ward Foxton argues Talus resembles Groq in using an all-SRAM architecture, needs multiple chips to support large models, but is well suited to handling the decode portion alongside a GPU. She says the acquisition is not surprising, because Talus's software stack requirements are low and the technology is distinctive.

[14:18] (Sally Ward Foxton) **The price guess: billions, because Nvidia reset the bar** — Sally guesses the acquisition price could be in the billions of dollars, because Nvidia's $2 billion deal for Groq pushed up valuations across chip startups. ## The Church Used "Forgive and Forget" to Handle Sexual Abuse, and Victims Were Told to Stay Quiet

**A closed Minnesota sect wrote "forgive and forget" into its official guidance, letting sexual abuse be absorbed internally and kept out of the justice system. A prosecutor handed the case to a reporter, and only then did a systemic cover-up spanning three generations come to light.**

why listen: A complete narrative of investigative reporting, with medium information density. Worth listening to for anyone wanting to understand how religious institutions use doctrine to dissolve accountability, and how investigative journalists pry open closed communities.

### points

[1:01] (Jessica Lussenhop) **The prosecutor reached out to a reporter himself** — Minnesota prosecutor Mike Ryan proactively contacted ProPublica reporter Jessica Lussenhop about a child sexual abuse case he was handling. The case took place in a church community called OALC (Old Apostolic Lutheran Church). Ryan said the defendant was a popular member of the church, the abuse had continued for years and was almost an open secret, and some of it even happened on the pews during services. Victims or their families had reported it to church leaders, but the church suppressed it. He suspected there were more sexual assaults in the church that he and the police had not discovered. According to church doctrine, if you ask another believer for forgiveness, the sin is washed clean, as if it never happened. If a victim brings it up again, that is "refusing to let go" and "having an unforgiving heart," and the responsibility falls back on the victim. The reporter obtained an official OALC document titled "Guidelines for the Prevention of Violence, Harassment and Sexual Abuse and the Handling of Such Incidents," which described a process of "talking with the victim alone, talking with the perpetrator alone, talking with both together," which the reporter called a "forgiveness session." The document says to respect the law and authorities, but never states "report to police under mandatory reporting law."

[21:58] (Jessica Lussenhop) **The pastor admitted he knew, but said he kept silent** — The reporter obtained police video of pastor Daryl Brucklemyer. In the video he calmly admitted knowing about Massey's sexual abuse, and when the investigator said six victims had mentioned his name, he asked, "Who's the other one?" The investigator asked whether he understood Minnesota's mandatory reporting law, and he said, "No one ever discussed it with us." But the reporter found a recording of another call three years earlier in which the investigator read him the state law point by point, and he said he understood it. When pressed on why he did not report, he said: "As part of the church, we keep silent." He said victims and families could go to law enforcement themselves, and that the church had also warned Massey to stay away from the church's children.

The stories Andy heard were identical to Duluth's: the pastor knew, everyone knew the perpetrator, but it was all handled internally through "forgiveness sessions." [32:23] (Jessica Lussenhop) **The girl who disembarked in 1951 already carried the wounds** — Andy reached a former church member, Terry Lee Martinin, whose grandfather brought the first OALC church from Finland to Canada in 1951. ## The FCC Used a Blunt Rule to Shut Chinese Robots Out

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-chinatalk-fcc-用一份笨规则-把中国机器人挡在门外/
- show: ChinaTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/chinatalk/)
- original episode: The FCC's New Robot Rules
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 51:44
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7874 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The FCC put mobile robots on the covered list, barring all new models from import. The reason isn't technological superiority — it's that supply chain dependence gets harder to fix the longer you wait, so a crude rule beats a finely tuned exemption.**

why listen: An FCC insider lays out the real logic behind the US robot import ban: it's not fear of robots rebelling, it's fear of repeating the Huawei-style supply chain dependence. Medium information density, but the mechanism is explained thoroughly.

### points

[3:23] (Adam Chan) **The covered list is not a sanctions list, and the FCC can't change it alone** — The FCC's covered list is not the same as the OFAC sanctions list or the BIS entity list: the FCC has no authority to update the list itself. Another national security agency or an interagency body must make a determination first, and only then can the FCC update and enforce it. Devices on the list cannot get import or marketing authorization. The FCC doesn't just regulate spectrum and broadcasting — nearly every electronic device that emits radio frequency must pass FCC certification before it can be imported, marketed, or sold. That little FCC logo is the tool, and it's also the switch that can cut off new models at the border.

[5:28] (Adam Chan) **Robots are the only bet that hasn't taken shape yet** — Adam sorted the FCC's recent covered list actions into categories: undersea cables, telecom, and drones all have clear industries and demonstrated impact, while mobile robots are still a very early industry. His read is that there are good reasons to see this action as staking out position five years ahead of time. The driver is the lesson from telecom networks in 2019 and 2020 — at the time, US domestic telecom networks depended almost entirely on Huawei and ZTE equipment, forcing a large-scale rip-and-replace. The US government's thinking now is: don't let the same thing happen again in a critical industry like robotics.

[10:40] (Adam Chan) **A crude rule moves faster than a finely tuned one** — Facing the charge that this is too blunt, Adam's response is that simple, even dumb, rules are often the best rules. It avoids two things — naming specific entities, and the whack-a-mole problem that comes with writing complex definitions and long transition periods; at the same time it sends a strong signal to the market, drawing in capital and investment. He also acknowledges the tool will cause collateral damage, but argues it can be patched afterward: the drone definition was initially very broad, and a later determination exempted toy drones; the robot determination also builds in a conditional approval process that lets companies apply for exemptions.

[17:52] (Adam Chan) **The real risk isn't not being able to buy — it's not being able to build at all** — The host raises a sharp counterquestion: the choice may not be ‘Chinese robots vs. American robots’ but ‘Chinese robots vs. an American robot ecosystem that doesn't exist at all.’ Adam's answer has two layers: first, the cheapest and easiest moment to fix supply chain dependence is now, and the longer you wait, the more commercial incentives lock the dependence in; second, the covered list generally only affects new models, which amounts to a transition period of several years, not a sudden cutoff. His evidence: after the drone action there has already been more than five billion dollars of investment, over a million square feet of manufacturing capacity, and thousands of jobs; in routers, where there were originally zero domestic US manufacturers, dozens of companies have now committed to expanding production.

[22:09] (Adam Chan) **Research use and teardown practice both get carve-outs** — The rule builds in several categories of exceptions: imports and sales for US government use are unaffected; small-batch imports for product development can also continue. Adam mentions a specific scenario — some US counter-drone companies import foreign drones precisely to practice shooting them down, and as long as they meet other FCC rules and stay under the quantity cap, that's still allowed. He also mentions an exemption on the drone side: any drone or component on the Defense Department's blue UAS list gets a pass, and many of those are actually made overseas or in allied countries, such as Ukraine.

[25:22] (Adam Chan) **To get an exemption, you first have to hand in an onshoring plan** — The conditional approval process requires companies to submit an onshoring plan explaining how they intend to move production back to the US. Adam says the enforcement branch does not intend to hand companies a blank exemption to ‘keep producing overseas,’ even if the company has no obvious risk from an ownership or cybersecurity standpoint. He also gives a quantitative threshold: if it meets the ‘US domestic end product’ definition — assembled in the US, with 65% of components by value made in the US — that's enough, which also means some components can still be imported.

[31:42] (Adam Chan) **You don't need to believe in AGI to support this rule** — The host asks: how much would you have to believe in AGI to think this rule matters? Adam's answer is that most people should be uncertain about AGI anyway — humanoid robots could turn out to be a complete dud after 2027, or they could genuinely be crucial, and the rule means completely different things in those two cases. But he points out it holds up without the AGI narrative: mobile robots in warehouses and quadruped robot dogs for public safety don't need the kind of AI model we dream about to already play an important role in the economy, and mobile robots sourced from foreign suppliers pose a risk all the same.

[38:00] (Adam Chan) **Enforcement is already moving: a company lied about US manufacturing** — Adam says the FCC will stay busy on both the rulemaking and enforcement tracks. He gives one case currently under investigation: a company claimed on its application form that it manufactured in the US when it actually didn't, and the manufacturer listed on the form confirmed it had never heard of the company. The FCC is also dealing with drone companies that won't cooperate with investigations, and with behavior that may circumvent covered list restrictions through rebranding. The FCC also has a program called bad labs, aimed at the labs that do device testing for the FCC.

### verbatim quotes

[10:40] Adam Chan: "I think there's actually a strong argument in this case and other examples of sort of FCC policy of the sort of simple and stupid policy actually being the best policy whereby it allows for fast action."

[18:56] Adam Chan: "the least expensive and easiest time to address a supply chain dependency is right now. It's only going to get harder as these industries grow and as all the sort of basic commercial incentives are to continue to entrench the dependency."

[20:00] Adam Chan: "We've seen something like routers. Actually, there were zero entities that produce routers in America. But as of now, there are dozens of companies that have committed to actually expanding production of routers in this country."

[32:44] Adam Chan: "you don't need to be, have the sort of AI models that we can only dream of to, you know, have those play sort of significant role in the economy."

[33:51] Adam Chan: "if Unitree wants to set up a factory in the United States and produce robots, nothing is, nothing is stopping them under the FCC action."

[44:13] Adam Chan: "all the national security rules, um, and, you know, enforcement action, penalty, fine type things that we've brought have all been bipartisan, unanimous."

### figures

- Total FCC employees: about 1,200 [43:12]
- FCC budget: about $400 million [43:12]
- Investment attracted after the drone action: more than $5 billion [15:50]
- Component threshold in the US domestic end product definition: 65% by value made in the US [26:22]
- China's share of components such as magnets in the robot ecosystem: 99% [17:52]
- Public comment period for the drone rule: 30 days [41:08]

### glossary

- covered list: A list of equipment and services the FCC established under two laws in 2020 and 2021; listed devices cannot get import or marketing authorization.
- conditional approval: A process by which companies can apply for an exemption; they must submit an onshoring plan, and review is led by the Defense Department.
- blue UAS list: A list of drones approved by the US Department of Defense for sale to the military; those on it are exempt from FCC restrictions.
- bad labs: An FCC program targeting the labs that perform device testing for the commission.
- onshoring plan: A plan that must be submitted with a conditional approval application, explaining how production will be moved back to the US.

who it is for: Founders and investors watching US-China tech decoupling, hardware supply chains, and the robotics sector; policy researchers who want to understand how the US export control toolbox actually works.

## AI Didn't Kill Jobs — Herding Agents Is the Real Bottleneck

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-whatsnext-单个智能体再强也成不了团队-ai需要生产关系/
- show: What's Next｜科技早知道 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/whatsnext/)
- original episode: 贾扬清：我所经历的「人工智能已死」到「AI 颠覆世界」的数年巨变丨串台「声东击西」S10E24
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 2:10:08
- transcript: Machine transcription · 40316 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Jia Yangqing, from Caffe to two startups, looks back on fifteen years of AI: model capability is already sufficient, the bottleneck is how to make a swarm of agents collaborate like a human team, and he asserts AI hasn't brought mass layoffs — it's just the scapegoat.**

why listen: He is one of the few AI witnesses who spans academia, big tech and startups, and his judgments on agent organization and the layoff scapegoat carry strong information gain; the second half is especially worth hearing for founders and technical managers.

### points

[8:19] (Yangqing Jia) **The industry once declared AI dead** — Jia Yangqing first encountered the concept of artificial intelligence in 2005 and 2006 while looking for a graduate research direction, but at the time the entire industry had already declared the field ‘dead’, treating artificial intelligence as a historical concept; the more common terms were machine learning and pattern recognition. He recalls studying automation as an undergraduate and switching to pattern recognition in graduate school, when people believed the wave of artificial neural networks had passed and that more direct mathematical methods were needed to identify cats and dogs. It wasn't until AlexNet appeared in 2012 that AI returned to the center of the economy. This background explains why the later rise of deep learning was seen as such a huge leap.

[17:46] (Yangqing Jia) **Caffe was born from a GPU in a courier box** — During his PhD, because AI compute demands exploded, Jia Yangqing wrote the open-source framework Caffe. It started as a side project, because at the time there was almost no open-source code to reproduce AlexNet. He applied to Nvidia's academic hardware donation program, and they sent him a single GPU, packed in a courier box. Jia says that back then you received the package and assembled the machine yourself. That GPU drastically cut training time from 1 to 2 months on CPU, and also led Nvidia to establish a collaboration with Berkeley. Caffe later became a foundational open-source AI tool, and it gave him his first taste of the positive impact of open source.

[37:56] (Yangqing Jia) **AlphaGo didn't keep him, pay did** — For Jia Yangqing, AlphaGo beating Lee Sedol in 2016 was ‘a pretty big shock’, but his colleagues at Google Brain weren't surprised, because the model's predicted win rate never dropped below 50%. He admits he never imagined at the time that an algorithm for playing Go could upend every industry a decade later. Even so, he chose to leave Google and join Facebook, because Facebook was ‘more chaotic and vibrant’, more like undergraduates getting together to do things. Another very practical reason was ‘pay good’ — he had just had a child and was carrying a mortgage, so a bit more money was nice. This also reflects the pragmatism of Silicon Valley talent flow.

[50:28] (Yangqing Jia) **What he learned at Alibaba was guts** — In 2019 Jia Yangqing joined Alibaba Cloud, heading the computing platform business unit. Alibaba Cloud CTO Xing Tian told him: you can keep deepening your technology, but do you want to try spreading this technology across all industries? Jia believes Alibaba gave a technical expert a stage, and took a big risk. His biggest gain was ‘guts’: at Google and Facebook he was more like a good student producing perfect answers, while at Alibaba he faced problems from ‘half of China's internet’ and had to define the problems himself. The ability to handle complexity that he learned there was later applied directly to his startup, for example helping customers solve supply chain problems rather than just providing a software platform.

[1:05:05] (Yangqing Jia) **GPT-3.5 turned AI into a generalist** — Jia Yangqing recalls that when GPT-3.5 came out in November 2022, it was still a rough prototype and couldn't reliably answer math questions. But the whole industry spent months understanding its capability boundary, and the mindset shifted from ‘there's something to use slowly’ to ‘try it to death’. He says AI used to be ‘general technology, specialized products’, requiring domain knowledge to specialize; after large language models it became a generalist you can interact with in natural language. His startup idea actually came slightly earlier than GPT — he was already talking with partners in September and October — but the AI inflection point amplified demand for a new kind of cloud and GPU systems.

[1:28:38] (Yangqing Jia) **Don't copy big-tech frugality when you start up** — Lepton AI became profitable in its second year, and Jia Yangqing was very proud, but in hindsight he reflects that he could have been more aggressive. He brought the big-tech mindset of building a ‘solid business’ to his startup: valuing profitability, idle efficiency, saving money. But the task of a startup isn't profitability, it's growth; when the rocket is taking off you shouldn't be calculating fuel efficiency. He says the untold context of decisions differs between big tech and startups — for example, idle resources are a huge waste in big tech, but in a startup with rapid business growth, idle resources quickly get filled. This reflection resonates with many people who leave big tech to start companies.

[1:37:56] (Yangqing Jia) **A bunch of agents isn't a team, it's a gang** — Jia Yangqing's motivation for his second startup came from seeing that a single agent is already smart enough, but multiple agents without a good coordination mechanism are an ‘agent gang’ rather than a team. AI agents slack off like humans: for instance, if they can't iterate to a result they suggest recording the requirement as a to-do item, and the review agent will also say ‘you have a point’. He believes a verifiable mechanism is needed, such as validating with business systems or simulated environments, rather than letting AIs chat with each other. What his new company wants to build is the organizational relationships between AIs, letting people define ‘what is wanted’ and ‘what counts as done’, and leaving ‘how to do it’ to the agents. This may be the direction that breaks through in the next 6 to 12 months.

[2:04:51] (Yangqing Jia) **In the layoff wave, AI is the scapegoat** — Facing the social backlash against AI, Jia Yangqing's view is somewhat unwelcome: AI has not brought mass unemployment the way the media portrays it — it's mostly speculation. He gives the example of a company like Brex (which does SRE) announcing layoffs because of AI more than half a year ago, but the more fundamental reason was that it pushed into crypto and doubled its headcount during the pandemic, and is now paying for earlier mistakes, with AI conveniently serving as a ‘plausible reason’. He also says any organization will find reasons for itself, and AI has become the scapegoat. He admits AI practitioners do pay relatively little attention to trust issues, and Silicon Valley's arrogant posture has intensified the antagonism, but positive changes exist too, such as electronic payments increasing trust between people.

## Three Trillion-Dollar Companies in Five Years, but the Next One Won't Come That Fast

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-nopriors-三位万亿公司五年内出现-但下一个不会这么快/
- show: No Priors (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/nopriors/)
- original episode: Chasing Trillion-Dollar Companies, Founder Ambition, Token Budgets, and Regulatory Capture with Sarah & Elad
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 39:29
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7824 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Three companies going from zero to a trillion-dollar valuation in five years is a historical anomaly, not a new normal. What's genuinely scarce isn't a big market — it's the speed to reach $50 billion in revenue within five years.**

why listen: Sarah and Elad give concrete judgments on the number of trillion-dollar companies, whether founders should sell, and how to allocate token budgets; the second half on regulatory capture is worth more than the first.

### points

[2:04] (Elad Gil) **Three trillion-dollar companies in five years is an anomaly, not a new normal** — Elad points out that over the past five years Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX each went from near zero to a trillion-dollar valuation, whereas historically SpaceX from the early 2000s and Google from the 90s followed a 15-to-20-year arc. He thinks many people now assume another batch of trillion-dollar companies will emerge within three to five years, and that this doesn't hold. He can think of "maybe one more" himself, but refuses to say which. Sarah pushes back from the other side: what she encounters more often is investors lacking imagination, valuing AI companies on old per-seat, per-lawyer TAMs, when coding has already proven that consumption and value can grow 100x.

[6:06] (Elad Gil) **A trillion-dollar market needs $50 billion in revenue, not a big TAM** — Elad reframes the question from "is the TAM big" to "where is there a revenue stream of $50 to $100 billion for a single company." He mentions a blog post he wrote in 2010 about how hard it is to reach a $10 billion market cap, a number that today is just some neolab's seed round. His judgment: plenty of companies can reach $5 billion or $10 billion in revenue, very few can reach a trillion — that's an order-of-magnitude difference. Sarah adds the key distinction — people conflate market size with speed of arrival; what she doubts isn't the size of markets like energy or robotics, but whether physical-goods companies have enough footprint to get there that fast.

[8:08] (Sarah Guo) **The best founders are building small businesses out of fear of the labs** — Sarah observes two things happening at once: in the mid-to-late stage market, investors keep betting on "can reach a trillion" speed, and she doesn't believe that speed exists; meanwhile a cohort of very strong founders is turning to niche markets because there's far less fear of neolabs and far less head-on competition. She names Harvey, Open Evidence, Decagon, Sierra and Cognition as companies that at the time entered large markets that could plausibly appear on a lab's roadmap. Elad pushes this further: what worries him isn't the median founder, it's that the best founders are turning timid — a shift in the trend line, and in his view a negative signal.

[10:32] (Elad Gil) **Every company has a 12-to-18-month window to sell at its best price** — Elad's framework: a tiny handful of companies (he names Anthropic and OpenAI) should absolutely not sell anytime soon; but most companies in any era should at least consider selling, and there's usually a 12-to-18-month window in which the company is worth the most it will ever be worth. He cites Ben Horowitz's practice — a pre-scheduled annual board meeting whose agenda is to ask, unemotionally, "should we consider an exit in the next six months," driven by process rather than by the founder or an investor. Sarah adds a new question: are you capturing value on the curve of falling costs and rising capability, or are you on the wrong side of it? If the latter, and you have no plan to get to the other side, you should sell.

[14:14] (Elad Gil) **Raising will get easier; your real cost is your time** — Elad judges that because a few three-trillion-dollar-scale companies rose so fast, a lot of VC capital is flowing back, funds are getting bigger, and the money has to be deployed, so valuations will keep rising over the next year or two and raising will get easier rather than harder. He therefore shifts the decision's center of gravity from "can I raise" to "what is your company's true expected outcome" — don't listen to investors, the media or Twitter; sit down and do the math yourself, including future dilution and the number of years it will take. He stresses that the biggest opportunity cost isn't money but time: the cohort of founders from 2020 and 2021 who are still running companies that don't work five years later missed the entire AI shift. Sarah cautions that private markets can stay irrational for a long time, and that the ability to raise is equivalent to avoiding a margin call.

[18:17] (Sarah Guo) **RSI arrives every 18 months, and it's been arriving for five years** — Elad describes the restlessness inside the labs: code is basically solved by the end of the year, some kind of light RSI may arrive by the end of next year, models start training large parts of themselves, and early on it's mostly post-training. Sarah offers a counterpoint — her data is that a group of very smart and self-reflective scientists have felt, every 18 months for the past five years, that recursive self-improvement or ASI is 18 months away. She thinks extending from code to training code and data pipelines is easier to believe, but the hard part is how to collect data in unverifiable, more complex domains, and the accessibility of physical compute, which may be more of a limiting factor than algorithmic feasibility. She also mentions people from labs coming to ask her whether they should get married, because they don't know what the world will look like in 18 months.

[21:49] (Elad Gil) **Compute scarcity lets a few dozen researchers capture 80% of the results** — Elad proposes a "human power law": in any field at most a few dozen people drive most of the progress — breast cancer research, subfields of math, subfields of physics, the startup ecosystem — and AI research is no exception. When compute becomes the truly scarce resource, compute starts being allocated differentially to those people, and some labs have slowed researcher hiring unless the candidate clears an extremely high bar — because the bottleneck isn't the researcher's salary, it's the compute allocated to them. From this he draws out the concept of ROIT (return on invested tokens): given a token budget, who should get it and why. He also draws an analogy to internal tools teams, which have historically been starved of resources, and thinks this explains why "the death of SaaS" has been exaggerated.

[28:52] (Elad Gil) **California is pushing the whole ecosystem out** — On California's billionaire tax, Elad argues the bill is written quite broadly, and once passed it could be re-enacted and thresholds lowered in future years, and around 2028 there's also talk of adding an exit tax, effectively penalizing those who leave a second time. His judgment is that lawmakers want this outflow to happen, and the two genuinely negative signals from California are this bill and ballot-harvesting-related measures. Sarah says she already knows quite a few people leaving now or planning to leave before the fall. She thinks the key to migration isn't weather but whether you can gather enough smart people doing the same thing — Boston was Silicon Valley's counterpart in the 80s, lost the competition in the early 90s, yet biotech is still there today. She names Texas, where an ecosystem around energy and hardware is forming.

[34:03] (Elad Gil) **Architecture isn't the variable; regulatory capture is** — Sarah presses on whether non-transformer architectures could change the landscape, and Elad's answer is: whatever the underlying architecture, the industry will eat all available compute and power, so the pressure toward more memory-efficient, more power-efficient architectures is greater than ever, but catching up to transformer at scale while matching hardware is still very hard. He offers two low-probability scenarios: some neolab secretly builds something better and uses it to raise more compute, or one person on a team jumps to Anthropic or OpenAI and the knowledge spreads — the latter being what has actually happened so far. He then cites an interview with Janssen of Janssen Pharmaceuticals on regulatory capture: drugs get more expensive and slower for two reasons — regulatory capture, and an FDA that looks only at risk and not at benefit. He worries the same structure will form inside the labs.

### verbatim quotes

[2:04] Elad Gil: "And so suddenly we had this massive inflection in terms of valuations of these companies. And I think a lot of people now are assuming that there's a bunch of other trillion dollar companies that will be formed in three to five years. And, you know, that's unprecedented in human history."

[6:06] Elad Gil: "You need a hundred billion of revenue or 50 to a hundred billion pretty easily. And so then the question with good margin, right? So then the question is, where are the 50 to a hundred billion dollar revenue streams for single companies?"

[8:08] Sarah Guo: "People are conflating the two things right now, in my opinion."

[10:32] Elad Gil: "It's like a 12 to 18 month period, usually where the company's worth the most it'll ever be worth."

[15:15] Elad Gil: "But the biggest opportunity cost is your time. Your most productive years of your life are on the line right now."

[19:17] Sarah Guo: "The data I have is that a number of very smart and even very self-aware research scientists have felt that, you know, there was some knee in the curve on recursive self-improvement or ASI 18 months away, every 18 months for the last five years."

[22:27] Elad Gil: "Which is a really interesting human power law, right? If you actually look at it in any field, there's at most a few dozen people who drive the field."

[36:10] Elad Gil: "70% of France is still nuclear in terms of its power generation. Right? 70%! Where are all the accidents? And where are all the kerfuffles? And nothing. Nothing's happened."

### figures

### glossary

- punctuated equilibrium: An evolutionary theory: long periods of stability interrupted by short bursts, which Elad uses as an analogy for technology waves.
- RSI: Recursive self-improvement: models participating in improving their own training, seen as a key step toward ASI.
- ROIT: Return on invested tokens: a term Elad coined for how a given token budget should be allocated and what return it yields.
- regulatory capture: When a regulator is swayed by the interests of the industry it is supposed to oversee, so that the bar ends up serving incumbents.
- exit tax: A tax on asset gains levied when leaving a jurisdiction; California is discussing adding one.
