## A billionaire's economic forecast is no more trustworthy than financial advice on short video

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-rationalreminder-亿万富翁的经济预测-和短视频里的理财建议一样不可信/
- show: The Rational Reminder Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/rationalreminder/)
- original episode: Barry Ritholtz: How Not to Invest | Rational Reminder 421
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 1:40:34
- transcript: YouTube captions · 16037 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 10 quotes matched verbatim, 11 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The halo effect makes people treat everything a successful person says as insight, but outside their own field they are just as ignorant; good advice is humble and probabilistic, bad advice is confident and specific.**

why listen: Ritholtz compresses decades of mistakes into checklists for spotting bad advice, valuation, concentrated positions and spending — high information density, worth listening to more than once.

### points

[5:14] (Barry Ritholtz) **The halo effect makes billionaires' forecasts look credible** — Ritholtz says billionaire economic forecasts have two features: first, like everyone else they talk their book — they hold assets so they are naturally bullish, and that bias cannot be avoided; second, most of them are simply not qualified to make economic forecasts. What is genuinely dangerous is the halo effect — people see someone who is extraordinarily successful in one field and extend the halo to everything he touches. But spoiler alert: they are not successful in other fields, they are just good at the one thing they are good at, and they are just as ignorant about the future.

[10:22] (Barry Ritholtz) **Good advice is humble and probabilistic, bad advice is confident and specific** — The tells for spotting bad advice: appeals to emotion (scaring you, stoking your greed, pushing FOMO), manufactured urgency (‘the market is going to crash in September’ is a huge red flag, not insight). Good advice tends to be both humble and probabilistic — ‘I don't know what's going to happen, but here are the various outcomes and their probabilities’. Bad advice sounds very confident and very specific. Ritholtz also offers the ‘3D’ framework: doubt (people with no self-doubt usually don't know their own blind spots), depth (a long track record backed by a repeatable process), Dunning-Kruger (not just overconfidence, but the degree to which you understand the boundaries of your own skill). The most expensive sentence for a novice investor is ‘how hard can this be’.

[13:25] (Barry Ritholtz) **The news is a daily beast that must be fed** — The media always has column inches to fill, newsletters and columns to write, 24/7 broadcast to air — but that unrelenting demand on your attention is fundamentally incompatible, on a time scale, with the investor's goal of letting a portfolio compound over years and decades. For a long-term investor, following the news isn't merely useless, it's negative — it damages your returns, because the media constantly pushes you to act, and people are born with an action bias; history tells us most financial decisions are not good ones, and the fewer decisions you make the better the outcome tends to be. Ritholtz cites new research by Henry Bessembinder: if you had bought at the inception of the S&P 500 and then done nothing, you would have significantly outperformed all the rebalancing, adding and trimming in between.

[15:26] (Barry Ritholtz) **The IRS had to issue 42 announcements to debunk short-video finance** — Ritholtz says the algorithm rewards the loudest, most extreme views, and this content is ‘financial junk food’. He gives two examples: first, the US IRS had to issue a 42-point press release debunking, one by one, 42 things on TikTok and Instagram — following them isn't just wrong, some get you fines, some get you clawbacks plus interest, some get you prison. Second, mothers' old saying: don't take candy from strangers. You don't know who the person giving you advice is, what their record is, what their method is, or whether they fly off the handle the moment something happens; taking advice from a rando on social media is financially the same as taking candy from a stranger.

[17:29] (Barry Ritholtz) **Gell-Mann amnesia: you know a source is wrong and still trust it** — Michael Crichton told a story: he read an article about an event he had personally lived through, and the reporter got it completely wrong — but he turned the page and believed what was on the next page. That is Gell-Mann amnesia — you see that a source is wrong in an area where you have expertise, yet you keep giving that source credit. Ritholtz's response is to build a list of sources he has verified over many years, but he stresses ‘that's my list, you have to make your own list’ — don't outsource your thinking. He also says the media on the whole does a good job reporting the news, but you need to be skeptical of exaggerated claims — extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof, and we often don't see that proof.

[30:41] (Barry Ritholtz) **Sturgeon's Law: 90% of financial products are crap** — Ritholtz says several of his favourite pieces of investing philosophy come from books. The first is Sturgeon's Law: when science fiction writer Ted Sturgeon was criticised for sci-fi being terrible, he replied ‘90% of everything is crap’. Ritholtz turns it into Ritholtz's Corollary — 90% of financial products are crap: most mutual funds are bad, SPACs are bad, most stocks are bad, and a lot of bonds are bad too. The second is statistician George Box's ‘All models are wrong, but some are useful’: a model is just a mathematical projection of the world, not a hologram, and every model has built into it the assumption that the future will look like the past, so when the future changes the model breaks. The third is William Goldman's ‘nobody knows anything’ — Hollywood passed on Star Wars, The Princess Bride and Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Keanu Reeves couldn't get a major studio to make John Wick, which went on to become a two-billion-dollar franchise.

[46:55] (Barry Ritholtz) **Expensive valuations are not a reason not to buy stocks** — Ritholtz says the most common mistake is: seeing high PE, CAPE or price-to-book and deciding to stay out of stocks. He asks in return — that judgment would have kept you out of US equities since 2015, and would have kept you out of large growth stocks for decades. Valuation is a ‘flexible snapshot’; what you should look at is the full moving picture. He concedes valuation has directionality — expensive means future returns below average, cheap means above average — but in 1977 and 1978 stocks were cheap, and buying in still took three or four years to turn positive, so it can't be used as a timing system.

[51:59] (Barry Ritholtz) **Your world is shutting down, the index is going up** — During the pandemic he was asked the same question over and over: restaurants, retailers, airlines and hotels around me are going under, so why is the market rising? He says this is classic availability heuristic — what you see is your own real-world experience, but the market is weighted by market cap. They went and counted: all those failing industries combined made up only about 6% of the S&P 500. And the S&P 500 rose about 69% from its March low over the rest of that year. Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Target and Walmart were fine, and so were the companies that could pivot to delivery. The same mismatch shows up today with AI: why is the market rising if we're all going to lose our jobs? He asks in return, how do you know we're all going to lose our jobs.

[55:04] (Barry Ritholtz) **All equity value comes from 1-2% of stocks** — Ritholtz cites research by Hendrik Bessembinder of Arizona's business school: almost all equity value is driven by 1% to 2% of stocks, with slight variation by region and country. So why do you think you can win at 100-to-1 odds, or to be generous, 50-to-1? His analogy is a plane going down with only one parachute, and the 1-in-50 chance is yours — you would not be happy. Conversely, indexing gets you into the top half of market performance over ten or twenty years, and the top quartile over 25 to 30 years. He cites Bogle: everyone is chasing alpha, but you can't get alpha without starting from beta; the index is the Christmas tree, and everything else is just ornaments hung on it.

[1:07:14] (Barry Ritholtz) **The danger of concentration comes from being forced to hold** — Ritholtz lists a string of companies that went to zero: Lehman, AIG, General Motors, General Electric. Concentrated positions arise in a few ways: founder stock, inherited stock with a low tax basis, ESOP shares granted by your company. He gives the GE example — the ESOP match, as he recalls, was around 15%, and the result was that employees' 401(k)s were 50%, 60%, 70% GE. His assessment of Jack Welch is scathing, calling him the most overrated CEO in history: he took over as the 1982 bull market began and left at the 2000 top, leaving behind an old industrial company trading at 47 times earnings and a brewing GE Capital accounting scandal, while the people who took over cleaned up the mess and took the blame.

[1:10:16] (Barry Ritholtz) **The price of not wanting to pay capital gains tax** — Many people refuse to sell a concentrated position on the grounds that ‘I don't want to pay capital gains tax’. Ritholtz's response: the way to make sure you never pay capital gains tax is to never have any gains. He gives Cisco: from its March 2000 high, it took 25 years to get back to break-even, having fallen 93% in between. He also notes that Cisco and Qualcomm in 1999 were hotbeds of this kind of conversation.

[1:33:39] (Barry Ritholtz) **Financial success is defined as freedom and optionality** — Barry defines portfolio success as freedom, opportunity, optionality — being able to create meaningful value for yourself and your family, and reducing the stress money causes. He was poor when he was young, and says the worst part of being poor isn't not being able to buy a nice car or watch, it's the endless stress at the bottom of Maslow's hierarchy: food, rent, insurance. Once you're past that line, you have to recognise that the marginal utility of every extra dollar is diminishing, and that income hits a plateau at some point.

[1:34:41] (Barry Ritholtz) **Comparison is the thief of joy** — Barry throws out the line he didn't put in the book and is saving for the next one: Comparison is the thief of joy. He calls social media a cancer, precisely because it makes comparison the norm. He offers a concrete exercise: if you want to make yourself miserable, open Zillow and look at what's for sale in the nice neighbourhoods closer to the water or downtown. His father-in-law built an 800-square-foot, three-bedroom, one-bath cottage in the Hamptons in 1961 — crude conditions but a wonderful experience: drop the dog and the luggage and head to the beach. Later, when they went looking for a vacation home themselves, they were stunned by sale prices of 40 million, 50 million, 60 million.

[1:36:42] (Barry Ritholtz) **Once you have enough, the hardest part is starting to spend** — Barry says the biggest challenge with clients who have already hit their number and entered the decumulation phase is getting them to spend the money. You've spent your whole life working and saving, and making that turn is very hard. The directions he offers include: give the inheritance away early, while you're still alive and can watch your kids enjoy it; or build a structure that lowers stress and means you no longer have to worry about it. He thinks that is everything a person can ask of a portfolio.

## Yo-Yo Dieting Doesn't Wreck Your Metabolism — Healthy Habits, Not Weight Swings, Decide How Long You Live

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-sciencevs-体重循环不毁代谢-健康行为比体重重要/
- show: Science Vs (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sciencevs/)
- original episode: Weight Loss: Why Won't It Stick?
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 39:39
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7002 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Weight cycling (yo-yo dieting) does not permanently damage metabolism, and for ordinary people the weight regained rarely means muscle loss; what actually shapes health and lifespan is the healthy habits themselves, not the up-and-down of the scale.**

why listen: It takes the claim that "yo-yo dieting wrecks your body" and tests it along four lines — metabolism, muscle, inflammation, disease — and the conclusion is more reassuring than intuition suggests. Suited to anyone worn down by repeated failed diets.

### points

[3:37] **Failing at weight loss nine times is not a willpower problem** — Research estimates that as many as half of American adults have experienced weight cycling at least once, and among people who weight cycle, the average is 8 times by midlife. Drummer John is on his ninth attempt at losing weight; he says he has gained and lost hundreds of pounds on and off over his life, and each regain makes him feel like he "succeeded and then failed," blaming his own self-control. But as the episode goes on to show, the hunger hormones and metabolic mechanisms in his body make it hard to keep the weight off, and they matter far more than willpower.

[12:47] **Your body claws the calories back below the level of awareness** — Researchers gave one group of subjects a diabetes drug that makes sugar exit in urine; the subjects lost calories and lost weight, and they had no idea. As a result, the drug group felt hungry sooner and ate more than the placebo group. This happened below the level of consciousness, showing the body automatically compensates for a calorie deficit. Holding your weight is like keeping a rubber band stretched taut — slack off even slightly and it snaps back.

[18:39] **Slowed metabolism is an extreme case, not the general rule** — The Biggest Loser study had 16 contestants lose about a third of their body weight on average, and six years later their resting metabolic rates were still about 500 calories a day below predicted — the equivalent of a Big Mac. But University of Copenhagen professor Faan points out that this group is extreme and the sample is too small. Meta-analyses show that for ordinary people metabolic suppression is on average very small, and may even fall within measurement error. So after nine cycles, John's metabolism most likely is not damaged.

[22:21] **There is no evidence cycling makes you fatter; the variable is age** — A North Carolina study found that 74% of the weight lost was fat, but 88% of the weight regained was fat, which sounds like muscle is being lost. A German study found no such difference. The key distinction is age: the former's participants were 50-70, the latter's were 20-40. People lose muscle as they age anyway, regardless of whether they weight cycle. Almost no studies follow people through more than one full cycle, so "each cycle makes you fatter" has no evidence behind it.

[29:49] **Mice return to their starting weight, but the immune system remembers** — Fat tissue contains large numbers of immune cells; when visceral fat cells die from lack of oxygen, macrophages come to clean them up, triggering inflammation. Alyssa Hasty put mice on a high-fat diet for 9 weeks to gain weight, then a low-fat diet to lose it, then high-fat again for 9 weeks. Compared with mice that stayed obese throughout, the cycling mice ended up with exactly the same body weight and visceral fat mass — but more T cells, and more "excitable" ones. She says the body remembers the weight swings. Still, this comes from mice on extreme diet switches, and the human evidence is murkier.

[34:20] **Regain it all and your diabetes risk is still lower** — Observational studies show people who weight cycle have higher risks of heart failure and death, but this kind of study cannot prove causation. The answer from randomized controlled trials: even when people in a supervised weight-loss program regained all the weight, their risk of type 2 diabetes was still lower than people who never tried, and their cholesterol and blood pressure were lower too. A survey of 12,000 people found that what actually predicted mortality was healthy habits — fruits and vegetables, exercise, smoking and drinking — not BMI. So regaining the weight is not wasted effort; the healthy behavior itself is protecting you.

### glossary

- weight cycling: The process of repeatedly losing weight and regaining it, known medically as weight cycling.
- visceral fat: Fat wrapped around the organs, more likely to trigger inflammation than subcutaneous fat.
- macrophage: A type of immune cell responsible for clearing away dead cells and tissue debris.

who it is for: People currently dieting or who have regained weight, and anyone scared off from trying again by the idea that yo-yo dieting is harmful; also for science readers who want to tell observational studies apart from randomized controlled trial evidence.

## The US Joins Japan to Intervene in the Yen: Selling Euros, Not Dollars, and Betting on a BOJ Hike

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-oddlots-美国为何联手日本干预日元-新工具与旧逻辑/
- show: Odd Lots (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/oddlots/)
- original episode: Brad Setser on the US's Unusual Japanese Yen Intervention
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 42:00
- transcript: Official transcript · 7088 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 2 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The US Treasury has unusually joined Japan in intervening in the yen, selling euros rather than dollars and drawing on the FIMA repo facility. Brad Setser argues the intervention works as long as the Bank of Japan raises rates, and that Japan's fiscal position is far better than America's.**

why listen: A deep dive into the new tools and motives behind US intervention in the yen, challenging conventional wisdom and offering a unique window into how currency and Treasury markets move together.

### points

[4:06] (Brad Setser) **What the BOJ fears isn't inflation, it's a return to deflation** — The Bank of Japan is raising rates slowly, with its short-term policy rate around 1%, while inflation has long been above that level. Its concerns include: not wanting to end the hard-won 2% inflation target prematurely and slip back into a zero-rate deflationary economy; and, on the technical side, that rate hikes push up bank deposit costs while banks hold large amounts of low-yielding assets, potentially hitting the banking system. There is also a market view that rate hikes raise government financing costs, though Brad thinks that worry is somewhat overstated.

[6:10] (Brad Setser) **East Asia piles up global surpluses, yet its currencies weaken** — Global trade surpluses are concentrated in East Asia. South Korea's current account surplus is set to rise from $100 billion to $300-400 billion, and Taiwan's surplus will reach 25%-30% of GDP, yet their currencies are broadly weakening. Taiwan's central bank has guided the New Taiwan dollar lower through regulatory loosening, while in South Korea a stock market rally triggered foreign ownership concentration limits, causing foreign investors to sell Korean equities and capital to flow out, compounded by pension outflows — a "good news turns into bad news" trap. The yen's weakness stems more from extremely low interest rates.

[12:20] (Brad Setser) **The US is stepping in to save the yen, but what it really wants to save is Treasuries** — Traditionally, weak East Asian currencies hurt US manufacturing, especially autos, but Bessent did not stress that. What concerns him is the overall pressure that yen weakness puts on Asia's currency system and the potential shock to the Treasury market. If the BOJ intervenes by selling Treasuries, it would add to pressure on Treasuries. A joint US intervention both supports the yen and reduces the need for Japan to sell Treasuries, thereby protecting the Treasury market.

[15:23] (Brad Setser) **Selling euros, not dollars, is a way of saying this has nothing to do with the dollar** — The US sold euros rather than dollars partly because Bessent, a former FX trader, wanted to "have some fun," but the more important signal is that this is not a view on the dollar's exchange rate but a purely yen-focused operation. By selling euros, the US shows it still supports a strong dollar while avoiding a direct dollar sell-off that markets could misread. It also makes the operation more flexible — for instance, conducting rate checks in the euro-yen market to create a surprise effect.

[19:29] (Brad Setser) **Japan would rather borrow against Treasuries than sell them, but the facility is too small** — The FIMA repo facility lets foreign central banks use Treasuries as collateral to obtain dollars from the Fed, avoiding outright Treasury sales. Brad was a proponent of this tool, arguing it can prevent the Treasury market from falling into a selling spiral during stress. But its rate is above market, and its size cap of about $60 billion may limit its effectiveness. Still, for Japan's Ministry of Finance, which holds high-coupon old bonds, using FIMA may be more advantageous than selling, because it keeps the bonds and earns the spread.

[23:30] (Brad Setser) **America's intervention ammunition can't sustain an exchange rate target** — The US Treasury's own ammunition is limited: the Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) holds about $20 billion in foreign currency and $20 billion in cash, plus roughly $160-170 billion in SDRs, but it is not unlimited. Setting a yen exchange rate target would require cooperation from Japan's Ministry of Finance and institutions like the GPIF — for example, adjusting pension investment guidelines so they hedge FX risk. But setting a fixed target is very risky: once the world changes (an oil price shock, a Fed rate hike), it may have to be abandoned.

[26:33] (Brad Setser) **Whether the intervention works all depends on a September hike** — Brad argues that if the Bank of Japan raises rates in September, the intervention will work; otherwise it will face a test. He rebuts Adam Posen's view that intervention is ineffective, pointing out that the yen is already severely oversold and fundamentals are improving: oil prices are not high, Japan's current account surplus is 5% of GDP, and long-term rate differentials have narrowed. The key is changing market expectations, and the Japanese government, as the largest holder of foreign exchange assets, has an enormous influence on the exchange rate through its behavior.

[32:41] (Brad Setser) **Shorting the yen means going long the worse fiscal position** — Japan's fiscal position is far better than the market perceives: its primary balance (excluding interest) is already balanced and even trending toward surplus, better than the US, UK, France and Germany. Although rising rates increase the interest burden, the Japanese government holds huge overseas assets whose returns can offset part of the cost. Net debt has been falling for five years, while US net debt will soon catch up. Brad argues that shorting the yen and going long the dollar is effectively going long US fiscal policy — and the US fiscal position is the worse one.

### verbatim quotes

[26:33] Brad Setser: "I think it will be enough if the Bank of Japan is going to raise rates and maybe raise rates several times. I think the only reason why it wouldn't be enough if the Bank of Japan is going to raise rates."

[37:45] Brad Setser: "Just always remember Japan is selling dollars at by between eighty and one hundred depending on when they bought it, and somewhere around one sixty. This and the worst you can say this operation. It reduces gross debt in a really big way."

### figures

- BOJ short-term policy rate: about 1% [4:06]
- Taiwan current account surplus as share of GDP: 25%-30% [7:13]
- Japan current account surplus as share of GDP: 5% [9:17]
- Japan foreign exchange reserves: about $1.2 trillion [9:17]
- Japanese government pension foreign assets: more than $900 billion [9:17]
- Japan GDP: about $4 trillion [9:17]
- FIMA repo facility size cap: about $60 billion [19:29]
- US Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) foreign currency assets: about $20 billion [23:30]

### glossary

- FIMA Repo Facility: A Fed facility that lets foreign central banks use Treasuries as collateral to obtain dollars, avoiding outright Treasury sales.
- ESF: The Exchange Stabilization Fund, the US Treasury's pool of money for FX intervention, limited in size.
- Primary Balance: Government revenue minus spending (excluding interest), a measure of fiscal health.
- Carry Trade: Borrowing in a low-rate currency (such as the yen) to invest in higher-yielding assets and earn the spread.
- Big Mac Index: A purchasing power parity comparison based on the price of a McDonald's Big Mac, used to gauge currency valuation.

who it is for: Investors watching currency markets and Treasuries, macro strategists, central bank watchers, and anyone studying Japan's economy and fiscal policy.
what to skip: The closing chit-chat between the two hosts (after roughly 38:47) can be skipped.

## 222nm lamps kill pathogens but sell only a few hundred a year — the bottleneck isn't the technology

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-06-complexsys-222纳米杀菌灯便宜有效-缺的是认知而非技术/
- show: Complex Systems (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/complexsys/)
- original episode: The economics of putting germicidal light in every room, with Misha Gurevich and Vivian Belenky of Aerolamp
- published: 2026-08-06 · duration: 1:16:20
- transcript: Official transcript page · 13520 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Far UVC uses 222nm light to inactivate pathogens in the air while leaving human skin unharmed; a South African TB trial has already seen 90% suppression, yet the world sells only a few hundred units a year. The real bottleneck is awareness.**

why listen: It lays out the safety mechanism, the cost structure, scaling and failure modes; the middle and later sections on building codes and the business case are especially worth founders' time.

### points

[3:25] (Vivian) **222nm is safe for humans because of a layer of dead skin** — The 200–235nm band of far UVC (especially 222nm) is absorbed by pathogens' DNA, RNA and nearly all proteins, inactivating airborne pathogens — equivalent to 30–50 extra air changes per hour. The reason it's safe for humans is mainly mechanical: human epidermis has a dead-cell layer about 20 microns thick, full of protein, that absorbs almost all far UVC; conventional UVC at 254/265nm lacks that strong protein absorption and shouldn't be exposed. The eyes are protected by eyelids, eyelashes and other structures, tolerate a lower dose than skin, but long-term damage risk is very low.

[9:24] (Misha) **A corner-mounted lamp is a proof of existence, not the final form** — Current products are mostly corner-mounted because the beam angle is narrow, and firing from a diagonal maximizes path length and average dose. The emitter is only about 100 milliwatts, decaying to near zero at the other end of the room; but the dose needed to kill is very small. Misha calls the current lamp a "proof of existence": there's no insurmountable technical or logistical obstacle, ordinary people can buy and install it, and in the future it becomes an ordinary ceiling fixture. The real obstacle isn't cost or regulation — it's that too few people know about it.

[13:55] (Vivian) **Elementary schools need it most, but workplaces get it first** — Vivian thinks the biggest payoff is probably elementary/middle schools: ventilation is usually poor and children's immune systems aren't mature; but parents demand high safety, schools are conservative, and workplaces, long-term care centers and hospital waiting rooms will go first. The economics: each lamp covers about 250 square feet, a normal classroom needs 2–3, a university needs hundreds; a small building costs only four to five figures for the whole thing, a large building reaches six figures; professional installation costs about as much as the lamps. Patrick adds that waiting rooms have high foot traffic, so any one person's cumulative dose is low, but total dwell time is very high.

[23:24] (Vivian) **TB is the most UV-resistant, yet its transmission has been cut 90%** — Preliminary results from the South African TB ward trial have already seen 90% transmission suppression: guinea pigs were exposed to patients only through the air. Tuberculosis is not especially sensitive to far UVC, with roughly 10 times the resistance of influenza/coronavirus, so the effect on common respiratory viruses may be even better. TB hotspots and nursing homes will be among the first sources of strong evidence. Vivian says pandemic prevention is the most exciting scenario: the more transmissible the pathogen, the bigger the leverage of environmental intervention; old-style UVC once successfully controlled measles with R0≈20, so pushing R from slightly above 1 to slightly below 1 is enough to avert a pandemic.

[34:23] (Vivian) **Once it's in building codes, UVC is the cheapest path to compliance** — ASHRAE 241 is currently the only infection-prevention standard, but it hasn't yet been widely adopted by any jurisdiction with authority; once it's written into building codes, UVC becomes the cheapest way to comply and enters the existing building stock on a ten-year renovation cycle. The alternatives don't suffice: upgrading HVAC in existing buildings is often impossible or extremely expensive; portable filters (MERV 13 is enough) work, but pathogens are only one of many air pollutants and need to be used alongside UVC. In high-density large spaces like auditoriums and gymnasiums, meeting clean-air standards through ventilation alone is basically cost-infeasible — you have to use UVC.

[42:33] (Misha) **Lamp prices can fall like LEDs, but adoption doesn't depend on price** — The best emitters today are made by a single Japanese company, with a high-margin business model; even if you cut all profit, a single emitter costs 15–20 dollars, and manufacturing uses hydrofluoric acid gas, making it harder to scale than LEDs. The end market is still tiny; some sell lamps for 2000 or even 3500 dollars, AeroLamp prices at 500 dollars, targeting around 100 dollars within a year or two, with no technological innovation required. Patrick judges that going from a few hundred units a year to a billion-dollar market, unit prices will fall as fast as LEDs; Misha cautions that falling prices won't automatically change willingness to deploy — information is the bottleneck.

[47:35] **Whether home use is worth it depends on whether disease spreads at close range** — Misha thinks ordinary households don't have much transmission, 500 dollars isn't worth it, and 100 dollars is justifiable; Vivian counters: she just had a baby, keeps two lamps at home on during gatherings and when guests come, and once a baby gets a fever it's the ER, hospitalization or even a spinal tap — preventing a few illnesses pays for itself. Behind this disagreement is the biggest failure mode: if most common illnesses spread mainly at short range within two feet at high dose, environmental intervention can only do so much, reducing severity rather than preventing infection; but even then, lowering viral load may make the course of illness milder.

[1:06:04] (Misha) **The first money should buy global awareness, not more lamps** — Misha thinks the first money should go to building global awareness: the world may sell only a few hundred lamps a year, and almost no one has heard of 222nm. Vivian leans toward formal trial deployments, arguing that hype can backfire and expansion must be responsible; Paris Hilton is a better spokesperson than Taylor Swift. The commercial shortcut doesn't require convincing the public: companies have already internalized the cost of sick leave and caregiving absences, companies like Google have people dedicated to employee health, and they'll install once the math is clear; building owners can decide unilaterally, bypassing the "blocker veto."

And this is very important, because the fact that it's so heavily absorbed by proteins is a thing that makes it much safer than other germicidal UV wavelengths."

### glossary

- far UVC: Ultraviolet light at 200–235nm, mainly 222nm, absorbed by proteins, germicidal and safe for human surfaces.
- krypton chloride excimer lamp: The main current far UVC emitter; its manufacturing process is more complex than LEDs and requires hydrofluoric acid gas.
- ASHRAE 241: An indoor infection-prevention standard set by the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers, not yet widely incorporated into building codes.
- R0: The average number of people one infected person infects; above 1 it spreads exponentially, below 1 it dies out on its own.
- hygiene hypothesis: The idea that being too clean causes allergies and asthma; the modern version holds that immune training comes from environmental bacteria, not from actually getting sick.

who it is for: Founders working on respiratory disease prevention, building/HVAC professionals, hospital operators, and parents who want to upgrade the air in their kids' schools.

## The USSR Forged Women Into Superhumans and Spoiled Men Into Wrecks

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-05-tyler-苏联把女人炼成超人-把男人宠成废物/
- show: Conversations with Tyler (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tyler/)
- original episode: Julia Ioffe on Russian Women, Missing Men, and the Roots of Autocracy
- published: 2026-08-05 · duration: 55:14
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9327 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**After World War II killed 27 million Soviets, men became a scarce resource; the state used abortion bans, rewards for out-of-wedlock births, and the decriminalization of domestic violence to forge women into superhumans and spoil men into wrecks — an order that still underpins Putin's patriarchal mobilization.**

why listen: Ioffe uses family history to connect Russian women and population politics, explaining the roots of Putin's war propaganda and the decriminalization of domestic violence; her observations on flowers and gender signals are a key to opening up Russian society.

### points

[3:04] (Julia Ioffe) **The Soviet female elite was a product of the radical tradition of tsarist Russia** — Under tsarist law women could not do many things without their husband's permission; but the radical tradition bred women revolutionaries — Sofya Perovskaya, who assassinated Alexander II, was a woman, and there were so many women revolutionaries that the tsar had to build a separate women's prison. Radical women were shut out of universities, and those who could went to Switzerland to study medicine, until the secret police, worried they would be radicalized abroad, had Russia open a women's medical school to "keep an eye on them nearby." After the 1917 revolution free higher education opened to women and Jews, and two generations of Julia's family benefited — but the roots lay in the pre-revolutionary radical tradition.

[8:41] (Julia Ioffe) **Abortion became the only contraception Soviet women had** — The Bolsheviks legalized abortion in 1920 and followed with contraceptives in 1923, but contraception was always in short supply, and abortion became the only means of birth control for Soviet women. By the end of their childbearing years, the average Soviet woman had had 3 to 12 abortions, and many far more. In 1936 Stalin recriminalized abortion, but elites could still find doctors while ordinary people went underground. Ioffe says there is an old Russian saying: the severity of the law is diluted by the need to circumvent it.

[16:50] (Julia Ioffe) **The Soviet Union used population policy to split childbearing from fatherhood** — World War II cost the Soviet Union 27 million lives, 20.1 million of them men. To "replace the dead," Stalin and Khrushchev rolled out a 1944 policy: divorce became extremely difficult, locking men into marriage; at the same time they were encouraged to father children outside it — children born out of wedlock could not carry their father's name and could not claim child support from him, while the state paid a monthly allowance and awarded medals by number of children, a medal system copied directly from the Nazis. The result was that a third of the postwar baby boom was born out of wedlock, and a whole generation had a blank father's name on their birth certificates. Childbearing was thus decoupled from fatherhood, single motherhood became a protected legal status, and men gradually became superfluous at home.

[20:00] (Julia Ioffe) **"Men don't grow on trees" is a belief left behind by policy** — The gender imbalance evolved into an intergenerational belief. Ioffe says her grandmothers often said "men don't grow on trees," and her mother warned her to catch a husband in university or "all the good men will be picked over." Women were taught to maximize their attractiveness, or another woman would "lead their husband away by the rope" — as one Russian sociologist grumbled: are men calves, that you can lead them by a rope to another barn? After the war a whole generation of women never married because there were no men to marry, becoming pitied "old maids," and that trauma still distorts Russia's marriage market today.

[23:06] (Julia Ioffe) **The cost of being a superwoman was 40 extra hours of housework a week** — The Soviet Union required women to work — as early as 1920 women were mandated to be employed; after the war, to boost births, they were not allowed to go home, and food rations and daycare were tied to female workers. So women had to take on all housework and child-rearing on top of their jobs, and still "look effortless." Ioffe's grandmother was a chemical engineer running a water-treatment lab, picked mushrooms in the forest on her lunch break, and after work queued three times with her children for bread, milk, and meat; at night, with no washing machine, she boiled water and scrubbed the whole family's clothes on a washboard, then ironed each piece. By the late Soviet period, urban women spent an extra 40 hours a week on housework, rural women 55. One reader wrote to a newspaper: "A Soviet woman can do anything — we just don't want to anymore."

[29:45] (Julia Ioffe) **The bias of low expectations spoiled Soviet men into wrecks** — After the war men became an endangered species, fought over by women and protected by the state, and almost nothing was demanded of them. Ioffe calls it "the prejudice of low expectations" — expectations were so low, and men met them exactly. Add to that a definition of a "real man" as someone who drinks, smokes, takes risks, and dies young, and they had even less incentive to take care of themselves or invest in family life. American men will marry Russian women, but American women don't want to marry Russian men — that is the signal the market gives. The one exception is Jewish men: they don't drink, don't beat, and care for family, so Russian women are willing to marry Jews — yet the same poll says they don't want a Jewish president.

[34:43] (Julia Ioffe) **Giving flowers is not etiquette but a loyalty signal in a low-trust society** — Russia has an extremely high density of flower shops; birthdays, March 8, New Year, and visiting someone's home all require bringing flowers to the hostess. Ioffe argues this is not just politeness but a repeated proof of ongoing loyalty in a low-trust society. The most telling is the gender gesture at the very top: Putin always presents flowers when awarding medals to women; at the Minsk peace talks, Russian negotiator Surkov brought each of two American women diplomats a bouquet of the "Donetsk People's Republic" national flower — as if to say, "you are a woman first, a negotiator second." Westerners treat flowers as etiquette; Russians treat them as a reaffirmation of the gender hierarchy.

[44:41] (Julia Ioffe) **The wartime division of labor is men die, women give birth** — After the war broke out, one Russian Defense Ministry ad turned a lazy man drinking beer on the couch into a soldier in the trenches, with the slogan "Be a real man, go fight in Ukraine"; another ad used "Europe has no heating, but Russia is warm as spring at home" to attract Western women. Meanwhile, Putin, in the name of "protecting the traditional family," restricted abortion and made the "child-free movement" a crime; the Duma speaker said the most important course for girls is learning to cook and care for men, and a minister advised girls not to bother with university and to have children early. In 2016 Russia also decriminalized domestic violence; Ioffe relays a striking explanation: it is a "steam valve" letting men's pent-up aggression in a stagnant economy be vented at home. Ukraine is the opposite — both after the war and today it is bringing women into the military.

- Postwar gender ratio in some areas: 100 women to 19 men [16:10]

- Russia's birth rate in September 2024: the lowest since Putin took power [46:50]

### glossary

- woman question: The 19th-century European intellectual shorthand for women's emancipation and social role.
- single sex family: A family structure with only mothers and grandmothers, no male role.
- gender essentialism: The belief that men and women have fixed natures and should each stay in their place.
- pronatalist policy: State interventions that reward childbearing in order to increase population.
- steam valve: A mechanism that gives pressure somewhere to escape; here, using domestic violence to soothe male aggression.

who it is for: Investors watching Russian markets and political risk, analysts studying gender and population policy, and readers curious about how postwar society reshaped the sexes.
what to skip: Those with little interest in Russian cultural minutiae can skip the names segment at 37:35–39:51; the rest is very information-dense.

## xAI's Best Days, and Why It Couldn't Keep Her

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-05-sv101-xai-最美好的时代-为什么留不住她/
- show: 硅谷101 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sv101/)
- original episode: E247｜对话盛颖：xAI，Infra的浪漫，SGLang，开源，平权与“甄嬛传”
- published: 2026-08-05 · duration: 1:46:26
- transcript: Machine transcription · 35753 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Sheng Ying calls early xAI v1.0: under 100 people, no politics, and both support and freedom at once. She left two months early for the SGLang community, walking away from a one-year cliff.**

why listen: The first half is a personal account of school and a low period, and the information density is average; the second half, on Infra aesthetics, open-source equality, and disenchantment with fundraising, is worth listening to.

### points

[34:37] (Sheng Ying) **What xAI gave her was support plus freedom** — Sheng Ying says her few months at Databricks trying to promote SGLang were not successful: Databricks is a mature company, everything needs a sufficient reason, and she was a new grad researcher with not much power, and she would not drive a big effort inside a mature company. xAI gave her two things at once — support and freedom, and she describes it as ‘when I have support and freedom at the same time, I can do this thing’. Some of her other opportunities offered only support, some only freedom. When she joined, xAI had fewer than 100 people, and she says that was the best period she remembers, the first time she experienced a company with no people games at all, no politics.

[44:07] (Sheng Ying) **Two months of vesting was still too long to wait** — The SGLang community became a pure community project very early on; the core developers were all people met online, working together for two years without ever turning on a camera, and the understanding was ‘as long as I see your code, I know who you are’. In 2025 demand surged, but everyone was contributing in their spare time, staying up at night and working a bit more at noon, and the growth got so fast that this model could not hold, and delivery became a borderline fly-by. By July and August, Sheng Ying's anxiety had reached the point of ‘if we don't come out and fill in the hollow state, we are about to disappoint the outside world’. She was on a one-year cliff, had only been there ten months when she left, and two more months would have gotten her the first year's vesting, but by May she could no longer stand it.

[51:10] (Sheng Ying) **Infra is not support, Infra itself is the product** — Sheng Ying says Infra people have long been underestimated within the full stack: they have to support researchers in getting experiments running, and support product people in running the product stably and fast, yet they are always forced to do hacky things themselves. Her rebuttal is ‘Infra itself, in my eyes, is the product’ — when you make a product you think about whether it is beautiful, whether it is usable, whether it hits human nature, and no one would say they hope Infra hits human nature, but the impact Infra produces is transmitted from the bottom up. She calls this relationship romantic, and says this is not her special case; the whole group of people who write Infra can understand it. RadixArk's approach is the mirror image: when a training job gets stuck, solve the problem systematically rather than patching it so it has to run.

[1:05:28] (Sheng Ying) **RadixArk's long-term mission is not in the inference race** — Sheng Ying states plainly that although SGLang is Infra, RadixArk's long-term mission does not belong to this track. The goal she gives is ‘bring the best AI to everyone’, and she says the ultimate mission is to make the next generation of AI — not purely an Infra implementation, and not necessarily a model, but ‘something that does not exist in the world right now’. So she does not consider herself in the same category as the existing Inference Players, and precisely for that reason she is willing to keep good relations with every Inference company: SGLang does not belong to RadixArk, it belongs to the community, all the company's contributions are open source on the market, there is no private fork, and the company's lifeline is not here.

[1:19:33] (Sheng Ying) **Open source is air, not deliberate insistence** — Sheng Ying corrects the phrasing ‘insistent on open source’: she was born in Jiangxi, and when she wanted to learn programming the textbooks and resources on the market were extremely scarce, so her learning came almost entirely from random posts on the internet, CSDN, online judges; she did not know who wrote the code, or where in the world they were. She says she was raised by this group of people, so the culture of sharing openly exists like air, as a matter of course, ‘you have an idea, you do a thing, and if you don't share it, that is what feels strange’. She also points out the side effect of open source getting better: the admiration has mixed in something impure, and the presence of utilitarians makes those who originally believed unable to tell which parts are pure.

[1:27:03] (Sheng Ying) **Equality is not an education problem, it is a power problem** — Sheng Ying gives an example from her competition days: play equally well, and if you are a boy everyone says he is a genius, if you are a girl they say she works hard, is obedient, got lucky. Every match she won had to be explained — the opponent was off form, this problem had been done before — while others' wins needed no explanation. She says each such thing on its own is very small, but it happens every day, every minute, every second, and the impact on the people affected has to be multiplied by a hundred million. Her conclusion is hard: there is only one way to solve this, and that is for women to truly have rights; through education you cannot reach any goal. She admits she cannot change structural problems, but ‘if I can change 1%, I am willing to spend my whole life changing that 1%’.

[1:39:36] (Sheng Ying) **Before fundraising she did not know what a Termsheet was** — Sheng Ying says when she first went out to raise money she knew nothing about this system: she did not know what a Termsheet was, did not know what valuation was, had never even heard the word P-S-D-K, and had no idea how many pages to write or what went on each page. She read books, and the books all described something beautiful — investors and founders in lifelong friendship, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Reality is far more complicated, but in the end she really did return with her P-S-D-K investors to the kind of relationship the books describe. Her summary is: there exist in the world such pure mentors, investors and interviewers, it is just that the vast majority of people do not persist to the end of that ups-and-downs process, do not persist to believing that the good thing exists.

[1:42:39] (Sheng Ying) **Being split is fine, you don't have to escape it** — Asked how a rigorous thinker faces a world that is random and a slapdash outfit, Sheng Ying says she is very emotional, small things cause big emotional effects, but she can separate emotional effect from value construction: seeing something she does not want to happen, she will be unhappy, but she will not therefore consider it normal. She says her positive feedback loop lets her wait longer and longer — the first time she waited a few months and was validated, the next time she waited years, the next time she would wait ten years. She thinks being split is completely OK, it is not really painful, people are just afraid; the only key point is ‘are you perceiving and acting according to your own ideas, or are you actually being led by someone else’.

### glossary

- SGLang: An open-source large-model inference engine that uses RadixAttention for prefix cache reuse; the capstone of Sheng Ying's PhD work.
- RadixAttention: Uses a radix tree to index the common prefixes of requests, reusing already-computed KVCache to avoid recomputation.
- KVCache: Caches the keys and values of attention computation at inference time, so later requests in a multi-turn conversation can reuse the earlier history.
- Miles: An RL framework developed by RadixArk; when DeepSeek released a new model it was the first to achieve day zero RL compatibility.
- day zero: The inference engine completes adaptation and support on the very day a new model is released; the market's expectation of the Infra side.
- one year cliff: Equity vests only after a full year; leave early and you get not a single share.

who it is for: Engineers doing AI Infra, maintainers of open-source projects, and technical people leaving big companies to start up, especially those interested in the part about an organization moving from rule by people to systems.
what to skip: The stretch from 2:16 to 26:01 on school, the low period, and Empresses in the Palace has nothing to do with AI judgment.

## The Real Hard Part of Self-Driving Isn't the Technology, It's the Last 5% of Surprises

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-04-cnf65bb3-自动驾驶真正的难关不是技术-是最后那-5-的意外/
- show: 科技这碗饭 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cnf65bb3/)
- original episode: 美国无人驾驶20年兴衰：天才、小偷、叛徒，从沙漠到法庭的大冒险
- published: 2026-08-04 · duration: 2:34:39
- transcript: Machine transcription · 45292 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In 1995 a Mercedes drove 1,758 km of highway on its own; the machine could already handle 95% of the miles. But as long as the remaining 5% of surprises remain, a person must stay in the driver's seat, and not a cent of the driver's wages can be saved.**

why listen: Two and a half hours that lay out 22 years of industry history, from the DARPA desert to the Tempe fatality; the mechanisms and numbers land on specific people and accidents, worth hearing in full.

### points

[13:08] **Write rules, or let the machine learn on its own** — At the second DARPA Challenge in 2005, Carnegie Mellon and Stanford gave two completely different answers. Carnegie Mellon's approach was to write as many situations as engineers could imagine into the system in advance: what surfaces are passable, how to handle obstacles, prepared one by one. Stanford's Stanley had a secret weapon that wasn't hardware but machine learning, letting the machine watch how human drivers drive and then learn from driving data what kind of ground can be crossed. At the time it looked like just two teams' ways of solving the problem; looking back today, this is exactly the core question the industry has argued over again and again—should the world be written as rules, or should the machine learn the world from data on its own.

[14:10] **The race was lost to a poorly connected filter** — For the second race Carnegie Mellon prepared two vehicles, thinking it had double insurance, but neither won. Highlander's engine developed a problem two hours into the race, it couldn't climb a slope, and the organizers had to make it pull over and pause. The cause of the failure was investigated for years without being found, until 2017 when the old car was pulled out of storage for a commemorative display; while cleaning the engine bay someone touched a small component on the wiring, engine power suddenly dropped, and pressing it again killed the engine outright—it was a filter between the engine control computer and the fuel injectors, with a poor connection, and on race day the severe desert vibration ultimately caused the engine to lose power. This failure cost Highlander more than 40 minutes, while Stanley reached the finish only 20 minutes faster. Even Thrun admitted they won this race purely on luck.

[34:42] **Employee test footage killed the L3 path** — In 2012 the team gave Google employees cars with self-driving capability for their commutes; before departure everyone was told they must keep watching the road and be ready to take over at any time. When the footage was collected, it turned out: they texted, opened laptops to do work, charged their phones, put on makeup, and some fell asleep. As soon as the car takes over the steering wheel and the first few times go well, people quickly develop the illusion that "it probably won't crash," and once attention leaves driving it cannot be reconnected in an instant. What this footage negated was not self-driving itself, but the product design of "let the machine handle the vast majority of driving, then leave the most sudden and dangerous few seconds to the human." Google therefore cut the entire assisted-driving product line around 2013 and turned completely to full autonomy.

[41:47] **Page replaced the line with a bonus** — Levandowski had approached Google competitors under the name 510 Systems, pitching the sensors and positioning equipment being used on Google's test cars; an internal investigation was launched, and an email titled "It's finally happening" spread like wildfire among engineers. But Page made a completely opposite decision: not only did he not fire him, he ordered the purchase of both 510 and another Levandowski company, paying more than $20 million. His own words remain in an internal email: if the driver project succeeds, let Levandowski get rich. This later became a system—a bonus plan designed specifically for the self-driving team, not tied to Google's stock price but to the self-driving project's own valuation, with a mark recorded for each technical milestone completed. Page managed him not by drawing a line that could not be crossed, but by binding him inside Google with money and interests.

[53:03] **The fuck-off money didn't buy loyalty, it bought courage** — This bonus plan, accumulating by milestone and recalculated as the project valuation grew, was designed without anyone expecting the team to complete milestones so fast or the valuation to grow so much. One member's accumulated bonus over four years was multiplied more than tenfold when paid out; by the time executives realized it would compute to astronomical figures, the contracts had long been signed. By 2015 the team privately called it "fuck-off money"—with that money, you could tell your boss you didn't want to work anymore at any time. Levandowski's share in this plan was worth more than $120 million, while Google had spent only a bit over $20 million to acquire all of 510 Systems. But once a colleague said his life goal was to earn 100 million, and Levandowski thought that target was too low; he set his own number at a billion. This money did not buy his loyalty; it gave him the courage to leave.

[1:44:02] **In 5.6 seconds every line of defense failed** — On the evening of March 18, 2018, on a four-lane road in Tempe, 49-year-old Herzberg was pushing a bicycle across the road at a non-crosswalk location. When the Uber test car hit her, its speed was still close to 63 km/h. The accident report reconstructed the 5.6 seconds before impact: radar first detected her, classified as a car; 0.4 seconds later lidar saw her and reclassified her as an unrecognizable object; after that her identity kept changing among car, position object and bicycle, and each reclassification lost the previously accumulated motion track. At 1.2 seconds before impact the system finally identified her as a bicycle and calculated an imminent collision, but Uber's system had another rule—when it judged that only hard braking could avoid the accident, it would not brake immediately but first wait one second to reconfirm. This second was originally meant to reduce needless hard braking. By the time that second passed, only 0.2 seconds remained before impact.

[1:49:04] **Three chances to stop the testing, none taken** — The first chance was in the fall of 2017: previously every test car had two safety drivers, one in the driver's seat watching the road and one in the passenger seat watching the screen; five months before the accident Uber merged the two jobs into one, and although an employee warned that it was hard for one person to stay alert for long, the company did not stop. The second chance was a number visible across the company: Uber wanted its test cars to drive 21 km independently before needing a takeover, but internal documents showed that at the time they often needed a takeover before even 20 km, while in the same period Waymo disclosed to California an average of 9,000 km before a human takeover. The third chance was an email: five days before the accident, an operations manager warned that test cars were frequently having damage accidents, with a damaged vehicle almost every other day in February, and recommended cutting the fleet by 85% and restoring the two-safety-driver configuration; no executive replied. Three days later this manager left, and two days after that the fatal crash occurred.

[1:57:20] **Cruise fell on the unspoken 6 meters** — In October 2023 in San Francisco, a woman was thrown by a human driver and landed in the path of a Cruise self-driving car; Cruise braked hard but did not stop in time, and its wheels ran over her. The car stopped for a moment and then continued forward; the system misjudged the impact as a side scrape and initiated its post-collision pull-over procedure, dragging the injured person under the car forward about 6 meters at 11 km/h before stopping again. What really killed Cruise was not these 6 meters, but how the company explained these 6 meters to regulators after the accident: at a meeting with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration the next day, more than 100 people inside the company already knew the vehicle had moved forward after first stopping, but the oral report did not include these 6 meters; at a meeting with the California DMV it chose to let the video speak for itself, and the video the DMV saw stopped at the point where the vehicle first braked. The formal accident report submitted that afternoon still did not disclose those 6 meters.

## Big Tech's Off-Balance-Sheet Debt Isn't Fraud, It's That Nobody Reads the Footnotes

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-04-patrickboyle-表外债务不是欺诈-真正的风险是没人读脚注/
- show: Patrick Boyle (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/patrickboyle/)
- original episode: Big Tech's Hidden Debt Problem
- published: 2026-08-04 · duration: 32:18
- transcript: Machine transcription · 4855 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The so-called $1.65 trillion in hidden debt is not Enron-style fraud but long-term leases and purchase commitments for data centers not yet in service — legal, but buried in the footnotes; the real danger is AI giants telling their story through mutual financing and adjusted earnings.**

why listen: This episode takes apart Big Tech's off-balance-sheet debt: not fraud, but a product of accounting rules and footnote disclosure; it also explains how adjusted earnings and circular financing prop up valuations.

### points

[3:07] (Patrick Boyle) **$1.65 trillion isn't hidden debt, it's stuff not yet delivered** — The $1.65 trillion in off-balance-sheet debt reported by Nikkei is mostly long-term GPU purchase agreements and leases on data centers not yet in service. Under standard accounting rules, when goods haven't been delivered or buildings aren't running, you don't have to record a balance-sheet liability — you just disclose it in the footnotes, just as signing a two-year phone contract doesn't mean booking a $1,200 liability that day. Meta added $233 billion in commitments last quarter, of which $96 billion in leases will move onto the balance sheet once the data centers come into service. So this isn't Enron-style fraud, it's a timing gap.

[5:12] (Patrick Boyle) **Willing to borrow but not to sell stock means management really believes** — If management believed it could turn $1 into $5, it would tend to borrow rather than sell equity, so as to keep the excess profit for itself; only when uncertain about the outlook would it bring in outside shareholders. Alphabet completed nearly $85 billion in equity financing in June, the largest ever, with Berkshire investing $10 billion and buying in at roughly a 6% discount — a company that normally doesn't pay a premium for a story. The signal isn't the method of financing but the record scale of simultaneously using debt, equity and convertibles: the company thinks there's something behind the massive spending worth fighting for.

[8:22] (Patrick Boyle) **Ignoring depreciation assumes equipment never wears out** — Tech giants prefer to talk EBITDA, but Munger advised reading EBITDA as BS earnings. Depreciation is reverse float: cash goes out first, the expense shows up later; ignoring depreciation assumes equipment never wears out. In the latest earnings season, the four big hyperscalers together generated only $7 billion in free cash flow, and Alphabet went cash-flow negative for the first time since going public. Stock-based compensation shouldn't simply be added back either — it's barter: issuing shares directly is as much a cost as selling shares to pay salaries. To offset dilution, companies have to buy back on a fixed schedule and can't wait for a low price.

[11:29] (Patrick Boyle) **When they default you lose the customer and the money you lent** — Nvidia is pushing more than $750 billion in AI deals: $250 billion of support for OpenAI leases, then financing for $350 billion of chip purchases, plus $5 billion invested in Ilya Sutskever's startup; Google is providing $35 billion in lease support for Anthropic; SoftBank has committed $65 billion to OpenAI and borrowed $40 billion in bridge loans. The giants are investing in each other and buying from each other. It's like carmakers lending customers money to buy cars, but it's also old-fashioned vendor financing. The risk is that on default you lose both the customer and the money you lent the customer.

[15:46] (Patrick Boyle) **Everyone is priced as a winner, which is mathematically impossible** — Aswath Damodaran and Bradford Cornell call it the big market delusion: every investor treats the company they're betting on as the future winner, but add up the money each is expected to earn and the number exceeds the market itself — mathematically impossible. The Economist estimates about $900 billion of AI buildout spending this year, more than $400 billion of it borrowed; earning that back would require roughly $2.5 trillion a year in AI revenue, more than the entire global tech industry generates today. Actual adoption is modest: US executives use AI about 100 minutes a week on average, and median enterprise spend per person is just $10.66 a month.

[20:06] (Patrick Boyle) **93% of SpaceX's market space comes from AI, not rockets** — In its IPO prospectus, SpaceX attributed $26.5 trillion of its $28.5 trillion TAM — 93% — to AI/Grok, leaving about $2 trillion for actual businesses like rockets and satellites. Analysts then put out an $800 target price, implying a market cap above $10 trillion, while the company's revenue last year was under $19 billion. The reason: SpaceX disclosed roughly $235 billion in spending commitments through 2030, and IPO proceeds cover only a small part — the roughly $170 billion gap has to be filled by repeatedly issuing stock and debt over many years, which is exactly Wall Street's underwriting feast. Analysts at 18 underwriting banks published bullish calls at almost the same time, and only one independent firm gave a sell rating.

[26:17] (Patrick Boyle) **Burying debt on page 83 is a rational bet** — Public doesn't mean usable. Robert Bloomfield's incomplete revelation hypothesis holds that the harder information is to extract, the less fully it gets priced; putting debt on page 83 of a 200-page document, scattered across four footnotes, is choosing that most people won't look. Richard Sloan found in 1996 that the market treats cash earnings and accruals the same, even though accruals are less persistent. Limits of arbitrage then explain that someone who reads the footnotes can short, but may be blown up before the market corrects, so smart money often stays away from hype stocks. Companies burying inconvenient numbers in the footnotes is a rational bet: it disclosed them, it's legal, and it often works.

[30:36] (Patrick Boyle) **The AI winner is the person paying $20 a month** — This round of "hidden debt" panic isn't the discovery of the next Enron; it's people finally reading the footnotes and realizing the true scale of spending. AI isn't fraud, it's obviously useful, but the biggest returns don't go to the giants burning hundreds of billions — they go to the founders using AI to start one-person businesses at about $20 a month. For the renter it's a great deal; for the side that spent enormous sums building and is still waiting for $20 monthly fees to accumulate into $2.5 trillion in annual revenue, it's terrible. As Jamie Dimon said: AI may pay off like the internet, but not on the timetable you expect.

### verbatim quotes

[8:22] Patrick Boyle: "every time you read the word EBITDA you should replace it in your head with BS earnings."

[9:29] Patrick Boyle: "If options aren't a form of compensation, what are they? If compensation isn't an expense, what is it? And if expenses shouldn't go into the calculation of earnings, where in the world should they go?"

[15:46] Patrick Boyle: "The story is doing all the work and nobody's minding the numbers."

### figures

- Alphabet equity financing (largest ever): nearly $85 billion [5:12]

- SpaceX's disclosed 2030 spending commitments and financing gap: about $235 billion, with a gap of about $170 billion [21:09]

### glossary

- off-balance-sheet vehicle: A special-purpose entity that keeps debt off a company's books, though it still must be disclosed in the footnotes.
- vendor financing: A seller lending to a buyer so the buyer can purchase its product, locking in the customer while taking on default risk.
- big market delusion: Investors price every company in a new sector as the eventual winner, pushing total valuation beyond the truly addressable market.
- incomplete revelation hypothesis: The harder information is to extract, the less fully the market prices it; facts buried in hard-to-read footnotes get undervalued.
- limits of arbitrage: Even when mispricing is spotted, shorting can blow up because the market stays irrational, keeping smart money out.

who it is for: Investors who care whether AI capex is forming a bubble, and founders and analysts who need to read tech company financials.
what to skip: Listeners already familiar with the Enron case can skip the first 3 minutes of background.

## AI revenue up 700% year over year, but grunt-work tasks still 6x behind humans

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-04-eightythousand-agi-时间线提前一年-但脏活仍是瓶颈/
- show: 80,000 Hours Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/eightythousand/)
- original episode: What the hell happened with AGI timelines in 2026? – Rob Wiblin
- published: 2026-08-04 · duration: 49:28
- transcript: Official transcript · 10455 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The 2026 evidence on AI progress: revenue exploding, coding agents maturing, but grunt-work tasks still lag; timelines shortened by about a year, though the long run remains uncertain.**

why listen: Rob Wiblin systematically sorts through the key 2026 evidence on AI, separating real progress from hype — directly useful for judging AGI timelines.

### points

[1:29] (Rob Wiblin) **The reversal isn't a new breakthrough — scaling still works** — In October 2025 AI sentiment was pessimistic: GPT-5 was seen as a failure and agents as unreliable. Two months later Claude Opus 4.5 changed everything, programmers found agents genuinely usable, and figures like Karpathy shifted their stance. The key isn't breakthrough technology but that scaling and RL keep working: as models get smarter, error rates on long-chain tasks fall. The Epoch Capabilities Index shows that after reasoning models appeared in September 2024, the pace of progress accelerated 2-3x and has held there since.

[4:46] (Rob Wiblin) **Gross margins rose to 70% — this isn't buying revenue at a loss** — OpenAI and Anthropic grew annualised revenue 700% over the past six months, and 1600% over the past three. Anthropic grew annualised revenue 8400% over the past 5.5 months, reaching a $47 billion annualised run rate in May. Gross margins rose from 38% to above 70%, showing this isn't loss-making sales. Revenue growth proves real value, investors keep putting money in, and the industry is in a positive loop.

[9:30] (Rob Wiblin) **The doubling period is down to 4 months — but only on clean tasks** — METR's task-completion timeline shows AI can complete tasks that take humans 12-24 hours, and the doubling speed has accelerated from every 7 months to every 4 months. But be careful: this holds only for clean tasks like coding, where feedback density is high; AI companies focus their investment there; the benchmark compares against new programmers rather than people familiar with the code; and 50% success is an arbitrary threshold, while real use needs higher reliability.

[15:38] (Rob Wiblin) **That jump may just be a bigger model, not faster progress** — Anthropic's Mythos model produced a jump in the ECI index, equivalent to 6 months of progress in 3 months. But progress returned to its previous pace over the following two months, suggesting the jump came from training a bigger model (roughly 5x the parameters of the previous generation) rather than a new acceleration trend. Jumps like this may repeat every 1-2 years, but they aren't continuous acceleration.

[17:37] (Rob Wiblin) **80% of code is Claude's, but the evidence is coding-only** — Anthropic reports that 80% of merged code is written by Claude, that employee code output rose 8x, that code quality matches humans, and that it expects to surpass humans within a year. Claude's success rate on open-ended tasks rose from 10% to 75%. But most of the evidence comes from coding, and employee surveys may overstate AI's contribution.

[22:29] (Rob Wiblin) **Let AI run a shop: it earns $10k, humans earn $60k** — AI performs excellently on clean tasks like coding and math, but still lags on grunt-work tasks like running a business. GDPval shows AI beating humans on specific tasks, but in Vending-Bench 2 the AI earned $10,000 versus $60,000 for humans; the AI Village project produced limited results; and Andon Labs' cafe and shop operated but ran at a loss.

[33:46] (Rob Wiblin) **AI disproved a math conjecture and still didn't move the timeline** — An unreleased OpenAI model solved the unit distance problem conjecture by proving it false. The method was human-like, but relied on cross-domain knowledge and patience. Mathematicians think humans missed it because they believed the conjecture was true, lacked cross-domain knowledge, and found the proof tedious. Rob thinks this doesn't update the timeline, because math is an area of AI strength and there was no sign of AI having a flash of inspiration.

[38:54] (Rob Wiblin) **AI does the same work for 3% of the human cost** — Redwood Research's analysis shows AI completes tasks at about 3% of the human cost, and that hasn't risen. Although chains of thought have grown longer, the tasks have grown larger too, and token costs have fallen. Rob previously worried that inference scaling would make AI uneconomical; he now thinks it isn't a big problem.

## Getting Kicked Out of the Friend Group Isn't a Verdict: It's a Chemical Bond Reinforcing Itself

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-04-asklisa-友谊破裂是成长章节-不是人生判决/
- show: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/asklisa/)
- original episode: 283: ENCORE: Best of Ask Lisa: Friendship Breakups & Conflict
- published: 2026-08-04 · duration: 23:42
