## Open models have caught closed ones, and the distillation charge doesn't hold up

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-01-sv101-开源模型追平闭源-蒸馏指控站不住脚/
- show: 硅谷101 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sv101/)
- original episode: E246｜何谓蒸馏？聊聊硅谷如何看中国开放模型逼近前沿
- published: 2026-08-01 · duration: 1:07:12
- transcript: YouTube captions · 21576 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Only about 15 days separate the K3 and Fable releases — far too little time for distillation to be possible. What actually rattles the closed labs is that models have gone from monopoly goods to commodity goods, and the valuation math has to be redone.**

why listen: Both guests go deep on the technical definition of distillation, how strong the evidence behind the accusation really is, and how an open-source license can actually collect money — useful for anyone trying to judge the shockwave from Chinese open models.

### points

[4:01] (Wang Tiezhen) **Open models caught closed ones, and the moat vanished overnight** — Tiezhen walks through three shifts in Silicon Valley's mood. At DeepSeek R1, everyone thought open models had already closed in on the frontier; a year later they realized it was a cry-wolf story — closed models shipped monthly, open models quarterly, and Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8 were far ahead. The turning point was GLM 5.2: he himself had already replaced some Opus 4.8 functions with it, but Silicon Valley still figured that as long as closed models stayed a generation ahead there was nothing to worry about. Then K3 arrived — not merely on par with Opus, but essentially caught up to Fable and better in some scenarios. Closed models suddenly found they had no moat, and FOMO and fears of a valuation bubble erupted together.

[5:01] (Wang Tiezhen) **A fifteen-day gap means the distillation charge cannot stand** — On the question of whether K3 distilled Fable, Tiezhen offers a timing argument: only about 15 days separated the releases that Fable and K3 users could actually use. In ten-odd days you cannot even finish preparing a model release, let alone collect enough corpus and complete distillation. Keith breaks the accusation down further. The first layer is that some labs may have made large-scale unauthorized calls to frontier model APIs to extract training signal — that kind of automated request can be caught by detection systems. The second layer, that K3 got its capabilities by distilling Fable, has very weak evidence. And even if the first-layer behavior exists, it does not mean the core capabilities came from distillation.

[14:09] (Wang Tiezhen) **Distillation is a neutral word that has been turned into a slur** — Tiezhen starts with the technical clarification: classic distillation has a small model learn the logits probability distribution output by a large model, but a closed model only gives you sampled tokens — you cannot reverse-engineer the distribution, so classic distillation could never learn Fable. What people now call distillation is really training on text generated by a closed model, and that is where the controversy lies. He offers an analogy: a closed model learns from all of humanity's data, and then after it outputs something, no one else is allowed to use it to train the next model — as if someone read books and wrote a work, then told everyone you are not allowed to read what I wrote. And because closed models do not expose their chain of thought, it is hard to learn behavior from outputs alone, so a closed model can easily distill an open model, while the reverse is extremely hard.

[24:13] (Wang Tiezhen) **The K3 License shuts down the free riders** — K3 uses a separate Kimi K3 License: if a company sells models and the company and its affiliates have had more than $20 million in total revenue over 12 consecutive months, or uses K3 and derivative models for commercial services, it needs a separate agreement; end applications embedded in specific product features are not counted. Tiezhen sees this as progress at the license level: Llama had similar restrictions back then but enforcement was unclear, whereas Kimi wrote the enforceable content clearly, so dedicated inference providers and cloud vendors can no longer free-ride. He also offers a counterintuitive judgment — cloud vendors and MaaS providers actually welcome Kimi collecting money, because paying means getting official certification, and tokens sold carry guarantees on accuracy and performance; customers are unwilling to buy uncertified tokens.

[34:18] (Keith Zhai) **Monopolizing intelligence is worth more than monopolizing goods — and more fragile** — Keith argues the first shock lands on the valuation system. Before open models caught up to Fable, the closed model itself was seen as scarce, deserving a premium, even monopolistic, and therefore naturally worth a trillion-dollar market cap. Once many players can train models, a very smart model becomes a commodity, gets democratized, even becomes basic social infrastructure — and then what OpenAI and Anthropic are worth becomes an open question. The second shock is the business: if every new cloud in the US becomes their competitor, paying a small licensing fee still beats selling data centers to Anthropic at a low price; if the new clouds undercut each other on price, the closed labs may be dragged into a price war. He also observes that Anthropic's account bans are less crazy and that ChatGPT has started handing out reset coupons — all of which will show up in earnings and competition.

[37:39] (Keith Zhai) **Nvidia backs open source because a shovel seller doesn't care who strikes gold** — The July 24 open letter "Open Weights and American AI Leadership" was initially signed by about 25 companies and individual organizations, and reached 75 a few days later; Anthropic never signed. Keith points out the business logic is fundamentally opposed: every time an open model is released it hits closed vendors selling APIs, whereas Nvidia, from the chip and infrastructure angle, wants everyone to be able to freely build the best systems, so it can sell more shovels — it does not care who strikes gold. Tiezhen adds that Nvidia has built its moat on an open ecosystem since the CUDA era: Caffe, TensorFlow and PyTorch all sit on its hardware, and AMD has to negotiate integrations one by one to get in. A good part of the so-called CUDA moat is created by the open ecosystem around it.

[49:26] (Keith Zhai) **OpenRouter's valuation was lifted by Chinese open models** — Asked whether multi-model platforms like OpenRouter only took off with this wave, Keith says they had been under a lot of pressure, because the market narrative was to use the best model, and the best model was closed, leaving them few advantages. Over the past few months, OpenRouter and a batch of similar companies have seen ARR and valuations double and grow fast, and the core of that is tapping the large supply of open models, mainly Chinese. Tiezhen draws an analogy with IBM clones and Apple's all-in-one machines: in an industry's early days everyone does what they are best at — model makers make models, inference providers do inference, enterprise service firms do enterprise services — each making the most efficient decisions and iterating fastest, which is far better than the traditional Chinese internet pattern of doing everything end to end and beating rivals through traffic support and content bans.

[55:40] (Wang Tiezhen) **K3 scores low on offense, and the safety debate has been oversimplified** — Responding to whether a model near the frontier should have its weights opened, Tiezhen cites the Exploit Bench cyber offense-defense test: K3 scores only in the 30% range, far below the 75%-plus of frontier models. He offers two explanations: one is that distillation may have limited its capabilities, the other is that it may not have opened up its strongest offensive cyber capabilities. He stresses the need to separate two questions: whether open models are inherently safe, and whether K3 specifically has known safety problems; so far K3 has no known safety problem backed by evidence. He also says intelligence and safety are not the same thing: someone can be as smart as Einstein but not know how to hack NASA's website, while an 18-year-old high schooler might be able to get in.

[58:31] (Wang Tiezhen) **Closed models are both player and referee** — Tiezhen tells the story of Hugging Face being accidentally attacked by one of OpenAI's test agents: the agent decided copying the answer directly beat fumbling around, so it hacked someone else's website to grab the answer. Hugging Face wanted to use a model to analyze the attack process, but the closed model said this is unsafe and it cannot help you analyze cybersecurity corpus, so it had to turn to open models for auxiliary analysis. From this Tiezhen questions why such an important topic as cybersecurity is left to the two most frontier model companies to judge — letting them both assess whether others are safe and, intentionally or not, send their own agents out to attack others. He also mentions a Japanese big-company executive saying the real shock of Fable being unusable is not the features themselves, but the realization that this thing was unsafe all along and could be banned or have its permissions adjusted at any time.

### verbatim quotes

[4:01] Wang Tiezhen: "A year later, everyone realized it was a cry-wolf story, because over the past year the performance divergence between open and closed models was actually very large. Closed models could ship monthly, open models maybe quarterly."
    original (zh): 结果过了一年 大家发现是一个狼来了的故事 因为过去一年的开源和闭源模型 性能的分化实际上是非常大的 闭源模型可能能做到月更 开源模型可能是季更

[5:01] Wang Tiezhen: "I personally lean toward no, because in ten-odd days you cannot even finish preparing a model release, let alone collect enough corpus and distill Fable."
    original (zh): 我个人倾向于是没有的 因为你十多天连模型发布的准备 都来不及 你何谈说收集到足够多的语料 并且蒸馏Fable

[15:10] Wang Tiezhen: "A closed model can take all of humanity's data to learn from, and then after it outputs what it learned, no one else can use it to make the next model. Isn't that ridiculous?"
    original (zh): 闭源模型可以拿 所有人类的数据去学习 然后学完的东西 在被闭源模型输出之后 不能被别人用来做下一个模型 这不是很可笑吗

[20:11] Wang Tiezhen: "Distillation can get you to a passing grade very quickly, whereas something like Kimi K3 has already gone far beyond the passing grade."
    original (zh): 蒸馏可以让你很快地 去达到一个及格线 而像Kimi K3 它其实已经远远超过及格线了

[35:18] Keith Zhai: "So monopolizing intelligence is in fact far more terrifying than monopolizing any commodity, so it naturally deserves a trillion-dollar market cap."
    original (zh): 所以它垄断智能这个事情 实际上是比垄断任何商品威力 要恐怖得多得多 所以它天然就值得万亿的市值

[38:20] Keith Zhai: "Because it doesn't care who strikes gold, whereas for model vendors the core is protecting their own moat."
    original (zh): 因为他并不在乎谁能挖到金子 而对于模型厂商 其实核心就是保住自己的护城河

[1:02:32] Wang Tiezhen: "However you look at it, the absence of open source is in fact the most unsafe thing about this era."
    original (zh): 不管怎么看 没有开源 反而是这个时代最不安全的事情

### figures

- Gap between K3 and Fable usable releases: about 15 days [5:01]
- K3 scaling efficiency gain over K2: 2.5x [11:07]
- K3 model size: under 3T [12:07]
- Fable model size (rumored): 8 to 10T [12:07]
- Signatories to the open weights letter: from about 25 to 75 [37:39]
- K3 score on Exploit Bench: in the 30% range [55:40]
- Frontier model score on Exploit Bench: 75% or above [55:40]
- Drop in cost per unit of intelligence over the past few years: about a thousandfold [54:28]
- Expected further drop in cost per unit of intelligence over the next three years: about another thousandfold [54:28]

### glossary

- logits: The probability distribution a model outputs over every token at each position; classic distillation has a small model learn this distribution.
- scaling efficiency: Whether you can drive costs down while scaling; Chinese open models have been competing hard on this metric.
- KV cache: Caching already-computed key-value pairs during inference; reuse rates are very high in agent workloads with long inputs and short outputs.
- harness: The engineering layer wrapping the model, controlling the interface for communicating with the model and the KV cache lifecycle.
- Exploit Bench: An authoritative benchmark measuring a model's offensive cyber capabilities; K3 scores clearly below frontier models.

who it is for: Founders and investors watching the commercialization of Chinese open models and the valuation logic of closed labs; engineers who want to judge whether the distillation accusation holds and whether open-source licenses can collect revenue.
what to skip: The part after 1:04:01 about whether open or closed models are more easily abused — it overlaps heavily with the safety discussion earlier.

## Using AI only to cut costs is a pretty sad thing

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-31-nopriors-ai-只用来砍成本-是件很可悲的事/
- show: No Priors (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/nopriors/)
- original episode: Building an Autonomous Enterprise for Real-World Services with Netic Founder Melisa Tokmak
- published: 2026-07-31 · duration: 34:29

**Netic founder Melisa Tokmak says private equity's first meeting with her always starts with cost cutting, but what she actually sells is net new revenue for these companies — her customers have already made $600 million more because of it.**

why listen: The first half is a conventional startup narrative; the second half, on how private equity is being changed by AI and how she screens for people with agency, is noticeably denser.

### points

[3:08] (Melisa Tokmak) **Answering a phone call is much harder than the model** — Netic handles scenarios like "it's -20 degrees and the heat is broken": a customer finds a service provider through search, an aggregator or an LLM, then calls, texts or goes to the website, and the one answering is Netic's agent. The hard part isn't speech recognition, it's the reasoning chain behind it — what kind of house you live in, whether there's a history, whether to send someone today or tomorrow, whether to send an old hand who can only fix boilers or a younger one who can handle new systems, whether this customer's lifetime value justifies priority dispatch. Melisa says these operational requirements are "very complex," not as simple as "Eli's heat is broken, Melissa goes to fix it."

[5:10] (Melisa Tokmak) **The pain point in this business is nobody answers the phone at 6am** — She describes the daily reality of a billion-dollar-revenue company: the business starts at four or five in the morning, but at that hour there's not a single person in the office, and technicians don't start until six. By the time the manager arrives, three people may have quit and five may not have shown up. Meanwhile customers start pouring in from six in the morning — because there's a heat wave across the country. These businesses are cyclical: winter, summer, holidays, the season when people start working out, and the value has to be captured in those few months to support yourself and your employees. So Netic first entered through "answering overflow calls," but today more than 70% of its customers are AI first, and every one of their customers' first contact happens on a Netic agent.

[9:14] (Melisa Tokmak) **She doesn't do roll-ups because that isn't her skill** — Faced with the question "why not just buy up a bunch of companies and optimize them with AI," she gives three reasons. First, the most important thing in a roll-up is M&A itself, and she isn't an M&A person — she's an engineer and a product person — and she doesn't want to be in a business where "what I can offer isn't the most important thing." Second, in a roll-up the product you build for the company you just bought can't really be reused for other companies, which amounts to locking yourself into a handful of industries. Third, what she wants is for "every real-world business to be able to run on Netic" — letting these companies focus on what's genuinely differentiated, namely labor and quality of service, and leaving the rest to Netic.

[11:16] (Melisa Tokmak) **For robots to take over, every building would have to be torn down first** — She compares AI for the real world to different chapters of the same book: the robot chapter is in the future, but in the industries she serves it's still quite far off. The reason is the non-standardization of the physical world — if robots were to do what these companies do today, every building outside the window would first have to be 3D-printed or thoroughly standardized, and she doesn't see that happening. Today's robots are still far off in dexterity: different kinds of screws, differently built houses, how to climb up, how to get into tight spaces — often you have to open up an entire wall before you know what needs fixing. Add the human factor — these moments are often the worst day of a customer's life, the house is flooded, or they just want to relieve stress by playing tennis.

[13:16] (Melisa Tokmak) **The big labs aren't competitors, they're partners** — She thinks this question ten years ago was "can Google do it," and now it's "can the labs do it." Her judgment: on core capabilities the labs certainly can, but there are things they won't invest in. She gives two specific points — OpenAI ships products extremely fast, but "kills products extremely fast too," and companies in these industries don't want that cadence; Anthropic leads on coding agents because of focus, but in the enterprise setting you see roughly 20 products and can't tell what's actually happening. She also says lab researchers care about the most generalizable solution, which in this setting amounts to "wait for AGI and then ask how to solve essential services" — which she considers operationally and intellectually "a bit lazy."

[15:16] (Melisa Tokmak) **Founders are now too afraid of the labs** — The host observes that four years ago he was investing in vertical applications like Harvey, Perplexity and Decagon, whereas now many founders worry too much about the labs' roadmaps and so don't dare enter new verticals — in an earlier era people would have just fought it out first. Melisa's response: that's because many people now build things thinking "how do I exit immediately," rather than treating founding as something you commit decades to. She says that before building her company she seriously looked for a job — first asking whether there was anything she wanted to build, then whether there was anything else she was interested in, and finally whether there was anyone whose mission she wanted to advance. She also calls out the "permanent underclass" mindset popular among Gen Z: if you haven't made money within 18 months and haven't learned everything within 6 months, you'll be poor forever.

[19:21] (Melisa Tokmak) **Screening for agency means seeing whether you stuck with it** — Her way of screening for agency isn't asking one question, it's digging into life experience: if you're a new grad, what did you do in college? What did you do to get into college? Is there a project you genuinely cared about? The key isn't "I did this over the weekend," it's whether you kept doing it. One question she often asks is "what's the hardest thing you've ever done in your life" — the answer can come from anywhere, and it may not even be something you chose; what matters is how you reacted, what you controlled, and how you turned the part you could control into a different future. She gives an example of someone she just hired: the person said their life is very simple, they care about work, and they have a crazy discipline around health, and the hardest thing was keeping that routine for over 15 years without getting bored. She says that's a very creative answer.

[23:53] (Melisa Tokmak) **These industries aren't old school, they're primitive and tech-forward at once** — She thinks seeing these industries as old school is a big misunderstanding, and that the most tech-forward, most business-focused people she's met are precisely in this industry. She gives a number: a deal just signed might be a $500,000 contract, 14 days from start to finish — not because AI is a magic potion, but because they check very carefully whether the value is really there. She gives the example of roofing companies: these people were already going to hire people to knock on doors, and now Netic plugs in satellite data to judge how hurricanes affected roofs in different blocks and what materials to use, feeding all of that automatically into the agent's context, so it can both talk to customers better and identify who to go after.

[27:24] (Melisa Tokmak) **The private equity playbook has already changed** — She says the old private equity playbook — find a gem with a beautiful multiple, swap out the team, create value, sell it again — no longer works, because those undiscovered gems no longer exist, and the playbook has become "how do you create real value in these businesses." She observes two extremes: some go too deep, treating AI as software and expecting results in the first week; others move too slowly. She thinks the right posture is to separate AI from vaporware, look at real ROI, and look at whether results keep getting better rather than worse over a full year. She also mentions that private equity now hires AI operating partners, or keeps a few AI-oriented engineers to do internal education.

[30:26] (Melisa Tokmak) **The first meeting always starts with cost cutting** — She says private equity's first round of conversation always focuses on cutting costs, because they've never seen a product like Netic, while what she really wants to talk about is net new revenue. She thinks this requires proactively opening the conversation and showing them concrete examples, otherwise the topic falls back to how to squeeze the bottom line and cut some costs. Her words: if AI is only used to cut costs, that would be pretty sad. She also stresses that private equity is more about advising portfolio companies and can rarely shove things down a company's throat, but it can be a good advisor, telling companies what to examine.

## The Female Con Artist Anatomised After Death: What She Threatened Wasn't Money, It Was Order

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-31-cautionary-约克郡女巫罪案-骗局的核心是权力欲/
- show: Cautionary Tales with Tim Harford (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/cautionary/)
- original episode: Arsenic and Lace: The Trial of the Yorkshire Witch - with Maddy Pelling
- published: 2026-07-31 · duration: 43:31
- transcript: Official transcript · 7548 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In 18th-century England, the female swindler Mary Bateman ran fortune-telling and poisoned-pie scams — not for money, but for the pleasure of control. Her tricks hit human longing with precision, and after death she was dissected and put on display, revealing society's fear of those who upend its order.**

why listen: Rich in historical detail, and the second half's leap from a single case to the mechanics of modern scams is especially rewarding; if you only care about crime stories, the middle drags a little.

### points

[5:22] (Maddy Pelling) **When the con artist melts into the crowd, the magician's pact collapses** — In the 1740s, a magician announced he would climb into a bottle at London's Haymarket Theatre. The audience paid for tickets, expecting to enjoy clever trickery in suspended disbelief. But the performer never appeared, the crowd rioted at being fooled, and soldiers put them down. Maddie points out that until then a pact existed between magician and audience: the illusion on stage was safe, and the audience knowingly played along. When a con artist breaks the contract and melts into the crowd, becoming any stranger at all, every bit of trust fails. The episode is a metaphor for its age: every established rule was being rewritten.

[11:29] (Maddy Pelling) **She didn't need money — what the con gave her was intimate control** — The mill burned down, and a pregnant Mary went door to door collecting bandages for the hospital — then turned around and sold them all. She didn't lack money; her husband John was a wheelwright with a respectable income and a militia post. Maddie stresses that Mary acted out of a craving for intimate control, not economic motive. She was skilled at using her pregnancy to win trust, reading others' fears, offering what looked like precise comfort, then destroying them utterly. That pattern of manipulation runs through her whole life and foreshadows the graver crimes to come.

[19:35] (Maddy Pelling) **The scam's endpoint isn't money, it's a pie laced with arsenic** — Rebecca Perigo suffered from chronic illness, and Mary claimed a spell had to be worked through an intermediary, Miss Blythe, inducing the couple to hand over almost everything they owned, including a new bed, ham and gold coins. When William grew suspicious, Mary's final instruction was to eat a pie mixed with powder, then take honey to mask the bitterness. Rebecca ate a few bites, rolled on the ground vomiting, and died miserably days later; William survived because he ate only one bite. He set a trap to catch Mary, who was carrying a small bottle of arsenic, and multiple items belonging to victims were found in her home. The scam had escalated from psychological manipulation to lethal poisoning.

[24:38] (Maddy Pelling) **The letter she told him to burn became the evidence that hanged her** — At trial, William produced the letters Mary had written him — she had asked him to burn them after reading, but he kept them, and they became the strongest physical evidence. Several doctors examined the pie residue and vomit, and one even suffered a heart attack in the courtroom. After being sentenced to hang, Mary asked to plead the belly; the judge closed the court, women present examined her, and the conclusion was that she was not pregnant. A prison guard recalled that at the end she nursed a baby, handed the child to her husband, and walked to the gallows. Mary lied to the very end, but the chain of evidence could no longer be overturned.

[28:45] (Maddy Pelling) **Hanging her wasn't enough — she was boiled and put on display** — After Mary was hanged, her body was taken back to the Leeds anatomy school, where the anatomist William Hay charged admission to exhibit it for three days, dissecting the corpse in public and holding up the uterus to declare, "There is no baby here," while spectators joked that her heart wasn't black enough. Her remains were boiled and displayed, and her bones stayed on show in a museum until 2015. Visitors queued to touch the bones, afraid she would come back for revenge. Maddie argues that this extreme treatment shows she shook the emerging capitalist hierarchy and had to be erased completely, not merely executed.

[30:46] (Maddy Pelling) **She made a living by defying the system, so she had to be erased** — Maddie notes that Mary feels eerily modern — she read weaknesses, offered hope, faked authority, just like so many con artists today. That she could make a living inside the social system by defying it was precisely what threatened the consolidating structure of capitalist power. So she was dissected, boiled and publicly displayed to eliminate her symbolic threat. This exposes the era's fear of losing control: when society changes too fast, people seek an outlet in irrational explanations, and Mary was both a product of that need and its scapegoat.

[33:56] (Maddy Pelling) **A con artist doesn't sell a product, but the hope reality can't give** — A listener named Stuart's aunt paid $15,000 for a "magic box" built from a low-spec computer, on the reasoning that expensive means good. Maddie analyses that the most powerful thing about a con artist's story is that it offers hope reality cannot deliver, while faking authority and expertise. She warns that in the Enlightenment the definition of knowledge and the location of authority were shifting violently, leaving ordinary people unable to tell the difference; the modern internet amplifies the danger of "authority mimicry" even more. When a person is drawn to the certainty a stranger projects, that is often the most vulnerable moment.

[40:03] (Tim Harford) **The cruellest forgery proves the authenticator was right all along** — Tim uses the Van Meegeren case to show how precisely a con can hit its target. The art critic Abraham Bredius spent his life convinced that Vermeer had travelled to Italy and been influenced by Caravaggio, though the evidence was thin. Van Meegeren painted a Vermeer in Caravaggio's style, letting Bredius see his long-held theory confirmed, and so fooled an authoritative authenticator. Tim stresses that this is more like "pressing a button" than mere forgery — it proves the other person has been right their whole life. Anyone can be brought down by their own background and blind spots, and that is the hardest part of guarding against fraud.

### glossary

- bottle conjurer: A street magician who claimed he could stuff himself into a wine bottle — in practice a byword for a hoax.
- ill wishes / well wishes: Objects sewn into clothing and believed to cast or break a curse.

## AI Research's Next Breakthrough: Build a Physics for AI First, Then Let It Discover Architectures on Its Own

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-30-zhangxiaojun-ai-for-ai-关键在于建立ai的物理学/
- show: 张小珲·商业访谈录 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/zhangxiaojun/)
- original episode: 149. 亲历中美neo labs资本狂潮，和清华刘子鸣聊：AI for AI、机制可解释性和Max Tegmark
- published: 2026-07-30 · duration: 1:40:35
- transcript: Machine transcription · 30707 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 3 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Liu Ziming argues that real AFAI is not writing papers or tweaking training pipelines, but using physics methods to structure research first, then training a meta model to predict training curves, and ultimately letting AI discover the next generation of architectures itself.**

why listen: A frontline researcher's distinctive definition of "AI auto research," having lived through the neo labs funding wave in both China and the US, and a candid comparison of Anthropic's mechanistic interpretability and the limits of RSI — high information density.

### points

[2:05] (Liu Ziming) **After ChatGPT, physics should turn around and explain AI** — Liu Ziming studied physics as an undergraduate at Peking University, then went to MIT to work under Max Tegmark, starting out in AI for physics. After ChatGPT appeared, he decided to swap the roles of AI and physics, turning to physics of AI — using physics methodology to understand and design AI. He counts both himself and Max as "bird people," good at migrating methods across fields, which laid the foundation for his distinctive definition of AFAI.

[13:32] (Liu Ziming) **A worst-case impossibility proof does not stop a physicist** — KAN is Liu Ziming's breakout work, but Max opposed it at first, because a 1989 paper proved that the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem cannot be turned into an algorithm in the worst case. Coming from physics, Liu Ziming held that you need not care about the worst case — the actual universe is not the worst-case universe. He built a prototype in two weeks, then spent one more week on visualization, and only after Max saw the network's internal structure did he exclaim and approve. This reflects his research style of "build the thing first, explain it later."

[18:40] (Liu Ziming) **LLM success comes from language, not architecture** — Liu Ziming agrees with Xie Saining's view: large language models are anti-bitter-lesson. The key to LLM success lies in language itself — language is a compression produced over millions of years of human evolution, and a model only needs to be able to "eat" this gift to succeed, so it places little demand on architecture. By contrast, modalities such as vision have not been well compressed, and world models need architectures designed to learn abstract representations — which is exactly why model design becomes important again in the post-LLM era.

[21:53] (Liu Ziming) **Most AFAI only goes neuron-to-neuron, with no closed loop** — Liu Ziming sums up his own research as one main thread: grafting the neural and symbolic worlds together. AI for science uses neural methods to capture symbolically expressed scientific laws; science of AI turns around and uses symbolic and scientific methods to understand and improve the AI black box. He points out that what people usually call AFAI is mostly neuron-to-neuron, with no closed loop back to the symbolic part; his AFAI is "AI for physics of AI" — using AI to accelerate understanding of AI itself, then guiding the design of better models.

[37:20] (Liu Ziming) **Top talent would rather go solo than be a big-company grunt** — Liu Ziming believes the root cause of the many neo labs appearing simultaneously in China and the US is that top talent's choices have changed: between academia, being a grunt at a big company, and going solo, more and more people choose the last. At the same time, the current paradigm (transformer + scaling) has obvious low-hanging basins it cannot reach, such as AutoResearch and world models, which need a lot of early-stage research rather than pure engineering grind — and these directions happen to be the living space for new labs.

[43:35] (Liu Ziming) **Hot money is all in world models and AutoResearch** — Liu Ziming judges that the directions where capital is most active right now are world models and AutoResearch. A world model is essentially giving a robot a "brain," serving the robotics track; AutoResearch is training an AI researcher to do research. AFAI, meanwhile, is currently mostly classified by investors under AI for science. His firsthand feel from fundraising is that it is "insanely crazy" — investors probe each other for information and move extremely fast on projects, and after a seed round there can be unlimited follow-on rounds.

[47:41] (Liu Ziming) **RSI competes on diligence, AFAI competes on hit rate** — Liu Ziming compares Tian Yuandong's Recursive Superintelligence (RSI) with his own ideas. He thinks RSI's current route is more like a "diligent" coding agent, emphasizing action and iteration count; what he wants to build is a "smart" AFAI, emphasizing the hit rate of the ideas it proposes. He gives an example: a coding agent may propose 100 ideas and only 1 works, whereas he wants a model where 3 proposals yield 1 that works. The two are orthogonal directions that will ultimately need to be integrated.

[50:56] (Liu Ziming) **Training curves can be predicted in advance, and he is his own evidence** — Since the start of this year, Liu Ziming has treated himself as a model being trained: each day he randomly pulls a dataset and a model, predicts the training curve first, then runs the experiment. For the first forty or fifty days his predictive ability was poor, then it suddenly became accurate. This "human experiment" convinced him that a meta model exists — a model that takes conditions such as model architecture as input and outputs the training curve. With a meta model, AI could rank ideas and predict experiments in advance, greatly accelerating AI research.

[1:21:11] (Liu Ziming) **People who cannot train models should still be able to train models** — Liu Ziming envisions the final product as a "training autopilot." Users need not know about transformers or understand training; they just have to state their needs clearly (for example, a budget of only 100 yuan), and the system can design, train, deploy and deliver a model end to end. He draws an analogy: coding now lets people who cannot write programs write programs, and in the future training autopilot will let people who cannot train models train models, and incubate "OpenAIs" in every vertical domain.

### glossary

## Knowledge-creators outlive stars, so epistemology is physics

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-30-tokcast-知识创造者比恒星活得久-所以认识论是物理学/
- show: ToKCast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tokcast/)
- original episode: Ep 264: David Deutsch's "The Fabric of Reality" Chapter 14 "The Ends of the Universe" Part 1
- published: 2026-07-30 · duration: 44:29
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7669 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 2 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Twist quantum mechanics, computation, evolution and epistemology into one strand, and the conclusion is: as long as humans keep solving problems, the long-term structure of the universe will be determined by knowledge, not gravity.**

why listen: A sentence-by-sentence close read of the first half of Chapter 14 of Deutsch's book. Concept density is high but the pace is slow — suited to anyone who wants to get clear on the argument chain for why epistemology is physics.

### points

[3:24] (Brett Hall) **Unpredictable does not mean non-deterministic** — Brett Hall first dismantles a common misunderstanding: physics determining everything does not mean physics can predict everything. He gives three kinds of unpredictability: a system so complex that any computer we could build cannot out-compute the universe itself; a single photon on a half-silvered mirror, which can only be given a definite 50-50 probability; and, most crucially, the creation of knowledge. The laws of physics permit knowledge to be created, but the same laws forbid us from predicting which path that knowledge will take, because that would amount to possessing the knowledge before it is created. So ‘physical determinism’ and ‘the future is predictable’ are two different things, and conflating them leads people to think epistemology will sooner or later be swallowed by physics.

[6:26] (Brett Hall) **Proof requires matter, so proof can go wrong** — In the original text Deutsch admits he changed his mind: he once thought human knowledge would unify under ‘ever-deeper fundamental physics’, and later rejected this. Brett lays out the reasoning: a mathematical proof requires a person or a machine to carry it out, the thing doing the proof is made of matter, matter obeys quantum physics, and quantum physics means the possibility of error can never be ruled out. So a proof is never a proof of ‘necessarily true’, and mathematical knowledge is conjectural too. He calls the belief that mathematicians can intuit certain, error-free truths the mathematician's misconception, and quotes Deutsch: necessary truth is merely the subject matter of mathematics, not the reward of doing it.

[11:32] (Brett Hall) **‘This theory could be wrong’ is a vacuous remark** — Brett treats this sentence as the bugbear he finds most irritating when explaining this kind of material: there is always someone saying ‘but this theory could be wrong’, as if no one had thought of it. He concedes it is true, trivially true, part of fallibilism — but ‘could be wrong’ by itself solves nothing. The right move is to take the current best explanation seriously and see where it takes you; if you assume from the start that it is wrong, then anything goes, and what is left is supernaturalism, magic and wizards. He gives ‘the Earth is approximately spherical’ and ‘energy is conserved’ as examples — these could also be wrong, but you cannot refuse to use them on that account.

[12:32] (Brett Hall) **Once proved, the Turing conjecture is upgraded to a principle** — Deutsch's 1985 paper proved the Turing conjecture, so many people now call it the Turing-Deutsch principle. Brett explains the difference between a conjecture and a principle: a conjecture is a guess that looks reasonable and that no one has a deep criticism of; a principle is a law about laws, a level deeper. If quantum theory is the total explanation of matter and energy, and from this conjecture the Church-Turing conjecture can be proved to hold, then it deserves the title of ‘principle’ — any law discovered in the future within quantum theory must conform to it, or quantum theory itself would have to change. Deutsch also stresses that this principle has an emergent character, bearing directly on the properties of complex machines and only indirectly on subatomic processes, with a status comparable to conservation of energy and the laws of thermodynamics.

[14:32] (Brett Hall) **Over the long run, the universe's structure is decided by knowledge** — Following Deutsch's hint, Brett pushes to a picture: on the largest timescales, the structure of the multiverse will increasingly be determined by people and the knowledge they create. What people build and control in different universes will outlast any single star; knowledge across different universes will converge, because everyone has to exploit the same set of physical laws. He describes explanatory knowledge and its technological consequences as ‘like a crystal that persists’. So epistemology is the most important discipline on the long-term scale of cosmic evolution — this sounds very strange the first time you hear it, but its only premise is: humans keep solving problems and never go extinct.

[17:37] (Brett Hall) **Treating one strand as the whole world leads you astray** — Deutsch says that quantum physics swallowing the other three strands is merely ‘the parochial view of a physicist’, possibly contaminated by reductionism. Brett gives three examples of treating a single strand as a worldview: computer-science types who see everything through the lens of deterministic computation, who think that with enough compute, hardware will ratchet itself up to AGI, then ASI, and take over the world, and who even think we already live inside a computer simulation; Brett Weinstein and others who want to explain all human activity, including politics, religion and social movements, by biological evolution; and Cartesian epistemological foundationalism. His judgment: each strand on its own is rich enough to support an entire worldview, but doing so is both limiting and misleading.

[21:39] (Brett Hall) **Descartes and the Buddhists arrived at the same place** — Brett points out that cogito ergo sum does not appear where the full argument is given in the Meditations; what is said there is ‘that I think and that I exist is a necessary truth’, resting on ‘clear and distinct ideas’. He finds this reads as very Buddhist: Descartes sits in his armchair by the fire, uses the method of doubt all the way down to doubting the body, and finally finds there must be something doing the doubting. Buddhists, modern meditators and Descartes, each by their own method — looking inward at subjective experience — arrived at the same conclusion. Brett says this is perhaps no coincidence, because they come from the same place.

[29:47] (Brett Hall) **If the simulation hypothesis were true, it would expose itself** — Brett relays Peter Boghossian's challenge: even if the simulation hypothesis solves no problem, it could still be true. Brett disagrees, on the grounds that ‘problems are solvable’: if the universe is a simulation, there must be consequences that show up in our reality and are eventually discovered by us. He gives a concrete mechanism — the computer a simulation runs on has finite memory and speed, so physical constants may stop gaining digits once measured to some precision. He takes the gravitational constant G as an example: it is now 6.6743 times 10 to the minus 11, and as instruments get more precise the digits should keep increasing; if one day a measurement reads 6.6743108 followed by all zeros and never changes again, that would need an explanation, and the simulation hypothesis would explain it exactly. But for now there is no reason at all to think it is true.

[41:09] (Brett Hall) **To predict a star you must first factor in human choices** — Brett explains Deutsch's precise use of ‘fundamental’: something is fundamental if it is caught up in the explanation of many things — gravity, for instance, is used to explain tides, falling leaves, the Moon's motion, stars shining and the evolution of the universe as a whole. So why is epistemology fundamental? Because on cosmological timescales — thousands, millions, billions of years — predicting the far future requires first considering what the people alive then will do. A star would otherwise expand, cool, contract, reheat and cool again according to astrophysical models, but if there are people there, with knowledge, resources and wealth, they may choose to slow down or speed up the star's evolution and reactions. Human choices, economics and preferences enter the prediction, so epistemology is not only about belief and subjective psychology, but also about stars, galaxies and the universe.

### verbatim quotes

[4:24] Brett Hall: "the most important kind of unpredictability is that of knowledge creation. Physics, deterministic physics, physics that consists of... regularities of nature or laws allows for knowledge creation. But those same laws seem to prohibit our predicting of the route knowledge creation will take."

[8:29] Brett Hall: "necessary truth is merely the subject matter of mathematics, not the reward we get for doing mathematics"

[11:32] Brett Hall: "In the meantime, it doesn't get you anywhere. In the meantime, it doesn't allow you to solve problems. In the meantime, what you should be doing is taking the best explanation seriously and see where it leads."

[14:32] Brett Hall: "the structure of the multiverse will be increasingly dictated by people and the knowledge they create. Those structures will persist longer than individual stars"

[26:44] Brett Hall: "It's exciting to create knowledge and it's a dead end to claim that you're absolutely certain and without doubt. And it's completely unnecessary."

[34:59] Brett Hall: "investigating fantasies, and they are fantasies, seems like a waste of cognition"

[41:09] Brett Hall: "We can't predict what a star will do in billions of years unless we take into account the choices of people that might be there at that time."

### figures

- Current measured value of the gravitational constant G: 6.6743 × 10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²) [31:52]
- Year Deutsch proved the Turing conjecture: 1985 [12:32]

### glossary

- Turing-Deutsch principle: The physical principle that the Turing conjecture was upgraded to after Deutsch proved it, constraining every information-processing system.
- mathematician's misconception: The belief that mathematicians can intuit certain, error-free, incorrigible truths.
- Omega Point Theory: The end-of-the-universe hypothesis put forward by physicist Frank Tipler; Deutsch considers its core valuable but exaggerated.
- crypto inductivist: A critic of Popper's epistemology who says it only describes the conditions for the growth of scientific knowledge and not why it grows.

who it is for: For people who have read or are reading The Fabric of Reality and want to understand how Deutsch elevates epistemology to the status of a physical principle; also for engineers with their own views on the simulation hypothesis and AGI determinism.

## Leveraged Investing Works on Paper, but Nobody Executes Step Two

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-30-rationalreminder-杠杆投资理论上成立-但没人真的执行第二步/
- show: The Rational Reminder Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/rationalreminder/)
- original episode: Is Sequence of Returns Overrated? (& Other Questions) | Rational Reminder 420
- published: 2026-07-30 · duration: 1:51:28
- transcript: YouTube captions · 20466 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The paper says young people should lever up on their lifetime wealth, but clients who pay off the mortgage never borrow it back. Sequence-of-returns risk is only a problem when withdrawals are fixed; make them variable and the portfolio gymnastics become unnecessary.**

why listen: This is a listener Q&A episode. The first half on leverage and parenting is more anecdotal; the second half's reframing of sequence-of-returns and withdrawal-sequence risk is worth hearing.

### points

[22:27] (Benjamin Felix) **Borrowing to invest works in theory, and is very hard psychologically** — A resident physician asks: is it worth borrowing against a line of credit at roughly 4% to put into a 100% stock ETF? Benjamin cites the 2013 Journal of Portfolio Management paper "Diversification Across Time": people who are young, whose future human capital is high and bond-like, and who currently hold few financial assets should in theory use leverage, because their ideal stock allocation is far above their current investable assets. The paper argues for setting the stock share based on "lifetime wealth" rather than "current savings," and for young people even suggests investing 200% of current savings. But Benjamin's landing point is: it ultimately comes down to risk tolerance, and 100% stocks looks good on paper — not everyone can execute it.

[27:31] (Benjamin Felix) **Samuelson himself publicly opposed this paper** — After the paper came out, Paul Samuelson argued against it in a 2008 talk, on the grounds that using leverage carries the risk of being wiped out entirely, and you have to stay at the table to collect the long-run result. The paper's authors counter that having your financial assets wiped out doesn't really matter, because most of your assets are future income you haven't earned yet — technically true, but Benjamin adds: bankruptcy still hurts. Robert Merton also agreed that leverage makes sense for young people, but opposed using margin, arguing that options, or building leverage into a financial product, are more appropriate, because "expecting people to execute this idea themselves is crazy."

[29:34] (Benjamin Felix) **Dan Bortolotti doesn't question the numbers, he questions the behavior** — Dan Bortolotti of Canadian Couch Potato reviewed the book these authors wrote on the back of this in a 2010 blog post. He doesn't dispute the paper's numbers, and thinks the theoretical and empirical results probably hold, but the behavioral layer makes the whole strategy very hard to implement: you're borrowing to invest, and you could lose a lot or be wiped out. Benjamin adds the picture: if you blow up your RBC line of credit, RBC probably won't like you very much, and even maintaining the banking relationship may be difficult. The paper's authors acknowledge the psychological aversion is real, but argue people don't truly understand the cost of forgoing this strategy.

[35:38] (Benjamin Felix) **Adjust asset allocation first, then talk about borrowing** — Benjamin proposes a practical order of operations: think of borrowing as a negative fixed-income position. Rather than borrowing $500,000, first move the portfolio from 80% stocks to 100% stocks — in financial planning software the results come out very close. So if you're at 80% stocks and considering leverage, maybe first go to 100% stocks; if that already gets you the outcome you want, you may not need to borrow. Louis adds this can double as a behavioral test: a 70/30 investor can first experience 100% stock volatility, and only consider the next step if they can stomach it.

[39:42] (Multi-person conversation) **After paying off the mortgage, nobody wants to borrow it back** — A client asks how to optimize the mortgage and free up money to invest, and the advisor's plan is: use taxable assets to pay off the mortgage, then borrow against the home to invest. The model was run, and the long-term net worth projection for one family was a "huge improvement." The result: once the mortgage was paid off, that client never borrowed back to invest. Ben says he's seen this many times, and almost nobody actually executes step two. The reason isn't that the math doesn't work — it's that the sense of relief from clearing the debt is too strong, and with improved cash flow, people simply stop at being debt-free.

[56:58] (Ben Felix) **It's not the sequence of returns, it's the sequence of withdrawals** — Ben directly reframes the question: rather than thinking "how big does the portfolio need to be to not fear sequence-of-returns risk," think about the withdrawal sequence. Sequence-of-returns risk is only a problem when withdrawals are fixed — if you take out the same amount every period, a few consecutive bad years really do hurt; but withdrawals don't have to be fixed. Allowing variable withdrawals lets you raise lifetime spending overall while not raising (or even lowering) the risk of ruin: spend less in bad years, more in good years. This flexible spending comes from the lifecycle model.

[1:19:16] **Static allocation has the lowest failure rate** — A 2016 paper, "Retirement Glidepaths: An International Perspective," used data from 19 countries spanning 110 years from 1900 to 2009 to test three types of stock allocation strategies: declining, rising, and static. The conclusion is that the static strategy had the lowest or near-lowest failure rate, the highest or near-highest expected legacy, good upside potential, and the best downside protection. The authors specifically note that the static strategy of staying fully in stocks the whole way had the lowest failure rate, held up reasonably in tail-risk shocks, and had higher upside potential than the other strategies. Its outcome standard deviation is indeed higher, but the authors' explanation is that this standard deviation reflects uncertainty about how much better off the retiree will be after 30 years, not how much worse.

[1:23:19] **The optimal solution switches to 27% Treasury bills at retirement** — One finding in the Cederberg paper directly relevant to the listener's question: if the investor is allowed to adjust allocation once a year, the optimal solution stays 100% stocks until retirement at 60, switches 27% into Treasury bills at retirement (equivalent to a high-interest savings account), then takes about seven years to gradually shift back to 100% stocks. The paper itself says this Treasury bill allocation is the simulated investor's response to the sequence risk created by the 4% rule's fixed real withdrawal amount. But the paper also tested variable withdrawals — taking a percentage of the portfolio each year rather than a fixed dollar amount based on the first year's portfolio — and once you switch to variable withdrawals, this cash allocation disappears.

[1:37:25] (Louie) **The worst case clients describe isn't a 10% drop** — Louie says that after the asset allocation episode he read through all the RR community, YouTube, and Spotify comments, and then started asking clients directly: how do you define risk? What's the worst that could happen? Nobody said the worst case was a 60/40 portfolio dropping 10% and staying down for a year. Every answer was: I'm afraid I won't have enough money to retire, I'm afraid I can't help my family, I need to care for my parents or kids, I'm afraid of running out of money. That made him realize that framing risk as short-term volatility and emphasizing the psychological comfort of investing may miss the bigger risk — not having enough money to meet your goals. His new approach is to guide clients toward becoming more comfortable with investing over time, rather than only optimizing at the portfolio level.

### verbatim quotes

[27:31] Benjamin Felix: "you risk being entirely wiped out by using leverage and you have to stay in the game to have a good long-term outcome"

[30:36] Benjamin Felix: "We are taught to think of leverage investments as instruments for short-term speculation, not long-term diversification."

[35:38] Ben Wilson: "the amount of leverage has to be pretty meaningful, like six figures or seven figures to make a material impact to their long-term financial plan"

[40:44] Multi-person conversation: "And then we paid off the mortgage and then he never raised, rebarorrowing to invest again."

[1:21:18] : "it does not seem to have been a key determinant of portfolio failure in the broad global sample"

[1:25:19] : "You can do a lot of portfolio gymnastics like that initial cash allocation to make fixed withdrawals work or you can build variable withdrawals into your plan and you have to do less gymnastics."

[1:39:26] : "I basically pay for this twice. I hire you guys and pay PWL fees to coach me into becoming a more comfortable investor. So, I kind of view that as a bit of like a behavioral bond-like element of my broader net worth."

### figures

- Initial stock position suggested by the paper: 200% of current savings [26:31]

- Number of countries covered by the paper: 19 countries [1:19:16]
- Years covered by the paper: 1900 to 2009, 110 years [1:19:16]
- Treasury bill allocation at retirement: 27% [1:23:19]
- Domestic/international split of the optimal stock portfolio: about one-third domestic stocks, two-thirds international stocks [1:22:18]

### glossary

- Sequence of Returns Risk: The risk that bad returns early in retirement cause a portfolio to deplete faster under fixed withdrawals.
- Sequence of Withdrawals Risk: The effect of changing withdrawal amounts and timing on portfolio longevity, which is more controllable than the sequence of returns.
- Block Bootstrap: A statistical method that resamples contiguous blocks from historical data to generate many hypothetical market paths.
- Lifecycle Model: An economic model that plans saving, investing, and spending based on lifetime wealth and future income.

who it is for: Investors with mortgages, those considering leverage, or anyone planning retirement withdrawals — plus advisors who want to understand the sequence-of-returns risk framework.
what to skip: The parenting and experiential-consumption discussion from 44:47 to 51:57, which has weak relevance to the investing topic.

## Brain Signals Show Up Seven Seconds Early, but the Original Author Says Free Will Is Still Here

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-30-sciencevs-大脑早七秒做决定-自由意志依然存在/
- show: Science Vs (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sciencevs/)
- original episode: Free Will: Does It Exist?
- published: 2026-07-30 · duration: 31:49
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5473 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 4 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Libet's and Haynes's experiments show brain signals arriving half a second to seven seconds before ‘you decide’, but the original authors deny this means free will is dead; compatibilism holds that the will may be a macroscopic emergence from microscopic brain processes, the way temperature emerges from atoms.**

why listen: This is not just philosophical speculation: people who read that free will is an illusion cheat more and help others less. It has real consequences for decision-making, responsibility, and AI prediction of behavior.

### points

[0:00] (Wendy Zuckerman) **If choice is an illusion, the ‘I’ is not the decider** — A genre of video circulates on social platforms: people say ‘I just remembered I have free will’ and then do something arbitrary — dumping all the cutlery into a drawer unsorted, climbing into the attic and eating chips like a goat. The routine celebrates freedom, but another corner of the internet says everything was determined long ago. The host points out that scientists have been publishing papers arguing free will does not exist for decades, and the question is no joke: if choice is an illusion, is the ‘I’ still the one making the decision?

[5:00] (Merrill Horn) **Read one line saying free will is an illusion and people cheat more** — Merrill cites a body of psychology experiments: subjects are given something to read claiming science has proven free will is an illusion, and then their behavior is observed. The results show people cheat more, help others less, and are more likely to behave aggressively. Wendy's reaction is immediate: if I listen to the end and conclude I have no free will, I can say ‘I had no choice’ and offload everything. Merrill corrects that it may not necessarily come to that, but the answer on free will does affect people's sense of responsibility and moral behavior.

[7:20] (Merrill Horn) **Humans are trains stuck on tracks, unable to escape physical law** — The usual definition of free will is: between chocolate and caramel, it is ‘I’ who decides, and it is not a random dice roll. But classical physics paints a clockwork universe: a ball rolls downhill because of gravity, every event determined by prior causes; the human body is likewise a collection of molecules whose next move could in theory be predicted from physics and biology. John Dylan Haynes of Charité in Berlin uses the image of railway tracks: a person is like a train stuck on rails, unable to escape the path laid down by natural law.

[14:05] (Merrill Horn) **The brain decides seven seconds early; consciousness is just a passenger** — In the 1980s Benjamin Libet's experiments had already found that about half a second before subjects reported ‘deciding to move’, a small signal appeared in the scalp EEG. John replicated and pushed this further with fMRI: 14 subjects freely chose to press a left or right button, and brain signals appeared a full 7 seconds before people reported making the decision. Wendy counts out 7 seconds live to demonstrate how long that is — your brain may have already prepared the decision, and consciousness is only a passenger catching up.

[16:25] (Merrill Horn) **Sixty percent accuracy cannot carry ‘the decision was already made’** — John used machine learning to analyze brain signals and see whether he could predict left or right before subjects were aware of it; accuracy came out around 60% — above the 50% of a coin flip, but far from perfect. Merrill is not impressed by 60%; another group using a different technique pushed prediction to 80% just before the decision. These studies became the ammunition of the debate: John's paper has been cited by other papers nearly 3,000 times. But for opponents, the core message is: the brain is already leaning toward a choice before you know it.

[23:11] (Merrill Horn / Sean Carroll) **Temperature is not in a single atom, and choices are just as real** — Theoretical physicist Sean Carroll offers a compatibilist framework: weather forecasting depends on temperature, pressure, and humidity, but you cannot see temperature on a single atom — only when a large number of atoms gather do these quantities appear, and this is called emergence; waves in the ocean likewise exist only at the macroscopic level, yet no one doubts the ocean is real. By analogy, he says, the ‘you’ who makes decisions is a macroscopic emergence from all the microscopic processes of the brain; the fact that every neuron below obeys physical law does not mean the experience of choosing above is an illusion.

[27:59] (Merrill Horn) **Pressing a button cannot tell you whether to have a child** — Merrill aims at the soft spot of the opposition: the lab tasks are just pressing a button or flicking a wrist, far removed from ‘should I have a child’ or ‘should I marry this person’. Using the most basic motor decisions to infer life's major choices is itself an untested assumption. Even granting that brain signals precede consciousness does not mean free will has been falsified — it only shows that the process of deciding is more complex than we thought.

[30:00] (John Dylan Haynes) **Neurons fire first, and it is still ‘you’ deciding** — John Dylan Haynes, who ran the 7-second experiment, clarifies personally: in the 2008 paper he deliberately did not write ‘there is no free will’, because he wanted to publish the findings first and set the philosophical controversy aside. He himself leans toward thinking that even if neurons fire before the decision, it is still ‘you’ deciding — the definition of the ‘self’ needs to include unconscious processes too. The episode's landing point is therefore not ‘free will has been defeated’ but ‘free will needs to be reunderstood’.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] Wendy Zuckerman: "in these videos, you'll see people saying, I just remember, I have free will."

[5:00] Merrill Horn: "And these studies find that people will act worse.They're more likely to cheat less likely."

[23:11] Merrill Horn: "Like you can't look at one little atom and see that it's 20 degrees outside."

[30:00] John Dylan Haynes: "We were quite careful, So, by the way.Not to say in that 2008 paper that there's no free will."

### figures

- Time by which the readiness potential preceded the subjective decision in Libet's experiment: about half a second [9:41]
- Time by which brain signals preceded the reported decision in Haynes's fMRI experiment: 7 seconds [14:05]
- Machine-learning prediction accuracy for left/right button presses (John's experiment): about 60% [16:25]
- Prediction accuracy in another group's experiment: over 80% [17:36]
- Times Haynes's 2008 paper has been cited by other papers: nearly 3,000 [17:36]
- Number of subjects in the fMRI experiment: 14 [14:05]
- Number of references cited in this episode: 22 [31:15]

### glossary

- Emergence: A new property that appears when a large number of microscopic parts form a whole, as temperature does from atoms.
- Clockwork universe: The classical physics picture: everything is like a wound-up clock, and every event is determined by prior states.
- fMRI: An imaging technique that measures where brain activity occurs; Haynes used it to record signals before a decision.
- EEG: Electrodes on the scalp measure electrical activity; Libet used it to discover the readiness potential.

who it is for: Founders wrestling with whether their choices are really theirs, product leads who need to define where decision responsibility lies, and tech readers who have been fed fatalism by algorithmic feeds but have never heard the compatibilist case.
what to skip: The sponsor reads in the front and back segments can be fast-forwarded; the core content is concentrated in 0:00-31:15.
tags: Free will, Neuroscience, Emergence, Compatibilism, Libet experiment, Consciousness

## For an AI application company, surviving matters more than innovating: Liblib turns cash-flow positive

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-30-latetalk-ai-应用公司的最优解是活下来-而不是创新/
- show: 晚点聊 LateTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/latetalk/)
- original episode: 175: 对话Liblib陈冕：关于活下来，以及所有接近死亡的时刻
- published: 2026-07-30 · duration: 2:08:33
- transcript: Machine transcription · 39053 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**An AI application company accused of "only copying + buying traffic" has been cash-flow positive since May, with paid advertising revenue at just 4%. Founder Chen Mian says: the era of applications hasn't arrived yet, and the most important goal is to stay alive; between being first to find PMF and ultimately winning the market lies a vast distance.**

why listen: High information density. Chen Mian rarely breaks down pricing, gross margin and cash-flow details, and also confronts the originality controversy, team turmoil and personal moments of collapse. For founders building applications in the shadow of model giants, this is a rare tactical sample.

### points

[5:14] (Chen Mian) **Chasing high gross margin at the application layer actually suppresses demand** — The outside world says we blew up, but in May and June the company's cash on hand kept growing and cash flow was positive; they say we buy traffic, but we spend less than 1 million RMB per month on traffic, and paid advertising revenue is only 4%, because mainstream video media can't open accounts for AI tools — we couldn't spend the money even if we wanted to. Chen Mian attributes the outside attention to AI being too hot and the application layer being a topic, and says he "doesn't deserve" so many comments. On gross margin, he states his short-term target clearly: no more than 30% and positive — the application layer doesn't control the model, its greatest value is users, and chasing high gross margin would instead suppress demand.

[12:41] (Chen Mian) **AI membership pricing bets that users won't use up their credits** — The 3.9 discount on LibTV memberships at launch was understood by outsiders as a 3.9 discount on Chat API, but Chen Mian says this is a misunderstanding: it was a 3.9 discount on the monthly-annual package. The essence of pricing is balancing two assumptions — renewal rate and consumption rate. If a user buys 1 million credits and only uses 200,000, the remaining 800,000 is profit; the bet is that "the vast majority of users won't use up their credits over the year," the same logic as a gym betting that annual-card holders won't come often. He admits that if users used all their tokens at the original pricing, the company would definitely lose money; but this was the norm in the previous era of tool software, except that this era adds the token scale.

[22:13] (Chen Mian) **The real panic wasn't at 4,000 RMB left, it was at 6 million** — The story of having only 4,000 RMB left in the early days is true, but Chen Mian says the real panic began when there was only 6 million left on the books. At the time he had just finished a vicious fight with a wealthier rival: because he put all his energy into competition, he turned down all fundraising, didn't even add investors on WeChat, and burned 3 million to 4 million USD in a few months. The first mistake he identifies in retrospect is "founders don't look at the books, thinking that once the business takes off there will be money." Only after the battle ended did he frantically meet investors, and found no one willing to invest in a company about to go under. This experience shaped the "trade time for space" undertone of his later strategy, and explains why he is extremely sensitive to cash flow.

[37:51] (Chen Mian) **Being first to find PMF is a world away from winning the market** — Facing the originality controversy, Chen Mian admits LibTV was not the first product to find PMF, but stresses that "being first to find PMF and ultimately winning this market are a world apart." He believes it's hard for an interface to have 0-to-1 original innovation, that the optimal interface for a vertical will converge, and that engineering innovation has a shelf life of only days to a week. He is criticized harshly because "it wasn't the first PMF, yet it reached relatively the largest scale at extremely fast speed." The real moat isn't the interface, but marketing rhythm, word-of-mouth touchpoints, and the ability to scale quickly. He also responds to acquisition rumors: initially he wanted to invest a little, but the other side ignored him; later he judged this market to be bigger than his main business, so he entered it himself.

[49:20] (Chen Mian) **Management matters least, but ignoring it is already costing you** — Chen Mian quotes "management doesn't matter but organization and culture do," then adds his own line: management is relatively the least important in this era, but the cost of ignoring it is now showing. He breaks out two reward models: the first is business-oriented — whoever fits goes up, whoever doesn't gets pulled — which he did well, and which is why the company grew; the second he didn't do well — what happens to the people pulled down? The company didn't give them enough respect or feedback to find a new place. He admits he is sometimes hasty in hiring, having casually introduced 10 co-founders externally in the early days because he "didn't take titles seriously," but the other party treats it as a promise. Only one CTO truly left, because the company was about to go under, but 4 technical leads reporting directly to him left.

[1:08:36] (Chen Mian) **The near-death moment wasn't running out of money, it was the day Sora launched** — The moment that truly approached death wasn't having only 4,000 RMB left, but seeing Sora launch in January. The team had spent a year exploring the "workflow control" direction, but a new model directly internalized the workflow — "it just hit the next stage directly." Chen Mian was in Shanghai at the time; the moment he opened his laptop and saw the page he was in tears, and called a shareholder who was fundraising to say "we're finished." Later, on the flight from Shanghai back to Beijing, he figured out the direction — shifting from asset production to providing context, a new product combining agent and workflow. After landing he excitedly found the marketing lead and said "do it now." This was also the first time he cried in front of a shareholder, but he later said that cry was closer to a breakdown than the one after a startup failure.

[1:28:10] (Chen Mian) **While the giants fight for the Central Plains, you can first unify Jiangdong** — Chen Mian uses the Three Kingdoms metaphor to explain the independent survival path: when the giants are contending for the Central Plains, they have a priority order, and Jiangdong is not their highest priority — that's the startup's time gap. "When he enters the Central Plains, your unifying Jiangdong has nothing to do with his entering the Central Plains." Trade time for space, then space for resources, and finally pour resources into building a moat — a real moat needs time to be watered, "any moat built overnight is not a real moat." Geographic advantage is also dynamic: at first it might be Bashu, and only by building the Yangtze River natural barrier does it become Jiangdong. Today's Bashu is the "Shu Road is hard" between multimodality and text — general products can't easily become professional creation tools, but he also admits this path "isn't that thick."

[2:06:34] (Chen Mian) **Only by surviving first do you earn the right to talk about innovation and moats** — In closing, Chen Mian sums up his three years of entrepreneurship as "driving a super-fast car, fixing it while driving, people getting on and off, scenery passing by outside the window," but with no time to stop and say hello and say goodbye. He admits his biggest regret is not having time to say goodbye, and can only grip the steering wheel and look ahead. Asked about the scenario "suppose the model company is a train and you might just be a small car attached outside it," he says he too fears being thrown off, but wants even more to build the car well in the process. This echoes the opening — the survive he repeatedly stresses, above all specific tactics, is ultimately a philosophy about time: only by surviving first do you earn the right to talk about anything else.
