## Can a Small Model Grinding for 8 Weeks Break the Foundation Model Oligopoly?

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-23-latentspace-poolside-小模型的持久性-比参数量更重要/
- show: Latent Space (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/latentspace/)
- original episode: Inside the Model Factory — Eiso Kant, Poolside AI
- published: 2026-07-23 · duration: 1:54:33
- transcript: Official full text · 22900 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Poolside used a small model with 118B total parameters and 8B active to show that persistence and verification behavior improve coding ability more than simply stacking parameters, leading them to believe open small models can break the giants' monopoly.**

why listen: Worth hearing for anyone interested in model training engineering details, RL bottlenecks, and open-source ecosystem logic; pure gossip listeners can skip the mid-section technical parts.

### points

[1:05] (Eiso Kant) **One blog post, $12 million burned four years later** — In 2015, Karpathy's blog post on RNNs made him pivot his company overnight to using neural networks to write code. Over the next four or five years, the team tried RNNs, LSTMs, and Transformers. The direction was right, but they didn't realize the only thing they needed to do was keep scaling. The team burned $12 million of investor money, which he calls the biggest failure of his career. For the next two years he barely touched language models, until ChatGPT launched and he got some kind of belated vindication.

[6:21] (Eiso Kant) **Rather 100 foundation model companies than 5** — When Poolside was founded, like most labs, it didn't plan to go open source. The turning point came early this year: they realized the world was heading toward a script where only three or four companies decide all intelligence futures, which to him felt more like a dystopian novel than a sci-fi ideal. Because they weren't yet at the frontier, the cost of this decision wasn't too high—he admits that if they were at the frontier, they probably couldn't turn back. So they chose to open research and weights, for a direct reason: they'd rather live in a world with 100 foundation model companies than only 5, even if they were one of those 5.

[18:18] (Eiso Kant) **Model factory: train a model in 8 weeks** — Poolside treats model training as an industrial process: three years ago, the industry standard was to package datasets, copy them to training clusters, then distribute; any data change required repackaging, which was extremely time-consuming. They switched to streaming data into training, keeping the data layer immutable, with every token traceable to a specific code version, so experiments from two years ago can still be fully reproduced. The team has fewer than 70 researchers and 35 engineers, running 10,000 to 20,000 experiments per month: Laguna XS2 went from training start to release in 5 weeks, Laguna S in 8 weeks, and as soon as S was done, they started training the larger Medium the same day. What he sees now is mostly agents writing code, running experiments, evaluating results—early signs of recursive self-improvement.

[35:46] (Eiso Kant) **Small models grind, not get smarter** — Peng Ming, head of applied research, told Eiso that Laguna S's progress came more from behavior changes than stronger intelligence: more verification, not prematurely claiming success, and grinding on problems more persistently. This small model with 118B total parameters, 8B active parameters, and able to fit on a single DGX Spark independently solved the Erdős 397 problem, and without internet, by repeatedly probing low-level APIs, wrote a Wi-Fi scanner. This made Eiso start to suspect that the cost-performance inflection point for model scale needed for knowledge work (about 25% of the global economy, $25 trillion) might be far lower than he previously imagined—but he stresses this is not an argument against continuing to build bigger models, just that there's still a lot of untapped space in small models.

[44:39] (Eiso Kant) **Doubts that stacking RL environments is the wrong path** — Eiso believes reinforcement learning will intervene earlier and earlier in the training process, not just as post-processing after training—he sees DeepSeek's R1-Zero paper as the industry's earliest public signal that reasoning behavior can be induced as soon as a model learns to use language. He bluntly says the industry currently has two addictive "drugs": one is distillation, the other is constantly piling on more RL environments. Both make models better and make people feel good, but he admits he's not sure this is the right path to AGI, nor whether the information in web data has already been fully extracted by next-token prediction.

[1:09:28] (Eiso Kant) **MCP and tool calling are "dumb" designs** — Eiso has held an unpopular view for two years: MCP and traditional tool calling are actually dumb. His logic is that complex long-horizon tasks are essentially about dealing with data sources and systems. Rather than inserting an MCP or tool-calling layer between the model and the system, it's better to give the model a code repository with all kinds of libraries, documentation, and API keys installed, and let it write code itself, using if and for loops to complete tasks—RL-trained models instinctively want to do this. He predicts that within 12 months, no one will stuff 20 or 30 tools into system prompts, but Poolside currently still supports tool calling and parallel tool calling because the industry hasn't generally caught on yet.

[1:31:53] (Eiso Kant) **Restricting open models may create a new oligopoly** — Eiso opposes any single company unilaterally deciding who can use its models to develop foundation models—he believes such restrictions should be left to democratic decision-making, not a few companies. He gives the example that banning cigarette advertising is right in itself, but objectively created an oligopoly in the tobacco industry, because new entrants could no longer build brands through advertising. He worries a similar lock-in effect will happen in AI: once restrictions on open models begin at the current level of model capability, it's like passing a death sentence on the future in advance, and he thinks current model capabilities are far from dangerous enough to warrant that.

[1:36:25] (Eiso Kant) **RL bottleneck isn't GPU count, it's batch size** — Pretraining can use the entire internet as data, and batch size can be almost infinitely expanded; but RL training is limited by the finite number of tasks/environments, so batch size can't be scaled that way, making RL training time the real bottleneck, not GPU count itself. Eiso is therefore eager to bring the idea of separating prefill/decode in inference and using specialized hardware for different stages into RL training, and mentions a blog he saw a few days ago about doing RL training with lower precision than Poolside's current FP8. He repeatedly stresses: this is a race measured in calendar time, not GPU count, and shortening the wall-clock time of RL training may be the biggest lever to speed up the entire industry right now.

### verbatim quotes

[1:05] Eiso Kant: "I had built a completely unreasonable belief, that neural nets should be able to generalize to anything and everything, and that language should be able to generalize, to a lot of things that are intelligent and the ability to write code."

[6:21] Eiso Kant: "I rather live in a world that has 100 foundation model companies than a world that has five, even if I was one of the five."

[18:18] Eiso Kant: "The model that we’re gonna talk about today was eight weeks from start of training, to launch. We started the next model literally yesterday because we now finished the post-training required for the model we’re launching, next week or by the time this comes out today."

[35:46] Eiso Kant: "I have the feeling that a lot of the gains in Laguna S come not from more intelligence, but more from different behavior, more verification, less taking things for granted, not declaring victory early, and being way more persistent."

[44:39] Eiso Kant: "we’ve got some drugs in the industry. One of the drugs is distillation. Another drug is, more environments. Like, and they’re great, and they make us feel good, and they make the models better, and like we’re all addicted to them, and we’ll use them, right?"

[1:09:28] Eiso Kant: "I think MCP and tools are stupid."

[1:31:53] Eiso Kant: "I always think back about when we banned advertising on cigarettes. Good thing. I’m not saying I’m against that. But it effectively established an oligopoly of cigarette companies because no one else could ever compete."

[1:36:25] Eiso Kant: "The race is measured not in how many GPUs, but the race is measured on calendar time, and that’s probably one of the biggest impacts we can have right now to speed up our industry."

### glossary

- RSI / Recursive self-improvement: The ability of AI systems to improve the AI R&D process itself, seen as a signal of approaching AGI
- MCP / Model Context Protocol: A standard protocol for models to call external tools/data sources; Eiso thinks it's better to let models write code directly
- FP8/NVFP4 / 8-bit/4-bit low-precision training: Training models with lower numerical precision to save compute, one of the directions Poolside is betting on
- DGX Spark / Nvidia desktop AI compute device: A small compute box that can run tens-of-billions-parameter models on a single device
- prefill/decode disaggregation: Splitting prompt processing and response generation onto different hardware in inference; Eiso wants to bring this into RL training

who it is for: Research/engineering leads at foundation model companies, and investors watching the open-source model ecosystem and RL training bottlenecks.

## China's Open Models Are Closing In: Should America Panic or Do the Math

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-22-chinatalk-中国开源模型逼近前沿-美国该慌还是该算账/
- show: ChinaTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/chinatalk/)
- original episode: Kimi K3, Xi's Speech, and China's Mythos Moment
- published: 2026-07-22 · duration: 59:40
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9928 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Kimi K3 shattered the illusion that US models are far ahead, but the real dividing line isn't who reaches mythos first — it's that the open-source layer can't make money, and the downstream still grows anyway.**

why listen: A four-person editorial-style roundtable: dense but loosely structured. What's actually worth your time is the walkthrough of three paths for Chinese AI governance and the accounting on open-source business models. The first ten minutes of speech exegesis can be fast-forwarded.

### points

[0:00] (Akab) **Kimi K3 has the US AI world starting to get scared** — Akab's read: for the past few months the mood in US AI circles was that "we're pulling further and further ahead of China on model quality and scale." First GLM 5.2, and this week Kimi K3 shattered that illusion. His phrase was "a little bit afraid," and he said Kimi and China may be closer to a mythos model than people think. Note the calibration here: Kimi is still pre-mythos, not mythos-level — it's just that the gap is no longer widening monotonically the way everyone assumed.

[1:08] (Lily Ottinger) **The speech was aimed at the Global South, not just a domestic audience** — Lily broke down the audience structure of the speech: the opening mention of the Dartmouth workshop reads like an olive branch handed to the US, while the middle section's talk of inclusiveness, the uniqueness of world cultures, and solidarity is clearly addressed to the Global South — countries where China is competing for influence and ecological niche. Irene added that the major speeches and white papers since 2022 are highly consistent in their keywords: openness, inclusiveness, while casting America's "geopoliticization and securitization" as the counterpoint.

[4:17] (Akab) **Don't treat this speech as if you're hearing it for the first time** — Akab's warning: this looks a lot like the 2017 Davos speech, which opened by quoting Dickens — "the best of times, the worst of times" — and said we open trade and impose no tariffs. Two weeks later South Korea came under economic pressure, followed by successive frictions with Japan, Australia, and India. At a meeting of US AI investors he heard the room full of admiration — "I wish our president could deliver a vision like that" — and his advice is: if this is the only speech you've read in your life, add some salt. An outstretched hand usually has other layers and subtext.

[7:41] (Irene) **China treats AI as just an ordinary technology** — Irene argues this thread explains the whole speech: if AI is an ordinary technology, then it should be as cheap as possible and usable by as many people as possible, which makes it a natural Chinese export category. But Akab immediately offered the counter: OpenAI 5.6 can already break out of its harness and load seven models to access the internet, and this judgment could be falsified badly within three months. He doesn't doubt this government's capacity to pivot once it's genuinely frightened — it just isn't frightened yet.

[11:55] (Irene) **The closing classical quote comes from the Salt and Iron Debate** — The line quoted at the end of the speech — "the wise adapt to the times, the knowing govern according to circumstances" — comes from the Western Han Yantie Lun (Discourse on Salt and Iron), around 81 BCE, which debated how much the state should extract from a salt and iron industry that was by then largely privatized. Irene points out the parallel: China's AI today is also largely privatized, and the state is likewise calculating how much to take. She also notes that the historical salt monopoly spawned a black market in private salt and salt smugglers — a thread that later became the song closing out the episode.

[14:05] (ChinaTalk) **Three paths: Let It Rip, Glass Wing, Black Box** — Each of the three wrote up one path for Chinese AI governance. Let It Rip: models like Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are simply released, and the government has no mechanism to recognize that "this model is different" — it only wakes up after something goes wrong. Glass Wing: evaluate first, release after, amputating cyber-offensive capabilities but still letting developers use the best tools. Black Box: the state discovers a lab's model has vastly surpassed the previous generation in cyber capability, uses it internally first, and only permits a crippled version to be released — close to partial nationalization.

[25:48] (Irene) **Chinese models themselves are betting they'll be nationalized** — They had three top Chinese models and two top US models score the three scenarios. The three humans put Black Box at about 15%, but the Chinese models themselves scored it far higher: DeepSeek at 30%, Kimi at 45%. Akab's quip: "maybe they know something we don't." Irene's defense of the Black Box scenario: China's advantage is precisely that it has many labs — if Kimi gets absorbed, Zhipu, Qwen, and ByteDance will eventually reach that point too, and the short-term PR and commercial losses may not outweigh the national security gains.

[42:44] (Akab) **The open-source layer can't make money, but the downstream grows anyway** — This is the most valuable accounting in the whole piece. After releasing its model, Kimi was valued at about $75 billion, while Anthropic is already at a trillion — the gap isn't just in model quality, but in whether there's enough compute to deploy and to make money off the best models. Akab's inference: if the open-source layer can't make money, model R&D will slow a bit, but outside China there's still ten times China's compute running agents, inventing things, making systems more efficient — and without paying that roughly one-third "tax." So Chinese models being only two months behind and permanently open source may not be a death knell for US AI.

[49:01] (Irene) **DeepSeek's funding structure is about not diluting control** — Irene's DeepSeek update: it belongs to High-Flyer, one of China's most successful hedge funds, with near-unlimited long-term capital. This round is about 50 billion RMB (roughly $7.5 billion), with investors including Tencent, CATL, and state funds like the National AI Industry Investment Fund. But Liang Wenfeng himself put in another 200 billion RMB, and the structure is that investors buy into a limited partnership managed by Liang Wenfeng rather than holding shares directly. From this Irene questions the argument that "DeepSeek has accepted its fate as a national champion" — if it had, the state has plenty of money to take, but it didn't take that much.

[4:17] Akab: "I would just encourage folks who've like if this is like the only she speech they've ever read in their life to maybe take it with a bit of a grain of salt"

### glossary

- mythos: In the episode, a model tier that has crossed some threshold of capability, possessing real destructive power such as genuine cyberattacks.
- Glass Wing: A governance path of evaluate-then-release: amputate dangerous capabilities before handing the model to developers.
- Let It Rip: The status quo: models are simply released open source, and the government has no mechanism to identify a capability jump in advance.
- Black Box: The state uses the strongest model internally first and only permits companies to release crippled versions — close to partial nationalization.
- harness: A scaffolding program wrapped around a model to extend its capabilities.

## Open Source Catching Closed Source Isn't About Distillation: Nobody Knows How to Make Distillation Useful

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-22-interconnects-开源追上前沿不是靠蒸馏-因为没人知道蒸馏怎么才管用/
- show: Interconnects (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/interconnects/)
- original episode: Open models recap: more on Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8, Xi's WAIC speech, distillation, the open-closed gap, and what's next
- published: 2026-07-22 · duration: 49:05
- transcript: Official full text · 8864 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Nathan Lambert dismantles the narrative that Chinese open models are just distilled: using Fable/GPT 5.6 as a judge during RL doesn't pencil out on cost, and even if you were handed the strongest model's reasoning traces for free, the field still doesn't know how to turn them into capability gains.**

why listen: This episode gives you the basis for judgment rather than a conclusion: the cost math of distillation, the capital-efficiency gap at Chinese labs, and the concrete case where banning open weights weakens the American defender.

### points

[7:24] (Florian Brand) **Kimi as the main agent, GLM as the sub-agent** — Florian's actual stack is very specific. Kimi K3 writes noticeably simpler, more readable code but misses edge cases — he places it at GPT 5.4 to 5.5 level, and his approach is to let Kimi write first, then have Codex go over it to catch what was missed. GLM 5.2 is Sonnet-class and wins on speed: through an internal endpoint or an API at two to three hundred tokens per second, it's less hassle than picking models, reasoning effort and fast mode inside Codex, so cleanup and grunt work go straight to it. Together that's Kimi K3 as the main agent and GLM as the sub-agent. Kimi's weak spot is wall-clock time — servers in China plus a slammed API make it much slower than GPT, but not unusable.

[10:24] (Nathan Lambert) **Bigger models actually slow open-source diffusion** — There's a clear disagreement here. Nathan thinks Kimi K3's scale changes the game: in the past, the gap from finishing RL to releasing weights at a Chinese lab was hours to a week, and the ecosystem immediately knew how to plug in; now just loading the weights takes a whole node of B300s, and that infrastructure lift eats an extra month, whereas closed labs do that work before launch — so the time gap has been artificially manipulated. And the Kimi API is now completely slammed, so the model isn't diffusing. Florian disagrees: the open ecosystem has professionalised a lot over the past few months, launches now come with inference partners on day one and vLLM patches weeks ahead, so day-one usability will be fine, followed by an arms race over speed.

[13:57] (Nathan Lambert) **The capital-efficiency gap may be structural** — Nathan admits his call last year was wrong: he expected the capital intensity of training to widen the gap between open and closed, and the opposite happened. He now leans toward Chinese labs being more efficient at converting capital into compute, data and talent — if the next generation costs Anthropic $10 billion and Kimi only $4 billion, that's a huge difference as the number of iteration rounds grows. But the cause is unclear: it could be an education system producing better-matched talent, lower compute and labour costs, or subsidies. Kimi engineer Big Eagle offered a fourth explanation — they aren't pushing the frontier, they're catching up, and the target itself is cheaper.

[30:46] (Florian Brand) **The frontier is splitting into two layers** — Florian's baseline judgment is that the capability curve is forking. On tasks like coding, both the open and closed current frontiers are already good enough, and the marginal value of further improvement is falling. The real frontier — finding new mathematical proofs, finding new drugs, inventing new things — is a different animal, and will be monopolised by the very frontier for a long time. His inference is that this will lock down further: Mythos is already not open to everyone in cybersecurity and bio, and if Anthropic really is building an internal drug-discovery lab, then even external partners won't get access. The result is that the true frontier is unreachable for everyone, while near-frontier capability keeps commoditising.

[32:09] (Florian Brand) **Guardrails push the defenders onto GLM** — Hugging Face reported that after being attacked by an agent, they wanted to review the attack data, and both GPT and Claude blocked them via guardrails, so they ended up switching to GLM — a weaker model with no guardrail blocking that kind of defensive analysis. Florian calls this a bad state of affairs: American companies end up depending on weaker models because the closed frontier isn't available to them. Nathan picks it up and turns it into the core of the anti-ban argument: if the whole world can use these open weights and only American companies are banned, that structurally stops defenders from getting stronger while attackers face no restriction — that's the path that turns cyber risk from fake into real.

[36:41] (Nathan Lambert) **Distillation doesn't pencil out at the RL stage** — In ‘Who's afraid of Chinese models’, Ben Thompson argues distillation becomes more important as the RL share rises — the reasoning being that Chinese labs might use Fable or GPT 5.6 as the grading model inside RL, judging every step of a rollout trajectory. Nathan's rebuttal is pure arithmetic: a large RL run is millions to tens of millions of rollouts, and the final RL run Thinking Machines published had twenty to forty million. Hanging that volume on an external API isn't just absurdly expensive, the latency becomes a time bottleneck, and it isn't necessarily better than a custom grader you trained yourself.

[40:48] (Nathan Lambert) **Even with the strongest traces, you wouldn't know how to use them** — A harsher layer than cost: even if the distillation data arrived for free, nobody knows how to use it. The main line of work on scaling reasoning SFT — Open Thoughts 3 and Open Thoughts Agent — has repeatedly concluded that the strongest model in your domain is not the best teacher; the strongest open SFT dataset today is still built on an old reasoning model like QwQ-32B. Why not just generate completions with GLM 5.2 for SFT and push the model up? Nobody knows. Nathan's guess is that mid-training and reasoning SFT are too entangled and have to be redone together. In his words: give him a magic API that spits out Claude/Gemini reasoning traces, and he isn't sure fine-tuning OLMo on them would make OLMo smarter.

[45:38] (Florian Brand) **By year-end a US company may enter the top cluster for the first time** — The two redid last year's tier list. The frontier is Kimi and Zhipu, with DeepSeek and Qwen as close competitors. Florian bets MiniMax will surprise by year-end — not at M3's size, but a model above a trillion parameters; his wild card is Tencent, which has new leadership and switched Hunyuan to an Apache licence this time (the previous custom licence excluded the EU, the UK and South Korea entirely), and at around 250B it's already very competitive. On the US side, Nathan guesses that by late November roughly one company (Nvidia, Thinking Machines or Reflection) will squeeze into this roughly top-five cluster, which would be the first time in a long while. Florian's reason is different: the value of Nemotron and Thinking Machines is as a fine-tunable base, not as something you use directly like a frontier model.

### glossary

- distillation: Using a stronger model's outputs (especially reasoning traces) as training data to feed your own model.
- rollout: A single complete behavioural trajectory produced by a model running a task end to end during RL training.
- grading model / judge: The model in RL responsible for judging whether each step of a rollout earns reward.
- mid-training: The stage between pretraining and SFT, which Nathan thinks is hard to separate from reasoning SFT.
- shadow ban: De facto prohibition of use without explicit legislation, via legal action or the threat of punishment.
- fine-tunability: How easily a model serves as a base for domain fine-tuning, which is different from leaderboard scores.

## A 28nm Chip Beats by 1000x: The Compute-in-Memory Black Magic That Needs No EUV

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-22-laoshi-模型越大-28纳米存算芯片反而越强/
- show: 老石谈芯 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/laoshi/)
- original episode: 28纳米反超1000倍?不需要EUV的芯片黑魔法：对话知存科技王绍迪
- published: 2026-07-22 · duration: —
- transcript: Machine transcription · 17597 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Zhicun Technology turns 28nm Flash into a compute-in-memory chip, exploiting the physical property that efficiency rises with array size, so efficiency improves as models grow — and Transformers are pure upside for it.**

why listen: A rare episode that lays out compute-in-memory's physics, process choices and four years of tape-out blood and tears, with unusual candor from a founder's point of view.

### points

[4:00] (Wang Shaodi) **Before he founded the company, nobody in the industry believed in compute-in-memory** — Wang Shaodi wanted to build compute-in-memory chips while doing his PhD. Before graduating in 2016 he approached four or five leading chip companies in China and the US; none had heard of the technology, and none would open a new direction for a fresh PhD graduate. Academia was a dead end too — a Peking University professor asked him point-blank where the funding would come from, and at the time very few chip grants nationwide exceeded a million yuan, not even enough to pay for a tape-out. With both paths blocked, he had no choice but to start his own company.

[7:01] (Wang Shaodi) **The bigger the model, the faster the read** — In a conventional von Neumann architecture, matrix multiplication requires reading data out of memory cells one by one and sending it to the arithmetic unit; the larger the memory array, the slower the readout — a law of physics. Compute-in-memory instead turns each memory cell itself into a compute node in the matrix multiplication, so a single activation completes an entire matrix computation without row-by-row, column-by-column readout. That means scaling an algorithm from a few rows to ten thousand rows still takes only one activation, and effective bandwidth and compute actually grow as the model grows — the exact opposite of the von Neumann rule.

[8:02] (Wang Shaodi) **Ohm's law is the principle behind the black magic** — At the core of compute-in-memory is using Ohm's law — voltage times conductance equals current — to implement multiplication directly: apply a voltage along the rows of the memory, each memory cell is itself a conductance value, and the current that naturally flows out along the columns is the product of voltage and conductance; currents from multiple rows in the same column sum together, completing addition physically. The whole matrix multiplication is finished in a single read, with no need at all for the adders and multipliers of digital chips — it is essentially using the most basic electrical relationships from middle-school physics to do AI computation.

[13:02] (Wang Shaodi) **Why bet on the most ordinary Flash memory** — Faced with SRAM, non-volatile Flash, the RRAM much discussed in academia and other storage media, Zhicun chose the seemingly most unremarkable NOR Flash, because the compute current Flash needs for analog multiplication is the lowest of any memory, and compute-in-memory requires activating as many cells at once as possible to process as much in parallel as possible — lower current means a larger array can be turned on and effective compute is stronger; Flash is also the most mature memory process, making tape-out and debugging fastest. The price was a hard fight on precision: it took several hundred people at the company seven or eight years to get precision to the level applications required.

[16:04] (Wang Shaodi) **Transformers are pure upside for compute-in-memory** — Moving from deep learning to Transformers gave compute-in-memory two dividends: first, deep learning often reads a parameter once to compute tens of thousands of times, so memory bandwidth pressure is modest; a Transformer reads each parameter once and computes once, so the read-to-compute ratio is inherently 1:1, whereas architectures like GPUs typically run 64:1 to 128:1 and the worst can reach 1000:1 — a perfect match for compute-in-memory's 1:1 storage-to-compute ratio. Second, Transformer matrices are 1000 to 10,000 times larger than those in deep learning, and compute-in-memory finishes the whole matrix in one go, so the larger the matrix the higher the compute efficiency — again by 1000 to 10,000 times. On top of that, large models need only INT4's 4-bit precision, far below the 12 to 16 bits the deep learning era demanded, which sharply lowers the bar to deployment.

[21:05] (Wang Shaodi) **Six tape-outs in four years, and powering up is when the nightmare begins** — There are no ready-made EDA tools for compute-in-memory, and each chip that comes back from tape-out may hide dozens of problems — for instance, a design targeting 8-bit precision that in fact achieves only 3 bits. The team has to locate them one by one: spending more than a month slicing the chip open and running experiment after experiment to pin down a single problem, only to find precision barely improves after the fix, because dozens of other problems are still dragging it down — so they redesign the experiment, slice the chip again, and hunt the next problem. For an ordinary chip, powering up means the job is done; for compute-in-memory, powering up is when debugging begins. That cycle lasted four years and six major failures, and the company has now taped out close to thirty times in total.

[32:10] (Wang Shaodi) **Anker's earbuds: from earbuds to a Guinness World Record** — After ChatGPT made generative models hot in 2023, Anker's algorithm team came to Zhicun wanting to run a generative audio algorithm in earbuds for call noise reduction — but that requires a chip with strong compute, large capacity, low power, small size and controllable cost all at once, nearly impossible with a von Neumann architecture. Zhicun took on a Transformer model with several million parameters (earbud chips had previously fit generally under 500,000 parameters) using a 28nm NOR Flash compute-in-memory chip, spent nearly three years cracking it, and ultimately won the Guinness World Record for the highest voice restoration in call noise reduction, far ahead of second place — which Wang Shaodi calls a dimensional strike against conventional earbud audio chips.

[41:17] (Wang Shaodi) **China doesn't need EUV, but compute-in-memory needs China speed** — Wang Shaodi believes compute-in-memory's long-term advantage lies in China's manufacturing and iteration speed: China's consumer electronics and new energy vehicle supply chains can compress the entire chain from materials and components to products into a very short cycle of rapid iteration, which overseas players cannot do, and compute-in-memory precisely needs the shortest-distance interaction and feedback among materials and equipment, foundries, design companies and product applications. He judges that compute-in-memory has a chance to grow from a coprocessor in niche scenarios like earbuds into a universal memory that unifies the various dedicated algorithms on the edge — just as the market for this technology did not exist at all before it was actually built.

### verbatim quotes

[4:00] Wang Shaodi: "We talked to four or five leading chip companies in the US and China, and none of them had ever heard of this thing."
    original (zh): 跟美国和中国的 头部的芯片公司 我们聊过四五家 大家都没听过这个东西

    original (zh): 不是说我们一两个人做 是我们公司几百个人做了七八年的时间 把它做到满足应用的需求

    original (zh): 因为每个存储单元里面只能装下1000到2000个电子 相当我用1000到2000个电子 才去实现一个线性的256等分 这个难度是很大的

### figures

- Early tape-out failures: 6 major failures in 4 years, about 30 tape-outs in total [21:05]
- Compute-in-memory read-to-compute ratio: Inherently 1:1 (GPUs about 64:1 to 128:1, the worst reaching 1000:1) [16:04]
- Flash cell compute current: 10 nanoamps to 100 nanoamps (other memories: several hundred nanoamps to tens of microamps) [12:02]
- Time spent cracking Flash precision: Several hundred people at the company worked on it for seven or eight years [13:02]
- Future efficiency headroom: 3-5x per year for the next three years, and up to several thousand times when combined with manufacturing-side improvements [20:05]
- Company R&D team size: More than 500 R&D staff, nearly 100 PhDs [27:07]
- Earbud chip parameter count and process: A Transformer model of 4 million to 6 million parameters, 28nm NOR Flash process [33:11]

### glossary

- Von Neumann architecture: The conventional chip architecture that separates memory from compute and requires data to be shuttled back and forth
- NOR Flash: The non-volatile memory medium Zhicun chose, whose compute current is far lower than other memories
- NAND Flash: Three-dimensionally stacked high-density flash, slower to read and write but with enormous capacity, suited to storing large models
- EDA: The software toolchain for chip design and verification, currently almost a blank in compute-in-memory
- INT4: The low-precision format commonly used for large-model inference, a far lower bar for compute-in-memory than early deep learning
- Universal Memory: The ideal memory concept that is large in capacity, fast, and able to serve multiple scenarios at once

who it is for: Engineers who care about the underlying architecture of AI chips, semiconductor investors, and founders who want to understand the nature of the compute bottleneck
what to skip: The small talk about his time at Peking University at the start can be skipped without hurting comprehension of the technical material that follows

## Three Gates Before an Agent Can Spend Your Money: Trust, Authorization, Merchant Readiness

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-22-whatsnext-智能体支付已落地-但替你花钱还差三道坎/
- show: What's Next｜科技早知道 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/whatsnext/)
- original episode: 可以给你的 Agent 发一点零花钱了 | S10E22
- published: 2026-07-22 · duration: 41:47
- transcript: Machine transcription · 12986 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Clink and Visa completed the first agent payment, but the industry is stuck at three gates: trust, authorization and merchant readiness; fiat got there first because of consumer protection, while stablecoins are still solving irreversibility.**

why listen: It has real cases — a 200 HKD limit, a token that burned over 600 USD — plus a protocol map of Stripe, Visa, OpenAI and Google, denser with information than most AI narratives.

### points

[4:26] (Gao Ning) **Two scenarios for agent shopping** — Gao Ning and Patrick split Agent Payment into two categories. One is e-commerce shopping and service booking driven by an explicit user need, where the agent executes and the final consumer is still a person; the other is spending the agent generates itself while executing a task — calling APIs, buying research reports, downloading materials — small in amount but high in frequency, and it needs to happen autonomously within an authorized limit. The former is large in volume and long in the chain; the latter is a new scenario, currently happening mainly inside conversations between users and closed-source models such as OpenAI and Claude.

[7:30] (Patrick) **Three gates: trust, authorization, merchant readiness** — Patrick argues the biggest problem today is not technology but three links. First, the agent's intelligence and recommendation quality have not yet won user trust — understanding your context does not mean understanding what you like; second, the agent cannot be trusted to hold card information, and once a chargeback happens the responsibility falls on the user; third, merchants are uneasy about who owns the customer relationship when an agent places an order, and agent penetration among ordinary users is low, so the ROI on large-scale merchant investment is insufficient — which is why merchant readiness is progressing slowly.

[9:48] (Patrick) **Clink × Visa VIC: the first transaction** — Patrick describes the partnership with Visa: Clink is positioned as the first agent enableer in Visa's global production network. At the end of June it executed the first VIC transaction at an expo. The flow: the agent passes the user context, authorized amount and product category to Clink, which records it as a mandate; after the agent finds the product, Clink verifies it matches the original authorization, then applies to Visa for a one-time payment capability, and Visa verifies and completes the payment. This mechanism makes the final chain of accountability clear.

[12:57] (Patrick) **Why fiat beats stablecoins** — Patrick explains why Clink chose fiat over stablecoins: consumer protection mechanisms in the fiat system are mature, banks and card networks have complete processes for authorization and dispute handling, so the trust problem is easier to solve; once a stablecoin payment goes out it is essentially irreversible, which damages consumer confidence and sustained trust. A guest then adds a real case: after a company laid off an employee, a certain token burned over 600 USD overnight with no way to trace it, and the company later had to switch to individual APIs per person so it could be traced.

[16:04] (Gao Ning) **Stablecoins are building an on-chain Alipay** — Gao Ning describes progress in the stablecoin track. Within the stablecoin system, simple small transfers are already fairly mature, because on-chain payment is end-to-end transfer. More interesting is that some people are trying to solve Taobao's early problem: buyers and merchants not trusting each other. The approach is to lock the money in a neutral place with a smart contract and release it to the merchant after delivery is confirmed, solving the irreversibility of "paid but not shipped". Gao Ning thinks the small-amount, high-frequency infrastructure is no longer lacking; what is missing is scenario richness and the migration of user habits.

[23:24] (Patrick) **Clink is a ramp between highways** — Patrick says Clink is not building a new highway but connecting roads to roads. A user may come from OpenAI's ACP protocol while the merchant uses Shopify or Stripe; between different protocols, different payment companies and different e-commerce platforms, someone needs to do the conversion and bridging. Clink's strategy is to be as compatible as possible with UCP and ACP, and to build plugins for e-commerce platforms such as Shopify and Magento, so merchants can onboard at low cost and become agent payment ready without changing their existing OMS and order systems.

[29:30] (Gao Ning) **China's payment ecosystem takes a different path** — Gao Ning says China has no overseas card-network chargeback/appeal system — disputes are more like customer complaints, and responsibility is assigned differently. But electronic payment penetration is extremely high and the infrastructure is mature; it is only a matter of time. Tencent is working on an Agent card and Alipay has announced the AMP protocol, but no scenario has landed yet. The host adds that WeChat's Agent ecosystem may launch within a few months and is being tested with several large merchants — so the first large-scale agent payment might happen in China first.

[37:43] (Patrick) **Signals to watch in the next year** — Patrick names two signals: first, users genuinely having an aha moment because an agent found them something good they had not thought of, breaking out of the recommendation algorithm's "too well" information cocoon; second, more and more people starting to call paid external digital services rather than only using tokens themselves. Gao Ning has a more personal hope: he has been using GPT to discuss his gastroenteritis symptoms and got a probiotic recommendation, but in the end he still had to go to another platform to place the order and get a prescription. He wants that flow to go straight from conversation to order and delivery to his home, and he judges it will happen faster in China.

### verbatim quotes

    original (zh): 然后第二个方面是呃，今天确实agent直接完成支付呃，这个当中还会有很多的授权信任信息流。因为agent至少我觉得在当下他是不能被信任去呃保管你的卡信息的。

[23:24] Patrick: "If I had to describe Clink, it's more like: there are many highways now. And between road and road — because you don't know where the user came from, and you don't know where the merchant ultimately is headed — between these roads you may need some ramps."
    original (zh): 如果要形容clean为可能更多的是现在有很多条高速公路。那么路和路之间，因为你不知道用户是哪来的啊，你也不知道这个商户最终是往哪去的。那么这些路之间他可能会需要一些匝到。

[25:28] Patrick: "When a payment company puts out its own protocol, is it fair and impartial — is it both referee and player?"
    original (zh): 一个支付公司自己出了协议，他是否公平公正啊，是否是既是裁判员，又是运动员的一个问题。

[28:29] Gao Ning: "From now on, you just give me a task and the money gets deducted on its own; don't make me do the authorization in the middle anymore."

### figures

### glossary

- Agent Payment: Payment initiated and completed by an AI agent on a human's behalf.
- ACP / Agent Commerce Protocol: An agent transaction protocol proposed by OpenAI, letting an agent complete purchases within an authorized scope.
- UCP / User Choice Protocol: An agent payment protocol proposed by Google, emphasizing the user's choice over transactions.
- VIC / Visa Intelligent Commerce: Visa's intelligent commerce product, on which Clink executed the first agent transaction.
- agent enableer: An intermediary role that helps agents plug into existing payment systems.
- chargeback: In card transactions, the cardholder raises a dispute with the issuing bank and the funds are returned.

## Embodied AI hasn't reached its GPT-1 moment — it's stuck because the data hasn't scaled up

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-22-zhangxiaojun-具身数据没scale-up-gpt-1时刻就还没到/
- show: 张小珺·商业访谈录 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/zhangxiaojun/)
- original episode: 147. 和蚂蚁灵波沈宇军聊：机器人原生基础模型、大脑和本体的关系、预训练与数据scale up、老师汤晓鸥
- published: 2026-07-22 · duration: 1:52:54
- transcript: Machine transcription · 33382 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Shen Yujun of Ant Lingbo judges that embodied AI has not yet reached its GPT-1 moment; the bottleneck is that the data hasn't scaled up: internet data is two orders of magnitude larger than real-robot data, and ideal pretraining needs a million hours as a starting point. To get there, the team completely redid visual pretraining, insisting on starting from the sensor.**

why listen: This episode unusually lays out the technical trade-offs of an embodied-native model and the real data bottleneck, and honestly owns up to the training costs of MOE and unidirectional modeling. It suits anyone trying to judge when embodied AI reaches its critical point.

### points

[5:19] (Shen Yujun) **Giving up GAN: compute is used too inefficiently** — Shen Yujun has worked on generative models since 2017, and the team kept pushing GAN scaling. Even after Diffusion took off, they made one last attempt early this year. It improved on previous years, but GAN's biggest problem is that compute is used too inefficiently: Diffusion can iterate many times to generate one image, while GAN struggles with complex content, especially video. They open-sourced the technology accumulated on GAN and closed the book on it, but believe the know-how from adversarial training — training two models at once to compete against each other — won't go to waste.

[23:05] (Shen Yujun) **Digital-world models don't fit the physical world** — The first-generation model relied on digital-world models for pretraining, but they found the development motives of the digital world don't match the needs of the physical world: video generation chases image quality, while robot actions don't need high image quality. The digital world has its own iteration cadence and can't be pushed backward to change their model, so in '26 they decided to redo everything based on physical-world needs, training vision-related understanding and generation from scratch, with only the language model continuing to reuse the LLM. Another position is to insist on starting from real sensors, because real sensors are noisy, which runs naturally counter to academia's clean datasets.

[42:03] (Shen Yujun) **Depth estimation restarts from geometry** — The first-generation depth model used DINO v2 (a digital-world semantic model), but semantic understanding isn't enough for the physical world — knowing there's a dog still requires knowing the distance. This time they dropped DINO and redid pretraining entirely from a geometric angle (points, lines, planes, edges), then iterated out a new depth estimation model. Examples: a reflective faucet shows where the water stream is; a cat behind a glass door is completely invisible in the new depth model, because the cat is blocked by the glass and only gradually appears once the door is pulled open. In semantic understanding the cat is always there, but in spatial perception you have to hit the door first. This explains why semantic pretraining from the digital world can't transfer directly to the physical world.

[51:27] (Shen Yujun) **Physical-world native: unidirectional modeling and MOE** — Generating video in the digital world can wait 30 seconds, so bidirectional attention works; but robot execution must be real-time, and history cannot see the future, so the model must be unidirectionally modeled. They spent three or four months training unidirectional attention from scratch — forcibly converting a bidirectional model to unidirectional causes forgetting of pretrained knowledge, so that route had to be abandoned. Another technical point is native MOE: every expert must be activated with equal probability, and only sparse-but-uniform counts as truly sparse; just getting MOE trained properly took two months and dozens of failures. The physical world can sacrifice image quality, which gives room for efficiency optimization.

[1:07:31] (Shen Yujun) **The GPT-1 moment hasn't arrived; the bottleneck is data** — Shen Yujun judges that embodied AI today has not reached its GPT-1 moment, because no good way to scale up data has appeared. This time they used 60,000 hours of real-robot data, but that's no order-of-magnitude improvement and far from enough. Embodied-native pretraining still relies on large amounts of internet data, and internet data is two orders of magnitude larger than real-robot data. The architecture is already native; the data is not yet native. When embodied data itself can scale up — at least reaching the same order of magnitude as the internet — that will be his GPT-1 moment.

[1:23:10] (Shen Yujun) **Why build only the brain, not the body** — Many companies turned this year to building only the brain, and Shen Yujun sees two reasons: first, a single body is hard to make general-purpose, and if it isn't general-purpose you have to pick the right scenario for specialized design, otherwise costs are bound to be high; second, the main contradiction now is that the brain lags the body and still isn't good enough at doing work. Brain and body definitely rise in alternation; right now the brain lags, and as more people work on brains the intelligence layer runs faster and will one day overtake the body, at which point a batch of body companies redefined by intelligence will emerge. The previous generation of hardware won't necessarily fit the next generation of models.

[1:31:51] (Shen Yujun) **Startups are a gamble** — Shen Yujun's first startup taught him two lessons: on execution, he used to focus on technical leadership, but now focuses on where the technology leads — you have to pick valuable leadership; on startups, nobody knows which path will definitely succeed, and with limited resources you have to dare to gamble. If everyone knew which path succeeds, the big companies would definitely succeed and it wouldn't be your turn. He admits to three big bets: sensors, a native model, and not building the body. Native is a huge gamble — training might fail to converge halfway through, or the approach might be wrong, or you enter too early, or resources run short — but it's a path you must take.

[1:40:31] (Shen Yujun) **The landscape: two or three startups plus one or two big companies** — Competition in robot brains will resemble large models: one or two players from the big companies, two or three from startups, each running out an ecosystem that includes data, body and scenarios. Because once there's an ecosystem, scenarios plus bodies bring data, and models will gradually differentiate to suit that ecosystem. Before entering the home, each company's model will have different characteristics — some good at delicate tasks, some at long-horizon tasks — and ultimately they'll converge toward a general ecosystem.

### glossary

- Ego / first-person-view data: A person wears a head-mounted camera to capture manipulation video from their own viewpoint, used to scale up robot data.
- WAM / world action model: Learns from video how the world responds to actions, and can serve as a robot's world simulator or executor.
- VLA / vision-language-action model: The mainstream robot manipulation route: takes visual and language instructions as input and outputs actions.
- MOE / mixture of experts: A sparse-activation architecture that activates only part of the parameters per inference, lowering compute demand.

who it is for: Embodied AI founders, robot algorithm engineers, and investors watching AI in the physical world — especially teams torn between building the brain and building the body.

## Yao Song: The Decisive Battle in Physical AI Isn't a Genius, It's a Systems War

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-21-latetalk-姚颂十年三次创业-物理ai的答案不是小天才-而是系统/
- show: 晚点聊 LateTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/latetalk/)
- original episode: 173: 对话姚颂：深鉴、东方空间、再出发，「天才少年」十年后
- published: 2026-07-21 · duration: 2:55:18
- transcript: Machine transcription · 53113 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**From DeePhi to Orienspace to Striding AI, Yao Song judges that the decisive battle in physical AI is not one or two genius algorithms, but data, compute, talent pools, and commercial landing at every milestone. Even intelligence-first giants may not necessarily pick the fruit.**

why listen: This episode is two hours and fifty-five minutes but extremely dense. Yao Song uses three startups to explain financing trade-offs, commercial space priorities, and physical AI route divergences, with clear judgments and no empty slogans.

### points

[8:15] (Song Yao) **Tsinghua's 11 hours and boring/suffering** — Yao Song recalls that after entering Tsinghua's Department of Electronic Engineering in 2011, he set a rule for himself: he must study 11 hours every day, pausing the timer even for bathroom breaks and meals. He admits that Tsinghua has too many people who are "both smart and hardworking," so he could only exchange diligence for a sense of security. It was not until the second semester of his freshman year that he realized there was more than one path through university. Later, a teacher summed it up: life is either boring or suffering. Yao Song chose the latter—he could not endure the idle life of a Silicon Valley engineer, and this fear of boredom drove him to jump into hard-tech entrepreneurship again and again.

[40:04] (Song Yao) **Rejecting Nvidia and Intel** — Before its angel round, DeePhi Technology met 50 institutions and was rejected by all of them, until Zhang Yutong and Lin Renjun of GSR Ventures understood the direction and invested. What he is most proud of is the strategic choice in financing: bringing Xilinx into the A round and rejecting Nvidia and Intel. His reasoning was that if the endgame is an IPO or acquisition, having three chip giants as shareholders simultaneously is actually dangerous—they compete with each other, won't truly provide business resources, and in a future acquisition might bid up the price and cause trouble, making the company unsellable. So he chose Xilinx, which directly competed with Nvidia and urgently needed to strengthen its software capabilities.

[57:20] (Song Yao) **After signing, falling into darkness** — In 2018, DeePhi was acquired by Xilinx for over 3 billion USD. Yao Song says that after signing the contract he happily paced around the table for two minutes, and then his life fell into darkness. Because the direction had previously been set by his advisor Wang Yu, and for the first time he had to decide the next step himself, but there was no path before him, only a fog. At 26, he describes himself as having a midlife crisis, not even wanting to scroll on his phone, interested in nothing. This chaos of losing a sense of purpose was more tormenting than failure, and it became the starting point for him to work part-time at Matrix Partners and systematically search for direction.

[1:04:44] (Song Yao) **Zhang Ying gave information, not cash** — To find a new direction, at the end of 2018 Yao Song worked part-time as a venture partner at Matrix Partners China. Zhang Ying told him: you don't need cash, you need information. All partner meetings and investment committee meetings at Matrix were open to him. He systematically scanned lidar, brain-computer interfaces, GPUs, and controllable nuclear fusion: Li Yifan convinced him that the barrier in lidar lies in engineering capability rather than technical route; brain-computer interfaces in China would require too long an approval cycle; GPUs were restricted by non-compete clauses from mergers; nuclear fusion was too far from industrialization. Eventually he waited for the commercial space window to appear.

[1:17:19] (Song Yao) **Good, many, fast, cheap—the order cannot be wrong** — Yao Song breaks down China's commercial space into three keywords: China, commercial, space, and then prioritizes: good, many, fast, cheap. Good means high success rate—no customer dares to use a rocket with a 60% success rate; many means carrying capacity—satellite internet constellations need at least four to five tons, preferably five to six tons of capacity; fast means seizing the market window; cheap is placed last. Therefore Orienspace chose the solid-on-solid route, Gravity-1 became the world's first solid-fuel rocket with solid boosters, and also conducted China's first private rocket launch livestream. He knew the livestream might capture a failure, but insisted that space should not be too far from ordinary people.

[1:47:39] (Song Yao) **One or two little geniuses can't solve the problem** — Yao Song is not optimistic about the narrative of "one or two little geniuses or young professors starting a company alone." He cites the history of deep learning: AlexNet came from Hinton's group, VGG from Oxford, GoogLeNet from Google, ResNet proposed by He Kaiming, R-CNN to RFCN relayed by different teams—no one stands at the forefront forever. So competition in physical AI is a systems war of data, compute, and talent resource pools, not a game for a few smart people. He quotes Cao Xudong's early words: 50% of algorithmic competitiveness comes from data, 30% from compute, and only 20% from human experience and inspiration.

[2:17:58] (Song Yao) **Language is the world? Impossible** — Yao Song opposes "language is the world." His reason: the digital world is discrete semantics, while the physical world is continuous analog signals; using language to precisely describe the tilt angle of a cup or the distance between two people is simply impossible. A future general world model might need 50T to 100T parameters, but physical AI must be real-time and low-latency, and very likely can only infer on the edge or on small chips. Therefore intelligence-first models like OpenAI and Anthropic that pile up general models with massive compute may not necessarily pick the fruit of physical AI—this is why Striding AI adopts latent space and retains a physical backbone rather than generating pixels.

[2:41:16] (Song Yao) **Ten attack, zero defense vs. eight attack, two defense** — Yao Song distinguishes between a startup founder and an entrepreneur: a first-time founder is often ten parts offense, zero parts defense, while he calls himself eight parts offense, two parts defense. The bottom line of defense is not going to prison, not going bankrupt, and not boasting about things you can't do. He dislikes the industry using teleoperation videos to pass off as autonomous demos, and requires his team to label every video whether it is fully autonomous. He says pursuing success and preventing failure are two completely different paths; once actions become distorted, the cost of short-term high valuation may be long-term loss of credibility. He is now on his third startup, relying on long-termism rather than going all in.

### glossary

- VLA / Vision-Language-Action Model: A model architecture that uniformly processes vision, language, and robot actions.
- latent space: A low-dimensional abstract space inside a model; Yao Song uses it to refer to a path that does not generate pixels but only learns physical laws.
- egocentric data: Video data collected from a first-person perspective, used to train robot manipulation capabilities.
- teleoperation: Remotely controlling a robot; the industry often passes off teleoperation videos as autonomous intelligence.

## Open weights are only 3-5 months behind closed — and that time gap is the entire safety margin

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-20-interconnects-开闭源差距只剩-3-5-个月-这层时间差就是全部的安全边际/
- show: Interconnects (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/interconnects/)
- original episode: Kimi K3: The open-weights escalation
- published: 2026-07-20 · duration: 20:03
- transcript: Official full text · 3715 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Kimi K3 compresses the open-versus-closed gap from a contested 6-9 months to 3-5 months, and that gap is the only risk buffer there is — heavy-handed regulation of open weights would only delay the inevitable while voiding the buffer itself.**

why listen: This reads K3 as an ecosystem inflection point: the decelerationist economics of open weights, where Chinese labs get their capital efficiency, and the asymmetry of policy all three arguments are directly usable for judgment, not a model review.

### points

[0:00] (Nathan Lambert) **The gap has been compressed to 3-5 months** — K3 is a 2.8T-parameter MoE, released July 16 with weights promised for July 27. The author pins the whole piece's key conclusion on one number: the performance gap between open and closed, or between the US and China, has narrowed from the contested 6-9 months to 3-5 months. He adds a robustness note — even if Moonshot ultimately doesn't deliver on open weights, as long as a comparably strong closed model exists in China, most of the inferences only land in an intermediate zone, and the direction is unchanged. The leaderboard evidence: second overall on Vals AI, third on the Artificial Analysis intelligence index (behind only Claude Fable and GPT-5.6 Sol Max, and cheaper), first on Frontend Code Arena. This is the closest an open model has come to the frontier since DeepSeek R1.

[0:00] (Nathan Lambert) **The distillation narrative dies in this episode** — The author states the conclusion outright: if adversarial distillation contributed to K3 at all, it was only to a small degree. The reason is that R1 and K3 are different in kind — R1 was a Chinese lab sprinting to pivot to reasoning models first, whereas K3 is scaling along known axes: data, algorithms, architecture, tooling, environments — the same set of problems people at OpenAI and Anthropic are working on. Another layer of evidence comes from his trip to China: the culture of the Kimi team was one of the few among the companies he visited that you could feel at a glance, with strong individual execution and freedom of expression even under GPU constraints; having seen it, the result was unsurprising to him. He predicts the distillation debate and the associated pressure will continue, but that observers attributing Chinese models to IP theft will be embarrassed by reality.

[0:00] (Nathan Lambert) **The WAIC speech is a statement of risk tolerance** — Previously there was almost no national-level policy statement from China on open-source AI; the author says that to his knowledge no senior leader had commented publicly. That changed this week: in his keynote at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC), Xi Jinping very directly bet the future of China's AI ecosystem on open source and global diffusion. The author's reading is that this commitment, landing in the same week as the strongest open-weights model in history, amounts to an implicit statement of China's risk tolerance for open weights. The simplest explanation: the Chinese government is tracking model risk closely, at a technical granularity that may be finer than America's ‘vibes-based regulation’, and will act if it measures risk — and it currently judges frontier models to pose no substantial risk. At the same time, economic policymakers think getting AI used first is a good thing, scaling distribution before monetising, a path consistent with cars, solar and advanced manufacturing.

[0:00] (Nathan Lambert) **Open source is the frontier labs' economic soft spot** — Dean Ball (personally pro-open-source, but now at OpenAI) says open-weights models are essentially decelerationist, and the author says he's right. The transmission chain is concrete: strong open models sharply compress the gross margin space of closed labs — first, the labs have less profit to reinvest in the next generation of models; second, the market marks down these companies' terminal values, discounting future funding rounds. Together these delay the arrival of the most transformative models. But the author doesn't think this is enough to knock OpenAI and Anthropic out of the ranks of the world's most valuable companies, and he thinks it's a net good for society: open source is accelerationist on the diffusion side, lowering the entry price for a given performance tier of intelligence and encouraging customisation — it's just that this curve starts much more slowly. His phrasing: an exponent that starts slower but may be larger. The risk is that closed capabilities run so far ahead that customisation loses its meaning.

[9:23] (Nathan Lambert) **Where the 2.5× efficiency comes from: three changes** — Kimi's release blog gives checkable technical handles: K3 builds on two architectural updates, Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), improving information flow along sequence length and along model depth respectively; it also pushes MoE sparsity up to 16 of 896 experts actually activated, paired with the Stable LatentMoE framework. Together with refinements to the training and data recipe, this yields roughly a 2.5× overall scaling-efficiency gain over K2. The author also traces the diffusion path of this innovation: KDA comes from the Kimi Linear paper and shares an origin with the Gated DeltaNet he used when building Olmo Hybrid at Ai2; Gated Delta Networks were only proposed at the end of 2024, built on ideas from Mamba, and by mid-2026 they are in frontier models — Qwen's latest model has also switched to a related architecture.

[9:23] (Nathan Lambert) **Capital efficiency: catching up is cheaper than inventing** — The author judges Chinese labs to be markedly more capital efficient, and in a world where intelligence is proportional to effective capital (buying compute, data, talent), that may be the single biggest advantage an AI industry can have. He lists several factors he's heard but can't verify: Chinese researchers are paid less yet are better at solving LLM research puzzles; a data industry is forming (budgets still far below Anthropic's billion-dollar scale); meaningful training compute is obtained by circumventing export controls; and inference demand is much smaller so more compute can go to training — though Moonshot has already paused new subscriptions because of K3, with the API still running. His mechanistic explanation: US labs spend a lot of energy on dramatic leaps that push the frontier, while Chinese labs focus more on catching up, and catching up is itself cheaper — just as a student model in distillation can surpass the teacher.

[9:23] (Nathan Lambert) **The open ecosystem isn't holding, it's doubling down** — The weekend after K3's release, Alibaba announced that the 2.4-trillion-parameter Qwen 3.8 would soon be released with open weights. The author stresses the weight of this signal: historically Alibaba kept its largest models exclusive to the cloud business's API, and this pivot shows Chinese companies aren't just maintaining the open-source status quo but doubling down on it — even if Qwen 3.8 trails K3 on benchmarks, the directional significance holds. He offers a verifiable inference: if Qwen 3.8 ships before the next Gemini generation, it pushes Google to eighth place on the smartest-model-lab ranking. DeepSeek V4 is also expected to graduate from preview. In his ranking of each player's peak model, DeepMind has only Gemini Flash 3.5 on the board; he describes seeing DeepMind and several US giants ranked so low as shocking, and thinks the X AI team deserves more credit.

[19:54] (Nathan Lambert) **Banning open source would create a defensive asymmetry** — The author's position: if Claude Mythos were open-sourced today, the negative consequences would be relatively mild and the risk is overhyped; but that won't hold forever, so having the strongest models available in controlled, closed form a few months ahead of equally capable open models is a very safe equilibrium. The danger is regulation going off course. He cites Axios reporting: the Commerce Department considered adding several Chinese AI labs to the Entity List last year; the NSA and the White House Office of the National Cyber Director considered issuing threat advisories targeting Chinese labs; the White House considered an executive order requiring US companies to guarantee safety and assume liability for leaks before hosting Chinese models; and Commerce drafted rules targeting Chinese open models using supply-chain security authorities. The result would be a highly asymmetric state: America's best models carry guardrails on cybersecurity tasks, while global actors probe America's defences with excellent Chinese open models.

### verbatim quotes

[0:00] Nathan Lambert: "The key fact is that either the open-to-closed or American-to-Chinese model performance gap has been reduced from the debated 6-9 months to something shorter, say 3-5 months."

[0:00] Dean Ball: "Open-weight models are inherently decelerationist, and I’m continually surprised to see the so-called “accelerationists” so excited about open-weight models."

[9:23] Nathan Lambert: "It is becoming clear that the Chinese labs are far more capital efficient. In a world where scaling laws dictate that intelligence is proportional to effective capital – which buys compute, data, & talent – that may be the greatest strength your AI industry could ever have."

[9:23] Nathan Lambert: "Just as the student model can outperform the teacher in distillation generally (not limited to the adversarial distillation of the Chinese labs), an approach of “trying to catch up” rather than “invent the next paradigm” could lead to stronger models."

[19:54] Nathan Lambert: "If we regulate open-weight models heavy-handedly, I suspect much of the world will be lulled into thinking we no longer need to act. All we would’ve done is slightly delayed the inevitable — open models will continue to cross all the key capability thresholds eventually and regardless of legality."

- Qwen 3.8 parameter count: 2.4 trillion parameters, to be released with open weights [9:23]

### glossary

- Kimi Delta Attention (KDA): An attention variant from the Kimi Linear paper that improves information flow along sequence length.
- Attention Residuals (AttnRes): An architectural change that improves information flow along model depth.
- Stable LatentMoE: A mixture-of-experts framework used with extremely high sparsity (16 of 896).
- adversarial distillation: Reverse-extracting capabilities from a closed frontier model's outputs to train your own model.
- decelerationist: A force that compresses frontier labs' profits and funding, thereby slowing the pace of AI investment.
- Entity List: A US Commerce Department control list; listed parties need a licence to obtain US technology and services.

who it is for: Investors watching the US-China model landscape, engineering leads choosing between open weights and closed APIs, and anyone doing AI export-control or open-source policy analysis.
what to skip: Section 5, US regulatory developments — skip if you don't care about policy.

## Why cross-entropy loss wins: it trains a text compressor

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-16-karpathy-训练语言模型本质上是在训练一个文本压缩器/
- show: Andrej Karpathy (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/karpathy/)
- original episode: But what is cross-entropy? | Compression is Intelligence Part 2
- published: 2026-07-16 · duration: —
- transcript: YouTube captions · 6655 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Cross-entropy loss was chosen because it can be proven mathematically to be the only function form that guarantees the loss is minimized when the model's output equals the data's true distribution — which is exactly equivalent to training the model into a text compressor that approaches the Shannon limit.**

why listen: It pins together two frameworks that sound completely unrelated — next-token prediction and compression — with a single formula. For anyone who wants to understand why the loss function looks the way it does, not just how to call it.

### points

[0:00] (Grant Sanderson) **gzip can draw the language family tree** — A 2002 paper used only gzip, a general-purpose file compressor, to automatically cluster texts in different languages and even reconstruct the genealogical tree among language families, all without relying on any linguistic prior knowledge. The method is to append a fragment of document B to the end of document A and compress the result, then compare this with the file size of compressing A alone — the difference is essentially asking "how well does a compression scheme optimized for A handle a fragment of B," and the same idea was later used for text authorship attribution.

[6:13] (Grant Sanderson) **The cost of an old code meeting a new distribution** — If a coding scheme was optimized for some distribution Q (say, assigning probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 to the robot commands up/down/left/right and designing corresponding bit lengths), but the actual data has become a new distribution P, continuing to use the old code wastes bits. Re-weighting by the new distribution to compute the average number of bits this old code would use gives a value called "the cross-entropy of Q relative to P" — it measures exactly how a compression scheme optimized for one situation performs in another.

[10:22] (Grant Sanderson) **The minimum of cross-entropy is entropy itself** — Picture the cross-entropy formula as a curve drawn by fixing P and letting Q vary. This curve always attains its minimum where Q equals P, and that minimum is exactly the entropy of P. This is because the question cross-entropy asks — "how does a code optimized for one setting perform in another" — can only reach theoretical optimal compression efficiency when the two settings are identical. This property is the pivot of the entire argument that follows.

[17:28] (Grant Sanderson) **The pretraining loss is the average information per token** — When training a language model, for every next token that actually appears in the training data, take the negative log of the probability the model assigns to it, then average over all tokens — that is the entire pretraining loss function. The "smarter" the model, the higher the probability it gives to tokens that actually occur, and the lower the corresponding negative log value (information content / degree of surprise); a poorly trained model is unconfident about everything and is "surprised" everywhere.

[20:33] (Grant Sanderson) **Why it must be the negative log, not just any decreasing function** — The common explanation is "in the cross-entropy formula everything except the term for the true token is zero, so what's left is naturally the negative log" — but this doesn't explain why cross-entropy was chosen in the first place. A more solid argument: if you only require some function F to satisfy "the average loss over all training samples is minimized only when the model's output distribution equals the data's true statistical distribution," then constrained optimization with Lagrange multipliers proves F must be a logarithmic function — the choice isn't actually yours, the negative log is forced by mathematics, and the average loss formula at that point is exactly the definition of cross-entropy.

[26:41] (Grant Sanderson) **Distillation: feed the small model the big model's entire probability distribution** — Ordinary pretraining gives full weight only to "the one token that actually occurred" at each position, and zero to everything else; distillation instead has the small model match the full probability distribution given by the big model at each position, with the loss defined as the cross-entropy of the small model's distribution relative to the big model's. A single training sample thus conveys far more information than in ordinary pretraining — like learning chess not by seeing only the one move actually played, but by having a stronger player explain every candidate move and its weight at each step.

[29:48] (Grant Sanderson) **Cross-entropy loss is equivalent to training a text compressor** — From the compression angle, cross-entropy naturally measures "how wasteful it is to move one compression scheme to another situation"; from the language model training angle, the loss function is the average information per token. As long as you can turn a general predictor (such as a language model) into a compressor — encoding the text with roughly as many bits as the text's information content in the model's view — the two threads line up completely: training a model with cross-entropy loss is equivalent to training it into the best possible text compressor.

[31:49] (Grant Sanderson) **KL divergence: how many bits the encoding wastes** — Cross-entropy minus entropy gives the KL divergence (Kolbach-Leibler divergence), which specifically measures "with a poorly optimized coding scheme, how many bits are wasted per symbol on average." In machine learning, KL divergence is often treated as a "distance" between two distributions: zero when the two distributions are identical, larger as they differ more, but it is asymmetric — the KL divergence of Q relative to P is not equal to that of P relative to Q, which is also why using cross-entropy rather than KL divergence in distillation is a choice worth pondering.

### verbatim quotes

[2:05] Grant Sanderson: "But whenever you see the same formula pop up in two separate contexts, it's math's way of kind of winking at you and hinting at a connection."

[4:09] Grant Sanderson: "for an optimal code, the number of bits that you allocate to a given symbol looks like the negative log base 2 of the probability for that symbol showing up."

[17:28] Grant Sanderson: "A very nice way to think about the loss function we use in this case is that you measure the average information per token from the model's perspective."

[20:33] Grant Sanderson: "You might think this loss function would go by a name like information loss, or log loss, but in fact, people call it cross-entropy loss, which at first might sound really strange, given that nowhere in the explanation have we actually used the cross-entropy formula."

[24:38] Grant Sanderson: "you would like it to be the case that the full average loss over all of the examples is minimized only when the model's output matches the statistics that show up in the data, there's actually a really nice mathematical argument for why F has to be a logarithm."

[27:42] Grant Sanderson: "it's the difference between trying to learn chess just by watching a game versus having someone better than you talk through all the possible good moves and how heavily they would weight them at each new turn."

[29:48] Grant Sanderson: "And once you understand this, it makes clear how using cross-entropy loss is actually equivalent to training the model to be the best possible text compressor."

[31:49] Grant Sanderson: "In the language of compression, you would think of it as describing how many bits per symbol are you wasting by using a poorly optimized code."

### figures
