- Publication year of the paper "Language Trees and Zipping": 2002 [0:00]

### glossary

- cross-entropy: The average number of bits per symbol required to encode data from distribution P using a code optimized for distribution Q
- KL divergence: Cross-entropy minus entropy; measures how many bits a coding scheme wastes relative to the optimal scheme
- distillation: Training a small model using the full probability distribution output by a large model rather than a single correct answer
- Lagrange multiplier: A mathematical method for finding extrema of a function under constraints
- Shannon limit: The theoretical lower bound on the optimal number of bits achievable in lossless compression

who it is for: Engineers and researchers interested in the intersection of loss function design, information theory and deep learning, especially those who want to understand where the name "cross-entropy loss" comes from.
what to skip: The rigorous derivation with Lagrange multipliers at 24:38 can be skipped without affecting the conclusions that follow.

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-16-sv101-机器人操作比运动控制难两三个数量级-硅谷却押错了方向/

**Sudo believes the mainstream Silicon Valley end-to-end imitation learning route has a fundamental flaw in open-world manipulation, and that a hierarchical top-down/bottom-up structure will return to the mainstream in the second half of this year.**

why listen: This episode is information-dense, suited to founders and investors who want to understand the divergence in embodied AI technical routes, the feasibility of Sim2Real, and the landscape of Silicon Valley robotics companies.

### points

[13:21] (Han Zheng) **Video training cannot reach sub-millimeter precision** — Han Zheng explains why you cannot directly train robot manipulation on internet video. 2D images and video do contain three-dimensional information, but it is "not quite complete, and not quite accurate." Autonomous driving navigation only needs precision of around 10 centimeters, but robot manipulation demands sub-millimeter precision — for example, inserting a cable into the corresponding hole. Only datasets built from 3D modeling can achieve that precision. The simulator requires the robot's understanding of geometric precision to reach millimeter or even sub-millimeter level.

[28:05] (Han Zheng) **Zero-shot general grasping hits 98% single-attempt success** — In internal tests in November and December last year, Sudo R1 operated over 100 objects for a continuous hour, 240 pick-and-place cycles, and none of these objects had ever appeared in the training data. Single-attempt pick-and-place success rate was close to 98%, and if the first attempt failed, the robot would use closed-loop control to rapidly adjust its strategy and reach 100%. Han Zheng calls this the first time the Sim2Real route has closed the gap. Afterwards they had nearly 1,000 people test it with random objects on site at ICRA and CVPR, something no one had done at academic conferences before.

[34:22] (Han Zheng) **Short-skill generalization matters more than chaining long-horizon tasks** — Han Zheng argues that zero-shot stable short skills for manipulating basic objects in the open world are more core than reproducing long-horizon tasks. If short skills are stable and reliable enough, with sufficiently high generalization, they can be assembled into all kinds of long-horizon operations. This is also the core idea of the ManiSkill framework. Around the same time the Sudo team proposed chain of thought in 2023, there was a piece of work called Chain of Thought Predictive Control, specifically addressing the chaining of short tasks into long-horizon tasks.

[44:51] (Han Zheng) **Manipulating objects is two to three orders of magnitude harder than motion control** — Han Zheng points out that reinforcement learning in simulation and Sim2Real have already been fully validated in motion control for Boston Dynamics and Unitree humanoid robots and quadruped dogs, and part of the reinforcement learning engine inside Nvidia Isaac was contributed early on by members of the Sudo team. But when a robot manipulates objects, the difficulty is two to three orders of magnitude higher. Because motion control only needs to focus on its own actions, it does not need to understand object shape or material, nor does it need to know how to move near an object and make adjustments.

[53:27] (Han Zheng) **Tesla cannot be replicated; cold start must rely on simulation** — Han Zheng explains why robots cannot collect data by selling cars the way Tesla did. Tesla started selling cars over a decade ago, millions of drivers drive on the road every day, and data accumulates naturally. But it is very hard for a robot to sell 5 million units into offices and homes before it has any function, with a worker standing next to it remote-controlling it. Domestic companies might reach a scale of a hundred or even a thousand units, but that is far from 5 million or 10 million units entering every household. So the cold start must rely on simulation, requiring millions or even tens of millions of full data collected in open environments.

[55:38] (Han Zheng) **The hierarchical structure Silicon Valley abandoned is about to return to the mainstream** — Han Zheng reveals that when Physical Intelligence was still at Google Robotics before it was founded, everyone tacitly assumed that once the low-level model had stable manipulation capability, the high level would handle environment understanding and task decomposition. But when they founded their startups in 2023 and 2024, everyone chose the end-to-end playbook they were good at and familiar with, and stopped mentioning hierarchy. Han Zheng's hot take is: starting in the second half of this year, the hierarchical top-down/bottom-up structure will return to the mainstream, and may be the final commercialization solution. After exchanges between academia and industry in recent weeks, some people have already realized this could be the new direction.

[1:05:40] (Han Zheng) **Most bullish on DeepMind plus Boston Dynamics Atlas** — Han Zheng considers the biggest competitor to be DeepMind plus the electric version of Boston Dynamics Atlas. Last year's Demis Hassabis interviews and documentary showed that Google's bet on physical-world AI is the most resolute among all the big companies. They have already switched their hardware platform from Apptronik to the electric version of Atlas, and poached core people from Boston Dynamics' hardware division to DeepMind. Google also acquired the MuJoCo team, has its own world model Genie 3, and has almost unlimited GPUs and the best talent. Han Zheng believes this is simply not on the same order of magnitude as other companies.

[1:09:01] (Han Zheng) **Amazon has many scenarios but integration is difficult** — Han Zheng believes Amazon has always been the big company investing the most in robotics, with warehousing and logistics AGVs, Kiva, various robotic arms and humanoid robot companies such as Agility and Covariant. It will provide scenarios, but in the end it will either acquire these companies or do it itself. Covariant at the time also counted Amazon as one of its core customers. But integrating multiple robot systems is difficult.

## He wrote poetry in the conqueror's language, and was sewn into a sack and thrown in the river

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-15-litandhist-他用征服者的语言写诗-最后被缝进袋子扔进河/
- show: Literature and History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/litandhist/)
- original episode: Episode 127: Bashshar ibn Burd
- published: 2026-07-15 · duration: 2:02:18
- transcript: Official transcript page · 17735 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Bashshar ibn Burd was the grandson of a slave and a blind poet who mocked Arabs in Arabic and insulted a caliph and lived twenty more years — until one poem put him in the Tigris.**

why listen: Medium information density, but it strings together the political freedom of the eighth-century Abbasid dynasty, Persian nationalism and the golden age of Arabic poetry into a single line — suited to listeners interested in literary history and imperial politics.

### points

[9:03] **Persians counterattacked the Arabs in the Arabs' own language** — Bashshar ibn Burd was an early literary representative of the Shu'ubiyya movement. The word comes from "peoples" in Quran 49:13: "We made you into nations and tribes, that you may know one another." For Persian Muslims, if the scripture plainly said Muslims were equal, there was no reason to bow to Arab elites just because they were Arabs — Arab Muslims should not live in garrison cities lording it over other Muslims in the provinces. The movement was mainly started by Persians, but it also included other conquered peoples, and its demand was equal rights. Bashshar wrote poetry in the conqueror's language, but his origins left him sympathetic to the conquered.

[27:00] **His grandfather was a slave, his father a freedman** — Bashshar was born in Basrah around 713. Two generations earlier, his grandfather had fought the Muslim conquerors in Tukharistan in the Oxus valley (today northern Afghanistan), was taken captive as a slave, and died in Basrah; his father was freed and joined an Arab tribe. Bashshar later told stories about how noble his paternal lineage was, but the episode states plainly that the truth of these stories is unknown. He was disfigured by smallpox in childhood, was blind, and was large and heavy of body. He himself said blindness actually helped him write poetry: "lack of sight strengthens the acuteness of the heart and cuts out interference from things which are visible."

[30:56] **He wrote poems mocking Arabs for eating lizards** — In one satire, Bashshar declared that his grandfather and father were the noblest of Persians, that the Roman emperor was his uncle, and that they all wore crowns; his father wore Persian sable and drank from gold cups, never followed mangy camels singing camel songs, never dug up desert melons to stave off hunger, and never dug lizards out of stony ground to eat. The episode notes that this lineage was mostly invented, but the satirical intent is clear: Persia is the land of civilization, and the Arabs can keep their wretched qasidas that romanticize the dry desert. His attitude toward Bedouin poetry was playfully irreverent, and at the same time he could wield its conventions with complete fluency.

[36:25] **One poem put him in the Tigris** — Bashshar had a tense relationship with the caliph al-Mahdi (r. 775-785), who once ordered him to stop writing love poetry; he ignored it. According to the historian al-Tabari, around 783 Bashshar wrote a poem saying: wake up, sons of Umayya, you have slept too long; the Persian bureaucrat Ya'qub b. Dawud is the caliph, your caliphate is ruined, go look for God's caliph among the tambourines and lutes. This amounted to saying the Abbasid dynasty could be replaced by the Umayyads they had usurped — crossing from insolence into sedition. He was imprisoned, beaten half to death, sewn into a sack and thrown into the Tigris to drown, at about seventy years old.

[1:08:00] **He insulted a caliph and lived twenty more years** — In 762, descendants of the Prophet's daughter Fatima rose in revolt against the Abbasids in Medina; Bashshar sided with the rebels and wrote a poem telling the reigning caliph al-Mansur, then in his eighth year in power, directly: you are a bad Muslim, more guilty than the Umayyad caliph Marwān whom you overthrew, and those descendants of the Prophet who rose up are better suited to rule than you. After writing this poem he lived another twenty years. There are accounts that he later altered the verses to turn their edge against al-Mansur's enemies. This shows that the newborn Abbasid monarchy, though a total state, was still a "new, soft" state, and the first generation of writers enjoyed a great deal of political freedom.

[1:14:17] **Insulting someone by declaring you won't insult them** — Eighth-century Arabic satire often used a rhetorical device called apophasis (paralepsis): saying a thing by declaring that you will not say it. Bashshar used it against members of the Abbasid royal family — first advising his target to "seek my satisfaction, do not provoke me, a weak and decrepit man cannot bear the burden I lay on him," then offering fake praise: "how noble this man of Quraysh is, we do not deny his kinship with the Prophet, even if his mother is of low birth," then driving the knife in: his ancestors were lions of the tribe when they went to the evening feast, and jackals before the enemy. Bashshar compared his poetry to a branding iron searing into the other man's flesh.

[1:34:10] **Panegyric was a meal ticket, and also art** — Beeston pointed out back in 1977: Abbasid poets sang the praises of the fabulously wealthy nobles who occasionally fought on the Byzantine frontier, and those lists of exaggerated courage and generosity "had little basis in reality" — writing panegyric was mostly about squeezing money out of the person being praised, and if the reward fell short of expectations, the poet turned around and wrote satire. But the host adds another layer: panegyric was both a calculated transaction and, at the same time, genuine gratitude and superb art. Early Abbasid society was astonishingly tolerant of political dissent — even satire aimed at the caliph and his family could exist; and the other side revealed by panegyric is that the Islamic cities along the Tigris and Euphrates were packed with the newly rich, and the private relationships between poets and patrons, based on appreciation of art, grew into the cross-cultural market of the later Islamic Golden Age — because the Golden Age really did need gold in the literal sense.

[1:45:16] **Poetry was the empire's pressure valve** — The scholar Salma Jayyusi wrote that early Muslim society was full of tensions: a new hierarchy was emerging, different from the old tribal order, and rapidly gaining status as a source of power and wealth; society was moving steadily toward a more urban way of life; and a Bedouin people, suddenly thrown by conquest into a completely different world, produced a kind of anxiety — it took more than four generations of Islamization and urbanization to erase the influence of the pre-Islamic Arab way of life. From this the host concludes: eighth-century Islamic civilization was uneasy, and the new power relations left whole swathes of social groups feeling dispossessed. But in a city like Basrah, poetry and literature were the pressure valve — as a young man Bashshar watched the previous generation of poets, Jarir and al-Farazdaq, hurl coarse and hilarious verses at each other, and laughed along with the crowd until he could not stop; when he grew up he discovered that although certain strata of Arab society were closed to him, the Arabic language was public property for anyone with talent.

### verbatim quotes

### glossary

- Shu'ubiyya: The eighth- to ninth-century Persian-led anti-Arab cultural movement, which held that non-Arab Muslims were equal to Arabs.
- badee: An Arabic poetry term literally meaning "the newly made," which came to denote an emphasis on rhetorical devices such as metaphor and wordplay.
- apophasis: A rhetorical device that says a thing by declaring one will not say it, common in eighth-century Arabic satire.
- al-adab: An Arabic word meaning both "literature" and "good breeding," emphasizing ethics and aesthetics together.
- qasida: A pre-Islamic Arabic poetic form, often opening with desert and camel imagery, which Bashshar both mocked and used with fluency.

**The reproductive-suppression signal in naked mole-rats has finally been found: queens alone produce isopropyl myristate. Add it to a colony that has lost its queen and peace holds; stop and the fight for the throne erupts. The same molecule also shows up in lactating women.**

why listen: The spine is a complete new evidence chain from molecule to social behavior, and the later "intuitive gamer" model has direct implications for low-compute AI; the two-minute Highlights segment in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

### points

[2:35] **The queen mystery: social suppression, not genetic** — Naked mole-rats are a rare social species among mammals: a colony has only one breeding female, the queen, while the other females do not reproduce and only find food, guard the nest and care for pups. The structure resembles bees, but a bee queen is destined before birth, whereas every female naked mole-rat could in principle become queen. Melissa Holmes says this is not a genetic trait but the social environment exerting control — the question is what signal makes one female queen and suppresses all the others. Earlier work looked for pheromones only in queen urine and came up empty.

[4:05] **A molecule made only by queens** — The team collected all kinds of odors from 16 colonies and more than 450 animals, and had in particular to pick the queen out of a pile of stacked rodents. They found a volatile molecule produced only by naked mole-rat queens: isopropyl myristate. It is structurally simple, common in plastics and skincare products, and can be bought in the lab for about $5. Gary Lewin says this made the experiments extremely easy: you can just buy it and run behavioral tests. By contrast, rodent pheromones were thought to belong in urine, but there was nothing at all in queen urine.

[4:05] **Add it back and peace holds; stop and war begins** — Brain scans show isopropyl myristate activates the odor-processing regions in worker brains and suppresses other females from entering a sexually active state — effectively a "scent contraceptive." Add the molecule to a colony that has just lost its queen and everything stays calm, with workers behaving as if the queen were still there; once the addition stops, high-ranking females immediately begin fighting among themselves for the throne. The authors think the mechanism is clear: whoever gets pregnant first starts making the molecule and thereby suppresses all the other females. Melissa Holmes calls it the holy grail of research on naked mole-rat social structure.

[4:05] **The same molecule and lactating women** — Isopropyl myristate is not unique to naked mole-rats. Gary Lewin notes that a study years ago measured the volatile molecules given off by the breasts of lactating women, and isopropyl myristate was among them; when researchers put the mixture on cotton swabs, newborns would start sniffing and even try to suckle. But he says that paper was an isolated case and no one followed up. Now that the molecule has such a strong social effect in naked mole-rats, researchers perhaps ought to revisit whether it does anything in other mammals.

[10:34] **Two cotton-candy planets and Hannibal** — This week's Highlights has two number stories. One is two newly discovered exoplanets, close to Jupiter in size but more than 20 times lighter, with a density lower than cotton candy — among the lowest-density planets known; they orbit the same star, with periods of 232 days and 139 days. The other is the metabolic ledger of Hannibal crossing the Alps: the most likely route requires 15 days and 230 tons of supplies, and even with enough food, maintaining body weight would have been impossible, with the war elephants expected to lose 4%. These two segments are unrelated to the main thread but are enough to refresh your intuitions.

[11:49] **How novices evaluate a new game** — Game research has long focused on experts, but Katie Collins's team looked at novices judging a game the first time they hear its rules. In the experiments, participants read the rules of different games and predicted who would win, whether there would be a draw, and whether they thought it would be fun. They modified tic-tac-toe and Connect Four — for example, a three-by-three board requiring two rows to win, or a five-by-five board won with three in a row — creating rule variants people had never seen. The core question is not "how to play well" but "before making the first move, how does the human brain judge whether a game is worth playing."

[16:09] **Three features of the "intuitive gamer" model** — The team's intuitive gamer model imagines novices doing fast, shallow, probabilistic, goal-directed mental simulation. Fast means only a few simulations, more than 1 and fewer than 10; shallow means the simulated players do not think very far ahead; probabilistic means they assess which action is good but do not necessarily always pick the best one. The model explains both people's judgments about new games and data from their first actual play. Katie Collins says this shows novices are not entirely unsystematic, but do not expect them to match the optimal predictions of classical game theory.

[18:42] **Two implications for AI** — The first AI use of this model is saving compute: in many situations, you do not need massive simulation or enormous computation to approach game-theoretic optimality. A system could work like an intuitive gamer, doing only a little thinking to quickly judge whether a path is worth exploring. The second use is AI as a thinking partner: if an AI has a more accurate model of human computation, it can simulate the user's judgment and point out ahead of time that "you may think a position will go one way, but it won't." The next step in the research is to expand from analyzing existing games to how people create new games, which is closer to open-world games.

## The autonomous driving supplier endgame is down to two or three players, and the window closes at year-end

**Momenta's Cao Xudong judges that autonomous driving is like batteries: there is only good and better. The endgame for third-party suppliers is two or three in China and three or four globally; the first tier already holds 90% market share, the data flywheel and mass production are the entry ticket, and the next stop is physical AI and home robots.**

### points

[4:12] (Cao Xudong) **The competition window closes at year-end** — Cao Xudong still insists that competition in assisted driving will end in 2026: China will ultimately have 2-3 third-party suppliers, and the world 3-4. The mechanism he gives is that this industry has extremely strong first-mover and scale advantages; the leaders roll revenue and gross profit back into R&D, while the second tier cannot win customers and cannot afford core R&D. Currently the first tier (Momenta and Huawei) together hold 90% market share and have clear pricing power; he believes this opportunity window may close by the end of this year, and concentration will continue to increase.

[8:37] (Cao Xudong) **Autonomous driving goes from toy to necessity** — Cao Xudong believes that two years ago autonomous driving was still a "fun toy," and now it has become a "usable product," but it has only just crossed the usability threshold; at a rate of 10x per year, by 2028 the driving capability of L2++ passenger cars will reach human level, thus moving from nice to have to must have. One piece of evidence is the change in customer organizations: the autonomous driving lead becomes the intelligentization lead, then the R&D lead, and even the chairman, making it a number-one engineering priority. Another piece of evidence is that in Nielsen surveys, autonomous driving has already ranked fourth in car purchase decisions, behind only price, appearance, and space.

[13:42] (Cao Xudong) **Autonomous driving is a battery-style business** — Cao Xudong uses batteries as an analogy for autonomous driving: there is only "good and better," not a matter of taste where everyone likes something different; differentiation accounts for only 10%-20%. This kind of industry has extremely strong first-mover and scale effects, and the final players will be two or three in China and three or four globally. He rebuts the common prediction that "there will be many third-party suppliers, price wars will drive gross margins low," pointing out that the number of automakers doing autonomous driving will not decrease because of electrification, but suppliers will become highly concentrated; Momenta's gross margin rose from less than 20% in 2023 to over 70% in 2025.

[27:41] (Cao Xudong) **World model unifies the foundation** — Cao Xudong says he will not do robots this year, and plans to invest in 2027. Two judgments support this: first, working backward from China as the starting point, home robots will reach an inflection point in 2030 and begin scaled commercialization; second, R7 validated the world model—pretraining on massive physical world data, then post-training on proprietary scenarios. Autonomous driving and robotics R&D paradigms are highly similar, and the infrastructure is reusable. He observes that Silicon Valley robotics companies were talking about LA a year ago, and this year they are all talking about world models; for example, one company used body-less data for pretraining and may have raised its success rate from 50% to 90%.

[41:12] (Cao Xudong) **RoboVan ranks first** — Asked about new players like JD, Meituan, and Hello entering last-mile delivery, Cao Xudong gives his business ranking for the next 5 years: RoboVan first, RoboTruck second, RoboTaxi third. [1:24:54] (Cao Xudong) **Data-driven physical reasoning** — Cao Xudong explains why he was convinced in 2016 that autonomous driving must be data-driven: he comes from a physics background and is used to using dimensional analysis to validate hypotheses. Human driving safety is about one major accident per 100 million kilometers; for autonomous driving to be widely adopted, it must be at least 10 times safer, and considering statistical confidence, about 100 validations are needed, so the amount of data required can never be accumulated by an owned fleet—it can only be collected through mass-produced vehicles. This reasoning established from day one the two-legged strategy of "data flywheel + mass production + fully driverless," unchanged for ten years.

[1:34:22] (Cao Xudong) **From research institute to fighting** — Cao Xudong looks back at the company's transformation from the end of 2018 to 2019: before that it was like a loose research institute, over-promising to investors, so severely that outsiders could see it; in 2019 he used philosophy guidance and organizational adjustment (whoever makes products according to customer value gets promoted) and it took half a year to turn around, while now it can be done in a month. The transformation crystallized the principle of "reuse the main line, develop the main line"—when encountering problems, prioritize solving them with the main line architecture, and never open a branch line outside the main line, otherwise you will be dragged down by "chimneys"; the first customer project made him understand that the R&D and delivery systems must be data-driven and highly automated.

[2:02:51] (Cao Xudong) **Fox and hedgehog decision-making** — Cao Xudong says he does not take the path of "making the decision only now" for major decisions; instead, he spends one or two years, or even three to five years, repeatedly brewing and discussing within the organization in advance, so that when the time comes to actually do it, it is no longer a choice of whether to do it, but when and with what entry point. He repeatedly emphasizes returning to the front line to get first-hand information rather than listening to reports; for a CEO, the most important thing is not efficiency, but the correctness of cognition and judgment. Finally, he summarizes his methodology with "the fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing": underlying principles matter more than multiple paths.

## The optimal linear-programming solution is never interior: simplex climbs only along boundary vertices

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-13-statquest-线性规划最优解不在内部-单纯形法只沿边界顶点爬/
- show: StatQuest (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/statquest/)
- original episode: The Simplex Algorithm, Mathematical Details!!!
- published: 2026-07-13 · duration: 27:06
- transcript: YouTube captions · 3812 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The optimum of a linear program always sits on some boundary vertex, so the simplex algorithm never searches the interior: starting from the origin, it picks a direction from the most negative column, sets the step size by the minimum ratio, and keeps moving to a more profitable adjacent vertex.**

why listen: This episode turns the geometric intuition of "climbing along boundary vertices" into matrix operations at every step, spelling out direction, step size and stopping condition. Once you've worked it by hand, optimizer documentation reads completely differently.

### points

[1:06] (Josh Starmer) **Climbing between adjacent vertices** — A linear program seeks the extreme value of an objective function inside a feasible region bounded by straight-line constraints. The simplex algorithm does not search the interior of that region; it starts at the origin and moves along an edge to an adjacent vertex that raises revenue, then from the new vertex looks at the next adjacent vertex, until no move increases revenue any further. Because the algorithm "cannot see" the picture, all the seemingly complicated matrix operations that follow are essentially answering two questions with numbers: which direction, and how far.

[4:06] (Josh Starmer) **First normalize every constraint to less-than-or-equal** — Before the iterations proper, standardization is required: a constraint with a greater-than-or-equal sign must be flipped into less-than-or-equal by multiplying both sides by -1; a constraint with an equals sign is split into a less-than-or-equal and a greater-than-or-equal inequality, and the greater-than-or-equal one is then multiplied by -1 and flipped, so the two inequalities form a kind of "inequality sandwich" equivalent to the original equality. The episode explains the purpose: the algorithm then only has to handle one kind of sign at every step, with no branching checks for different constraint forms during iteration.

[5:08] (Josh Starmer) **Slack variables pad inequalities into equalities** — Even after an expression becomes less-than-or-equal, the left and right sides may still not be equal. The fix is to append a non-negative slack variable to each equation, filling in exactly the shortfall. The episode's example: when producing 10 kg of cookie mix and 8 kg of doughnut mix, only 8 kg of flour is actually used while 10 kg is available, so the slack variable for flour is set to 2 kg; the slack variables of the other constraints vanish from the calculation because their coefficients are 0. Only after the slack variables are added do all equations share one format and can be put into a matrix uniformly.

[7:10] (Josh Starmer) **Load the matrix, then negate the first row** — The last formatting step is to fill all coefficients and totals into the matrix and multiply the first row by -1. The negation is only to match the usual definition of the simplex method, so that "where to go next" can be read directly as the most negative coefficient in the first row; at this point the initial revenue is 0, because the search starts at the origin. Once the matrix is in order, every iteration revolves around the same action: first choose a direction, then fix a distance, and finally use row operations to read the new vertex's coordinates explicitly.

[9:11] (Josh Starmer) **Only the minimum ratio lands on the boundary** — The algorithm itself cannot see the feasible region, so it uses the ratio test to set the step size: take the total on the right-hand side of each constraint row and divide it by the corresponding positive coefficient in the current column; the quotient is the coordinate reachable along that axis. The episode uses three candidate points on the cookie mix axis to illustrate: the ratios 25 and 16.7 correspond to where the yellow and blue lines meet the axis, both outside the feasible region; the lowest, 10, lands on the brown line's intersection, i.e. on the boundary. So the minimum ratio is always chosen; a point with a larger ratio necessarily overshoots. If the minimum ratio is tied, the convention is to pick the row with the smallest row number.

[16:17] (Josh Starmer) **Gaussian elimination makes the coordinates surface on their own** — Once the pivot column and pivot row are chosen, Gaussian elimination turns the pivot position into 1, then clears every other position in that column to 0 by adding multiples of rows. After elimination the reading rule is simple: if a column has a single 1 and zeros everywhere else, read the total on that column's row as the current vertex's coordinate on that axis; when several variable columns satisfy this at once, the coordinates appear together, and the value in the top-right corner directly gives that vertex's revenue. The episode reads off the second vertex (10,10) and revenue 50 this way.

[18:19] (Josh Starmer) **Stop when the first row has no negatives** — When to stop matters as much as how to move. As long as the first row still holds a most negative coefficient that can serve as a candidate, the algorithm keeps testing whether revenue can be raised; once the first row has no negatives left, the simplex method declares the current vertex optimal. The second stop of the first example, (10,10), satisfies this condition, and revenue 50 is the best value attainable under the three constraints of flour, sugar and chocolate. This stopping condition is exactly the matrix-language equivalent of the geometric intuition that "no adjacent vertex can raise revenue any further."

[25:33] (Josh Starmer) **The three-dimensional example adds no new machinery** — Extending the example from two products to three, the simplex method still holds. The episode labels doughnut, cookie and brownie mix as x, y and z, gives each of the five constraints its own slack variable, and after starting from the origin every step is still the same procedure: use the most negative coefficient in the first row to pick a column, use the minimum ratio to pick the pivot row, then do Gaussian elimination. When several most negative coefficients tie, take the leftmost column first. After a few moves the first row has no negatives left, and the algorithm stops at (9,9,4), corresponding to a maximum revenue of 22.

### verbatim quotes

[1:06] Josh Starmer: "The simplex algorithm starts at the origin and then moves to neighboring vertices that increase revenue until moving to the next vertex does not increase the revenue. Bam."

[4:06] Josh Starmer: "Now the two inequalities give us a sort of inequality sandwich that is the equivalent of the original equality."

[5:08] Josh Starmer: "The idea is that when the total amount of something like flour used by the cookie and doughnut mixes on the left is less than the amount available on the right, the slack variables make up the difference."

[8:10] Josh Starmer: "In this example, the largest negative number in the first row, -3, is in the first column, the column for cookie mix. So, we could decide to go along the cookie mix axis."

[15:16] Josh Starmer: "Again, in general, the simplex algorithm selects the lowest value because larger values are always outside of the feasible region."

[18:19] Josh Starmer: "In other words, the point 10, 10, which represents a revenue of 50, is the best we can do given the constraints on the amount of flour, sugar, and chocolate that we can use."

### figures

- Endpoint of the first move in the first example: cookie mix = 10, doughnut mix = 0 [13:16]
- Revenue at that vertex: 30 [13:16]
- Endpoint of the second move in the first example: cookie mix = 10, doughnut mix = 10 [17:17]
- Revenue gain at that vertex: from 30 to 50 [18:19]
- Optimal vertex of the three-dimensional example: x = 9, y = 9, z = 4 [25:33]
- Maximum revenue of the three-dimensional example: 22 [25:33]

### glossary

- simplex algorithm: An algorithm that starts at the origin and moves step by step along adjacent boundary vertices to find the optimal solution of a linear program.
- feasible region: The region containing all feasible solutions, bounded by all the constraints together.
- objective function: The linear equation to be maximized or minimized; in the example, the revenue equation.
- slack variable: A non-negative variable added to pad an inequality into an equality.
- Gaussian elimination: Using row operations to reduce a matrix to echelon form so the intersection coordinates can be read off.
- ratio test: Dividing each constraint total by the positive coefficient in the current column and taking the smallest ratio to set the step size.

who it is for: Engineers who call optimization libraries but have never derived the simplex method by hand, operations-research students, and teachers preparing to lecture on linear programming.
what to skip: The Gurobi ad at the top, the linear-programming recap at the start, and the book-and-merch pitch at the end are skippable; everything else is hand-calculation detail.
tags: Linear programming, Simplex method, Slack variables, Gaussian elimination, Operations research, Algorithm details

## A black hole is a 100%-efficient power plant; fusion only reaches one percent

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-10-dwarkesh-黑洞是效率-100-的发电厂-聚变只到百分之一/
- show: Dwarkesh Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/dwarkesh/)
- original episode: Adam Brown – A deep but accessible introduction to general relativity
- published: 2026-07-10 · duration: 1:38:24
- transcript: Official transcript page · 16695 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Lower a brick slowly to just above the horizon and let go, and its rest mass can become work at a distance with 100% efficiency; chemical burning gets only one part in ten billion and fusion only one percent, because nuclear reactions never touch the rest mass of protons and neutrons — only gravity does.**

why listen: One hour takes general relativity from the equivalence principle to the black hole power plant; it's a lecture, not an interview. Only the last eight minutes touch AI doing theoretical physics, so don't expect industry news.

### points

[4:09] (Adam Brown) **The equivalence principle is the only clue** — In electromagnetism, charge and mass have nothing to do with each other — a neutron is heavy but uncharged, an electron is light but fully charged. Gravity is not like that: the inertial mass that resists acceleration in Newton's second law and the gravitational mass that gets pulled in the law of universal gravitation are the same number. In Newton's system this is a pure coincidence, but Newton himself verified it to one part in a thousand, Einstein's era to one part in a billion, and today to one part in 10^15. Einstein treated this coincidence as the only clue: a force that can be explained as an inertial force must have inertial mass as its "charge"; conversely, only a force whose charge equals inertial mass is even eligible to be an inertial force. Electromagnetism never has that eligibility; gravity does.

[19:35] (Adam Brown) **The price is redefining what a straight line is** — Swing a bucket in a circle and the water doesn't fall out; someone sitting in the bucket would say that's centrifugal force. The charge of an inertial force like centrifugal force must be inertial mass, because its source is just mass's tendency to travel in a straight line. From this Einstein makes the leap: gravity itself is a kind of inertial force. The price is enormous — you must accept that the parabola of free fall is the straight line, and that you, sitting still, are not. This is no more absurd than a flight map on which San Francisco to London has to curve over Greenland: draw something curved as if it were flat and you will inevitably get wrong which line is straight. So matter curves spacetime, curved spacetime defines what a straight line is, and treating curved spacetime as if it were flat makes you see a fictitious force called gravity.

[31:44] (Adam Brown) **The infinite-energy paradox forces out black holes** — Lower a brick of mass m slowly on a pulley from far away to radius r and release it, and the fraction of its rest mass energy you can extract is GM/(c²r). Lowered to Earth's surface it's only 7×10^-10; to the Sun's surface, 2×10^-6; to a white dwarf like Sirius B, larger still. But the formula has no upper bound: once r is less than GM/c², the fraction exceeds 1 — you extract more energy than the brick's rest mass energy, and using that energy to make another brick and lower it again gives you a machine that creates energy from nothing. Adam says explicitly that this is a purely Newtonian calculation and only suggestive, but it shows that something must break down near that radius.

[45:54] (Adam Brown) **Gravity's resolution is to get stronger, not weaker** — In electromagnetism the analogous paradox is resolved by the force getting weaker: two charges brought too close smear out quantum-mechanically and stop attracting so hard. General relativity goes the other way — the acceleration needed to stay at rest carries a factor of 1/√(1-2GM/c²r), which diverges at 2GM/c², and the brick is torn straight out of your hand. The same square root also gives time dilation and redshift, and gives the exact extraction fraction 1-√(1-2GM/c²r): lowered to just above the horizon it is exactly 1, no more and no less, 100%. So a black hole is a power plant at the efficiency limit: chemical burning 10^-10, fission 10^-3, fusion 10^-2, because neither fission nor fusion changes the total number of nucleons — 99% of the energy is locked in the rest mass of protons and neutrons.

[1:10:34] (Adam Brown) **Doomed, but not yet dead** — I watch you fall toward the black hole from far away: first faster and faster, then slower and slower, your clock running ever slower, your light ever redder, and after a last photon you fade to black — I never see you cross the horizon. Early physicists therefore thought something violent must happen at the moment of crossing; that is wrong. You cross with nothing unusual happening to you; tidal forces would hurt for a solar-mass black hole, but the bigger the black hole the gentler, and at galactic-mass scale you wouldn't notice at all. Once you cross the horizon you are doomed, but not dead — only on hitting the singularity are you spaghettified by tidal forces. The horizon is not something locally measurable; it is a teleological fact: inside a sufficiently large black hole you can live out a whole life and leave several generations of descendants.

[1:16:02] (Adam Brown) **Three kinds of evidence for black holes** — For half a century after the Schwarzschild solution was written down, people thought it was a mathematical monster that required finely tuned initial conditions, and Einstein himself wrote mistaken things like objects bouncing back from the horizon. The theoretical reversal was Penrose, and later Hawking and Penrose, proving that black hole formation is a generic property of general relativity, not a finely tuned artifact. Experimentally there are three lines: decades of stellar orbits around Sagittarius A* at the galactic center, which imply something extremely heavy, extremely dark and extremely compact; LIGO, which picked up spacetime jitters right after turning on in late 2015, with multiple sites shaking in exactly the same way, ruling out trucks and earthquakes; and the Event Horizon Telescope, using a global radio array to see the radiation of infalling matter. Seen, felt, and calculated from orbits.

[1:22:07] (Adam Brown) **Two failed eclipses actually saved him** — Mercury's orbit came out right, but that was a known answer and only weakly persuasive; what really made general relativity consensus was the bending of light. Plug the speed of light into Newtonian mechanics and you also get a deflection value; general relativity gives twice that. The 1911 eclipse expedition to Argentina was clouded out; the next was a German team funded by Krupp to Crimea, and war broke out before the eclipse, with the whole team interned until the war ended. These two failures were good for Einstein: his early prediction based on the equivalence principle was wrong and happened to equal the Newtonian value, and it was precisely in the wartime window when no one was observing that he changed it to twice. In 1919 Eddington's British expedition reported exactly twice — a British experiment confirming a German theory, which also became part of postwar reconciliation.

[1:27:41] (Adam Brown) **What string theory bets on is uniqueness** — Dwarkesh's provocation is: the most beautiful theory barely needs experiment, so why spend tens of billions building machines. Adam's answer is that general relativity is an extreme case — you need only that the speed of light is finite, plus the symmetry that protects it, plus the empirical fact of the equivalence principle, and after that the available options are limited: it is feasible to have a large number of models lay out the whole tree, with each "Einstein" taking one set of options (say, giving up simultaneity). But the branching ratio differs by field. String theory bets entirely on this path: it believes there is only one consistent quantum theory of gravity, reachable by consistency checks alone, because seeing it would require a galaxy-scale collider. Condensed matter physics, by contrast, often has no choice but to do experiments.

[45:54] Adam Brown: "The bulk of the energy—99% of the energy—is stored not in the electromagnetic interaction, not in the strong interaction, but in the rest mass energy of the protons and neutrons, something that neither chemical reactions nor nuclear reactions can touch. ### figures

- Precision to which inertial and gravitational mass are verified equal: Newton's era 1/1000, Einstein's era 1/10^9, now 1/10^15 [4:09]
- Earth's escape velocity: about 11 km/s [31:44]
- Fraction of a brick's rest mass energy extractable by lowering it to Earth's surface: 7×10^-10 [31:44]
- Fraction of rest mass energy in the chemical binding energy of hydrogen-oxygen rocket fuel: 1.5×10^-10 [31:44]
- Gravitational redshift at the Sun's surface: 2×10^-6 [31:44]
- Mass-energy conversion efficiency of fission and fusion: about 10^-3 and 10^-2 [45:54]
- The two black holes of LIGO's first event: about 30 solar masses each, about 1.6 billion light-years from Earth, detected in late 2015 [1:16:02]

### glossary

- equivalence principle: Inertial mass and gravitational mass are exactly equal — the reason a feather and a brick land at the same time.
- fictitious / inertial force: A force that arises from the reference frame, whose charge must be inertial mass, such as centrifugal force.
- Schwarzschild radius / event horizon: 2GM/c²; past it, no matter how much thrust you have, you must fall toward the singularity.
- gravitational time dilation: Clocks deeper in a potential well run slower, independent of relative motion; GPS must subtract it out.
- spaghettification: Tidal forces stretch and shred an object radially; fatal only near the singularity.

## US Capital Controls 11 Premier League Clubs — Through Finance, Not Football

**American money already controls 11 Premier League clubs and has reached into UEFA commercial development, rights distribution and player-transfer finance; with broadcast fees peaking, they keep the game going by pushing valuations and evergreen funds.**

why listen: From the Glazers' debt to the Ipswich returns, the numbers and the chain of operations are concrete; fans may hate it, but investors can see how capital collects rent across borders.

### points

[0:00] (Mahua) **Trump's "suspended sentence" phone call** — At this year's World Cup knockout stage, an American player was due to serve a one-match ban after a red card; reportedly, after Trump phoned FIFA president Infantino, the punishment was suspended for a year. The Wall Street Journal analysed that Infantino needs the World Cup held in North America for greater exposure and commercial revenue, and has therefore catered to Trump's preferences for years. The episode is used as an entry point: it is not just FIFA — across European football, whether the Premier League or Europe's big five leagues, Americans loom large behind the scenes.

[6:21] **Half the Premier League is American-owned** — Of the 20 Premier League clubs, 11 are now controlled by Americans, including Manchester United, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea from the big six. Most investment came after 2008, and more than half after 2018. The reasons: US quantitative easing flooded the system with capital seeking assets; some European economies recovered slowly from the financial crisis, leaving football assets undervalued; and around 2020 the pandemic shut down the game, leaving clubs short of cash, so American money bought in heavily at the bottom. American owners do not treat clubs as standalone assets but as part of their sports portfolios, linked with NFL and NBA teams.

[16:14] (Mahua) **The Ipswich sample: small clubs can pay off big** — In 2021, GameChanger Twenty, led by an Arizona pension fund, bought then-League One Ipswich for £30 million. In 2024, another American private equity firm paid £105 million for 40%, meaning early investors effectively made a pure profit of 2.5 times their acquisition cost. That same year the club was promoted to the Premier League, shirt sales rose from 10,000 to 100,000 a year, and season revenue jumped from £13 million to £155 million. American consortia do not have to buy giants; small clubs can also deliver high multiples through promotion within the system and commercial development.

[22:47] (Zhang Bin) **The Glazers' blood-sucking leveraged buyout** — In 2005 the Glazer family used a £790 million leveraged buyout of Manchester United, putting in only £270 million of their own money and borrowing the rest. For over 20 years they have paid only interest each year, never principal, and now they have borrowed again at an interest rate in the low 5s to repay old debt. As of the end of 2024, they had extracted £1.2 billion from Manchester United, including dividends, board compensation and share sales. Meanwhile, Old Trafford has fallen into disrepair — leaking roof, rat infestation — and lost its hosting rights for Euro 2028. This playbook became the template for American acquisitions of European clubs and the root of Manchester United fans' resentment.

[30:04] (Shi Hualun) **Arsenal's stadium debt** — Arsenal spent £450 million to build the Emirates Stadium, securitising the next 25 years of matchday ticket revenue into bonds and raising £260 million in one go. To service that debt, Arsenal pinched pennies in the transfer market for years and was forced to sell its captain, until Kroenke's full takeover and debt restructuring eased the interest burden and restored spending power. Shi Hualun points out that matchday revenue now accounts for only about 20% of big six clubs' income, but 20 years ago broadcast revenue was nowhere near today's levels; those who decided to build the stadium did not foresee that broadcast would replace tickets as the largest revenue source.

[52:47] (Shi Hualun) **Chelsea's speculation blew up** — In 2022, the Boehly and Clearlake consortium took over Chelsea from sanctioned Abramovich for £2.5 billion. They applied American experience, signing players to 8- to 10-year contracts to stretch amortisation, manoeuvring the books, and buying a dozen or twenty players at once. This rule-bending prompted the Premier League to repeatedly amend its rules to close loopholes. The result: Chelsea's form fluctuated, finishing as low as 12th, with 50 players crammed into the training facility. Shi Hualun believes the owners entered at too speculative a moment, and every move in the Premier League is watched by the media; the playbook failed under such high exposure.

[57:10] (Zhang Bin) **American capital sits at every gate** — American penetration of European football goes beyond clubs. In 2012-2013, US-based CAA took over UEFA national-team competition commercial development; in 2024, Relevent Sports wrested the commercial rights to three major tournaments from Team Marketing, effective from 2025. Broadcast platforms are also often backed by American money, such as DAZN. Even instalment payments in player transfers have been turned into factoring products, with banks offering receivables at a discount for cash; such financial tools come mainly from JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs. Zhang Bin sums it up: every time money moves through European football, Americans have set up a gate to skim a fee.

[1:05:46] (Zhang Bin) **After the rights peak, it's a valuation game** — Premier League domestic broadcast revenue, adjusted for inflation, is down 31% from the 2016-19 cycle, while player wages and transfer fees keep rising, squeezing costs. From a revenue and margin perspective, football clubs are not a good business; American capital relies more on the valuation game: push asset values up, then exit through consortia, selling 1% stakes, or evergreen funds that roll over indefinitely. In theory, as long as there is a next buyer, valuations can keep inflating. Zhang Bin warns this is essentially like speculating on concept stocks in the A-share market and distributing at the top — you need a continuous stream of willing buyers.

## Two Ways to Survive in Short Drama: Scale Plays for Principal Safety, Content Plays on Character Relationships

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-09-luanfanshu-月产-300-部短剧不靠灵感-靠本金安全与人物关系/

- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Short drama has two ways of living: the scale play relies on principal safety and the certainty of 300 episodes a month, the content play relies on character relationships to determine motivation; both sides agree AI cannot yet replace a real actor's micro-expressions.**

why listen: Two frontline company bosses talk it out face to face — the books, the casting, the post-mortem logic of the scale play and the content play are all in specific numbers, which is worth more than a general industry discussion.

### points

[3:13] (Hou Chao) **Short-Drama Capital: Why Xi'an and Zhengzhou** — Hengdian's backlots were designed for horizontal screens and deep depth of field, so converting them costs more than in Xi'an and Zhengzhou. Short drama was commercially born in Xi'an because at the tail end of the pandemic Xi'an was a tourism city, the real economy needed to recover, and people in entertainment were more eager to embrace short drama. What Zhengzhou and Xi'an share is convenient transport, a population above 13 million, an information-feed gene, lots of cheap labour and people willing to try. Zhengzhou is more cutthroat than Xi'an, its industrial structure is more complex, and even its top companies have more varied names.

[5:17] (Hou Chao) **300 Episodes a Month Is a City's Capacity Ceiling** — At the peak, 200 projects were shooting at the same time. Counting the number of people in key skilled positions in Zhengzhou alone, capacity maxed out at roughly 300 episodes a month. Short drama is a coordination-heavy trade: the more projects, the more coordination pressure multiplies. 300 episodes is the city's carrying limit, and previously no company in the whole industry could manage one or two hundred projects at once. What supports that rhythm is a script IP library, genre tags, high-frequency reuse of the same directors and similar sets and props, and mid-office control.

[8:33] (Li Jiajia) **Paid to Free: Resisted First, Then Validated** — The biggest change in going from paid to free is the metric — completion rate replaces the strong hook. Li Jiajia (李佳佳) resisted it at first, felt inferior, thought her method could not keep up with the free rhythm; only when “时间节” was both a paid hit and a free hit did it validate that the character-relationship logic holds on the free side too, a milestone for the team. After that the method shifted from concentrating effort on the first ten episodes to spreading it relatively evenly across every episode, telling the story properly.

[11:35] (Li Jiajia) **Anti-Typecasting: Character Relationships Are the Cornerstone** — The methodology is ‘character relationships determine character motivation, motivation determines events, events determine story’. The core of the hit “苏太太高调离婚了” is that each person is closer to or more distant from different people, so their tone and the information they reveal differ; the details are made solid and typecasting is avoided. A story is unwatchable precisely because of typecasting. Ensemble scenes are the hardest to shoot, because every line each person says must carry a different attitude toward each other person.

[33:28] **Admit First That You Started a Business to Make Money** — One guest admits he did a deep breakdown and concluded his own goal is actually to make money. The company's number-two is a super high-achiever who gave him ‘a small goal’ to keep him making money; he found he could not bring himself to throw away his experience, connections and team, so he kept going to work, making money and making dramas, forming a loop. He also judges that no long-form film/TV company has lasted by doing content well, unless the boss himself is that content person.

[48:22] **Two Post-Mortem Logics: Fatal Factors vs. Ceiling** — In Hou Chao's (侯超) 300-person content team, only two or three people can really put 3-5 million into a single project, so the post-mortem looks only at ‘fatal factors’: genre dividends, whether an ordinary person can pull it off, shooting-scheduling difficulty — the fatal weak spots — and after checking, it is circulated that repeating them is banned. Li Jiajia's cases more often fell short of expectations without dying outright, so she analyses the ceiling from the production side and the topic-selection side; the two sides can complement each other, and the production side often fails to patch the hard flaws on the topic-selection side. A big hit always comes down to the long board; only a drama whose long board is exciting enough can blow up.

[51:29] **AI and Live Action Are Becoming Two Separate Lines** — AI and live action are already two lines: AI is better at presenting spectacles people have not seen but can imagine, such as the Classic of Mountains and Seas, effects, animals; live action suits emotion and relationship-driven content like harem intrigue. A real actor's micro-expressions and a good actor's tension are things AI cannot learn in the short term, and as long as that difference exists, live action has room to survive. The defensive logic on the other side is only to run past the ‘kill line’ — a single episode not losing money is enough, protect the floor and chase the ceiling. AI has also landed in script tools, digital continuity sheets and overload-prevention scheduling, not just content assistance.

[1:02:27] **Interactive Film-Games: Not Betting on This One** — Facing the interactive film-game boom, one guest says that after AI arrived he seriously considered dissolving the company and starting over, because of path dependency. But not doing interactive film-games like “盛世天下” is not because it is hard, but because there is still no genuinely proven demo, no industry consensus and no sound rules, and he is unwilling to be the first to eat the crab. The other adds: the newer the company, the thinner the talent pipeline, and the worst thing is scattered energy — ‘wanting to do everything, getting into nothing’ — the opportunity cost of the boss's and partners' time is too high.

## AI self-evolution could close the loop in as little as six months, but models will quietly drift off course

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-06-sv101-ai最快半年跑通自进化-验证与品味是最后门槛/
- show: 硅谷101 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sv101/)
- original episode: E242｜最快半年AI跑通自进化？与陈天桥首席科学家聊聊硅谷模型必争之地
- published: 2026-07-06 · duration: 1:10:54
- transcript: Machine transcription · 20897 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The inflection point for RSI is a model that can handle long-horizon tasks. Apodex's chief scientist says the self-evolution loop could close in as little as six months, but recursive drift and model taste still need humans minding them for a long time to come.**

why listen: A frontline researcher breaks down the RSI technical path, verification methods and timeline. High information density, and direct material for understanding the real progress of model self-evolution.

### points

[7:21] (Bei Bing) **Recursive self-improvement became possible because of long-horizon tasks** — Self-evolution is not a new idea. Two or three years ago there were already approaches like LM-as-optimizer and agent optimizer, but back then a model could only optimize for two or three hours; one small mistake would compound on itself and it could not keep iterating. What is different this year is that models have gotten stronger and can complete long-horizon tasks that take a human 1.5 hours or even 12 hours, so they can self-correct many times within a single task, and the "R" in recursive finally holds up. At Anthropic, 80% of code is written by Claude — it is precisely coding ability that makes it natural for a model to train itself.

[10:30] (Bei Bing) **Three technical bottlenecks stand in the way of long-horizon tasks** — Long-horizon tasks are not just a context-length problem. First, standard attention has quadratic complexity, so million-token inference is extremely resource-hungry and needs architectural innovation. Second, long-context support alone is not enough: the model must have been trained on very long data, otherwise it goes out-of-distribution. Third, the training and inference infra also has to change, including GPU optimization and kernel-level code. Stack those three difficulties together and the difficulty of long-horizon tasks rises exponentially. Simon adds that even with a million-token context, truly ultra-long-horizon tasks still need agent architecture and memory mechanisms to digest.

[14:37] (Bei Bing) **Recursive drift is the fundamental obstacle to self-evolution** — When a model generates its own training data, reasoning errors accumulate and amplify across generations — that is recursive drift. Apodex's countermeasure is verification: code and math are easy to verify, using test scripts or formal proofs, so they are relatively controllable; but the tests themselves can be too broad or too narrow, and subtle drift still occurs. So Apodex specifically trains verification ability, and during reinforcement learning it has the judge learn alongside, to keep the model from learning bad behaviors like reward hacking.

[16:58] (Simon) **Verification relies on sub-agents checking each other plus redundancy** — The name Apodex comes from the Greek word for "proof." Verification methods differ by domain: code uses unit tests, math uses formal proofs, but more problems depend on human judgment. Apodex 1.0 uses an agent team: first decompose the problem, one sub-agent solves it and another sub-agent verifies it separately, avoiding context contamination; then have multiple agents work the same problem to produce redundancy, with a global agent judging which answer is more accurate. During training it also has agents judge the credibility of information sources — a forum, for instance, is less reliable than a textbook.

[21:06] (Bei Bing) **The three self-evolution paths have very different moats** — Beibing divides self-evolution into three paths: pretraining, post-training, and harness (scaffolding). Evolving at the harness level is the cheapest — you can do it just by calling APIs — and the open-source community and academia have produced plenty of results there, so the moat is the shallowest. Post-training is the more core and more difficult battlefield: you first have to diagnose model defects, create targeted problems, and verify training results, which takes a lot of resources. Pretraining is currently mostly toy-level tasks and has not really scaled to product level. Apodex does all three; post-training and scaffolding are like the left foot stepping on the right foot, iterating alternately. To judge a company's capability, first ask which layer it evolves at.

[29:29] (Simon) **Why an agent team beats a single smart AI** — Simon states it plainly: one smart AI cannot beat a team that checks each other. The reason is the nature of self-attention — the longer the context, the worse attention works, and linear attention does not solve ultra-long context either, so a single model has a ceiling under current technology, just as a person's working memory is limited and needs notes. So multiple agents must divide the work and share information through memory mechanisms to handle ultra-long-horizon problems. Model capability and agent engineering are one plus one greater than two; agent teams in vertical domains still have a moat, though the scaffolding has to be fine-tuned as models iterate every month.

[36:34] (Bei Bing) **The hard part of a discovery model is verification, not generation** — Generative models already have mature training recipes, but a discovery model's goal is not to generate answers but to propose and verify out-of-distribution hypotheses. The first step requires a creative hypothesis, and the hard part is that it is far from the pretraining data; the second step is judging whether the hypothesis holds, which brings us back to verification. You can use deep research to gather existing information to assist the hypothesis, and you can write code to run simulations to build confidence. But unknown domains often have no standard answer and no trustworthy simulation environment, so self-evolution is Apodex's main route toward a Heavy Duty Solver.

[57:29] (Bei Bing) **A six-month loop, but drift will take years** — Beibing expects the first self-evolution loop to close in as little as six months to a year: in some domain (coding, say) the model finds its own problems, generates its own training data, verifies itself, and iterates one round. But the recursive part of RSI requires many rounds, and recursive drift is still unsolved; he is confident it can be fully solved within a few years. What keeps him up at night is not knowing whether the model has drifted off course while self-evolving — both safety goals and performance goals can drift. For now the only option is to manually read model outputs every day and intervene in agent behavior; in the future, "distilling yourself" could inject that monitoring ability into the model and speed up the process.

### glossary

- RSI / Recursive Self-Improvement: The ability of a model to train itself and improve in a loop.
- Recursive Drift: When a model self-generates training data, errors accumulate across generations and it gradually deviates from the goal.
- Heavy Duty Solver: Apodex's goal — a general model that solves hard problems for which humans have no standard answer.
- Discovery Model: A model that does not rely on known answers but proposes and verifies new hypotheses.
- Agent Team: A collaborative system in which multiple sub-agents divide work and verify each other, used for ultra-long tasks and verification.

## AI Has Not Produced a Single New Theory, So It Is Not an Artificial Person

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-07-04-tokcast-ai-至今没造出一个新理论-所以它不是人工人/
- show: ToKCast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tokcast/)
- original episode: Ep 263: David Deutsch's "The Fabric of Reality" Chapter 13 "The Four Strands" Part 4 - and final.
- published: 2026-07-04 · duration: 1:30:56
- transcript: Machine transcription · 15137 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Deutsch's test: AI only fills in the parts of known theories that nobody has bothered to compute — it is coloring in the existing picture of organic chemistry. To reach the threshold of creating new knowledge, you first need problems — and LLMs have no problems; the problems are the ones we give them.**

why listen: This is the wrap-up of the final chapter of The Fabric of Reality: the first half covers induction, the many-worlds test and the explanatory gap, and only in the second half do the four strands come together. Dense, but it takes a little patience.

### points

[3:07] (Brett Hall) **Induction is not a source of knowledge, it is extrapolation under a new name** — Deutsch takes Popper's line: induction is a pseudo-problem. Inductionists wanted a mechanical process for science corresponding to mathematical deduction, so they invented the word "induction." But for induction to work you must first assume the theory that "this trend will continue" — so it is really conjecture plus extrapolation, and extrapolation itself is deductive. At best it gives you a prediction, never an explanation. The host uses this to rebut "AI is doing induction": if induction in Popper's sense were what AI does, then AI would be making scientific discoveries — and it is not.

[7:13] (Brett Hall) **AI has never produced a single new theory** — The host offers a concrete test: what AI can do is fill in the parts of known theories that have not yet been computed. Take a given number of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen atoms — which molecules could physically exist? The theory of atomic bonding and carbon chemistry has long existed; nobody just had the leisure to compute it, and AI can do it for us. Same in mathematics: the axioms and rules of inference are already there. This is "coloring in the existing picture of organic chemistry," not generating new explanatory knowledge. Reaching the threshold of creating new knowledge — and thereby counting as AGI or an "artificial person" — requires the latter.

[14:31] (Brett Hall) **Opponents of many-worlds shout "untestable" first** — The host observes that the most common objection today is not a refusal of the explanation but the reflex "it's untestable." Yet Deutsch published an experimental scheme for testing many-worlds decades ago; the host, Maria Violaris and Sam Kuypers have all explained it, and after pointing to the paper and the video, the other party — physicists included — still will not budge. The experiment requires a "conscious observer" in superposition, so then people say we have no AGI capable of doing it. The host cites Deutsch: needing AGI to run this decisive experiment is not a fault of the many-worlds theory.

[32:34] (Brett Hall) **The explanatory gap: the Turing principle cannot answer what a person is** — Deutsch says that some of those who deny the possibility of AI are in fact expressing a more reasonable criticism: Turing's computational explanation seems in principle to leave no room for a physical explanation of mental properties like consciousness and free will. AI partisans respond bluntly that "the Turing principle guarantees a computer can do anything a brain can do" — true, but that answers with a prediction, whereas the problem lies in the explanation; there is an explanatory gap. The host adds: this is why we still cannot build AGI; saying the brain is some kind of computer does not settle what a person is.

[42:59] **Simple rules do not specify a peacock, yet peacocks appear** — Deutsch uses a Darwinian analogy: the laws of physics do not contain the shapes of elephants and peacocks; they are merely emergent results of atoms interacting by rule. Brett Hall connects this directly to Conway's Game of Life — the rules are minimal, and unless you run it you cannot know what it will produce. From this he criticizes Michael Levin: Levin claims the bubble sort algorithm does unpredictable things and therefore is conscious, but Hall checked the paper and found Levin deliberately altered the algorithm methodologically and introduced randomness — that is no longer standard bubble sort, and is in effect rediscovering a low-resolution version of the Game of Life.

[49:25] **Not knowing where the line is drawn does not mean there is no line** — The standard panpsychist argument is: walk down the phylogenetic tree from humans — cats and dogs, birds, mice, insects, fish — and you find no point where a line for consciousness can reasonably be drawn, so no line exists, and consciousness goes all the way down to elementary particles. Hall says this smuggles in "there is no line" in place of "we don't know where the line is" — "Just because you don't know where to draw a line doesn't mean there isn't a line." He offers several candidate lines: whether something is a universal explainer, whether brain capacity reaches some threshold, whether a nervous system exists — and concedes there is currently no good explanation, so none can be ruled out.

[50:27] **LLMs are not people, because they have no problems** — Hall ties consciousness to knowledge creation: knowledge creation depends on problems, a problem is a conflict between ideas, and in a person the conflict produces a feeling of wanting to resolve it — and it is precisely in that "wanting," a subjective, conscious state, that a person begins seeking a solution and creating knowledge. From this he draws his judgment on LLMs: LLMs do not prompt themselves, they are not interested in anything, they have no problems — the problems are the ones we give them. This rebuts the claim that "LLMs are artificial people"; when they truly become artificial people, they will have problems, and vice versa.

[1:22:55] (Brett Hall) **20th-century fundamental science was adopted and ignored at once** — Deutsch's observation: the history of the four strands shows that for most of the 20th century fundamental science and philosophy suffered something deeply unpleasant. The vogue for positivist and instrumentalist views of science went together with indifference to genuine explanation, loss of confidence and pessimism — precisely when the prestige, utility and funding of fundamental research stood at an all-time high. The theories of the four protagonists were simultaneously adopted and ignored, and that unprecedented manner is itself telling. He admits he has no complete explanation, but thinks we are now emerging from this phase.

[1:22:55] Brett Hall: "Despite all the excuses I've been making for the critics of the central theories, the history of all four strands shows that something very unpleasant happened to fundamental science and philosophy for most of the 20th century."
